en: Preface to the *Huìfǔ Hóngjì* Commentary on the *Tiāntái Sìjiào Yí Zhù*.
A single volume of the *Tiāntái Sìjiào Yí Jízhù* has long been included in the canon and circulated widely.

However, because its text is concise while its meaning is profound, how can those newly entering the study of Buddhism penetrate its inner sanctum without extensively searching through the sūtras and śāstras to elucidate it? [This work] serves as an aid...

The *Hongji* (Record of Propagation) is traditionally said to have been compiled by a successor of the Shanjia school. It was assembled as a supplement to the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) in order to propagate the teachings and contemplations.
It is also known as the *Fuzongji* (Record for Supporting the School). Alas, it has not been printed on woodblocks since ancient times;

it remains hidden within lecture halls, its value exceeding even that of the Dragon Palace Canon (*Longzang*). Consequently, those who transcribed it have omitted characters and misplaced punctuation, rendering the script illegible. This is because...

Upon unrolling it once, my fingers could not bear to fold it back. Since I first composed this record in the Dinchu year of the Qianlong era, I was finally able to obtain a transcribed copy of the *Yizhu* (Commentary on Rituals) and various annotated editions by former masters.

Thereupon, over the course of four years of leisure, I joyfully set aside sleep and forgot my meals to compile these into ten volumes, changing the title to *Zhufuhong* (Annotated Supplements to the Great).
Postscript: I intended to carefully revise and recompile this work to share it with my fellow practitioners, thereby completing an essential manual for upholding the teachings.
Yet, before the draft was even finished, my sight failed me. Is this due to the meager roots of merit planted in past lives? Or is it because the conditions and timing still await their fulfillment?
I leave this behind as a gift for future worthies, who may examine and edit it in detail before entrusting it to the press for circulation; thus, may [the teachings] flourish.
May it continue until the end of the future, so that all who see or hear it may together enter and roam within the secret treasury of the three virtues.
Recorded on the first day of the seventh month in the year of Jihai, the forty-fourth year of the Great Qing Qianlong era,
by the Bhikṣu Shisan Shi Xingquan.
Preface to the Supplementary Revision by Fuhong:

From the site of enlightenment at the beginning of the Tathāgata’s dispensation throughout his lifetime, until his passing beneath the twin śāla trees, there were various sections concerning the sudden and gradual, the provisional and the real, as well as discourses on the partial and the complete, and the half and the full.
It was at the Lotus Sūtra that he revealed the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; this is truly the Great [Dharma].

This fully expresses his original intention. What is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision is the wondrous Dharma of the inconceivable, non-contingent, and marvelous three thousand realms within a single thought-moment—emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.
To take this as one's fundamental principle is called the Perfect Teaching; to understand this is called perfect understanding;
to cultivate this is called perfect cultivation; and to realize this is called perfect realization. As a verse in the *Lotus Sūtra* says:
When a Son of the Buddha dwells in this stage, it is the very enjoyment of the Buddhas; they are constantly within it, whether walking, sitting, or reclining—is this not the intent?
Reaching the thirteenth transmission after Kāśyapa, Nāgārjuna composed the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* (Treatise on the Middle Way) and translated it into China.

When Master Wen of the Northern Qi read it, he awakened to the meaning of the single verse concerning the identity of dependent origination, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. By means of this—
He transmitted it to Huisi; Master Huisi transmitted it to Zhiyi. The Great Master Zhiyi entered into the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra and gave rise to the *Svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī*.
He established two types of the Fourfold Teaching and determined the five periods of the Buddha’s lifetime.

Truly, this is what is known as the "Teaching and Contemplation of this One School," which comprehensively encompasses the entire Dragon Canon. Those who succeeded him were Zhang’an Zhizheng, Jingyun Huiling, and Dongyang Huiling.
Zuoxi Lang and Jingxi Ran caused the treatises on both the Teaching (jiao) and Meditation (guan) of Tiantai to be fully perfected.

Following Jingxi, those who inherited his legacy were Xingdao Sui, Zhixing Xiu, Zhengding Wai, Miaoshuo Xiu, Gaolun Song, Changzhao Ji, Weiyuan Tong, and Fazhi Li; thus, the Teaching once again flourished as a "Second Revival. Fazhi...

And those who followed him were Nanping Zhen, Congjian Bian, Chexi Qing, Yi’ung Guan, Yuanshi Yin, Foguang Zhao, Zitong Xun, Dongming Ri, Puzhi Ai, Tianzhu Hui, and Dongchan Weng. Baisong Jue and Wujin Deng also appeared.
Lingfeng Xu—Master Xu was the progenitor of the Lingfeng branch—composed the *Jiudou* (Prayer for Drawing Lots).
Regarding the Buddha, he attained the teachings of the Tiantai school. Those who transmitted them were Canghui, Cheng, Jingxiu, Ming, Luyuan, Hong, Sulian, Zhu, Daolai, and Cheng.
Master Cheng was the sixth patriarch at Lingfeng; his sons and grandsons now all occupy seats in various quarters.
When Master Cheng was preaching the Dharma in Wulin, he once instructed Shan Zihua of Fuchun.

Zang took the essentials of the threefold contemplation within a single mind as his core principle. He thoroughly mastered the teachings of the various schools, including Xianshou and Cien, and frequently investigated the great purport of the Western Transmission.
One night, upon hearing the sound of crickets, he attained a profound realization. He composed a verse which says: "Cicada, cicada, you are far too talkative;
the dew is cold and the wind is cool, yet you cry out until your blood flows with every sound. Thus, when he expounded the Dharma, every word emerged from the depths of his heart.
His erudition flowed forth, neither biased nor mired in dogma; he penetrated all schools of thought with a majestic eloquence as vast as clouds, meeting no obstruction wherever he turned.
Was it not as if he had attained the *pratibhāna-samādhi* (the samādhi of inspired eloquence)?

Among his disciples was one named Qian Yian, who devoted himself to the inner scriptures (*nèi-diǎn*) and maintained a relationship of external friendship with me. He requested that I collate and revise a certain work titled *Fùhóng Jì*. Therein, occasionally...
Second is the section on "Damage and Benefit," into which the *Qianziwen* has been incorporated. Alas! Those in the Chan forests cling to principle while disregarding practice;
lecturers vie for erudition while dismissing contemplation. Such a degeneration of the tradition is particularly severe today. Why not take the time to savor and reflect upon this?
By gathering these points, one comes to know the inconceivable and non-referential essence in which object and contemplation are of one suchness;

with both understanding and practice advancing together, one may swiftly reach the ocean of all-knowledge and avoid becoming a person of overweening pride—is this not a source of lifelong joy and fulfillment?
The book by Master Qian was completed, yet Master Shan had already passed away. He requested a preface from me.
I consider that Master Qian has already described in detail the origins of this collection as well as his intention to guide future worthies.

Therefore, I have specifically composed this preface concerning the source of the transmission of the Tiantai school, so as to make it public for the sake of future sages, enabling them to hear of its reputation and be inspired to arise and practice.

Written on the day of the winter solstice in the second month of winter in the year of Bingzi, the twenty-first year of the Longfei Jiaqing era, by the Bhikṣu Yirun (also known as Yuanhong) at the Zhenji Hermitage on the banks of the Tiáo River in Wulin.
Recorded for the purpose of supplementing and revising the *Fuhong Ji*. Autobiographical Preface.
Regarding the *Jiuzhu Fuhong Ji* (Collected Annotations on the Fourfold Teaching Ritual) by the one whose name has been lost: the lecturers have transmitted it as a secret within their lecture halls.
I received it from Mr. Huazang Dan; subsequently, I was shown the three families’ supplementary annotations by Master Yuanru;
finally, I obtained the *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) by Venerable Shao Tan from Master Yuanhong. These are all essential texts for explaining the ritual annotations. My wisdom... [text truncated]
Meeting with meager fortune and lacking pure wealth, I have collated and edited [this work] more than twenty times.

Praying morning and evening for the protection of the Triple Gem, I finalized it after five years. I commissioned the *Juzhen* (Assembly of Treasures) characters and diligently brought it to completion.

Beginning the project and the carving of the printing blocks on the twelfth day of the fifth month of the Bingzi year, three days after the first day of the eleventh month, at the hour of [the sun being in]... (the text ends).
The work was completed at the winter solstice. During this interval, I collated and corrected errors; the master who assisted in these matters was Master Yuan.
Someone asked: "You received the single transmission from Caoxi; why then do you study the various teachings so extensively?
Moreover, why are you now so urgently engaged in circulating the *Fuhongji* of the Tiantai school? I smiled and said: "As for the School of the Lineage..."
Carrying water and hauling firewood, or speaking coarse and refined words—all these are the meaning of the West’s coming. Why should it be any different for the sutras and śāstras?

Yet, while principle is realized suddenly and, through that realization, is simultaneously extinguished, phenomena must be eliminated gradually and exhausted through successive stages. Do you suppose that a single awakening makes one a Buddha, such that there is no need for cultivation?
Although the First Patriarch did not establish reliance on words and letters, he entrusted the *Lengyan Sūtra* to the Second Patriarch.

Kāśyapa, have you alone not heard this? Moreover, as for those like us with shallow knowledge and superficial vision, whose three poisons are still rampant—how would we dare to destroy the Vinaya (*mukha*), reject the Sūtras (*sūtra*), and act as "lion-insects"? Furthermore, I once heard the instruction of Master Huazang:
since the Buddha-dharma flowed eastward, it has flourished extensively until now primarily through Tiantai; yet, outside of that, there are those who manifest the "Direct Pointing."
There was Bodhidharma, who expounded the Dharma-realm; there was Xianshou, who established the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*; and there was Cien, [who established the Huayan school].

As for the others, such as the Pure Land, Esoteric, and Vinaya schools—these patriarchs all took great compassion as their core intent, each opening gates of skillful means to act as messengers of the Tathāgata.
Yet, they distinguished between the partial and the perfect, discerned the heterodox and the orthodox, and understood the ailments [of sentient beings] to provide the appropriate remedies.
Medicine: Administering medicine according to the ailment, encompassing all dimensions both horizontally and vertically, the teachings and contemplations are exquisitely complete.

For those who wish to evaluate the provisional and the ultimate across various schools, none can compare to Tiantai. As for those who study it yet achieve no success at all, it is not that their empty words are of no benefit;
rather, they are like one day of exposure followed by ten days of frost, or perhaps they have failed to apply the methods of expedient means and correct cultivation to the stages of practice.

Such omissions and deficiencies are not the fault of Tiantai. Nevertheless, if we examine the works of the Tiantai school alone—those of Zhiyi, Zhizhe, Zhang’an, Jingxi, and Siming—their compositions are voluminous and their meanings profound.
They are so subtle, deep, and expansive that they dazzle the eyes and startle the spirit.

Furthermore, the doctrinal positions established by various schools each have their own specific focus. For instance, regarding the four types of scriptural evidence from the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages), the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) borrows two interpretations, while the *Fuxing* (Aids to Practice) borrows three.
Additionally, the *Bie xing* (Separate Practice) borrows the four gates of the non-arising (*anabhisamskāra*) of the horizontal study.
At a shallow stage, one should merely be "intermediate" (*chung*). Yet, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states that this is "attached to that teaching.

Such points of agreement and difference are difficult to enumerate exhaustively. Since the *Jizhu* (Collected Annotations on the Ritual of the Four Teachings) was first compiled, subsequent works have appeared in succession.

To provide a summary of their major outlines and general purports, later students can easily extract their essential points. Thus, the Tiantai school compiles the twelve divisions of the Buddha’s teachings.

This constitutes the ultimate perfection [of the teachings]. Furthermore, the *Yizhu* (Commentary on the Rites) serves as the master key to the Three Great Works of the Tiantai school; how could it not be considered of great importance?

Indeed, when the *Yizhu* is held in high esteem, those who expound upon it to propagate the teachings and contemplations (*jiaoguan*) are likewise esteemed. A prime example of this is the single volume of the *Fuhong Ji* (Record of Auxiliary Propagation).
The *Yizhu* draws extensively from the sūtras and śāstras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions, citing no fewer than one hundred and ten works. Although there are...

The various texts on the "Equipping," the "Simplicity," and the "Virtue and Righteousness" are still not yet exhaustive or complete. This record, however, meticulously transcribes their cited passages and elucidates their textual meanings.

If those of us with dull faculties in the final stages of learning can, through this record, come to understand the Tiantai school, then the distinctions between the partial and the perfect, the heterodox and the orthodox, and the provisional and the real according to the various masters will become as clear as looking at one's own palm. Only then may one employ these principles for one’s own practice.
One should immediately employ this to transform others; dedicating this profound resolve to serve every dust mote and world-system is what is called repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
This was what I previously heard from Master Huazang, and it reflects his earnest intention for its widespread circulation.

As for the words of Master Lingfeng: "When the *Sijiaoyi* appeared, the Tiantai school fell into obscurity"—this was likely said out of a sense of exasperation, and he offered these words as a response.
There is no need for me to add further commentary.
On the day of the winter solstice in the eleventh month of the twenty-first year of the Jiaqing era of the Great Qing (the Bingzi year), Qian Yian,
a humble disciple of the Three Jewels from Wulin, respectfully composed this preface.

Preface to the Supplementary Revision of the *Fuhong Ji* (Record of Aiding and Expanding) Regarding the original title, *Tiantai sijiaoyi jizhu fuhong ji* (Collected Annotations on the Ritual of the Four Teachings of Tiantai with the Record of Aiding and Expanding), Master Shi added the character "zhù" (annotation) above "fuhong ji.
This has now been deleted. Furthermore, the characters "buding" (supplementary revision) have been added below "ji" (record). Thus it is settled.
The meaning of the title is found at the beginning of the volume.
The *Jiben* (Original Record) contains a detailed compilation; Master Shi’s commentary further increased it by one-third.

Now, within the *Yanji* (Study Record), I have deleted those passages where the meaning was not certain or where the content was redundant and non-essential. Regarding the supplementary notes added by Master Shi, I have likewise [edited them].
However, for each section, the headings of the topical divisions (ke-tí) are placed two spaces lower than the preceding ritual text (yí-wén).

As for the ritual text itself, it begins on a new line and is set at a higher level. Regarding the [■ Original Note]: the upper portion is marked as the main text (yīn-wén), followed by the collected commentaries (jí-zhù).
Then add the character 【□註】 (Zhu), leaving the preceding space blank; mark the top of this with the "yang" (male) stroke.
Where the original notes (*yuánzhù*) and the collected commentary (*jízhù*) are joined in meaning, do not separate them with a mark. Next, above the *Jì* (Record) text, add the character 【■記】 (Ji).
If there are omissions in the record, record what the Master has supplemented and add the character 【■補】 (Bu) separately to indicate the supplement.
It was still not fully clear; I have consulted various commentaries again for reference and added the character 【備】 (preparatory/for reference) above them, so that the texts may not be confused.
Aside from the manuscript copied by Master Shi, I have further obtained a copy of the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) edition, though I do not know which master recorded it. Therefore...

I have merely added the four-character headings provided by Master Shī; the rest follows the *Jiéyì* (Analysis of Meaning) by Master Língyào and the *Bèijiǎn Bùyí* (Supplement to the Essential Simplifications) by Master Tiānxī.

Regarding the *Jízhù Wèndá* (Questions and Answers on the Collected Commentaries) and the *Jízhù Biànhé* (Discrimination of Errors in the Collected Commentaries) by Master Shàotán, where the meanings were deemed worthy of adoption, they have all been included and their respective titles recorded.

This is the edition preserved at Lêng-yen Temple. The original headings were listed at the beginning, but they have now been deleted. Following the master’s recorded text, supplementary headings have been added separately.
However, the purpose of dividing into sections is to identify the general outline of the chapters; if the divisions were too fine, they would become overly cumbersome.
Therefore, the current headings follow the general structure.
Regarding the printed edition of the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries), three versions have been seen, each containing mutual discrepancies and errors.

As for the manuscript of the *Fuhong ji*, it has likewise inherited many such errors. Although it has now been collated, I still fear it may not be exhaustive. Should anyone later discover the actual truth through further examination, I beg that they correct it;
the same applies to erroneous points in the various commentaries. This holds true except for the citations of sūtras and śāstras within the record itself.
In some cases, because the original text was prolix, it has been abridged; in others, because the meaning was profound and subtle, auxiliary words have been added.
There are many such instances within this collection. Do not disparage it on the grounds that you have not seen the original sūtras or śāstras.
Furthermore, when citing other sections in the future, do not cite this edition as proof.
This edition has been produced by carving characters on xylographic blocks and printing two hundred copies to serve as the vanguard for its circulation.

May those who see it treasure it. Should there be the conditions for carving woodblocks, then all the illustrations ought to be redrawn according to the original line-drawings and subsequently printed from them.
The Preface to the Newly Carved *Tiantai sijiao yi zhu huibufu hongji* (Supplementary Record for Aiding and Expanding the Commentary on the Ritual of the Four Teachings of Tiantai).
Originally, the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs consists solely of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Without contemplation (*guan*), there is no means to penetrate deeply;

without teaching (*jiao*), there is no means to understand profoundly. To have teaching without contemplation leads to delusion; to have contemplation without teaching leads to peril. Teaching is what is received...
Fu Xun: Contemplation arises from one’s own practice. "Contemplation" (guan) refers to the *prajñā* of words and letters; "practice" (xing) refers to the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination.
Only then can one realize the *prajñā* of true reality (*dharmatā*).

For instance, our founder, the Great Master Zhiyi, heard the teachings at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in a former life, attained wondrous enlightenment at Mount Dasu, and subdued the celestial Māras at Mount Huading.

At Waguan Temple, he turned the Wheel of Dharma, employing unimpeded eloquence to proclaim the teachings in accordance with the nature of reality. Relying upon the two gates of original and manifested traces (*honjaku*), he opened up the two subtleties of the provisional and the ultimate (*tairai*).
To elucidate this wondrous sutra, he composed the *Profound Meaning* (*Hannya Gen gi*), the *Words and Phrases* (*Kanjō*), and the *Cessation and Contemplation* (*Shikan*);

these are renowned in the world as the Three Great Works of the Tiantai School. These works exhaustively clarify the great causal conditions for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world, leaving no residue of meaning unexhausted. However, because...
The breadth of its texts and the profundity of its meanings are such that scholars of later generations have all sighed in awe like those gazing at the vast ocean.
It was then that we relied upon the High Priest of Goryeo, who skillfully recorded and refined this single scroll, naming it *Sijiao yi* (The Ritual of the Four Teachings).

He compiled the essential outlines of the Three Great Works to serve as the key for unlocking the entire Taishō Canon. If one can immerse oneself in its ritual texts, one will be able to penetrate the medicinal teachings for saving sentient beings.
This means that by tasting a single grain, the flavors of all others are present; by beholding a single bubble, the waters of a hundred rivers are contained therein.

Yet, though the text is concise, its meaning is vast and profound, making it difficult even for the most attentive gaze to grasp. Fortunately, there exists a ten-volume annotated commentary from South India, which may be said to be both detailed and complete.
Alas! We live in an age of decline, where cleverness has degenerated and wisdom is fading. Were it not for the Dharma of Expedient Means (upāya) inherent in one's nature...
Master [Zhi]hui’s *Supplement to the Record of the Aids to the Great Dharma* (Fuhong ji) exists; yet, although the *Collected Commentaries* (Jizhu) are detailed, they still fall short as a reference.

From this, one knows that the *Record of the Aids to the Great Dharma* is truly the most essential book for the Dharma gate, providing immense benefit to both doctrinal study and contemplative practice.
It is a pity that this work has not long been available for longevity; scholars rarely have had the opportunity to study it personally.

For instance, in the summer of the Jiawu year of the Guangxu era (1894), when our late Great Ancestor, the Venerable Elder Min, was expounding the *Jizhu* at Longhua Lecture Hall, there were over two thousand people assembled, yet those who possessed this book numbered only five or six—and these were still the *Zhujin* (mechanical printing) editions from the Jiaqing period. It is more precious than the Dragon Canon itself.

I have treasured it as a secret. Other fellow practitioners who sought it could not find it, and those who wished to behold it had no copy. (Xian) Although I am dull-witted and decayed, I have been nourished by its moisture for many years.

Originally, wishing to repay the kindness of my ancestors, I intended to have it carved into woodblocks for printing. Yet, I am ashamed that my nature is foolish and ignorant, lacking skill in worldly correspondence;
my mind rests in tranquility, and I lack the art to transform base metal into gold. Thus, unable to bear it any longer, I have set aside my shame and produced this work.
[The Master] said: "I venture to inform the donors that we should rejoice that the conditions for the Dharma have gathered here and this undertaking may now be fulfilled.
However, the old manuscript has long been sprawling and its punctuation remains unclear; if it were not briefly edited and refined, it would be difficult for beginners to read.

Lately, I have had no leisure to attend lectures, and although I have occasionally cleared my mind to immerse myself in the study, my progress has been repeatedly interrupted and neglected. Within this interval, the arrangement of the lines and the classification of the sections..."

My eyebrows have parted and my eyes have opened; I have largely fulfilled my humble aspirations. Counting on my fingers, three autumns have passed. As for the unsolved kōan of the late Master Dao-wan Xianquan, how could I dare say it is not yet resolved?
This was written in the spring month, on the day of the full moon, during the twenty-third year of the Guangxu era of the Great Qing, the year of Dingyou.
Written by the junior monk Dixian, a direct descendant of the Tiantai lineage, at the Xingji Hall of Miaozhi Chan Monastery on Mount Gudoutuo by the Ou River,
regarding the new edition of the *Fuhong Ji* (Record of Aiding and Propagating): General Principles.
This book is the structural outline of the Great Canon and the heart-essence of the Tiantai school. Master [Zhiyi] expounded the great treatises during the Sui dynasty;
Master [Zhanran] recorded the core teachings in Wu; and Master [Jingxiu] composed the collected commentaries in the Yuan dynasty.

It was shown that these three masters obtained the *Fujiji* (Record of Aided Remembrance) in the Dingchou year of the Qianlong era, and the layman Qian produced the *Juzhen* (Assembly of Treasures) edition in the Bingzi year of the Jiaqing era. Up until now...
Now, at last, the printing blocks have been completed. Alas! To expound the sutras is difficult; to compose them is even more difficult.
Yet, to carve the blocks and circulate them has likewise not been undertaken lightly. I pray that my fellow practitioners will not treat this matter with negligence.
Fu Hong was the recorder. Tradition holds that he was a successor of the Tiantai school; he compiled and recorded these accounts.
It is a pity that his name has been lost, so that the primary compiler cannot be clearly identified.
This book’s original title was *The Auxiliary Record for Expanding [the Teaching] with Collected Annotations on the Ritual of the Four Teachings of Tiantai*.

The Master added the character “zhù” (annotation) above the word “jì” (record). Layman Yī’ān deleted this character and further added the characters “bǔdìng” (supplemented and revised) below the word “jì.
Now, subsuming the specific for the general, it is simply titled *The Comprehensive Supplement to the Auxiliary Record for Expanding [the Teaching]: Annotated Ritual*.
The *Ji* (Record) in this original compilation was already detailed; Master Shi further increased it by one-third.

When the lay practitioner [Wang] revised and finalized it, he deleted what was redundant and supplemented what was incomplete. In the present edition, whenever ritual texts (*yiwén*) occur, they are all set with topical divisions (*kēpàn*).
Both the annotated texts (*zhùwén*) and the recorded texts (*jìwén*) are each started on a new line; both the ritual and annotated texts are aligned at the top margin.
Regarding the layout: if there is an original note within the two lines of text, it shall still be entered in small characters beneath those two lines.
If it is a commentarial note, prefix it with the character "注" (zhù) in large characters; however, for a record (jì), lower it by one space.

This is because such a note serves as an explanation of the preceding two lines, and thus it is appropriate to do so. Consequently, the character "記" (jì) is listed at the beginning in small characters, yet it indicates the master’s own [teaching].

In the text of the supplements, the character "supplement" (補) shall be marked in small print; likewise, in the text of the collations by the Layman, the character "collation" (備) shall also be marked in small print.
In this way, when students open the volume, they will understand it clearly, as if looking at the palm of their hand.

The text obtained by the layman Xiān has been inserted as a supplement; it retains the four characters "yǒu shī biāo yún" (the teacher’s original notation) and follows the previous conventions for the remainder, etc.

The Lêng-yen Temple edition lists the headings in a suspended format (*hsüan-k'o*). The Layman [Hsü-an] deleted these; I have not seen the version he presented to the Master with the headings attached (*tiē-k'o*).

However, the original purpose of dividing the sections was to facilitate the recognition of the chapters and their general outlines. The Layman, finding the detail tedious, deleted the fine subdivisions.
To my dull eyes, it seems that such omissions are not yet sufficient for comprehension. Therefore, I now rely on the traditional text according to the ritual manual.
Judgment: With a slight addition of clarity and ease, I have augmented the text preceding the main body. I pray that those of like mind will deign to examine and grant their approval.

[Signature] The postscript states: "If there is the karmic condition for carving woodblocks, then the various diagrams shall still follow the hanging-line (suspended) format; this is now the appropriate course.
Therefore, I have converted the direct prose explanations into diagrams, all of which have been cross-referenced and corrected according to the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries)."

In the ancient commentaries, the topical outlines (kaimoku) following the text often do not list all sections together; for instance, when one section is divided into three, only the first section is indicated.
I shall follow this precedent here as well. How could I dare to display my own ingenuity by arranging them differently?

The ancients established models for outlining and formatting their works, skillfully employing the heavenly stems and earthly branches to distinguish the levels of the topical headings (*kēmù*). I now follow this tradition;

however, because the chapters and sections of this book are so numerous and overlapping, twenty characters would not suffice as a heading. Therefore, I have further employed numerical figures to mark the headings in sequence.
This is truly intended to facilitate those who seek the source by following its current, and is not an exhibition of my own ineptitude.

Within the structural divisions of the chapters, although the major sections are divided into several parts, and some sub-sections are further subdivided, only the beginning of each section has been indicated;
they have never been listed in their entirety. Therefore, I have separately established a brief outline of the structural headings prior to this commentary.
This is merely for the convenience of seeking the root and investigating the source.

(I, the unworthy one,) have lacked study since my youth; my wisdom does not equal that of others. Moreover, I have not yet had the opportunity to personally attend upon the high sages or extensively peruse the ancient commentaries.
Now, in carving this book, I have followed only the principles, phrasing, and sequential order of the previously printed commentaries, not daring to act arbitrarily.

Although these have been rearranged and included in the printed editions, they offer little by way of supplementation; each instance has simply been recorded according to the original notes as a supplement to what was omitted, merely correcting the wording on the surface of the text.
The Commentary consists of ten fascicles, and the Sub-commentary likewise consists of ten fascicles. Now, in organizing the text of the Sub-commentary, I have likewise divided it into ten fascicles.
However, because the number of pages is excessive and the revised edition is very thick, I fear it may be inconvenient for those who wish to consult it.

Therefore, I have split each into an "upper" and "lower" volume. This is intended so that the revised edition may be more portable; it is done out of reverence for the Buddha-Dharma, and not out of any audacity on my part.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* constitutes the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The various Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, speak of existence while discussing emptiness;
these are mutually unimpeded and constitute the gate of both existence and emptiness. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and other treatises state that all phenomena are existence that is itself emptiness.
"It is neither existent" is the emptiness of existence; "it is neither empty" is the mutual cessation and mutual fusion [of existence and emptiness], which is the primary meaning (paramārtha).
This constitutes the gate of "neither empty nor existent. Regarding the four teachings of Guangzhai:

the sheep cart is compared to the śrāvaka, the deer cart to the pratyekabuddha, the ox cart to the bodhisattva, and the white ox cart is modeled after the Mahāyāna bodhisattva. —From Yuanxiao of the Tang Dynasty.

Regarding the four teachings: First, the distinct teaching of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna-vibhakti-śāsana*). This refers to the *Catuḥsatya-sūtra*, the *Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, and so forth. These are studied in common by the three vehicles;

however, within them, the two inner vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) do not clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), as these are taught as distinct characteristics (*vibhakta-lakṣaṇa*). Second, the common teaching of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna-sāmānya-śāsana*).

This refers to the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and so forth, which are studied in common by the three vehicles. Within these, the emptiness of all phenomena is explained; this constitutes the common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). Third, the one [vehicle]... [text fragment ends].

The *yāna-vibhāga-śāsana* (teachings categorized by vehicle), such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* and others, are called the "One Vehicle" (*ekayāna*) because they are not shared with the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).
Within these, because the all-pervasiveness of the Dharma has not yet been fully revealed, they are termed "partial" (*vibhāga*). Thus, there are four types of One Vehicle partial teachings.

The "complete" (*pūrṇa*) One Vehicle teachings, such as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and others, are so named because they fully elucidate the perfect fusion and all-pervasiveness of the *dharmadhātu*. Master Yuan [Chengguan] established these four categories.

As for the "Teacher," this refers to Master Yuan, a disciple of the Tang dynasty’s Master Xianshou (Fazang). Because the *Ratnagotravibhāga* (Treatise on the Jewel Nature) posits four types of sentient beings who do not recognize the Tathāgatagarbha, he established four teachings.

First is the Teaching of Deluded Truth and Diverse Attachments (*mizhen yizhi jiao*). This refers to ordinary people and non-Buddhists who, being deluded regarding the truth, extensively give rise to diverse attachments.

Second is the Teaching of One Part of the True [Nature] and the Half-Teaching (*zhen yifen banjiao*). This refers to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), which are like the immutable following the mutable... [text continues].
Based on two meanings, it is called "one part" (*ekadeśa*) because it only attains accordance with conditions (*anuparivartana*) and does not attain non-transformation (*avikāra*).
Within this accordance with conditions, it speaks only of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and not the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); therefore, it is called "half.

Third, the True One-Part Complete Teaching (*tattva-ekadeśa-paripūrṇa-deśanā*) refers to the bodhisattvas at the initial stage who only attain non-transformation and do not attain accordance with conditions; therefore, it is called "one part. Regarding non-transformation...
In the middle [section], both types of emptiness are explained together; therefore, it is called "complete. Fourth, the True Complete-Part Teaching:
this refers to the Bodhisattva’s possession of the two meanings of "changing according to conditions" and "unchanging," which reveals the true principle and realizes the Tathāgatagarbha.
[Note] Tiantai is the name of a mountain. "Tian" (Heaven) means the summit. Before the primordial qi was differentiated, all was blended into one.

Once the two polarities were divided, that which was clear became Heaven and that which was turbid became Earth; this is its original secular name, and for now we rely on the secular explanation. As for "Tai" (Platform):
This is the name of a star. Its terrestrial division corresponds to the Three Terraces (San Tai) of Heaven; therefore, it is named accordingly. See *Fuxing* 1 (upper, 17).
[Commentary] "Dian" means the summit; it is the highest and unsurpassed. When the primal qi had not yet divided, it was the Great Ultimate (Taiji); once the clear and turbid had separated...
It is judged as the two polarities (*liangyi*). That which is said to be the light and clear aspect of the vital breath (*qi*) floating upward is Heaven;

that which is the heavy and turbid aspect of the vital breath coagulating downward is Earth. This is according to Confucianism and Buddhism. However, if one relies on the Buddhist sutras and treatises, that which is radiant and pure, sovereign, and possesses divine function is called Heaven.
Furthermore, that which excels in body and excels in bliss is called Heaven, as explained in the third fascicle on the Heavenly Realm (*deva-loka*).
"Star" (xing) means "to disperse. The twenty-eight lunar mansions are arranged and distributed in their respective positions, each having its own assigned territory;
hence they are called "divisions" (fenye). Since that land corresponds above to the Three Terraces (Santai) star, the mountain is likewise named after it as Mount Tiantai.

[Note] This mountain is the very place where the Great Master took up residence and entered into *nirvāṇa*. Generally, in the customs of the Western Regions (India), one honors by using a person's name;
in this land (China), one shows respect by avoiding the use of their name. Therefore, this location is used here to manifest the person himself.
Furthermore, regarding the human lifeblood of the lineage, Tiantai is its fundamental school. The intent of the present title lies therein.
[Commentary] This clarifies that the Great Master was associated with this mountain from beginning to end; therefore, he used it as the title for his work. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"In the West (India), using a name is considered an honor, much like a child’s name, which is shared by both parents.

Since the Buddha was to be born there, [the Master] established these rites in advance so that others might admire his virtue and call upon his name. In this land (China), however, one avoids using names out of respect; therefore, he used the place..."

"Residing" (*ju*) reveals the person [who practices]. [Note: *Bei*] The "Discerning Errors" (*Bian'e*) states: "To 'rest the body' (*qi shen*) should be 'resting in the truth' (*qi zhen*), because the Great Master [Huiyuan] withdrew from the world to preserve the profound mystery.
In the Vinaya, the Western lands also use the term 'avoidance' (*bi*) as a form of reverence. For example, it says: 'One must not utter the names of the two masters.
If someone asks [for their names], one should indicate a single character; if asked again, one should say: 'Because of the causal conditions of the meaning.'"
The name is [insert name]. Furthermore, in the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, the formula for requesting ordination says: "I have come here for this purpose. [Then] one states the name of the *upādhyāya*:
"O *upādhyāya*, my name is [insert name]. Based on this, the ancient masters used the designation "Upper [Name]" and "Lower [Name].
As for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their magnificent names consisting of myriad virtues are not tabooed; this is similar to how posthumous titles (*shì*) are used in this land.
The title "Wúyì" (No Difference) should also be discussed separately. I have examined that Ānanda and Rāhula were both names rather than posthumous titles;
however, within the Vinaya, there are instances where these terms are used as euphemisms, and there is also a doctrinal basis for this. Thus, it may be appropriate to preserve both usages.
[Note] Regarding the "Four Teachings": while the specific text clarifies the *Huayi* (Methods of Conversion) and the *Huafa* (Methods of Teaching), there are actually eight types of teaching.

The reason we speak only of the "Four Teachings" here is that the title is established based on the general name, which encompasses both types. Indeed, without the *Huayi*, there would be no means of discernment; without the *Huafa*, there would be no means of explanation.
The essential purport of this single work does not exceed these two. "Teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the words of the Sage directed toward those below. It is also...
The definition of "teaching" (*jiao*) is the act of explaining and transforming sentient beings.

[Note: The present title designates the "Four Teachings," namely the four teachings of the transformative ritual (*huayi*), such as the Sudden and so forth, and the four teachings of the transformative dharma (*huafa*), such as the Tripitaka and so forth.
Although there are differences between their rituals and methods, they are all collectively subsumed under these four characters as their general names. This is because...
Regarding the teachings of this one lifetime, they are determined by the modes of transformation and analyzed according to the methods of transformation;
thus, the four-character title serves as a general name that encompasses both types of the Fourfold Teachings. As for the phrase "universally benefiting those below" used to define "teaching" (jiao):

it means that through the great compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in benefiting sentient beings, their words universally benefit those of the present time, and their teachings universally benefit future generations. This refers to the elucidation of principle.

Regarding "transforming beings as the meaning" (*yì*): this refers to discerning their capacities and expounding the principles to transform their minds. Thus, in the methods of transformation (*huà yí*), there is a distinction between sudden exposition and gradual exposition;
in the teachings of transformation (*huà fǎ*), there is a distinction between the exposition of the ultimate truth (*zhēn*) and the exposition of the conventional (*zhōng*). The *Sìjiào yì* states:

"These four are collectively termed 'teachings' (*jiào*) because their meaning consists in transforming beings through the exposition of principles. The Great Sage, regarding that which is inexpressible within these four..."
He speaks by means of the four *siddhāntas* in accordance with conditions, for he teaches the principles that can express [the truth] in order to transform the minds of sentient beings.

[Note: Question: Or, the title may be established based on the "Method of Conversion" (*huayi*), according to the commentary on the *Fenbie gongde lun*. The four teachings of the Method of Conversion are complete in both text and meaning.

It is established as proof that [the teachings] spontaneously encompass the four categories, such as the Tripitaka; or it may be said that the proclamation of the Pitakas and so forth constitutes the "sudden" and other [teachings].

This implies that the modes of transformation (*nirmāṇa-vidhi*) have no inherent substance. Furthermore, it is argued that while the four teachings—Sudden and the rest—were already employed by the masters of antiquity, the four teachings beginning with the Tripitaka originated with Tiantai, who established these titles based on the methods of transformation (*hua-fa*). Why, then, do you now follow the general names?

[■ Record] This selection of topics establishes the title based on the general [classification]. [■ Commentary] There are three types of questions posed. The first concerns the titles of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), specifically regarding the *huayi* (the ritual of conversion).
This is according to the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), which, in its explanation of the "Secret" and "Indeterminate" [teachings], states: "For now, we rely upon the three dharmas."

This is because it reveals their characteristics. Why? Because when these three methods—sudden, gradual, and indeterminate—are contrasted with the secret [teaching], the four teachings of the transformative ritual (*huayi*) become complete in both text and meaning, spontaneously encompassing the four [vehicles] such as the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared).

Second, the titles of the four teachings specifically concern the methods of transformation; this is based on the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), where the text clarifying the judgment of the teachings states: "As for..."

The "Coming" refers to skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). It is because [the Buddha] was well-versed in the capacities of sentient beings that he proclaimed the *pitakas* and so forth as being "sudden" (*tun*) and so forth;
thus one may know that while the *pitakas* and other teachings as methods of transformation (*huàfǎ*) possess substance, the "sudden" and other modes of transformation (*huàyí*) lack substantiality.

Third, the titles of the four teachings (*sìjiào*) belong specifically to the Tiantai school in terms of the teachings as methods of transformation. Indeed, the four teachings as modes of transformation were also employed by ancient masters. As the *Miaoxuan* states: "In the South..."

The Northern Masters generally employ three types of doctrinal systems: first, the sudden; second, the gradual; and third, the indeterminate. The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra is for the transformation of bodhisattvas;
like the sun shining upon high mountains, it is called the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*). The Tripiṭaka is for the transformation of those of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);

it first teaches the "half-letters," and is thus called the Teaching with Characteristics (*youxiang-jiao*). After twelve years, for the sake of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), he preached the Prajñāpāramitā in five stages. Now...
Reaching the state of eternal abiding is called the Teaching of Signlessness (*animitta*). These are all categorized as the Gradual Teachings (*anupūrva-vinaya*).

There is another class of sutras that are neither Sudden nor Gradual, which clarify the eternal abiding of the Buddha-nature; these include the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, and others.

These clarify the Partial, Non-fixed Teachings (*prādeśika-aniyata-vinaya*). These three meanings are common to all paths. Only the four teachings, such as the Tripitaka, [are specifically addressed by] Tiantai.

This is a unique creation. Therefore, if one were to establish the title based on the *huayi* (the ritual manifestations of transformation), there would be the criticism of being redundant with the ancients;
whereas if one establishes the teaching based on the *huafa* (the methods of transformation), it possesses the excellence of being a specialized school. Why, then, do we now follow the general name?

[Supplement] "Spontaneous" (*renyun*) means that, for example, "sudden" (*dun*) subsumes both the *bie* (separate) and *yuan* (perfect) teachings, while "gradual" (*jian*) subsumes the four teachings. "Proclaiming" (*banxuan*) refers to distributing and disseminating; it refers to the proclamation of the *zang* (scriptural treasury).
The four dharmas [of the Tripitaka] are gradual; the proclamation of the two dharmas of the Perfect and Distinctive [Vehicles] is sudden;

the proclamation of the [three] Pitakas where the listeners are the same but what they hear differs is indeterminate; and that which is mutually unknown is secret. Therefore, the modes of transformation have no fixed substance. [Note:
*Shiqian* explains that by relying on the three methods of sudden, gradual, manifest, and indeterminate, one reveals their characteristics; the secret method of preaching is thus established.]
Its characteristics are difficult to manifest; therefore, they are presented by means of three dharmas.

By juxtaposing them against the Secret [Teaching] to bring it forth, the characteristics of the Secret can be known, and the four teachings become complete and sufficient. Miaole states: "The Secret was not transmitted to anyone below the Buddha."
Because it is not what has been described, it must be set forth later before it can be transmitted.

Furthermore, while the ancient masters established only three types—such as the "indeterminate" (aniyata) and so on—the present text speaks of four teachings being employed as well, because both the "exoteric" (prakaṭa) and "esoteric" (guhya) are subsumed under the category of the indeterminate.
This is explained in the two fascicles of the *Piānfāng* (Eccentric Teachings).

[□ Note] Answer: Regarding the methods of transformation (*huayi*) and the teachings of transformation (*huafa*), as well as their having substance or lacking substance, and their mutual inclusion—each passage has its own specific meaning and was not established for the purpose of setting forth this title.
Furthermore, the "sudden" (*dun*) and other categories established by ancient masters differ from those of the present [school].
Therefore, Miaole considers the titles and the *pitakas* to be the primary framework for the Tiantai school’s system of classification and interpretation; this present work follows that approach.
Since the titles of the four teachings have already been clearly analyzed and explained, how could they belong exclusively to one side?
[■ Record] The two phrases regarding the "teachings of transformation" (*huàfǎ*) cite the meaning of the *Fùxíng* (Sub-commentary). "Mutually inclusive" cites the meaning of the *Qiān* (Commentary).

Each has its own intended significance. [■ Supplement] The *Qiān* uses the *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) to merely list the Sudden, Gradual, and Indeterminate, thereby contrasting them with the Esoteric; therefore, it does not...
Regarding the mention of the "Treasury" (Zang) and so forth, and the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) which proclaims the "Treasury" and so forth as being the "Sudden" (Dun) and other categories:

these are intended to apply the purport of the teaching and to clarify the structural framework of the doctrinal gates. Since they do not specifically cite the "Sudden" and so forth [as the primary title], one knows that these two texts each have their own specific focus;

neither was established for the purpose of providing a formal title for this work. As for the different titles established by ancient masters, the *Miaoxuan* states: "The masters of the North and South both generally employ the three types."
Regarding the classification of the teachings (*shōsō*): it is like the sun shining upon a high mountain; this is termed "Sudden" (*ton*) and so forth. The *Shigiki* states:

"From the beginning at the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra down to the end at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Sūtra, all possess the meaning of the Sudden. Within the 'Manifest' (*kenryo*) category, with the sole exception of the Deer Park [teachings], the other sections all possess the Sudden, and are thus termed the Sudden Teaching.
Indeterminate [teachings] are likewise so. Furthermore, it clarifies that even the initial establishment of the Deer Park teachings possesses the meaning of the Sudden.

How much more so for the various Sautrāntika schools. [Commentary: The masters of the North and South generally employ three types [of teachings], yet those they establish as "indeterminate" (aniyata) specifically refer to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
Our school’s judgment, however, is that within each and every flavor [of the Dharma] there are indeterminate elements. As the *Mysterious Text* (*Xuanyiwen*) states:

"Within a single time, a single teaching, and a single thought-moment, all indeterminate elements are fully present. This differs from the old interpretation, which was exclusive [to specific sūtras].
This belongs to the two divisions [of the *Sifen lü*]. Thus we know that the Great Master did not merely innovate the four teachings for the transformation of beings;

even the ritual procedures he established for this transformation were truly distinct from those of antiquity. Therefore, Miaole states: "The four teachings—Sudden and so forth—are the great outline for the judgment of teachings within this school;
the four baskets—*piṭaka* and so forth—are the detailed table of contents for the interpretation of meanings within this tradition. As for the present ritual text:
Since both the *Jian* (Judgment) and the *Shi* (Exegesis) are clearly elucidated herein, it is appropriate to establish the title according to these general names.
[Note] "Ritual" (*yi*) refers to the ritual protocols for judging and explaining the Four Teachings according to the Tiantai school. Since the end of the text states:

"From here below, I shall briefly clarify the ritual protocols for judging the teachings used by various schools," it is evident that this single work is intended to clarify both judgment and exegesis.
[Tiantai]: How could this be called the sequential ritual for the Tathāgata’s manifestation of transformation?

[Note: Since the following section clarifies the ritual systems for doctrinal classification according to various schools, it is evident that the character "yi" (ritual) here specifically refers to the Master’s own system of classification and interpretation.
It appears there is a concern that the current character "yi" might be mistakenly taken as referring to the Tathāgata’s ritual of manifesting transformation.]
Thus it is explained and set forth; therefore, it is analyzed and determined.
Recorded by the Koryo Sramana Diguan (谛观).
[Commentary] Next, the person is identified. The Master’s name was Diguan; his school is that of the Three Truths (三谛) and Three Contemplations (三观), wherein object and wisdom are one and the same.
This is the naming established according to the contemplative practice (*guanxing*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). The *Tonghui lu* states:
When the Wuyue King Qian Zhongyi was reading the *Yongjia ji*, he realized that both [he and the Master] had eliminated the four abidings (*sizhu*).

Taking this as a point of commonality, he questioned National Teacher Shao, who replied, "At Tiantai Guoqing Temple, Master Ji must understand this statement. The King then invited Master Ji to his presence and questioned him. The Master said:
This work, the *Miaoxuanwen* (Profound and Mysterious Text) by the Wise One [Zhiyi], suffered destruction during the military upheavals of An Lushan and Shi Siming.

Recently, it was further burned during the Huichang Persecution, such that the scriptural treasury was nearly completely lost. Now, the propagation of the teachings flourishes once more in Goryeo, where the complete canon is preserved.

King [Wen-tsung] was deeply moved and dispatched a mission to Goryeo; the Goryeo ruler issued an imperial decree for the monk Diguān to serve as an envoy to the Tiantai school. He subsequently returned with the texts.
Zhiguan (Zhi Guan) arrived in China and received instruction from Master Jì. At this time, the Tiantai teachings and contemplations flourished once again.

Zhiguan explored the fundamental texts and produced, in brief, two fascicles of the *Sijiaoyi* (Outline of the Four Teachings). In the upper fascicle, he elucidates the system of doctrinal classification and the establishment of tenets according to our own school;
in the lower fascicle, he clarifies the divergent views and sectarian paths of the various masters of the North and South. Later, Master Gushan remarked that the upper fascicle...
The words and intent are concise and essential; scholars rely upon them to grasp the general outline of a single transformation (*ekavyūha*).

The lower fascicle consists of refutations of ancient masters and may be set aside; therefore, only the upper fascicle is circulated. [Supplement] The *Tongji* states: "When Master Guan composed the *Sijiaoyi*, no one knew of it.
After Luoxi’s passing, it shone forth from his old chest; upon opening it to view, it was found to be the *Sijiaoyi*."
This is the ritual manual (*vidhi*). From this, it flourished widely. It removes the four abodes (*catur-vāsa*) equally and explains the nine fascicles.

[Note] Goryeo: the name of a country among the Eastern Barbarians (*tong-i*). *Śramaṇa*: translated here as "diligent cessation. This means to diligently practice all manner of goodness and to cease all evils.

[Commentary] All wholesome dharmas do not transcend the Three Studies; all unwholesome dharmas do not transcend the Three Poisons. This refers to diligently cultivating precepts, concentration, and wisdom, thereby extinguishing greed, anger, and delusion.
[Supplementary Note] If one discusses perfect contemplation, it is the "three thousand realms in a single thought-moment," which is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle.
When one is destroyed, all are destroyed; when one is established, all are established; when one reaches ultimate realization, all reach ultimate realization.
"What good is not practiced? What evil is not ceased? This is the diligent cessation of those with the highest faculties.
[Note] Furthermore, as for why śramaṇas take "Śākya" as their clan name, it began with Dharma Master Jin’an. Later, when the *Ekottarika Āgama* arrived in this land, it said:
"As the four rivers enter the sea, they all share the same salty taste; so too do those of the four castes who leave the household life—all are called [śramaṇas]."
[This is] the commentary on the text. [■ Record:
This simultaneously explains the general designation "Śramaṇa" as "Śākya. Dao'an said: "Having shaved their hair and dyed their robes, they continue the lineage of Śākyamuni;
therefore, they should take 'Śākya' as their clan name. Later, one additional character was added to confirm this. As for the "four rivers," they are the Anavatapta...
Within the lake, the Gaṅgā River flows from the east into the southeastern ocean; the Sindhu River flows from the south into the southwestern ocean;
the Vakṣu River flows from the west into the northwestern ocean; and the Sītā River flows from the north into the northeastern ocean—it is the source of the Yellow River in this land.
There are four castes: first, the Kṣatriya, translated as "Lord of the Fields," who loves the people and governs the state; they are the kings.

First, the Kṣatriyas, translated as "Warriors," referring to those who govern the state and wield military power. Second, the Brāhmaṇas, translated as "Pure Conduct," referring to those engaged in the study of the Way and who abide in integrity.

Third, the Vaiśyas, which refers to the merchant class. Fourth, the Śūdras, which refers to the agricultural class. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that other miscellaneous castes are difficult to record in detail;
however, there are four distinct lineages among them. Furthermore, the *Kaiyuan lu* (Kaiyuan Catalogue of the Tripitaka), citing the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, states: [text continues].
He said: "O bhikṣus, you who have left the household life from various backgrounds have all abandoned your original surnames and are collectively called sons of Śākya.
Since this accords with the Sūtras and the Vinaya, it shall thus become an eternal rule."

【□Note】The *Xiànxìng lù* (Record of Manifesting the Nature) uses four propositions to distinguish them as follows: 1. One who is a śramaṇa but not a son of Śākya: an ascetic from a non-Buddhist tradition. 2.
One who is a son of Śākya but not a śramaṇa: a member of the Śākya clan living at home; this refers to those of the royal lineage of the Śākyas.

3. One who is both a son of Śākya and a śramaṇa: monks of the two lands (India and China); these are those who have left the household life from any of the four castes and are collectively termed "Śākyas. 4. Neither a son of Śākya nor a śramaṇa.
"Disciple, you are not a śramaṇa. Thus, the customs of the two lands [India and China] have been exhaustively distinguished by these four propositions.
[■ Record] Although this is now cited generally, the intent lies in corroborating the third proposition.

[■ Supplement] The *Xianxing lu* (Record of Manifesting Nature) was so named because Master Yuanyan of Gushan explained the "Buddha-nature of insentient beings" in his *Jingang pei*. [■ Note] Non-Buddhists also...
This does not accord with the designation of a *śramaṇa* as one who exerts effort and seeks cessation.

For now, I shall tentatively provide an explanation based on the discourse regarding those who have left the household life (*pravrajita*). [Commentary: Some may ask: "The son of the Śākya is a *śramaṇa*, and he is one who has left the household life from the Śākya clan.

Furthermore, those who have left the household life from other clans in the land of India, as well as the monastics here in this land, are all called 'Śākya-sons' (*śākyaputrīya*) *śramaṇas*. Under which category should they be subsumed?"
[Commentary: This section alone explains the third phrase. First, a divergent interpretation is presented. Now, the intent of the interrogation and refutation is as follows:

Since those who have gone forth from the Śākya clan are initially called "Śākya-sons" (śākyaputrīya) and "śramaṇas," one must judge whether the monastics of both lands are subsumed under this third phrase or not.
Under which phrase, then, would they be included? By means of this single interrogation, the proponents of the divergent view fall silent and submit.
[□ Note] "Record" (Lu) refers to the Master Guan’s transcription of the essential outlines of the Tiantai teachings.
[■ Record] By citing the main framework, the various details unfold of themselves; by transcribing the essentials, the full text can be understood in detail.
△ Second, the Explanation of the Text (Shiwen), in its major divisions, is divided into three parts. First, the Narration of the Time, Teaching, and Meaning (Xushi Jiaofayi San Guang).
Second, the Actual Narration (Zhengxu). First, Establishing the Authority Who Judges (Lining Napanzhu).

Tiantai Master Zhizhe. [Commentary] The Dharma relies on individuals for its propagation; the teaching is established through individuals. Therefore, the patriarch who first established the teaching is designated at the outset.

[Sub-commentary] The *Shiyiji* (Record of Supplementary Omissions) states: "Tiantai" is a place where the true reality dwells; "Zhizhe" is the title bestowed by the Sui Emperor; "Dashi" (Great Master) refers to one who is... [the leader of] the multitude.
He became a living model and was also a teacher to emperors and high ministers.
[Commentary] Regarding the one who dwelt in truth at Tiantai, *Fayi* states: "The Master received the tally through a dream; his auspicious resonance caused the bell to ring."
Specters and demons vanished upon beholding his virtue; a Brahman monk descended from the void to pay him homage. He propagated the sutras at Luoshui and entered nirvana at Shicheng;
this was because his karmic affinity lay with Tiantai. As for what the Sui sovereign praised:

when Emperor Yang was still the Prince of Jin, after he had received the Bodhisattva precepts, the Prince said, "My teacher transmits the lamp of the Buddha-dharma; he should be called 'The Wise One' (Zhìzhě). This refers to that very title. Great.

Regarding the teacher as the model for the multitude, the *Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā* states: The Sūtra says that a "Great Teacher" (Mahāśāstṛ) is one who is able to skillfully instruct and admonish his śrāvaka disciples regarding what should and should not be done;
he is thus called a Great Teacher. Furthermore, he is one who can transform and guide immeasurable sentient beings.

He is so named because he has realized suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Furthermore, he is so named because he appears in the world to destroy the heterodox and defiled teachings of outside paths.
Thus, only the Buddha is entitled to be called the Great Teacher of the Three Realms (*triloka-śāstṛ*).

That he is now called the "Great Teacher" is truly due to the veneration of the fourfold assembly, just as when a Buddha appears in the world. The *Commentary on the Sutra of the Avalokiteśvara Dharani* states: "Great" is a term of praise and excellence.
These are his words. "Master" (*shī*) is a title for one who teaches others the Way. In antiquity, those whose understanding and practice served as a model were called "Great Masters.
"Wise One" (*zhìzhě*) was a designation used because he was a paradigm of his time. "Emperor and Kings" refers to great ministers such as the Later Chen Emperor.

During the reigns of the two emperors Wen and Yang of the Sui dynasty, Shen Junli and others, who held the rank of Yitong, [prepared the following account]. The Great Master previously dreamed that on a mountain peak there was a monk who beckoned to him;
extending his arm all the way down to the foot of the mountain, he guided the Master upward and led him to ascend.

Later, when the Master entered Tiantai, he saw the southern peak of Fulong and lingered there with deep attention. That night, he stayed at the grass hut of Dingguang, where everyone heard the sound of a bell.

There was the sound of voices, light, and long-drawn chants accompanied by hand gestures; one could only hear the striking of the wooden mallet to assemble the monks—this was the sign that he had attained abiding.
He recalled the past, when they beckoned and led one another, or when he went alone to practice *dhūta* on the Flower-Peak of a distant mountain.

Later at night, a great wind uprooted trees and thousands of *chi-mei* (goblins) swarmed about; yet, with his mind settled in empty stillness, they naturally dispersed. When the Master lectured on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, Yuan...
Zixiong saw several dozen foreign monks coming out, holding incense burners in their hands.
△ Second, clarifying the methods of doctrinal classification, in two parts: first, the general heading.
By means of the five periods and eight teachings, he classified and interpreted the entirety of the holy teachings that flowed eastward; there was no fragrance left unexhausted.
[Commentary: Our Buddha, out of his great compassion, universally transformed beings throughout the ten directions. Consequently, the holy teachings were transmitted to China.

Upon the appearance of the Great Master Zhiyi, he established definitive interpretations through the framework of the five periods and eight teachings; thus, the essential purport was fully exhausted, neither prolix nor deficient.
This is precisely the text recorded in the book; therefore, it is first presented as a general heading.
[Note] The Five Periods and Eight Teachings are originally the Dharma spoken by the Tathāgata; the Great Master established these names based on their underlying meaning.
[Supplementary Note] The Tathāgata observes the capacities of sentient beings to evolve them; thus, his timing never misses its mark, and his teachings are never established indiscriminately.

Therefore, imparting the teaching according to the time is the fundamental protocol for the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma. Yet, as its intent is profound and subtle, it cannot be fathomed except by those who are Great Beings of the Four Reliances.
Who could fathom its origins? The Great Master personally beheld the assembly on Vulture Peak as if it were still present, unscattered;
he attained the *pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*—the first of the four reliances—and was thus able to rely upon the sacred meaning to establish the five periods and eight teachings.
[Note] This is used to judge and explain the holy teachings of a lifetime; hence the word "by" (*yi*) is employed.

[Supplement] The five periods and eight teachings constitute the original method of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma. By now adding the character "by," it becomes the definitive system of interpretation established by Tiantai.
[Note] However, the Tiantai Master Zhiyi of the Upper Heaven is the person who judges and explains; the holy teachings flowing from the East are the dharmas that are judged and explained;
and the five periods and eight teachings are the methods for such judgment and explanation.

[Supplementary Note] This commentary is divided into three distinct parts for the sake of interpretation: that which pertains to the person, that which pertains to the dharma, and that which pertains to the timing and teaching of the ritual.
This is intended so that future students may have a clear understanding when they encounter the actual text.

[Commentary] Tiantai, following the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*, judges and interprets all other scriptures. As the *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "The judgment and interpretation are based upon the categories of the teachings (*bu-jiao*).
The meaning of these categories of teachings resides solely in the *Lotus Sūtra*."

[Appendix] The Great Master personally realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. Therefore, he interpreted all the various sūtras according to the *Lotus Sūtra*, as in the case of the "Five Periods" and the "Four Teachings of the Conversion Ritual.
This is evidenced by the fact that his commentaries frequently cite passages from the "Belief and Understanding" chapter (*Adhimukty-adhyāya*). Regarding this point, the *Jieyi* states:
"The *Shiqian* contains no text explicitly stating that his interpretations are based on the specific divisions of the sūtras and teachings; rather, every dharma possesses this underlying intent."
As stated in the *Jingmiaozhongyan* (Discourse on the Subtlety of the Objects): "If one does not rely upon the teachings, one will not know the subtlety of the teachings;
if one does not rely upon the schools (*nikāya*), one will not know the subtlety of the schools. This is merely a brief summary of such meanings.
[□ Note] "Jiàn" (判) means to analyze and discern; "shì" (釋) means to explain and expound.

[■ Supplement] The "Transformation Ritual" (*huàyí*) constitutes the general framework and is appropriate for analysis and discernment; the "Transformation Dharma" (*huàfǎ*) constitutes the specific method and is appropriate for explanation and exposition.

[Miao-leo] says: "The categories of 'sudden' and so forth constitute the great outline for the classification of teachings within this school; the categories of 'pitaka' and so forth constitute the general table of contents for the interpretation of meanings within this tradition."

[Commentary] The "General Outline" (*dàgāng*) is the place where the eyes are located as a whole; thus it is likened to the "Method of Transformation" (*huàyí*), which establishes the general teaching of a single transformation.
The "Detailed Items" (*wǎngmù*) are the individual meshes of the net; thus they are likened to the "Teachings of Transformation" (*huàfǎ*), which explain the specific meanings of various sutras.
[Note] For example, if one judges the *Avataṃsaka* to be "sudden" based on its pedagogical method (*huayi*), yet explains it according to the distinct and perfect teachings (*biyuan*) of the Dharma;
or even if one judges the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to be "neither sudden nor gradual," yet explains it as being purely perfect and uniquely sublime.
[Note] A detailed explanation of the classification of the five periods (*pañca-kāla*) is found below.
[Record] The following text provides a detailed exposition of the periods and teachings (*kāla-śāsana*). As the textual meaning is extensive and dispersed, it is presented here in summary.
[Commentary] "Flowing eastward" means that the Buddha-dharma flowed from the West to the East.

[Record] During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty, Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna first arrived in Zhendan (China). From this point on, the Buddha-dharma spread extensively throughout the Eastern lands.

[Note] "Generation" (dài) means a cycle. The Tathāgata’s fifty years of preaching the Dharma constitute one generation. Now, by means of the five periods and eight teachings, his explanations are judged and interpreted without omission.

[Commentary: Although the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma spanned a long duration and its teachings were vast, this present classification and interpretation by means of the Five Periods and Eight Teachings alone accords with the Buddha’s intent;
there is no further room for dispute. Were it not for Tiantai, to whom could I turn?
[Commentary] If this is so, why does the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) ask: "Why was [the teaching at] the Amra Garden not included among the 'Lesser' [teachings]?

One must understand that the *Miaoxuan* refutes the ancients based on the timing. That is to say, when the *Dīpavaṃsa Sūtra* (Tiwei jing) was preached, it was prior to the turning of the Wheel of Dharma;

since the Jewel of the Sangha did not yet exist, [Zhiyi] refuted the ancient masters who claimed that one should separately establish the teaching for humans and devas at the Amra Garden as a "Lesser Teaching."
If one classifies the sūtras according to their doctrinal content (*dharma*), it is as stated in the *Sijiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings):

"The Three Piṭakas clarify worldly generosity, precept-keeping, and meditative concentration; these constitute the teachings for humans and devas, and are all wholesome dharmas produced by correct causes and conditions.
Since these are already subsumed within the Three Piṭakas, the former masters have said that when classifying by time, one should not rely on the five periods, but rather classify by doctrine."
[Sūtra]: In meaning, this should be subsumed within the Tripiṭaka.
[Commentary] This selection refers to the *Paiṅgula-sūtra* mentioned previously regarding the Jeta Grove. The *Paiṅgula-sūtra* should be subsumed under the Hīnayāna.
The *Myōzen* (Miaoxuan) asks: "Why was the *Paiṅgula-sūtra* previously categorized as being subsumed under the Hīnayāna? [Supplement]: Since it is not subsumed under the Hīnayāna...

If it is subsumed [under the *She dasheng lun*], then it does not belong to the Eight Teachings. Since it predates the Jeta Grove (the period of the *Lotus Sūtra*), it does not belong to the Five Periods.

Would this not result in the failure to encompass the Dharma exhaustively? [Commentary] One must know that the section beginning with "Below" constitutes the response. This is as explained in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) within the refutation of ancient views based on the chronology of the teachings.
The *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis) states: From the beginning at Vārāṇasī until the final Parinirvāṇa, all that was taught as the Dharma of the Hīnayāna was compiled into the Three Piṭakas.
From the attainment of enlightenment until the twin trees, all that was taught as the Mahāyāna was compiled into the Mahāyāna [Piṭaka].
That which occurred prior to the Jeta Grove is not included within the Hīnayāna. Why? Because at that time, the Jewel of the Saṃgha did not yet exist.
[Note: Although this constitutes a virtuous discourse for the worlds of humans and devas, it does not yet turn the supramundane Dharma-wheel of the Hīnayāna;

therefore, one should not definitively establish that the *Purāṇa* (Tiwei) represents the initial period of the Hīnayāna teachings. This is because the Buddha defines "time" by the turning of the Dharma-wheel;

thus, the statement [in question] is not included within the Hīnayāna category. It specifically refutes the error of those who maintain that the initial period was established [by the Buddha]. If we consider it from the perspective of the Dharma...]

This clarifies that the correct judgment of the Tiantai school is that [the *Tiwei jing*] should be subsumed under the Tripiṭaka, because the *Tiwei jing* speaks of the merit of precept-observance and goodness.

Therefore, it cites the *Sijiao yi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), which states: "The worldly giving, precepts, and meditative concentration of the Tripiṭaka serve as proof," following the previous masters.

The explanations provided by the former masters of the Tiantai school are easily understood. [Record] In antiquity, there was the recluse Liu Qiu of the Qi dynasty, who established the doctrine of the Five Periods:

first, the Teaching for Humans and Devas, which is the *Tiewei jing*; second, the Teaching with Characteristics, which is the *Āgamas*; third, the Teaching without Characteristics, which is the *Prajñāpāramitā*;
fourth, the Teaching of Common Return, which is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and fifth, the Teaching of Eternal Abiding, which is the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*. [Supplement]
The question in this section arises because the previous passage concerning the Jeta Grove did not employ the terminology of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

Based on the Tiantai school’s doctrine of the five periods (*pañca-kāla*), if there were any omissions, this objection would follow. The *Tongji* states: "The tree deity knew that the Buddha had sat in meditation for seven days and had not yet eaten.
As five hundred merchants passed by, two great men named Trapusa and Bhallika went to the deity and made their request."
Puṇya. The deity said, "The Buddha is by the water's edge; first offer him food. The two men offered honeyed parched grain (*madhupāyasa*) to the Buddha.
The Buddha bestowed upon them the Three Refuges and further preached the Five Precepts. Regarding the refuge in the Saṅgha, he said: "I take refuge in the future Saṅgha."
△ Second, the detailed enumeration is divided into two parts. First, the five periods are divided into two. First, the inquiry and the designation of the names.
Regarding the "five periods": first is the Avataṃsaka period.
[Commentary] When the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, he manifested the nature of the Dharma-realm and preached the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, desiring to cause sentient beings—
This is the realization and entry into the Dharma-realm.

[Commentary] From the perspective established by the title of the sutra, although it spans seven locations and eight assemblies—or nine assemblies in the new translation—it constitutes but a single sutra.
[Commentary] This explains the meaning of "time" as established from the title; the section on "place and assembly" follows below for further explanation.
[Sub-commentary] The causal practices are like flowers, adorning the fruition virtues.
[Commentary] It is adorned by the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices and possesses the meritorious virtues of the fruit of the One Vehicle.
