[Sub-commentary] The full title is *The Mahāvaipulya Buddha-avatamsaka Sūtra*. This title is established through the complete presence of the three elements: person, dharma, and metaphor.
There are also cases where these three are presented individually or in combination.
[Commentary] Amitābha is translated as "Immeasurable Life" and also as "Immeasurable Light. The Buddha is the speaker, while Amitābha is that which is spoken of;
both are persons who have attained the fruit. The title is established based on a single individual. Nirvāṇa is translated as "Great Extinction" (Mahā-parinirvāṇa); this refers to the Dharma.

The explanation is found below. This title is established based on a single dharma: the "Brahmajāla" (Net of Brahmā). The Great Brahmā King possesses a *jāla-dhvaja* (net-banner), upon which red light rays radiate back and forth and multicolored hues shine in mutual brilliance;

the layered reflections of pearls interpenetrate one another without end. The Buddha contemplates this banner and, because of it, speaks of worlds that are immeasurable and boundless, like the mesh of a net.
The Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma-gates is also like this. [Single] (Note: The term *jāla-dhvaja* refers to a banner featuring a net motif, symbolizing the interconnectedness of all phenomena.)

The title is established through analogy. Mañjuśrī (Wénshū) means "Wonderful Virtue" (Miaode). If one perceives the Buddha-nature, one is endowed with the three virtues; because these are neither vertical nor horizontal, it is named "Wonderful Virtue.

Prajñā (Bānrě) is the Dharma; the explanation for this will follow below. Thus, the title is established by way of both person and dharma. Regarding *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (Miàofǎliánhuá), the explanation will follow below.
As for the lotus flower (*puṇḍarīka*), cause and effect are simultaneous; this is used as a metaphor for the fact that the provisional and the real are of one essence within the Wonderful Dharma.
The title is established through the combination of dharma and metaphor. "Tathāgata" is explained below. "Lion’s Roar" refers to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma;

that is, his single voice universally reaches all, and beings of different kinds understand it equally, causing demons and heretics to submit their hearts—this is what is called the Lion’s Roar, the fearless teaching.
Upon hearing this, the brains of all the hundred beasts would split asunder. "Human" is like setting forth a title: *The Great Vaipulya Buddha Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because its substance is boundless, capable of encompassing the entirety of space. It is called "Vaipulya" (*vaipulya*) because its Dharma-gates are inexhaustible, capable of emptying the vast ocean.

It is called "Avataṃsaka" (*avataṃsaka*) because its functions are unfathomable, capable of counting every atom within all lands. It is "separated from awakening" [because it transcends the dualism of subject and object].
That which is awakened illuminates the profound depths of the myriad dharmas—this is the Buddha. It spreads the fragrance of the myriad practices and brings glory to all virtues—this is the Flower.
It perfects these practices and virtues to adorn the ten bodies—this is the Adornment. It penetrates and gathers the mysterious and subtle to form the radiance of true light—this is the Sūtra.
"Mahāvaipulya" refers to the Dharma; "Buddha" refers to the person; "Avataṃsaka" is a metaphor. To be fully endowed with these constitutes [the title].

Title. [Supplement] The Ten Bodies. First, the Bodhi-body (*bodhi-kāya*). *Bodhi* is translated as "the Way" (*mārga*). This refers to the body of the Buddha who has attained Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Second, the Vow-body (*praṇidhāna-kāya*).

This refers to the descent from Tuṣita Heaven, explained as being based on the power of vows to deliver sentient beings. Third, the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). This refers to manifesting transformations according to the various classes of beings to respond to their capacities.

Fourth, the Sustaining Power-body (*bala-dhāraṇa-kāya*). This refers to the sustaining power of spiritual penetrations (*ṛddhi*) that maintains the entirety of the True Body (*dharmakāya*) for the sake of transformation.

1. The physical body and the fragmented *śarīra* relics remain indestructible for all eternity. 5. The body adorned with the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), meaning the attainment of the true recompense body (*vipāka-kāya*) characterized by these subtle marks and signs.
6. The body of majestic power (*prabhāva-kāya*), which refers to subduing the māras, externalists, and borderlands through one's awesome authority.

7. The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*): assuming bodies in various places according to the intentions of oneself and others; wherever the mind goes, the body immediately follows, thereby liberating sentient beings.
8. The merit body (*puṇya-kāya*): so called because it is fully endowed with merit. 9. The dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*):

taking the pervasive nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) throughout the entire dharma-realm as its body. 10. The wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*): possessing the perfect clarity of sublime wisdom that definitively discerns all phenomena.
True Light. It is the One True Dharma-realm.
[Note] The old translation was produced by the Jin dynasty in either fifty or sixty fascicles. The new translation was produced by the Tang dynasty in eighty fascicles.
As for the three versions from the Dragon Palace, the upper version contains verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms.

The middle version consists of one hundred and twenty-four thousand *śloka* verses and one thousand two hundred chapters, equal in number to the atoms within four sets of four continents (*cāturdvīpaka*).
The inferior version consists of one hundred thousand *śloka* verses and forty-eight chapters (of which there are currently only thirty-nine,
as noted in the *Shiqian*, fascicle 18).

[Commentary] Regarding the old translation: during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, Buddhabhadra (translated as Jue Xian) translated thirty-six thousand *ślokas* from the Sanskrit original at Xie Sikong Monastery in Yangzhou, producing the Jin version in either fifty or sixty fascicles.
Regarding the new translation: during the Yonglong era of the Tang dynasty, Prajñā (Rizhao) relied upon the Jin version to translate the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter (*dharmadhātupraveśa*).

There were omissions in two places. In the first year of the Zhengsheng era, Śikṣānanda, who was translating the *Xi-xue* (Joyful Learning), retranslated the portions completed by Jñānagupta and supplemented various deficiencies, resulting in eighty fascicles. However, the passage in which Mañjuśrī placed his hand upon Sudhana’s head was still missing.
Xianshou took the portion supplemented by Jñānagupta and inserted it into the omission in Śikṣānanda’s version; thus, the text was joined and the meaning made continuous.
However, these two sutras are both abridgments from among the one hundred thousand verses;

because the translation was not yet complete, the three versions in the Dragon Palace were compiled by Mañjuśrī and Ānanda at Sālaguha (Mount Cakravāḍa), and the Dharma-protecting deities took them into the Dragon Palace.
When Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna personally visited the Dragon Palace, he saw that the upper and middle versions were extensive, beyond human capacity.

That which was held [in the original] was transmitted among humans solely through the recitation of the lower text. What exists today as only thirty-nine chapters refers to the number of chapters in the Tang translation.
Regarding the old translation, there were seven locations and eight assemblies; the new translation adds one assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall.
First, the six chapters on the Magadha Āraṇya: 1. The Sublime Array of Worldly Lords; 2. The Manifestation of the Tathāgata...
1. The Marks; 2. The Three [Bodies]; 3. Samantabhadra Samādhi; 4. World-Formation; 5. The Flower Adornment World; 6. Vairocana.
Second, the six chapters of the Assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance: 1. The Names and Titles of the Tathāgata; 2. The Four Noble Truths.

3. *Prabhāsa-avabodha* (The Enlightenment of Radiance); 4. *Bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-prabhāsa* (The Questions of the Bodhisattvas on Radiance); 5. *Śuddhacaryā* (Pure Conduct); 6. *Bhadrapāla* (Worthy Leader). Third:

The *Trāyastriṃśa-parivarta* (Assembly of the Heaven of the Thirty-three), which explains the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*). It consists of six chapters: 1. *Sumeru-śikhara-abhirohaṇa* (Ascending the Summit of Mount Sumeru); 2. *Sumeru-śikhara-gāthā-stotra* (Verses of Praise on the Summit of Mount Sumeru).
3. The Ten Abodes; 4. Holy Conduct; 5. The Merit of Arousing the Mind; 6. Clarifying the Dharma. Fourth:
The Assembly of the Yāma Heaven, which explains the Ten Practices in four chapters: 1. Ascending to the Yāma Heaven; 2. Ascending to the Yāma Heaven with Verses of Praise; 3. The Ten Practices.
Four: The Ten Inexhaustible Treasuries. Fifth: The Assembly in Tuṣita Heaven speaks of the Ten Dedications in three parts:
first, ascending to Tuṣita; second, ascending to Tuṣita with verses of praise; third, the Ten Dedications. Sixth: The Assembly in Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven speaks of the Ten Grounds.
One fascicle. Chapter Seven: The Assembly at the Universal Radiance Hall, wherein the superior progression of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is expounded.

Eleven fascicles: 1. The Ten Samādhis; 2. The Ten Supernatural Powers (*abhijñā*); 3. The Ten Endurances (*kṣānti*); 4. The Incalculable Eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); 5. The Lifespan; 6. The Abodes of Bodhisattvas; 7.
The Inconceivable Dharmas, which clarify the virtues of the Buddha-fruit; 8. The Ocean of Marks (*lakṣaṇa-samudra*); 9. The Radiance Following the Marks.
The tenth is the "Chapter on Merit. The eleventh is the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra. The eighth is the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata.

The eighth [section] consists of one chapter—the "Chapter on Leaving the World"—which explains the six stages in the Hall of Universal Radiance during the third assembly. The ninth is the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm," spoken at the assembly in the Jeta Grove.
[Note] Regarding the fourfold classification of the *Avataṃsaka* established by earlier scholars, there is no explicit textual basis from the Patriarch [Zhiyi].

Examining the intentions of the Great Master [Zhiyi] and Jingxi [Zhanran], there are differences based on time, place, and principle. Based on principle, it is called the "Dharmadhātu"; based on place, it is sometimes called the "Site of Quiescence" (Gṛdhrakūṭa);
and based on time, it is said to be "thirty-seven days," or sometimes "extending through the limits of the future. How can one cling to these mere names?
One might then claim that the *Avataṃsaka* has four distinct divisions; however, this involves contradictions regarding its doctrinal meaning.

It is improper to designate the later period as the site of the *Vaiśālī* assembly simply because the *Avataṃsaka* spans a long duration, nor should one take the "universal teaching" (*pāryāyika-deśanā*) common to all five periods and treat it as a long-duration period.
[Appendix] Formerly, based on the site of the Bodhimanda, the duration of time, and the ultimate limit of the future throughout the *dharmadhātu*, four types of *Avataṃsaka* were established.
Examining the intent of the Great Master [Zhiyi] and Jingxi [Zhanran], they differ only in terms of time, place, and principle. Regarding principle, it is called the *dharmadhātu*;
regarding place, it is called the Bodhimanda; regarding time, it is called the thirty-seven days—or, alternatively, the long duration until the end of the future.

How can one recognize this conventional expression regarding time and, conversely, divide it into two types—long duration and "until the end of the future limit"—and further add "Dharmadhātu" and "Site of Quiescence" to claim there are four distinct kinds?

Furthermore, in the section below [the text] refutes errors, stating: "One should not take the subsequent division of 'long duration' as the phrase for the 'Site of Quiescence. According to the old [version]..."

In the translation of the *Avataṃsaka*, it says that Sudhana’s southern journey does not depart from the site of enlightenment (*śīta-vana*). The new translation states he does not depart from before the seat of Vairocana.
Since all subsequent sections likewise state he does not depart, these should be harmonized with the scriptural language.

Furthermore, one should not take the meaning of the five periods as extending through the later periods to constitute a phrase regarding the length of time. According to the *Miaoxuan*, the duration of the *Avataṃsaka* period is long.
Now, upon hearing the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one is able to enter it immediately. The *Zhìshēn* (Commentary) states: "First, taking the Dharma-realm as the *Avataṃsaka*;

second, taking the length of time to extend into the later [periods]. Since both the Great Master [Zhiyi] and Jīngqī [Zhili] take "extending through the meaning" (*yìtōng*) to mean "length of time," this should be harmonized with the words of the Patriarch [Huisi].
Having read what he has distinguished, I find it possesses great insight. Master Yù refutes this based on three points.
The meaning of the four traditional [periods] has already been established. Furthermore, regarding the latter two sections therein, they originally belonged to a different intent.

Now, following the intention of Master Yù, I provide a comprehensive interpretation: since the tradition already established two types based on time, one should not eliminate the specific divisions of the "thirty-seven" [days], but rather establish the subsequent period as being long in duration in order to encompass the [teachings of] the Jīvaṃdhara Grove. This extends through the five periods.
Later, there is "pervasion by meaning" (*yìtōng*); up to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, there is "pervasion by text" (*wéntōng*). There is a slight distinction between them;

one cannot assume that because the period of pervasion by meaning is long, the period of pervasion by text is likewise long. [Commentary] Miaole says: "That which is expounded has nothing external to it;
this is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Zongjing says: "The Dharma-realm is the general name for the One Mind and the myriad phenomena."
The destination is the site of tranquility. Unfurling the original scroll: for twenty-one days. As it is said, during the first seven days, the first five assemblies were taught.

This is because the beginning of the sutra states that from the moment of attaining perfect enlightenment, in all three locations, [the Buddha] did not rise from his previous state. During the second seven days...
The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth are taught because, at the beginning of the sutra, it is stated that the Bhagavat had not long attained enlightenment, being in his second week.
The ninth assembly is said to have been taught after the third week, as Śāriputra, Jeta Grove, and others are present.
This is based on Bodhiruci’s explanation regarding the preservation of the sequence of events. [Supplement] The *Tongji* states that formerly...
The site of tranquility (the Bodhimaṇḍa), the duration of time, the limit of the future, and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are arranged as the fourfold *Avataṃsaka*.

Furthermore, the first three are categorized as pertaining to phenomena (*dharma*), while the last one pertains to principle (*tattva*). This has been a persistent flaw through successive generations;

now, when discussing its meaning, there are only three names. The first is the "site of tranquility" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) quotes the *Fangbian pin* (Chapter on Expedient Means): "From the moment he first sat at the site of enlightenment, he contemplated for twenty-one days."
This refers to the Buddha’s initial, sudden teaching. From the first chapter up to the thirty-sixth chapter constitutes the first division, which is twofold;

that is, the "long period," as cited in the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) from the *Faxing lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Dharmas), referring to those of dull faculties entering the Dharma-realm in three stages.

From the thirty-seventh chapter onward constitutes the second division, which is threefold, referring to the "limitless future. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states: "In the *Avataṃsaka*, [this is] not yet..."

The *Xi* (Platform) first opened with the gradual teaching; this was spoken by Miaole, who provisionally relied upon a single period of transformation within the Sahā world to convey his present intent.
One should know that the *Avataṃsaka* extends to the end of the future; it is just as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* constantly abides on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa—how is this different from the ten directions?
Though they mutually serve as the principal and the attendant, although there are three names, the sutras taught therein are none other than the *Avataṃsaka*.

The principle that is expounded is none other than the Dharma-realm; this is the summary that refutes the old interpretations. Furthermore, the *Tongji* (Comprehensive Record) states that the duration of time is long.

Regarding those that encompass three locations, these refer to the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Sūtra of the Ocean of Emptiness*; the Buddha-wisdom of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; and the Lotus Treasury Ocean of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
[Appendix] Master Zhi, by means of his seven-times-three days of contemplation, brought all back to the site of the tranquil assembly. Thus...
The time and place seem not yet distinguished.

[□ Note] Question: The *Avataṃsaka* spans a long period; to what time does it extend? Answer: As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states, its meaning corresponds to the period of the "Transmitted Teaching" (*tenkyō*).
The compiler of the sutra took the later sections and, following their thematic categories, concluded them within the preceding section of the *Avataṃsaka* division. This is...

The "pervasion" (*tong*) in the texts of the five periods refers to the category of pervasive [teachings]. For instance, in the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the ocean-like emptiness of the *Avataṃsaka* is clarified;

it is like the sun, when about to set, casting its final rays upon a lofty peak. This [emptiness] is connected with the Lotus Treasury Ocean (*padmagarbha-samudra*) and extends even to after the *Nirvāṇa*.

This is not a case of clarifying the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* within another division [of the canon] and then concluding that it belongs to that specific division; rather, it is a case where the meaning is pervasive throughout the five periods. This is the category of pervasive [teachings].
It is not that the duration [of the teaching] was long.

[Commentary: This refers to the transmission of the teaching. It explains the original fascicle. Subsequently, at the single assembly in the Jeta Grove, the various categories were grouped together and integrated back into the preceding division within the Avataṃsaka section.
This constitutes the textual continuity across the five periods. Regarding the Prajñā, Avataṃsaka, Saṃdhinirmocana, and Śūnyatā: they are wondrous.

Xuán yún: "The *Avataṃsaka* is distinct in that it pertains only to the beginning, whereas it is pervasive throughout to the end. Thus, through cultivation over successive kalpas, one reaches the ocean-like emptiness of the *Avataṃsaka*;
at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one realizes the wisdom of the four Buddhas. This is what it means to pervasively reach both sutras. Furthermore, the *Xiàngfǎ juéyí jīng* says:
'Some see the Reward Body within the Lotus Treasury World-Ocean as the hundreds of thousands of myriads of Śākyamunis.'"

The Buddha preached the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi-dharmamukha*). Just as when the sun rises it first illuminates the high mountains, and when the sun sets its lingering radiance still rests upon the steep peaks, so too does the Lotus Treasury Ocean (*padmagarbhasāgara*) extend through to after the *Nirvāṇa*. By means of the Semblance Dharma (*pratirūpaka-dharma*), doubts are resolved;

thus, this is the concluding scripture of the *Nirvāṇa*. One should know that what was explained above clarifies the meaning of the *Avataṃsaka* from another perspective; it cannot be concluded [as the final word] here.

This main section refers to the "pervasive meaning" that permeates all five periods [of the Buddha’s teaching]; it does not refer to the "pervasive text" of the *Avataṃsaka* in terms of its temporal duration.
[Supplement] Regarding the long duration of the later sections, this refers to a single assembly at the Jetavana Grove.
When Mañjuśrī emerged from the Jetavana Grove, Śāriputra spoke to his six thousand disciples, saying: "Do you see the majestic power, the physical marks, and the minor signs of Mañjuśrī? etc.

When it comes to the passage where Mañjuśrī says to the bhikṣus, "You have all been well able to accomplish the ten kinds of great resolve," the *Jujì* (Record of Phrases) states that one may only say this upon reaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

This is because it corresponds in meaning to the time when the teaching is being transmitted. Furthermore, the *Tǒngjì* (Comprehensive Record) states: "By virtue of having cultivated and studied the *Prajñā* over successive kalpas, [they] now give rise to..."
Through the wisdom of emptiness, one enters the Dharma-realm and contemplates the ocean of the Avataṃsaka-treasury as being ultimately empty. [Appendix] Clarifying Errors:

It is said that "non-temporal" (*fēishí*) is incorrect; it should be changed to "non-literal" (*fēiwéntōng*). Personally, I maintain that both "literal penetration" (*wéntōng*) and "doctrinal penetration" (*yìtōng*) carry the sense of "temporal length.
However, the temporal length of literal penetration extends only to the Prajñāpāramitā, whereas the temporal length of doctrinal penetration reaches the limits of the future.
[The Buddha] heard.
Second, during the period at the Deer Park, he preached the Four Āgamas.

[Commentary: Since those of small capacity would have no benefit from the sudden teaching, the Buddha concealed his excellence and manifested inferiority; without moving from the site of tranquility, he traveled [to the Deer Park].
The Deer Park. To provide assurance for those of inferior capacity, he provisionally certified them to the minor fruits.
[Note] Established according to location and time: although many sūtras were preached, they share the same location.
[Supplement] Regarding the mention of the four Āgamas: this does not restrict [the location] to a single place; rather, it refers specifically to the site where the Wheel of Dharma was first turned.
[Appendix] *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) states: "The phrase 'in one and the same place' is extremely restrictive. One should know that the initial conversion by all Buddhas occurs at the Deer Park."
Therefore, it was established as the time [of the teaching].
[Note] This is the place where the Tathāgata formerly manifested his transformative influence during his previous birth; for the conditions, see *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), Vol.
1, Section 7. [Record] The *Fuxing* quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, saying: "The King of Vārāṇasī went out hunting and saw two leaders of deer. One was..."
Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was once Devadatta. The Bodhisattva, Lord of the Deer, informed the king:
"If you wish to provide a meal, you should designate deer in turn to be sent one by day. The king approved of these words, and it was Devadatta’s turn to be among the herd.
There was a doe who said to her master, "It is my turn to die, yet I am pregnant. My offspring has not yet reached its time; I beg you to grant me your favor.
The master replied angrily, "Who does not cherish their own life? Since it is your turn, simply depart. The doe went to the presence of the Lord of the Śākyas and related the matter in detail.
The Lord said, "If I do not intervene, her offspring will be killed unjustly. If she is exempted from this turn, [the others will follow suit] later..."
"What did you send next? "I alone went in my place. The King asked in astonishment, "Are all the deer gone? The leader replied, "They are merely flourishing;
it was for the sake of those deer that I returned to inform you. Because I took pity on them, this body of mine will not last long and must inevitably face death.
To compassionately rescue others from suffering and distress brings immeasurable merit. The King spoke in verse: "I am truly but a beast."
He was named "The Human-Headed Deer," while you, though a beast, were named "The Deer-Headed Human.
By principle one is human, not by physical form. From this day forward, I shall not eat any meat;
I offer this gift of fearlessness, which may also bring peace to your mind. By these causes and conditions, know that this was Śākyamuni manifesting his transformative power in a former birth.
This is the place [of the Deer Park].

[Commentary] It is called the Deer Park because it is the dwelling place of a herd of deer. It is also named the Pomegranate Garden (*Nāvana*) after the trees. Furthermore, as it was the dwelling place of two seers (*ṛṣi*), it is also called the Seers' Garden.
[Commentary] The Āmra Garden (Naiyuan): Because there are many *āmra* trees on the ground, it is called such. Regarding the Rishi Garden (Xianyuan), the *Vibhāṣā* states:
When a Buddha appears in the world, Arhat Great Rishis have dwelt, do dwell, and will dwell there. When no Buddha appears in the world, Pratyekabuddhas dwell there;
when there are no Pratyekabuddhas, Rishis with the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) dwell there. These two types of rishis may be either Ārāḍa or Kālāma.
Regarding the "Two Sages" (Erxian): [Note] Bian’o states that those who claim it derives from a tree are referring to the *vana* (grove) as "tree," not specifically to the crabapple (*nai*).
It simply refers to the grove of Vārāṇasī. As for the two characters "Two Sages," I suspect they were written down by Jingxi in a single moment of inspiration.

Regarding Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma: since these two sages were in the kingdom of Magadha and were not in this grove, although the current commentary cites them to establish the text, it seems necessary to change the wording to "the Place where the Sages Fell.
This is because five hundred sages heard music from the sky and, giving rise to defilement, lost their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and fell to this spot.
[Note] *Āgama* is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anupama-dharma*).
[Record] This refers to the wisdom of the sages which, in discerning the meanings of dharmas, is beyond compare.

[Commentary] The first part of the *Miaoxuan* states: The *Ekottarika Āgama* clarifies the causes and effects of humans and devas; the *Madhyama Āgama* clarifies the profound meaning of true stillness;

the *Saṃyukta Āgama* clarifies various dhyānas and samādhis; and the *Dīrgha Āgama* refutes non-Buddhists while universally teaching impermanence, the knowledge of suffering, the severance of its origin, the realization of cessation, and the cultivation of the path.

[Commentary] The *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: For the sake of devas and worldlings, he preached the Dharma according to the occasion; these were compiled as the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
To encourage people to practice, for the sake of sentient beings with sharp faculties, he expounded various profound meanings;

this is called the *Madhyama Āgama*, practiced by those who study. He expounded various methods corresponding to dhyāna; this is the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, practiced by those who practice seated meditation. [He also] refuted all non-Buddhists.
Regarding this *Dīrgha Āgama*, the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-śāstra* states: Ānanda further reflected that the texts and meanings of the *Sūtras* were intermingled;

it was appropriate, therefore, to arrange them according to their subject matter and principles, placing the larger first and the smaller in subsequent order. First is the *Ekottarika*; second is named the *Madhyama*;
third is named the *Dīrgha*; and fourth is named the *Saṃyukta*. Starting from one and proceeding up to ten, they follow the sequence of the subjects.
"Superior" (*adhipati*) refers to the *Ekottarika* (Increasing by One). "Middle" refers to matters that are neither large nor small, neither long nor short, but which abide in the Middle Way.

"Long" refers to the teaching of events from remote antiquity, continuing unceasingly through kalpas; it concerns the fundamental origins and the history of the Seven Buddhas, the Holy Kings, and the Seven Treasures.
"Miscellaneous" refers to various sūtras for severing the fetters that are difficult to recite and difficult to remember, as their contents are numerous and fragmented, causing people...
This is joy. Although there are four [truths] in the Sūtra, that which they expound is the same: impermanence. Why is this?

The worldly, out-flowing fruits of suffering are produced by the accumulated causes of afflictions and karma; the supramundane, out-flow-free state of quiescence is attained through the primary and auxiliary factors of the Path.
Because sentient beings do not understand suffering, they do not sever its accumulation; because they do not yearn for cessation, they do not cultivate the Path.

Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke in segments: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent; they are dharmas that do not endure for long, dharmas that change rapidly, and dharmas that cannot be relied upon.

This was intended to cause [beings] to know suffering (*duḥkha*), abandon its accumulation (*samudaya*), aspire toward its cessation (*nirodha*), and cultivate the path (*mārga*). [Supplement] Regarding the profound meaning of true tranquility (*śānti*):

it is called "true" (*satya*) because it is free from the false imaginings of views and thoughts; it is called "tranquil" (*śānta*) because it is detached from the flux of birth and death. This is the supramundane state.

The Dharma. Therefore, it is called the profound meaning. It long refuted the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), clarifying that dharmas arise from correct causes and conditions, thereby refuting the heterodox.
There are no two kinds of causes and conditions.
Third, during the period of the Vaipulya [sūtras].

[Commentary: Since those of inferior capacity are guaranteed only the partial truth, the Buddha extensively employs methods of praise and censure, bestowing both encouragement and reprimand, so that they may feel shame for their inferiority and aspire toward the superior.

[Commentary] Extensively discussing the four teachings, they are equally bestowed upon all capacities. Since the sutras preached are numerous and the locations are not uniform, the time is established here based on the Dharma.
[Commentary] It is called "Universal" (fang) because it discusses all four teachings together; it is called "Equal" (deng) because it universally benefits those of the three capacities.
The locations are also not uniform, such as Rājagṛha, Śrāvastī, Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain, the Nairañjanā River, and so forth.

[Note] If the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra* is called "Vaipulya" (Universal/Equally Great), it derives its name from the principle (*li*). As stated in the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes on the *Zhiguan*), fascicle 6, section 15:

"This [sūtra] is named a Vaipulya scripture because it is equal in terms of principle. Furthermore, as stated in the *Zhi guan* (Stop and Contemplation), fascicle 2, section 6: "Entering the Cool Pond through the four gates is called 'Va' (direction/square)."

The principle realized is called "equality" (*samatā*). This is discussed in terms of the convergence of practice and principle; however, as for the present "Prajñāpāramitā" (*Vaipulya*), which is the method for refining and subduing through the "fresh butter" stage, its meaning should pertain to the phenomenal level (*vastu*).
[■ Record] There are four gates, namely the gate of existence, the gate of emptiness, and so forth. [■ Commentary] The *Tongji* states:

Previous explanations regarding the designation of the Vaipulya (fangděng) scriptures merely distinguished between phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), failing to exhaust their full meaning. I shall now provide a detailed explanation. The *Guanfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha) states:
"Recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya scriptures. The *Guangming Xuan* states: "The teaching of Vaipulya extends to the three vehicles. The *Xin Guang*...

The *Ming jing yan* states: "Those who wish to be born among humans or devas, those who wish to attain the four fruits, pratyekabuddhahood, or Buddhahood, should all perform repentance to extinguish and eliminate their karmic obstacles and establish themselves in the Vaipulya. The *Anchu fangdeng xuyiji* says: "The name 'Vaipulya' has two meanings.
If the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* [states] that fresh butter is produced from curds, this is an analogy for how the Vaipulya emerges from the Sūtras. This refers to the second [meaning]."
The three periods are called Fangdeng (Vaipulya). These are intended for those with the capacities of the four teachings of the One Vehicle.

If the *Puxian guan jing* (Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sādhana) is designated as Fangdeng, it directly elucidates the principle of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). Now, regarding the citations [from that text], one might fear that, like the *Puxian guan*, the title is established based on its underlying principle.

Therefore, the titles for the repentance texts of the Three Vehicles are established by citing them according to their specific scriptural divisions (*nikāya*), rather than being based solely on their substance or principle.
According to the established treatises of old, there are three theories. First, [classification] by way of substance: the *Mahāvaipulya* (Great Extensive) Sūtras emerge from the *Sūtra* (Vaipulya);

next, the *Anantārthasūtra* (Sūtra of Infinite Meanings) speaks of the *Vaipulya*; the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) refers to the "milk-curd" stage as the *Vaipulya* that refutes and subdues; and the *Prabhāsa-sūtra* (Light Sūtra) is read [in this context].
Recite the Mahāyāna Vaipulya *Guanzhi Xuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Illumination). The Vaipulya teachings encompass the three vehicles;

these all refer to the teachings of the third period. Second, from the perspective of principle: the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* states that this Vaipulya scripture is the eye of all Buddhas.
Third, both phenomenon and principle are encompassed: the *Zhi guan* says, "There are four methods for Prajñā, namely, entering the Cool Grove through four gates."
The "pool" (hrada) signifies squareness; the principle it accords with is the Great Wisdom of Equality, which is "equal" (sama).

Therefore, regarding the third period, according to the established doctrines of the Four Illuminations (Sishiming), its name is determined specifically from the perspective of the *nikāya* teachings, rather than being restricted solely to phenomena and principle (*dharma*).

Now, Master Yu takes the Vaipulya as his guiding framework and speaks from the standpoint of the *nikāya* teachings; since these *nikāya* teachings encompass both phenomena and principle, it is not as if one were merely using fresh butter for seasoning.
"Rejection" (*chì*) refers to the Buddha’s transformative activity; it is a name established based on that activity.

However, among the three traditional interpretations, the *Contemplation Sūtra* follows the principle (*lǐ*), while the "rejection" of the Vaipulya (*fāngděng*) follows the activity (*shì*). These two are identical. Now, my commentary on the Vaipulya as following activity and principle is also slightly different:
since entering the pond by way of the four gates belongs to practice (*xíng*), it is said here that this concerns the synthesis of practice and principle.
Clarifying erroneous statements: Your critical rebuke regarding "fresh butter" (navanīta) has never departed from principle.

If it were to pertain solely to the phenomenal (the particular), it would seem as though there exists a separate realm of phenomena outside of principle, like the Vaipulya (fangdeng) scriptures. This would present the difficulty that the Vaipulya school fails to encompass all sutras.

I privately maintain that transformative phenomena are invariably inseparable from principle. Master Yu merely follows the old interpretations and, while re-criticizing the peripheral views, judges [this matter] to belong to...

Regarding these matters, there will likewise be no cause for difficult objections; those of future wisdom may simply approach them with an open mind and achieve a harmonious integration. As for "harmonizing and refuting":

harmonizing refers to reconciling the minds of those in the three vehicles so that they may attain universal benefit; refuting refers to chastising those who are like scorched sprouts or rotten seeds, causing their hearts to aspire toward the Great Vehicle.
Regarding the *Vimalakīrti*:

[□ Note] The full title is the *Sūtra Spoken by Vimalakīrti*. It is titled after both a person and a dharma. This is translated as "Pure Name" (*Jìngmíng*), and it is also rendered as "Stainless Renown" (*Wúgòuchēng*).
[Commentary: Ordinary beings are stained by existence; those of the Two Vehicles are stained by emptiness; and Bodhisattvas are stained by the Middle Way; none of them attain the name "Pure.
The Layman (Vimalakīrti) does not cling to either of the two extremes, yet he does not rest in the Middle Way. Although he dwells in a household, he is not attached to the three realms (*tridhātu*).

He manifests having a wife and children, yet he constantly cultivates pure conduct (*brahmacarya*). Like a lotus flower emerging from the water, he is not defiled by it; therefore, he is named Vimalakīrti ("Stainless Renown").
This is an explanation based on the traces (*liǎo*). If one relies on the fundamental source (*běn*), it is the manifestation of the Tathāgata Suvarṇa-śālaka (Golden Grain).
All evils are utterly extinguished, and all virtues gather extensively. Even "purity" cannot be named; yet, within that which cannot be named, it is designated by the name "Purity."
"Stainless" (vimala) means pure. "Renowned" (yaśas) means fame.
"Samparigraha" [is translated as] *Siyi* (思益). [Note: The full title is the *Siyi Fantian Suowen Jing* (思益梵天所問經). It was answered by the Bodhisattva Jālinīprabha.]
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "To the east, beyond seventy-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands, there is a land named Pure and Clean.
The Buddha there is named Sun-Moon Radiance Tathāgata. There is a bodhisattva named Manojña (Beneficial Thought).

Because my Buddha has proclaimed the 'Radiance of Tranquil Adornment,' he has emitted this light, which universally illumines the Buddha-lands of the ten directions. Therefore, [this is spoken by] the Brahmā-deva Manojña.

They came to this land to praise the Buddha with verses and to respectfully request further instruction. Jālinīprabha asked about the Buddha’s physical marks, which surpass the radiance of thousands of millions of suns and moons;
therefore, the Buddha emitted light. Brahmā Viśeṣacintin arrived and engaged in mutual dialogue with the various bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the scripture clearly describes the practices of Mañjuśrī and others, as well as Kāśyapa, Subhūti, and all the other noble ones.
There are responses and challenges [to this]. Here, we specifically point to Jālinīprabha because he was the one who initiated this sutra.
Regarding *Laṅkā*:
[□ Note] it is translated as "Inaccessible."
[Commentary] Laṅkā is the name of a city located on the summit of Mount Malaya. The *Avataṃsaka-śāstra* states that its base overlooks the great ocean;

it is broad at the bottom and narrow at the top, with no path by which to ascend. The city is composed of various precious jewels, its radiance outshining the sun and moon, and it has no gates through which to enter. This mountain city is occupied by the great yakṣa king Māpila.

Only those endowed with great supernormal powers (*mahābhijñā*) are able to ascend and proceed; this is a metaphor for the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*), which cannot be reached by speech or thought, nor can it be traversed through mere silence; it is entered only by those who possess inconceivable realization.

Śūraṅgama Samādhi. [Note] Śūraṅgama is translated as "heroic aspect. Samādhi is translated as "harmonious and upright concentration," and is also called "the sphere of practice for rectifying the mind."
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Leng-yen" (Lakṣaṇa-vibhāga) means in the language of Qin, "Distinguishing the Characteristics.
This refers to knowing the number, depth, and degree of the various characteristics of samādhis. When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, no afflictions, demons, or demonic beings can destroy it.
Regarding "Tiao-chih-ding" (Samyak-samādhi), the *Fourfold Teachings* (*Sijiaoyi*) says: "Generally speaking, samādhi is named 'Tiao-chih-ding' (Right Samādhi). It is true..."

The samādhi of the [four] truths is "straightening" by means of departing from craving and views. The samādhi of conventional truth is "straightening" by means of conforming to the capacities [of sentient beings].

The samādhi of the Middle Way is "straightening" by means of being free from the curvature of the two extremes. Regarding the locus of the practice of the upright mind, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"All meditative concentrations that collect the mind are termed samādhi; this refers to what is called the locus of the practice of the upright mind."
The mind has been constantly crooked and unupright since beginningless time; once it attains the sphere of upright mental practice, it becomes straight and correct.
Master Yuanhong stated that the *Mahābuddhatoṣaṇī Śūraṅgama Sūtra* translates as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.
During the time of the Master Zhi, this sutra had not yet arrived; this [term] refers to the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi*.

*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. [□ Note] "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "light" (*prabhā*) is Prajñā; "clarity" (*sūrya*) is liberation (*vimukti*). This title is established based on individual dharmas.

[■ Record] The *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is, in its divisions, the three virtues (*triguṇa*); all are based upon the essential nature (*svabhāva*), which fully possesses gold, light, and clarity."

The meaning of "true reality" (tattva) is as follows: the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is worthy of honor and esteem; in its essential substance, it is called "gold. It is quiescent yet ever-illuminating;
in its essential substance, it is called "light. Its great compassion benefits all things; in its essential substance, it is termed "clarity."
[□ Note] The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) follows the ancients and provides another interpretation based on analogy. It finds that other interpretations of the analogies are incomplete.

[■ Record] This is because the *Xuánwén* again interprets it by means of analogy; therefore, it is explained here now. The *Xuánwén* clarifies that there were three schools of ancient commentators regarding the title:
first, the Numerical School (*Shùlùn jiā*), who compared "Gold" to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Light" to Prajñā, and "Brightness" to Liberation (*vimukti*).

The Great Master refutes this, saying: "The Sāṃkhya school explains only two bodies, the Real (satya) and the Responsive (nirmāṇa). To explain three bodies based on these two is inconvenient for their treatise.
If one follows the scriptural texts, there is no passage that clarifies the three qualities (triguṇa). If one were to provide an interpretive explanation, what meaning would not be applicable?
Yet they specifically use them as a metaphor for the three qualities. This both contradicts their own treatise and fails to accord with the scriptures; it is not what we employ here. (2)

The followers of the *Dharmatā* school say: "The substance of gold possesses the capacity for luminosity. Just as the *dharmatā* gives rise to its functions from its essence, it inherently possesses the power of *prajñā* and liberation.
One need only establish the two meanings of essence and function; there is no need to distinguish luminosity as something separate."

The Great Master refuted this, saying: "The *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages) fortunately clarifies the three Buddhas. To explain the title [of the scripture] by means of the three Buddhas is naturally convenient in terms of meaning.
Yet, you discard the three bodies (*trikāya*) and instead follow the 'essence and function' (*tǐyòng*). This does not accord with the meaning of the treatise.

Furthermore, if both the new and old versions of the text equally speak of the three bodies and do not mention essence and function, then your position contradicts your own treatise and fails to harmonize with the sūtra. Whether you advance or retreat, where can you go? This is not the case now."
Regarding its application, there are three points. Tripitaka Master Paramārtha stated that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) is a metaphor for three kinds of triple dharmas, namely:

the three bodies (*trikāya*), the three virtues (*triguṇa*), and the three stages (*tristhāna*). As for the metaphor of the three bodies: the true substance of gold is compared to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);

the function of light, which is able to illuminate, is compared to the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*); and the clarity, which is able to benefit all universally, is compared to the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). As for the metaphor of the three virtues: gold possesses four meanings.
First, its form does not change; second, its substance is unstained; third, its transformation is unimpeded; fourth, it causes people to become wealthy.

These correspond to the four virtues of the Dharmakāya: permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Regarding light, there are two meanings: first, it can illuminate and clarify; second, it can dispel darkness.
The analogy of "prajñā" illuminating the object and eliminating delusions has two meanings: first, it is free from darkness; second, it is vast and far-reaching.

The analogy of being "liberated" from all burdens and forever exhausting them to universally benefit those with whom one has a karmic connection is illustrated by three stages: the nature of gold exists inherently, which is like the stage of the primary cause prior to the Path;
its brilliance fuses and its essence becomes manifest, which is like the stage of the contributing cause during the Path; and its clarity is free from flaws and impurities, which is like...
Regarding the subsequent position concerning causes and conditions, the Great Master refutes it, stating: "The explanation of the three sets of three does not clarify the three meanings;

furthermore, it entails three faults: first, the causal conditions are not universally applicable; second, it contradicts the Perfect and Distinct [teachings]; and third, it does not accord with the Dharma-nature.

Having thus refuted it, he then accords with it, explaining by means of an analogy: "One should know that the three characters 'Jin-guang-ming' (Golden Light) serve as a universal metaphor for all things."
The horizontal dharma-gate is termed the teaching of the boundlessness of the *dharmatā*; the vertical dharma-gates are universally illustrated as the profound purport of the dharma-gates.
Only thus does it accord with the King of Sutras, which universally encompasses all things. This meaning is profound and vast.
Furthermore, let us provisionally take ten sets of three dharmas as the initial gateway. These are:

the three virtues, the Three Jewels, the three nirvāṇas, the three bodies, the three Great Vehicles, the three enlightenments, the three prajñās, the three Buddha-natures, the three consciousnesses, and the three paths.

These threefold dharmas encompass the beginning and the end; they are profoundly deep and immeasurable. This is called the first interpretation based on analogy, which, while comprehensive, does not exhaust all possibilities.

Furthermore, the *Shiyiji* (Records of the Supplementary Omissions) states: "An analogy is one interpretation; it was used by various masters to explain the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* for the sake of worldly phenomena.

While the Tathāgata’s profound Dharma uses analogies to manifest the teachings, those masters, though they employ them, do not in fact understand that the characteristics of the Dharma are perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*).
They provide restricted interpretations according to specific names, and thus cannot use analogies to encompass all dharmas. The Great Master [Zhiyi] wished to demonstrate the gold..."
The Ocean of Radiance: there is no dharma that is not complete therein, and no dharma that is not fused within it. Therefore, one accords with this.
By means of the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light), the analogy is fully established to compare it to the sphere where the Buddha wanders. This is abbreviated as ten kinds;
expanded, it encompasses all dharma-gates, each of which is mutually fused and inconceivable. This, then, rectifies other analogies for dharmas that were incomplete or broad.

This refers to the manifestation of the essence of nature as being fully endowed with all dharmas. [Supplement] In the commentary, three explanations are given for two points; if one follows one's own school’s position, it would be undermined, which is inconvenient for the treatise.
This refutation contradicts that school’s tenets. If one takes the scriptural text itself, there is no passage that clearly illustrates the three virtues through analogies.
This refutation contradicts the sutras; cause and effect do not correspond, as the cause and its fruit are mutually inconsistent.

Regarding the ten sets of three dharmas: the three paths (of affliction, karma, and suffering); the three jewels (Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha); the three bodies (Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya); and the three nirvāṇas:

first, intrinsic purity, which is the true mark (*dharmatā*); second, perfect purity, which is the manifestation of the perfected principle through the purification of afflictions; and third, purity through expedient means, which is...
Skillful purity consists of three virtues: the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), prajñā, and liberation (*vimukti*). Regarding the three types of bodhi:
first, the bodhi of true nature (*tathatā-bodhi*), which takes this true nature as the path; second, the bodhi of actualized wisdom (*jñāna-bodhi*), which is the wisdom capable of illumination;

and third, the bodhi of skillful means (*upāya-bodhi*), which refers to mastery in skillful transformative application. Regarding the three Buddha-natures (*buddhadhātu*): first, the Buddha-nature abiding in its own nature (*prakṛtistha-gotra*), which refers to—

1. The self-nature of *tathatā* is eternally abiding. 2. The buddha-nature that is drawn forth (*nirmocana-buddhatva*), meaning that the nature is manifested through cultivation and thus drawn forth. 3.

The buddha-nature of attaining the fruit (*phala-prāpti-buddhatva*), meaning it is manifested upon realizing the stage of fruition. The three consciousnesses refer to the seventh consciousness and the eighth consciousness.

Ninth, the nine pure consciousnesses. Furthermore, there is one: the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), which refers to the true mind. Second, the manifesting consciousness (*pratibhāsa-vijñāna*), which manifests the sense organs, the body, and the world.

Third, the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). Third, the three vehicles of the Mahāyāna: first, the vehicle of principle (*tattva-yāna*), which refers to the nature of reality; second, the vehicle of accordance (*anuvartana-yāna*), which is wisdom functioning in accordance with that principle;
third, the vehicle of attainment (*prāpti-yāna*), which is the attainment of the fruit—attaining liberation for oneself and attaining the capacity to bring others to liberation. Third.

Prajñā has three aspects: first, the true mark (lakṣaṇa), which is the actual substance; second, contemplative observation (vipaśyanā), which is the wisdom of illumination; third, skillful means (upāya), which is the transformative application of expedient artistry.
[□ Note] As in the title of the sutra: "This is the Dharma, not a metaphor.

[■ Record] Some may say: "Since the Great Master follows the ancients in using metaphors to clarify the Dharma, why does he further establish his own two types of explanations for the title—'conforming to the text' and 'corresponding to the essence'?
Therefore, we now explain this. As the Record says: "Nevertheless, although he follows the ancients in using metaphors to clarify..."

Regarding the term *dharma*: as the title of this sutra indicates, this is the actual *dharma* and not a metaphor. Therefore, [the author] subsequently establishes his own interpretation based on the text, providing three types of explanations according to the essence [of the dharma].
This serves to refute those who rely on remote analogies; by relying on the sutra and approaching the *dharma* directly, it becomes truly intimate.

This is because the Great Master deeply understood the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and fully possessed the true meaning of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, thereby achieving ultimate perfection. (Excluding the concluding phrase.)

Beyond the dharmatā, all names and expressions lack any substantial meaning. These three dharma-gates of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* are such that raising one is the three, and the entirety of the three is the one.
They are neither one nor three; yet they are three and one. Neither vertical nor horizontal, they transcend thought and transcend discourse;
this is the secret treasury, the dwelling place of the Buddhas.
[□ Note] Furthermore, one must not allow both the Dharma and the parable to coexist in order to accommodate those of sharp and dull faculties.

[■ Record] This refutes the simultaneous preservation of both to suit two types of capacities. [■ Supplement] Regarding the refutation of their simultaneous preservation: The *Xuánwén* (Profound Meaning) poses the question: "The ancients said that this sutra is named based on its parables;
why do you distort the meaning and rely instead on the literal text? The answer is: "It is not that we are currently following the literal text."
Yet this harms the analogy; if one stubbornly clings to the analogy, it further harms the text. There are two paths for the meaning, which ought to be preserved both.

Therefore, the previous statement that "meaning is remote when inferred" while "the text is proximate" was made. The Record says: "Using analogies in this manner, although they lack scriptural authority, preserving them is beneficial.
Both [text and analogy] should not be discarded unilaterally. You, however, exclusively cling to the analogy, abandoning the proximate to pursue the remote."
I now exist as both simultaneously; thus, both the intimate and the distant may attain me. As the *Xuanwen* (Mysterious Words) states: "For those of dull faculties, the dharma is used as a metaphor;

for those of sharp faculties, the dharma itself serves as the metaphor. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Abiding within this profound dharmatā, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni Buddha, within this very scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Furthermore, the "Chapter on Emptiness" (*Śūnyatā-parivarta*) states: "For the sake of those of dull [faculties]..."
Because of their faculties, they give rise to the mind of great compassion. Those of dull faculties guard the finger and guard the stump;
how could they know of the hare or the moon? Those of sharp faculties understand through transcendence; they do not require the stump or the finger. Furthermore, the Record states:

"Since the Buddha’s teaching of this scripture covers both types of faculties, those who explain the sutra must also provide two interpretations to accord with their sharpness or dullness. Moreover, the derogatory [comparison] follows the metaphor, such as 'guarding'..."

The "finger" refers to the one who relies on the teaching. To have a suspended understanding [of the moon] is like the rabbit in the moon; there is no need for the finger. This sufficiently reveals the subtle intention behind not permitting the use of metaphors.
Master Yu feared that later generations would fail to understand that the two explanations—relying on the Dharma versus relying on metaphors—are not the definitive intent.

Therefore, he set it forth, stating that according to the title of the sutra, this is the Dharma and not a metaphor. Furthermore, he feared that people would take the distinction between those of sharp and dull faculties as proof [that the metaphor is definitive].
Based on this, it is further stated that [the teaching] cannot be applied to both sharp and dull faculties simultaneously;
thus, they are preserved as equals.
Regarding the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* and other scriptures: [□ Note] The full title is the *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-vaipulya-sūtra*.
[Commentary: King Prasenajit summoned his daughter, Queen Śrīmālā, and she returned to the kingdom to see the Buddha.
The queen spoke these verses: "The Tathāgata has appeared in the world for the sake of all sentient beings; he should likewise take pity on us and swiftly descend to this place.

Having finished speaking, the Tathāgata manifested his body so that she might see him. She then spoke further verses in praise of the Buddha and various teachings, which were approved by the Tathāgata.

It is so; therefore, this sutra exists. There are three kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): first, the provisional application of expedients for the sake of the ultimate truth, which is the artful and subtle skillful means;
second, the great skillful means of using words where the principle is fundamentally wordless; third, the great skillful means in which the provisional and the ultimate are without obstruction.
The first is, for example, the teaching of the three vehicles as a differentiation of the single Buddha-vehicle. The second is, for example, "the mark of the quiescence of all dharmas."
It cannot be proclaimed through words. By the power of skillful means, he spoke thus for the sake of the five bhikṣus. (3) This is as follows:

just as one who traverses existence has never been deluded regarding emptiness, and one who contemplates emptiness does not neglect existence—this is the perfection of the Buddha’s skillful means, knowledge, and vision, all of which are already fully complete. This refers to the latter two kinds. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "If the Tathāgata..."

He teaches through skillful means according to their inclinations; this is precisely the One Vehicle. The One Vehicle is the ultimate truth (paramārtha), as seen previously in the Lion’s Roar of the Vaipulya.
[Note] Queen Śrīmālā was the daughter of King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī and the daughter of Queen Mallikā;
she served as the queen consort of the King of Ujjayinī.
[Commentary] The Sanskrit name *Mallikā* is translated as "Victorious Garland" (*Shengman*), because she is a mother of supreme physical marks and signs.
*Prasenajit* is translated as "Harmonious Joy" (*Hoyue*), because the king is preeminently compassionate and benevolent. *Mallī* is translated as "Garland" (*Man*).
Fourth, the period of Prajñā.
[Commentary: Because of the aforementioned equality and so forth, although the followers of the Two Vehicles have resolved their minds toward the Great Vehicle, their habitual tendencies remain firm.
Since one must use the water of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) to wash away these attachments, there is the period of Prajñā.

[Note] The temporal designation is established based on the title of the sutra. "Prajñā" is translated as "wisdom. That wisdom is "light and thin" is one of the five reasons for not translating [the term].

[Commentary] That which possesses conceptual discrimination is called "knowledge" (jñāna); that which is non-conceptual is called "wisdom" (prajñā). Furthermore, the fundamental [wisdom] is called "wisdom," while the subsequently attained [wisdom] is called "knowledge.
Here, by using both "wisdom" and "knowledge" as translations for *prajñā*, it is revealed that the provisional and the ultimate are a single entity within the Great Wisdom (*mahā-prajñā*).
Regarding the five reasons for not translating [Sanskrit terms]: first, there is the "secret" non-translation, such as various *dhāraṇī* mantras; second, there is the "multivalent" non-translation.

There are five reasons why certain terms are not translated [into Chinese]: 1. As with the term *Bhagavān*, which contains six meanings; three of these meanings have no equivalent in this land (China). 2. As with the *Jambū* tree;
it is a term that follows ancient precedent and is not translated. 3. As with *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; it has been preserved in its Sanskrit form since antiquity. 4.

To inspire wholesome states of mind, terms are not translated; for example, "Prajñā" is revered while "wisdom" (*zhìhuì*) is considered slight. To inspire people toward wholesome states, the term "Prajñā" is retained. [Appendix] Record.
The analysis of the middle [truth] is wisdom (*prajñā*). This too is spoken of in a general sense;

one should not adhere to it dogmatically. There are various *prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, such as the *Māyā-prajñā*, the *Prasphulla-prajñā*, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñā*, and the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñā*.

[Commentary] Because the followers of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) understood the Dharma-gates at the assembly of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Lotus Sūtra* is taught to reveal that the provisional teachings of the four periods were opened.

This reveals the subtlety of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). However, as for those with the karmic capacity caught in the net of outflows (*sāsrava*) and those who have arrived unexpectedly, who have not yet heard the previous teachings, how could they understand the Buddha-vehicle?
Therefore, he preached the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* once more to gather them in, universally causing them to realize and return to the Buddha-wisdom;
thus, both sūtras constitute the fifth period.

[Note] The full title is *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Wondrous" (*miao*) means inconceivable. "Dharma" refers to the provisional and real dharmas of the ten realms and the ten suchnesses.
The lotus flower serves as a metaphor for the aforementioned provisional and real dharmas.

[Commentary] There are three versions of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The translation by the Jin [dynasty] is titled *Zhengfahua* (The Lotus of the True Dharma) in ten fascicles. The translation by the Qin [dynasty] is titled *Miaofa Lianhua* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma) in seven fascicles.
The translation from the Sui [dynasty] is titled *Tianpin Miaofa Lianhua* (The Expanded Version of the Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma) in eight fascicles.

The present version is the Qin edition. The term "Wondrous" (*miao*) refers to that which is inconceivable; it is where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases. The "ten realms" refer to the four... [text continues].

The six classes of noble beings and ordinary beings. Regarding the analogy of the lotus: the lotus represents the simultaneity of cause and effect, serving as a metaphor for the fact that the provisional and the real are of one essence within the wondrous Dharma.

[Supplement] The wondrous Dharma is the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). As for the "ten suchnesses": first is "suchness of appearance" (*lakṣaṇa-tathatā*); "appearance" refers to external characteristics which can be distinguished.

Such is its nature (*svabhāva*); nature refers to that which is internal and unchanging. Such is its substance (*dravya*); "substance" is the name for the primary material. Such is its power (*bala*); functional capacity is called power.
Such is its activity (*karma*); construction is termed activity. Such is its cause (*hetu*); the habitual cause is the cause. Such is its condition (*pratyaya*);
the assisting cause is the condition. Such is its fruit (*phala*); the habitual fruit is the fruit. Such is its retribution (*vipāka*); the retributive fruit is the retribution.
The retribution is thus: from beginning to end, they are ultimately equal. The initial characteristic is the "beginning," and the subsequent retribution is the "end.
That which they return to as their destination is "ultimate equality. Within a single dharma-realm, there are ten suchnesses; within ten dharma-realms, there are one hundred suchnesses.
Furthermore, one *dharmadhātu* possesses nine *dharmadhātus*, thus there are one hundred *dharmadhātus* and one thousand such [realms].
[Note] *Nirvāṇa* is fully called *mahāparinirvāṇa*; this is translated as "Great Extinction" (*dà mièdù*). "Great" refers to the *dharmakāya*.

“Extinction” (*nirodha*) is liberation (*vimukti*); “crossing over” (*tāraṇa*) is wisdom (*prajñā*). These constitute the secret treasury of the three virtues. [Commentary] “Great” (*mahat*) refers to being all-pervasive in accordance with its essence;
this is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*), for its essence pervades the ten directions. “Extinction” means being free from the burdens of bondage;
this is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*), as it extinguishes the bonds of the two kinds of birth-and-death. “Crossing over” means shattering the obstruction of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*).
The virtue of *prajñā* (wisdom) illuminates and shatters the ignorance of the five abodes.
△ Second, the conclusion establishing alternative names:
these constitute the five periods, which are also called the five flavors.

[Note] This refers to the "Periods" (jié). Regarding the five periods, they are sometimes arranged as the "five flavors" within the *Mahāvaipulya* [scriptures]; hence the word "also" (yì) is used. The verse on the preaching of the Dharma during the five periods states:
The *Āgama* for twelve years, the *Vaipulya* for eight; The *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught for twenty-two years;
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and *Nirvāṇa* together for eight years; And the *Avataṃsaka* at the very beginning for twenty-one days.

[■ Supplement] Now, to clarify a distinct meaning, the verse on the Five Periods of Teaching by Gushan is cited. [■ Appendix] The *Jiaoguan gangzong* (Outline of Teaching and Contemplation) cites the words from the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning):
"The discourse on the five flavors distinguishes between the specific; the specific has its limits. The discourse on the universal applies to both the beginning and the end. Zhanran (Zhang'an) says:
"Some say that during the second period, within twelve years, the specific teaching of the Three Vehicles was preached. If that were so, it would exceed [the duration]."
At twelve years [of the teaching], there were those who were fit to hear the Truths and the Means of Crossing Over (*pratisaraṇa*); how could one not speak to them?

People say that during the third period, for thirty years, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, *Vimalakīrti*, and *Saṃghabhedavastu* (or *Suvikrāntavikrāmī*)—the schools of Emptiness (*śūnyatāvāda*)—were taught. On what scriptural passage does one know that it was thirty years?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Subhūti, within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, heard the teaching of raising the hand and lowering the head."

All shall attain Buddhahood. For this reason, I now inquire about the meaning of "retrogression. If that is so, then how are the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* determined in their sequence?

The clear explanations of the Venerable Zhiyi and Zhizhe are as such. Yet people today still transmit the teaching of twelve years for the *Āgamas* and eight years for the *Vaipulya*, even going so far as to distinguish five distinct periods;
these are merely based on one type of most dull-witted śrāvaka who has fully passed through [the stages].

It is only after five stages of smelting and casting that one attains the true essence. Nevertheless, these distinct teachings for the five periods are not strictly bound by fixed years, months, days, or times.
To clarify erroneous claims: the verses concerning the five periods are extremely restrictive.

However, the reason ancient critics were troubled by this was that they saw the *Lotus Sūtra* mention "twenty years of clearing away dung," and consequently concluded that the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) period must also contain the Tripitaka teachings.

Therefore, it is determined that the Vaipulya [sūtras] consist of eight [categories], as the Āgamas themselves contain explicit textual evidence stating that these were spoken within twelve years [of the Buddha’s enlightenment].
Furthermore, one observes within the sūtras the statement: "For twenty years, he managed the affairs of the household; then, after a short time had passed..."

Thus, he judges that the *Prajñāpāramitā* was taught when [the Buddha] was twenty-two years old. In my humble opinion, Master Yu’s citation of the verse is not due to ignorance of the meaning of the "five periods" (pañca-kāla) as it relates to what Zhiyi (Zhang’an) refuted;
rather, it is simply a case of adhering to the specific [classification] while failing to recognize how it differs from the inclusive [perspective].

Now, since this treatise discusses the distinctions between different times and the relative length of practice before and after, it introduces [the *Ekottarika-āgama*] because a sequence must exist within that which lacks a fixed sequence.
If the compilers had included it within its own original section, this would belong to the category of "general" (pervasive) texts.

Future scholars should certainly not be dogmatic about specific dates, nor should they use a general text to challenge a specific one. Regarding the five periods mentioned in the *Commentary*, these are used to categorize the sūtras.
The *Saṃyuktāgama* and other texts state this; these shall be reserved for future examination. [Commentary] The "Five Periods" scheme collects the scriptures:

the Deer Park period collects the four *Āgamas* and various other Hīnayāna sūtras; the Vaipulya period, excluding the other four periods, generally collects all Mahāyāna sūtras; and the Prajñā period...
The *Prajñāpāramitā* assemblies collect the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* collects the *Anantamukhasādhaka*, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*;
the *Nirvāṇa* assembly collects the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saddharma-vyākaraṇa*; the *Avataṃsaka* assembly collects the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Brahmajāla*.
If one discusses the sūtras concluded at each of the five periods, then for the *Avataṃsaka* assembly, the *Brahmajāla* serves as the concluding sūtra. [The *Mṛgadāva*...]

The *Yuan* [Sūtra] takes the *Bequeathed Teaching* as its concluding scripture; the *Vaipulya* takes the *Adornment* as its concluding scripture; the *Prajñā* takes the *Benevolent Kings* as its concluding scripture;
the *Lotus* takes the *Universal Worthy’s Contemplation* as its concluding scripture; and the *Nirvāṇa* takes the *Resolution of Doubts in the Semblance Dharma* as its concluding scripture.
Thus, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for over fifty years, delivering more than three hundred assemblies of sūtras. Now...
This verse encompasses everything without omission. [Supplement] There is a version of the *Prajñāpāramitā* that includes all the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras as well as the *Anantārthaviniścaya-sūtra*.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* includes the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* itself along with the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryā-dhyāna-sūtra*. Furthermore, it states that the *Prajñāpāramitā* takes the *Anantārthaviniścaya* as its concluding sūtra.
