It further says: "Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable kalpas, practiced the six pāramitās; yet, if they have not heard this sutra..."
If one hears [the teaching] yet does not believe it, does not understand it, does not accord with it, and does not enter into it, they are not called a true Bodhisattva;

therefore, they are categorized among those who are not vessels for the Dharma. That one does not move from the tranquil site of enlightenment (Ajapāla-nigrodha) yet wanders in the Deer Park is due to the uncommon supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata.

Manifesting spontaneously in response to conditions: it is the beginning of the teaching of sudden enlightenment preached at the site of tranquility (Vajrāsana), and the beginning of the teaching of gradual enlightenment preached at the Deer Park.
Being neither before nor after, it is said that "the two aspects are suspended together. [Supplement] The *Tongji* states: "The discussions found in various texts..."

The initial [teaching] is sudden and the subsequent is gradual; these are the ritual arrangements established according to the conditions of those to be transformed. Now, by explaining both the Great and Small [Vehicles], one fully realizes the intent of discerning capacities and delivering sentient beings.
△ Second, manifesting the body through analogies.
He cast off his precious and noble robes of *vimala-śānti* and donned a tattered, filthy garment sixteen feet in length.
[Commentary] This clarifies the sequence of the transformative ritual: laying aside the Great Vehicle while manifesting the Lesser Vehicle.

[Commentary] This refers to the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*). Seeing his son from afar, emaciated and haggard, he immediately removed his necklaces, fine soft garments, and ornaments, and put on coarse, tattered, and soiled clothes;
thus, by means of skillful means (*upāya*), he was able to draw near to his son, as described in the text.

【□Note】 From the perspective of the Buddha’s intention, he set aside the reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* to bestow provisional teachings. According to the sequence of the stages of transformation, he set aside the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* to bestow gradual teachings.

[Commentary] The perfection of the *Avataṃsaka* is the reality of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. It is the original intent of our Buddha, desiring only to cause sentient beings to open, show, awaken to, and enter the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Because their faculties were not yet capable, he provisionally bestowed expedient means (*upāya*).
[Commentary] The passage states that while remaining unmoved, he wanders; regarding clothing, it discusses casting off the precious to wear the coarse. These texts mutually clarify one another.
However, if one does not understand "remaining unmoved while wandering," there is no way to see that the two beginnings occur simultaneously.

If one does not understand "casting off the precious to wear the coarse," there is no way to see the cessation of the great and the manifestation of the small. This text exhaustively describes the Tathāgata’s wondrous response, the aspect of his unpremeditated establishment of transformation.
[Commentary] These two passages clarify each other; neither can be omitted. Together, they exhaustively describe the Buddha’s wondrous responsive manifestations.
[Sub-commentary] The *Vairocana* (Śākyamuni) as the supreme response-body (*vipākakāya*) is adorned with wisdom and meditative concentration; thus, it is likened to a precious treasure.

The sixteen-foot inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which undergoes the afflictions of birth and the Dharma, is likened to something worn and defiled. This is a dual clarification through both the literal description and the metaphor.
[Commentary] The Honored One’s *vairocana-kāya* (body of universal manifestation) is adorned with the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama and the Great Wisdom of the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

In contrast, his inferior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), subject to arising and ceasing, is tormented by sentient beings such as mosquitoes and gnats, as well as by insentient things such as cold and heat. [Supplementary Note] A certain master states:

"In the *Myōryaku* [the *Fahua wenju*], it is said that enduring the afflictions of sentient beings is 'patience toward beings' (*sattvakṣānti*), while enduring the afflictions of insentient things is 'patience toward phenomena' (*dharmakṣānti*). This is the Great [Patience].
The treatise states: To endure all forms of respect, offerings, and the afflictions of sensual desire constitutes patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*).
To endure respect, offerings, and the phenomena of anger, vexation, and desire constitutes patience toward dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*).
△ Second, the cessation of great giving and the persistence of small giving. First, his descent into the world and attainment of enlightenment:

manifesting his descent from Tuṣita Heaven, taking birth in the womb of Māyā, remaining in the womb and emerging from it, marrying a consort and fathering a son, renouncing the world and practicing austerities;
after six years, beneath the Bodhi tree, using grass as a seat, he attained the body of inferior response.

[Note] This clarifies the "Small Beginning" (xiǎoshǐ). Originally, he is the Perfect Buddha; he manifests downward as the appearance of initial accomplishment within the Tripitaka, and thus it is said that he "shows" [himself].
Tuṣita is translated as "Contentment. This heaven has both an inner garden and an outer garden; the Bodhisattva dwells in the inner garden and then descends to manifest his spirit there.
However, among the seven heavens of the Six Desire Heavens and the Brahma World, he always resides in this one [Tuṣita].
[Commentary] Tuṣita is translated as "Wondrous Fulfillment" (Miaozu). It is also translated as "Contentment" (Dushidu); this is because the inhabitants are content with their enjoyment of desires.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* names it "Joyful Contentment" (Xizu), because Bodhisattvas in their final birth teach therein and extensively cultivate joyful contentment.
The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* clarifies that this heaven does not descend to the realms of humans or devas of the lower worlds, even until the destruction of the kalpa.

The three calamities do not reach it; only the inner garden is thus suitable, and therefore the Bodhisattva dwells there. Regarding why the Buddha constantly resides therein, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one is born in a lower realm, one’s life is short and ends before the Buddha has appeared in the world.
If one is born in a higher realm, one’s life is long and does not end until after the time of the Buddha’s appearance in the world has passed. Only the lifespan of Tuṣita Heaven [is appropriate]."
Because the Buddha appears in the world at the opportune time. Furthermore, because the Buddha always abides in the Middle Way:
among the desire-realm heavens and the Brahma heavens, he is above three and below three; from those heavens he descends to be born in a central land; at midnight he enters the womb;
at midnight he leaves the country; he practices the Middle Way; he attains enlightenment by the Middle Way; he teaches the Dharma to people by the Middle Way; and at midnight he enters nirvana.
This refers to *nirvāṇa-with-remainder*. [Note:
He descended from that realm and took birth by entering the womb of Māyā. Māyā means "Heavenly Queen"; she was the consort of King Śuddhodana.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) says: "All Buddhas do not appear among the other two lowly castes. When the times are noble and honored, they appear among the Kṣatriyas;
when the times require great learning, they appear among the Brāhmaṇas. Furthermore, when the age is turbid and difficult to discipline, they appear among the Kṣatriyas;
when the age is clear and easy to discipline, they appear among the Brāhmaṇas. (Text)
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When a Bodhisattva in his final birth comes from the heavens, it is because he rides upon the supreme path.
Furthermore, when descending from heaven, there are various auspicious omens; moreover, humans revere the heavens. The treatise further states:
"When a Bodhisattva is about to descend to be born, he first observes the place of birth. Only in the kingdom of Kapilavastu, with the Queen of King Śuddhodana, is he able [to be born]."
This refers to one who conceives the thought of becoming a Bodhisattva in their final existence. Below, the *Myōryaku* (Subcommentary) is cited to clarify the meaning of *kṣatriya*.
These are the royal lineage, esteemed as the most noble in the world; the *brāhmaṇa*, who are extensively learned and pure in conduct, renowned for their vast knowledge in the world.

Furthermore, the *kṣatriya* possess power and are able to harmonize the defilements of the *kalpa*; the *brāhmaṇa* are free from contention and can harmonize times when the era is pure. Thus, the Buddhas act according to the circumstances.

What is most precious arises precisely therein. Now, in the world of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the noble and honorable are especially esteemed; furthermore, this is because we are in an era of the *kalpa-kṣaya* (degeneration of the age), when sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform.

[Commentary on the Square Symbol] Regarding the descent into the womb: for a Bodhisattva, the entry through the side occurs naturally. One who relies on Right Wisdom perceives the descent into the womb;
those of the Hīnayāna see [the Bodhisattva] riding a white elephant, the essence of the sun-piercing radiance. Those of the Mahāyāna see [him] riding upon a sandalwood pavilion and the like.
[Commentary] Question: When ordinary people enter the mother’s womb with a defiled mind, they do so with continuity and in association with all manner of false wisdom.

How, then, does a Bodhisattva enter the mother’s womb with right wisdom? Answer: Because the Bodhisattva enters the womb while maintaining mindfulness without loss, dwelling within the intermediate state (antarābhava) and knowing that he dwells within the intermediate state; at the time of entering the womb, he knows he is entering the womb; [and thus enters] the kalala stage.
At that time, one knows from the stage of the *kalala* up until birth; thus, one knows that this is birth.
Regarding the perspective of the Hīnayāna, as stated in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*: "He manifested as a white elephant and descended into his mother’s womb.
Furthermore, Subhūti’s verse says: "His form was like a white elephant, with four feet and six tusks; when he entered his mother’s womb, it was as if he were strolling through a garden."
This is the visualization. Regarding those who see according to the Mahāyāna, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"The Bodhisattva Vairocana has already passed away from here and been born in the human realm within the house of King Śuddhodana; riding upon a sandalwood pavilion, he dwells within the womb of Queen Māyā.
[Supplement] The elephant is the king of elephants, possessing great power and utility, symbolizing that the Bodhisattva is able to bear the burden.
"Carrying sentient beings. "Guan" (貫) signifies the analytical contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). "Ri" (日) signifies the principle of partial emptiness;

for the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) practice the contemplation of emptiness and perceive it according to their own limited capacity. "The sandalwood pavilion" signifies the non-obstruction between form and mind (*rūpa-citta*), and the mutual fusion of the body and the land (*kāya-bhūmi*);
for the bodhisattvas practice the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) and perceive it according to their own limited capacity. [Appendix] Bian'e says: Bai...

"The Elephant Piercing the Sun" appears in the *Puyao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Radiance) and belongs to the Mahāyāna; it is thus a vision shared by both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. [This] is preserved for examination.
The supplementary explanations regarding the "Elephant King’s Pavilion" and so forth are likewise preserved for examination.
[Note] Regarding "dwelling in the womb": if one follows the eight phases of birth according to the Hinayana, dwelling in the womb is included within the phase of entering the womb (*garbhāvakrānti*).
Here, however, the intent is to demonstrate the historical deeds of the Buddha’s initial descent into manifestation, rather than to provide a formal exposition of the eight phases.

[Commentary] The eight phases of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) are explained in detail in the seventh fascicle. The phase of dwelling in the womb is discussed here in conjunction with the others. [Supplement] The *Caiguō jīng* (Sūtra on Cause and Effect) states:

While the Bodhisattva was in his mother’s womb, he preached the Dharma to the gods of the Form Realm (Rūpadhātu) in the morning, to the gods of the Desire Realm (Kāmadhātu) at midday, and to the spirits and deities (bhūta-deva) in the afternoon.
He did likewise during the three periods of the night. [Appendix] *Biàn'é rì* states: "In the Hīnayāna, there is no account of preaching while dwelling in the womb;
therefore, it is not mentioned. My personal view is that the reason it is not mentioned should be understood according to the seven-fascicle Hīnayāna [Vinaya].
No discussion of the doctrine of eternal abiding. [Note] Regarding the birth from the womb: on the eighth day of the fourth month, he descended as a spirit from his right side.

This is recorded in the *Ruiying jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses). [Record] The *Ruiying jing* states: From the time the Lady became pregnant, the heavens provided offerings for her; she did not partake of the royal kitchen. For four...
On the eighth day of the month, he was born from the right side [of his mother]. He immediately took seven steps and, raising his right hand, declared:

"In the heavens above and on the earth below, I alone am the most honored. All three realms are suffering; what is there to delight in? At that time, heaven and earth shook violently, and the palace was filled with light.
Brahmā, Śakra, and the celestial deities waited upon him from the air, while the Four Heavenly Kings received him and placed him upon a golden pedestal.
With celestial fragrant water, they bathed the Prince’s body. His body became the color of gold, endowed with the thirty-two marks, its radiance shining through to the ultimate realm of the Buddhas;
there was nothing that was not brilliantly illuminated. Heaven sent down thirty-two auspicious responses:
first, the earth shook greatly, and all mounds and ruins were leveled. This continued until the thirty-second: a tree spirit appeared in human form and bowed his head.
The attendants at court—those on both sides of the frontier—could not help but marvel and exclaim that such a thing had never before occurred;
this was the manifestation of the [birth] phase from the womb. [Note: There were three consorts: first, Gopī; second, Yaśodharā; third, Mṛgajā.]
[Commentary] The *Sūtra on the Twelve Wanderings* states: "The family of the Bodhisattva’s wife was of the Gautama clan. She was the daughter of a Śākya elder named Jyotipāla (Water-Light).
Her mother was named Candraprabhā (Moon-Woman). When the girl was born, as the sun was about to set, a remaining radiance illuminated her home;
therefore, she was named Gopī. She was the first consort. If the second consort had given birth to Rāhula..."
Her name was Yaśodharā, which is the same as Yaśu. Her father’s name was the elder Yaśas. The third lady’s name was Mṛgajā;
her father’s name was the elder Śākya.
[Note] The son born was Rāhula. Because the Buddha appeared and dwelt among them, he manifested the ways of human beings.
[Commentary] In the "Chapter on the Four Marks" of the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, Kāśyapa asks: "For what reason did Yaśodharā again give birth to Rāhula?"
"Furthermore, you should know that the Tathāgata has not yet crossed the great ocean of all fetters. The Buddha told Kāśyapa Bodhisattva:
"The manifestation of such immeasurable supernatural powers and transformations cannot be fathomed by any sentient being.
How then can you now claim to know that the Tathāgata indulged in desire and fathered Rāhula? Good son, I have already—"
He dwells long in this Great Parinirvāṇa; this is what he manifests.
[Note] He left the household life at the age of nineteen. On the night of the fifteenth day of the second month, at midnight, he mounted a celestial horse and leaped over the city wall.

[Commentary] The *Mahāvyūha-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva reflected to himself: 'Within the wilderness of afflictions and the river of birth and death, if I do not practice, it will be difficult to escape in the end.
After everyone had fallen asleep, he immediately called for Chandaka to prepare his horse and depart."
Śakra opened the gate; the Four Kings supported his feet, and Śakra and Brahmā led the way as he proceeded to the forest of the Great Seer. There, he took up a sword and shaved his hair.

According to another account, after the Prince had returned to the palace and reflected upon seeing old age, sickness, and death, desiring to escape such suffering, he saw the various ladies of the harem that night appearing like corpses, which intensified his sense of revulsion. Furthermore, he saw the Four Heavenly Kings standing there.
From within the window gap, he announced that the time for his renunciation had arrived. He then immediately opened the window and, treading upon the heavenly white horse, leaped over the city walls.
Arriving at the forest of the seer Bhārgava, he shaved his head. [Appendix] Bian’e says: "He rode the palace horse;
because the heavens supported the horse's hooves, it is called a 'heavenly horse' (*tianma*), not a horse from the heavens. In my private opinion, the *Tongji* agrees with this. However—
Regarding the account in the *Jì* (Commentary) concerning the white horse of the deva, this is merely a difference in perspective arising from varying mental capacities and views.

[Note] As for the necessity of six years of ascetic practice, the *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 7, section 19, states: "However, while the Way of all Buddhas is the same, the circumstances and events differ.
Śākyamuni practiced asceticism for six years; grass grew so thick that it reached his elbows, yet he was unaware of it. The devas wept and cried out, shaking [the earth]."

The earth did not hear [the sound]. By shifting his seat, he attained the Way. Maitreya attained the Way on the very day he left the household life. Although that Buddha had been present for ten kalpas, he still did not appear before him.

It is not that there are sharp or dull faculties, nor that the Way has difficulties or ease; rather, it is because the conditions were appropriate to be distant or near, and thus the manifestation was shown to be brief or long.
(Text) The *Fuxing* says: "The reason for the six years of ascetic practice was to subdue those with [wrong] views and to outshine the non-Buddhists."

[The Life of the Buddha] (Text). The verse says: Nineteen years spent leaving the city and practicing the six austerities; five years traveling abroad; thirty years until his attainment [of enlightenment];
fifty years preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings; thus, his total lifespan was eighty years.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions share one and the same Dharma-body; they are one in mind and one in wisdom, and likewise in their powers and fearlessnesses.
This refers to the identity of the Way, though the circumstances differ. These are clarified through the three distinct Buddhas.

Specifically, it refers to Śākyamuni’s time at Mount Hastikakṣa, when he ate hemp and wheat with the non-Buddhists for six years, until the grass and vines grew so long that they clustered and hung over his thighs.
When it reached his elbows, he still felt nothing. Seeing that their retinue was diminishing day by day, the devas wailed and cried out so loudly that the earth shook;
yet because he had practiced worldly dhyāna, he did not hear them. Furthermore, the Prince reflected for himself that asceticism was not the true path to liberation.
"I shall receive food and attain Buddhahood. Therefore, he shifted his seat and attained the Way. According to the *Maitreya-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha said:

"The four oceans will gradually diminish by three thousand *yojanas*. This Jambudvīpa will be ten thousand *yojanas* long and eight thousand *yojanas* wide, as level as a mirror and adorned in various ways. Within the city, there will be a great Brahmin lord."
The father is named Subrahman; the Brahmin wife is named Maitrāyaṇī. Maitreya will take birth as their son.
His body will be the color of purple gold and possess twenty-two marks. He will be one thousand *zhang* tall, with a chest thirty *zhang* wide and a face twelve *zhang* four *chi* long.
With his physical eyes, he will see for a thousand *yojana*; his constant radiance will shine for a hundred *yojana*. Śaṅkha...
The King offered the seven-jeweled platform to Maitreya, and Maitreya gave it to a Brahmin.

Seeing its destruction, [the King] cultivated the perception of impermanence and left the household life beneath the Dragon-Flower Bodhi tree. The trunk, branches, and leaves of that tree were five thousand *li* high;
on the very day he left the household life, he attained the Way. Regarding that "ten *kalpas*" of that Buddha, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū..."

This refers to the Buddha Jñānavijaya, who sat at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas, yet the Buddha-dharma did not manifest before him. By this standard, one knows that the conditions for Śākyamuni were particularly remote;
thus, he practiced austerities for six years. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which says:
"The austerities of non-Buddhists may last for three months, half a year, or one year, but none can endure them for six years while consuming only one sesame seed and one grain of wheat per day."
Furthermore, it is said: "If the Buddha had not practiced asceticism for six years, no one would have believed or accepted his rebuke that [other paths] were not the Way.
Because he attained Buddhahood through asceticism that surpassed others, people all believed and accepted his rebuke of those ascetic practices. Someone may ask: What does the verse say?
He left home at nineteen and attained the Way at thirty. Yet the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that he left home at seven and attained the Way at thirty.
Why is this? The answer is given in the *Fayi*: "The Great Sage’s manifestations have no fixed rule.
Some say that after the Prince entered Mount Dandaka to practice the Way, he first spent three years under Ārāḍa Kālāma learning the 'sphere of nothingness' (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*)."

He attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Realizing it was not [the ultimate], he abandoned it. He then went to the abode of Udraka Rāmaputra for three years, where he studied the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
realizing this too was not [the ultimate], he abandoned it again. Later, he went to Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and practiced with the non-Buddhists by subsisting on hemp and wheat for six years;
upon receiving food, he attained Buddhahood. Thus, the verse states that he left home at nineteen and attained the Way at thirty, totaling twelve years. This is correct.
This is the same as the number of years for practicing the path in the three locations. However, it seems to differ from the statement in the verse regarding "wandering for five years.
This should still be explained by demonstrating that there is no fixed rule. [Supplement] The *Tongji* states: "The *Śrīmat-bhadrakalpika-sūtra* (Ruiying) and the *Karmaprajñapti* (Yinguo)."
The *Benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Events) and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* both state that he left home at nineteen.
The *Catuṣpariṣat-sūtra*, the *Chuyao jing* (Sutra of Essential Excerpts), and the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-vyākhyā-śāstra* all state that he left home at twenty-five. Which of these should one follow?

Now, taking his total lifespan of eighty years and subtracting fifty years spent preaching the Dharma, we shall definitively adopt the accounts from the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, the *Nirnimitta-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, and other such texts, which establish his attainment of enlightenment at thirty.

Regarding the path: setting aside the account of six years of ascetic practice, it is definitively established that he left home at twenty-five and combined this with the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*’s teaching that he attained enlightenment at thirty.
If one determines this based on the sequence of these events, there are two points that can serve as proof.
First, after leaving home, he practiced asceticism for six years; this accords with the total number of years until his attainment of enlightenment.
Second, when he was about to leave the household life, he pointed to his consort’s womb and said, "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son.
Subsequently, in the year of his attainment of enlightenment, Rāhula was indeed born. The *Adbhutadharma-paryāya Sūtra* states that the Prince fled to the mountains and marshes.

He practiced austerities for six years. Upon attaining Buddhahood, he returned to his kingdom. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states that after six years of renunciation and ascetic practice, he attained all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).

Furthermore, the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* records that when the King, his father, heard that the Crown Prince had become a Buddha after six years, he sent Udāyin to invite him back, saying that it had been twelve years since they were last separated. It further records that when the Buddha returned to his kingdom, [the people]... the *Rā...* (text fragment).
Yun asked after his health. The ministers wondered how the Crown Prince could have a son after having abandoned the kingdom for twelve years.
These scriptural passages all refer to his attainment of Buddhahood six years after leaving home, followed by another six years before returning to his country.
According to the *Shang tong ji* (General Record), up to the verses of Gushan, it is stated that he traveled for five years; some point to three years at Ārāḍa and three years at Udraka.

[Carrying forward. [Note: Master Yuan says that in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, it states "seven years old for leaving home. Regarding the character "years" (suì), there were those in antiquity who interpreted it as "years" (nián);
this is quite ingenious. However, when taken together with the subsequent phrase "at thirty, he attained the Way," one should take "leaving home at twenty-five" as the standard.
In short, since the Tathāgata’s manifestations have no fixed rule, and furthermore, the various kingdoms of the Western Regions... [text ends]

Regarding the dates of the years and seasons, there may be some discrepancies. In the process of transmission and compilation, variations naturally arose; furthermore, as these were translated again and again, it was difficult to achieve perfect uniformity.
Thus, we have simply left points of uncertainty as they were. Later scholars need not trouble themselves to debate these matters to demonstrate their own erudition.

In "Discerning Errors," it is stated that phrases such as "grass growing on his mounded thighs" originate from the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisāgara-sūtra*. This is because [the Buddha] had entered the meditative concentration of the cessation of mental activity (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

"He neither heard nor perceived" belongs to the later teaching. If it concerns a *piṭaka* bodhisattva who has already suppressed the afflictions and is practicing the causes [of enlightenment], then he would be unable to enter the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It would be best to cite the *Tripiṭaka-buddha-pūrva-carita-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Former Deeds of the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka).

However, that text lacks accounts of such matters as grass growing and pressing against his thighs. Furthermore, in the *Pūrva-carita-sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva enters the *āniñjya-samādhi* (the immovable samādhi), then—
In the fourth dhyāna, because breathing does not function, one knows the mental states of others; however, those below do not know those above. "Heaven" (tian) refers to weeping at the end of life;
"private" (si) refers to such expressions as "the growth of grass. The present commentary cites this from the *Wenju* (Textual Explanations).
[Note] *Bodhi* tree. *Bodhi* is translated as "the Way" (*mārga*). Because the Buddha attained the Way beneath this tree, it is called the "Tree of the Way.

Regarding the grass seat: the *Caiguojing* (Sutra on Cause and Effect) states that Śakra transformed himself into the auspicious youth Maṅgala and offered grass to the Buddha, upon which he sat and attained enlightenment.
[Commentary] The *Sutra on Cause and Effect* (*Hetuphala-sūtra*) states: Śakra-devānām-indra manifested as a man holding clean, soft grass. The Bodhisattva asked, "What is your name?
He replied, "Auspiciousness" (*śrī*). The Bodhisattva rejoiced, saying, "I shall destroy inauspiciousness and thereby achieve auspiciousness."
"Can you provide me with some grass? Śiva-datta offered the grass and made this vow: "May I be the first among those whom you deliver upon your attainment of the Way.
The Bodhisattva sat cross-legged, in the manner of sitting used by all past Buddhas, and made this solemn declaration: "Until I have attained perfect enlightenment, I shall not rise from this seat."
[Commentary] The seats of wood, trees, and grass all symbolize that the Tripitaka elucidates arising and ceasing.
[Record] Grasses and trees sprout in spring, grow in summer, wither in autumn, and fall in winter.
[Note] "Inferior response" (劣應): This is judged to be inferior in contrast to the "superior response" (勝應) of the Mahāyāna.
[Record] The "superior response" refers to the *parasaṃbhogakāya* of Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas; the "inferior response" refers to the body of one *zhàng* and six *cùn*.
△ Second, the establishment of the teaching according to the capacity of the audience.
Initially, at the Deer Park, he first taught the five people the doctrine of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the practice of the Six Perfections.
[Commentary] The five men spoke in verse: "Aññā-Koṇḍañña and Bhaddiya, along with Vappa—these three were paternal kinsmen. Kaundinya was a maternal kinsman of the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha).
When the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, these were the ones first delivered."

[Commentary] This verse is from the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning). Regarding the "Dharma Wheel" (*dharmacakra*), first is the sense of "turning. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states:

"Because the Dharma for transforming others within the Buddha’s mind enters the minds of others, it is called 'turning the Dharma wheel'. Second is the sense of "crushing and grinding. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: [as follows].

By means of the wheel of the Four Noble Truths, one turns it to deliver others and crushes the fetters and delusions. Just as the Wheel-Treasure of a universal monarch can both destroy and bring peace, so too is the Dharma-wheel:
it destroys the enemies of the afflictions and establishes one in the principle of the Truths. Regarding the first turning, the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:

There are two kinds of turning the wheel of Dharma: first, within one's own body; second, in another person. Turning the wheel of Dharma beneath the Bodhi tree is turning the wheel within one's own body.
Turning the wheel of Dharma in the country of Vārāṇasī is turning the wheel through another's body, because it occurs within the body of another.
Because this was the first turning of the wheel of Dharma, it is called "the first. Regarding the prior deliverance of the five people: there were three stages of delivering people at the Deer Park.
According to the *Dharmaskandha*, first he taught the Four Noble Truths to Kauṇḍinya, and they attained the Way; next, he [taught them] to Aśvajit and Bhadrika.

He preached that through giving one attains the blissful merit of rebirth in heaven and that they would equally realize the fruit [of the path]. Thirdly, for Kāśyapa and Kauṣṭhila, as previously stated, they all attained the Noble Path.
[Commentary on the *Wenju* (5.5) states: Question: For what reason did he first turn the Wheel of Dharma for the five persons? Answer: Because people first saw them.
Because it is the truth; because humans are directly perceived; because humans serve as witnesses; because the Buddha’s activities are the same as those of humans;
because the devas obtain wholesome benefits from among humans; and because there are the fourfold assembly within the human realm.
[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā* states: Humans first realize the Truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), while gods do so later; humans perceive through direct observation (*pratyakṣa*), whereas gods do not;
humans serve as witnesses, whereas gods do not; the Buddha’s conduct is identical to that of humans;
the various gods also obtain wholesome benefits from among humans; and because the fourfold assembly exists among humans.

【□Note】The *Miaole* (Vol. 5, no. 31) states: "Question: Although the discussion involves five [categories], the intent lies precisely in the person. Therefore, all answers are given in terms of the person (text)."
[Commentary] Although the question addresses only five individuals, its intent actually applies universally to all people.

[Sub-commentary] If it were addressed solely to these five, there would be three underlying meanings. As Miaole (Vol. 16) states: first, to repay Śākyamuni Buddha for his past causal practices and original vows;
second, to fulfill the original vow of these five individuals to be the first to attain enlightenment; and third, to recompense them for their labor in serving him on this day.
[Commentary] Regarding the Śākyamuni Buddha’s practice of causes and original vows, Miaole states: "When King Kali was cutting [the Buddha's body] limb from limb, the Buddha made a vow:
'Upon attaining the Way, I shall deliver him first. King Kali was none other than Cunda. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) says:

"In a past age of famine, the Buddha transformed himself into a great fish. Five carpenters were the first to cut its flesh; the Buddha vowed that he would deliver these five men first. These five men were originally...
Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas, Miaole says: During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, nine people studied the Way; five of them had not yet attained the fruit.
They vowed that within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, they would be the very first to attain enlightenment. Regarding those who serve him today, Miaole says:
When the Prince studied the Way, his father sent five men to follow and attend him. Once he had attained the Way, he first preached the Four Noble Truths to them.
(*Fahua Wenshu*, Fascicle 5).

[Note] *Mānava* is a general term for the eldest son. Since *mahat* is translated as "great," *Kauṣṭhila* was the eldest son of King Droṇodana, and *Bhadrika* was the eldest son of King Amṛtodana; therefore, they are all called *mānava*.
[Commentary] The scriptural tradition states: The Four Heavenly Kings have eight sons. King Śuddhodana has two sons:
first, Siddhārtha; second, Nanda. King Śuklodana has two sons: first, Devadatta; second, Ānanda. King Droṇodana has two sons:
first, Mahānāman; second, Nandika. King Amṛtodana has two sons: first, Bhadrika; second, [the third son].
Tiṣya. The phrase *mahā-kulika* refers to Mahānāman. [Appendix] Bian’uo states: "The character for 'male' (*nan*) in *mohe nan* is also a transliteration of the Sanskrit sound;
thus, some sources refer to him as Mahānada. Vatsa: All sutras state that he was the second son of King Amṛta.
I have personally examined the *Dazang yilan* (A General Survey of the Great Canon) and found the *Qiyin shijian benjing* (Sutra on the Fundamental Causes of Arising in the World).
It is said: Śuddhodana had two sons, Siddhārtha and Nanda; Śuklodana had two sons, Tiṣya and Nandika;
Droṇodana had two sons, Aniruddha and Bhadrika; and Amṛtodana had two sons, Ānanda and Devadatta. This Bhadrika was also the biological father of [Ānanda].
They differ, however, in their ritual texts which follow the divination slips (*zhān*). Since Śāriputra (Cīrṇa) was considered the Buddha’s eldest son, he was called "Māna" (Son).
Thus, "Māna" should be understood as a general designation for the eldest son; it is not a mere fabrication.
Furthermore, when the *Dharmasaṃkhyā* cites him as the "eldest son of Amṛta," this too must have a scriptural basis. As for the discrepancies among the various sūtras—
[Location]. The visualization is as previously explained; this is due to the circumstances of its transmission, compilation, and translation.

[Note] Śāriputra (Śramaṇa-māna) is the same as Cunda. Just as those of the four castes who renounce the world are all equally called Śākya, he was the very first to attain liberation when the Buddha first realized the Way, preceding all humans, devas, and arhats. As stated in *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy), fascicle 1, section 37.
The *Pinfen gongde lun* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit) states:
"The eldest son of the Buddha is Cunda. [Commentary] Miaole says: "Kulinda was the first to perceive the signs of the Buddha-way;
because he stood before all humans, devas, and arhats, he is called Śāriputra. As cited in the lower section of Miaole, the treatise states: "Five hundred arhats..."

Each has their own particular excellence: some in wisdom, some in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), some in eloquence (*pratibhāna*), some in merit (*puṇya*), some in guarding the precepts, some in contentment, and some in preaching the Dharma;
each is foremost in its respective field. Regarding the discussion of the elder brothers preceding the younger:
Kauṇḍinya was the eldest and Subhadra was the youngest; thus, the eldest son was Cunda (Ajñātakauṇḍinya).

[Note]: The three categories of Truths (satya), Objects (ālambana), and Crossings (pāramitā) are fully detailed in the following text. These five individuals are Śrāvakas; strictly speaking, one should only speak of the Four Noble Truths.
Here, however, the teachings expounded at the Deer Park are cited collectively.
[■ Note] The phrase "the following text" refers to the Tripitaka Teaching (Zàngjiào) below.

[□ Commentary] Regarding those who practice the six perfections as phenomena (*dharma*): the Tripitaka Teaching discusses actual, substantial phenomena because they do not identify with principle (*lǐ*).

[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are two ways of practicing the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*): first, practicing the six perfections with a mind that grasps at existence;

second, practicing the six perfections with a mind that does not grasp at existence. What is discussed here is the practice of the six perfections with a mind that grasps at existence; thus, the practice is incomplete.

If judged by time, then the sun illuminates the deep valleys (the second period).

[Note] The "Chapter on the Manifestation" (*Prakāśa-parivarta*) in the old translation of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "For example, when the sun and moon appear in the world... and so forth, down to "even the deep..."
The deep mountain valleys—there is nowhere it does not universally illuminate (text).
[Commentary] This refers to time.
[Sub-commentary] *Fuxing* 1.1 (28) states: "Deep valleys" refers to the remote and secluded reaches of mountains and rivers (text).
[Commentary] "Sui" means profound.
△ Third, the judgment according to flavor (*rasa*).
If judged by flavor, then from milk comes curd; likewise, from the twelvefold scriptures (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) come the ninefold *sūtras* (the flavor of curd).
[Note] Milk produces curd; this is like the Tathāgata’s sequential method of teaching, which proceeds from the sudden to the gradual in terms of the principle of mutual production.
If one considers the capacities of sentient beings, there is a variation in the intensity [of their faculties].
[Note] This is an explanation based on "flavor" (*rasa*). It is explained in terms of the arising of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by proceeding from sudden bestowal to gradual [instruction].
It is explained in terms of "intensity or dilution" (*saṃkṣepa-vistara*) by transforming the ordinary person into a sage for those of small capacity, just as milk is transformed into curd.
[□ Note] As stated in the text below: first, one merely takes up the sequence of the arising of marks; second, one takes up their intensity and subtlety.
