[Note] From the twelve divisions [of the canon], nine divisions emerge; this is merely a matter of their mutual generation (*xiāngshēng*). In reality, however, the nine divisions emerge from the Buddha.

[Commentary] The term "mutual generation" appears in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Chapter on Holy Practice (*Śīla-carita-parivarta*). Here, too, we shall for now discuss their mutual generation—how the nine emerge from the twelve.
In truth, they emerge from the Buddha. As the Sūtra says: "These ninefold teachings of mine follow along with..."
The sentient beings say: "It is so.
△ Fourth, judging according to the sutra, in two parts. First, citing the sutra to raise the inquiry, in two parts. First, citing the sutra:

The *Śraddhābhūmi-parivarta* (Chapter on Faith and Understanding) says: "And by means of skillful means, he secretly dispatched two persons (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) whose physical forms were haggard and who lacked majesty..."
"O Virtuous One, you may go to him and speak gently to that impoverished son, saying: 'I will hire you to remove the filth.
[Commentary] This is based on the judgment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The "Chapter on Faith and Understanding" states:
"At that time, the elder, wishing to entice his son, established a skillful means. He secretly dispatched two men who were haggard in appearance and devoid of majesty, saying to them: 'You..."
"You may go to him and speak gently to that impoverished son, saying: 'There is work here; I will pay you double wages.
If he asks what it is he should do, you may tell him: 'I hire you to remove this refuse; the two of us shall also work together with you.'"

【□Note】 "Skillful means" (*upāya*): "Means" (*fang*) refers to method; "skillful" (*bian*) refers to application. To skillfully employ these methods to accord with the capacities of sentient beings is what is meant by "skillfulness."
[Commentary] To be skillful in employing expedient means (*upāya*) to deftly accommodate sentient beings is the meaning of "expedient" (*upāya*).

[Sub-commentary] Regarding "secretly dispatching": the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6, section 23, states: "Initially, it was intended as Mahāyāna, saying 'immediately dispatch an attendant,' which symbolizes the One True Truth (*ekasatyam*), the one teaching of Mahāyāna, and the one person who is a Bodhisattva.
Now, it is clarified that 'expedient' refers to concealing the reality; this points to the partial [teachings]."

"True" refers to elimination (*kṣepa*). In terms of the teaching (*śāsana*), the *pūrṇākṣara* (full syllables) is hidden and thus "secret" (*guhya*), while the *ardhākṣara* (half-syllables) is eliminated and thus "expelled.

In terms of persons (*pudgala*), internally concealing the bodhisattva practice is "secret," while externally manifesting as a śrāvaka is "expelled. In terms of the pedagogical method (*vinaya*), setting aside the Great [Vehicle] to bestow the Small is "expelled," while the Small not fathoming the Great is "secret" (as the text says).

[Commentary] This citation from the *Avataṃsaka* serves to dispel [misconceptions]. Regarding the interpretation of the main text, "secretly dispelling" refers to manifesting the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya-satya*).

Among the five periods of teaching—excluding the *Āgama* period—all clarify the ultimate truth; however, here it specifically points to the *Avataṃsaka*, which, while including the distinct teaching (*bye-ba, vyatireka*), also encompasses the perfect teaching (*rdzogs-pa, paripūrṇa*) as the single ultimate truth.
"The first Great Vehicle teaching" refers precisely to the perfect and distinct teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*. "The first bodhisattva person" [refers to the practitioner of this teaching].
"Those" refers to a class of bodhisattvas of great capacity. Now, regarding the phrase "to clarify the lower," this is the formal explanation of the "secret dispatching.
From the perspective of skillful means, the ultimate reality is that which is concealed; thus it is "secret. Because it points toward the partial truth, it is "dispatched. As Miaole says:
Now, regarding "clearly and secretly dispatching": to conceal the reality is called "secret"; to employ the provisional is "dispatching. Regarding the teaching:

the Sudden Teaching of the Full Word conceals and does not speak [the ultimate], thus it is "secret"; the Gradual Teaching of the Half Word employs it to explain and demonstrate, thus it is "dispatching."
Regarding the classification by person, it is as the sutra says: "Therefore, bodhisattvas manifest as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

Regarding the classification by mode of teaching, the preaching of the Lesser Vehicle is for the purpose of dispelling [obstacles], while its being unfathomable to those of lesser faculties constitutes its secrecy.
[Note] Regarding "two persons": The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6 (23), states that the four great disciples each led their own respective groups and did not involve the bodhisattvas;
therefore, it says "two persons. In terms of the Dharma, these are the Four Noble Truths of Dependent Origination; in terms of principle, they are the conditioned ultimate and the conventional;
in terms of persons, they are the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. (Text) For now, we shall consider them according to persons.
[Commentary] The four great disciples each took charge of one portion. Because they abide in the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles, they are referred to as "two persons.

The causal conditions are precisely the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing. Regarding the distinction between the conditioned-true and the conventional: the analysis of form into emptiness is the conditioned-true;
that which exists outside of this principle is the conditioned-conventional.
[Commentary] Their physical appearance is haggard. Textual Passage 6 (23) states: "In the teachings of the Two Vehicles, one does not cultivate the primary and secondary marks;
they speak only of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and impurity—this is what is meant by a haggard appearance. Furthermore, (25) states: "Internally fearing impermanence."
It is said: "Worn out. This refers to encountering the eight sufferings externally. It is said: "Emaciated" (the character *wen* is used).

[Commentary] Miaole says: Although what was planted over a hundred kalpas is mentioned in the *Abhidharma-śāstra*, it does not pertain to the two vehicles; therefore, they lack beautiful form and color.
[Commentary] "Lacking majestic power" means that he does not possess the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*).

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the ten powers: the first is the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*), which is the knowledge of the fixed nature of all causes, conditions, and their karmic results.
1. By means of such causes and conditions, such retributions arise; he knows fully that such retributions do not arise. 2. The power of knowledge regarding karma:

he knows the various karmas and their resulting experiences of all sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. 3. The power of concentration: he knows all dhyānas and samādhis. 4. The power of the faculties:
he knows the superior and inferior degrees of the faculties of sentient beings. 5. The power of desires: he knows [the inclinations of] sentient beings...

1. The power of knowing various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*): knowing the diverse inclinations of the world. 2. The power of knowing various dispositions (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*): knowing the diverse dispositions of the world. 3. The power of knowing the paths leading to destinations (*sarvatraga-mārga-jñāna-bala*):

knowing the characteristics of all paths that lead to their respective destinations. 4. The power of recollecting past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*): knowing from one lifetime up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.

[He knows] names and surnames, suffering and pleasure, the length of lifespan, and so forth. Ninth is the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), by which he sees beings at the time of their birth and death, as well as their rebirth in good or evil destinies.
Tenth is the power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), by which he knows for himself: "My births are exhausted; I shall not undergo further existence.
Regarding the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): the first is the fearlessness of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*) concerning both the mundane and the supramundane.

1. Regarding all phenomena, he knows them completely and sees them completely. As the Buddha said: "I am one who possesses all-encompassing right knowledge," he thus attains peace and security, and attains fearlessness.
2. Fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-vaiśāradya*): Delusion, karma, and birth-and-death are all exhausted. As the Buddha said:
"I have exhausted all outflows," he thus attains peace and security, and attains fearlessness. 3. [Fearlessness] in proclaiming the obstacles to the Path...
The fearlessness regarding the teaching of the dharmas that obstruct the noble path. As the Buddha said: "Because I have taught the obstructing dharmas, I have attained peace and security;
I have attained fearlessness. Fourth is the fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path that exhausts suffering.
This refers to teaching the path capable of exhausting all suffering. As the Buddha said: "The noble path I have taught can transcend the world and can exhaust all [afflictions]."
Because of suffering, one attains peace and security, and attains fearlessness.

From the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise). [Commentary] "You may go to him and speak slowly to that impoverished son. The twenty-fourth section of the six-part text states: "This refers to employing the Small Teaching for those with small capacities.
The Great Teaching clarifies principles that are direct and substantial; therefore, it says to 'run quickly and seize him. The Small Teaching clarifies principles that are circuitous..."
"Hidden. Therefore, it is said that one speaks slowly. (Text) "I hire you to remove dung. "Hire" means to rent for wages. *Wenju* 6.24 states:
"To remove the dung of suffering and its origin, and to take the price of the Path and Cessation. (Text)
[Commentary] Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) can defile the true nature (*tattva*), like excrement and filth.

The path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) can lead one to realize the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), like obtaining a price—namely, obtaining the "daily wage" of *nirvāṇa*. "Zhu" (紆) means "crooked."
△ 2. The inquiry: What meaning does this summarize?
△ 2. The answer and explanation of what was summarized.
Answer: Following the sudden teaching, the Tripitaka teaching was expounded. For twenty years, he was constantly made to remove filth;
this signifies the meaning of destroying the afflictions of views and thought.

[Commentary] During twenty years, one uses the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which together constitute one unimpeded [knowledge] and one liberation.

One then uses nine unimpeded knowledges and nine liberations to sever the afflictions of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), totaling twenty. (In the sutra, there are two further instances clarifying these "twenty years.
If one abides in the stage of the Two Vehicles and turns toward the Mahayana teaching, it is called "managing the household affairs for twenty years. From this...
The capacities of those of the Two Vehicles have come to inspire the Buddha; thus it is said: "It has been twenty years since you, my sons, came.
Each of them has attained the ten knowledges (daśajñāna) characteristic of the Two Vehicles.

[Commentary] First, the abandonment of views; ninth, the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa*). Altogether there are ten kinds of unimpededness (*ānantarya*) and ten kinds of liberation (*vimukti*), totaling twenty.

Regarding "views" and "afflictions," this explains the lower Tripitaka teachings. As for the mention of "twenty years" in two places in the Sūtra, it does not refer to the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
It is because the Buddha commanded [the disciples] to turn the teaching over to the Bodhisattvas that he spoke of "twenty years. The phrase "managing household affairs" intends to clarify...
When the followers of the Two Vehicles received their mandate and turned the teaching, they secretly eliminated their specific delusions of both views and thoughts; hence it is said, "twenty years.
One verse from the *Lotus Sūtra* describes the long interval between the separate assembly of father and sons, stating, "Since I saw my son, twenty years have passed.
This is intended to clarify that the capacities of the Two Vehicles have, since coming, moved the Buddha to respond, and thus the designation of the "Two Vehicles" was established.
Therefore, it is said that [this occurs] after twenty years. Regarding the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), the *Renwang jing shu* (Commentary on the Benevolent Kings Sutra) states:

first is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*). This refers to the untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) regarding phenomena bound to the desire realm; untainted knowledge regarding the causes bound to the desire realm; untainted knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena bound to the desire realm;
untainted knowledge regarding the path for abandoning phenomena bound to the desire realm; and the category of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānapakṣa*).
This refers to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the middle [realm]. Second is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

Within the untainted seed-knowledge of the two higher realms, when distinguished according to the Four Noble Truths, there are four types of untainted knowledge, as clarified above in the section on dharma-knowledge; the only difference is the distinction between dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.

Third is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), which consists of the present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) bound to the two realms of desire and form, as well as untainted minds.

1. A small portion of the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). 2. Four types of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*). Knowledge of all worldly things that is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) is also called "equal knowledge" (*samvṛti-jñāna*), because it is possessed by both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*).
3. Knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*): contemplating the five aggregates as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self.

Sixth is the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) when contemplating the causes of tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as having origination through causes and conditions. Seventh is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*):
the untainted wisdom when contemplating exhaustion, cessation, and the sublime transcendence. Eighth is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*):

the untainted wisdom when contemplating the path as the realization, the track, and the vehicle. Ninth is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*): the wisdom that has already seen suffering and completed the cultivation of the path. The treatise says: "I have seen suffering."
Having done so, having abandoned the origin [of suffering], having realized cessation, and having cultivated the path—there are ten knowledges of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Having seen suffering, one no longer sees it again, and so forth.

【□Note】Regarding the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* (viewing) and *klesa* (thinking): "viewing" refers to conceptual discrimination; "thinking" refers to craving and attachment. The *Zhiguan famen baokan wen* (Questions on the Essentials of Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 8, states:
"The dharma of darkened affliction disturbs and confuses the mind and spirit. (Text)

[Commentary] To give rise to conceptual discrimination by being deluded regarding the principle is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). To give rise to craving and attachment toward objects is called "name" (*nāman*). Its essence is obscure and vexing;
its function is to cause affliction and confusion.

[Note] This refers to the destruction of the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*). It answers the previous [point regarding] "removing filth. Filth is that which can defile; thus it is used as a metaphor, meaning it pollutes the True Reality (*tattva*).
△ Second, the Vaipulya [sūtras] are fivefold. First, they are categorized by school;
next, the Vaipulya school is explained. Sūtras such as the *Vimalakīrti* refute the partial and subdue the Hinayana, praising the Great Vehicle and extolling the Perfect.
[□ Note] Next, the Vaipulya section and others are explained; this concerns the classification of sections and the inclusion of sutras.
[■ Record] This is a classification based on sections. The Vaipulya serves as that which includes, while sutras such as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* serve as that which is included.

[Note] "Criticizing the partial," etc., clarifies the intent of the [Lotus] section. Although the collection of scriptures is vast, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* possesses the merit of criticizing and refuting; thus it is specifically designated as the foremost.

It criticizes the partial, subdues the Small Vehicle, extols the Great, and praises the Perfect. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), fascicle 4, section 36, states: "These eight characters belong to our own school."

The judgment that exhausts all principles refers to disparaging the Small [Vehicle] and criticizing the Partial [Teachings], while praising the Great [Vehicle] and extolling the Perfect [Teaching]. (Text) The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 10, part 2, states:
"For example, the 'Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings' is the praise of the Great; the eulogy of Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti is the extolling of the Perfect.
Therefore, it causes those of small faculties to feel shame for the Small and to aspire to the Great. (Text)
[Commentary] Vimalakīrti clarifies that the Bodhisattva is like an illusion, like the moon reflected in water, and like a conjured person; his afflictions are like those who have attained *nirvāṇa*.
He manifests the reception of a body to contemplate sentient beings. Furthermore, he clarifies that the Bodhisattva practices the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Moreover, he clarifies that all phenomena are established based on the "root of non-abiding" (*apratiṣṭhita-mūla*). The commentary on the fascicle indicates this as a praise of the Great [Vehicle]. Furthermore, Vimalakīrti says: "Mañjuśrī..."
"Coming, he comes without the mark of coming; seeing, he sees without the mark of seeing. Mañjuśrī said: "If there is coming, it has already come and does not come again;
if there is going, it has already gone and does not go again. That which comes has nowhere from which it comes;
that which goes has nowhere to which it goes. That which can be seen cannot be seen again. This is the meeting of masters, presenting face-to-face, even unto entry."
Regarding the Gate of Non-duality: Mañjuśrī dispels words with words, while Vimalakīrti dispels words with wordlessness.
This is because words are like dregs; were it not for the dispelling of words, one could not attain the essence. Yet even the "dispelling of words" is still a form of speech;

were it not for silent stillness, one could not realize its ultimate limit. The commentary identifies this as the "Praise of the Perfect," precisely intended to cause those who disparage the Small Vehicle to aspire toward the Great.

[Commentary] Regarding the necessity of refuting and rebuking [the disciples]: this is because those of inferior capacity cling to the "True" (the Lesser Vehicle) to preserve their fruits, seeking realization and entering extinction.
Thus, as soon as they realize the Lesser Fruit, they are fit to be rebuked; it is not strictly necessary to wait until after twelve years.

Later, when Vimalakīrti manifested illness in Vaiśālī, the Buddha ordered his disciples to go and inquire after his health. Consequently, they all recounted how they had previously been scolded and declined to go, saying they were incapable of the task.

This refers to the "recounting of past reproaches" (*pūrvakṛta-nirbhartsana*), which is a form of indirect censure. If one were to reprove someone while they are actually present in the seat, it would be like the case of removing flowers from a seat during a formal ritual.

[Commentary] The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* contains two types of reproaches. As in the "Chapter on the Disciples," when the Buddha dispatched his disciples to inquire after Vimalakīrti’s illness, they all recounted past reproaches they had received, stating they were unable to go.
Śāriputra said, "I recall once sitting beneath a tree," to which Vimalakīrti replied: [The remainder of the passage follows the citation of the scripture.]
It is not necessarily sitting on this seat that constitutes "serene sitting" (*yansuo*). Not manifesting body, speech, or mind within the three realms is serene sitting.

Not arising from the meditative concentration of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while manifesting all dignified deportments is serene sitting. Not abandoning the dharmas of the Path while manifesting the affairs of ordinary people is serene sitting.
"This is tranquil sitting (*śānta-āsana*). Even until the non-interruption of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the entry into *nirvāṇa*, this is tranquil sitting.
Sitting in such a manner is what the Buddha has authorized. At that time, O World-Honored One, having heard these words, I remained silent and was unable to offer a reply.

Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. This is what is called "recounting the past" and subtly rebuking [the interlocutor]. Regarding "paying homage at the seat," it is as stated in the sutra:
Śāriputra saw that there were no seats in the room and thought, "Where shall the great assembly sit?
Vimalakīrti said, "Venerable sir, have you come for the sake of the Dharma, or for the sake of a seat? ... Indeed, one who seeks the Dharma..."
They do not cling to their own bodies or lives, much less to their seats. Having asked Mañjuśrī, "In which buddha-field are there excellent, sublime merits that produce such lion thrones?
Mañjuśrī replied, "To the east, passing through lands as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sumeru-lakṣaṇa.
The Buddha there is named Sumeru-pradīpa-rāja. His throne is eight [yojanas] high."

It was fourteen thousand yojanas in extent and was the most exquisitely adorned. When Vimalakīrti manifested his supernatural powers, that Buddha sent thirty-two thousand lion thrones into Vimalakīrti’s room.

Even until Mañjuśrī and all the bodhisattvas and great beings were seated together, each had to manifest their own body to match the form of those thrones. Those bodhisattvas who had attained supernatural powers immediately [manifested themselves accordingly].
He transformed himself to a height of forty-two thousand yojanas and sat upon a lion throne.
The bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds and the great disciples were all unable to ascend it.

Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "Pay homage to the Tathāgata Sumerudīparāja, and then you shall be able to sit. Thereupon, Śāriputra and the others paid homage and were able to sit; they then removed the flowers.
The Sūtra says: A goddess scattered flowers over the Bodhisattvas and the great disciples (*mahāśrāvaka*). When the flowers reached the Bodhisattvas, they fell away;
but when they reached the great disciples, they stuck and did not fall. All the disciples attempted to remove the flowers through their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), but were unable to do so.
The goddess asked Śāriputra, "For what reason do you try to remove the flowers? He replied, "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma. This is...
He removed them. The deva said, "Do not say that these flowers are improper. These flowers have no discrimination;

it is you, O virtuous one, who give rise to discrimination. As for the bodhisattvas to whom the flowers do not adhere, it is because they have already severed all conceptualizations of discrimination.
For example, when a person is afraid, non-human spirits find an opportunity to take advantage of them; likewise, the disciples fear birth and death."
Therefore, forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, and tangibles find their opportunity [to disturb]. For one who has already abandoned fear, all five desires are powerless to act.

If the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted, the flowers merely adhere to the body; once the tendencies are exhausted, they do not adhere. This is what is meant by "reproving on the spot."
△ Second, the classification according to the teachings (*jiao*).

All four teachings are expounded herein. The *Tripitaka* (Zang) is the "half-syllable" teaching; the *Shared*, *Distinct*, and *Perfect* [teachings] are the "full-syllable" teachings. Because it speaks of the full in contrast to the half and so forth, it is called "classification according to the teachings."

[Note] "The four teachings are all taught," etc., clarifies the application of the teachings within the *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) section. This is because, in order to extensively censure the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and to accommodate both those suited for the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*) and those suited for the Lesser, the four teachings are required;
thus, all four are taught. Regarding the teaching of the *Tripiṭaka* within the *Vaipulya*: first, it serves as the basis for censure and refutation;
second, it serves for those whose spiritual capacities have arisen unexpectedly.

[Commentary] As for those who come as sudden opportunists: they have not yet attended the assemblies of the Āgamas, have not heard the Four Truths of Arising and Ceasing, and have not realized the True Principle;
therefore, it is necessary to preach the Tripitaka teachings.

[Note] As stated in the *Shiqian*: "Furthermore, within the gradual [teaching], there is first the entry into minor practices. Outside the chambers of the lay assembly, he preaches the Way of Impermanence.

[Commentary] This citation is used to corroborate the aforementioned horizontal [responsive] capacities. In the "Buddha-land" chapter (*Buddhakṣetra-parivarta*) of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, the Buddha says that according to [the capacity of] each...

"When the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure. Śāriputra thought to himself, "When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, how could his mind not have been pure, yet the Sahā world is so impure as this? The Buddha said, "This land of mine is pure, but you do not see it.
Thereupon, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the great trichiliocosm was adorned with precious jewels, like...
The Buddha Ratnavyūha, the land of Immeasurable Merit Adorned with Jewels, and the Buddha’s withdrawal of his supernormal power caused the world to return to its former state.

Thirty-two thousand gods and humans who sought the vehicle of the śrāvakas, realizing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are entirely impermanent, became free from dust and defilement and attained the pure Dharma-eye. Eight thousand bhikṣus did not accept [further existence].
All dharmas, the exhaustion of outflows, and the liberation of the mind—this is the initial entry into the practice of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
As for those among the lay multitude who discourse on the Way of impermanence outside the chamber, this refers to the "Chapter on Skillful Means" in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*.
When the Elder manifested illness, the king, ministers, elders, householders, brahmins, princes, and other officials all went to inquire after his illness. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti...
This is explained in detail by means of the bodily illness, as it is said: "O worthy ones, this body is impermanent; it is without strength, without power, and without solidity.
It is of a nature that quickly decays and cannot be relied upon. It is afflicted by suffering and is the gathering place of manifold diseases.
Indeed, this body is like a venomous snake, like a hostile thief, and like an empty village—a composite formation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas)."

This is so. [Supplement] The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* originally contains no explicit mention of "inside" or "outside" the room. Now, it is said that being unable to enter the Mahāyāna room is, in meaning, equivalent to being outside the room.

[Commentary on the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Vol. 10, p. 24] states: "In the Vaipulya [teachings], the Tripiṭaka is used subsidiarily, while the three teachings are used as the primary means to censure the Two Vehicles.
By incorporating those of the Two Vehicles, they secretly achieve universal benefit. Those who were not previously spoken of as Bodhisattvas are now transformed into persons within the Mahāyāna."

[Appendix] *Bian'e* (Discriminating Errors) states: "The phrase 'the Bodhisattva further transforms into one among those of the Mahāyāna' appears in the second volume, lower section, of the *Xuanqi hui-ben* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning, Collated Edition).
However, since it is now stated that they 'rebuke the partial,' the Bodhisattvas of the *Āgama* (Tripiṭaka) stage are also included therein;
how much more so regarding the matter of transformation, whether in the Vaipulya or Prajñā periods? As for those who do not transform, there are still such cases even after the Prajñā period."
This seems not to be restricted solely to the Vaipulya (fangděng) period; it must certainly be understood as evolving into the Mahāyāna (yán).

In my private opinion, the "reproach and expulsion" (*tánchì*) found in the Vaipulya teachings seem to refer specifically to those of the Two Vehicles (*ērshèng*) who were small-capacity recipients of transformation.

Speaking from the perspective of one who has fully traversed the five periods, such as the *Lotus Sūtra*’s bestowal of the eightfold prediction (*bāxiàng shòujì*), it appears that even those of the Two Vehicles are all of the Mahāyāna capacity (*púsà jī*). Nevertheless, regarding the passage in the *Xuánqǐn* concerning the evolution into the Mahāyāna:
This inherently possesses profound meaning.

[□ Note] It speaks of the "Full" (Pūrṇa) in contrast to the "Half" (Ardha), thereby using the Full to refute the Half. Thus, although it refutes both the Great and the Small, its primary intent is to refute the Small.

The *Shiqian* quotes the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, saying: "For example, there was an elder who had only one son; his heart was constantly filled with love and concern for him. He intended to take him to a wise [teacher]..."
The teacher, fearing that [the child] would not achieve mastery quickly, soon brought him back.
Out of affection, he diligently taught him only the "half-syllables" day and night, but did not instruct him in the *Vyākaraṇa* treatise. This was because his son’s strength was as yet insufficient.
The *Vyākaraṇa* treatise is the translation of the "root of syllables," meaning the foundation of all worldly characters; it is what is called the "full-syllable. To provide an analogy:
The "half-syllable" refers to the ninefold canon (*navāṅga-śāsana*). The *Vyākaraṇa* treatises refer to the Vaipulya scriptures;
these are the "full-syllables. [Commentary] In the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha said:

"I teach the initial half-syllables as the foundation for all grammatical treatises (*vyākaraṇa*), incantations (*mantra*), literary compositions, and the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*). Ordinary people study these as the root of letters."

Later one will be able to know what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma. Furthermore, the meaning of the "half-syllables" (ardhakṣara) is that they are all the basis for the verbal expressions of afflictions;
the "full-syllables" (pūrṇakṣara), however, are the fundamental basis for the verbal expressions of all wholesome dharmas. This is the Vyākaraṇa-śāstra.
As stated in the *Fuxing*: "This treatise is the root of written characters. The Master of Hexi said:

"It is the foundation of all worldly writing and the treatise on the phonetics of the scriptures. It expounds the four types of eloquence, censures worldly dharmas, and praises the dharma of renunciation."
The phrasing is elegant and refined, and the principles are profound; although these are non-Buddhist treatises, they contain no heterodox teachings.
They must have been composed by a Mahāsattva of skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), and for this reason, they are now compared to the Vaipulya sūtras.

[Supplement] Regarding *Vyākaraṇa*, the *Guangming ji* states that this translates as "Explanatory Treatise" (*Jilun*) and was composed by Pāṇini. [Note] This also refutes the *Mahāvyutpatti*, not merely indicating its expansion.
The Bodhisattva says: as cited below from the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī was also rebuked.

[Note] This is based on the Vaipulya (fangděng) sutras, which use the Great Vehicle to criticize the Small Vehicle. Thus, the fulfillment of the three teachings of the Mahāyāna gate is contrasted with the partiality of the Tripiṭaka.
If the *Wénjù* states that there are no "three" to be contrasted by the Vaipulya, this reveals the section of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
"Exquisite! It is the unique, perfect vehicle (*ekayāna*), not the same as the 'perfect' [teaching] of the Vaipulya (fangděng) which is contrasted with the three [other vehicles].

[Commentary: Regarding the passage "if one looks at the words and phrases," it means that the *Lotus Sūtra* is purely perfect and uniquely exquisite, being free from any admixture, partiality, or juxtaposition.
Therefore, the "perfection" of the Vaipulya, which is contrasted with the three [vehicles], differs from the pure perfection of the *Lotus Sūtra*.
△ Third, the judgment according to time.
If judged by time, it is the mealtime (the third period).
[Note] This is precisely the first mealtime in the "Illuminating the Level Ground" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (the hour of the dragon, 7–9 a.m.). The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* has four [sections].
At dawn, it is the time for humans to eat. At midday, it is the food of the devas. At noon, it is the food of the Buddhas of the three periods of time. In the afternoon, it is the food of animals.
At dusk, it is the food of ghosts and spirits. Now is the time for the devas to eat.
[Commentary]: This refers to the time. The *Vīra-samādhi Sūtra* states that there are four types of eating times: at dawn, the food of devas; at noon, the food of Buddhas;

in the evening, the food of animals; and at night, the food of ghosts and spirits. Because the Buddha severed the causes for the six realms of existence and caused himself to be equal to the Buddhas of the three periods, it is said that noon is the time for the Dharma-food. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states that only devas may eat past midday.
Regarding the *Āgama*’s definition of "mealtimes" (*bhojana-kāla*) as "at dawn" (*prabhāta*), this refers to the "dawn atmosphere," which is taken because it is pure.

If categorized by the twelve-hour system (*dvādaśa-lagna*), then the hours of *yīn*, *mǎo*, and *chén* constitute the dawn period; *sì*, *wǔ*, and *wèi* constitute the midday period; *shēn*, *yǒu*, and *xù* constitute the evening period;

and *hài*, *zǐ*, and *chǒu* constitute the night period. Thus, the present *Vaipulya* [sūtras] refer to the hours of *yīn*, *mǎo*, and *chén*. [Supplementary Note: The *Biàn'é* (Discerning Errors) states that the mealtimes should...
This is discussed in reference to human beings, not those in the heavens. In my humble opinion, "three meals a day" refers to the time of a person's initial meal each day;
however, it may also be harmonized with the observation that one partakes of celestial food when rising early, as seen in the sutras.
△ Fourth, the judgment according to flavor (rasa).
If judged by flavor, then from curd (dadhi) comes cream (navanīta); this [Mahāyāna] emerges from the ninefold canon (navāṅga), like the flavor of ghee (ghṛta).

[□ Commentary] Regarding the arising [of the teachings], this is discussed in terms of the doctrinal systems; regarding their intensity, it is discussed in terms of the capacities of the practitioners. Since they feel shame for the Lesser Vehicle and aspire to the Great Vehicle, it is like boiling curd to produce fresh butter.
[■ Record] This concerns the flavor [of the teaching]. In the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Kāśyapa says: "Why have we eternally severed our roots of goodness?"
For those in this Mahāyāna who are like withered seeds, all the śrāvakas, upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation, should weep aloud, their voices shaking the great trichiliocosm;
all the bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crowns of their heads.
When these words were spoken, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon Bodhi. This...
This refers to being ashamed of the small and aspiring toward the great, like boiling thin curd to produce thick butter.
From the ninefold Sūtras emerges the Vaipulya, which arises as a sign of its manifestation.
△ Five: Judging according to the sutra, there are two parts. First, citing the sutra to raise the inquiry, which has two sub-sections.

First, citing the sutra: The *Śraddhādhimukti-parivarta* states: "After this period had passed, their minds were in mutual trust; they entered and left [the dwelling] without difficulty. However, as for where they stayed..."
It remains in its original place.
[Commentary] After this period—following the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) at the Deer Park—it is now the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras). Their minds accord with one another in essence;
father and son trust each other. Fully understanding and believing in compliance, because the son trusts the father, the attainment of the fruit is not in vain; because the father trusts the son...
Therefore, having heard the Great [Vehicle], one does not slander it.
[Commentary] This is based on the judgment of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The *Wenju* states:

"If obtaining the price of *nirvāṇa* through the *Hīnayāna* teachings is not false, then now, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, the preaching of the Mahāyāna Dharma is likewise not false; the son trusts his father. Thus says the Buddha.

Knowing these things, they have already severed the afflictions of view and thought; upon hearing [the teaching], they will certainly not slander it. Possessing sharp untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), they give rise to faith immediately upon hearing it—this is like a father believing his son.
[Note: Entering and exiting without difficulty. *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6 (29), states: "By means of this, one beholds the body of sublime marks and hears the Mahāyāna."]
The teaching is called "entry," yet it is further criticized; because one still perceives the sixteen-foot [form] and preaches the *hīnayāna* dharma, this is called "exit.
Regarding these entries and exits of the Great and Small Vehicles, there is no doubt or difficulty. (Text) The third fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Explanatory Sub-commentary) states:
"It is not like the time when one is terrified by kings and the like; therefore, it is said that there is no difficulty" (Text).
[Commentary] Fearful of the king and others. As stated in the *Śraddhādhimuktiparivarta*: "At that time, the impoverished son happened upon his father’s house and stood by the side of the gate.
From afar he saw his father seated upon a lion throne with a jeweled footstool supporting his feet, surrounded by all the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders who paid him respectful homage...
When the impoverished son saw that his father possessed such great power, he immediately—"
Filled with terror, he regretted having come here and thought to himself: "This must be a king or someone of royal rank;
this is no place for me to earn a living through hired labor. It would be better to go to a poor neighborhood where there is scope for exertion and food and clothing are easily obtained.
Thinking thus, he even ran away in haste. This was a time of doubt and difficulty, yet now it has been realized as the truth.
Therefore, there is no difficulty.

[Commentary] Nevertheless, when practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one employs the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (active consciousness) and perceives the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), abiding in the provisional principle.

When practicing the Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamā-pratipad-vipaśyanā*), one employs the *karma-vijñāna* (karmic consciousness) and perceives the sublime body (*vairocana-kāya*), abiding in the ultimate principle. Now, although those of the Two Vehicles practice the contemplation of emptiness, they may enter into the perception of the sublime body.

Due to the karmic consciousness (*karmavijñāna*). For it is the two consciousnesses of activity (*karma*) and perception (*vijñapti*) that serve as the basis for both the seeing and the perceived; thus, the *Jieshi* (Exegesis on Refutation) states:
"Entering the vision of the Honored One’s sublime form is due to the merit of the karmic consciousness; because the teaching has not yet been opened, one dwells temporarily in a grass hut."
[Commentary] This clarifies the reason why the Two Vehicles perceive the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa* (the sublime physical form). The *Miaozong* states:

"The root from which the marks arise is precisely the two principles of the provisional and the real, the two contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the middle way (*madhyamā*), and the two consciousnesses of activity (*karma*) and reality (*vastu*).

When divided according to these, the distinction between the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the *viśiṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*-body is as clear as pointing at one's own palm. The *Jinguangming shu* states: "The Buddha of the sixteen-foot body..."

The Buddha of True Reality dwells in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The Buddha of the Honored Special Body (*vairocana-viśeṣa-deha*) dwells in both the ultimate and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
The Dharma-body Buddha dwells in the Middle Way. Because these rely on two principles, there are thus two Buddhas. Sentient beings possess two consciousnesses;
because there are causes for two types of contemplation, they invoke two Buddhas. Below this section on "Activity" (*karma*), it explains and clarifies the Two Vehicles (*dvi-yāna*). Due to...

Because the consciousness of karma perceives the Sovereign-Specific (zuntè) [form], the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* states: "Regarding the two types of consciousness, there are two kinds of Buddha-activity.

The first is based on the consciousness of differentiated phenomena (*fenbié shìshí*). That which is perceived by the minds of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles is called the Response Body (*yīngshēn*)."
Because they do not know that the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) is manifesting, they perceive [the Buddha] as coming from without and grasp at the boundaries of form;

because they cannot fully comprehend this, [they do not see the true body]. Second, based on the *karma-vijñāna*, it is said that for all Bodhisattvas, from their first aspiration until the ultimate stage of a Bodhisattva, what the mind perceives is called the *saṃbhoga-kāya*. This body possesses infinite forms, and these forms possess infinite [qualities].
Marks. These marks possess immeasurable secondary characteristics (*anuvyañjana*). The fruits upon which they depend are likewise immeasurable.
Their various adornments, manifesting according to what is shown, are boundless and inexhaustible, transcending all marks of limitation. They appear in accordance with what is appropriate.
It is always able to abide and maintain itself, neither decaying nor being lost.

Such merits as these are all accomplished through the permeation of immeasurable practices such as the various *pāramitās*, as well as through inconceivable permeation; they are fully endowed with the characteristics of immeasurable bliss.

Therefore, it is called "retribution. Based on this, one knows that the two consciousnesses—karma-consciousness (*karmavijñāna*) and seeing-consciousness (*darśanavijñāna*)—are the basis of both the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*).

Thus, the followers of the Two Vehicles perceive the "Venerable and Extraordinary" (the *vairocana-kāya*) through the karma-consciousness. Regarding the section "Refuting Misinterpretations" below, it provides a corroborating explanation; its intent clarifies the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the provisional (*upāya*) to reveal the ultimate.

He then abandoned the thatched hut. Since this had not yet been discussed as an opening [of the teaching], he remained in the hut according to the provisional principle (*upāya*). He performed manual labor for others;

it was solely through the functioning of his *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) that he beheld the *vairocana-kāya* (the Body of Sovereign Marks). [Supplementary Note: The *phenomenal consciousness* (*vastuvijñāna*) perceives the birth-body (*janma-kāya*), while the *karmic consciousness* perceives the *vairocana-kāya*.
This is merely a rough distinction made for the time being. In reality, even when perceiving the birth-body, one still employs the *karmic consciousness*; this is because...

The followers of the Two Vehicles do not know that there are the seventh and eighth consciousnesses; they do not realize that objects manifest through the mind. They merely employ the six preceding consciousnesses for mental discrimination;

therefore, it is said that they "employ the active consciousness" (*saviṣaya-vijñāna*). Even when perceiving the *vairocana* (the Universal Radiance) Buddha, they do not abandon the active consciousness.

This is simply because, having already severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃskāra-kleśa*), they are free from conceptual discrimination; and because, having already heard the Great Dharma, they have gradually reached a state of maturity.

At that time, the remaining afflictions consist solely of ignorance (*avidyā*), and thus what they employ is likewise the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*); it is not necessarily the case that they are exclusively practicing the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*).
Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles originally regressed from the Great Vehicle to adopt the Lesser; they possess the seeds of having previously practiced the Middle Way in the past.

One attains the vision of the *zhuntè* (exalted special body). The *Guangming ji* states: "The Tathāgata, through the functioning of the *dharmadhātu*, accords with the two consciousnesses of sentient beings' activities and manifests the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*.
The *nirmāṇakāya* is the *janmakāya* (birth-body); the *saṃbhogakāya* is the *zhuntèshēn* (exalted special body)."

And as for the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*): those who rely on the *saviṣaya-vijñāna* (consciousness with objects) can see only the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and cannot perceive the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body), because their [understanding] is coarse and superficial and does not fathom the profound.
Those who rely on the *karma-vijñāna* (consciousness of karma) can perceive both the *saṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*, because they know True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it gives rise to two functions, one should know that the function of True Suchness manifests as the greatness of the Buddha’s marks. There are three grades:
first, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* discusses the number of his marks and signs as being equal to the atoms in ten lotus-treasury worlds; second, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.

Whether many or few, they are all boundless; therefore, they are all termed "oceans. None of them fail to be the *vairocana* (Universal Radiance) form, yet there is a distinction between the universal and the specific.

The eighty-four thousand [teachings] contained therein are restricted to the vision of the *karmic-consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*); the thirty-two [marks], however, are universal to the vision of the *phenomenal-consciousness* (*vastuvijñāna*).

The Unshared Middle Way dharma is taught in common with the Two Vehicles; this serves as an analogy for the Vaipulya section, which is not devoid of this meaning.

However, because the Vaipulya sutras frequently employ censure and rebuke, their shared meaning is somewhat sparse. In the case of the Prajñā [sutras], they constitute a shared teaching for Bodhisattvas (this is based on the source of the three faculties of understanding).

This is spoken in common with [other vehicles], yet the underlying intent is to censure and rebuke them, causing those who cling to the small to aspire to the great;

therefore, while the shared meaning is somewhat superficial, when the *Prajñāpāramitā* is applied to the Separate and Complete [teachings], it constitutes a common exposition. Regarding the source of the three faculties' understanding, the *Miaoxuan* states:

That which is neither outflow (*āsrava*) nor mundane is not the case; that which is neither non-outflow nor mundane is the removal of attachment. Why?

Because practitioners may give rise to attachment toward the non-outflow, just as they give rise to latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by taking cessation as an object. To shatter this mind of attachment, one returns to the non-outflow. This is one cycle of the two truths.
Next, when a person hears that it is neither outflow nor non-outflow, this indicates that it is free from the two extremes and specifically reveals the Middle Way—the principle of the Mean.

This is the truth. It is also another instance of the two truths. Furthermore, when a person hears "neither outflowing nor non-outflowing," they immediately understand the "double negation," which correctly reveals the Middle Way.
The power and function of the Middle Way Dharma-realm are vast and great, equal to empty space.
All dharmas tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing. This is yet another instance of the two truths. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) explains: "It is not non-..."

The outflows (*āsrava*) are that which dispel attachment; the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is non-attachment. Because practitioners take it as an object with an attached mind, it is now used to shatter that attachment;

therefore, it is called "neither outflow-free. Furthermore, it is said: "outflow" and "outflow-free" are originally universal dharmas; for the sake of establishing the meaning of connection, they are called "both negations.
"Empty" and "not empty" are originally distinct dharmas. That all dharmas converge [upon the ultimate] is the original [nature].

Regarding the Perfect Teaching (*yuanfa*), because the three types of people attain different understandings of each and every dharma, the source of their understanding is demonstrated by means of the outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth.

As for establishing the meaning of "reception" (*jie*), it refers to the reception of the Distinct Teaching by the Perfect, and the reception of the Perfect by the Distinct. This explanation is found in the seventh fascicle.

Why, then, when categorized according to the teaching (*jiao*), is it only designated as "Common"? Answer: When categorized according to the section (*bu*), it refers to the period of the two *sūtras* [the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra*].

The Two Vehicles also hear [the teachings], yet they are called "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) only within the context of the Shared [Teaching]. In the *Avataṃsaka*, they are called "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).

In terms of the classification of teachings (*śāsana-vibhāga*), the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings are therefore "uncommon. In the Shared Teaching, however, the Three Vehicles practice together; thus, it is "common.

Nevertheless, while it is termed "common" with respect to the specific scriptural division (*nikāya*), it remains "uncommon" in terms of the teaching itself. This is because although they hear it, they lack the aspiration to seek and attain it; hence, it is "common."

In terms of flavor, just as clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is produced from fresh butter (*navanīta*), so too does this [Mahāprajñāpāramitā] emerge after the Vaipulya sūtras; it possesses the flavor of the fourth stage of clarified butter.

The "Judgment" refers to passages concerning the one provisional and one real [teachings] during the Avataṃsaka period.

the Subtle within the Vaipulya and Prajñā teachings is no different from the present Subtle. Therefore, the single Subtlety of the Sudden division is non-dual and indistinguishable from the Lotus Sūtra."

The various flavors of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) are inherently and originally interfused. Nevertheless, in terms of their doctrinal meanings, there are levels of coarseness—namely, the "combined" (*jian*), the "single" (*dan*), and the "corresponding" (*duidai*)—which must necessarily be opened and revealed to become wondrous.

Therefore, it is said that "opening" [the provisional to reveal the real] constitutes the primary intent. [Supplement] Regarding those who judge through the theory of relative dependence (*xiangdai lunpan*):
Waiting upon the coarseness of the preceding four periods serves to manifest the subtlety of the present One Vehicle.

To say that it transcends the three teachings and four periods is because the various sutras of the past—whether combined, single, paired, or transitional—do not equal the pure and perfect nature of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Regarding the "opening" discussed in terms of absolute transcendence:
it transcends all previous coarseness such that nothing remains to be compared against it; for the subtlety of the *Lotus Sūtra* possesses the power to absolutely transcend the coarse. Thus...
It is opened by means of the Treatise. Beyond the wondrous there is no coarse; the coarse is itself the wondrous. As the Sūtra says:

"The definitive realization of the Śrāvaka Dharma is the king of all sūtras. It points out that what is practiced by the Two Vehicles is the Bodhisattva path, and that there is no other vehicle, directly revealing the single reality.
Therefore, it is said that "opening the former makes it wondrous," and so forth. Nevertheless, these two forms of the wondrous are indispensable; neither can be lacking.
If it were not distinguished through relative dependence, the teaching of the *Lotus Sūtra* as transcendent would not be revealed;
if it were not opened through absolute transcendence, one would not know that the *Lotus Sūtra* is wondrous beyond all dharmas.
[Note] Generally, when discussing the revelation of the provisional (*upāya*), there are various perspectives: by *piṭaka* (division), by teaching, by realm, by principle, and so forth.
What is here termed "sudden" and "gradual" refers to the universal revelation according to the *piṭaka*. "Sudden" and "gradual" are provisional and belong to the first four periods;

that which is neither sudden nor gradual is the real, namely the present *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, "three" is the provisional and "one" is the real. Therefore, the conclusion is reached through the opening, the abolishing, and the merging of the three.
It is said: "Therefore, it is called 'opening the provisional and revealing the real,' and so forth.

[Commentary] This explains the teachings of the section that is opened. The first line generally demonstrates that there are four aspects of the provisional and the real; namely, with respect to the sections [of the canon].

Regarding the provisional teachings (*kyōkyō*), they follow the sequence [of the nine realms]. Regarding the realms (*kai*), it opens up the breadth of the nine realms to reveal the loftiness of the Buddha-realm;

thus it is said that "the nine realms are all opened, such that there is none who does not become a Buddha. Regarding principle (*ri*), it opens up the capacities for birth-and-death, non-arising, and the immeasurable to reveal the reality of non-action (*musa*);
thus it is said that "the gate of expedient means is opened to show the mark of reality. Now, as for what follows...

This clearly explains the opening of the divisions. That is to say, the "one sudden" and "three gradual" [teachings] are all provisional. Because the *Lotus Sūtra* does not strive to preach [the truth] immediately, it is not the sudden;

because it speaks only of the unsurpassed path, it is not the gradual. This is precisely the reality (*tattva*). Furthermore, from "the three below," it clarifies the teachings within the opening of the divisions.

That is to say, since the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), *Vaipulya* (Shared), and *Pṛthaktva* (Distinct) are all provisional, they should be opened, abandoned, and harmonized. The *Pariniṣpanna* (Perfect) [is the reality].

Since the teachings are indeed real, they must likewise be manifested and established so that all may return to the One. [Appendix] Bian’e cites the *Tongji* (Comprehensive Record), which quotes the *Jijie* (Collected Explanations):
"The four periods and three teachings are all that have been opened; they are not like the *Avataṃsaka*, which is [only for those who are] deaf and mute."

Therefore, it is not sudden; because it does not follow the sequential order of the three periods, it is not gradual. Now, this sutra reveals and clarifies that there is no one who will not attain Buddhahood;
hence it is said that the convergence and entry is neither sudden nor gradual.
[Commentary] "Opening" (kai) means to initiate or to expand. Previously, it was not stated that the three [vehicles] were expedient means; therefore, the gate of expedient means was closed.
Now, it is stated that the three are expedient means; therefore, the gate of expedient means is opened. "Abolishing" (hei) is another name for relinquishing. Once opened, both are equally real.

There is no authority to debate this; in principle, it ought to be abolished. If we rely on the Dharma, then at the very moment of opening [the teaching], it is simultaneously abolished. If we rely on analogy, the meaning necessarily requires that it be opened first.
If we rely on the underlying principle, opening and abolishing occur at the same time, because it is already abolished at the moment of opening.
[Commentary] This explains the opening and closing [of the gates]. [Supplement] In the past, because the provisional concealed the real, the gate was closed.

Now, by perceiving the real within the provisional, one knows that this is the power of the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya*), who, within the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), has distinguished and taught three. Thus, the gate of skillful means is opened.
When [the provisional] is discarded, the provisional is itself the real. What the followers of the Two Vehicles practice is the Bodhisattva path; there is no longer any provisional to be discussed.

However, according to the Buddha’s method of transformation, once the Real is opened, one immediately abides in the Provisional. By way of analogy, when the flower opens, the lotus appears; logically, the opening must come first.
Yet, regarding the ultimate principle of reality, that principle transcends priority and sequence; it is such that opening and discarding are simultaneous.

[Note] Some may say: "The current text opens [the teaching], abandons [the provisional], and reunites [with the ultimate], which accords with the first volume of the *Xuánzàn* (Profound Commentary). While there is no doctrinal contradiction in matching this with the 'Four and One,' that passage does not explicitly pair them;
its phrasing is redundant there. In the present context, it simply serves to conclude the preceding section on the opening of the divisions."

This interpretation seems somewhat plausible; for it is the nature of the *Lotus Sūtra* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) to open, abolish, and reunify the three vehicles. This is as stated in the following passage:
"It universally opens, reunifies, and abolishes the coarseness of the preceding four flavors."

[Supplementary Note] This selection differentiates [the teachings and the principle] from the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and the *Jian* (Commentary), which correspond to the "Four" and the "One. The preface to the *Xuanyi* states:

"It sweeps away the attachment to the teaching of the 'City of Transformation' and abolishes the stagnant sentiments of the 'Thatched Hut. The *Jian* judges this to be the Teaching; it opens the provisional gate of skillful means and reveals the wondrous principle of reality.
The *Jian* judges this to be the Principle; it unifies the minor practices of various virtues and returns them to the One, which is vast and great."

The "vehicle" (yāna) refers to the practice; the "prognosticating tally" (shanjian) refers to the person. Those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties are all granted the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).

Thus, the three categories—abandonment, convergence, and so forth—are combined with the superior, middling, and inferior faculties to correspond to the "four ones" (the four teachings and the one vehicle). However, in that [previous] context, they do not correspond; there, the text seems to be a redundant restatement.
In the present text, there is no need to correspond them to the "four ones"; it merely serves to conclude the preceding section and open the current division, which is logically sound.

This is the constant [truth]. [Commentary] It says below: "Coming to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one universally opens and sets aside the coarse [teachings] of the four preceding flavors, causing them to become the wondrous One Vehicle.
Therefore, it is appropriate to conclude the meaning of what precedes."
[Note] Previously, regarding the "opening of the provisional" (*kaiken*), there was a distinction made between "same essence" (*dōtai*) and "different essence" (*itai*).

However, if one discusses it from the perspective of the Buddha’s intention—concerning both the essence of the Dharma that is opened and the wondrous [wisdom] that performs the opening—all are of the same essence. It is simply that the mental dispositions of the sentient beings to whom the provisional is opened were formerly attached to them as being different;
therefore, they had to be opened. As the *Shiki* (Sub-commentary) says: "The Dharma is fundamentally wondrous; its coarseness arises from the mental dispositions of beings. But...
When their dispositions are opened, principle naturally returns to its source. Furthermore, the *Xuánwén* states: "It opens up the differences of the past to reveal the sameness of the present.
Thus, opening the dispositions of the capacities specifically means opening the distinct bodies.
[Commentary] This distinguishes between those of the same substance (*ekadravya*) and those of different substances (*nānādravya*). As the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:

"Some claim that the Perfect [Teaching] and the three other teachings are distinct from one another; thus, 'opening up the provisional' (*kaikuan*) refers to opening up the different substances of these three teachings.

If the present Perfect and the former Perfect were non-dual and without distinction—being of the same substance—then there would be no need to open them up. This is explained in terms of the distinctions between the teachings.

This is my view. Some say that it not only opens up [the teachings of] different entities, but also opens up those of the same entity; this is the sense of a comprehensive sublation based on the various schools.

However, the "Dharma-body" opened up in the present treatise refers precisely to the Dharma of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), *Vaipulya* (Shared), and *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) vehicles discussed in the preceding four flavors.
The "subtle" [wisdom] that performs the opening refers to the pure, perfect, and subtle Dharma of the present *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Nevertheless...
Regarding the fact that all aspects of the Buddha’s intent share the same essence: the Sūtra states, "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, expound all dharmas through countless skillful means;
these dharmas are all for the sake of the Single Buddha Vehicle. Therefore, they are of the same essence.

It is only because of the dispositions of those to be awakened that they are grasped as being different. As Kāśyapa said: "World-Honored One, since the World-Honored One has long been preaching the Dharma in the past, at that time I..."
While sitting, the body becomes weary and lax; one merely contemplates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Regarding the Bodhisattva teachings—such as sporting with supernatural powers, purifying Buddha-lands, and maturing sentient beings—the mind finds no joy. This is the attachment to divergent sentiments.

It must be opened. Below, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) and *Xuanyu* (Profound Meaning) are cited to prove that from the perspective of the mental dispositions of the faculties (*indriya*), the specific opening [of the teaching] constitutes a distinct entity.

[Appendix] In the "Chapter on Various Names of the Dharma Jewel" within the *Fanyi Mingyi Ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings), there is a discussion distinguishing between identical and distinct entities.
△ Second, the names "expedient" (*upāya*) and "real" (*tattva*) apply universally.
Regarding these terms "expedient" and "real," their names are common to both the ancient and the present, yet their meanings differ.

[Commentary] "Expedient" refers to a strategic device; it is employed temporarily and then discarded. "Real" refers to the actual record; it is the ultimate destination. In the past, there was a partiality...

The meaning of the equality between the provisional and the real for both self and others is perfected. Now, there is the meaning of establishing the provisional for the sake of the real and opening the provisional to reveal the real;
thus, the meanings differ. In the past, the provisional and the real each followed their own paths; now, all that is provisional leads toward the real; thus, the intentions differ.

The *Myōryaku* (Tiantai’s *Commentary on the Lotus Sutra*), fascicle 10, states: "The terminology of 'provisional' and 'real' is not unique to this sutra alone. The words regarding their mutual identity originate from [the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*]."
[This passage. [Commentary:
This explains that the intended meanings of the provisional and the real differ between the ancient and modern [interpretations]. As Master Zhi said: "The first three teachings..."

The provisional and the real are not identical; the Great and the Small are separated by a gulf. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional and the real are non-dual: the provisional is itself the real, and the real is itself the provisional.
This meaning differs from that of the former sutras, where the provisional and the real were merely expedient means (*siddhānta*) employed to accord with the capacities of sentient beings.

In this present sutra, the real is used to establish the provisional, with the intent being directed toward the real; the opening of the provisional to reveal the real has as its intent the real itself.

The meaning of "provisional" (*quán*) here differs from that [in other texts]. Miaole states: "In various sutras where provisional wisdom (*quánzhì*) is taught, the provisional is not identical to the real;
consequently, the teachings are not all-encompassing and the various capacities of beings are not harmonized. Thus, the teaching masters differ accordingly.

In those sutras where real wisdom (*shízhì*) is clarified, it is the real external to the provisional; therefore, the dispelling of doubts is not universal, as it does not reach the extent of what is taught in this sutra regarding the bestowal [of the Dharma]."
Regarding the meaning of "expedient" (*upāya*): since all delusions have already been shattered, it is said that the expedient is identical to the real.

Furthermore, as this present sutra is fundamentally intended to reveal the Real and sever all doubts, it is said that the expedient is identical to the Real. Thus, the relationship between the expedient and the Real is not unique to this sutra alone.

The identity of characteristics arises from this. [Note: "Separate and Perfect" regarding self and others refers to the meanings of the separation between the partial and the perfect, such as the distinction between one's own practice and the transformation of others.
△ Second, listing the two categories of the provisional and the real from the past. First, a general indication of the distinctions between the sudden and the gradual:
that prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the provisional and the real were not the same, and the Great and Small Vehicles were separated.

[Note] The following section explains the provisional and the real according to the present [teaching], wherein the underlying meaning differs. At the beginning of the text, the opening was made universal across the various divisions [of the teachings];

therefore, the sudden and gradual were treated as provisional, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* was taken as the real. This distinguishes the teachings within the former divisions, which possessed both the provisional and the real.

However, in the past, the real was subtle and wondrous while the provisional was coarse; now, by opening up the coarse so that it is immediately wondrous, the difference in their underlying meanings is finally revealed.
Now, let us first clarify the provisional and the real of the past; therefore it is said: "Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the provisional and the real were not the same.

[Commentary] At the beginning of the text, this is discussed in terms of the scriptural divisions (*piṭaka*); thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is neither sudden nor gradual, and is termed the "One Real" (the One Vehicle). The preceding four periods [of teaching] are as follows:

The sections on the Sudden and Gradual teachings are collectively termed "expedient" (*upāya*). This serves to distinguish the teachings within the previous sections, wherein there are both expedient and real aspects—such as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra, which possesses one reality alongside one expedient means.
However, in the previous teachings, the expedient and the real were divided into two distinct categories of coarse and subtle;
in the present sūtra, the coarse is itself the subtle. Now, first, the following section clarifies the expedient and the real of the past. For...
The foundation for what follows below is revealed here.

[Note] "Provisional" and "real" refer to the partial and the perfect; "small" and "great" refer to the half and the full. Alternatively, "provisional" and "real" may refer to the teaching (dharma), while "small" and "great" refer to the person.
In times past, these meanings were all present.
[Commentary] This explains the meaning of the provisional and the real, as well as the Great and the Small, through two pairs of analogies. First, the pair of principle and metaphor:

the principle of the partial and small is called provisional, while the principle of the perfect and full is called real. The "half-syllable" (ardhamātrā) is a metaphor for the Small Vehicle, and the "full-syllable" (pūrṇamātrā) is a metaphor for the Great Vehicle.
Second, the pair of persons and dharmas: the teachings of the Three Vehicles are called provisional, while the teachings of the One Vehicle are [called real].
In truth, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are "great persons," while the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are "lesser persons.

Furthermore, regarding the explanation of the terms "Great" and "Small," or "Half" and "Full" in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), one must first distinguish them by speaking of them in their general sense.

That is to say, "Great" and "Small" may refer to the practitioners of the three teachings within the Mahāyāna (*Yan*), or they may refer to the persons of the three vehicles within the *Zang* (Tripitaka) teaching. As for the "Great among the Great," it may...

This refers to those who have attained the ultimate fruit of the Three Teachings; alternatively, it may refer to those at the causal stage of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); or it may refer exclusively to those who have attained the ultimate fruit of the Perfect Teaching.
Regarding "small, medium, and great," these may refer to Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka (Sanzang) school, or they may refer exclusively to those who have attained the Buddha-fruit.
Since this is the case regarding the "Great" and "Small," it is likewise so for the "Half" and "Full.

[Commentary] However, while the intent of the text primarily clarifies the provisional and the real within the former divisions, its further clarification of the "Great" and "Small" must be understood as follows:

the provisional permeates the partial teachings, yet it does not specifically reveal the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) practitioners of the Tripiṭaka within the provisional. Throughout the preceding four periods, they remained separated from the Great Vehicle.

Only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does one finally attain entry into the Perfect [Teaching]. Therefore, while the treatise discusses the provisional and the real, it further clarifies the Great and Small Vehicles;

yet, although it clarifies the Great and Small, these do not transcend the provisional and the real. As stated in the following passage: "Reiterating the provisional teachings of the previous four periods" refers precisely to those of small capacity.
[Commentary] This explanation further clarifies the meaning of "Great" and "Small. The first two phrases state the intent and cite the text. "One must know," and so forth, is an exhortation.
Regarding "the provisional [teachings] that encompass the partial teachings": this refers to the three teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka), *Vaipulya*, and *Pratyekabuddha*.

Since these are the skillful, provisional manifestations of the Tathāgata, they may be termed "partial. Within these provisional teachings, "those of small capacity for the Tripitaka" specifically points to...

The preceding four periods represent those of dull faculties. As for the entry into the Perfect [Teaching] of the *Lotus Sūtra*, Śāriputra said, "Only today do I know that I am truly a son of the Buddha," and the five hundred disciples said, "Only now do we know that we are indeed Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, by clarifying the Great and Small Vehicles in addition to the provisional and the real, the meaning is finally complete and sufficient.

△ Second, the separate enumeration of the two categories of the former period: the coarse and the subtle. First, the explanation of the Sudden (Dunbu) school. First, the separation of the provisional from the fundamental intention.

As in the time of the *Avataṃsaka*, one is provisional and one is real (the Perfect Real [the ultimate] distinguishes itself from the provisional); they do not mutually interpenetrate. Because the Great does not contain the Small, the Small...

Although they were seated there, they were as if deaf or mute; therefore, although the Dharma-gate he preached was vast and perfect, it did not fully encompass all those with karmic affinity, nor did it fully express the Tathāgata’s original intent for appearing in the world.

[Note] "One provisional and one real" explains the difference between the provisional and the real. "The Great does not admit the Small" explains that the Great and the Small are separated from one another.

Now, this specifically refers to the Great being separated from the Small; thus, although the Small is present in the assembly, they are as if deaf and mute. The *Jieshan* (Explanatory Subcommentary), Fascicle 1, section 11, states:

"In the *Avataṃsaka*, even those with the great capacity are still separated from the distinct [teaching], and those with the small capacity are obscured, hearing nothing at all. Therefore, it is simply..."
To establish the names "Sudden" and "Great" without establishing the designation "The Sole Subtlety of the One Vehicle" is not the Buddha’s original intent;
it is for this reason. If even the "Sudden" and "Great" of the *Avataṃsaka* are not yet his original intent, how much more so the case of the Deer Park?

Therefore, at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka teachings and within those sections, because the coarse aspects have not yet been fully exhausted, the title "Subtle" is entirely absent. This can be understood by comparing it with the *Vaipulya* and *Prajñāpāramitā* teachings (as stated in the text).
[Commentary] This clarifies the sudden and great teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*. Compared to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it is still separated by the "distinct" (or "separate") teaching;

furthermore, because those of the Lesser Vehicle do not hear of the Great, it does not establish the designation of the "solely wondrous One Vehicle. Therefore, it does not fully express the Buddha’s original intent.
Regarding "the Tripitaka being the foremost": the Tripitaka is the foremost among the four teachings; it is the shallowest among the shallow. How could it be called "wondrous"?
Furthermore, as for the section expounded at the Deer Park assembly, what is elucidated therein is merely the coarse level of the Shared Teaching, which is still not yet comprehensive.

How much more so regarding the subtlety of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao)! Thus, the designation "subtle" is entirely transcended. This "entire transcendence" is spoken in contrast to what is not yet transcended.

If one were to apply the milk and the two types of cream across the various teachings (bù) in a general manner, it would not accord with the original intent. For example, if one applies them according to the specific distinctions of the teachings (jiào), there may still be a sense of subtlety;
therefore, they have not yet reached total transcendence.
△ Second, the coarse teachings must be revealed and clarified.

Why is this? In the initial Sudden Teaching (the *biejiao*), there is one coarse [teaching] (the Separate Teaching) and two sublime [teachings] (the Perfect Teaching). If it were merely one sublime teaching, it would be no different from the *Lotus Sūtra*.
If it is indeed one coarse teaching, it must wait for the *Lotus Sūtra* to reveal, harmonize, and subsume it before it can finally be called "sublime."
【□Note】Why is this so? This inquiry arises because the previous explanation failed to fully express the original intention.

All of this is due to the fact that in the past, one was unable to reveal the subtle within the coarse. Therefore, from here on, the various sections are examined to distinguish the teachings, clearly judging and clearly revealing them.
