This records the intent of the inquiry and its explanation: it means that the texts of the initial *Dunbu* (Sudden Division) and others clearly establish [the teachings] as distinct, whereas they must await the texts of the *Fahua* (Lotus Sūtra) and others to be revealed as one.
[Note] Regarding the "initial *Dunbu* and others," this specifically clarifies the coarse teachings within the Sudden; they must await the "opening and unification" because of the timing.
People say this is because the *Avataṃsaka* is superior.
[Commentary] This judgment that the *Avataṃsaka* is "coarse" refers to the Master Xuánxuān of the Huánxian school. The *Huáyán Chāo* (Notes on the Avataṃsaka) states:
In the *Fǎhuá Shū* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), while praising Śāriputra’s three requests, it says: "No other sutra contains such earnest and persistent requests as these. Only...
The Bodhisattva Vimukticandra in the *Avataṃsaka* requested [the teaching] from Vajragarbha; this may be cited as a parallel case.
However, in that instance, the requester was a person seeking the causal dharma, whereas here, the request is for the Buddha-wisdom; thus, they are not the same.

This current *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is inferior to the *Avataṃsaka*, because the former involves a request by a single family, while the latter involves requests by three families; furthermore, the former was requested by Śrāvakas, whereas this is...

In the *Avataṃsaka*, the request is made by Bodhisattvas alone and consists of only three requests; in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there are five requests, and these include a request made by the Buddha himself.

Consequently, some claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is superior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Therefore, the *Shiqian* states: "The various masters who have propagated the sutras since antiquity did not understand the Buddha’s intent.
Seeing that the *Avataṃsaka* has extensive matters and voluminous texts and that the Bodhisattvas presented their requests, they claimed that the *Avataṃsaka* was [superior]."
The *Lotus Sūtra* is superior. Since recent times, those who have read the teachings of our mountain school (the Tendai) have still maintained this view:

that teachers merely compare the status of the patrons to determine superiority or inferiority, rather than asserting that the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* is superior to this [other teaching].

Yet, contemporary masters claim that the essence of the teaching (*shikishin*) is superior to the *Lotus Sūtra*. Is this not an error? Therefore, following the judgment at the end of the present text, it concludes: [...the *Lotus Sūtra* is superior.]
He opens up one aspect of its coarseness to demonstrate that the *Lotus Sūtra* alone is uniquely wondrous, supreme, and perfect.

[Note] This refers to the ancient master’s *Huayan Chao* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka), not the sub-commentaries of Master Qingliang. *Bian'e* states: "This is a treatise by Master Guan that strikes the mark. Jingxi said:
'When the Buddha preached the *Avataṃsaka*, first, it did not encompass those of small capacity; second, it did not open up the provisional.'"

Because he did not reveal his origins, his original intent was not yet fully expressed. Since Qingliang studied under Jingxi, when he interpreted the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he entirely employed the *Lotus Sūtra*’s method of revealing and clarifying the perfect meaning to integrate it.

For instance, in the *Xuántán* (Profound Discourse), he takes the "causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching" as the first section, stating that the Tathāgata appeared in the world for the sake of the one great causal event (*ekamahā-karaṇīya-hetu-pratyaya*), desiring to cause all sentient beings...
"Generating the opening, revealing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. This marks the beginning of the "Chapter on the Exquisite Adornments.

At the very moment of attaining perfect enlightenment, the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*—which was established long ago—is pointedly introduced. Throughout every section, the principle of opening, revealing, and perfectly realizing [the truth] is applied;
this remains consistent from beginning to end. Had the *Lotus Sūtra* not come to this land, those who comment upon this scripture would have remained entirely ignorant of its opening and revealing.
How can the coarse be transformed into the sublime? In my humble opinion, the text of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* also subtly hints at this in one or two phrases that reveal its true origin;
however, it is not as explicit and fully manifest as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Therefore, Jingxi [Zhiyi] judged it to be "not yet revealing the origin.
Since Master Qingliang already understood the revelation and manifestation [of the Buddha-nature], his commentary on the *Avataṃsaka* logically ought to be thus. Future scholars should simply...
One should take it as one’s duty to investigate the teachings and contemplations with precision.
△ Second, the judgment of the three gradual stages:

Next, at the Deer Park, there is only the coarse and no subtle (the Tripitaka Teaching); next, at the Vaipulya, there are three that are coarse (the Shared and Distinct Teachings) and one that is subtle (the Perfect Teaching); next, at the Prajñā...
If there are two types of "coarse" (referring to both the general and specific) and one type of "subtle" (the Perfect Teaching).
[Note] This is a judgment of coarse and subtle within the preceding sections based on the principle of mutual relativity (*dai-tai*).
Regarding this textual analysis of the "Severance" (斷), the first three gradual stages can be understood.
△ Third, the unique excellence of this present sutra has two parts. First, opening up the previous sections. Second, first, opening up the partial and coarse to reveal the wondrous.

Arriving at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the former four flavors are all opened up and subsumed; their coarseness is discarded, and they are made to become the wondrousness of the One Vehicle.
[Note] This opening of the former four flavors refers to the coarseness of the three teachings within the "heavy" category, which are made to become the wondrousness of the present One Vehicle.

Furthermore, as for the provisional persons of the three teachings within the former sections, upon arriving at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they must be exclusively opened up. As for the provisional fruits of the three teachings, fundamentally...

This is the perfect fruit; how could it be further opened so as to become a perfect Buddha? If it concerns the provisional [teachings] adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, there is no impediment to discussing such an opening, as when it is said that the six-foot form in its soiled robes was revealed, and so forth.
[Commentary] The first line clarifies how the coarse teachings are opened to become sublime. The *Tongji* states:

"The coarse aspects of the preceding four flavors are opened, the coarse aspects of the preceding four flavors are unified, and the coarse aspects of the preceding four flavors are discarded; therefore, the single character 'total' (zǒng) is prefixed, signifying 'opening, unifying, and discarding.'"
In the first four periods, the two teachings and the two vehicles, as well as the bodhisattvas of the three teachings, possessed coarse distinctions in person, teaching, principle, and practice;
now, with the arrival of the Lotus Sūtra, these have all become subtle and wondrous. Thus it is said that they are perfected into the wondrous One Vehicle.

Furthermore, in the previous sections below, it was clarified that those of coarse capacity are opened to become wondrous. As for the statement that those of provisional capacity in the three teachings must invariably be opened, it is because:
Since the coarse teachings received have already been opened, the coarse persons who receive them must likewise be opened.
This is because, by practicing according to the coarse teachings, they can only create [rebirths] up to three or four hundred *yojanas* in height; they ultimately cannot reach the Precious Place.
Therefore, it is necessary to open them exclusively. As for the provisional fruits of the Three Teachings not being opened, it is because the [Ultimate] is subtle...
Xuán says: Where else could there be four distinct teaching masters, each with their own body and each speaking with their own mouth?
One should know that this is merely the concealment of his infinitely adorned body to manifest as the six bodies of the written word.

If one opens the gate of skillful means and reveals the true aspect, then these very bodies are the perfect and eternal body. [Supplement] A provisional discourse for the sake of those to be converted.

"Open. Regarding the phrase "like opening a soiled garment," the *Miaoxuan* states: "The provisional and the real of transforming others are identical to the provisional and the real of one's own practice (*xing*).

This is like a person inside a soiled garment who is actually an elder. The provisional and the real of the self-practice that embodies both self-benefit and benefiting others is the treatise on one's own practice.
It is like all activities of livelihood and production, which are entirely non-different from the true aspect (*shixiang*)."

They are mutually contradictory. Yet, in every single form and every single fragrance, there is nothing that is not the Middle Way; how much more so for the reality of one's own practice—could it possibly not be real?
△ Second, opening up the past to perfect the wondrous [reality]. First, it is wondrous because it is fundamentally fused.

The Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of the various flavors does not require further opening; it is inherently perfect and harmonious from the beginning, and thus does not depend on being opened. [Commentary:
Furthermore, since the three teachings have already been opened within the previous sections, must the "Perfect" [teaching] of those previous sections also be opened?

Therefore, the text below immediately states, "the Perfect of the various flavors," and so forth. This is because the present Perfect and the past Perfect are not distinct as two separate Perfections; this is based on the distinction between the teachings (*jiao*).

[Supplement] This clarifies that the original perfection of the past was inherently wondrous. The first line raises a question regarding the partial [teachings] in contrast to the perfect; the subsequent "Therefore" section provides the answer;

and the final three lines provide a definitive explanation that the original perfection of the past was inherently wondrous and not yet opened [to its full potential]. The *Tongji* states: "In the past, the Perfect and Sudden did not require..."
Regarding further openings: in the *Avataṃsaka*, the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are the three non-differentiated; in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, all that is defiled and pure is interpenetrating;
in the *Vimalakīrti*, inconceivable pores contain and encompass all; and in the *Cintyagupta* and *Jālinīprabha*, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.
Prajñā: All phenomena are intermingled and non-dual. These perfect principles are no different and no distinct from the Buddha’s knowledge and vision in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
How could there be anything further to be revealed?

[Commentary] If Miaole says that a person of the Perfect [Teaching] at the initial stage must hear the revelation of the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena, this is because there are two possible directions for a person of the Perfect [Teaching] from the past.

Regarding the "initial stage of names," this refers to the Perfect being separated from the Partial; upon hearing the Buddha’s revelation of the provisional, the attachment to the separation from the partial is extinguished, yet the Perfect essence itself has not been revealed.
If one has already entered the Real through the stage of contemplative practice (kuan-hsing), then one only discusses further progress, as follows:

The sutra distinguishes the assembly by stating: "Except for the multitude of bodhisattvas whose power of faith is firm. This refers to those [of the ten stages of faith] whose five grades of faith-power are firm (the ten *śraddhā*).

[Commentary] This explains that those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan) at the initial stage must hear the text on the revelation of the provisional (kaixian). There are two directions: namely, that the former Perfect was separated from the Partial (pian), whereas the present Perfect is not separated from it.
Therefore, one is a person of "Name-Identity" (mingzi-ji) by virtue of hearing the revelation of the provisional; through this, the attachment to the separation from the partial is extinguished.

As cited below from the sutra, the Bodhisattva of the Power of Faith (Xinli) refers to the stage of contemplative practice (guanxing-wei), who has already perfectly subdued the five abodes (wu-zhu) and is firm and stable.

The Bodhisattva refers to the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Since they have already shattered the *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions of views) and *kleśa-heya* (delusions of thought), as well as the *rajas-aṇu* (delusions like motes of dust), this section discusses only their further advancement.
[Note] Furthermore, Miaole states: "This present sutra is the Perfect [Teaching], yet it must still be opened and revealed; this is because it reveals the Perfection within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."
It is not merely that it transcends the previous four periods; it must also open and reveal all the teachings.

[■ Record] This citation explains that the *Lotus Sūtra* is the Perfect [Teaching]. It refers to the passage concerning its necessity to "open and reveal," meaning that the *Lotus Sūtra* is purely perfect and uniquely wondrous;
it not only stands far beyond the four periods, but can also open and reveal all the sudden and gradual teachings. Now, it is established as the Perfect.
"Exquisite.
△ Second, "exquisite" is used only here [in this section].

However, because this merely involves a partial inclusion or a relative comparison within the same category, it does not equal the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, which is pure, singular, and without admixture.

[Commentary] To judge correctly, the schools of the past belong to the coarse category. With the exception of the Deer Park [teachings], although they all possess the Perfect [teaching], because they are mixed with other elements, they cannot be called "sublime.
Whether a coarse person or a subtle person, both commit an error. This is a general refutation based on the categories of the schools.

[Commentary] This explains that the former Perfect [Teaching] was still coarse. That is to say, the *Avataṃsaka* was coarse in relation to the One Vehicle; the *Vaipulya* was coarse in contrast to the Three Vehicles;

and the *Prajñāpāramitā* was coarse in comparison to the Two Vehicles. Therefore, the former Perfect Teaching was still within the realm of conceptual thought and could not be called "wondrous" (*miau*).
Therefore, those who are coarse individuals have obstructions that prevent them from reaching the pure, perfect, and uniquely wondrous state. [Appendix] The supplementary note states:

regarding the terms "coarse person" and "subtle person," this phrase originates from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. A "coarse person" refers to one who commits coarse offenses; a "subtle person" refers to one who commits subtle offenses.
Now, borrowing this for comparison: there is certainly a fault in the "coarse" that is being encompassed;
likewise, there is also a fault in the "subtle" that encompasses it, as it cannot cause the coarse to become subtle.

[Commentary] The *Shiqian* (Expository Notes on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 1, part 10, states: "From the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at its beginning to the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* at its end, although the names differ, they are all subsumed within the sequential three truths (*tisraḥ satyāni*).
Only when this present sutra brings them together with reality can it be called 'perfectly interfused' (*pariniṣpanna-yuganaddha*). (Text)
[Commentary] This citation explains that what was previously coarse is now sublime. Regarding the "successive three truths": the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya) sweeps away [delusions];
the Truth of Conventional Reality (saṃvṛti-satya) establishes [phenomena]; and the Truth of the Middle Way (madhyamā-satya) negates both, being neither ultimate nor conventional.

One practices these in succession, with the three truths remaining distinct. The scriptural collections of former times were considered coarse for this reason. Regarding the "perfectly integrated three truths": the three—ultimate, conventional, and middle—are simultaneous.

They are identical; neither before nor after, they transcend thought and transcend discourse. Since this present sutra opens up and unifies all dharmas, it is said that "square" (fang) is now termed "perfectly interfused" (yuanrong).

[Commentary] Therefore, at the beginning of the text, when opening up the teachings according to the various sections, one must say that it "opens up" the preceding sudden and gradual teachings, and so forth.
This section concludes the text and clarifies the intent behind opening the provisional.
△ Second, revealing the present division has two parts. First, the reason for receiving its name:
it alone receives the name "wondrous" (miao), and this is truly for a specific reason.

[Commentary] As discussed above regarding the provisional and the ultimate, the theory of the "absolute" (juedai) reveals the truth. From the perspective of the distinct teachings (*yijiao*), there is differentiation; from the perspective of the various sections (*yubu*), there is universal sublation.

Through this process of alternating suppression and exaltation, it is finally revealed that the *Lotus Sūtra* transcends all other teachings. Its section is perfect and its teaching is perfect; its subtle excellence surpasses all other scriptures, fulfilling the Buddha’s original intent for appearing in the world.
This is fully expressed herein. Therefore, the text immediately cites the "Fourfold One" (*sishi*) from the sūtra as proof.

[■ Record] This follows the preceding text regarding the "one coarse and one subtle" of the Sudden Teaching (*tōbu*). It is a judgment based on relative comparison (*sōtai ronhan*). Reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* (*Hokke*), all are universally opened to become "sublime" (*myō*);
this is a discourse based on absolute transcendence (*zettai ka-ron*). The distinction between "separately granting" (*betsu-yo*) and "generally revoking" (*tsū-tatsu*) is seen above.

[■ Commentary] *Bennyō* states: "Relative comparison" (*sōtai*) is for the purpose of overturning; "absolute transcendence" (*zettai*) is for the purpose of covering over. "Separately granting" (*betsu-yo*) is for the purpose of exalting; "generally revoking" (*tsū-tatsu*) is for the purpose of suppressing.
△ Second, citing evidence for the "purely one" [vehicle]. Thus the text says:
"In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third" (the unity of teaching).

"Directly abandoning expedient means, he speaks only of the unsurpassed path" (the unity of practice). "He acts solely for the sake of bodhisattvas, not for those of the Lesser Vehicle" (the unity of persons). Worldly...
The intermediate characteristics are eternally abiding (the principle is one).
[Note] Because it is pure and singular, it alone receives the name "wondrous. Therefore, "one" is cited to manifest the "wondrous"; for indeed, one is precisely the wondrous.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "The 'Fourfold Identity' originated with the Guangzhai [School]. Today’s school follows the old [tradition], yet also establishes a 'Fourfold Identity.

The old [tradition] spoke of 'Identity of the Fruit,' while today we speak of 'Identity of Principle. Without the seal of principle, one's teaching is identical to that of Māra. The old [tradition] spoke of 'Identity of the Cause.'"

Now, it is said that "practice is one. Because it is spoken of as a cause, it is singular; because practice extends through both cause and effect, it involves both person and teaching. This is no different from the previous [teachings]. [Note:
The phrase "the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are equal" is stated according to their commonality and is also based on the Buddha’s intention. It refers to the Dharma of the One Vehicle.

This is because the *bù* (division) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*) is perfect. "Neither two nor three" means that, regarding numerical categories, there is no duality of the "half" and "full" teachings characteristic of the Shared Teaching (*tōngjiào*);

there is no triad of vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching (*sānzàngjiào*); and there is no "remaining vehicle," which refers to the absence of the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*) and the Perfect [Teaching] entering the Distinct.
Regarding divisions (*bù*), there is no duality implied by the *Prajñāpāramitā* [Sūtras], nor the triad contrasted with the Vaipulya [Sūtras].

The Vaipulya treasury subsumes the Deer Park [teachings]; the distinction between the two *sūtras* (the *Prajñāpāramitā* and *Saṃdhinirmocana*) encompasses the *Avataṃsaka*. Because there is only the single Buddha-vehicle, it is said that the teaching is one.
[Commentary] This explains that the teaching is one. Regarding the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there are two perspectives. First, speaking according to their commonality:
it means that just as space is boundless, so too are the worlds and the various Buddha-lands boundless; within them, he provides guidance and transformation.

Each [teaching] is according to what is appropriate for the occasion. Sometimes the One Vehicle is used to reach those of lower capacity; sometimes the Three Vehicles are employed to respond to various needs.

The present mention of "the Buddha-lands of the ten directions" refers to those places where the One Vehicle Dharma is equally expounded. Second, this is from the perspective of the Buddha’s intention.
This means that the original intention of all Buddhas is to lead those to be transformed in their lands solely by means of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) Buddha-way;

there are neither two nor three. Regarding this, there are two interpretations. First, concerning the teachings: the "Shared" (Tongjiao) teaching encompasses both the "Half" of the preceding Tripitaka teaching and the "Full" of the subsequent Distinct (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) teachings.
However, the present sutra is uniquely wondrous and transcends all oppositions; therefore, it is free from the relative distinction between the Half and the Full.
Second: this present sutra is intended solely to teach the great bodhisattvas; therefore, it contains no śrāvaka disciples and no vehicle of the Tripiṭaka.

The Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddhayāna) is intended only for bodhisattvas who accumulate practices, as well as for those of a certain class of complete-capacity practitioners who enter the Separate Teaching and undergo successive cultivation over kalpas through a sequential and distributed dharma-gate.
This present sutra involves complete cultivation and complete realization; therefore, there is no Separate Teaching here.

This also includes the remainder of the distinct vehicles that are fully entered. Second, regarding the [classification by] *bù* (sections): the present sutra is neither "opposed to" (*duì*) nor "accompanied by" (*dài*).
Therefore, it lacks the three [categories] opposed by the Vaipulya (*fangděng*) and the two categories accompanied by the Prajñāpāramitā.

Furthermore, it can be understood that the Vaipulya Piṭaka subsumes the Three Piṭakas, while the distinction of the two *sū* (milk products) subsumes the Avataṃsaka. [■Note: The *Biǎn'é* says: "According to their commonalities..."

The phrasing seems to suggest there is yet another difference. In my private view, there is no difference in the Buddha’s intent; however, in the present discussion regarding the capacity of the audience (*mārga*), the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) specifically adds these words.
It is as in the case of the ancient Dīpaṃkara, who did not yet preach the Dharma. The *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) further states:

"Regarding the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), one should explain that even if there is the employment of provisional means (*upāya*), there is nothing that does not reveal the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*); therefore, it is said that there is 'only' [the One Vehicle]."

"There is only the One Vehicle; there is no other vehicle. According to the verse in the sutra, there is indeed no mention of "no other vehicle," yet its appearance in the commentary (*shu*) is actually a reversal of the phrasing used to explain the phrase "there is only the One Vehicle," thereby supplementing the distinct teaching (*biejiao*). The term "supplement" (*changchu*) should refer to the prose section (*changxing*).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Directly abandoning expedient means and teaching only the Unsurpassed Way," the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 5, part 5, states: "The five vehicles are crooked rather than straight;
they are partial and biased rather than correct. Now, all such biases and crookedness are abandoned, and only the single, direct path is taught.

(Text) According to the *Shu* (Sub-commentary), this refers to the category of "Teaching" (*jiao*) because it concerns the exposition of the extremes; however, here, based on the name "Way" (*dao*), which signifies the capacity for universal penetration, it is therefore categorized as [the category of "Principle"].
"Practicing the One.
[Commentary] This explains "practicing the One. It means that the five vehicles are the Tathāgata’s skillful and expedient teachings according to circumstances, rather than direct discourse.
Furthermore, it causes those of the two vehicles to sever their afflictions, realize bodhi, and depart from birth and death.
Attaining nirvana through these means is entirely crooked rather than straight. Regarding the terms "comprehensive," "distinctive," "partial," and "peripheral":

the comprehensive teaching (tongjiao) is peripheral to the two vehicles; the distinctive teaching (biejiao) is partial to the bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is said that they are partial and peripheral rather than central.

This present sutra abandons those partialities of the comprehensive and distinctive teachings, as well as the crookedness of the five vehicles, and speaks only of the pure, perfect, upright, and direct single path. That is to say:
This is the wondrous practice of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Some claim that the commentary explains this passage as belonging to the "unity of teaching" (*ekavidha-śāsana*).

Why, then, do you now say it belongs to the "unity of practice" (*ekavidha-caryā*)? Therefore, it is said: the commentary relies on the aspect of verbal expression and thus belongs to the unity of teaching, for the speech of the Sage is called "teaching.

Now, we follow the sense of being able to penetrate [to the Way], and thus it belongs to the unity of practice; for through the forward progression of practice, one is able to penetrate to the Way. Its...
The meaning is the same.

[Note] "But for the sake of the bodhisattvas" refers to the Buddha’s intention; it means that while previously, according to expedient means, he taught and transformed those of the three vehicles, now they are all of one kind—bodhisattvas—and thus it is said that "the persons are one."

[Commentary] This is the first explanation of persons. It means that although the Buddha, according to his true intention, taught the three vehicles (*triyāna*), he did so solely for the sake of transforming bodhisattvas.

However, based on the past, he employed skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) to teach the dharmas of the Truths (*satya*), the Causal Links (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the Perfections (*pāramitā*) in order to transform those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities.
Nevertheless, while in the past there may have been distinctions between the three types of persons, in the present they are all of one kind: the bodhisattva cause.
He is a person.

[Commentary] Regarding "the marks of the world are eternally abiding": the distinct and differentiated marks of the ten realms, both the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhipati*), are called the "marks of the world.

Because they are identical to the Principle (*li*), they are all eternally abiding. If one views them through the lens of emotional perception (*qing-jian*), they appear as arising and ceasing, shifting and flowing; yet, when this emotional perception is cleared away, they are vast and empty.

Forget it. All phenomena are eternally abiding. Since the eternal is identical to the nature, it is neither eternal nor non-eternal. This is what is meant by "the words are partial, but the meaning is perfect.
Students should understand and realize this.

[Commentary] This interpretation is based on the single principle. That is to say, whether it be the four noble ones or the six classes of ordinary beings, whether it be the environment as the support or the sentient beings as the supported—whatever their various forms and distinct appearances may be, these are called "worldly marks. Because these marks are identical to the principle, they are all eternally abiding.
Thus, the singing of birds, the smiling of flowers, the movement of the wind, and the flying of dust—all phenomena (dharmas) span from antiquity to the present. Head... [text breaks off].
The head is without transition or change; that is to say, whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, its nature and characteristics abide eternally.

It is only when viewed with the eye of the Way that it is thus. However, if one views through the discriminations of emotional perception regarding arising and ceasing, then the lands undergo formation, subsistence, destruction, and emptiness.

The birth, aging, illness, and death of sentient beings all arise from delusive confusion; thus, there is constant flux. Therefore it is said: "When a single speck of film is in the eye, illusory flowers fall in disarray.

If one can immediately understand and immediately practice, turning the hearing back toward one's own nature, then in a single moment, when the mind is vast and empty and emotional attachments are forgotten, all phenomena will abide eternally.
[Supplementary Note: This means that the sense faculties do not pursue external objects, and external objects do not drag the mind away. The faculties...
When the dust of sensory objects is freed from its attachment, discriminatory thought does not arise. The revolving flow of delusion returns to true nature;

once nature is tranquil, its manifestations are likewise eternally abiding. In every land and every particle of dust, phenomena abide in their respective positions. And within this abiding of phenomena in their positions...
Non-characteristic is itself characteristic; characteristic is itself non-characteristic. It is neither characteristic nor non-characteristic; it is neither abiding nor non-abiding.
Beyond the paths of speech and thought, where cessation and illumination occur simultaneously, one then realizes the true, eternally abiding principle of all characteristics.

This should be realized at the moment when the numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the faculties and their objects, and when, having passed away, one revives once more. Suddenly, one attains spontaneous awakening; this is not a matter of discursive thought.
This cannot be understood through the discrimination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is identical to the state of awakening in the Chan school; thus, the ancients said:

"Exhaust all ordinary sentiments, and there will be no separate 'sage-understanding'. As for the *Fahua wenju*, it holds that the Buddhas' births all take Suchness (*tathatā*) as their station and all take Suchness as their characteristic;
therefore, "the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding. In the *Ji* (Commentary), however, it takes purity...
Turbid waves are not different from their moist nature; they both take moist nature as the wave. Therefore, all are explained by taking "Suchness" (tathatā) as their characteristic.
Likewise, they both take the wave as moist nature; therefore, all are explained by taking "Suchness" as their state. [Commentary] Now, regarding the permanent and the impermanent:
This is a discourse on two extremes. However, the principle within this context is the permanence of the eternally abiding nature;

it does not reside in either extreme, but is neither permanent nor impermanent—the Middle Way that negates both poles. If one speaks through verbal expression, to say "existence" loses "non-existence," and to discuss this excludes that.
If one seeks to comprehend it through the mind, to raise up one side encompasses the middle, and to contemplate the internal includes all.

Externally, one knows that while the words are partial, the meaning is perfect. Generally speaking, if one seeks through words, one misses the mark at every turn; if one realizes through wisdom, then every phenomenon is revealed.
Therefore, it is appropriate to forget emotions and dissolve [dualistic thought], so that one may silently accord with the truth.

The final two lines exhort one to resolve what can be resolved. [Supplement] There are three meanings of "realization" (*hui*): first, the mundane world; second, the world of correct awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*); third...
The world of sentient beings, the world of the three types of receptacles, and these three [worlds]—their very substance is principle (*li*).

Since the nature of principle is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, each and every one is eternally quiescent and not subject to change; each and every one is nothing other than the station of the Dharma. It is only that sentient beings are deluded and obscured.
They are unable to perceive it; within that which is eternally abiding, they falsely perceive arising and ceasing, and within True Suchness (*tathatā*), they falsely perceive flux and change.
Therefore, although the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding, they do not know them.

Only I, the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, having sat at the site of enlightenment and known it as it truly is, [realize] the ineffable, transcendent of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), and quiescent nature of reality.
One can, through skillful means, explain that this principle is one. Since the characteristics of the three worlds are all eternally abiding, the principle is therefore one.
Question: Awakening to this rational nature is called the world of true enlightenment; because it accords with the nature, it is appropriate that both the nature and its characteristics are eternal.
However, being deluded regarding this rational nature constitutes the world of sentient beings; since they are deluded regarding the nature, as for the nature—

Although the fundamental nature is eternal, its manifestations are not necessarily eternal. How could the characteristics of the world-receptacle (*bhājanaloka*) inhabited by sentient beings also be eternally abiding?
Answer: If ice and water share moisture as their common nature, then if moisture were eternal, ice would also be eternal.

Furthermore, it is like a drunkard who perceives a house as spinning; yet the house itself does not actually spin. All sentient beings possess only a "constancy of principle" (*li-chang*); they can hear [the truth] and...

Explanation: To understand [the teachings] is called "permanence of name. To contemplate and examine their essence continuously, moment after moment, is called "permanence of contemplative practice" (*guanxing*).

When coarse defilements first fall away and the six sense organs become pure, it is called "permanence of semblance. Then, there is a sudden awakening, wherein one realizes the true cause of the forty-one stages.
To partially realize the eternal is to manifest it fully and without deficiency or remainder; this constitutes ultimate eternity. [Supplementary Note] Bian’ē cites Guǎnbiāo, who says:

"All phenomena take *tathatā* (suchness) as their essence. To penetrate this essence of *tathatā*, there is no separation across the three periods of time and no obstruction throughout the ten directions.
Being doubly free from the eight inversions is precisely the true eternity of nature. As for the phrase 'the words are partial but the intent is complete,' it means that the intent transcends..."
Beyond permanence and impermanence, it further posits one form of permanence, which thereby encompasses bliss, selfhood, and purity; thus, the intention is complete.
△ Second, the refutation of errors:
People of that time had not yet attained the wondrous purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and saw only within its sections the three carts, the impoverished son, the illusory city, and so forth.

The analogy is said to be inferior to other sutras because it is not understood that the four previous stages of provisional teaching are reiterated here to uniquely manifest the Great Vehicle, to entrust the family inheritance, and to reach only the place of the supreme treasure; thus, the fault of slander is incurred.

[Commentary] Those who propagate the teachings in the present age have not yet understood the subtle and profound purport of the *Lotus Sūtra*—the opening up of provisional means (*upāya*) and the ultimate transcendence of all limitations.
Seeing only the parables of the three carts and so forth within the sūtra, they claim it does not equal the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other scriptures.

This is because they do not realize that the parables of the three carts and so forth are merely a reiteration of the provisional means of the past; the underlying intent is to show that these very provisional means are themselves the reality (*bhūta*). Thus, the three carts are cited.

The Great Vehicle, the impoverished son, the entrustment of the family estate, and the transformation city leading to the place of treasure— those who do not understand the meaning of these [parables] incur the fault of slandering the Dharma.
[Commentary] This is a general explanation of those who propagate the teaching in the present age. The "three carts" were expedient means (*upāya*) of the past;

their intent is that they are revealed as the reality (*bhūta*) in this present sutra. Therefore, the three carts, the impoverished son, and the "city of transformation" (*nirmāṇa-pura*) are cited again to manifest that what is now [offered] is the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
It is the entrustment of the family inheritance; it is the arrival at the place of treasure. [Supplementary Note] *Biànyó* states: "The 'three carts,' etc.—the 'etc. refers to..."

Regarding the term "characters" (or "names"): this refers to the seven parables as set forth in the *Dharmapada-śāstra*. Generally, for something to be counted among the parables, it must necessarily be explained in terms of the provisional and the real, as well as their bestowal and revelation, thereby manifesting the single transformation of the Buddha's teaching;
only then does it qualify for inclusion in this number. As for those who claim there are nine parables, that is incorrect.
[Note] The three carts: the sheep cart represents the Śrāvaka-yāna; the deer cart represents the Pratyekabuddha-yāna; and the water buffalo cart represents the Bodhisattva-yāna.
These are the three vehicles [taught] at the Deer Park.

[Commentary] This clarifies the analogy of the three vehicles. As the Sūtra says: "If there are sentient beings who, having heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, accept it with faith, and apply themselves with earnest diligence, desiring to quickly escape the triple world and seek their own nirvāṇa—this is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
They are like those sons who, seeking the goat-drawn carts, emerged from the burning house. If there are sentient beings who... [text continues]

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, hears the Dharma and receives it with faith; he practices with earnest diligence, seeks spontaneous wisdom, delights in solitary seclusion, and deeply understands the causes and conditions of all phenomena—this is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

It is like those sons who, seeking the deer-cart, emerged from the burning house. If there are sentient beings who, from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, hear the Dharma and receive it with faith, practicing with earnest...
With diligence, he seeks all-knowledge, the Buddha-knowledge, self-existent knowledge, and teacherless knowledge; the Tathāgata’s insight and vision, the powers, and the fearlessnesses;
out of compassion for the peace and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings, he benefits devas and humans, delivering and liberating them all.
This is called the Mahāyāna. Because Bodhisattvas seek this vehicle, they are named Mahāsattvas. They are like those sons who, seeking ox-carts, emerged from the burning house.
[Supplement] Regarding "spontaneous wisdom" (*svayambhū-jñāna*): the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states that one enters through the gateway of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This gateway is inherently present; it was not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans, and is thus called spontaneous wisdom. It is as if one were looking upon...
"One awakens to the Way through the blooming and falling of flowers. The *Kezhu* (Commentary on the Sections) states: "The Śrāvakas cannot transform others;

they are like sheep that do not look back at the herd. The *Bie xingshu* (Separate Commentary on Practice) states: "The Pratyekabuddhas are likened to deer; they still possess the intention to look back. The *Bai song jiang lu* (Lectures by Bai Song) states:
"The 'Omniscient One' (Sarvajña) is one who understands all internal and external phenomena without exception; this refers to the stage of the cause (*hetu*)."

The "Buddha-wisdom" (*buddhajñāna*) that is cultivated is the wisdom realized upon the fruition; it is the spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) obtained by one who has reached the fruit at the conclusion of the Three Piṭakas.

This is the wisdom that arises subsequently for the sake of manifesting transformative teachings, because it is able to preach the doctrine according to the capacities of sentient beings, such that the capacity and the teaching are in perfect harmony.
As for the "teacherless wisdom" (*anācārya-jñāna*), according to the explanation of the Hīnayāna, it refers only to a single Buddha transforming the world, with no others [of his kind].

There is none who can act as a teacher to the Buddha. The sixteen modes of knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), the ten powers (*bala*), and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are explained in detail within the categories of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the *Jianglu* (Lectures and Records) states: "The analogy of the ox is that the ox possesses the power to carry heavy burdens over long periods;
all such functions are the merit of transforming others."

[Commentary] Regarding the "transformed city" (化城): the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 7, section 18, states: "By means of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), that which did not exist suddenly comes into being; this is called 'transformation' (化)."
That which wards off wrongs and resists enemies is called a city. (Text) This is analogous to how the True Dharma and Nirvana can ward off the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*).
[Record] This clarifies the analogy of the conjured city (*nirmita-pura*). As the Sūtra says: "Just as that guide, for the sake of providing rest, conjured a great city.
This is called "conjured" because it exists where there was nothing and then suddenly appears. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "The Buddha-dharma is like..."
A city can protect travelers from wrongdoing and ward off enemies. However, the *nirvāṇa* of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is not the Great *Nirvāṇa* of the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
This is because the Great *Nirvāṇa* is not a mere fabrication; it does not solely serve to ward off enemies, as its nature is identical to reality and it is endowed with all virtues.
Furthermore, this *nirvāṇa* of the ultimate truth merely involves the departure from false views and the afflictions of thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). It is thus named [as such].
"Though they have attained liberation, in reality they have not yet attained ultimate liberation; therefore, it is likened to a conjured city (*nirmāṇa-pura*).
However, this single analogy of the conjured city is taught for those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).

The treatise states that [the city] does not truly exist, because for those with overweening pride (*abhimāna*), there is no actual *nirvāṇa* in their worldly, outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) samādhis and samāpattis, yet they give rise to the notion of *nirvāṇa*."

This is a perverted conceptualization. To provide an antidote to this, the parable of the conjured city is taught. [The *Jiansi jie* (Exposition on the Severing of Views and Thoughts) in four fascicles states:
"The 'place of jewels' is a metaphor for the Dharma-realm of tranquil light (*jiguang*); in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, it is called the 'jeweled island' (*baozhu*)."

[Commentary] This clarifies the analogy of the "jeweled destination" (*ratnasthāna*). Since the *śāntaprabhāsa* (tranquil light) is the true pure land upon which all Buddhas rely, it is likened to a jeweled destination five hundred *yojanas* away.

As for the "jeweled island," this refers to the four dharmas taught as the causes for *nirvāṇa* within the seventh merit described in the *Guṇarājaparivarta*: first, attending upon virtuous friends; second, single-minded...

1. Listen to the Dharma with the mind; 2. Contemplate it with focused mindfulness; 3. Practice according to the Dharma. Regarding the second point, "listening to the Dharma with a concentrated mind," it says:
For example, it is like a merchant who wishes to go to a treasure island but does not know the way; someone shows it to him.
That person followed the instructions and reached a treasure island, where they obtained many rare jewels. All sentient beings are likewise:
desiring to know the place of goodness and to gather the jewels of the Path, they do not know where the road is passable or obstructed. The Bodhisattva shows them the way;
the sentient beings follow it and reach the place of goodness, obtaining the jewel of unsurpassed Great Nirvana. By means of this...

For this reason, through the causal conditions of hearing the Dharma, one attains proximity to the Great Parinirvāṇa. The terms "treasure-place" (寶所) and "jewel-island" (寶渚) differ only in their phonetic transcription, like the dialects of Chu and Xia.

[Commentary] The first four periods were provisional; the three carts and so forth referred to the Three Baskets and the Three Vehicles of the past. Thus, it is said that these are again raised up from what preceded.

Regarding the "provisional teachings of the four periods," one must understand that through the three cycles of revelation and clarification (*kaikhen*), the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *en* (Perfect) teachings are contrasted.

Although these primarily reveal the provisional for those of small capacity, when the former provisional teachings are cited, they encompass all four periods. Furthermore, because these beings of small capacity have passed through the preceding four periods, this is termed the "provisional teachings of the four periods.
The *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy), fascicle five, page thirteen, states: "The statement 'establishing the one and opening the provisional' now constitutes two meanings. The first is..."

In the past, Tathāgata manifested provisional means; these two serve as the locus for revealing the ultimate reality. Without pointing to that which is opened [by the provisional], there would be no way to speak of the ultimate reality.

Moreover, by pointing out that the provisional is itself provisional, one knows it is not the final goal. Once the ultimate reality has been revealed, the provisional is entirely the ultimate reality. (Text)
[Commentary] This explanation reiterates the phrase "the aforementioned times. The first line cites the objection: that the preceding four times are collectively termed "expedient means" (*upāya*).
Furthermore, the parables of the three carts and so forth in the sutra refer specifically to the Three Vehicles of the Tripitaka from the past.
Now, as for the text stating that the provisional teachings of the previous four periods are raised again: why is this?

One must understand that what follows explains how, at the assembly of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the Tathāgata employed three cycles of revelation—through direct teaching (*dharmadeśanā*), illustrative teaching (*avadānadeśanā*), and teaching by causes and conditions (*nidānadeśanā*)—all of which contrasted the round teaching (*vaipulya*) with the *āgama* vehicles.
While this encompasses the general purport of the sūtra and primarily reveals the potential of those with inferior capacities, it nevertheless refers back to the past.
This refers to the power [of the teaching] that can encompass the four periods; this is the explanation according to the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*).

Furthermore, as for those with the capacities of the Tripiṭaka who have now come to the *Lotus Sūtra*, they have already passed through the preceding four periods; therefore, the parables of the three carts and so forth, as well as the ritual text, refer to the reiteration of the provisional [teachings] of the preceding four periods.
This is the explanation according to the capacities [of the audience]. In the lower section of the *Myōraku* (the *Fahua wenju*), he cites evidence to first clarify the bestowal of the past.
"Power" (*quan*)—as in "Teng"—takes "unfolding" as its meaning; this refers to unfolding the intent of the provisional (*quan*). Regarding the second point, "the locus for revealing the real":
this means that when the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the real, it simultaneously reveals that the former provisional was itself the real.

As for the statement, "Without pointing to what is opened, there is no way to speak of the real": the skillful means (*upāya*) of the *Lotus Sūtra* is the provisional within the essence of the body. Indeed, if one wishes to speak of the real...
In order to reveal the provisional [teachings], Śāriputra made three requests and the Tathāgata granted three refusals; only at the very end did he say:
"The Buddhas preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate for beings; their underlying intent is difficult to understand.

For instance, I have used countless skillful means, various causes and conditions, parables, and modes of expression to preach the Dharma. This Dharma cannot be understood through mere calculation or discrimination; it can only..."
Only the Buddhas are able to know this. It continues, saying: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach and transform only bodhisattvas;
all that they do is always for a single purpose—namely, to reveal and awaken sentient beings through the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
How much more so when it is said that the provisional is provisional, and one knows it is not ultimate? Śāriputra said: At that time, his mind spontaneously...
That is to say: having attained what was thought to be *nirvāṇa*, one now realizes for oneself that it was not true *nirvāṇa*.
This is so. Once the reality has been revealed, the provisional is seen to be entirely real. Śāriputra said:

"The Buddha, through various causes and conditions, skillful metaphors, and eloquent speech, has brought peace to my mind like the ocean; having heard this, the net of my doubts is severed. [Appendix] Now, the third commentary.

Regarding the vehicle (*yāna*), if one examines the first four periods [of the Buddha’s teaching] as a single volume, it is said that the Bodhisattva turns the *vaipulya* [wheel]. One should know that the intent of both granting and withholding [the teaching] can be understood through this.

[Note] Regarding "slander": the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 10 (3), states: "One should know that regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, if considered in terms of its division [of the teaching], it still surpasses the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*."
If one speaks in terms of the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), [the Lotus Sūtra] even refutes the final mind of the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*).
People do not see this, and thus they resort to slander. [Commentary: This explains the slander. Speaking in terms of the *nikāya* (sections), the *Lotus Sūtra* is pure and unadulterated;

therefore, it refutes the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which are termed "mixed" (*jiāndài*). Speaking in terms of the teachings themselves, the *Lotus Sūtra* alone possesses the name "Subtle" (*miào*). Therefore...

It refutes the final mind of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha), asserting that this is the true cause. The final two phrases conclude by addressing how delusion leads to slander—namely, the claim that the *Lotus Sūtra* does not equal sūtras such as the *Avataṃsaka*.
[Appendix] From the *Tianxi Jizhu Wen-da* (Questions and Answers with the Tianxi Commentary): Question:

If the path of realization in the Separate Ground (*bhūmi*) is identical to the Perfect [Teaching], why does it still refute the final mind of the Separate Teaching? Answer: This refers to the distinction between those on the Grounds and those prior to the Grounds within the Separate Teaching.
The two types of teaching and realization—those based on provisional doctrine and those based on practice—are entirely distinct and do not intersect.

The specific reference here is to the *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which constitutes the two practices of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Because the former is set aside in favor of the latter, it is termed "breaking" (*po*).
△ Second, the excellence [of the teaching] is revealed by way of time.
By way of time, it is when the sun is at its zenith, with no shadow cast to either side (the fifth period).
[Commentary: The ten realms are all opened; there is none that does not attain Buddhahood. It is like the sun at its meridian: there is nowhere that does not face south.
[■ Record] This refers to time. The nine realms are opened up to be the Buddha-realm; all are brought to extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata.
It is like the sun at its zenith. These are the words of Dharma Master Rui. [■ Commentary] *Bian'e* quotes from the *Zhong*: "One should only open up the nine realms.
That we now speak of ten realms is because they must also be opened as a provisional means to suit the capacities of sentient beings. *Bian'e* further states:

As in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (miaojue) is merely the true cause (zhenyin) within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjia). Therefore, the Buddha-realm must also be opened [as the ultimate fruit].

[Commentary] According to the *Zhouli*, one uses a soil-gnomon (*tuguī*) of one chi and five cun, sets up a pole eight chi high, and at noon on the summer solstice, measures the shadow of the sun to find the center of the earth and establish the state.

[Commentary] The Duke of Zhou wished to seek the center of the earth to establish the royal capital. Therefore, he measured the shadow using a *tugu* (earth-measuring rod) and found Yangcheng in Yingchuan;
thus, he established the capital there. Zheng Kangcheng said: "The *tugu* is one chi and five cun long.
On the summer solstice, when an eight-foot gnomon is set upright, its shadow falls exactly level with the length of the *tugu*. This is called the 'center of the earth.'"

[Commentary] During the Song dynasty, the two masters Yan and Guan, together with the Grand Astrologer He Chengtian, employed this method to measure the sun’s shadow to determine the location of the Central Kingdom.

To the north of the gnomon, they obtained a shadow of one chi and five cun, which was equal to the *tugu* (the standard measurement stick). On the ground, there remained an additional shadow of one cun.

Since it is ten thousand *li* from the heavens, one knows that India alone is the center of the earth. As for the current statement that "no shadow can be measured," this is based on the Indian account.
[Note] The *Liang Zhuan* states that He Chengtian of Donghai was renowned for his vast learning; he then asked Huiyan:
"What calendar does the Buddha-land use? Yan replied, "In India, on the day of the summer solstice, when the sun is at its zenith, a gnomon casts no shadow;

this is what is called the 'Center of Heaven. Regarding the five elements, they follow the virtue of Earth (*tǔdé*); yellow is the honored color, and five is the honored number. Eight *cùn* constitute one *chí*.
Ten *liǎng* there correspond to twelve *liǎng* in this land. The month of *Chén* (the third lunar month) is the beginning of the year. Upon further investigation, [it was found to be so].

The calculations for the solstices and equinoxes, the prediction of eclipses, and the observation of light and shadow were extremely detailed; the stellar positions, degrees, and years all followed established rules.
Zhen Chengtian had no grounds for raising objections. Later, when people from the country of Boli arrived, their accounts indeed coincided with Yan’s explanations.
Therefore, they used the measurement of shadows to determine the center of the Middle Kingdom. Zheng Sīnóng stated: "For every thousand *lǐ* on the ground, the sun's shadow differs by one *cùn*;
thus, one should know that Yángchéng is indeed the center of this land. This implies that [the calculation] was based on this specific territory as its own center.

Since there are already manifestations and shadows, how could these not be other aggregates (*skandhas*)? Moreover, in this land, the meaning is clearly demonstrated at the edge of the great ocean in the eastern extremity.
The Master Chengguan’s disciple said: "From Central India to China in the east is fifty-eight thousand *li*;
to the Golden Land (*Suvarṇabhūmi*) in the south; to the country of Aṅga in the west; and to Mount Gandhamādana and Lake Anavatapta in the north—each likewise [is fifty-eight thousand *li*]."
At fifty-eight thousand *li*, one knows that it is the Middle Kingdom. Thus, Zhu Falan said to Emperor Ming of the Han:
"Kapilavastu is the center of the great trichiliocosm. Huiyan and Huiguan, who received their training from Master Kumārajīva, saw this in the *Sengshi*.
[Appendix] Bian'e states: The *Fanyi ji* cites the words of Zheng Sionuo, saying that there is a difference of one thousand *li*...
"One inch. The divination slip says: "Ten thousand *li* are all mistaken. Furthermore, this calculation of distance is based on the north-south axis and does not refer to the east-west axis.
△ Third, revealing the subtlety by way of taste.

In terms of flavor, clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is produced from matured butter (*sarpis*); likewise, this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (the fifth flavor of clarified butter) is produced from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.

[Commentary on the *Fahua Xuanzan Shiqian*, Fascicle 1, Section 19] Question: That sūtra itself uses clarified butter as a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*; why can it now be used as a metaphor for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? Answer:
According to the doctrinal intent of our school, these two sections share the same flavor. However, even *nirvāṇa* is still inferior; how much more so [the others]?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* opens up the provisional [teachings], like breaking through a great army; when other capacities reach that point, they are like remnants who are not difficult to subdue.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the "great harvest," while the *Nirvāṇa* is the "gathering of gleanings.

Were it not so, the *Nirvāṇa* would not have distantly pointed out that eight thousand śrāvakas had received their predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and perceived the Tathāgata-nature—just as autumn is for harvesting and winter for gathering the remains.
[The text] concludes: "There is nothing further to be made. [Commentary]:
This is a concise analysis of the flavors, comparing the *Lotus Sūtra* to the *amṛta* (clarified butter). As stated in the "Tathāgatagarbha" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
This sutra has appeared in the world like that fruit; it brings great benefit and peace and happiness to all, enabling sentient beings to perceive the Buddha-nature.

Just as the eight thousand śrāvakas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* received their predictions of enlightenment and attained the great fruit, they are like the harvest gathered in autumn and stored away for winter, requiring no further labor. By this, one can know with certainty that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the Great [Vehicle].
It is a gathering. That there is nothing further to be done means: according to principle, it is the ultimate principle wherein there is nothing to be done;
according to teaching, having heard this teaching, one hears nothing more elsewhere;
according to practice, having cultivated this practice, one no longer changes course. Such various meanings of "nothing to be done" can be summarized as follows:
Through the wondrous awakening of wisdom, one attains the vision of the essence of the sutra.

[Note] However, that original scripture does not contain the statement that it "emerges from the Lotus Sutra. Here, we speak according to its meaning; therefore, it is simply said that this [Lotus Sutra] emerges from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
[Commentary] The *Prajñāpāramitā* takes charge of the family estate, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* entrusts the family estate [to others].
Since their meanings follow this sequence, it is said that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* emerges from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
△ Four: Citing Scriptural Evidence, Part Two. First, citing a sūtra to provide proof and explanation.
The *Śraddhādhimuktiparivarta* says: "He gathered his kinsmen together and immediately declared: 'This is truly my son; I am truly his father.'"
"Whatever I now possess is all yours; I entrust it to you as my family estate. The impoverished son was filled with joy, having attained what he had never experienced before.
[Commentary on the *Wenju* (6.31) states: "The Dharma-body Bodhisattvas of the ten directions who act as his kin are his relatives.
These followers of the shadow and echo were mostly those with whom Śākyamuni shared common karma in the past, and they all practiced together with the Tathāgata under twenty trillion Buddhas."
Those whom he transforms and enlightens together with him are, in that very context, his uncles and cousins; therefore, they are treated as his kinsmen (*bandhu*). (Text).

[Commentary] This is a judgment based on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. There are five grades of kinsmen: First, "kinsmen" refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body throughout the ten directions who act as manifestations and shadows;
these constitute the conduct of Śākyamuni’s uncles and cousins. Second, "kings" refers to those who are honored within their respective divisions.
"Powerful King" refers to the teaching master within the division acting as king. The "three great ministers" refer to those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The "four kṣatriyas" refer to those who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*). The "five householders" refer to those in the thirty minds of the ten stages.
Now, these initial close relatives are Maitreya and other great bodhisattvas serving as kin; this differs from the former interpretation which took them to be emanations of various Buddhas.
"For the sake of kinsmen.
[Commentary] "This is truly my son; I am truly his father. To reunite father and son, the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6 (31), states:
"Truly he has received instruction from me; truly he is my son. He has attained understanding through me; he is born of me. I have indeed [previously]..."
"In the presence of twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, he constantly taught the Great Dharma; therefore, I am truly his father.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: At that time, the Buddha addressed Śāriputra: "I now declare among this great assembly of gods, humans, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas:
In the past, I was in the presence of twenty thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas for the sake of the Unsurpassed Way."
Therefore, I have constantly taught and transformed you, and you have likewise followed me to receive instruction throughout the long night.

Because I have guided you through skillful means, you have been born into my Dharma. These twenty trillion Buddhas are precisely the twenty trillion Sun-Moon-Lamp Brightness (Sūryacandrapradīpa) Buddhas encountered during the sixty intermediate kalpas.
As for "constantly teaching the Great Dharma," this refers to what the Buddha has spoken.
The Mahāyāna sūtra titled *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma) is precisely this "Teaching of the Bodhisattva-dharma.
[Note] "Whatever I now possess is all yours; I am truly entrusting you with the family inheritance. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6 (310), states:

"All Mahāyāna teachings, the myriad virtues, and the myriad practices—therefore it says 'all that I possess. Furthermore, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha as a child is no different [from that of the Buddha].
Therefore, it is said that all these belong to the child (the sentient being). One should know that whatever belongs to the Tathāgata is precisely what the child originally possesses.
[Note: Regarding "whatever belongs [to the Buddha] is the child's possession": the Buddha’s possessions do not transcend the myriad practices and myriad virtues;

yet, because the Tathāgatagarbha is no different from the Buddha, they are thus the child's possession. Since these are all originally possessed by the child, when they reside in the Tathāgata, they are...)
Entrusting the family business to the impoverished son is like his experiencing joy at having attained what he had never before.
[Supplement] Regarding "the myriad practices and myriad virtues," Miaole states: "The Prajñā that is entrusted has both common and uncommon aspects; it does not transcend cause and effect.

The cause consists of the myriad practices, and the fruit consists of the myriad virtues. Furthermore, 'that which the son possesses' refers to what is manifested through the Tathāgata’s cultivation, namely the multitude of..."
It is inherently possessed within the nature of birth.
△ Second, the inquiry into the reason for this acceptance.

What is the meaning of this acceptance? Answer: Immediately following the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* was subsequently taught; [the disciples] had already accepted and understood it as a treasury.
Just as when one is about to die, one simply entrusts their household affairs to others; so too, in the previous transmission of the teaching, all were made to know the Dharma-gates.
When preaching the Lotus Sūtra, [the Buddha] merely opened, revealed, awakened, and led them into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and conferred upon them the prediction of attaining Buddhahood.
[Boxed Note] "At the time of the end of life" refers to the moment when [the Buddha] proclaimed on Vulture Peak that he was entering *nirvāṇa*.

[Commentary] This explains "at the time of the end of life": it means that the original intention for the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world was to cause all sentient beings universally to become Buddhas.

Now, this sutra bestows predictions upon those of the three capacities; this constitutes the entrustment of the family inheritance of the Dharma-king. Thus, as he was about to transmit the family [lineage]...
He performed his karmic duties and then first proclaimed his passing away. As the sutra says: "The Tathāgata shall before long enter parinirvāṇa.
The Buddha wished to entrust this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to those who would uphold it, just as a person entrusts their family estate before passing away.
[Note] This is analogous to the previous "turning of the teaching," wherein all know the Dharma-gates. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 6, states:

"Referring back to the former *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* where the teaching was received, there were both extensive and abbreviated versions of the *Prajñā*, as well as common and uncommon dharmas; these are what you have known, and thus they are what you possess.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies only the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*), and does not further elaborate on all the various aspects of practice.
(Text). [Commentary]:
This explains that the preceding analogies and the turning of the teaching are all dharma-gates. That is to say, speaking extensively is called "detailed," while speaking briefly is called "concise.

However, those that are neither detailed nor concise are the unique dharmas (*asādhāraṇa-dharma*). Those spoken for the sake of the two vehicles are called common dharmas (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*). Previously, they were the objects of...
