A cold wind blows, and the hell-wardens call out to them, "Ho! All you sinners, live again! For this reason, it is called the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.
Immediately they are restored to their former state and once more undergo agonizing suffering as before.

The sentient beings therein, by reason of their past karma and conditions, were fond of killing living creatures—such as oxen, sheep, birds, and beasts—for the sake of fields, lands, houses, slaves, and wives.
Sons, because of lands and wealth, they kill one another; due to various such karmic retributions for killing, they undergo this extreme suffering.

Regarding the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra*), the treatises state that the sinners within the great Black Rope Hell see evil rākṣasas, hell-wardens, and ghost-artisans who constantly use black, glowing-hot iron cords to measure out the sinners with the prison...
A great iron axe is used to instruct people to hack at them: making the long short, the short long; making the square round, the round square.
Their four limbs are severed; their ears and noses are cut off; their hands and feet are lopped away. With a great iron saw, they are dismembered and sliced apart;

their flesh is torn into pieces and weighed portion by portion. This is due to the karmic causes and conditions of this person’s past conduct: slandering the loyal and virtuous, speaking falsehoods, and committing evil deeds.

[Engaging in] double-tongued speech, frivolous speech, or the wrongful execution of the innocent; or acting as a corrupt official, committing acts of cruelty and violence to oppress and harm others—because of such various forms of harsh speech, slander, and treachery, one undergoes these punishments. Regarding the *Saṃghāta* (Crushing) Hell, the treatise states:
"One sees in the Great Hell of Crushing various evil rākṣasa hell-wardens assuming diverse forms, such as oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, muntjacks, and deer."

Foxes, dogs, tigers, wolves, lions, six-tusked elephants, eagles, vultures, and quails—assuming the heads of these various birds and beasts, they come to swallow, devour, gnaw, and bite the offenders, tearing and mauling them. Two mountains close together;
a great, glowing iron wheel rolls over the multitude of offenders, shattering their bodies. Within a glowing iron mortar, they are pounded until crushed to pieces. As...
They crush the grapes as if pressing oil; it is like treading upon a threshing floor where flesh is piled into heaps and blood accumulates into pools as high as mountains.
Vultures, eagles, tigers, and wolves each come to scramble and tear at them.

This is due to the karmic causes and conditions of this person’s past lives, having killed many oxen, horses, pigs, sheep, deer, wild boars, foxes, rabbits, tigers, wolves, lions, six-tusked elephants, and various birds.
Because they frequently harmed and killed one another—due to such various birds and beasts—they must again receive these heads of various birds and beasts to come and harm the offenders.
Furthermore, because they used their power and influence to oppress the weak and unjustly crushed them, they receive the punishment of two mountains closing together.
Because of greed, anger, delusion, and fear, they adjudicated matters of light and heavy offense without employing correct principles, or...
Regarding those who destroy the right path and subvert the true Dharma, they undergo the punishment of being crushed by hot iron wheels and pounded in hot iron mortars;
these are the "Wailing" and "Great Wailing" hells. The treatise states:

In this great hell, the sinners see rākṣasa wardens whose heads are yellow like gold, from whose eyes fire issues forth, who wear ochre-colored robes, whose flesh and bodies are firm and tough, and who run as swiftly as the wind.
His hands and feet were large and long; his mouth uttered evil sounds; he grasped a trident, and arrows fell like rain, piercing and shooting at the offenders.
The offenders were frantic with terror and struck their heads in supplication, crying, "Great General, please release us! Please have pity on us!
Immediately, they were led into the Hell of Hot Iron, which was one hundred *yojana* in length and breadth; there they were driven, beaten, and made to run until their feet [bled].
All were scorched; their fat and marrow flowed out like pressed ghee or oil. Iron clubs struck their heads until they were shattered and the brains spilled forth, like a broken jar of curd.
They were hacked, pierced, sliced, and flayed, their bodies becoming mangled and putrefied. Then they were cast into iron chambers, where black smoke billowed and suffocated them.
As they pushed and crushed one another, they harbored mutual malice and resentment, each crying out, "Why are you pressing me down?"
As soon as he sought to escape, the gate was already closed. He cried out with a loud voice, his lamentation never ceasing.

This was due to the karmic causes and conditions of his past conduct: all stemmed from deceiving others with false weights and measures, adjudicating matters unjustly, refusing to return entrusted deposits, and oppressing the lowly.
He had tormented the poor, causing them to wail; he had destroyed other cities and ruined people’s villages, inflicting injury upon them.

They are harmed, plundered, and their families harbor poisonous resentment; the entire city cries out in lamentation. At times, through deceit and fraud, they entice them to come forth and then harm them again.
Due to various causes and conditions such as these, one undergoes the retribution of the Great Crying Hell (*Mahāraurava*).
Regarding the "Heating" (*Tapana*) and "Extremely Heating" (*Pratāpana*) hells, the treatise states that within the Hot (*Tāpana*) and Greatly Hot (*Mahātāpana*) hells, there are two great iron...
There are cauldrons. One is named Nanda and the other is named Upananda. They are filled with boiling brine.
Rākṣasa demons and hell-wardens cast the sinners into them, like a cook roasting meat. While the person is inside the cauldron, their feet are up and their head is down;

they are like beans being boiled until they are thoroughly soft and rotten, their bones and joints disintegrating and their skin and flesh separating, so that one knows they have been completely decomposed.

Emerging from one torment by means of another, driven by the causal conditions of their past actions, they are revived by cold winds and then cast again into pits of charcoal, or placed amidst boiling ashes—like fish taken out of water and set upon hot sand. Furthermore, they are seared by pus and blood;
emerging from the charcoal pits, they are thrown onto flaming beds and forcibly driven to sit, [their] eyes, ears, nose, and mouth [being tormented].
Furthermore, fire issues forth from all his pores. This is because in past lives this person troubled and disturbed his parents, teachers, elders, śramaṇas, and brahmins;
he distressed virtuous people and fields of merit, causing their minds to burn with heat. Due to these karmic offenses, [this occurs].

They undergo the retribution of the Heat Hells. This may be due to various causes and conditions from past lives, such as boiling raw cocoons, roasting live pigs or sheep, impaling people on wooden stakes and roasting them alive, burning mountains, forests, villages, Buddhist temples, and monasteries, or pushing sentient beings into pits of fire. Through such various causes and conditions, they are born [there].

Regarding this Avīci hell within the hells, the treatises state: one sees the Avīci hell as being four thousand *li* in length and breadth, surrounded by iron walls. Among the seven hells, its location is the deepest.
The rākṣasa jailers use great iron hammers to strike the sinners, just as a smith beats iron; they flay the skin from their heads down to their feet.
Five hundred nails are driven through his body, tearing it apart like the flaying of an ox hide; they pull against one another until he is torn asunder at the mere touch of their hands.
Hot iron chariots roll over his body, driving him into a pit of fire and forcing him to embrace burning coals and emerge.
He is driven into a river of boiling urine, where within it dwell various insects with sharp beaks that enter through his nostrils and exit from the soles of his feet. From...

They enter through the soles of the feet and emerge from the mouth; they stand in the midst of the path of swords and drive them to run about until their feet are shattered like minced meat in a kitchen.
Sharp knives, swords, and spears fly into their bodies, falling in chaotic disorder like leaves from a frost-bitten tree blown by the wind.
The hands, feet, ears, noses, and limbs of the sinners are all ground away, flayed, severed, and cut down upon the ground, streaming [with blood].
Blood forms a pool. There are two great, wicked dogs: the first named Śyāma and the second named Śabala.
With sharp mouths and fierce prowess, they crush the sinews and bones of men; their strength exceeds that of tigers and leopards, and they are as fierce as lions.
There is a forest of great thorns where the offenders are driven and forced to climb trees. As the offenders ascend, the thorns point downward; as they descend, the thorns [point upward].
Looking upward, great-bodied venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and malevolent insects come in swarms to bite them. Great birds with long beaks split open their heads and devour their brains.

They enter the briny river, drifting up and down with the current; upon emerging, they tread upon ground of glowing red-hot iron and walk upon iron thorns, or sit upon iron spears that pierce them from below.
With pincers, their mouths are forced open, and molten copper is poured inside until they swallow it.
A red-hot iron ball enters the mouth and scorches it; it enters the throat and rots it; it enters the belly and sets it ablaze.

All five viscera are scorched, and the ball passes straight through and falls to the ground. One sees only hideous sights, constantly smells foul odors, and perpetually feels coarse and abrasive sensations.

One encounters various agonies, becoming bewildered, fainting, and exhausted; at times one becomes frantic and reckless, at times hides and flees or throws oneself about, and at times tumbles and falls.
Fall! This person’s past conduct involved the commission of many great evils and the grave offenses of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
They have severed all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), declaring the Dharma to be non-Dharma and non-Dharma to be the Dharma; they declared the real to be unreal and the unreal to be real;

they subverted cause and effect and harbored malice and envy toward virtuous people. Because of these sins, they enter this hell and undergo the most intense punishment. (Original Note: Cited from the *Cheng*).

Regarding the discussion of the five kinds of immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*): 1. **Immediate succession regarding the fruition**: Because one abandons the body and is born into the retribution [of the hell].
That is to say, upon abandoning this body, one is immediately born there. 2. **Immediate succession regarding the experience of suffering**: Because there is no pleasure in the interval.

3. **Immediate succession regarding time**: Because it is fixed at exactly one *kalpa*. 4. **Immediate succession regarding life**: Because there is no interruption in the interim. 5. **Immediate succession regarding form**: Whether it be a single person or many people.
Because they are all completely filled. The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that the suffering of Avīci is a thousand times greater than that of the preceding seven hells.
[Supplement] The verse on the eight cold and eight hot hells was composed by Dharma Master Taishui Cui.
Regarding *Aṭaṭa*, Yi Fu says: because the cold is so extreme, the mouth cannot open; one can only move the tongue to produce sounds. These three [terms] refer to the sensations experienced.
The names are established based on their suffering. For instance, when the lips cannot move and only the tongue produces sound, it is called *aṭaṭa*.

When the tongue cannot move and only the lips produce sound, it is called *hahava*. When neither the lips nor the tongue can move, but sound is produced by vibrating the internal breath, it is called *huḥuva*.
These are all sounds of pain. They correspond respectively to the three types of bodily coloration.
That is to say: blue corresponds to the *utpala*; red corresponds to the *padma*; and deep red corresponds to the *mahāpadma*.
These colors—blue, red, and so forth—are produced because their bodies are oppressed by cold; therefore, they correspond respectively. *Zhá*.
Yīnzhá (音劄). Bēng (綳, pinyin: bēng). Zhàn (顫, pinyin: zhàn). Wǔ (嗢, pinyin: wū). Jiāxiè (浹渫, pinyin: jié xiě). Shào (矟, pinyin: shuò).

*Maóu* (矛) means a spear. *Juè* (劊), pronounced like *guì*, means to mince finely. *Pīn* (拼), pronounced like *bēng*, [is used here]. *Rì* (刵), pronounced like *èr*, means to cut off the ears. *Zhuān* (剸), pronounced like *tuán*, means to slice.
Lì (轢): Pronounced lì; to be crushed by a vehicle. Zè (笮): Pronounced zà; to press. Xián (燂): Pronounced qián;
hot water. Zhé (磔): Pronounced jí; to tear apart. È (頞): Pronounced è.

【□Note】 Each [hell] has its own retinue, numbering in the countless. The eight hells, such as Saṃjīva (Reviving Hell) and others, each have four gates. At each gate there are four secondary hells, namely:

the Pit of Hot Ashes (Kukūla), the Quagmire of Corpses (Kuṇapa), the Forest of Sword-Blades (Asipattravana), and the River of Boiling Water (Vaitaraṇī). Thus, there are sixteen for each primary hell, totaling one hundred and twenty-eight.

These are all called the *Utsada* (Additional) Hells, because when sentient beings wander therein, their suffering increases. This is based on the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), Fascicle [X].
Sixth, the six clouds; eighth, the eight cold hells. These also possess one hundred and twenty-eight [subsidiary hells].

However, since treatises such as the *Nyāyānusāra* refer to them merely as "retinues," the *Abhidharmakośa* diagrams depict the hot hells vertically and the cold hells horizontally, without listing the *Utpala* (Flowering) or *Mahotpala* (Great Flowering) among the eight cold hells.

Furthermore, there are other hells such as the Solitary, the Diaphragm, and the Light-Binding, which exist everywhere—in oceans, rivers, mountains, forests, and mid-air. The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states: "In the south..."

The continents have both central and peripheral regions. The two eastern and western continents have only peripheral regions and no central ones. In the northern continent, there are neither central nor peripheral regions.

If the people of the three continents commit grave offenses, they all come to the central hells and the peripheral hells of the southern, eastern, and western continents to undergo suffering (*Miaoxuan*, fascicle 6, section 28).
It says: "These central hells are located twenty thousand *yojanas* beneath the earth; their sides..."
The hells are either upon the earth or within the Cakravāḍa mountains. [Commentary] Regarding the phrase "equal punishment" below:
these are the subsidiary hells of Heat (*tāpana*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Two thousand [yojanas] below this is the Avīci hell; its depth and breadth are equal.

Above it are the seven *naraka*s, and each of the eight increases has sixteen [subsidiaries], namely: the Pit of Hot Ashes (*kukūla*), the Pit of Rotting Corpses (*kuṇapa*), and the Pit of Razor Blades (*kṣuradhāra*)."

The *Uṣṇa* (Heat) River increases in size. Each of these is situated at the four cardinal directions of those [hells]. Each *Avīci* hell has four gates; as there are four for each, the same applies to the seven above.
Regarding the sixteen peripheral grounds (*utsada*) surrounding the four gates of the hells, there are four at each gate.

The four at the eastern gate are: Hunger, the Copper Cauldron, the Many Pots, and the Stone Mill. The four at the southern gate are: Pus and Blood, the Pit of Ashes, the River of Ashes, and the Iron Ball.

The four [hells] at the western gate are: the Hatchet, the Leopard and Wolf, the Sword-Tree, and the Cold Ice. The four at the northern gate are: Black Sand, Boiling Excrement, Iron Nails, and Burning Thirst.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that each of the eight hot hells has four gates, and at each gate there is a peripheral hell (*utsada-naraka*).
Sentient beings wander therein because their suffering increases. Next, following the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*, the cold satellites are described.

This refers to the hells. The first two phrases provide a general indication based on the *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity). The next phrase specifies the "proper realm" (*samyaktva-niyāma*) while referring only to its "retinue.

The *Śāstra* states "Naraka, etc.," which includes the entirety of the four lower destinies (*gati*) as well as a portion of the heavenly realms; these constitute the intermediate states of the retinue.

Together with the physical world (*bhājana-loka*), these are collectively termed the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). This constitutes what is referred to as the "retinue" (*pārśvaga*) of the *naraka* (hell).

As for the fact that the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* diagram does not list the cold peripheral hells (*śīta-pārśvaga*), this follows the intention of the *Nyāyānusāra*, which speaks only of them as a retinue.

Furthermore, there are solitary prisons (*ekāntika-naraka*) located throughout rivers, forests, and other places; regarding these solitary prisons, the *Dharmapada-śāstra* states that there are three types: those situated among mountains, and so forth.
In the waters and in the wilderness—there are hells in all three places. In the lower section of the *Vibhāṣā*, it indicates whether the primary hells exist at the periphery of the four continents.
The Southern version of the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Below Jambudvīpa, there are the primary hells; above Jambudvīpa..."
There are only peripheral hells—whether on mountains, in valleys, in wildernesses, or in the air.
In Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī, there are only peripheral hells and no primary hells. In Uttarakuru, there are neither primary nor peripheral hells at all.
Because that is the fruit of pure retribution. Question: For what reason is there a primary hell beneath Jambudvīpa, while there is none in other places?
Answer: The people of Jambudvīpa cultivate wholesome deeds with great intensity, and they likewise commit unwholesome karmas with great intensity.
Therefore, there is a primary hell; the others do not have one. Furthermore, it was asked:

"If other continents also commit the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) and other grave karmas, in what place is the retribution received? The answer is: "It is received beneath this Jambudvīpa.

In the *Miaoxuan* (Sublime Commentary), Part 2, the primary hell at the edge of this Southern Continent is indicated. As the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Beneath Jambudvīpa, passing five..."
At a distance of one hundred *yojana*, there are hells. Furthermore, it is said that on the surface of the earth there are only the peripheral hells (*prādeśika-naraka*).
Another sutra clarifies that the space between the two Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*), where the sun and moon do not reach, is called the Hell of Darkness (*andhakāra-naraka*).

However, the "peripheral hells" mentioned above are precisely the subsidiary hells (*utsada-naraka*). [Supplement] Herein it is clarified that the eight cold and eight hot hells constitute the great hells; these are ten...
The six *yūzō* (increasing wandering) hells constitute the subsidiary hells (*kwanshuku*).

This differs slightly from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), which designates the eight hot hells as the primary hells (*dàyù*) and the eight cold hells, along with the flames of fire, as the subsidiary hells. *Fǔ*: the phonetic reading is *fù*; it refers to a large-mouthed cauldron. *Lín*: the phonetic reading is *mó*.

[Commentary on the Square Symbol]: Light and Heavy. The lateral [hells] are light, while the central [hell] is heavy. Those who commit heavy offenses traverse all one hundred and thirty-six hells; those who commit middling offenses do not traverse them all;
and those who commit minor offenses undergo further reduction.
[Commentary] Grave offenses. One undergoes the full cycle of the eight fundamental hells and the one hundred and twenty-eight subsidiary hells.

[Sub-commentary] For kalpas and so forth. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "In the six hells beginning with Saṃjīva (Reviving), a day and night is respectively equal to the lifespan of the gods of the Desire Realm.

(Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Four Great Kings; five hundred years of the Four Great Kings constitute one day and night in Saṃjīva, which corresponds to nine million human years. Furthermore, human...)

One hundred years on earth constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa devas. One thousand years of the Trāyastriṃśa devas constitutes one day and night for the Kālasūtra hell (which corresponds to thirty-six million years in the human realm).

[Note] Their lifespans are likewise equal to those [of the heavens]. (The lifespan in Saṃjīva is equal to five hundred years of the Cāturmahārājika heaven; the lifespan in Kālasūtra is equal to one thousand years of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven; the lifespans in the hells of Saṃjīva and so forth are similarly so.
Should one not stand in awe?)

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: The lifespans of the six classes of gods of the Desire Realm, beginning with the Four Great Kings, are respectively equal to one day and night for each of the six hells, beginning with Saṃjīva (Reviving). Their lifespans in those hells are likewise equal to those of the respective heavens.
The lifespan of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years; this constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva hell. Based on these days and nights, [the lifespan is calculated].
The months and years are calculated in this same manner. Their lifespan is five hundred such years, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin [heavens], where the lifespan is sixteen thousand [years].
In the Tapana (Inferno of Intense Heat) hell, one day and night is equivalent to that [sixteen-thousand-year] lifespan;

by calculating months and years based on this day and night, their lifespan there is likewise sixteen thousand years. [Supplement: Two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Yāma [heaven]. The night...
Two thousand years in the [Heaven of] Yāma constitute one day and night for the Saṃghāta [Hell]. This corresponds to fourteen billion four hundred million years in the human realm.
Four hundred years in the human realm constitute one day and night for the Tuṣita [Heaven]. Four thousand years in Tuṣita constitute one day and night for the Raurava [Hell].
This corresponds to five billion seven hundred and sixty million years in the human realm. Eight hundred [years in the human realm...]

One year [of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations] constitutes one day and night for the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations. Eight thousand years of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations constitute one day and night for the Great Screaming Hell;
this corresponds to two hundred and thirty billion years of human time. One thousand six hundred years of human time constitute one day and night for the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
Sixteen thousand years of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations constitute one day and night for the Reviving Hell; this corresponds to human time...
Nine hundred twenty-one billion six million years.

[Commentary] The Extremely Hot Hell lasts for half an intermediate kalpa; the Avīci Hell lasts for a full intermediate kalpa; and the maximum lifespan of animals (such as the Nanda Dragon and others) is one *sthiti-kalpa*.

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "The lifespan in the Reviving (Pratāpana) Hell is half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*); the lifespan in the Unrelenting (Avīci) Hell is one intermediate kalpa.

Regarding the lifespan of animals (*tiryagyoni*), it is for the most part indefinite; however, the maximum is also one intermediate kalpa, as in the case of the great nāga kings such as Nanda and others.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said: 'There are eight great nāgas, all of whom abide for an entire kalpa and are capable of...'"
"Supporting the great earth. [Note] Bian’uo says: "A lifespan of one *sthiti-kalpa*. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this means the lifespan lasts for one *kalpa*.
This text, however, relies on the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*. In the *Kośa*, it is clarified that one increase and one decrease constitute a *madhyama-kalpa*.

The phrase in the text, "the maximum among animals is one *madhyama-kalpa*," intends to say they abide for one *madhyama-kalpa*, not that their lifespan is one *sthiti-kalpa*. This is because... [text continues].

Since an eon (*kalpa*) consists of twenty cycles of increase and decrease, I [the author] privately remark: the commentary states that these minor three calamities have not yet arisen within the intermediate eon (*antarakalpa*).

Furthermore, regarding the animal realm in the passage below, which says that all the great dragon kings dwell for an entire eon, the phrase "dwelling here for one" is a scribal error for "dwelling for one."
[Note] Ghosts have a lifespan of five hundred years (ghosts take one human month as one day; by accumulating such days into months, their lifespan is five hundred years).
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "For the hungry ghosts, one human month constitutes one day;
by this reckoning, they form their months, and their lifespan is five hundred years. The above explains the number of kalpas passed in the eight hot hells.

[Commentary] The lifespan of Arbuda is as follows: it is like a single *vāha* of sesame seeds (a *vāha* is translated as a granary; it holds twenty *hu* of sesame seeds, which is the same kind of vessel currently used in common parlance for storing rice).

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: Regarding the lifespan of those in the Cold Hells (*śītanaraka*), how long is it? The Blessed One illustrated their lifespan by means of a simile, saying:
"In this human world, twenty *kharī* make one *māghava* measure [of grain] in the kingdom of Magadha—a *māghava* being a bamboo basket for holding rice.
(The character for *zhuan* is pronounced *yan*. [It refers to a] bamboo basket used for storing rice.

[Note: □] One hundred years for each grain removed until exhausted (Suppose there is a person who removes one sesame seed every hundred years; when twenty *hu* have been exhausted, this is called the lifespan of Arbuda).
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: Suppose there were a vessel filled to the brim with sesame seeds (*tila*).

Even if one were able to remove a single seed every hundred years, such a quantity of sesame seeds might more easily reach its end than the lifespan of one born in Arbuda, which is difficult to exhaust.
[Supplement] "Huma" (胡麻) refers to the sesame seed (*tila*). It is not found in this region [of China].

【□Note】 Each subsequent [hell] is twenty times greater [than the preceding one] (The second is the Hell of Blisters and Cracks; with twenty *bāhā* of sesame seeds, the doubling for the six subsequent hells should be understood accordingly).
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Twenty times this [duration] constitutes the lifespan of the second [cold hell]. In this manner, each subsequent one is twenty times the preceding;
such are the kalpas that constitute the lifespans in the cold hells."
[Note] Regarding the eighty-four thousand cycles of birth and death, the *Vibhāṣā* states that each of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*) possesses its own inherent power.
Even when the physical form (*rūpa*) in hell is severed, it continues again. The *Wu miaole* (Treatise on the Five Pleasures), fascicle 30, citing the *Abhidharma*, says:

"At the moment of initial birth in any hell, all beings possess three cognitions: they know this place is a hell, they know by what cause they were born there, and they know from which place they came."
[Commentary] The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "When various brahmins die and are reborn in the Avīci Hell, they immediately have three thoughts.

First, they think, 'From where have I come? and upon being born, they know for themselves that they have come from the human realm. Second, they think, 'Where have I been born now? and they immediately know for themselves that it is the Avīci Hell.
Third, they think, 'By what karmic conditions have I come here? and they immediately know for themselves that they have come by virtue of slandering the Dharma."
Because he did not believe in Mahāyāna sūtras such as these, he was executed by the sovereign of the country and came to be born here.
Having reflected on this matter, he immediately conceived a heart of faith and reverence toward the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras; shortly thereafter, his life came to an end.

He was born in the world of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi, where his lifespan lasted ten kalpas. Now, the treatise introduces the beginning of the hells, stating that there are three thoughts upon birth.
Furthermore, the treatise says in nine words: "Among those in the hells, there are some who are able to recognize their own past lives.
As the Sūtra says: "The sentient beings in the hells have this thought: 'All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas...'"
Thus has greed been described. One should see its future perils and its terrifying consequences; therefore, one ought to sever greed.
It is solely because I was unable to sever greed that I now experience this extreme suffering and intense affliction.
Question: When he forms this thought, is it at the time of initial birth, the middle period, or the final period? Answer: At the time of initial birth.
It is not at the time of death, but rather at the time of initial birth; for at that time, one has not yet experienced suffering and pain.
If one were already experiencing suffering and pain, one would still be unable to remember events that ceased even a moment prior, let alone those from long ago.
[Commentary on the Text, Fascicle 4 (34): It says, "At first, all [utterances] are correct speech; however, when suffering pain, the sounds of agony can no longer be distinguished.
[The Miaole Commentary, Fascicle 5 (30): It says, "When first entering hell, one speaks as one did in life;
later, one merely makes sounds such as 'po-po,' which can no longer be discerned."
[Commentary] The sounds "po-po" and so forth are the sounds of enduring cold. However, those born into the hot hells also have speech; yet later, it becomes difficult to distinguish.
The *Old Sutra of Miscellaneous Parables* (*Jù zá pìyù jīng*) states: "In the past, there were six people who all fell into hell together.
They were in the same cauldron, and each wished to speak of their original transgressions. One person said 'sha'; two people said 'na'; three people said..."
Specifically: four people said "sha," five people said "gu," and six people said "tuo-luo. When the Buddha saw this, he smiled. Maudgalyāyana asked for the reason, and the Buddha said:
"There were six people traveling together who fell into hell. The boiling hot water surged up so violently that they could not speak further;
each uttered only one word before turning back. One person said 'sha,' which lasts for sixty billion years in the world."
One day in the hells is as long as [a human lifetime]. When will it ever end? Second, "na" means there is no time for escape;
one does not know when liberation will be attained. Third, "te" means: "Alas! Alas! I should have used my life to cultivate my livelihood, yet I could not restrain myself.
My mind was seized by the five thieves, and I divided my offerings among them instead of the Triple Gem. Foolish and greedy, I never had enough. What benefit is there now in regret? Fourth.
Regarding the term *yan-shê* (言涉): to say "I am managing my livelihood" is likewise insincere; for when property belongs to another, one suffers pain at its acquisition.
Fifth, regarding the term *gū* (姑): "Who shall protect me? Upon emerging from hell, one then refrains from violating prohibitions so as to attain the bliss of rebirth in heaven.
Sixth, regarding the term *tuó-luó* (陀羅): this matter is paramount; originally it was not a calculated plan of the mind. It is like a charioteer.
"A carriage that loses its way enters onto a deviant path; when the axle snaps and the carriage is destroyed, it is too late for regret.

[Commentary] The *Wenju* says: "The hell-wardens are transformations conjured to be seen; they do not belong to the category of sentient beings (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*). Those who initially lead the sinner, bind them, and bring them before King Yama do belong to the category of sentient beings.
However, when [the sinner] undergoes suffering, [the wardens] do not belong to the category of sentient beings. (Miaole, Fascicle 5)
(30) It is said that sentient beings and non-sentient things are both produced by common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karman*), yet they are transformations of the mind.
[Commentary: This explains the hell-wardens (*yamadūta*). Regarding those among them who are categorized as non-sentient:
the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that the people of Yama are not sentient beings, yet the sinners perceive them as sentient beings holding blazing torches in their hands.

Iron tongs. Once the evil karma of that hell-dweller is exhausted, after his life there has ended, he no longer sees the jailers of Yama, because they do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
Just as a lamp ceases to exist when the oil and the wick are spent, so it is with the exhaustion of karma;
one no longer sees the jailers of Yama in this same way. [This applies even to those with] evil eyes and evil speech.

Just as the terrifying forms of sentient beings are all completely worn away, like a painted wall being destroyed and the painting vanishing along with it, so too is the painted wall of evil karma. One no longer sees the terrifying forms of the jailers of Yama;
therefore, one knows that these jailers are merely transformations produced by the minds of sentient beings through their own sinful karma, and are thus merely self-delusions.

"Seeing these sentient beings" means that, in reality, they do not belong to the category of sentient beings. [Note: "Sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to the jailers of Yama and various malevolent birds and beasts.
"Non-sentient beings" (*asattva*) refers to the various great and small hells, as well as the mountains of knives and trees of swords.

However, within the *Wenju* (Textual Explanations), the phrase "not belonging to the category of sentient beings" actually refers to those who *do* belong to the category of sentient beings, excluding only those who have first been brought before the judge.
Those who are bound and brought before the king belong to the category of sentient beings;
all other beings—whether sentient or insentient—who experience suffering or sublime bliss, are manifestations produced by the retribution of karma.
[Note] Sentient beings are constantly oppressed by the suffering of heat. While the minor hells encompass both cold and heat, the major hells exist only in heat;
the *Sūtra on the Four Liberations* calls these the "Path of Fire," naming them after this heat.

[Commentary] Regarding those who experience slight sensations of cold and heat: the *Abhidharma* states that when people raise livestock and provide them with warm or cool food and drink, those [beings] in the hot hells obtain a respite of coolness, while those in the cold hells obtain a respite of warmth. This is what is meant by the existence of "concordant pleasure" (*niṣyanda-sukha*) within the hells.
The Great Hell of Sole Heat is as described: the fire from above penetrates below, and the fire from below penetrates above;
at the four gates to the east, west, south, and north, there are fierce flames everywhere. It is like a fish on a griddle, its fat and grease entirely consumed.
[□ Note] The five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): killing one’s father; killing one’s mother; killing an *arhat*; shedding the blood of a Buddha; and causing a schism in the harmonious Saṃgha.
[■ Record] According to the Mahāyāna, this is augmented by the murder of one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the murder of one’s teacher (*ācārya*), which are termed the seven heinous crimes.

[Commentary] The ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*). There are three types of bodily karma: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. There are four types of vocal karma: false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.
There are three types of mental karma: greed, hatred, and delusion.
[Commentary] The *Dharmadhātusthāna* states: "Killing" means to sever the life-force. "Stealing" means to take another's property.
"Sexual misconduct" means to engage in sexual acts with those who are not one's wife or concubine. "Lying" means to deceive others with words.

"Divisive speech" means using words that incite strife to cause discord between others. "Harsh speech" means using abusive words to cause distress. "Frivolous speech" refers to ornate and deviant talk.
"Speech" refers to words that deviate from the principles of reason. "Greed" refers to the state of having no sense of satiety in the mind when encountering objects that accord with one's desires.

"Anger" refers to the arising of resentment and fury in the mind when confronted with adverse circumstances. "False view" is equivalent to delusion; it refers to the denial of the reality of cause and effect, as well as seeking blessings through perverse beliefs—all such individuals are people of false views and delusion.
[Boxed Note] Regarding the "upper grade": wholesome and unwholesome karmas each have three grades, and these further divide into three. This is as shown in the *Zhahua chao*.
[■ Record] This explains the upper grade of unwholesome karma, which is described in relation to the three grades of wholesome karma.

The *Zhahua chao* is illustrated in the diagram. [■ Supplement] The character 摭 (zhé) is pronounced zhāi; it means to gather up or collect its remaining meanings. This is Guishan’s commentary on Guifeng Lanxi’s work.

Commentary on the *Běnshū* (The Summary of Categories). [■ Record] All actions performed do not exceed these three: namely, the mind contacting an object, the object confronting the mind, and the meeting of mind and object.

Since these must necessarily fall within a temporal division, there are thus three grades of wholesome and unwholesome karma. [■ Supplement] Regarding the term "dharma-number" (*fǎshù*), one is added.

Regarding the time of mental activity: "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) refers to the means, meaning that when a person wishes to commit an evil act, they must first give rise to the mental means and preparatory application.
Regarding the time of the two fundamental minds: this refers to the actual moment of committing the evil; at that time, the mind is resolute and cannot be uprooted or moved.
Third, the mind of subsequent action (*pṛṣṭhacitta*): this refers to the time after the deed has been performed, when one again gives rise to a mind that contemplates the action that was done.
Second, the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
It is also called "those who move sideways. This realm is found everywhere; they have fur, horns, scales, or shells.
Feathered creatures; those with four legs or many legs; those with feet and those without feet; those that travel by water, land, or air—devouring one another, they undergo endless suffering.
Those who, out of ignorance and craving, commit the five heinous crimes and ten evil deeds of middling gravity, receive such a body in this realm.

[Note] The Sanskrit term is *tiryak*. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), fascicle 2, part 1 (p. 25), states: "As for 'beasts' (*chusheng*), [the characters] are written as *chu* (six) and *xu* (six)."
Regarding "xiàngjiū" (向究): the three characters are interchangeable. "Zuòchǔ" (作褚) has six pronunciations, referring to the six domestic animals—namely, oxen, horses, chickens, pigs, dogs, and sheep.
However, this does not exhaustively encompass all realms of existence (*gati*). Now, in discussing this path in general, we do not restrict it to these six alone.
[Note] *Chǔ* (pronounced *chù*): to stop. *Xǔ* (pronounced *xù*): to nourish. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "to keep."
This refers to "raising" (chù). The character is pronounced as xiù (as in *xiū*). It means to produce food and drink by snorting;

because they mostly consume their food by sniffing it with their noses, they are called "sniffed-born" (*xiùshēng*). "Chǔ" (six) refers to the six domestic animals. This is what Zheng Xuan stated in his commentary on the *Liji*.
If one were to speak only of oxen, horses, chickens, pigs, dogs, and sheep, they would not encompass the entirety [of this category]. This is now a general discussion.
[Note: Regarding "animals" (tiryagyoni), the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Their forms are lateral, and their movements are lateral."
[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā* states: Because its form is horizontal, its movement is also horizontal; because its movement is horizontal, its form is also horizontal.

Furthermore, it is said that its form is horizontal because the body mostly lies across, and its movement is horizontal because the mind is mostly not upright. Moreover, the *Kangzheng* (Corrected Edition) says:

Its movements are not upright, and it receives its retribution horizontally, walking upon its back as it travels through the heavens; therefore, it is called a "horizontal mover" (*tiryañc*). This is roughly the nature of this path.
Because sentient beings mostly conceal their bodies while walking.

[Commentary] This path exists everywhere. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that it exists throughout the five destinies (*pañca-gati*). The *Wénjù* (Textual Explanations), fascicle 4, section 34, says:
"It exists in all four heavens and the Heaven of the Thirty-three; even the elephants, horses, and other mounts ridden by those in the higher heavens possess it."
This is a transformation produced by meritorious karma; it does not belong to the category of sentient beings. [Note:

This explains that the animal realm pervades all five destinies (*gati*). As the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Some later teachers say that because they exist everywhere, they are called the 'animal destiny'.
In the commentary on the text, it is shown that they also pervade the heavenly destiny, which likewise follows the *Vibhāṣā* in clarifying the four [destinies].
In the realm of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there are geese, sparrows, elephants, horses, and the like.

Furthermore, from the higher heavens upward, there are likewise patterns of geese, peacocks, and so forth. Question: Since the various heavens above also have [beings] that ride upon elephants and horses, why is it said here that they do not exist?
Answer: In those heavens, there are only those with two legs, such as birds of exquisite color and the like; all others are absent because they are celestial-dwellers (ākāśavāsin).
The elephants and horses ridden by the devas are produced through the causal conditions of the meritorious karma of those sentient beings;
they are not themselves sentient beings, yet they take the form of elephants and horses for the devas' own enjoyment.
[Note] Those with fur, such as wild beasts; those with horns, such as oxen and sheep; those with scales and shells, such as fish and turtles;
and those with feathers, such as flying birds.
[Commentary] Among these four, there are those with no feet, many feet, two feet, and feet that exist; they differ in this way, yet they pervade all five destinies.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "In the hells, those with no feet are such as the *Nandika* and others;
those with two feet are such as the *Kaurava* birds and others; those with four feet are such as dogs and others; and those with many feet are such as centipedes."
And so forth. Among the hungry ghosts (preta), those without feet include snakes and the like; those with two feet include birds such as the *kaurava* and others;
those with four feet include powerful beings such as elephants and powerless beings such as dogs; and those with many feet include centipedes and the like.
The human realm is to be understood accordingly. The celestial realms have been seen above.
[Note] Water, land, and air—these three are the abodes upon which animals depend. The *Miaoxuan* states: "Land [animals] are of three grades.
The heavy grade refers to those within the earth who do not see light; the middle grade refers to those in mountains and forests; the light grade refers to those kept as livestock by humans."
This explains those who travel by water, land, and air. The first phrase directly explains the environments they inhabit. As the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states:
"The abodes of animals (tiryagyoni) are water, land, and air; these include insects, fish, birds, and beasts, whose species are infinite in number."
Mountains, rivers, air, and land constitute realms that are boundless. In the *Miaoxuan* (Sublime Mystery), the section below provides a specific classification of the land into three grades:
those within the soil, such as earthworms and the like; those in the mountains and forests, such as birds and beasts; and the "light" category, which refers to domestic livestock and the like.

[Note] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn) subsumes all animals under three categories: those that roam by day, those that roam by night, and those that roam both day and night. [Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"There are three types of animal classes, namely those that move through the air, on land, and in water; furthermore, there are those that roam by day, those that roam by night, and those that roam both day and night.
Those that roam by night include creatures such as cats and mice. Those that roam both day and night include creatures such as ants and termites.
[Note] Regarding "devouring one another," the fourth fascicle of the *Wenju* (34) states: "As for 'beasts,' they are mostly blind and ignorant. To be blind and ignorant means..."
It is ignorance. The strong subdue the weak; they drink blood and devour flesh, facing a hundred forms of terror.
The *Sūtra on the Four Liberations* calls this the "Blood Path" (*rudhirapatha*), a name derived from the fact that beings there prey upon one another.

[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā* states: Some say they are called "beasts" (*tiryagyoni*) because of their blindness and darkness. Among the five destinies (*gati*), none possess more ignorance than beasts;
therefore, they rely on their strength to swallow the weak, while the weak face a hundred forms of terror with every step they take.

One must look around to the left and right. In reality, the realm of animals is the Path of the Knife. Because the sutra describes it from the perspective of mutual devouring, it is called the Path of Blood.
[Commentary] This is the medium grade. Their minds are inferior to those of the former [grade], and they feel some slight remorse after having committed their deeds.
[Commentary] They are inferior compared to those in the hells, yet superior when contrasted with the hungry ghosts (preta).

[Sub-commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The maximum lifespan of animals is one intermediate kalpa" (the lifespan of animals is generally without fixed limit; its maximum duration is one intermediate kalpa.
This refers to great dragon kings such as Nanda, who all abide for one kalpa and are able to sustain the great earth).
[■ Record] This is identical to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*.

[□ Note] The fourth fascicle (35) of the *Wénjù* states: "At the beginning of the kalpa, all understood the noble language (*ārya-bhāṣā*). Later, due to differences in food and drink and the arising of deceitful minds, their speech all changed;
some were even unable to speak. The fifth fascicle (30) of the *Miàolè* states: "Among the various teachings, animals are able to..."
[The text] says: "All [beings] were capable of speech at this time; furthermore, that animals could fly through the air was due to their own power. [Commentary:
This citation indicates that, at the beginning, animals were all able to speak. As the *Saṃyukta-ratna-piṭaka-sūtra* states:
The Buddha said, "In the past, the King of Videha subdued the army of the King of Kāśī with an elephant. The King of Kāśī thought thus:"
He said, "How shall I now obtain a fragrant elephant to crush and subdue the army of King Videha?

At that time, someone said, "I have seen a white fragrant elephant in the mountains. Upon hearing this, the king immediately recruited his troops, saying, "Whoever can capture this fragrant elephant, I shall grant them a great reward. Then the assembled troops went to seize that elephant. The elephant thought: "I..."
"If I go far away, my parents are blind and old; it would not be right for me to comply [with your request]. Let me go to the king's presence. The king said, "I will give you food and drink.
At that time, the elephant refused to eat or drink. In ancient times, animals were all able to speak human language.
The king asked, "For what reason do you not eat? The elephant replied, "I have parents who are old and blind; they have been given neither water nor grass. His parents—
"I do not eat. How could I eat? Furthermore, he said: 'If I wish to depart, none of the king's armies can obstruct me;
I have merely come here in accordance with the king's command. May Your Majesty now grant me leave so that I may go and provide for my parents, returning at the end of my life."
The king thought with joy: "I am indeed a man-headed elephant, and this is indeed an elephant-headed man. He immediately released the elephant.
When his parents passed away, he returned to the king's presence. The king wished to invade that country, but the elephant said: "Do not engage in conflict."
"Listen: let me go alone, so that those enemies will not dare to insult me, and none shall be able to obstruct me.
If I do not return," King Prasenajit heard that the elephant had arrived; he was exceedingly joyful and said, "Stay here in my kingdom immediately."
The Elephant said: "One must not remain here immediately. Previously, I promised that king that I would return to his kingdom.
You two kings should eliminate your enmity and settle yourselves in your own lands; would this not be most joyful? He then spoke a verse: "Victory increases enmity;
defeat adds only sorrow and suffering. For those who do not contend for victory or defeat, their happiness is supreme. At that time, the Incense...
After the elephant had spoken this verse, he immediately returned to his kingdom. From that time forward, the two kingdoms lived in harmony.
At that time, the white elephant king was my current self; the King of Kāśi was the current King Prasenajit;
and the King of Videha was the current King Ajātaśatru. One should know that even animals of antiquity were able to speak human language.
