III. The Realm of Hungry Ghosts. The Sanskrit term is *jārīta*. This realm also pervades all destinies (*gati*). Those with merit and virtue, having performed... [text fragment ends]
The deities of mountains, forests, tombs, and temples who lack merit dwell in impure places; they are unable to obtain food or drink and constantly suffer flogging.

They fill up rivers and dam up seas, undergoing immeasurable suffering. With minds characterized by flattery and deception, they commit the lowest grade of the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds.
Moved by this Dharma-body.
[Note] *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), Fascicle 2, Part 1 (p. 25), states: "The Sanskrit term is *ācārya*. This is translated as 'grandfather. Later generations say..."
As for the "grandfather" (pitāmaha): he is so named from the very beginning of his existence; furthermore, as one who is born later, he is also the grandfather of those born later.
[Commentary] The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "There are some sentient beings who, being the very first to be born within that realm, are called 'grandfathers. It further states:"
Subsequently, when sentient beings are born in that place of birth, those who continue that lineage are also called "grandfathers" (*pitṛ*).
[Note: The *Erya* states: "Ghost (*gui*) means 'to return' (*gui*). The *Shizi* says: "In antiquity, the dead were called 'returning persons.

It is further said that the spirit of humans is called a ghost (*gui*), the spirit of the earth is called a *qi*, and the spirit of heaven is called a *ling*. Furthermore, it is said that they are 'hungry,' referring to the hungry ghosts (*preta*)."
...and was constantly subjected to their service.
[Commentary] This citation from non-Buddhist texts explains ghosts. When King Yu of Xia was crossing the Yangtze River, a dragon carried his boat.
The boatmen were terrified, but Yu sighed and said: "I have received my mandate from Heaven; I exhaust my strength to labor for the myriad people. Life is a temporary lodging; death is a return."
What need is there to worry about the dragons? From then on, those who died were called "those who have returned" (歸人). Regarding hunger and so forth, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
Some say that because they suffer greatly from hunger and thirst, the bellies of those sentient beings are like mountains while their throats are like the eye of a needle.
For hundreds of thousands of years, they do not hear the sound of water, nor have they ever even seen it; how much less could they touch it? It further states that others say:
"Those who are driven. Because they are constantly driven about here and there by the various devas, they are also called *kumbhāṇḍa* (driven spirits).

[Supplement] "Ghost" (*preta*) means fear; it refers to those who are empty, timid, and full of dread. Furthermore, it means majesty, for they are able to cause others to stand in awe of their majesty.
[Note] This path also extends throughout all realms of existence (*gati*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 3, part 2, states: "This place is five hundred *yojana* beneath Jambudvīpa.
There is the realm of King Yama, whose length and breadth are equal [to Jambudvīpa]; this is the fundamental location. Furthermore, there are those who dwell within Jambudvīpa itself:
those with merit reside in groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, while those without merit dwell in impure places. East...

The two western continents also have ghosts. In the northern continent, there are only those possessing majestic power (*vaibhāṣika*). There are also ghosts among the various devas, taking on forms according to their place of birth.
Some dwell on islands in the ocean, while others reside among the mountains and forests of the human realm; some resemble human forms, while others resemble the forms of beasts.

[Commentary] Regarding those with virtue who dwell among the flowers and fruits: they preside over the groves of flowering and fruit-bearing trees, ensuring they do not wither, and thus enjoy the delights of wondrous blossoms and lush forests.
Regarding those without virtue who dwell in impurity, there are two types: first, those with power who preside over that place;
second, those without power who steal and consume filth, constantly suffering flogging and caning. These distinctions also apply to the eastern and western [purgatories].

There are two types regarding the absence of majestic power (*an-vaibhava*). Those who possess only majestic power reside in the North, because that land is the result of pure karmic fruition (*vipāka*).

As for those gods who take on the forms of their respective birthplaces, these refer to the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) and the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*), who possess only majestic power.
Regarding those who dwell upon ocean islands, mountain forests, and so forth, some say there are five hundred islands to the west of Jambudvīpa, consisting of pairs of islands.

In the interval, there were five hundred cities of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Of these, two hundred and fifty were inhabited by those possessing majestic power (*tejas*), and two hundred and fifty were inhabited by those lacking majestic power.
Therefore, the Cakravartin King Nimi said to his charioteer, Mātali: "I wish to ascend to heaven. You should proceed along this path so that I may see all sentient beings."

Regarding those who receive the retribution for evil or good deeds: at that time, as the Holy King passed by the various cities, he saw those possessed of majestic power, like the sons of gods, wearing celestial crowns and celestial robes, partaking of sweet food and delicious drink, each sporting and enjoying themselves.
Those lacking majestic power (avīrya) are naked and unclothed, covering themselves with their hair, and carry earthenware vessels in their hands, wandering for alms to sustain themselves.

Those with human or animal forms refer to those who stand upright, those who lean to one side, or those whose faces resemble pigs or whose heads resemble oxen, such as figures depicted in wall paintings. All of the above are based on the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Answer with a definitive explanation. [Supplement] Regarding the form according to the place of birth: for example, one born in Jambudvīpa takes on the form of a person of Jambudvīpa;
one born in the heavens takes on the form of a celestial being. Furthermore, the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the houses, dwellings, streets, and alleys where all people reside...
At crossroads, in butcher shops and markets, and among burial mounds, there are spirits and deities everywhere; there is no place left empty.
They are named after the people they inhabit and the villages they dwell in. As for all trees, even those as small as a chariot axle, [they are likewise inhabited].

All [beings] have spirits and deities as their support. A certain master states: "They assume the form of their place of birth," meaning that wherever one dies, one immediately takes on the form of that [place].
The critique says: One should not speak thus. If one passes away from the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu),...
Having been born in this place, could one be without form and without speech? One should say that according to the place of birth, form and speech are likewise [determined].
[Commentary] Regarding those who do not obtain food or drink: the most severe suffer from the blazing flames of the fire of hunger, not even hearing the names of broth or water;
the middling seek out and consume pus, blood, excrement, and filth; the least are occasionally satiated for a brief moment. Furthermore, they are driven and coerced with blades and staffs. Blocked...
The Sea-Filling River (Sāgarapūraṇa-nadī) is called the Path of Blades (Asipattravana) in the *Catuḥsmṛti-sūtra*. It is so named because beings are driven and coerced there by blades and staves.
[Commentary] However, the hungry ghosts should be called the Path of Blood, for they perceive clear water as pus and blood;
yet the Sūtra names it the Path of Blades because of the driving and coercion by blades and staves.
[Note] The lower grade. Because it is currently capable of repentance, it is called the "lower grade. The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"For the hungry ghosts, five hundred [human years] constitute one day; their lifespan is five hundred years. Furthermore, there are three categories and nine types, including those with internal obstructions (*antarāyika*).
Outer obstructions, absence of obstructions; as explained in the *Lanpen shu*.
[Commentary] There are three categories and nine types, as shown in the diagram below. Regarding inner obstructions, outer obstructions, and the absence of obstructions, the *Shu* states:
"When water reaches them, it transforms into pus and blood—this is an inner obstruction. A throat like a needle and a belly like a goiter constitute outer obstructions. [They] drink blood."
Consuming excrement and being scorched—these constitute the absence of obstacles (*anāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, it is said that there are three types:

first, external obstacles (*bāhyāvaraṇa*), wherein upon encountering water, one sees people wielding swords, staves, and other weapons as obstructions; second, internal obstacles (*ādhyātmikāvaraṇa*), wherein there are torches in the mouth, or the throat is like a needle;
third, the absence of obstacles, wherein one sees the river as a fierce fire, or consumes filth and excrement, or cuts one's own body.
[This refers to] the consumption of meat and so forth.

[Square Note: The present offering of food to beings of water and land is specifically for the sake of the *yankou* (flaming-mouth) spirits and deities, as well as the Brahmins and sages; it is the provision generated for their benefit.
[They are] wilderness spirits (*kṣetrapāla*) and the like, such as Hārītī.
[Note: The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-dhāraṇī-sūtra* (Yan kou jing) states: "Ānanda was practicing meditative concentration when he saw a king of ghosts at night, whose mouth spat forth flames."
The fires of hunger burned within him like kindling. He asked, "What is your name? He replied, "I am called Mianran (Face-Burning). "In three days' time," he said, "you shall fall into my own class.

Ānanda was struck with terror and sought refuge with the Greatly Awakened One, the Compassionate Honored One. He recounted the preceding causes and requested the method for deliverance from suffering.
The Buddha told Ānanda, "I recall that in the past, when I was a Brahmin, before Avalokiteśvara..."
From the Bodhisattva, you shall receive the dhāraṇī known as the *Dhāraṇī-dharma of the Tathāgata Immeasurable Majestic Virtue Sovereign Radiance*.
If you are able to properly perform this rite, by consecrating it seven times,
you can cause a single meal to transform into various kinds of ambrosial food and drink, thereby sufficing for hundreds of thousands of koṭis of beings.
By others—namely, all the *pretas* (hungry ghosts) numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the Brahmin seers (*ṛṣi*)—a verse was produced which says:
"The great garuḍa birds, the hosts of spirits in the wilderness, the rākṣasas, and the Mother of Ghosts—all have attained full satisfaction.
[Supplement] Regarding the "unification of water and land," Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty dreamed that a divine monk informed him to perform the Water [Rite].
Lu Dazhai performed a fast to deliver beings from the six realms and four modes of birth. The Emperor immediately dispatched an envoy to fetch the Tripitaka and established the ritual texts;
they were completed in three years. Thereupon, a *dharmapūjā* (sacred site) was constructed. Regarding those who emerge [from the realms], there are two conditions:

first, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, offerings are combined with those for the wild ghosts and spirits of the wilderness; according to the *Vinaya*, one is commanded to give to the Mother of Ghost Children (*Hārītī*) and others, as these beings originally subsist upon such offerings.

The Flesh-Eating Man was converted by the Buddha, who had him receive the precepts and instruct his disciples to provide food as alms wherever they went; this is why today’s vegetarian halls each produce [offerings] in this manner.
This practice is followed exclusively by those who have left the household life. Second, the *Yankou Jing* (Sūtra on Feeding the Hungry Ghosts) enjoins the giving of food to hungry ghosts;
thus, today in the vegetarian hall, small measures of grain are set out separately for each person, and after the meal is finished, the assembly performs the ritual for them. Or...
This is called the "Small Birth Measure" (xiǎoshēng hù). One performs the rite of reciting mantras and making offerings during the night;

this is a common practice among the general populace. [Commentary] The *Yulanpen shu* states: There are three kinds of hungry ghosts. First, those without wealth, who, because they lack merit and virtue, do not obtain food.
Second, those with little wealth, who obtain only a small amount of pure and exquisite food and drink. Third, those with much wealth, who obtain a great deal of pure and exquisite food and drink.

Because of their diet, there are again three types for each. Regarding the three types without wealth: first is the "torch-mouthed" (jùkǒu). This refers to those whose mouths constantly emit blazing torches.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "If a person, out of greed and envy, unjustly seizes the wealth of others, destroys their cities and fortresses, kills, plunders, and offers the plundered riches to kings and great ministers, thereby increasing their own cruelty and violence, they shall fall into the [Hell of] Blazing Flames."
Among the hungry ghosts, there are those with needle-like throats: their heads are as large as mountains, yet their throats are like the eye of a needle.

This is because they violated the precepts by eating at night and stole the food of the Sangha. Third are those with foul mouths: their mouths are putrid and stinking, as they undergo this evil retribution themselves.
Because they are excessively greedy for fame and profit, they judge themselves right and others wrong, praising the wicked and slandering the virtuous;

therefore, among those with little wealth, there are three types. The first is the "needle-hair" type: their body hair is as sharp as needles, which prick them whenever they move, due to their greed for profit.
They practice acupuncture and moxibustion improperly, or pierce living beings merely for the sake of seeking wealth rather than to cure illnesses. As for the second type, those with stinking hair:
their hair grows long and foul-smelling, and they suffer by plucking it out themselves because they traded in livestock, slaughtering, boiling, and flaying them alive.
The agony is unbearable. When their retribution for hellish sins ends, they fall into this realm of hungry ghosts. Regarding those with the three great goiters:

large goiters hang from their throats, and they tear them open themselves to devour the pus. This is because they were envious of others and constantly harbored resentment. Among those with many possessions, these are the three.
First, those who obtain discarded things: they constantly receive offerings of food that has been cast away.

Because their sins are many and their merits few, and because they were stingy with what little they had while casting away their own belongings, they now receive only what is discarded when they practice giving. Second, those who obtain lost things:

they constantly receive food left behind in streets and alleys. Because they were always attached to stinginess regarding their present wealth, they now give only after doubting whether they might lose it.
The three types of powerful beings refer to yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśāca spirits, and the like. The blessings and pleasures they receive are similar to those of humans and devas;
some dwell in trees, forests, mountain valleys, sacred shrines, or empty spaces. They move upright and belong to the realm of ghosts (preta-gati).
These beings possess manifold transformations because, in their previous lives, their merit and demerit were not refined. Regarding their suffering and pleasure—

This is because they act in mutual confusion. Now, regarding the single path of ghosts and spirits, there are many who do not believe in them. Formerly, Ruan Xiu maintained that there are no ghosts, saying:
"Now there are those who claim to see ghosts, yet they say [the ghosts] are wearing clothes from when they were alive.

If a person has a ghost, does the clothing also have a ghost? Proponents of the doctrine were silenced by this; however, he failed to realize that ghosts transform into clothing, appearing similar to the garments worn during life.
Furthermore, although worldly people speak of existence, they do not fully know that it exists;

thus, what the world speaks of merely perceives a small portion of humans and animals, failing to see the other four realms of rebirth. As Confucius said: "Birth and human affairs—these are things we have yet to fully understand."
"Death and the spirits and deities—how could I fathom them? Thus we know that the Buddhist Dharma alone fully elucidates the six destinies.
△ Fourth, the realm of asuras.
The fourth is the path of the asuras. This is translated as "without wine," or "without upright appearance," or "without gods.

They dwell either on seashores or at the bottom of the ocean, where their palaces are magnificently adorned. They constantly delight in combat and warfare, experiencing boundless fear and dread. During the causal stage, they harbored a mind of suspicion and jealousy;

although they practiced the five constant virtues, because they acted with the intent to surpass others, they performed the ten wholesome deeds of an inferior grade, thereby inducing birth in this realm.

[Commentary on the *Wenju* (21): It is said that flowers were gathered from the four continents and fermented in the great ocean; through the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor remained unchanged.
Because [the Buddha] vowed to sever anger and envy, it is said that there was no wine.

[Commentary] Asuras are fond of wine. They gather famous flowers everywhere and brew them in the ocean, desiring to produce fragrant liquor. However, due to the karmic power of fish and dragons, the taste of the water does not change.
Out of anger and jealousy, they vowed to abstain from wine; therefore, they are called "Wineless" (Asura).
[Box Note] There is no symmetry. The male asuras are ugly while the females are beautiful; Śacī is an example of this.
[Commentary] The male asuras have twenty-four heads and a thousand hands—their ugliness is evident. The female asuras are as beautiful as Śacī, whom Śakra took as his wife.
When a seer possessing the five supernatural powers hears her voice, he immediately loses those five powers.
Their excellence may thus be understood. Now, based on the male *asura*, they are called "those who are not upright" (*a-sura*).
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that *sura* means "upright"; since they are not upright, they are called *asura*.

【□Note】 "Not a deva. The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), fascicle 2, section 14, states: "The retribution of this spirit is most excellent, ranking next to the various devas, yet it is not a deva.
The *Miaole ji* (Record of the Sublime Joy), fascicle 2, section 29, states: "Because it lacks the virtues of a deva" (text).
[Commentary] Regarding the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*: this realm possesses the retribution of celestial bliss but lacks the actual virtues of a deva.

According to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, as cited by Miaole, the term "asura" means "heaven"; it signifies sovereignty (*vaśitva*). Because they lack the actual virtues of a deva, they are called *asura*.

[Note] "Or on the seashore or the ocean floor. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 2, Part 1 (25), states: "When the world was first formed, [the asuras] dwelt upon the summit of Mount Sumeru and possessed palaces there.
Later, when the beings from the Ābhāsvara Heaven descended, they moved successively down to the fifth heaven.
The asuras became angry and fled; finding no place to dwell, they were born here below. (Text). The *Wenju* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), Vol. 2 (21), states: "The realm of ghosts..."
Regarding those categorized as "gathering" (asuras): those dwelling on the shores of the great ocean are included within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).

According to this principle, one should understand that when the *Myōgen* (Excellence of the Profound) states they may dwell in rock caves on the slopes of half of Mount Sumeru, they are to be categorized among the celestial beings (*deva*).

Furthermore, the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy) cites the *Āgama*, which explains that the four classes of asuras dwell sequentially at the bottom of the ocean, each occupying a palace located twenty thousand *yojana* beneath the sea.
As for their dwelling places, they are exceptionally sublime; one must possess abundant merit to be reborn there.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies the distinctions between the four modes of birth—womb, egg, moisture, and transformation—and how they are subsumed within the four realms of ghosts, animals, humans, and devas, as detailed in that text.

[Commentary] In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*), it is explained that the asuras avoid the heavens. Counting backward from the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is precisely the fifth;
because they harbor anger and wish to avoid [the gods], they move their residence to the seashore and the ocean floor.

The *Wenzhongju* (Explanations of Terms) clarifies that ghosts, animals, and asuras dwell at the seashore and the ocean floor, as the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: "There are two kinds of asuras."

First, they are subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*); as for the *asura*s who possess supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), they belong to the body of Māra. Second, they are subsumed under the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*);

they dwell at the bottom of the great ocean and on the slopes of Mount Sumeru. The *Abhidharma-śāstra* states that because the *asura*s are characterized by deceit, crookedness, and concealment, they are subsumed under the realm of hungry ghosts;
yet because the *asura* king Rāhu was born from a lion, he is subsumed under the realm of animals. Thus, according to the scriptural passages...
Thus, those of the ghost lineage dwell by the seashore; those of the animal lineage dwell at the bottom of the sea.

By this standard, it is clearly known that those who dwell in the rocky caves of Mount Sumeru belong to the celestial lineage (*deva-gotra*). Regarding the term "celestial lineage," Miaole states: "These are all primordial ancestors.

Furthermore, they are manifestations of great skillful means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*); since their past conditions cannot be fixed, there are animals and asuras who are nonetheless subsumed under the celestial lineage."
In the *Myōryaku* (The Joy of the Sublime), it cites four asura abodes from the Āgamas:
namely, the asura Vemacitra, the asura Kharaskandha, the asura Vepacitti, and the asura Rāhu.
Each resides beneath the ocean at a depth of twenty thousand *yojanas*, where they have built palaces; only those who possess abundant merit are able to be born there.

Furthermore, examining the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* at the end of the text, it states that there are five classes of asuras: first, the extremely weak, who dwell in the mountain forests of the human realm;
to the west, within great mountain caves deep within the earth, there are palaces of non-gods (*asura*). Second, [those who dwell] to the north of Mount Sumeru.
Twenty-one thousand yojanas beneath the great ocean is the palace of Rāhu (3).
Again, twenty-one thousand yojanas [further down] is the palace of Śauṇḍa (4). Again, twenty-one thousand yojanas [further down] is the palace of Mālādhara;
"Mālādhara" here is translated as "Variegated Painting," for they paint their bodies with patterns (5). Again, twenty-one thousand yojanas...
In the ten directions, there is the palace of Vemacitrin, which is situated sequentially at the bottom of the ocean.
Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states that they are fond of strife and harbor a sense of superiority and inferiority; they may dwell among the various mountain ranges or beneath the sea.
However, those who possess great power do so because they have extensively cultivated merit. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The third..."

Within the realms, there are four kinds of asuras. Those who belong to the realm of hungry ghosts (preta), who by the power of protecting the Dharma ride upon spiritual penetrations to dwell in the void of humans, are born from eggs and are categorized within the preta destiny.

Those who, while among the devas, have their merit diminished and are cast down, whose dwellings are adjacent to the sun and moon, are born from wombs and are categorized within the human destiny. There are also asura kings who hold dominion...
Holding the world, their power penetrates all and they are fearless; they are able to contend for authority with the Brahma Kings, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the Four Heavenly Kings.
These asuras arise through transformation and are categorized within the realm of devas.

There is also a distinct class of inferior asuras who are born in the heart of the great ocean and dwell at the mouths of underwater caverns; they roam in the void by day and return to their watery abodes by night. These asuras...
Asuras exist due to moisture and are included within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*). [Note:
Their palaces are magnificently adorned. Regarding their exquisite pleasures, the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 18, states: "In the midst of the Vajra Mountains of Jambudvīpa..."
There are asura palaces, each sixty yojanas in extent, with railings and rows of trees. Yet, day and night, they undergo suffering at three periods;
instruments of torment come to them spontaneously as they enter their palaces. That those belonging to the four realms of existence suffer in this way is indeed for a specific reason. (Text)
[Commentary] The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states that the palaces, cities, and utensils of the asuras are equal to those of the earth-dwelling devas;
they also have marriage and sexual relations between men and women, with customs roughly similar to those of the human realm.

Now, citing the *Dīrgha Āgama*, it further says they suffer through three periods [of time]; therefore, they belong to the four realms of rebirth (*catur-gati*). [Supplement] The *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) points out that "suffering through three periods" refers to...
The Matter of Yama. [Commentary] He was always fond of fighting. *Wenju* (Text 2, Section 22) states: Vemacitra fathered Śacī, whom Śakra took as his wife.
Later, she slandered her father, leading to a military conflict. Śakra waded through the waters of the ocean with his feet and attacked Sudarśana with his hands. Śakra...
By the power of the *prajñā* mantra, [it] cannot cause harm.
[Note]: The *Buddhāvataṃsaka-samādhi-sūtra* states: A being from the Ābhāsvara Heaven was born upon this earth. The earth caused her to exist;

wishing to enter the ocean waters to wash away her impurities, she fell into the mud and transformed into an egg. After eight thousand years, a girl with a thousand heads and a few [less] [limbs] was born.
1. There were twenty-four hands. This woman played in the water, and the water-essence entered her body.
After eight thousand years, she gave birth to a son with twenty-four heads and one fewer than a thousand hands. He was named Vemacitra, so called because he caused the waves of the ocean to roar.
He took Śacī, the daughter of a Gandharva, as his wife. Through the karmic power of Śakra, he was made to dwell in a palace of the seven treasures. He took [her]...
As for his taking Śacī as his wife, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "When Śakra took Śacī as his wife, it was because the gods were greedy for her beautiful form;
he did not do so out of regard for her noble lineage. Because Śacī was peerlessly upright and handsome, Śakra took her as his wife.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "When the asuras and the devas fought, [the asuras] would either sever their limbs, break their bodies, or otherwise cause them..."
If they die, or if their hearts are wounded or their limbs severed, they are restored to their former state; however, if their heads are cut off, they perish immediately.
Thus, when the gods are victorious, they enter the palace of the asuras and take all their daughters;

when the asuras are victorious, they go to the celestial palace and take the delicious flavor of divine curd (*devadugdha*). [Supplement] Śakra, Lord of the Devas, made a great vow and upheld the Prajñāpāramitā. At that time...
In the void of space, blades and staves descended spontaneously; the ears, noses, hands, and feet of the asuras fell off all at once.
A master records that he also shook Mount Sumeru with his hand and moved the city of Sudarśana. The Śakra constantly recited the *Prajñāpāramitā*, whereupon the gods ascended to assist him.
The asuras were defeated and fled into the hollows of lotus roots.
[Note] Fear and dread are boundless. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā*, fascicle 2 (14), states: "In the past, because he was jealous and vexed others, he is constantly beset by much fear.
(Text) Regarding "suspicion and jealousy," the *Fuxing-zhuan* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*), Fascicle 2, Part 1 (25), states: "Furthermore, he was jealous of the Buddha preaching the Dharma.

When the Buddha preached the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) for the sake of the devas, that asura then preached five foundations of mindfulness. When the Buddha preached the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad bodhipakṣā dharmāḥ*)," [the asura likewise added more].
They speak of thirty-eight categories. "Constantly obscured by a crooked mind" means being suspicious; "suspicion" implies apprehension. The *Shi* commentary states:

"To take outward appearance as an object of envy and conduct as an object of jealousy; to harm the worthy is called 'jealousy' (*jí*). Thus we know that the asuras are jealous of the worthy and envious of virtuous conduct.
[Commentary] This explains the harboring of a suspicious and envious mind. As stated in the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*: "The asuras had this thought:
'The Buddha has taught us the four foundations of mindfulness; he must have taught the devas the five foundations of mindfulness.
The Buddha has taught us the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he must have taught the devas the thirty-eight factors of the path. Thus they were filled with such malice."
Because their minds are shrouded by crookedness, they are unable to attain right certainty; this is what is meant by harboring a mind of suspicion and jealousy.

Furthermore, it is said that the asuras suspected the Buddha was assisting the devas. When the Buddha taught them the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they claimed there were six aggregates, asserting that he did not teach one aggregate.
When the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*), they claimed there were five truths, asserting that he did not teach one truth. [Appendix]

Jieyi says: Regarding the five mindfulnesses (*pañca-smṛti*) and so forth, there are two interpretations. First, within the treatise it is clarified that Māra manifested as a Buddha and preached the five mindfulnesses and the thirty-eight articles to the fourfold assembly.

When the asuras heard this, they claimed that the Buddha had previously preached the five mindfulnesses to the devas, but for us he preached only the four mindfulnesses, implying that the Buddha was partial. Second, [the interpretation of] the asuras...
"Seeking victory" means increasing [one's claims] through false speech.

[□ Note] The *Changfu xing* (Commentary on the Constant Virtues), fascicle 1, part 3, states: "To nurture things with compassion is benevolence (*ren*); to advance and transform others through virtue is righteousness (*yi*);

to act appropriately in advancing and retreating is propriety (*li*); to be extraordinary and transcendent is wisdom (*zhi*); for one's words to be reliable and consistent is trustworthiness (*xin*"); internally..."
Only when virtue is fully possessed does one truly enter the human path; those who are arrogant, aggressive, and devoid of virtue are judged to belong to the asuras.
Furthermore, even according to their wholesome minds, they remain at the lowest grade, for while they outwardly display the five virtues, their fundamental intent lies in disparaging others. (Text)

[Commentary] The *Baihutong* states: "Ren" (benevolence) means to love life and cherish others. "Yi" (righteousness) means appropriateness; it is the attainment of the mean through decisive judgment. "Li" (propriety) means treading;
it is the completion of the person through treading the Way. "Zhi" (wisdom) means knowing; it is perceiving the subtle within affairs so as to know the manifest.
"Xin" (trustworthiness) means sincerity; it is being single-minded and unwavering. That which can be repeated is that which may later be practiced.
Regarding their speech: those who are arrogant, stubborn, and devoid of virtue, though they may outwardly practice the Five Constant Virtues, their intent is to disparage others;
they possess no inner virtue. [Appendix] A master has noted: "The treatise asks why asuras are not different from devas, yet now it speaks of them as 'good.
The answer is that this is divided into the section on the retribution of asuras. It replies: a person can leave the household life and receive the precepts, thereby attaining the Way."

The mind of an asura is full of flattery and crookedness; because it is difficult to approach the Way, they remain below humans. A critique of the error states: the character "yi" (宜) should properly be "yi" (儀).
According to the *Fuxing*, it ought to be the character "yi" (儀); otherwise, it would violate the interpretation that "that which is appropriate for one who errs in principle."

[Note] The ten wholesome actions (*daśa-kuśala*) are established in contrast to the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*); they refer to non-killing and so forth. Furthermore, each of these ten possesses both the wholesome of restraint (*saṃvara-kuśala*) and the wholesome of performance (*anabhisamskāra-kuśala*).
For example, non-killing is the wholesome of restraint, while releasing captive animals is the wholesome of performance, and so on.

[Commentary] As for the ten wholesome deeds being established in opposition to the ten unwholesome deeds: if a person can understand that evil invites suffering, they must cease evil and practice good;
only then can they bring about the fruit of pure ascent and happiness in a future life. Therefore, the ten wholesome deeds are established in opposition to the ten unwholesome deeds.

The general designation for "stopping" (*śamatha*) and "practice" (*vipaśyanā*) as "wholesome" (*kuśala*) is appropriate. "Wholesome" takes "conformity with principle" as its meaning. Because it quiets perversions and returns to the truth, it is called "conforming to principle.
Stopping means ceasing the evil of heavy perversions; practice means gradually returning to the goodness of the Noble Path.

This is understood through the contemplations of impurity, loving-kindness and compassion, dependent origination, and so forth, as explained in the five types of meditative stabilization (*pañca-vipaśyanā-sthiti*) within the *Āgama* teachings.
△ Fifth, the human realm.

The human realm consists of four continents, each distinct: namely, Pūrvavideha in the east (a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years), Jambudvīpa in the south (a lifespan of one hundred years), Aparagoyānī in the west (a lifespan of five hundred years), and Uttarakuru in the north (a lifespan of one thousand years; there is no premature death, and no noble ones appear therein—this constitutes one of the eight difficulties).

1) All experience a mixture of suffering and pleasure. During the time of the cause, one practices the Five Constant Virtues and the Five Precepts. The Five Constant Virtues are benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness.
The Five Precepts are: not killing, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and not drinking intoxicants.
By practicing the ten wholesome actions of the middle grade, one brings about this body of the realm of humans.

【□Note】The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 2, Part 1 (26), states: "In Sanskrit, it is *manas*; here [in Chinese], it is translated as 'mind' (*yi*). It refers to that which is produced among human beings."

All of these are preceded by mental volition (*manasikāra*). The *Book of Changes* says: "Only man is the spirit among the myriad things. The *Book of Rites* states: "Man is the heart of Heaven and Earth, the source of the five elements.
This is because they were unaware of the five destinies (*pañcagati*). The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "Beings in the five destinies are generally full of pride (*māna*)."
None surpasses humans. It is further said: among those in the five destinies, none who can still the mind surpasses humans. (Text) The *Fayuan* states:
"Human" (*ren*) means "endurance" (*ren*). Regarding the world’s adversities and favorable conditions, a human is able to endure them with equanimity.
[Commentary: The *Vibhāṣā* states: Formerly there was a king named Mūrdhaja who ruled over the four continents. He addressed all sentient beings, saying:

"In whatever you do, you should contemplate well with the mind, deliberate well, and maintain clear mindfulness. When sentient beings acted according to his instructions—deliberating and maintaining mindfulness—they were able to perform their tasks with skillful artistry.
Because they first intended [their actions] with the mind (*manas*), man is therefore called "the intentional one" (*manuṣya*).
The phrase "Man is the most spiritual among the myriad things" originates from the "Tai Shi" chapter of the *Shangshu*. The character for "man" (*ren*) is a scribal error.

Because man’s virtue is conjoined with Heaven and Earth, he is called "the heart of Heaven and Earth. This is spoken in terms of principle (*li*). "End" (*duan*) means "to tread upon" or "to lead"; it signifies the head.
A human being embodies the entirety of the five elements; therefore, it is said that humans are the "pinnacle of the five elements. This is spoken in terms of the vital energy (*qi*).

Confucian classics discuss only the human being in isolation, and thus they do not yet recognize the five destinies (*pañcagati*). Below the character "婆" (*po*), the Buddhist scriptures are cited to explain the human being.
The text states: Among the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), none possesses more conceit (*māna*) than the human realm; therefore, it is called the "human course.

Furthermore, among the five destinies, none is better able to bring the mind to rest than the human realm, because humans are capable of attaining the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya-kuśala-mūla*).

One is able to draw near to the four dharmas, such as approaching spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and is likewise able to practice these four dharmas of drawing near to spiritual friends and so forth.
The *Fayuan* states: "The character for 'human' (*ren*) is 'endurance' (*ren*). This means that regarding the extreme sufferings of the world, one accepts them with a willing mind (*ganxin*)."
[Note] Regarding the four continents: beneath this world are three layers—first wind, next water, and above that the golden wheel (*kāñcana-cakra*).
Above the golden wheel are nine mountains and eight seas, with Mount Sumeru situated in the center and the Iron Encircling Mountains (*cakravāḍa*) on the outside.
Surrounding Mount Sumeru are the seven golden mountains and seven fragrant seas. Outside the seventh mountain and within the Iron Encircling Mountains is the eighth, the salt sea. To the east...

To the south, west, and north lie the four great continents (*caturdvīpa*). These four continents rest upon the earth-circle (*pṛthivīmaṇḍala*), which itself rests upon the gold-circle (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*).
Along the borders of these four continents, there are further two minor continents (*antaradvīpa*), as described in detail in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa* states: To establish the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*) dwells at the very bottom.
Its extent is immeasurable, and its thickness is sixteen lakṣas. Above that is the water-circle; it is eleven hundred million and twenty thousand [yojanas] deep.
Eight lakṣas of this water solidify to form gold. This water-circle and gold-circle are equal in breadth, with a diameter of twelve lakṣas and thirty-four [thousand].
One hundred and fifty [yojanas]. Its circumference is three times this. It is further stated that there are eight intermediate continents (*antaradvīpa*), two for each side of the four continents.
Furthermore, regarding the two continents at the edge of Jambudvīpa: the first is Cāmara, and the second is Avara-cāmara.
Regarding the two continents at the edge of Videha: the first is Deha, and the second is Videha. Regarding the two continents at the edge of Godānīya: the first is...
Śāṭhā. Second, Uḍra-maṇḍala. Regarding the two peripheral continents of Kuru: first, Kūrma; second, Kaurava. All these continents are inhabited by humans.
[Supplement] One hundred thousand constitutes one lakṣa, which is a *koṭi*. The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The first Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand *yojanas* in both height and breadth."
The first fragrant ocean outside Mount Sumeru is eighty thousand yojanas in width.
The second mountain, Yugandhara, is forty thousand yojanas in both height and width. The second fragrant ocean is forty thousand yojanas in width.
The third mountain, Īṣādhara, is twenty thousand yojanas in both height and width. The fourth mountain, Khadiraka, is ten thousand yojanas in both height and width.
Yojanas. Fifth is Mount Sudarśana, five thousand yojanas in height and breadth. Sixth is Mount Aśvakarṇa, two thousand five hundred yojanas in height and breadth.
Seventh is Mount Vinataka, one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas in height and breadth.
The seventh fragrant ocean is one thousand two hundred and fifty yojanas in width. Eighth—
Mount Dharanidhara is six hundred and twenty-five yojanas in both height and breadth. The eighth salt-water ocean is three hundred and twenty-two thousand two hundred yojanas in extent;
within it lie the four continents. The ninth is Mount Cakravāḍa (Small Iron Ring), which is three hundred and twelve yojanas in both height and breadth.
All these mountains enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand yojanas, resting upon the Golden Wheel.
Above. All the oceans are eighty thousand yojanas deep. Based on this, the mountains, oceans, and four continents may be understood.
[Note] Pūrvavideha is translated as "Superior Body."

[Note] The *Xiyuji* states: "The eastern continent, Pūrvavideha—formerly called Fupo-ti, and also Fuyu-dai, which are corruptions—is here translated as 'Victorious' (*shèng*), because it surpasses the southern continent [Jambudvīpa]. It is also translated as 'Initial,' for it is the place where the sun first rises."
[Note] Jambudvīpa is also called Cāmpeya. Beside the Anavatapta Lake (Lake of No Heat), there is a Jambu forest; its trees cast tall and large shadows, and their fruit is sweet and delicious.

It is named after the tree. Since this [tree] does not exist in this region, it is not translated [into Chinese]. In the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions), it is translated as "foul tree" (*huidu*).
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Jambū" is the name of a tree. On this continent there is a forest of these trees;
within the forest is a river whose bed contains golden sand called Jambūnada gold. Because of the tree, the continent is named after it.

This continent is surrounded by five hundred smaller islands, collectively known as Jambudvīpa. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "Nanzhanbu [South Jambū], formerly called Jambū..."
*Pūrvavideha*. It is also called *Jambudvīpa*, which is a corruption. The *Zangchao* states that "Jambū" has no equivalent term in this land [China], and thus it is not translated;
only in the phonetic glosses of the *Xiyuji* is it translated as "foul tree" (*hèishù*). [Supplement] This does not carry the meaning of being filthy or impure.
That which provides high shade for all is called "defiled" (or "stained").

[Commentary] Jambudvīpa is translated as "Go-yen-i" (Cattle-Trade). The *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā* states: At the beginning of the kalpa, there was a precious ox beneath a tall tree, used for the purpose of trade.

[Note] Regarding the term *Go-varta*, the *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanation of Terms in Translation) states that it is also translated as "taking and giving. The *Zangshu* (Commentary on the Tripitaka) says that because there are many cattle there, they take cattle as their currency.
The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) refers to it as the continent of Aparagoyānī; it was formerly called Gōuní.

Furthermore, it is said that "Gokani" is a corruption [of Goyāni]. Regarding the section on "Principle and Righteousness," the *Dīrgha Āgama* states that in Aparagoyānī there is a great tree named Kiṃpila;
atop this tree is a stone ox banner, and furthermore, cattle and sheep are used as currency for trade.
Thus, the commentary incorporates these two meanings.
[Note] Uttarakuru is also called Kuru; it is translated as "Superior Place" because it surpasses the three continents. As the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states:

"The height of the people of Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits (or four cubits, i.e., eight feet). For the people of the eastern, western, and northern continents, the height doubles respectively."

(Eight cubits on Pūrvavideha; sixteen cubits on Aparagoyānī; thirty-two cubits on Uttarakuru. Only the inhabitants of Uttarakuru have a fixed lifespan of one thousand years; for the other three continents, it is not fixed.
Furthermore, speaking according to the ultimate classification, it is not necessarily the case that this is entirely so.
[Note] The *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Record of Translated Names and Meanings) states: *Uttara* is translated as "Superior Place" (*shèngchù*) and also as "Superior Birth" (*shèngshēng*).
Among the four continents, sentient beings dwell there; because this place is the most superior, it is also called "Exalted" (*gāoshàng*), as it rises above the other three directions. [West]

The *Yùjì* (Record of the Regions) states: "The northern continent of Kuru—formerly called Yùdānyuè (Uttarakuru), and also referred to as Jiūlóu (Kaurava), which is a corruption—is [described as follows].
In the long prose commentary on the verses of the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says: 'The people of Jambudvīpa are mostly three and a half cubits tall;
among them, a small portion are four cubits tall. In Pūrvavideha they are eight; in Aparagoyānī, sixteen; and in Uttarakuru, thirty-two. And so on."
The cubit (hasta) is one foot and eight inches long. Thus, the body size in Jambudvīpa is mostly six feet and three inches, though some are seven feet and two inches.
The body size in Pūrvavideha is fourteen feet and four inches.
The body size of those in Aparagoyānīya is twenty-eight feet and eight inches. The body size of those in Uttarakuru is five... [feet].
It is one *zhang* and seven *chi* six *cun*. Furthermore, regarding the lifespan of humans in the four continents, it is said in verse:

"In the Northern Continent, it is fixed at a thousand years; in the Western and Eastern [continents], it decreases by half each; in this continent, it is indefinite: ten years at the end, immeasurable at the beginning.

This means that at the end of the eon, the lifespan decreases until it reaches ten years, whereas at the beginning of the eon, it was eighty-four thousand years. Moreover, there is premature death in all places except for Uttarakuru.
Thus, one knows that the Northern Continent is superior.
[Note] Sages do not appear within it, nor are they born there; yet, in propagating their transformation, they are not absent from it.
According to the *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Pāṭhadatta, together with six hundred disciples, resided in Uttarakuru. As for the eight difficulties and the three miserable realms—

There are three [types of beings] among the gods; among humans, there are four: first, those who are blind, deaf, mute, or speech-impaired; second, those who possess worldly wisdom and eloquence; third, those born before or after a Buddha;
and fourth, those of the northern continent, Uttarakuru. Among the gods, there is one [group]: the non-percipient beings, or as some point out, the long-lived gods (*dīrghāyuṣka*).
Those who undergo these various karmic retributions cannot attain the transformation of the Noble Ones (*ārya*).

[Commentary] This explains the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). If one wishes not to undergo these eight difficulties, one must practice the four wheels of subjugation (*caturvidha-cakra-vinirghātana*).

As clarified in the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, a bodhisattva practices four wheels to subjugate the eight difficulties: first, the wheel of being born in a central land (*madhyadeśa*), which destroys the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and the difficulties of the northern continent (*uttarakuru*) and the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyu-deva*);
second, the wheel of cultivating right vows (*samyakpraṇidhāna*), which destroys the difficulty of worldly wisdom and cleverness (*loka-paṇḍita-vidagdha*). Third...

The wheel of planting roots of wholesome causes destroys the difficulty of being blind, deaf, or mute. The wheel of associating with virtuous persons destroys the difficulties of being before a Buddha or after the age of a Buddha.
Thus, if one lacks these four wheels, one cannot avoid the eight difficulties; among them, the northern continent of Uttarakuru is one such place.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra-vyākhyā* clarifies two kinds of "eight difficulties" (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*). These are: first, ordinary beings dwelling in the eight difficulties of phenomena; second, those of the Two Vehicles dwelling in the eight difficulties of principle.
Phenomenal [difficulties] refer to the eight difficulties within the realm of desire (*dhātu*), while principled [difficulties] refer to the eight difficulties beyond the realm of desire.
Jingxi stated: "If one wishes to explain this briefly, then those in the thirty minds within *nirvāṇa-with-remainder* take the three evil realms as their 'selflessness'."
The Dharma is called the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru). The craving for dharmas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) is like the gods of Long Life (*dīrghāyuṣka*).

Not yet possessing the ten kinds of six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) of the first stage is called "incompleteness of the faculties. Wisdom prior to the stages is shallow, like worldly cleverness and eloquence;
it does not exhaust the Middle Way principle, like being before or after a Buddha. If within the *sambhogakāya* realm, one proceeds through each stage and each section in comparison with the others.
This also obstructs the principle within [the intermediate state]. However, this is merely an explanation of the eight difficulties regarding abiding in a physical existence.

[Commentary] Regarding the alternation of suffering and pleasure, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 4, Part 1, page 9, states: "If one discusses karmic retribution, the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa) is the lowest of the low."
If one encounters a Buddha, Jambudvīpa is the most superior of all lands; thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 12, states:

"For three reasons, Jambudvīpa surpasses the various heavens and is not equaled by Uttarakuru: first, the ability to sever lustful desire; second, the power of mindfulness and recollection; and third, the capacity for diligent and courageous exertion.
Furthermore, because there are those who transcribe the Prajñāpāramitā, the various devas descend to hear the Dharma. Therefore, [Jambudvīpa is superior]. Great...

The Sūtra states: "Due to the lowest-of-the-low causes and conditions, one is born in the Northern Continent; ... up to: due to the highest-of-the-high causes and conditions, one is born in the Southern Continent.

(Text) The *Miaoxuan* (6.29) says: "Although the people of the four continents differ in the excellence or inferiority of their karmic retribution, they all equally undergo birth, old age, sickness, and death;
they are alike in being subject to the light retributions of hell" (text).

[Commentary] The teachings state that there are three continents, and among these, three aspects are superior to Jambudvīpa: first, longevity; second, physical excellence; third, the excellence of the land.
Therefore, Jambudvīpa is considered the lowest of the low. If a Buddha appears in the world, it is only in Jambudvīpa; he merely visits the eastern and western continents but is not born there.
He is neither born in nor does he visit the northern continent. This refers specifically to the Buddha’s teaching; thus, according to the treatise, one encounters a Buddha only in Jambudvīpa.
This is the supreme among the supreme. *Myōryaku* (Miaole) says: "The Buddha appears when there is no illness at the beginning of a kalpa, not when there is much illness at the end of a kalpa;

when life is long, not when it is short; when the eastern continent is wealthy and long-lived, and the western continent abounds in jewels, pearls, oxen, sheep, and cattle, and the northern continent is without 'self' or subjects—such times and places do not move the Buddha to appear. [When the lifespan is] eighty thousand..."
In the age of a hundred-year lifespan, the people of Jambudvīpa cultivate the cause before seeing the fruit; therefore, we know that the Buddha appears in this land.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Taishō Vol. 25), citing scriptural evidence, establishes Jambudvīpa as superior.

Furthermore, within the teachings, it is clarified that Jambudvīpa possesses five kinds of excellence over the three heavens above and even over the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*): first, valor and vigor; second, right mindfulness; third, the birth of the Buddha.

The stages are: first, the stage of the ordinary person; second, the stage of the practitioner; third, the stage of the noble one; fourth, the stage of cultivation; and fifth, the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
However, these do not go beyond the three matters set forth in the *Mahā-śāstra*. The *Mahā-sūtra* states: "Human karma consists of the ten wholesome paths, which further comprise four types:

first, the inferior; second, the middling; third, the superior; and fourth, the supreme. By reason of the inferior cause and condition, one is born in Uttarakuru; by reason of the middling cause and condition, one is born in Pūrvavideha; by reason of the superior..."
Due to these causes and conditions, one is born in Aparagoyānī. Due to superior causes and conditions, one is born in Jambudvīpa. The commentary states:

"The ten wholesome actions have four types of retributions within the four continents. Although the lifespan and karmic rewards in the southern continent (Jambudvīpa) are the most inferior—being the fruit of lower-grade karma—it is called 'superior' because it excels in the excellence of practicing the path and performing wholesome deeds. [Supplement] It is capable of severing lustful desire.

This is precisely the holy life (*brahmacarya*). Because it can attain the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and achieve right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), within the four divisions of dhyāna there are the stages of decline, maintenance, progress, and penetration.
"Penetration" refers to the arising of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) insight and contemplation within this concentration, whereby one is able to reach *nirvāṇa*.
"Power of mindfulness" is right mindfulness; it refers to the power of resolute mindfulness, by which one is able to cultivate extensively even without seeing the fruit.

Because of these causes, there are three forms of vigorous diligence, which is to say, valorous fortitude. One master identifies them as follows: first, the power of mindfulness, because one is able to recollect what was done long ago;
second, valorous fortitude, because one is able to extensively cultivate the causes even when the results are not yet seen.

[Note] The Five Constants and the Five Precepts. "Constant" (*chang*) means unchanging; "precept" (*jie*) refers to the prevention of wrongdoing. Benevolence (*ren*) entails not killing; righteousness (*yi*) entails not stealing;

propriety (*li*) entails not committing sexual misconduct; trustworthiness (*xin*) entails not speaking falsely; and wisdom (*zhi*) entails not drinking alcohol. This is because alcohol can cloud one's nature and give rise to transgressions.

[Commentary] This explains the five constant virtues and the five precepts. The first two phrases clarify the meaning of the constancy of the precepts; the following five phrases clarify the correspondence between the precepts and the constants.
For example, in the *Dabei jing* (Sutra of Great Compassion), an elder asks the Buddha: "For what reason do you speak of only five?"

He did not speak of four or six. The Buddha said: "The five are the root of heaven and earth, the beginning of the Grand Unity (Taiyi), the source of spirit and vital energy, and the ancestor of the myriad things;
therefore, there are only five. It is further said: "The Five Precepts cause one to perfect the five limbs in the future, and accord with the laws of the world’s five constants and five virtues.
To feel compassion and refrain from killing is called benevolence (ren). To be clear-sighted and discerning..."
Not stealing is called righteousness (*yi*). Preventing harm and avoiding licentiousness is called propriety (*li*). Governing the mind and abstaining from alcohol is called wisdom (*zhi*).
Not speaking what is not in accordance with the Dharma is called faithfulness (*xin*). These five may not be impaired even for a moment of haste, nor abandoned for even an instant.
The gentleman upholds them to establish his person and employs them without ever discarding them. Thus, these five precepts correspond to the Five Constant Virtues of the world.
Now, the Five Constant Virtues are thus made to correspond with the Five Precepts. As the Great Master Tiantai said:

benevolence, compassion, and caring for others such that one does not harm them is the precept against killing; righteousness, yielding, integrity, and frugality such that one draws from oneself to benefit others is the precept against stealing;
adhering to ritual forms and regulations and binding hair to form a marriage is the precept against sexual misconduct; and possessing clear and sharp wisdom—so that...

To maintain uprightness and act in accordance with the Way is the precept against drinking alcohol. To have faith that accords with reality and to be sincere and incorruptible is the precept against false speech.
The final sentence clarifies how alcohol gives rise to faults, as stated in the Brahmajāla Sūtra: "The transgressions arising from alcohol are immeasurable.
If one extends one's hand over a vessel of alcohol to give it to another to drink, [one will suffer] for five hundred lifetimes."
There are no hands [to offer]. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains that there are three kinds: first, grain wine; second, fruit wine;
and third, medicinal wine. None of these may be drunk. Furthermore, it was asked: "The prohibition against drinking for those who have left the household life goes without saying.
Yet the *Hanshu* states that wine is 'the beautiful bounty of Heaven,' used to nourish the world, for sacrifices and prayers, to support the weak, and to sustain the sick. Therefore, there is..."
"The state uses wine to bring about harmony and uses wine to perfect ritual propriety.
How can the world prohibit drinking? Answer: "Before the time of Xia Yu, there was no mention of wine. During the governance of Tang and Yu, rituals were complete and music was harmonious;
thus, the necessity of being cautioned against wine was already very clear. What further discussion is required? Furthermore, the Great Master’s *Commentary on the Precepts Sutra* explains:"
As for not being afflicted by calamities: why is this? Answer: This precisely clarifies the difficulty of avoiding such afflictions.

Truly, were it possible to perform a hundred prostrations and yet misfortune would not invade; to practice immeasurable virtue and yet disorder would not reach one; and for Wen Zhong never to have become intoxicated throughout his life.
Siyuan: "The intoxicated are superior to the sober. For those who can act in this manner, the *Shuwen* permits the opening [of the prohibition]; there is a specific intent behind this.
If they cannot, then total prohibition is best."

[Note] Furthermore, among the five precepts, four are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherently evil) and one is *prajñapti-sāvadya* (prohibited). Alcohol is a prohibition; the others are inherently evil. These constitute the foundation for the prohibitions and precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.

The *Zhi guan fu xing chuan hong jue* (Treatise on the Propagation and Protection of the Dharma through Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 4, states: "Regarding *prakṛti-śīla* (inherent morality), regardless of whether one has received the precepts or not, to violate them constitutes a transgression.
Whether one has received them or not, to maintain them constitutes virtue. If one has received the precepts, maintaining them generates merit, while violating them incurs guilt."
Not received; no merit. Not received; an offense; no transgression. (Text) *Fuxing* 4, upper (3), states: "As for what is called 'nature'..."

This refers to the "ancient precepts" (pūrvaśikṣā). They do not depend upon the Buddha’s formal enactment; because their nature is inherently good or evil, they are termed "nature-precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*).

Furthermore, it is said that among the five precepts, four are nature-precepts and one is a prohibitive precept (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*). Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Among the prohibitive precepts, only the abstention from alcohol is for the sake of protecting the other disciplinary rules.

However, once [the Buddha] has enacted the regulations, a further "enacted offense" (*prajñapti-āpatti*) is added to those that are nature-precepts. (Text) Nature-precepts are observed even by Wheel-Turning Kings (*cakravartin*), whereas prohibitive precepts are not.
Regarding the five precepts and ten wholesome actions established by the Tathāgata, there are differences in their expansion and contraction. The three physical actions are visible;
"not lying" subsumes the four types of vocal karma; and "abstaining from intoxicants" guards the mental ground, thereby subsuming the three mental actions.

[Commentary] This clarifies that among the five precepts, four are *prakṛti-sāvadya* (natural offenses) and one is *prajñapti-sāvadya* (proscribed offenses). As the *Bao’en jīng* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states:
“Of the five precepts for an upāsaka, four are natural offenses; the one precept regarding drinking alcohol is a proscribed offense.

They are collectively established as the five precepts because drinking alcohol is the root of heedlessness and can lead to the violation of the other four precepts. For example, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was an upāsaka...”
Upāsaka, because of drinking alcohol, one commits adultery with another's wife and steals and kills another's chicken. When asked why one acts thus, they reply, "I did not do it;
it was because I was intoxicated by wine. Thus, at once, one can destroy four precepts. Although these are not actual transgressions [of the precepts], they are equivalent to actual transgressions.
Regarding the root of the precepts of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the *Fajie Cidi* states that violating the five precepts constitutes a root offense.

Such a person destroys the fivefold Dharma-body and all the Buddha-dharmas. Since the five precepts are the root of the śīla (ethical discipline) for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, if one violates the five precepts, one may no longer receive the precepts of either vehicle. If one can maintain them firmly, they constitute the five great acts of giving.

In the lower section of the *Zhi guan*, it clarifies the nature of the two types of precepts—those received by nature and those received through ceremony—and the transgressions incurred in violating them.

There is a difference regarding merit. Regarding "the nature-precepts are inferior," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "This is a detailed analysis of whether or not there is non-manifest karma (*avijñapti*) within the three trainings.

First, as for the absence of non-manifest karma in the precepts: because the nature-precepts are not received [through formal ritual], they lack non-manifest karma. As for "if one receives the precepts," the *Fuxing* says: [and so forth].

It is clear that upon receiving the precepts, one immediately possesses non-informative action (*avijñapti*). Upon the basis of natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), there is added the transgression of violating the precepts of renunciation and so forth;
thus, a distinct non-informative action arises. Once the precepts have been received, they induce this non-informative action. Therefore, when maintained, the merit is as vast as space;
yet if broken, it is breached according to each specific limb or object. Thus, by exhorting others to uphold and receive them, one adds the offense of obstructing their observance.

Moreover, once a transgression has occurred, it can be removed through the methods of the Dharma, restoring one to original purity; this constitutes the "precepts received" (*śīla-samādāna*), which differs from the "inherent precepts" (*prakṛti-śīla*).

Thus, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "For example, in cutting grass or harming livestock, both involve the offense of violating a regulation (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), for which one performs repentance for a *pāyattika* offense, and both prohibitions are thereby extinguished.
Nevertheless, regarding the harm to livestock, there remains an inherent fault (*prakṛti-āpatti*). Therefore, it cites the *Mahā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* to explain this point.

The transgression of non-action (*avijñapti*) is extinguished simultaneously [with the act], yet the obligation for retribution remains; this constitutes a difference in the nature of the experience. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, fascicle 4, states:
"Those who drink alcohol have minds that are mostly dissolute and cannot guard the other vows (*saṃvara*); therefore, to protect those others, one is made to abstain from drinking alcohol.
Regarding the addition of one further offense of prohibition (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) after the rule was established, it is as in the case of the Great... [text fragment].
The treatise cites a sutra which says that the Buddha stated: "If an ordained person violates desire, they abandon [the precepts].

This is the first offense: violating what one has vowed for oneself. This is the second offense: knowing what the Buddha has prescribed, yet transgressing it. Regarding the section on the *prakṛti-śīla* (inherent precepts), the *Guangming ju* states:
"The five precepts open up the ten wholesome paths. The ten wholesome paths are the ancient dharma of the Wheel-Turning Kings."
It is also employed [in practice] and is likewise termed a "natural offense" (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). Natural offenses constitute the very root of all transgressions;

thus, one should know that the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) apply universally. The Vinaya clarifies that for various other bhikṣus who commit diverse offenses, the Tathāgata issues prohibitions one by one.
Just as ritual and music originate from the Son of Heaven, one should know that the prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*) are restricted to what was established by the Tathāgata.

This is the established rule. The final two lines clarify the differences between the opening and closing of the precepts and the wholesome acts (*śīla-kuśala*). As stated in the *Wenju* (Explanatory Passages) on the *Guanwuliangshoujing*: "The five precepts correspond to the ten wholesome acts.
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute the three bodily [precepts]. False speech subsumes the four verbal [precepts]. Drinking alcohol subsumes the three mental [precepts].
Since laypeople are unable to guard their speech, only one instance of false speech is briefly proscribed. The *Śāstra* states: "That which speaks of gravity refers to false speech."
As for speech, it already encompasses the [other] three [unwholesome actions]. Drinking alcohol is a form of wrong livelihood;
it increases hatred and delusion. In the supramundane realm, wisdom is primary; in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the three poisons are the root.
If one can refrain from alcohol, this prevents the three poisons of the mental faculty and nurtures supramundane wisdom. [Appendix: The shapes of the nine mountains and eight seas, and below...

The Way of Heaven is known only in brief; therefore, it is not recorded extensively. There is a diagram of the three thousand great thousand-fold world systems (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) for those who require it.
△ Six: The Way of Heaven, Part Two. First, the general judgment.
The six heavens of the desire realm, the eighteen heavens of the form realm, and the four heavens of the formless realm constitute the twenty-eight heavens of the celestial path.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), fascicle 2, upper section (26), states: "In the present Buddhist scriptures, that which is called 'heaven' is also termed 'supreme' and also termed 'radiance'.
The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), end of fascicle 4, states: "'Heaven' means natural and spontaneous; it is the excellence of bliss and the excellence of the body."

Therefore, all calamities have two fundamental causes: first, indulgence in fine food; second, a nature of indolence.
These minor three calamities arise at the end of a *madhyama-kalpa*. As for the three [major] calamities: first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.
This refers to the time at the end of a *madhyama-kalpa*, when the human lifespan is ten years, and people—due to unrighteous greed—have their mental continuums defiled by unequal craving.
Their minds are obscured; they are entangled in false teachings, and the poison of hatred increases until it arises as soon as they see one another.

They harbor a fierce and harmful intent, like hunters seeing birds or beasts. Whatever they grasp in their hands becomes a sharp blade, and each gives rein to their wicked madness, slaughtering one another;

Due to these various faults, non-human spirits emit poison and pestilential diseases spread. Encountering calamities, people meet their end;

Consequently, the devas and nāgas, filled with resentment, do not send down sweet rain. Because of this, the world suffers from famine for a long time. Much...
The period of division ends with death; therefore, it is said that due to famine, there arise the "accumulation," the "white bones," and the "counting of tally-sticks.

There are two causes by which these are called "accumulations": first, the accumulation of individuals, meaning that at that time people, being extremely emaciated from hunger, gather together and die;
second, the accumulation of provisions, meaning that at that time people withhold their own food in order to benefit those who come after them.
They place them in small baskets to serve as seeds; therefore, during times of famine, this period is called "The Accumulation.
Regarding the mention of "white bones," there are two causes: first, at that time, human bodies become withered and dry, so that not long after death, the white bones appear;
second, driven by the famine, people collect these white bones, boil them to extract a broth, and drink it. There is also the "Counting of Peas" (śalākā-vartana).
It is said that there are two causes: first, due to a scarcity of provisions, they resort to drawing lots (*śalākā*) for food;
that is, within a single household, from the eldest to the youngest, on whichever day a person's lot falls, they receive a small amount of coarse food.

Second, they use a stick to poke through old granaries to obtain a few grains of rice, which they boil with a large amount of water and share among themselves to sustain their remaining lives. Furthermore, it is stated in the Teachings that if...
If a person can observe the precept against killing for even a single day and night, they will certainly not encounter the calamity of war in the future.
If one can offer even a single *harītakī*—that is, a myrobalan fruit—brought by a celestial being, [the merit is likewise secured].
If one gives rise to a profound and pure mind and offers it to the Saṃgha, one will certainly not encounter the calamity of pestilence in the future.
If one can give rise to a profound and pure mind and offer even a single morsel of food to the Saṃgha, one will certainly not encounter the calamity of famine in the future.

Epidemic: on the seventh day of the seventh month. Famine: for seven years, beginning from the seventh day of the seventh month; once this period has passed, it ceases. Human lifespan gradually increases.

In the two continents of the East and West, there are no fundamental calamities (mūla-vyasanāni), though similar calamities do arise: namely, the intensification of malice resembles the calamity of war;
the weakness of physical strength resembles the calamity of pestilence; and the frequent occurrence of hunger and thirst resembles the calamity of famine.
In the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*), these do not exist at all. It was previously stated that the calamity of fire incinerates the trichiliocosm; the other two calamities are likewise.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, when the human lifespan decreases to thirty years, the calamity of famine arises, lasting for seven years, seven months, and seven days. When the lifespan decreases to twenty years, the calamity of pestilence arises, lasting for seven months and seven days. When the lifespan decreases to ten years, [the calamity of war arises].

When the calamity of weapons arises, it ceases after seven days and seven nights. As for the statement in the *Abhidharmakośa* that the thirteen calamities appear [at the end of the kalpa], this is said according to the extreme limit of the *apacayakalpa* (the aeon of decline). Therefore, when one proceeds in reverse order from the ten-year lifespan, the seven days of weapons correspond to the ten-year lifespan;

the seven months of pestilence correspond to the twenty-year lifespan; and the seven years of famine correspond to the thirty-year lifespan—thus, there is no difference whatsoever from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
