This refers precisely to the primary retribution of sentient beings; those celestial palaces arise when the sentient being arises and perish when the sentient being perishes).

[Commentary] These two lines of verse clarify solely that the fourth dhyāna is not permanent and immovable. This interpretation accords with the intent of the *Śāstra*, for the text of the *Śāstra* states:
"If that were so, the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) of that stage would have to be permanent. It is not so, because it is associated with existence..."
Because they arise and perish simultaneously with sentient beings. That is to say, in those celestial realms, there is no collective physical terrain;
rather, they are like the stars, each dwelling place being distinct. When sentient beings are born or die, the celestial palaces in which they reside arise and perish accordingly.

Therefore, the substance of those receptacle worlds (*bhājana-loka*) is not permanent. Although it is said that they are "immovable," this is because the treatise explains that such a statement is made based on this [specific condition].

The Buddha said: "That is named 'Immovable' because it is not reached by the three internal and external calamities; however, it is not an immovable state that is eternally abiding and indestructible."

[Note] It requires seven fires for one water. After seven fires, there is wind. (From the first dhyāna downward: seven cycles of fire disasters constitute seven periods of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, corresponding to seven great kalpas.

The eighth water disaster reaches up to the second dhyāna; another cycle of formation and destruction corresponds to eight great kalpas. Thus, from the first dhyāna downward, there are forty-nine fire disasters (seven times seven). From the second dhyāna downward, there are seven water disasters, totaling fifty-six kalpas.

From the first dhyāna downward, there are another seven fire disasters, totaling sixty-three kalpas. At sixty-four kalpas, the wind disaster destroys everything up to the third dhyāna. Furthermore, the arising of the fire disaster is due to seven suns appearing simultaneously. Before the kalpa is destroyed, six suns [appear].]

It is hidden beneath Mount Dvayadhara. When the world is destroyed, it gradually emerges during the final six days. During the onset of the calamity of water, it is due to the continuous downpour of rain; during the arising of the calamity of wind, it is due to the mutual striking of winds. From below the wind-circle (vāyu-maṇḍala), fierce winds arise;
furthermore, when the power of karma is exhausted, winds arise according to their respective locations.
[Commentary] This explanation of the verses and the treatise varies in detail and brevity. The treatise states: Regarding the three calamities mentioned, what is their sequence?
First, seven successive fire calamities must arise. Immediately following that, one water calamity must necessarily arise.

After this, there are again seven successive fire calamities. Once these seven fire calamities have passed, another water calamity occurs. This continues until seven water calamities have been completed.
Disasters. There are seven further fire disasters; this is the eighth occasion when a wind disaster arises.
Thus, there are a total of eight cycles of seven fire disasters, followed by one cycle of seven water disasters, and then one wind disaster arises. For what reason is it thus?

It is because those sentient beings, through the cultivation of the causes of meditative concentration, gradually attain superior states in the higher realms, and consequently experience a gradual increase in their physical stature and lifespan. In the First Dhyāna, the lifespan is one great kalpa.
In the third heaven of the second dhyāna, there are eight kalpas; in the third heaven of the third dhyāna, there are sixty-four kalpas.
Because of this, their dwellings also endure for increasingly long periods. This treatise explains these matters in detail, whereas the commentary is brief.

Regarding the simultaneous appearance of the seven suns, as stated in the *Saptasūryodaya-sūtra*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are impermanent and subject to change."
All things return to extinction. When the kalpa is about to end, there is a great drought that lasts for a long time; grasses and trees are all scorched.
When the second sun appears, all small streams dry up. When the third sun appears, even the great rivers run dry. When the fourth sun appears...
Within Jambudvīpa, the four great rivers and Lake Anavatapta will all become empty and parched.
When the fifth sun appears, the great ocean will dry up completely. When the sixth sun appears, smoke will rise from the great earth, Mount Sumeru, and all else, like the firing of pottery in a kiln.
When the seventh sun appears, everything will burn fiercely, and there will no longer be any smoke. The earth...
And Mount Sumeru, up to the Brahma Heaven, are all completely filled with blazing fire. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"These three great calamities force sentient beings to abandon the lower realms and gather in the higher heavens. First, the calamity of fire arises due to the appearance of seven suns;
next, the calamity of water arises due to torrential rains; finally, the calamity of wind arises due to the mutual clashing of winds. These three...
The power of the calamities destroys the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) until not even a single atom remains.

Furthermore, one should know that since these three calamities are caused by sentient beings' craving for food and drink and their fondness for indolence, within the monasteries (saṃghārāma), it is only through the upholding of the Buddha-dharma that the Buddha-dharma can endure for a long time. If it were to be maintained merely by means of food and clothing, it would cause—
When calamities arise, the Dharma perishes. We humans remain complacent while the Dharma perishes; do we then linger in indulgence, sitting idly to await the three calamities?
[Appendix] In the *Tianxi Wenda*, it is asked: "The six suns hide Mount Meru (Dvādaśāditya); why does Mount Meru not perish? The answer is: [text follows].

This should be determined by the karmic power of sentient beings. That the two supports (the body and its faculties) do not perish for six days is because the karmic power of sentient beings has not yet been exhausted.

(The *Fuxing* [Buzhi yaojue fuxing chuanhong ji], fascicle 6, upper section, line 2, states: "Those dwelling on earth engage in physical union; in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, they take the wind as their means; in the Yāma heaven, they embrace; in the Tuṣita heaven, they hold hands; in the Nirmāṇarati heaven, they gaze and laugh; in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, they merely gaze.")
[Commentary] The six heavens possess desire; they constitute the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*). This explains the first two lines of the verse regarding the experience of sensual objects.

When the gods of the six desire heavens are born through transformation (*upapāduka*), those of the Cāturmahārājika heaven appear like five-year-old children, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven, where they appear like ten-year-old children; thereafter, they gradually grow according to their respective physical dimensions. Those born in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) have their physical dimensions fully formed at birth and are already endowed with celestial garments.
It is like when the beings of the Brahma realm are first born; their height is half a yojana).
[Commentary] This explains the last two lines of the verse regarding the body size at birth. The total explanation provided above differs in detail from the wording of the treatise (*śāstra*).

According to the explanation in the treatise, it is only among the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*) that they experience the objects of exquisite desire; among these, at the beginning...
The Four Great Kings and the two classes of Trāyastriṃśa gods—those who dwell upon the earth—engage in sexual union that is no different from that of humans;
yet, when their vital energy is discharged, their feverish affliction is immediately removed, unlike among humans where residual impurities remain.
Among the Yāma devas, sexual union is accomplished merely by embracing; among the Tuṣita devas, it is achieved simply by holding hands; and among the Nirmāṇarati devas, it is [achieved] only...
In the Heaven of Mutual Facing, they smile at one another; in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*), they engage in sexual union by gazing at each other.

In the *Loka-prajñapti*, embracing and so forth are mentioned merely to illustrate the differences in the duration of time for those [heavens]. For the aforementioned heavens, the objects of desire become increasingly sublime and the greedy mind becomes increasingly swift;
therefore, it is made thus. On the laps of the male and female deities of those respective heavens, there appear spontaneously transformed boys and girls.
"Born. This refers to the sons and daughters born among those gods. The following two lines clarify the physical dimensions of the beings born in the heavens.

Furthermore, it is explained that for the various gods of the six desire realms, at the time of their initial birth, they are respectively like humans of five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten years of age.

First, regarding the father: Furthermore, Master Yuanhong said that all the heavens of the six desire realms possess lotus ponds. Whenever the various devas have been paired as husband and wife, they go together to roam the lotus ponds.
There, they see a breast-like bud emerge from the flower; the man and woman both stroke and knead this breast, causing it to receive the vital energies of yin and yang.
Within, a celestial form is conceived. When the months are full and the flower opens, the physical features are complete. This is an analogy.
Just as those born from eggs must rely on the warmth of their parents to be formed, they differ from the lotus-birth transformation seen in the Buddha-lands.
[Note] Regarding the Heaven of the Four Great Kings: the Heavenly King of the East is Dhṛtarāṣṭra, which here means "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó), for he protects and sustains the nation.
Because his realm is of earth, he dwells upon a terrace of gold and governs the gandharvas and pretas.

To the south is the Heavenly King Virūḍhaka, which in this language means "Increase," because he causes the roots of goodness in others to increase; he dwells upon a terrace of lapis lazuli and governs the kumbhāṇḍas.

Vaiśravaṇa. The king had ninety-one sons, as recorded in the *Linggan zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance). He is the Western Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, which here is translated as "Broad Eyes" (*Guangmu*).
He is also called "Non-Desirable Retribution" (*Feihao bao*) and "Diverse Speech" (*Zayu*), for he is able to produce all kinds of speech.
He dwells upon the terrace of white silver and governs the piśācas, venomous nāgas, and others.

To the north is the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, here called Duōwén (Much-Hearing), so named because the fame of his merit and virtue is heard in the four directions. He dwells upon the terrace of crystal and governs the yakṣas and rākṣasas.

The establishment of shrines for these heavenly kings in various locations is documented in the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, as seen in the *Sēngshìlüè* (A Brief History of the Sangha).
[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the translated names: *Tidrata* is translated as "Ruling the Kingdom. It is the lord of the *gandharvas* and *piśācas*.
The *gandharva* is the celestial deity of the inverted banner who delights in music; the *piśāca* is a ghost that devours vital essence (*ojas*), also known as a "mad-ghost.

He is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; this means "Holder of the Nation" (Chíguó) and is also translated as "Peace for the People.

Virūḍhaka is translated as "Growth" (Zēngzhǎng). He presides over the kumbhāṇḍas and the preta-s. As for the kumbhāṇḍas, they were formerly called "winter melons" (dōngguā); their private parts resemble winter melons.
He carries it upon his shoulder; when sitting, he squats upon it. Pūtimukta means "grandfather"; it refers to an inferior class of *preta*.

The *Shilüe* (Brief History) states: In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Táng dynasty, five Western Huī kingdoms invaded Ānxī.
On the eleventh day of the second month, a memorial was submitted requesting military reinforcements; however, it took many months for the troops to arrive from ten thousand *lǐ* away.

A close minister then memorialized that Tripiṭaka Master Fǎbùkōng be summoned into the palace to perform recitations. Emperor Xuānzōng held the incense burner while Fǎbùkōng chanted the *Rénwáng jīng*.
After reciting the *Rāṣṭrapāla-dhāraṇī* twenty-one times, the Emperor suddenly saw five hundred divine beings clad in armor and bearing spears standing before the hall.

The Emperor asked, "Who are these? Amoghavajra replied, "These are the second son of King Vaiśravaṇa, Durdharṣa, who has come at the command of the King to assist Your Majesty’s heart and go rescue Anxi. In the fourth month of that year, a report was submitted concerning this matter.

On the eleventh day of the month, at the hour of the Snake (6–8 am), thirty *li* to the northeast of the city, amidst a dense gloom of clouds and mist, there appeared spirits approximately one *zhang* in height, all clad in golden armor.
By the hour of the Rooster (5–7 pm), drums and horns resounded loudly; the earth shook and the mountains trembled.

After two days, the barbarian raiders were routed and dispersed. In an instant, a brilliant light appeared atop the city tower, and the Heavenly King manifested his form, glaring wrathfully at the barbarian army.

[The Emperor] carefully had an image painted and presented it along with a memorial. The Emperor issued an edict that the city towers of all prefectures and districts throughout the various circuits must house an image of the Heavenly King in the northwest corner. These Four Heavenly Kings reside within the belly of Mount Sumeru.
This is it. [Supplement] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Four World-Protecting Kings each have ninety-one sons who possess great majesty and virtue;

All ghosts and spirits are subordinate to these Four Kings. [Appendix] The *Record* cites that the Heavenly King Dhṛtarāṣṭra presides over the piśācas, which differs from the commentary.

Reaching the midpoint [of the mountain], the first terrace extends sixteen thousand [yojanas].
The second, third, and fourth terraces extend, in their respective order, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas]."

□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□□ Before the three luminaries existed, through the power of the merit of sentient beings, turbulent winds were stirred, blowing upon the essence of fire and the essence of gold; these two treasures formed the sun.
The city-gate of the Sun Deity (Sūryadeva) is sevenfold in circuit; it is two thousand li from east to west, and its height from south to north is—
The same applies below. Its circumference is eight thousand li. Furthermore, turbulent winds blow upon the two treasures of lapis lazuli and white silver to form the moon.
The sevenfold palace city where the Moon Deity (Candradeva) resides measures one thousand nine hundred and sixty li from east to west.
The same applies to its north and south, and its elevations and depressions. Its circumference is seven thousand eight hundred and forty *li*.
It is all sustained by great winds, like floating clouds, moving in a clockwise direction. As for the five winds: "Sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*) means having the power to support and maintain the palaces;

"Nourishing" (*poṣaṇa*) means being able to preserve and sustain the palaces; "Receiving" (*parigraha*) means containing and accommodating the palaces; and "Turning" (*vartana*) means causing the sun and moon to revolve.

"Harmonizing" (*tiáo*) means to harmonize the sun, moon, cold, and heat. However, the names of these five winds in this commentary are both identical to and different from those in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
As the Sūtra states: "Furthermore, they are sustained by five winds and thus revolve spontaneously: first, the sustaining wind; second, the abiding wind; third, the moving wind;
fourth, the revolving wind; and fifth, the circulating wind. The points of agreement and difference can be seen here. [The term] "equal" (*qí*) means "to hold together as a pair" (*shānchí*).

Regarding the mountain peaks: according to both the *Dīrgha Āgama* and the *Loutan jing*, these are the karmic retributions of the Sun and Moon Devas, which are equal to those of the Four Great Kings.
Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies that the Four Heavenly Kings reside in the Palace of the Sun and Moon within the Victorious Treasury Jewel Hall (*Jaya-garbha-ratna-vimāna*).
Thus, we know that the height of the palatial cities of the Sun and Moon is level with the Yugandhara Mountains, encircling the midsection of Mount Sumeru and illuminating [the world].

Regarding the four continents under heaven: according to Zhang Heng’s *Huntian tu* (Diagram of the浑天/Spherical Heaven), it states that the sun is like the yolk of a chicken egg and the heavens are like the white of the egg.
The sun rises in the east and gradually sets in the west; it then descends beneath the earth and emerges from the east, revolving around both heaven and earth.
Thus, it is said that the sun rises at Fusang and sets at Mengsi, according to these respective locations.
The treatise states that the sun and moon formerly moved vertically; now they revolve around the midsection of Mount Sumeru, illuminating the four continents.
Below the seven golden mountains and the Iron Ring Mountains, the dimensions of the nine mountain ranges are explained as follows.
As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "Sumeru stands in the center. Here, "Su" means "excellent" (*sādhu*), and "Meru" means "high" (*unnata*).
Next is Yugandhara, translated as "Double-Support," so named because its summit has two ridges that the mountain is able to support.
Īṣādhara is translated as "Axle-Support"; its peaks rise steeply upward like the axles of a chariot.
Because it is held at the mountain peak. Regarding Kailāsa, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā* states: "This is the name of a tree in the western regions;
the *Mahā-ṭīkā* merely translates it according to its appearance and does not provide its specific name. The *Gāthā-ṭīkā* says:

"In this region as well, there is a mountain named 'Carrying Wood' (*Dān-mù-shān*), because the precious trees upon its summit resemble those [in the west]. Sudarśana is translated as "Good to Behold" (*Shànjiàn*); it is so called because one beholds [it].
Because it is praised as "excellent" (*śubha*), [it is called] Śubha. Aśvakarṇa is translated as "Horse Ear," because the shape of the mountain resembles that.
Vinataka is translated as "Elephant Trunk," because the shape of the mountain resembles that. Regarding Nimiṃdhara, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* states: "It is the name of a fish;
its mouth is pointed, and the shape of the mountain resembles it. The *Huayan yinyi* (Explanations of Words and Meanings in the Avataṃsaka) says: "This refers to..."

Cakravāḍa is the mountain at the edge. It surrounds the other six mountains on the outer perimeter of the seven golden mountains. Outside of the great continents and so forth, there is the Iron Rim Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
The former seven are composed of gold; Sumeru is made of four jewels. All enter the water to a depth of eighty thousand [yojanas].
The height of Mount Sudarśana is likewise. The remaining eight decrease by half and half respectively. Their width is equal to their height. This is it. End.

Two phrases. Regarding the dimensions of the palaces of the sun and moon: the old [translation] states that the form of the sun is fifty *yojana* in length and breadth, and the form of the moon is forty-nine *yojana*.
This is based on the *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra). As for the stars, the smallest are one *krośa*, and the largest are sixteen *yojana*.
[Note] The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise [occur] simultaneously across the four continents.
[Commentary] These two lines of verse describe the rising and setting of the sun and moon.

(The *Fuxing* [Sub-commentary] quotes the *Dīrgha Āgama*, fascicle 22, as saying: "In Uttarakuru it is midnight; in Pūrvavideha the sun has set; in Jambudvīpa it is midday; in Aparagoyānī the sun has risen. The scriptural text thus describes the four directions by turning the description through them in succession. That same sutra further states:

"Jambudvīpa is the east and Pūrvavideha is the west," and so on, up to "Uttarakuru is the west and Pūrvavideha is the east. This is because the sun and moon revolve; therefore, the place where the sun rises is called the east. (Text)

[Commentary] This section is an original annotation that cites a sutra to explain the verse. Within it, a further citation from a sutra clarifies that the four continents serve as each other’s cardinal directions.
Now, the commentary on the Abhidharmakośa-śāstra states: "The underside of the solar disk is composed of *sphaṭika* (crystal) fire-jewels, which are capable of heating and illuminating.
The underside of the lunar disk is composed of *sphaṭika* water-jewels, which are capable of cooling."

It is capable of illuminating. According to the predominant karma of sentient beings, it is able to benefit or harm objects such as the sense faculties, bodies, fruits, flowers, crops, and medicinal herbs, as appropriate for each. Thus, the single sun and moon universally [affect] all four continents.
Regarding the performance of activities: are the activities performed on a single day simultaneous across the four continents? No. How so?

When it is midnight in the northern continent (Uttarakuru), it is sunset in the eastern continent (Pūrvavideha), midday in the southern continent (Jambudvīpa), and sunrise in the western continent (Aparagoyānī).

These four times are equal. Other cases should be understood by this analogy. Because the sun’s path over the northern continent has distinctions, it causes the days and nights there to increase and decrease.
There is diminution.

[Commentary] Because the moon is recently eclipsed by its own shadow, the lunar disk appears incomplete (as with the new moon, the moon is near the sun in the west; its own shadow covers the east, so it appears deficient in the east.
As with the waning crescent, the moon is near the sun in the east; its own shadow covers the west, so it appears deficient in the west).
[Commentary] This verse describes the waxing and waning of the moon. The annotation is identical to the explanation in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*.
The treatise states that in the *Lokaprajñapti*, it is explained as follows: when the lunar palace moves near the solar disc, the moon is eclipsed by the light of the solar disc;
a shadow is cast from the opposite side, which covers the lunar disc itself, causing it to appear incomplete at that time.

[Supplement] Regarding the phrase "the shadow of the sun covers [it]" from recent times: according to the *Huìxuán* (Compendium of Profound Meanings), which cites the *Abhidharmakośa*, it says that the shadow of the sun covers [the moon] because the sun’s motion is slightly faster and the moon’s motion is slightly slower, resulting in a difference in their orbital degrees.

For example, at the time of the new moon, as the moon gradually approaches the solar disk, the brilliant and radiant light of the sun shines upon it; its brilliance overwhelms the moon so that it does not appear, continuing until... [the full moon].
Illumination. Or it illuminates Mount Sumeru; when it is not being illuminated, its entire body is fully manifested.

The *Dīrgha Āgama* states that the city is square, measuring one thousand nine hundred and sixty li on each side, and its height and depth are likewise. From a distance it appears round, yet in reality it is square.
However, many such accounts exist within the teachings and cannot be recorded in full. This is also like the sun’s own shadow falling upon itself when it is near.
There are many explanations. Some say it is the moon's own shadow: because the moon is originally dark, it becomes bright by borrowing the light of the sun;

thus, when the moon moves westward toward the sun, its western side is illuminated. However, the eastern side remains dark due to the moon’s own shadow, which is inherently black, and therefore it does not shine.
Furthermore, it is said: Suppose the moon travels westward and approaches the sun; the moon is originally one *yojana* lower than the sun, yet the light of that sun illuminates it.
Consequently, its own shadow falls upon its eastern side. It is like a person standing in the sunlight:
if the sun is in the east, the shadow falls in the west.
[Note] *Trāyastriṃśa* (忉利). This means "Thirty-three. At each of the four corners of the mountain summit, there are eight palaces, with the palace of Śakra, the Lord of Devas, in the center.
In a former life, thirty-three people, with the Heavenly Emperor as their leader, cultivated superior karma in the kingdom of Magadha;
therefore, they were born together here.
[Supplement] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the past, there was a Brahmin of the Kauśika clan who, together with thirty-two others, cultivated merit and virtue.
At the end of their lives, they were all reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru; Kauśika became the Lord of Devas, and the thirty-two became his ministers.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "If this Śakra here [in our world] is the same as the one from the time of Kāśyapa Buddha..."
After his parinirvāṇa, there was a woman who resolved to build a stūpa. Furthermore, thirty-two people resolved to assist in its construction.
By virtue of the merit of building the stūpa, she was reborn as the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, while those who assisted in the construction were reborn as his ministers.
Together, these constitute the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "At the summit of Sumeru, eighty thousand [yojanas high], the Heaven of the Thirty-three resides. (This refers to the passage across eighty thousand *yojanas*.)
[Commentary] The following four verses clarify the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven. The commentary states that the Thirty-three Gods dwell upon the summit of Mount Meru.
Each of the four sides of this summit measures eighty thousand [yojanas], and its dimensions are no different from those of the four sides below.
Other masters say that the statement "eighty thousand in circumference" refers to the four sides collectively, while each individual side measures only twenty thousand.
[Note] At each of the four corners there are four peaks. This is where Vajrapāṇi resides (there is a yakṣa deity named Vajrapāṇi who wields a vajra and dwells therein to protect the devas).
[Commentary] Furthermore, the treatise states: At the four corners of the mountain summit, there is a peak at each; their height and breadth are each five hundred yojanas.
[Square Note] The central palace is named Sudarśana (the "Good-to-See," so called because seeing it is deemed excellent).
[Bullet Note] This verse describes the palace of Śakra. Furthermore, the treatise explains its dimensions, stating: "In the center of the mountain summit is a palace named Sudarśana;
each side measures two thousand and five hundred [yojanas]."

[Note] It is ten thousand *yojana*s in circumference. Its height is half a *yojana*, and it is made of gold (the outer wall of Sudarśana is made of gold; it is one and a half *yojanas* high, and the city has a thousand gates).
[Commentary] This verse clarifies the palace city, its height, breadth, and dimensions; the *Xiaozhu* (Minor Commentary) provides details according to the *Śāstra*.
[Sub-commentary] The ground is adorned with various ornaments and is soft; in its center stands a preeminent palace, measuring one thousand *yojanas* in circumference.
[Commentary] This verse clarifies the dimensions of the inner palace within the city. The commentary explains:
"The ground is level and composed of pure gold, adorned throughout with one hundred and one varieties of miscellaneous jewels. When touched, the ground is as soft as *tūla* cotton;
as one walks upon it, it yields and rises according to the movement of the feet. This is the great capital city where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides. Within it...
Within the city is the Palace of Supreme Excellence (*Vaijayanta*), which is the place where the various devas assemble for court. It is like the Taiji Hall of a royal household.
It is named "Supreme Excellence" because it is adorned with all manner of wondrous jewels that outshine the palaces of other devas;
thus it is called "Supreme Excellence. Each side measures two hundred and fifty *yojanas*, hence it is said to be one thousand *yojanas* in circumference. This is...
This explains the various delightful things within the city.

[Commentary] The four outer gardens are adorned as follows: 1. The Garden of Various Chariots (*Caitraratha*): various chariots appear according to the power of the devas' merit. 2. The Garden of Roughness (*Pāruṣyaka*):

coarse and harsh weapons appear when the devas wish to fight, such as swords and staves. 3. The Garden of Mixed Forests (*Miśrakavana*): because one experiences various sensual pleasures there. 4. The Garden of Joy (*Nandanavana*): it is a realm of supreme excellence; because those who behold it never tire of it, it is named the Garden of Joy.

[Commentary] The commentary and the treatise provide details for one another. The treatise states: "Outside the city, on its four sides, there are four parks that serve as places for the gods to sport together.
First is the Caitraratha Park, located outside the eastern gate; second is the Pāruṣyaka Park."
To the south of the sixth [gate] is the Trāyastriṃśa Grove; to the west of the western gate is the Nandana Grove; and to the north of the northern gate is the Caitraratha Grove.
These four groves are perfectly square, each measuring one yojana. They serve as the external ornaments adorning the Great City.

[Note] The Wondrous Pools are situated at the four cardinal directions. They are each twenty [yojanas] apart (there are pools at the edges of the gardens; they are each twenty yojanas from the gardens).

[Commentary] These two lines of verse refer to the ponds. As stated in the *Śāstra*: "At the four sides of the four groves, there are four wonderful ponds, each situated twenty *yojana*s from the center of its respective grove.
These are the places where those devas sport together; therein, the devas compete for excellence and enjoy themselves.
Some who claim these are [natural] grounds are likely in error.

[Note] To the northeast is the Pārijāta tree (located to the northeast outside the city wall; the tree is named Pārijāta. Its leaves stand tall and its flowers bloom, emitting a wondrous fragrance that permeates a hundred yojanas with the wind, and even fifty yojanas against the wind).
[Commentary] This explanatory verse is abbreviated compared to the treatise (*śāstra*). For the treatise explains: "To the northeast outside the city, there is the Pārijāta tree.
It is the supreme place where the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven enjoy sensual pleasures. Its trunk rises upward and its branches spread out to the sides;
its width and height are equal, measuring one hundred *yojana*s. Its leaves flourish and its flowers bloom, emitting a wondrous fragrance that wafts with the wind."
The fragrance permeates for a full hundred *yojana*s; even when blowing against the wind, it still pervades fifty [yojana*s].
Other masters say that fragrance does not actually perfume against the wind, but that this statement is made based on the principle that it does not exceed the boundary of the tree itself.
In reality, the *pārijāta* possesses such a quality that the scent it emits can perfume against the wind; although obstructed by the force of the wind, it is nonetheless able to continue.
It flows toward other directions, gradually becoming weaker and more subtle, and ceases upon reaching a nearby place; it is not capable of traveling far.

Just as when wind blows in a favorable direction, it carries [the scent] further to other places—is this because the wind alone perfumes it, or does a distinct fragrance arise? This point is not fixed;
all masters agree on this without fault. If that is so, why did the Blessed One say, "The fragrance of flowers cannot perfume against the wind"?
The same applies to the fragrances of roots, stalks, and so forth. The exquisite fragrance of these superior virtues is so aromatic that its beauty wafts against the wind and pervades all directions.
This statement is made based on the fragrances found among human beings.

[Note] The Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā) in the southwest (the Heaven of the Thirty-three). [The gods] gather there at times to discuss matters of what is in accordance with the Dharma and what is not. They practice the ten wholesome paths of action exclusively in their superior grade.

(Selecting those from Yāma Heaven and above, as they additionally cultivate meditative concentration. *Yāma* is translated here as "Good Time" (*śubhakāla*), and is also called "Time-Portion" (*kālabhāga*), because they repeatedly proclaim joy at every moment.
[Commentary] Yāma. In the new translation, it is called Suyāma. This is translated as "Excellent Time" (Kṣaṇasamaya), because they sing songs of joy from time to time.
The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states that this deva uses the opening and closing of lotuses to indicate the divisions of time.
It further says that the blooming of red lotuses signifies day, while the blooming of white lotuses signifies night; because the sunlight does not reach there, it is called "Excellent Time."

[Note] Tuṣita. This is translated as "Wonderful Fulfillment. According to the new [translation], it is called Dṛṣṭānta (or Tuṣita), which means "Contentment," because [the inhabitants] know contentment regarding the objects of the five desires.
[Commentary] Tuṣita. The inner court is where Bodhisattvas dwell; the outer court is where devas dwell. Furthermore, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, it is named "Contentment" (*tuṣita*).
Bodhisattvas in their final birth teach and transform therein, for they cultivate contentment extensively.
[Square Note] Nirmāṇarati (Delighting in Emanations). Because they delight themselves by emanating objects within their environment.

[Bullet Point Note] Nirmāṇarati means they emanate the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) themselves and take pleasure in them. In the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, it is called "Delighting in Emanations" (*nirmāṇa-rati*). "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*) refers to transmutation;

it means transforming the coarse into the subtle. "Emanation" (*nirmāṇa*) refers to manifestation; it means something suddenly appearing where there was nothing. When the gods of this heaven enjoy themselves, they...
By means of their supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) and merit (*puṇya*), they manifest various kinds of exquisite sensual pleasures for their enjoyment.

[Note] As for the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*): when they wish to obtain objects of desire, other devas create them; thus, they rely on what is produced by others to accomplish their own pleasure.
This refers to the Māra King. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Most of these are Bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation (*acintyavimokṣa*), abiding in the color red."
Samādhi. Neither grasping nor abandoning; one should [regard] this as the King of Māras.
[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To seize the transformations of others for one's own enjoyment is called Paranirmita-vaśavartin (Mastery over Others' Transformations).

It is also called the Heaven of the Response to Transformations (*Nirmāṇarati*). This is the highest heaven of the Desire Realm. By relying on the transformations of others to achieve one's own pleasure, it is precisely Māra."
Regarding the "King" and the "Māra King," the *Great Sūtra Commentary* states: "Māra is named 'the Killer. Pāpīyān (Waxun) means 'the evil among evils.
He dwells at the summit of the Desire Heaven (*kāmadhātu*) and serves as the lord of the Desire Realm. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Among those who act as Māra Kings in the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions, most are those who dwell in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*)."
The Bodhisattva, by means of the power of skillful means (*upāya-bala*), transforms sentient beings; he manifests as a Māra-king. Regarding the "red-colored samādhi" (*rakta-samādhi*):
the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that there are twenty-five kingly samādhis which destroy the existence of the twenty-five realms (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

One attains the red-colored samādhi because it destroys the existence of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*para-nirmita-vaśavartin*). [Appendix] Bian’e says: One should know that [this refers to] the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations.
Because he serves as the lord of the desire realm and is in opposition to the Buddha, he is called the Māra King.

In the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the Māra King is a distinct deity who dwells above the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations; it is not the case that the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations itself is the Māra Heaven.
[Note] The "not-yet-attained concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*) has not yet entered the fundamental dhyāna. The *Zhiguan Fuxing Zhuanhong Jue* (9.4) states:

"Abiding in the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*), from this point onward, the mind undergoes a sudden, total transformation. One becomes empty and vast, no longer perceiving the body, head, clothing, or bedding within the desire-realm concentration;
it is like empty space, bright and serene. The body is an obstacle to phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*). Phenomenal obstacles hinder the future; once these obstacles depart, the body [is transcended]."

Emptiness. When it is attained in the future, this is called the characteristic of the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*). (Text) However, regarding birth in the four higher heavens, this is due to the power of the desire-realm concentration itself;

it is spoken of from the perspective of the furthest limit of the desire realm. Thus, it is called "not-yet-arrived" concentration, though it is not necessarily the case that all four heavens are like this.

[Supplement] This explains the "preparatory concentration" (*anāgamya-samādhi*). The first sentence provides a direct explanation of the name of the concentration: that which is above the first *dhyāna* constitutes the "fundamental" [concentration].

The section beginning with "stopping and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) provides a corroborating explanation of the characteristics of the concentration: namely, sitting upright with the body straightened and harmonizing the breath.
All things vanish into profound stillness; the body is like a shadow in the clouds, vast, open, and pure.

Even if one still perceives the marks of body and mind, this is the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*). If one abides in the concentration of the desire realm, one should take the counting of breaths as the contemplation to settle the distraction.

Following this state of meditative concentration, one’s practice advances further. It becomes still and profoundly tranquil; with a total transformation, the realm of signs is transmuted into the signless.
Suddenly, all is vast and open; one no longer perceives the body, head, bedding, or clothing within the realm of the desire-dhyāna.

It is like the great void. *Jiong* (冏) means *huǎng* (迥), which signifies radiance. As for "peaceful and secure" (*ān-yǐn*), it is because while the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) still remain, the objective hindrances (*vastv-āvaraṇa*) have already been emptied.
Regarding "objective hindrances of the future," this refers to that which can obstruct future meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, as for "objective hindrances," the body, head, and so forth of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) act as the obstructing factors; [this pertains to] the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the dhyānas.

That which was obstructed is now removed, and the body is empty. The defilements of the desire realm and the objects of perception are both empty. Although the potential for future meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) has been awakened, the innate obstructions still remain;

as one has not yet entered the first *dhyāna*, this is called the characteristic of the "not-yet-arrived" concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*). Because it has not yet reached the fundamental state, it is named "not-yet-arrived" concentration.
Regarding the highest point of the desire-realm heavens, the term "Paranirmita-vaśavartin" (Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations) is used to indicate it.
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "For the gods of the desire realm, one *krośa* increases by one-quarter for each successive level (one-quarter being half a *li*.
The initial Four Heavenly Kings are half a *li* tall; for the five higher levels, it is likewise half a *li*, as the treatise explains the increase)."
[Commentary] This verse clarifies the body sizes of the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The commentary states:
among the six heavens of the desire realm, the body size of the lowest [heaven] is one *krośa*, divided into four quarters. In this manner, each successive [heaven] increases by one such quarter.
Up to the sixth heaven, [the distance] is one and a half *krośas*. [Commentary:
Fifty years among humans constitute one day and night in the lower heaven (Cāturmahārājakāyika). Based on this, their lifespan is five hundred years. Above that, it doubles five times in succession.

(The lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings is five hundred years, taking fifty human years as one day. In the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, it is one thousand years, taking one hundred human years as one day. This continues up to the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven, where it is sixteen thousand years, taking one thousand human years as one day.)
[Six hundred human years constitute one day].
[Commentary] This clarifies the lifespan. The treatise explains in detail: fifty human years constitute one day and night for the lowest of the six heavens.
Based on this day and night, thirty days make a month, and twelve months make a year.
Their lifespan is five hundred years. In the higher heavens of the five desires, both [lifespan and the length of the day] increase twofold respectively.

That is to say, one hundred human years constitutes one day and night in the second heaven; based on this day and night, months and years are calculated, and their lifespan there is one thousand years.
For the four heavens beginning with Yāma, it is as follows: two, four, eight, and sixteen hundred human years respectively constitute one day and night. Based on these...
Thus, days and nights constitute months and years, according to which their lifespans are calculated as twenty, forty, eighty, and one hundred and sixty million years respectively.

From the Yugaṃdhara mountain upward, there are neither suns nor moons; day and night are established by the opening and closing of flowers, such as the kuvalaya and padma, or by the differences in the singing and silence of birds, or by the waking and sleeping of the celestial hosts.
They are not the same. By relying on the radiance of their own bodies, they accomplish the function of external light.
[Note] The *Fahua wenju* (29) states: "The Three Radiance Devas are inner ministers of Śakra, like high-ranking officials."
The Four Kings are external ministers, like military generals. Furthermore, Śakra is the Lord of the Earth-dwelling Devas, and Māra is the Lord of the Six Desire Heavens;
although they rule over the Desire Realm, neither Śakra nor the Four Kings can be restrained by Māra when they wish to practice the Buddha-dharma.
As recorded in the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance). [Commentary: This section concerns the two celestial lords of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Although the realm presided over by Māra is vast, while that presided over by Śakra is limited, Śakra and the Four Heavenly Kings are able to practice the Buddha-dharma, whereas Māra can ultimately never restrain them.
As stated in the *Gantong zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance), Tianren Fei said: "Each King has eight generals, and the four kings have thirty-two generals.
They patrol the four worlds beneath heaven, coming and going to protect and assist all those who have left the household life. Within these four worlds..."
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the Buddha-dharma is sparse. In the other three continents, the Buddha-dharma is greatly propagated;

yet among those who have left the household life, many violate the prohibitions and precepts, while few act in accordance with the Dharma. In the eastern and western continents, there are few who possess wisdom, and their afflictions are difficult to transform.
Although the southern continent has many who commit offenses, they can be transformed to follow what is good, and their minds are easily subdued. When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa...
[The Buddha] personally entrusted [the Dharma] to you, charging you to protect it and prevent Māra from disturbing it.
If you do not guard it, who then would practice my Dharma-teachings? Therefore, the Buddha has bestowed his sincere charge; we dare not fail to act upon it.

Even if we see one who violates the prohibitions, we pity and protect them; if we see one who performs a single good deed, we do not blame them for ten thousand faults. This matter is like forgetting a flaw—one does not dwell upon it.
In the past, General Wei was preeminent in providing great protection. There were many daughters of Māra who would mock and toy with bhikṣus;
those whose power of the Path was slight were all deluded and disturbed by them. When General Wei rushed forth in alarm, he would eliminate them according to the occasion.
Therefore, when matters came before the Four Heavenly Kings, the Kings would all rise upon seeing him, for they said that General Wei cultivated the practice of celibacy.
They protect the teachings of the True Dharma; for this reason, the Māra-king is unable to subdue them.
*Tiantai sijiao yi zhu huibufu hong ji*, Fascicle 3b–4a.

collated and supplemented with auxiliary records by the Qing *bhikṣu* Xingquan.

△ Second: The Realm of Form (Rūpadhātu).
Next are the eighteen heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), which are divided into four *dhyānas*. The first *dhyāna* has three heavens: (Brahmapāriṣadya, Brahmapurohita, and Mahābrahmā).

The second *dhyāna* has three heavens: (Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara). The third *dhyāna* has three heavens: (Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna). The fourth *dhyāna* has nine heavens:

(Anabhraka, Puṇyaprasava, and Bṛhatphala—these three above are the abodes of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who have practiced the ten superior wholesome deeds and attained meditative concentration; the Asaṃjñisattva heaven is the dwelling place of non-Buddhist practitioners; and finally, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha—these five heavens above).

The third fruit-dwelling consists of the eighteen heavens above, which are free from coarse desires and distractions; however, they have not yet transcended the "cage of form," and are therefore called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Because beings therein abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they receive the name "Dhyāna."
This brief commentary briefly elucidates the nine heavens of the four dhyānas, the differing distinctions between internal and external ordinary beings and noble ones,
and the reasons for the two names of "dhyāna" and "meditation boundary" (*sīmābandha*).
[Commentary] The *Miaoxuan* states: "The body of the primary retribution is pure matter (*rūpa*), unlike the defiled matter of the desire realm.
These eighteen heavens are established according to the Sthavira school."
[Commentary] This refers to the general name for the eighteen devas as explained in the *Vibhaṅga*. Regarding the term "Elder" (*sthavira*), the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"One above whom there is no one else is called an Elder. The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "From those with zero summer retreats up to nine summer retreats are called junior monks (*navaka*).
From ten summer retreats up to nineteen summer retreats are called middle-ranking monks (*madhyama*). From twenty summer retreats up to forty summer retreats are called..."
Elder. [Note] According to the Sarvāstivāda school, only sixteen heavens are established; for the Brahmapurohita and Mahābrahmā are combined into one, as there is no separate location between them.
The Āsaṃjñika and Bṛhatphala are also combined into one, as their bodies and lifespans are identical. According to the Sautrāntika school (after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, four... [text fragment])...

At the beginning of the hundred-year period, a school emerged from the Sarvāstivāda known as the Sautrāntika. They established their tenets based on the sūtras and did not rely upon the vinaya or śāstras. They posited seventeen heavens, because the physical dimensions of the Brahmapurohita and Mahābrahmā deities differ.
[Commentary: This indicates that the number of heavens established by other schools differs. "Sarvāstivāda" in Sanskrit means "All-Existence.
More than four hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, a dissenting school named Sarvāstivāda was established within the Sthavira school due to a dispute over doctrinal matters.
They state that within the realm of the Brahmapurohita devas, there is a high terrace and pavilion called Mahā-...
Brahmā. Just as the World-Honored One sits with the fourfold assembly surrounding him, it is said that there is no separate location.

Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Brahmā King and the Brahmā-purohitas belong to the same heaven. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) says: According to the Sarvāstivāda school, within the first dhyāna there are only sixteen locations;
the superior place therein is called the Brahmā King and is not established separately. The Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Vast Fruit (*bṛhatphala*) are combined.
First, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, it likewise does not mention the "Non-conceptual" (asaṃjñin) realm;

rather, it includes it within the "Vipulaphala" (Broad Fruit) heaven because their bodies and lifespans are identical. As for the Sautrāntikas, they emerged from the Sarvāstivādins and established seventeen heavens.

The Sphere of Non-perception (*asaṃjñika*) and the Fruit of Vastness (*bṛhatphala*) are combined into one; the Great Brahmā (*mahābrahmāṇaḥ*) and the Retinue of Brahmā (*brahmapurohitāḥ*) are distinguished as two.
This is because the body-measure of the Retinue of Brahmā is one *yojana*, while the body-measure of the Great Brahmā is one and a half *yojanas*.
Therefore, the seventeenth chapter of the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* states in verse: "Above this, seventeen places are called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); therein, each of the three dhyānas..."
Three [in the third dhyāna] and eight in the fourth dhyāna, totaling seventeen heavens. [Commentary:
Within the Sthavira school, eighteen must be clearly explained. Although the lifespan and physical form of the Bṛhatphala and the Asaṃjñisattvas are identical, their causes and fruits differ.
For the Bṛhatphala, the absence of vitarka and vicāra constitutes the cause and fruit; for the Asaṃjñisattvas, the absence of mind constitutes the cause and fruit.

[Commentary] This clarifies the reason why the Sthavira school establishes eighteen heavens. The intended meaning is that the cessation of vitarka and vicāra within the Bṛhatphala heaven serves as the cause, while the non-arising of vitarka and vicāra for five hundred kalpas constitutes the result.
Within the causal state of the non-conceptual (asaṃjñika), one cultivates the meditative attainment of non-conceptuality (asaṃjñi-samāpatti);

by ceasing the constantly active mind and mental factors, the retribution of birth occurs within the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisattva-deva). [This lasts for] four hundred and ninety... [kalpas].
For nineteen kalpas, the perception of mind does not function. Since there is thus a difference in cause and effect, it must be distinguished to constitute eighteen heavens.
[Note] The fourth dhyāna:
the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is translated here as "concentration" (*ding*). It refers to the focused concentration of the mind so that it does not flow or scatter. Worldly...
Supramundane. This dhyāna serves as the foundation. Each possesses its own branches and secondary qualities (*aṅga-vipula-guṇa*), according to the *Dharmadhātu-krama*.
[Commentary] This explains the general name "Four Dhyānas. Regarding why these four stages are collectively termed "dhyāna," according to the *Dharmadhātu-krama*:

"Dhyāna" is a term from the Western land (India); here it is translated as "abandoning evil," for it is able to abandon the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and other such factors of the desire realm.

Because it is the opposite of evil. Alternatively, it is translated as "the branches and groves of merit," or "cultivation through reflection. Now, translating it as "concentration" (*samādhi*) is said in contrast to "distraction.
This means gathering and restraining the scattered mind, focusing it on a single object so that it does not wander among the six sense-objects or dissipate itself in the five desires.
When practiced for a long time, concentration is naturally accomplished. It is supramundane.

Regarding the root of the world, the *Fajie* (Dharmadhātu) says: Because the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the supernormal powers and transformations, as well as the untainted contemplative wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and various other samādhis, all emerge from within the four dhyānas.

Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) states that the holy practices of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ārya-caryā*) are briefly categorized into three types: first, the mundane...
Dhyāna (meditative concentration) is of three types: first, mundane dhyāna; second, supramundane dhyāna; and third, the supreme-to-supreme dhyāna. Mundane dhyāna is further divided into two:

first, the fundamental dhyāna of "tasting" (*āsvādana*), which is obscured, defiled, and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); second, the fundamental pure dhyāna (*śuddha-dhyāna*), which is unobscured, undefiled, and determinate (*vyākṛta*).

It is called "fundamental" because it is cultivated by ordinary persons, noble ones, and non-Buddhists alike; thus, it is the foundation for both mundane and supramundane dharmas. *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It is said: "The Buddhas' attainment of enlightenment, their turning of the wheel of Dharma, and their entry into nirvana all occur within dhyāna.

Because one can deeply contemplate the root and give rise to the most excellent and sublime higher concentration, it is called 'the root. As for 'disappearance,' it refers to dark realization lacking contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*).
As for 'having defilement,' it refers to the arising of craving and attachment in each stage (*bhūmi*). As for 'indeterminate,' it refers to the lack of clarity regarding the object. This—
There are three grades, namely: dhyāna, samatā, and śūnyatā; these constitute the twelve gates of dhyāna.
As for the fundamental purity, it is non-obscured, stainless, and determinate, differing from the aforementioned. This, moreover, has three grades, namely: the six subtle gates.

The sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśa viśeṣas*) and the nine supernormal powers (*abhiñjā*), etc. Second, regarding supramundane dhyāna, there are four types: namely, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), refinement (*pariśodhana*), perfuming (*vāsana*), and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

As for "contemplation," it refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*). As for "refinement," it refers to...
The nine successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*). "Perfuming" refers to the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s stretch samādhi).
"Cultivation" refers to the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (the leaping-over samādhi). Third, the supramundane, most excellent dhyānas are the nine kinds of great dhyānas:

first, dhyāna of intrinsic nature; second, all-encompassing dhyāna; third, difficult dhyāna; fourth, dhyāna of all gateways; fifth, dhyāna of virtuous persons; sixth, dhyāna of all practices; seventh...
The dhyāna that removes affliction; the eighth, the dhyāna of happiness in this world and the next; and the ninth, the pure and purified dhyāna, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
The *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* also records these, though they are not recorded here in full. These constitute the supreme mundane and supramundane dhyānas.

Because they arise from the four fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), they are called "roots. The qualities of their branches and forests are seen below [in the section on] the Twelve Gates and so forth. [Supplementary Note: The Twelve Gates, etc.

In the *Tripiṭaka-dharmasaṃkhyā*, the *Dhyānapāramitā* is recorded with equal detail. A master has noted: "The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that being neither distracted nor savoring [the taste] is called *pāramitā*.
As for why this is merely called 'dhyāna' and not 'pāramitā,' distraction has both coarse and subtle forms;
craving and pride/views are subtle, while the three poisons are coarse. To take pleasure in it with a single mind is 'savoring' (*āsvāda*). Thus he distinguished them.
The erroneous claim that this translates as "fixed phrase" (*dingju*) is likely mistaken; it should rather be called "dhyāna" (*jinglü*).

This is because the desire realm possesses *lü* (discernment) but lacks *jing* (tranquility), while the formless realm possesses *jing* but lacks *lü*; only the form realm is fully endowed with both. Therefore, *dhyāna* is specifically located within the form realm.

The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) pertain to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*). [Commentary: However, in this chart, only the names and characteristics of each have been indicated. I shall now record them in full. As stated in the *Dharmadhātu-vibhaṅga*, regarding the five factors of the first dhyāna:
first, the factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). When the initial mind is directed toward its object, it is called "awakening" (*vitarka*); the practitioner relies upon...
In the stage of "not-yet-reached" (*anāgamya*), one gives rise to the pure dharmas of the form realm belonging to the first dhyāna, which contact the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) of the desire realm.
The mind is greatly startled and awakened; at that moment, bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) arises, and one perceives this contact of the form realm as a hitherto unprecedented merit and benefit.
Second is the branch of observation (*vicāra*): the subtle mental discrimination is called observation. Having already realized the merits of the first dhyāna, one then—

The subtle mind discriminates these material phenomena within this meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and its various sublime qualities; the objects are clear and distinct, free from all obscurations.
Such qualities have never before existed in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Third, the factor of joy (*prīti-aṅga*):
the mind of exultation is called "joy. At the moment it arises, joy is produced, yet because discrimination is not yet complete, the joy is not [fully manifest].

It is accomplished. If one contemplates the mind through analysis, the pleasure of the desire realm that has been relinquished is very slight, whereas the benefit now obtained from the first dhyāna is exceedingly great;
thus, there is immeasurable joy. Fourth, the factor of bliss (*sukha-aṅga*): a heart of serene delight is called "bliss. At the moment it arises, there is indeed bliss;
however, when the agitation of the mind stirred by joy subsides, one then experiences the contact of tranquil, meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

*Pīti* (rapture) means joy, gladness, peace, and bliss. Five. The factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekaggatā*). Because the mind and the state of concentration are unified, it is called "one-pointedness of mind.
When the practitioner first realizes dhyāna, they immediately become attached to the concentration;

yet the mind still relies upon the factors of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), and bliss (*sukha*), and thus there remains a subtle degree of distraction. If the mind of rapture and bliss subsides, it naturally becomes one with concentration. Two.

The four factors of dhyāna are as follows: First, the factor of internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*). When the mind is free from the turbidity of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it is called "internal purity.
When the practitioner wishes to leave the first dhyāna, they variously censure applied and sustained thought; once these have ceased, the mind becomes internally pure.
The mind then corresponds with pure material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), becoming suddenly clear and luminous. Second, the factor of joy (*prīti*). The state of a joyful heart is called joy.
Joy (*prīti*). When the practitioner first attains internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), it arises simultaneously with joy, yet the mind of joy has not yet been fully established.
Subsequently, the mind rejoices in itself, having escaped the affliction of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) and attained the superior concentration of internal purity;
thus, its joy is immeasurable. Third, the factor of bliss (*sukha*). A state of mental serenity is called bliss. Once the practitioner’s feelings of exultation have subsided, then—
Tranquil in meditative reflection, one experiences the joy and bliss within internal purity. Four: the factor of one-pointedness of mind.

When the mind and the state of concentration are unified, it is called "one-pointedness. As the practitioner experiences bliss and the mind becomes stilled, the mind and concentration become one, becoming clear, still, and unmoving.
Three Dhyānas: Five factors. First: the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Being free from joy and without regret is called equanimity. The practitioner...
When one wishes to depart from the second dhyāna, one censures joy through various causes and conditions. Once joy has ceased and vanished, the third dhyāna immediately arises.
If one realizes the bliss of the third dhyāna, one abandons the joy of the second dhyāna without giving rise to regret.
It is also called the bliss of the third dhyāna. At the moment of its initial arising, this bliss is the foremost within the three realms and is capable of giving rise to mental attachment.

When the mind becomes attached, the dhyāna is destroyed; therefore, one must practice equanimity (*upekṣā*). Second is the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*). "Mindfulness" here refers to affectionate recollection.

Once the practitioner has generated this bliss of the third dhyāna, and since the bliss arises from within, they must cherish and protect it with affectionate mindfulness; thus, the bliss may increase.

1. The factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*). It extends throughout the entire body. 2. The factor of mindfulness (*smṛti*). It is the mind that maintains clear recollection. 3. The factor of discernment (*prajñā*). The mind that understands and knows is called discernment.
Once the practitioner has given rise to the bliss of the third dhyāna, this bliss is subtle and difficult to attain;

were it not for skillful discernment, one would be unable to employ skillful means to nurture it so that this bliss pervades the entire body. 4. The factor of bliss (*sukha*). The mind that is joyful and contented is called bliss.

Once the practitioner has given rise to these three dhyāna-blisses, if they can skillfully employ equanimity, mindfulness, and wisdom to protect this bliss, then since the bliss is faultless, it will increase and bring joy throughout the entire body; experiencing such blissful ease and well-being constitutes the supreme bliss.
If one is apart from the third dhyāna, there is no such pervasive bodily bliss in any other stage. Five: the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*).

When the mind and the state of concentration are unified, it is called "one-pointed mind. When the mind that experiences bliss comes to rest, the mind and concentration become one and remain unmoving.

Four: the fourth dhyāna has four factors. First: the factor of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukha*). A neutral state of mind is called "neither-pain-nor-pleasure. This is the mental formation (*saṃskāra*).
One who wishes to depart from the third dhyāna censures pleasure through various causes and conditions.

Once pleasure has subsided and ceased, the concentration of immovability (*āniñjya-samādhi*) arises together with equanimity (*upekṣā*); thus, the inner mind becomes serene, being neither painful nor pleasant. Second is the factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-aṅga*).

To be free from pleasure and without regret is called equanimity. Having attained the fourth dhyāna, the true concentration of immovability, one then relinquishes that which is difficult to relinquish.

One does not give rise to a mind of regret. It is also said that when one realizes the immovable concentration (*āniñjya-samādhi*) of the fourth dhyāna, one should not grasp at the concentration or give rise to discursive thoughts.
If one practices equanimity (*upekṣā*), there will be no deviation caused by such movement of thought. Third is the factor of pure mindfulness (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*).
As for "mindfulness," it means loving mindfulness. Having attained the true concentration of the fourth dhyāna, one should contemplate the faults of the lower stages and contemplate one's own merits.
Skillful means nurture [the mind], preventing it from falling away and causing it to enter superior stages; this is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).

It is also said that within the four dhyānas there is immovable illumination and clear understanding, which is the distinctness of right mindfulness. Fourth is the factor of one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*): the mind and meditative concentration are one.
This is called "one-pointed mind. Having attained the concentration of the fourth dhyāna associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), one relinquishes mindfulness and brings it to rest.

Since mindfulness has no further basis, it becomes utterly still and tranquil; the mind is focused on concentration as if a bright mirror were unmoving, reflecting with profound clarity so that all phenomena appear therein.

For what reason is the fourth dhyāna alone called "immovable"? It is because the first dhyāna is moved by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and the second dhyāna is moved by joy (*prīti*).
It is moved by the bliss of the third dhyāna; therefore, the fourth dhyāna is called "true concentration" (*bhūtadhyāna*).
If one skillfully illuminates and understands with clarity, then based on this concentration, one gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).

As for the outflow-bound practitioners of external paths who lack the skillful means of wisdom, when they enter this concentration, they do not destroy the physical form but instead directly extinguish the mind, entering the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), which they mistakenly claim to be *nirvāṇa*.
This constitutes a perverted inversion. As for the term "limb" (*aṅga*), it means a branch or division. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Although there are other factors within the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), because these [factors] are preeminent, they are established as 'limbs' for the practitioner of concentration, serving as objects of reflection."
[Commentary] *Fuxing* 9a (9) quotes from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, asking: Why are there five in the first three [categories], while there are four in the second and fourth?
Answer: It has been handed down from antiquity that the five desires of the desire realm constitute external distraction, while the joy of the second dhyāna constitutes internal distraction.
The first dhyāna marks the beginning of the remedy for external distraction, and the third dhyāna marks the beginning of the remedy for internal distraction; therefore, each has five factors.
In the second dhyāna, external distraction ceases, and in the fourth dhyāna, internal distraction ceases; for this reason, the second and fourth dhyānas are established as having only four factors.
[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā* states: "That which is conducive (*anuloma*) is a factor (*aṅga*). If a dharma is conducive to a particular stage, it is established as a factor.

Five factors are conducive to the first two [dhyānas], and four factors are conducive to the second and fourth. Furthermore, the desire realm is a sphere that is difficult to sever, difficult to eliminate, and difficult to transcend;
therefore, it requires a firm and powerful antidote. Consequently, five factors are established for the first dhyāna as its antidote."

The second dhyāna has joy (*prīti*), which is likewise difficult to sever, difficult to eliminate, and difficult to transcend; therefore, its antidote, the third dhyāna, also possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*).
Since the first dhyāna is not difficult to sever, eliminate, or transcend, its antidote, the second dhyāna, is established as having four factors (*caturaṅga*).
Furthermore, in order to counteract the craving for the five kinds of objects in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the first dhyāna is established as having five factors. For...
Regarding the five kinds of joy (*prīti*) in the second dhyāna, the third [dhyāna] is established as having five factors (*pañcāṅga*).

Because the first dhyāna lacks the craving for the five kinds of objects, and the third dhyāna lacks the liking for the five kinds of joy, the second and fourth dhyānas are not established as having five factors.

[Note] The three heavens of the First Dhyāna. "Brahma" (梵) means purity (*śuddha*), because they are free from the defilement of desire. All eighteen heavens are pure and free from desire, but this [heaven] stands at their head and thus universally receives the name "Pure.
The Brahma-kāyika are the subjects; the Brahma-purohita are the ministers; and the Mahābrahmā is the king.
He was born first at the beginning of the kalpa and perishes last at the end of the kalpa. He presides over a great trichiliocosm; however, generally speaking, there are ten billion such Brahmās.
O King, it is only within this Great Trichiliocosm that one may bear the name Śikhin and become its sovereign; beyond this, such a thing is impossible.
This is not a mere arbitrary claim, for in the First Dhyāna there exists speech and command, by which one can govern those above and preside over those below.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Lord of the Sahā World, the Brahmā King Śikhin Mahābrahmā, or Maheśvara."

Residing at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), he is the sovereign by virtue of his superior retribution (*vipāka*). There is no sense of a ruling king here; for from the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no dharma of speech.
Therefore, in each of the various dhyānas, one is likewise sovereign by virtue of superior retribution, not through the exercise of governance.

This vertical distinction is fully explained in the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra Commentary*. As for the statement in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary*: "The Lord of the Sahā World is precisely..."
Śūra, also called Brahmā-rāja, governs only a small chiliocosm; this is the explanation of the ancient masters and not the primary intent of our own school.
[Commentary] The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Freedom from desire and tranquility is called Brahma (*brahma*); in its full form it is *brahmā*. This is translated as 'purity' (*qingjie*)."
"Quiescence" (*śānti*) refers to the initial departure from the defilement of desire, which is termed "purity. Attaining the fundamental dhyāna constitutes "quiescence.

The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) refers to this as "lofty purity. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The heavens that have severed sexual desire are all called *brahma*; the First Dhyāna is their foremost."
This is specifically named "Pure. Next, it clarifies that the three heavens are divided into rulers, ministers, and subjects.

Because there is no language or dharma above the Second Dhyāna, kings and ministers are not established there; thus, we know that in the First Dhyāna, there exist language, commands, and governance, and therefore they are divided into rulers and ministers.
However, this general discussion below concerns the realm transformed by a single Buddha, namely the trichiliocosm.
Regarding the world in terms of its horizontal extent, there are ten trillion heavens of the First Dhyāna and ten trillion Brahmā Kings; yet all of these reside in the four directions.
Only this Śikhin presides over the Great Thousandfold World-system (Mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu). Śikhin is translated as "Crown Tuft" (Dingji).

On the crown of the King’s head is a fleshy protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) shaped like a conch; it is also called "Conch-Crest" (*śaṅkhacakraka*). Alternatively, it is called "Fire-Crown," because the calamity of fire reaches only up to this point.
His appearance is like that of a youth; his body is the color of white silver, and he wears garments of golden-yellow. He takes the joy of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-prīti*) as his food.

Furthermore, below this, there is a vertical classification of the Great Trichiliocosm according to the Kings [of the Heavens], stating that because the First Dhyāna possesses applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), it [is characterized by these].

Language and commands govern those above and crown those below. Question: In the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, Maheśvara is listed among the external protectors;
why is he called the lord of the Sahā world? Answer: Maheśvara dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*).

However, from the Second Dhyāna upward, there is neither applied nor sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), and thus no faculty of speech exists. Therefore, because his retribution is superior, he is [so designated].

"Lord" (*pati*) does not mean a sovereign ruler. Furthermore, as for *Śikhin*, this king originally cultivated the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), thereby destroying the afflictions of the desire realm;
he was named after this virtue. However, since the sutra mentions both the Brahma King and Śikhin, it appears as if there were two individuals.

According to the correct interpretation of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Shìlùn), Śikhin is the Lord. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* cites his rank to reveal his name, fearing that [if only one were mentioned] it might be a single person.
Furthermore, by practicing meditation alone, one becomes a Brahma-minister; by adding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), one becomes a king. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states:
"Maheśvara is Maheśvara [Mahesvaradeva], who dwells at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and presides over the trichiliocosm.
A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage manifests his traces therein. As for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it lists the World-Ruler as the Brahmā King.
What is the meaning of this? If one says "the lord of the Sahā world," it refers precisely to Śūra.
If one mentions Mahābrahmā Śikhin and others, these are further instances of citing the Brahma kings of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Furthermore, regarding the title "Brahmā Devānām Indra" as the lord of the world, I privately maintain that this refers to one who has attained the status of a Great [Brahmā] within a great trichiliocosm.

The Lord of a Thousand [Worlds] cannot descend here; therefore, we know that the claim that the Brahmā King governs only a small chiliocosm is the doctrine of ancient masters, not the intention of the present commentary.
[Supplement] The First Dhyāna is called the Stage of Joy and Bliss Born of Seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha-bhūmi*).

This means that by being separated from birth amidst the defiled and evil realms of the Desire Realm, one attains pure bliss. In the Vinaya, this is likened to the thorough soaking and moistening of a body during a skillful bath.

[Commentary] The three heavens of the Second Dhyāna are: 1) Parīttābha (Limited Light), so called because their radiance is slight; 2) Apramāṇābha (Immeasurable Light), so called because their radiance increases further until it becomes immeasurable;
3) Ābhāsvara (Light-Sound), so called because they use light as their speech and sound. The new translation calls this Abhāsvara (Extreme Light).

[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The second dhyāna is collectively termed 'Light-Sound' (*Ābhāsvara*). When the inhabitants of that heaven speak, pure light issues from their mouths.
Some say that because they have no applied or sustained thought internally and no speech externally, they use light in place of words; therefore, it is called 'Light-Sound.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* calls it 'Utmost Pure Light' (*Śubhakṛtsna*), meaning that pure light universally illuminates both one's own and others' locations. [Supplement] Second Dhyāna: Perception.

Contemplating both [joy and pain] as abandoned, one is not oppressed by anxiety or longing; having already subdued the coarse outflows (*āsrava*), this is designated as the stage of "joy and bliss born of concentration" (*samādhi-ja-prīti-sukha-bhūmi*).
This means that the water of concentration moistens the mind, which in the Vinaya is likened to a spring on a mountain peak. As for the "Limited Light" (*Parītta-ābhā*) and the others:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Because the purity and degree of the mind vary, the light has superior, middling, and inferior qualities.

The gods of the various heavens possess bodily radiance because their minds are pure and they practice generosity and uphold the precepts. Furthermore, there are those who light lamps in dark places, making offerings to honored images, stupas, and monasteries;
who constantly cultivate loving-kindness (*maitrī*); and who also practice the Buddha-recollection samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*), recollecting the light of all Buddhas."
