The other false speech—concerning the four aggregates such as feeling and perception, permanence and impermanence, finitude and infinity, and so forth—should be understood by analogy with these fourfold propositions.
Those who reckon [the self] as permanent do so because they cultivate merit for the sake of receiving retribution in future lives.

Those who reckon it as impermanent do so only for the sake of this present life, as they do not believe in retribution in future lives. Those who reckon it as both permanent and impermanent maintain that the spirit (*ātman*) possesses two aspects: coarse and subtle.

There are four types: first, that which is subtle and eternal; second, that which currently performs actions; third, that which is impermanent at the time of death; and fourth, that the subtle spirit (*sūkṣma-ātman*) is eternal.
Those who hold these four views all possess false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), for they merely falsely calculate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) to be the self (*ātman*).

"The world" (*loka*) here refers to the world of the physical realm (*bhājana-loka*); within the characteristics of this world, there are likewise four kinds of false views. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "From where does the self arise?"
If there were no cause from the very beginning, there would have to be error; yet the world exists. How then could this be the same as the heterodox view of a self (*ātman*)? The answer is:
[The Buddha] merely refutes the arising of the marks of permanence and impermanence regarding the world; he does not refute the world itself.

The Buddha refutes the perversion of the world’s permanence, but he does not refute the world. Why? Because it is directly perceived to be impermanent. Furthermore, one cannot say that it does not exist.

"Constant. This is because sins and merits are never lost. "Seeking the beginning of the world and not finding it" means that one seeks the fundamental origin of the world and does not find its beginning.
As for the calculation of eighty thousand kalpas, beyond this point one can no longer know;

it is merely a conceptual construction of a phenomenon, named the "constant nature of the world" (*lokadhātu-svabhāva*). Regarding the statement that the spirit (*ātman*) is like a mustard seed, the treatise says:

[The soul is] like a mustard seed, or like a jujube fruit, or said to be one inch [in size]. This is because they claim the soul (*ātman*) is a material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) that possesses parts.

Regarding the statement that the soul is finite or infinite: some say that the soul pervades empty space; it is able to perceive pleasure and pain only when occupying a body, and this is called the soul being infinite.
Regarding the mutual reckoning of the earth and the soul-self as existing or non-existing: some say that the soul...
The world is infinite; the world of lands is finite, or the world of deities is finite, while the world of lands is infinite, and so forth—these are termed "finite and infinite.

Some people perceive that there are faults in both the finitude and infinitude of the world, and thus they cling to the view that it is neither finite nor infinite, taking this to be the true nature of the world; such is the extreme view of limits (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). As it says:
As for "departing": it is like a person who comes to be born here and then departs to a future life; it is just so.

Some say that in a previous life there was nowhere from which one came, and upon extinction there is nowhere to which one goes. Others say that the union of the body and the spirit constitutes a human being.
After death, the spirit departs, but the body does not; this is called "thus-going" (tathāgata) and "not thus-going.
To perceive going and non-going is an error. Such a person cannot relinquish the spirit, yet clings to that which is neither going nor not going.
In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the passage "if earth or wood were absent" refers to an inquiry concerning the land alone. As for "the body goes while the spirit does not," it means:

The death and transformation and cessation of the body is "departure"; the non-transformation and non-cessation of the spirit is "non-departure. Regarding the statement in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* that "the spirit departs while the body does not depart":
the death and dissolution of the body is "non-departure," and the spirit's arrival in a future world is "departure. Both interpretations are logically consistent.

Furthermore, the *Śrīman-deva-vyākhyāna* states: "Regarding the sixty-two views, there are differing interpretations. For now, following the *Mahā-śāstra*, [the views] concerning the past are explained in relation to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as:
'The self and the world are eternal,' 'This is true, all else is false,' and so forth; the three phrases for each [of the other aggregates] are likewise."
The remaining aggregates (*skandha*) are also like this, thus forming twenty. Regarding the present as finite or infinite and so forth, applying these to the five aggregates also results in twenty.
Regarding whether the self exists after death, does not exist after death, and so forth, these also result in twenty. This makes sixty.
Adding "the self and the body are one" and "the self and the body are different" makes sixty-two.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, stating that there are sixty-five views. These consist of reckoning each of the five aggregates (*skandha*) as the self in four ways:
namely, "form is the self," "feeling is the servant," and so forth, including [the notions of feeling as] ornaments, a cave, or a dwelling. The same applies to the other three aggregates.

Combining the views of the self and what belongs to the self (*ātmiya*) results in thirteen propositions for each aggregate; thus, across the five aggregates, they total sixty-five propositions. Therefore, one...
One aggregate: the first is "I," and the other four are "mine. [Supplement] The *Ratnavali* states: "It is like a person who possesses wealth;
servants belong to me and are my subordinates. It is like a dwelling; oil exists within sesame seeds, and so forth."

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*) states: The *Wushi jiaojì jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Calculations) presents doctrinal characteristics that differ slightly from other sūtras. The *Zhi guan chao* quotes this sūtra as saying:
"If the eye perceives beautiful colors, ugly colors, or neutral colors, each contains *āśrava* (outflows) and *samudaya* (origination). This applies even up to the mind perceiving dharmas.
Thus, for each faculty there are three kinds of objects (*viṣaya*), and within these three kinds there are six types of *āśrava* and *samudaya*. This constitutes the six [bases].

The faculties (indriya) comprise thirty-six; when combined with the three periods of time, there are one hundred and eight. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "That sutra establishes only six faculties, each with six [aspects].
Although it lacks explicit mention of the three periods of time, it concludes by stating 'one hundred and eight. Thus we know that the three periods of time are reckoned in terms of moments (kṣaṇa).
Since the triad of mind (citta), mentation (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna) constitutes the three aspects of the mental ground (manobhūmi), they therefore pertain to all three periods of time."

As it is said: "The gathering and arising is called *citta* (mind); deliberation is called *manas* (intellect); and discernment is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

"If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, each of the six sense organs has three types of sensation (*vedanā*). These three sensations correspond to the three objects; when combined with the three periods of time, they constitute the one hundred and eight [afflictions]."

This is discussed in terms of karmic retribution (vipāka) in relation to the three periods of time. [Supplement] Regarding the momentary (*kṣaṇika*), it refers to the mind; regarding karmic retribution, it refers to the object (*viṣaya*).

The object is a phenomenon that constitutes retribution. As for the "aggregation of aggregates" (*skandha-samudaya*): the term "aggregate" (*skandha*) refers to pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral objects; the term "aggregation" (*samudaya*) refers to the arising of views (*dṛṣṭi*) upon those aggregates.

Some say that "aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of "covering" (*chādana*), while "aggregation" (*samudaya*) has the meaning of "accumulation" (*caya*). Pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral forms [are thus categorized].
If, with respect to the eye, the eye is that which is turned [toward objects], and it covers the eye, it is called a "skandha" (aggregate).

Furthermore, when these aggregates collect—whether they be beautiful, ugly, or neutral colors—with the seeds within, it is called a "samudaya" (accumulation). As it is with the eye faculty, so it is with the other faculties. This explanation is to be kept in mind.

[Note on the Square Box]: "Afflictions of thought" (*si-huo*). Upon entering the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one repeatedly contemplates the Truth (*satya*). The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states: "Contemplation" (*lü*) refers to deliberative thought.

Having already produced the outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) through the contemplation of Truth during the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*), one now contemplates it again; hence, it is called "repeated contemplation.

These afflictions are thereby eliminated and are termed "afflictions of thought" (*siwei-huo*). This name is derived from their function. If one speaks of "afflictions of thought regarding the conventional" (*si-jiā*) and "afflictions of craving" (*ài-huo*), these are names based on the essential nature of the phenomena themselves.

[Commentary] Regarding the term "cessation and contemplation" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), it is called "contemplation" (*manasikāra*) because it derives its name from understanding. Initially, when one perceives the Truth, it is still shallow and remains subject to objective hindrances.

Later, by repeatedly reflecting upon the Truth, these delusions are eliminated; thus, they are termed "delusions of contemplation. [Supplementary Note] As for "delusions of contemplation," they are fully constituted by the three types of false assumptions:
causal, continuous, and relative; hence they are called "false assumptions of contemplation. As for "delusions of craving," this is a technical term referring to *rāga* (greed/attachment).

It is called "thought" (saṃkalpa). This refers to the greedy attachment and defiled clinging toward the five external sense objects. It is the primary gateway to the dharma-realm and is termed the "affliction of craving.
This is a designation based on the very nature of the phenomenon itself.

[Commentary] However, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) arise from the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) and are able to obstruct the true principle (*tattva*). The delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) arise from the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and are able to draw one into the three realms (*tridhātu*).
These statements are all made with reference to the majority of cases in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); in detailed analysis, they are not restricted to this.

[Commentary] This clarifies that the hindrances of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) differ. Therefore, within the teachings, the delusions of view are termed "hindrances to principle" (*li-zhang*), while the delusions of thought are termed "hindrances to phenomena" (*shi-zhang*).
However, this is stated primarily with reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). [Supplement] The delusions of view do not merely hinder principle.
It can also draw forth rebirth, as it is said: "By means of these three, one returns to the lower realms.

Furthermore, the afflictions of volition (cetanā-kleśa) not only draw forth rebirth but can also obstruct the principle (li), as it is said: "Because of craving and attachment, one does not perceive the True Reality. *Biandongie* states:

This detailed discussion does not restrict itself to the literal phrasing of the text; rather, because the *Jiuzhu* (Collected Commentaries) establishes the "Diagram of the One Hundred and Eight Views," these words were spoken.
The above clarifies that the one hundred and eight views do not arise apart from the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

Since it is established that some views arise from the five sense objects (*pañcaviṣaya*), why is it said that "view" arises from the mental object (*dharmadhātu*) while "thought" arises from the five sense objects? In my private opinion, "not restricting" refers to the harmonization [of these points].
These are explained as being obstacles that hinder principle and lead to rebirth.
△ Second, different names for the same essence:

it is also called "viewing" (dṛṣṭi) and "cultivation" (bhāvanā); it is also called the "four abodes" (catvāra āśrayāḥ); it is also called "defiled ignorance" (kliṣṭājñāna); and it is also called "afflictions of grasping at signs" (nimittagrāha-kleśa). Furthermore...

It is called "ignorance at the branch-tip," it is also called "pervasive delusion," and it is also called "delusion within the realms. Although the names differ, they refer only to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*bhāvanā*).

[Commentary] "Views and cultivation" refers to the delusions of views, which are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and the delusions of thought, which are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). These names are applied according to the stage of the practitioner's capacity for abandonment.
These are the afflictions to be abandoned.
[Commentary] Those abandoned by the eight patiences and eight knowledges during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first fruit are called "afflictions of seeing" (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Those abandoned by the nine unhindered paths and nine paths of liberation during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) through reflection for the second and third fruits are called "afflictions of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

[Commentary] The four abodes (*catur-vāsa*) consist of the abode of views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsa*) as one, and the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) divided into three. Because of these two types of delusion, one dwells attached to the triple world (*traidhātuka*).
[Record] The abode of all views and the three abodes of craving for the desire, form, and formless realms.
[Note] "Defiled ignorance. *Myōraku* (Vol. 1, p. 24) states: "In the Hīnayāna, two types of ignorance are established:
defiled ignorance, which has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its essence; and non-defiled ignorance, which has inferior wisdom (*hīnaprajñā*) as its essence.

This refers to [knowledge of] taste, power, maturation, efficacy, time, number, and measure (the various flavors of phenomena; their power for benefit or harm; the efficacy of maturation; time such as proximity or distance; and numbers such as 'one by one' or measures such as 'large' and 'small')."
[Supplementary Note] Regarding the enumeration of dharmas: "Defiled ignorance" refers to the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *kleśa* (outflows), taking *avidyā* (ignorance) as its essence;

this means that it does not clearly comprehend the true nature (*tathatā*). "Non-defiled ignorance" refers to the *rajas-kaṣāya* (dust-like and sand-like [afflictions]), taking inferior wisdom (*hīna-prajñā*) as its essence;
this is because the seeds of the afflictions of *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa* within the sphere of others are as numerous as dust or sand, yet they are unable to defile [the true nature].
This is my true nature. The wisdom of the two vehicles is narrow and inferior; it cannot cause others to sever the afflictions of views and thought, and is thus termed "non-defiled ignorance.
[Supplement] That which does not obstruct the ultimate truth is called "non-defiled"; that which lacks comprehension of conventional truth is called "ignorance.
This inferior wisdom is the knowledge of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Although it can realize emptiness, regarding the infinite dharma-gates of the Buddhas, it is...
Those born with immeasurable faculties and natures are all unable to fathom it. Regarding the "equal flavor of all dharmas":

this means that within the Dharma-gates as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is the "flavor of all dharmas" in terms of the teachings; there is the "power of benefit and harm" in terms of the capacities of sentient beings;

there is the "maturation of virtuous function" in terms of the potential; and there is the "temporal distance or proximity" in terms of their characteristics. Each of these categories—whether great or small—is equal in number.

These are equal in measure; none of them are known by those of the Two Vehicles. The *Suixiang lun* (Treatise on Following Characteristics) states that lightness, heaviness, cold, heat, moisture, smoothness, softness, hardness, and so forth, are called "potencies" (*śakti*).
As for "maturation," it is like food or fruit entering the stomach, where the transformation and ripening differ.
As for "virtues" (*guṇa*), these are the majestic powers of plants and trees, such as roots that can emit light, repel ghosts, or eliminate poison, and so on. [End of] Supplement.

The Master Xingyan says that what others understand as "non-defiled" is actually the *vāsanā* (habitual tendencies). The intention of our own school is that, in the case of the Lesser Vehicle, these habitual tendencies are precisely the distinct delusions (*bhinna-kleśa*).

[Note] Regarding "delusions of grasping at marks" (*nimitta-grahaṇa-kleśa*): all three delusions are termed "grasping at marks. The *Guan-yin xuanyi ji*, Volume Upper (7), states: "View and thought (*dṛṣṭi-vikalpa*) grasp..."

The characteristic of birth and death is *rajas* (dust); the characteristic of taking up *nirvāṇa* is ignorance; the characteristic of taking up the two extremes is present *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* [afflictions];
and these take up the characteristics of birth and death within the six realms.

[Supplementary Note] To reckon birth and death as real is the grasping at marks (*nimitta-grāha*) of view-delusion and affliction-delusion (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). To illuminate the True [Ultimate] while failing to comprehend the Conventional is the grasping at marks of the "dust-sands" [of ignorance].

To be biased toward either the True or the Conventional without attaining accord with the Middle is the grasping at marks of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the clarification of erroneous terminology:

Master Guan (Zhiyi) names the grasping at marks "view-delusion and affliction-delusion"; this should be understood through both a general and a specific interpretation. The specific interpretation is as follows:...

The *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text) explains that Mahākāśyapa’s contemplation of the mind consists of shaking off and discarding the grasping for signs (*nimitta*). Regarding the statement that "cessation and contemplation return to the Great Place," it is said that grasping for signs obstructs *prajñā*.
Both the general and specific interpretations point to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*).
[Note] The secondary ignorance (*avidyā*) is named in contrast to the fundamental [ignorance]. Since views and afflictions take ignorance as their root, they are called "secondary.
Because it lacks clear comprehension regarding all phenomena, it is called "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
[Commentary] Ignorance (*avidyā*) serves as the basis for all defilements; therefore, the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) take it as their root.

[Sub-commentary] These are called "universal afflictions" (*sāmānya-kleśa*) because they are so named in contrast to "particular afflictions. Since the afflictions of views and thought are abandoned by practitioners of all three vehicles, they are termed universal.
The *rajas-resembling* ignorance (*rajas-sama-avidyā*) exists specifically within what is abandoned by Bodhisattvas; therefore, it is termed a particular affliction.

[Commentary]: Śrāvakas sever the afflictions of both views and cultivation separately at the beginning and end [of their path]. Pratyekabuddhas sever the afflictions of views and cultivation instantaneously, yet their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted.

Bodhisattvas, by means of thirty-four moments of mind, instantaneously sever the afflictions of views, cultivation, and habitual tendencies; therefore, these are termed "pervasive delusions" (*sāmānyakleśa*).
[Note] "Defilements within the realm" (*jìè nèi huò*) is a designation made in contrast to those "outside the realm.

The *dust-and-sand* (*chénshā*) [defilements] moisten untainted karma (*wúlòu yè*), while ignorance (*wúmíng*) moistens karma that is neither tainted nor untainted (*fēilòu fēiwúlòu yè*), thereby inviting birth in the *parināmika* (transformation) realm;
hence they are called "outside the realm. As for the dust-and-sand defilements, they pervade both the realms within and outside.
[Supplement] The delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā*) act as the moisture; tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*) acts as that which is moistened.

Delusion and karma act as the attractors; birth within the three realms acts as that which is attracted. Because they are moistened and attracted by the delusions of views and thought, they do not transcend the six destinies;

thus they are termed "delusions within the realm" (*dhātu-antar-kleśa*). As it is said in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "All tainted wholesome and unwholesome karmas, through the power of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*) acting as a contributing condition..."
The coarse resultant fruit of the three realms induced by [karmic] power is precisely the birth-and-death of segmented duration (*paricchinna-jarā-maraṇa*).
Regarding "dust-sands of moistening non-outflow karma": this non-outflow karma refers to the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness cultivated by those of the two vehicles.
However, it has not yet been examined from which sūtra or śāstra these "dust-sands of moistening karma" are derived. As for karma that is neither out-flowing nor non-out-flowing:

This refers to the practices cultivated by Bodhisattvas when they emerge from the conventional realm. Because these differ from the karmic actions of the birth-and-death cycle of the six realms, they are not "outflowing" (sāsrava).

Furthermore, because they do not share in the karmic activities of the two vehicles that cling to emptiness, they are not "non-outflowing" (anāsrava). Regarding the summoning of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*):

delusions and karma are the summoners, while the transformation body is that which is summoned. Through the power of compassion and vows, one transforms and sustains the physical life. There is no [other cause].
The fixed limit is called "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). It is like changing coarse matter for fine matter, or transforming short years into long ones. Question:
If it involves changing the coarse and transforming the short, why is it called "birth and death" (*saṃsāra*)? Answer: The exhaustion of the power of conscious awareness is called "death.

Entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and receiving further sustenance is termed "birth. Because these afflictions and karma only induce birth and death outside the realms, they are called "afflictions outside the realms. Only...

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All untainted (*anāsrava*) karma involving conceptual differentiation (*savikalpa*), through the auxiliary power of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), produces a distinct and subtle fruition of maturation (*vipākaphala*);

this is precisely the death and rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmikī cyuti*). Regarding the phrase "dust-like [afflictions] pervading both within and outside the realms," these delusions are spoken of from the perspective of conversion and guidance;
for example, while those of the two vehicles can sever their own view-delusions and afflictions (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*), they cannot sever those of others.
Regarding the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) of others: when one looks at the views and afflictions of other people, they are as numerous as dust motes and grains of sand.

Within this realm, views and afflictions constitute its substance. When a Bodhisattva has personally destroyed their own ignorance (*avidyā*) but has not yet been able to destroy the ignorance of all other people, and recognizes the stages of cultivation and realization beyond this realm, then the ignorance of others appears as numerous as dust motes and grains of sand. This is the realm [beyond].

Externally, it takes ignorance (*avidyā*) as its essence. [Note] Regarding "ripening" (*vipāka*): it refers to the deluded karma produced, which matures and brings about the fruition at a different time and in a different lifetime.
Regarding the "obstruction to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): "knowing" (*jñeya*) refers to the cause of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

When this applied and sustained thought is not extinguished, it obstructs the *dharmatā*, preventing one from attaining realization; thus it is called the obstruction to the knowable. [Note] *Bian'e* says: Ignorance...

The category of "moistening" (āsrava) is not [identical to] the category of "outflows" (āsrava). First, one should supplement the category of karma that is both outflowing and non-outflowing; this shall be reserved for final determination later.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two—view-delusion (dṛṣṭi) and thought-delusion (saṃjñā)—has two parts. First, the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) has three parts. First, the heading and enumeration of the names of the proclivities (anuśaya). First, the general indication of the names and numbers.
First, regarding the explanation of the delusions of view, there are eighty-eight *anuśaya*s (latent proclivities).
[Note] The *Fajie Cidi Shang* (7) states: "The term *anuśaya* has the meaning of 'driving and employing.
Because they can drive and employ the mind and spirit of the practitioner, causing them to transmigrate through the three realms, they are collectively given the name *anuśaya*."
[Commentary] The Hīnayāna does not speak of the eighth consciousness; therefore, it refers to it as the "mind-spirit" (*citta*).
△ Second, the specific enumeration of the ten *anuśayas* (proclivities):

namely, first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*); third, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); fourth, the grasping at precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); fifth, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—the above are the sharp proclivities (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*). Sixth...
1. Greed; 2. Anger; 3. Ignorance; 4. Pride; 5. Doubt (the above are the dull fetters). [Commentary] The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*):
within the aggregates, bases, and elements, one falsely calculates them to be a "self," forcibly establishing a sovereign master, and constantly giving rise to the view of self.

In various texts, it is sometimes called "view of self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and sometimes "view of selfhood" (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). In the *Shizhiguan* (Ten Transformations of Stopping and Contemplation), both names are listed:

"Because one seeks for a self and cannot find it, the view of self is destroyed; because the view of self is destroyed, the view of selfhood is destroyed. (Text). The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan), fascicle 5, part 2, states:
"The non-Buddhist outsiders postulate a self, [imagining it to be] like a sesame seed, a bean, or the thumb, or they postulate it as pervading the entire body, [identifying it with] the spirit-body."
The four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and [the categories of] identity and difference, etc.

(Text). [Commentary]: The *Zongjing* says that "self" (*ātman*) has two meanings: "lordship" (*prabhutva*) and "sovereignty" (*adhipatya*). That is to say, "lordship" refers to the power of autonomy, while "sovereignty" refers to the power of decisive judgment.

Since their meanings are identical to those of "self," lordship is the essence (*svabhāva*) of the self, and sovereignty is the function (*vṛtti*) of the self. Furthermore, lordship is innate (*sahaja*).

The "I" [which is] non-discriminative belongs to the seventh consciousness; the "I" that exercises sovereignty is discriminative and possesses the sense of severing [the continuity], belonging to the sixth consciousness.
Thus, while the notions of a master and so forth are established, the view of self arises. (From the *Fuxing* [Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*], Part 2, showing the view that clings to a self.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Some say the spirit resides within the heart, subtle as a mustard seed, and is called 'pure'."

The form-body (*rūpakāya*). Some say it is like a barley grain, or a bean, half an inch, or one inch in size; at the moment of first receiving a body, this is what is received first, being like the skeletal frame of a statue.
When the body is fully formed, it is like the statue having already become full-grown. Others say its dimensions vary according to the individual.

When the body perishes at death, this [consciousness] likewise departs beforehand. Furthermore, the term "consciousness-only" (vijñapti-mātra) excludes the "agent-self" (*kartṛ-ātman*) of the Vaiśeṣikas and the "experiencer-self" (*bhoktṛ-ātman*) of the Sāṃkhyas—entities that are eternal, omnipresent, and equal in extent to space, which supposedly perform karma in various places and experience pleasure and pain accordingly.
Furthermore, the shameless non-Buddhist Nirgranthas and others maintain that the essence of the self (*ātman*) is eternal yet its dimensions are indeterminate;

it expands and contracts according to the size of the body it inhabits. Moreover, the two schools of the Vātsīputrīyas and the Sammitīyas calculate that the essence of the self is eternal and extremely subtle.

It operates secretly within the body to perform various activities. Now, although the tenets and calculations of the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are numerous, they do not transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), such as identity and difference.
"Spiritual body" refers to the spiritual self (*ātman*). Identity and difference, as well as the [other] four propositions, have been explained previously.
Furthermore, "identity" means being identical with the aggregates (*skandha*), while "difference" means being separate from the aggregates.

[Note on the Square Symbol]: Extremist views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Based upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one calculates that the self is either annihilated or eternal; one clings to eternity rather than annihilation, or clings to annihilation rather than eternity, adhering to one extreme or the other.
[Commentary] This view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is explained in conjunction with the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). The *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:

"The one who clings to the view of extremes refers to one who, regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), adheres to the notions of annihilationism or eternalism; its essence is defiled wisdom (*kliṣṭaprajñā*). This was explained in detail within the preceding exposition on views.

[Boxed Note] *Dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (Adherence to Views): This refers to the belief that because of this view one will reach the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and the conviction that this is so and nothing else.

It consists of grasping what is inferior as being superior. [■ Record] The *Śāstra* states: Among all views and their underlying aggregates, to grasp them as supreme and as the means to attain the pure dharma of *nirvāṇa* is called *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*.
Because they mutually grasp each other as superior, quarrels arise. Furthermore, the *Fǔ*...
Xing said: "To falsely perceive nirvana within that which is not the truly supreme Dharma, and to give rise to a mind of attachment, is all termed 'clinging to views' (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Even when practicing the Path, although one may enter various gates of contemplation, if true illumination has not yet arisen and ignorance remains unclarified, one then erroneously calculates what has been attained as being real and supreme, giving rise to a mind of attachment; all such instances are termed 'clinging to views.'"
What is now referred to as "based on this view" means, for instance, the calculations of either permanence or annihilationism.

Based on these, one practices so as to attain the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), yet does not disparage other dharmas; rather, one clings to what is inferior as being superior.

For example, outsiders also practice the six subtle contemplations and engage in ascetic austerities; when they experience a slight degree of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), they take this to be a sign of having reached their destination.

[Note] *Śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances). To cling to what is false as being the Path is called "reckoning that which is not a cause to be a cause. The observances of chickens, dogs, and so forth are termed *śīlavrataparāmarśa*.

[Supplement] The *Xuánqiān* states: Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) also possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Seeing that chickens and dogs are reborn in heaven, they then undertake these observances, calculating that this will lead to birth in heaven.
They do not realize that once the karma [of those animals] has expired, it was a superior cause that drew them toward rebirth in heaven.

[The Buddha] heard that oxen and sheep were reborn in heaven after eating grass. Others also eat grass, yet they do not know that it is the oxen and sheep whose karmic retribution has ended that are reborn in heaven.
The *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*) states: "Non-Buddhists calculate six types of asceticism, namely: self-starvation, throwing oneself into deep water, and leaping into fire."

One who throws oneself down, remains in silent seclusion, or observes the precepts of cows, dogs, and so forth—this is called "regarding what is not a cause as a cause," and it is termed the clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
A certain master notes: Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner who observed the precepts of cows and dogs; Ānanda led him to see the Buddha, and he addressed him, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will explain the karmic retribution for him. The Buddha said, "I fear he would give rise to dread; it cannot be told.

That person requested again and again. The Buddha said, "If you observe the cow-vow (*go-vrata*), acting exactly according to the way of a cow without transgressing even a hair's breadth of its rules—"
Later, among the cattle, those who have committed minor offenses shall enter hell.

[Commentary] Regarding false views: these arise from reckoning existence as either eternal or annihilated, and failing to reckon in cause and effect; furthermore, they reckon this "self" (ātman) to be spontaneous, such as the primordial darkness (*ādi-tamas*) or the primal nature of the world (*pradhāna*).

This primal nature of the world refers to the twenty-five principles (*tattvas*): (1) primordial darkness, (2) the Great One (*mahat*), and the subsequent principles such as the intellect (*buddhi*), as shown in the diagram, as well as the six principles, and so forth.
Or to calculate that [the self] arises from parents, atoms, Brahmā, and so forth—all such views are termed wrong views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
[Commentary: Failing to understand the causes and effects of the Four Noble Truths, one uses a distorted mind to speculate, claiming that such principles do not exist.

One stubbornly adheres to the wrong views of nihilism (*uccheda*) or eternalism (*śāśvata*), and by means of this, cuts off supramundane roots of goodness, as well as even mundane roots of goodness, thereby becoming a nihilist (*nāstika*).

[New Paragraph] This constitutes wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, not understanding the principles of karma, rely on the power of worldly meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and see that a person who has spent their life practicing generosity is instead reborn in a lowly, impoverished, and famished state. They then think:

"There is certainly no such thing as giving, caring for others, or sacrificial offerings in this world. This is the denial of causes (*hetu-apavāda*). Moreover, they see virtuous people falling into the three [evil realms].

As for those who commit evil, they may be born into the good realms of humans or devas; yet immediately they reflect, "There is certainly no such thing in the world as a good cause producing a favorable retribution, or an evil cause producing an ugly fruit.
This is the slander of the fruit (*phala*). Regarding the twenty-five *tattvas*, there is no diagram in the *Jizhu* (Collected Annotations).

According to the text of the *Śata-śāstra*: from the primordial darkness (*avyakta*) arises intellect (*buddhi*); from intellect arises the ego-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*); from the ego-consciousness arise the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). From... [text continues]
The five objects of the senses (*pañca-viṣaya*) give rise to the five gross elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*). From the five gross elements arise the eleven faculties (*ekādaśendriya*).
With the *puruṣa* (the Self) as the sovereign principle, within the sphere of the characteristics of awakening (*buddhi*), it remains indestructible and imperishable, grasping all phenomena.

[Appendix] 1. From the primordial darkness (*tamas*) arises awakening; 2. from awakening arises the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*); 3. from the ego-sense arise the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), namely: 4. form, 5. sound, 6. fragrance, 7. taste, 8. [touch].

Tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*). Next, the five [subtle elements] give rise only to the five gross elements: namely, (1) earth, (2) water, (3) fire, (4) wind, and (5) space. Next, the five gross elements give rise to the eleven faculties:

namely, (6) the eye, (7) the ear, (8) the nose, (9) the tongue, (10) the body, (11) the mind, (12) the female faculty, (13) the male faculty, (14) the life faculty, (15) the faculty of pleasure, (16) the faculty of pain, (17) the faculty of joy, (18) the faculty of grief, (19) the faculty of equanimity, and (20) the faculty of will.
17. Tongue; 18. Body; 19. Hands; 20. Feet; 21. Mouth; 22. Great Excretory Organ; 23.
Small Excretory Organ; 24. Faculty of Mental Equanimity (citta-sāmya-indriya); up to 25. The Self as the Lord of Principles (ātma-pradhāna-tattva).
These twenty-five principles constitute the system established by the Sāṃkhya teachers, known as the *kārikā*.
Vīraśika is the foremost among the non-Buddhist outsiders of the western heavens; he knows the events of eighty thousand kalpas, yet he does not know what lies beyond that.
*Mingdi* (the obscure principle) is also called *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature). *Jue* (awakening) is the *mahat* (the Great One), which is wisdom. *Wo-xin* (self-mind) is *asmimāna* (ego-conceit).

When the self-mind contemplates and utilizes *svabhāva*, the obscure nature (*mṛtyu-prakṛti*) then transforms into the *mahat* and the other [evolutes], becoming bound by these objects and failing to attain liberation. This is the "self."
If one does not conceptualize, the nature of darkness remains unchanging, and one immediately attains liberation, which is called *nirvāṇa*.

This is a brief record from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* concerning the six truths (*ṣat-tattva*), which consist of six categories (*ṣat-padārtha*). These were established by the Vaiśeṣika masters; they are named Vaiśeṣika.
This is also that which I have accepted and utilized. While not yet liberated, one utilizes these six categories; to be apart from these six categories is reckoned as *nirvāṇa*. [Record]

The *Prakṛti-tattva* (the principle of primordial nature). The *Sāṃkhyakārikā-bhāṣya* explains this as being summarized into three categories, four when taken as intermediate, and twenty-five when expanded.
Regarding the summary into three: first, *prakṛti* (primordial nature); second, *puruṣa* (the self or knower); and third, *vikṛti* (transformation). *Prakṛti* is the primary principle;

it was anciently called *avyakta* (the unmanifest) and is also named *pradhāna* (the pre-eminent). It abides in its own state before the production of the "Great One" (*mahat*) and the other evolutes. This is termed...
Self-nature (*svabhāva*). If it gives rise to the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, it is called the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), because its function is most exalted.

The *Jñānaśāstra* states that the supernatural powers of non-Buddhists reach as far as eighty thousand eons, yet beyond this they remain in darkness and know nothing; thus they designate it the "Dark Principle" (*tamas-tattva*).

From this, awakening and cognition first arise, which is termed the "Dark Principle. Second is the "Knower of the Self," which is the twenty-fifth principle, the Divine Self (*puruṣa*). Third is transformation.
"Transformation" (*vikāra*) refers to the twenty-three principles (*tattva*) in between; because they are produced from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), they are called transformations.

Thus, there are three positions. Regarding "four being situated in the middle": first, primordial nature itself is without transformation. Second, the Great One (*mahat*) and the others are also transformations.
The five gross elements, the five cognitive faculties, the five organs of action, and the mind—these sixteen together are merely transformations.

Third: "The Knower is not a fundamental transformation" is the fourth [point]. The commentary explains: Because its nature (*prakṛti*) is able to produce the Great One (*mahat*) and so forth, it is called "fundamental" (*mūla*).
Because it does not arise from anything else, it is not a transformation (*vikāra*). The two Great Elements (*mahābhūta*), the I-principle (*ahaṃkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*):

these seven are both fundamental and transformations. The Great One is a transformation because it arises from the fundamental nature; it is a fundamental [cause] because it produces the I-principle. From the I-principle, the five [subtle elements] arise.
The *tanmātras* (five subtle elements) are both transformations and primal sources, because they give rise to the five gross elements, the five sense organs, and the five objects of perception.

The three—the five gross elements, the five cognitive organs, the five organs of action, and the mind as the single equal organ—arise solely from others; therefore, they are exclusively transformations (*vikāra*).
It cannot produce others; therefore, it is not called "fundamental" (*mūla*). Regarding the "four knowers": they take self-cognition as their essence.

They do not arise from another, nor do they produce another; thus, they are neither fundamental nor subject to transformation. If one follows the *Śata-śāstra*, the five great elements (*mahābhūta*) produce the eleven faculties;
in that case, the five great elements are both fundamental and transformative. Within the category of the transformative alone, there are only the eleven faculties. Six.

Regarding the "truths" (*satya*), the teachings of the vehicles state: first, *dravya*, translated as the "truth of the principal. This refers to the five great elements, time, space, the deities, and the mind;

these are called the "principal" because they serve as the basis upon which all things depend. Second, *guṇa*, translated as the "truth of dependence," referring to the five sense objects such as form, for they are that which depends [upon the principal].

Third, *karma*, translated as the "truth of activity," referring to actions such as looking up and down, bending and stretching, entering and exiting, and coming and going; therefore, it is called "activity."

Fourth is *samaya*, translated as the "truth of general characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-satya*); this refers to the fact that the myriad phenomena, despite their diversity, are one in their existence.
Fifth is *viśeṣa*, translated as the "truth of specific characteristics" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-satya*); this refers to how the myriad forms of the universe each possess their own distinct differences.

Sixth is *māpadya-satya*, which refers to the accomplishment of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) such that they do not obstruct one another; or alternatively, it is reckoned as arising from the subtle [elements] of the parents.

Regarding "dust" (rajas): it refers to those such as the masters of the Lokāyata school, who maintain that the atoms (paramāṇu) of earth, water, fire, and wind are substantially real and eternal, and are capable of producing coarse matter.
They claim that these atoms act as the "parent atoms," while the coarse matter they produce is the "child atom.
Alternatively, it refers to those who calculate [the origin] from Brahmā and others, such as the masters of the Vedas, who calculate that [the world arises] from the navel of the god Nārāyaṇa.
A great lotus flower arises. Upon the flower is Brahmā, the progenitor, who is the lord of all things.
From him are born all sentient and insentient beings. From the mouth of Brahmā are born the Brāhmaṇas; from his two arms, the Kṣatriyas; from his two feet, the Śūdras;
and from his two thighs, the Vaiśyas. The phrase "and so forth" includes the various temporal heretics who hold such calculations.
The teacher Bhāradvāja maintains that things arise from space; the teacher Mādhava maintains that they arise from the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*), which is the initial limit of the past;
the teacher Vātsīputra maintains that they arise from the power of speech; the teacher Akriyāvādin maintains that they arise without a cause;
the heretic Pāśupata maintains that they arise from the god Īśvara; and the teacher Pūrvakṛtavādin maintains that they arise from the fundamental conditions of past lives.

Karma is the creator; it serves as the cause for all things. This is recorded in detail in the *Dharmasaṃkhyā*. [Supplement] *Dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (Adherence to Views) refers to the stubborn attachment to what is inferior, asserting it to be superior.

*Śīlavrataparāmarśa* (Adherence to Rites and Rituals) refers to the false calculation of what is not a cause to be a cause. *Satkāyadṛṣṭi* (View of a Self-Entity) refers to the deluded attachment to "I" and "mine," asserting them to be a self.

*Antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (Extreme View) refers to the calculation of either annihilation or permanence based upon the view of a self-entity. *Mithyādṛṣṭi* (False View) refers to the denial of cause and effect.
"False views are the most widespread. This is explained according to the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings). [Supplement] The supplementary note states:
"The eight deva-kings are the parents of sentient beings; the Brahmā King is the parent of these eight deva-kings;
and Viṣṇu is the parent of the Brahmā King. Viṣṇu is none other than the deity Nārāyaṇa."
[Note] "To regard one's own dharma as [the object of] greed" refers to taking the five views (*pañcadṛṣṭi*) as one's own dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "dharma-realm": when the deluded mind confronts all objects of favorable conditions and draws them in with insatiable craving, this is greed (*rāga*).

Throughout the three realms and five elements, there are fifteen types of greed, all of which are driven by the underlying tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*). Here, it specifically points to craving and the five views as being one's own dharma.
[Note] As for anger (*dveṣa*): one feels anger because [the object] is not one's own dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu): when the deluded mind encounters all adverse conditions, anger arises; this is called *dveṣa* (hatred).

Throughout the five types of conduct within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this corresponds to the five forms of resentment (*āghāta*), which are themselves the underlying tendency of resentment (*pratighānuśaya*). Here, the reference specifically points to those phenomena that do not belong to oneself.
[Commentary on the Square Box] Ignorance (*moha*). It is the failure to recognize suffering and its origin within the [Middle Way] vision.

[Explanatory Record] The term "Dharma-realm" refers to the deluded and non-comprehending mind, which is called ignorance (*avidyā*). If this deluded mind conditions an object, [it constitutes ignorance].
Whatever arises, it is forever lost from moment to moment; those who do not know shame or remorse are all termed "deluded.

Throughout the three realms and five destinies, the fifteen types of delusion are none other than ignorance (*avidyā*). Here, we specifically point out that failing to recognize the first five views regarding suffering and its origin is what is called delusion.
[Boxed Note] Pride (*māna*): "I understand, while he does not. [Commentary] Regarding the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*):
the mind that relies on oneself and looks down upon others is called pride (*māna*). This extends to the fifteen types of pride found throughout the three realms and five destinies;
all of these are the underlying tendencies of pride (*mānānuśaya*). Here, specifically, it refers to the first of the five views: the pride of thinking, "I understand, while he does not."
This is called pride (*māna*).
[Note] Doubt (*vicikitsā*): To be hesitant and indecisive. [Commentary] The *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* states:
When the deluded mind deviates from principle and is hesitant and indecisive, it is called doubt. It traverses the three realms and four modes of conduct.
The twelve kinds of doubt are all the proclivities of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*). Here, "doubt" is explained as hesitation and indecision regarding what has been seen.

[Supplement] The *Fayuan* states: The Four Truths and the Path of Cultivation are called the "five practices. Within the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*), suffering, origin, cessation, and the path constitute four practices;
the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya*) constitute one practice. Since false views and doubt are not [delusions] of thought, [they are excluded from the four practices] within the three realms.

There are twelve types of conduct: greed, delusion, and pride; and the views and afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms. Because these are fully present, there are fifteen factors consisting of the five [afflictions] of the three realms.

Since hatred is not active in the upper realms, the views and afflictions of the desire realm constitute the five [afflictions] and the five types of anger (*pratigha*). However, what is intended here is specifically to speak of the views.
[Commentary] Sharp and dull. If sharp, they are constantly present even in moments of haste. If dull, they arise only after one has pushed for the sharp.

The five dull [afflictions] are also called "thoughts within views," "thoughts that push for the sharp," or "the latent tendencies on the back. If the sharp latent tendencies depart, the dull latent tendencies also vanish.
Therefore, they are subsumed under [the category of] views (*dṛṣṭi*).

[Commentary: That which arises immediately upon contact and is constantly present even in moments of haste is "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*). That which arises after a brief delay and only when one reflects upon its benefit is "dull" (*mṛdu*).
Below the five dull [faculties], it clarifies that the volition (*cetanā*) among the dull is also subsumed under views. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Three..."

There are two types of delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). First is innate view (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*), which exists as a sharp faculty within the five dull [afflictions], such as that of insects, beasts, and ordinary worldlings;

they are also able to give rise to the notions of "I" and "mine. This is because the sharp arises from the back of the dull, and thus it is categorized under the dull. Second is speculative view (*tarka-dṛṣṭi*).

Prior to the arising of the [supramundane] path of insight (*darśana-mārga*), although one may possess worldly wisdom, logical reasoning, and sharp discernment, their views and perceptions remain weak; therefore, the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) are collectively categorized as dull (*mṛdu*).

Once the three types of insight have arisen, they emerge from the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); because the mind of insight is intense and vigorous, the ten proclivities receive their designation according to this strength and are all classified as sharp (*tīkṣṇa*).
Regarding the three types of afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*): first, there are those that are innate (*sahaja*), which arise simultaneously with the physical form.

For example, when a man and woman conceive a fetus, they falsely give rise to feelings of love or hatred toward their parents; this is perverse thought and returns to the category of delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Second, based on views and thoughts: for instance, non-Buddhists give rise to anger based on their views; this is the dull [faculty] within the sharp [category], called the "latent tendency on the back" (*pṛṣṭha-anuśaya*).

At the time of abandoning the [delusions] through the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), the sharp [faculty] is abandoned, and the "back" is also abandoned. The thoughts bound to the three realms are thus threefold.
The nine grades of volition within the realms are called the dull afflictions (*mṛdu-kleśa*), also termed the obstruction of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), and designated as the primary three poisons.

However, the intent of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) clarifies that the sharp and dull aspects of both *darśana-heya* (afflictions abandoned by insight) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions abandoned by cultivation) are mutually inclusive; the present text, however, explains only the volition within the dull category.

It still belongs to the category of views (*dṛṣṭi*). If one wishes to reconcile this: the "concomitant volition" (*sahaja-cetanā*) mentioned in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) is precisely the volition within these views;
the "volition based on views" in the *Fuxing* is precisely the volition that drives and sharpens them from behind—the "instigator" (*pṛṣṭhataḥ-preraka*).

[Supplement] The *Abhidharma* states: although there is dullness within sharpness, this dullness belongs to the sharp; it arises from behind the sharp instigator (*tīkṣṇa-anuśaya*). The sharp instigator is like the edge of a blade, while the dull instigator is...
Like the back of a knife: when dull latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) arise subsequent to sharp latent tendencies, they are called "latent tendencies on the back.
[Supplementary Note: Regarding ordinary beings who give rise to the notions of "self" and "mine," *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Just as various wriggling insects, though in reality lacking any rational faculty, raise their claws and spread their fins, glaring with eyes of anger and self-importance—how could such lowly ordinary beings ever abandon their attachments? Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, they are constantly..."

Because it gives rise to my mind, the five dull [afflictions] are not without benefit. The remaining interpretations are detailed in the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings).
△ Second, the explanation by way of the realms (*dhātu*) is twofold. First, the general indication.
These ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), when traversing the four truths of the three realms, differ in their increase and decrease, totaling eighty-eight. [Note:

Regarding the differing increases and decreases of the afflictions under the four truths, the previous section stated that although the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) resides within both afflictions and karma, here we traverse all four truths because origination is the subject of delusion and suffering is the object of delusion.
Furthermore, although the truths of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are supramundane causes and effects, [they are included].

Due to delusion regarding suffering and its origin, one is likewise deluded regarding the path and its cessation. This is like failing to recognize a disease and consequently being deluded about the medicine.

[Supplement] Since the path and cessation are the primary antidotes to affliction, once one is deluded regarding suffering and its origin, one is necessarily deluded regarding the path and its cessation as well.
Therefore, there are also delusions.
△ Second, the specific explanation has two parts. First, the Desire Realm:

this means that in the Desire Realm, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of suffering are fully present; for origin and cessation, there are seven each, excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Regarding the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*), there are eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). When combined with those under the [other] four truths, these total thirty-two.
△ Second, regarding the upper realms:

in the two upper realms, all [tendencies] under the four truths are the same as in the desire realm, except that from each truth, the underlying tendency of hatred (*pratigha-anuśaya*) is excluded. Therefore...
Each realm has twenty-eight [afflictions].
[Commentary] Regarding these afflictions of the Four Noble Truths, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Under Suffering, all are present; for Origin and Cessation, three each are excluded;
for the Path, two views are excluded. In the higher realms, hatred does not function. (See *Fuxing*, Vol. V, Section 9). Question: Regarding the afflictions under the Four Noble Truths, based on...

What is the reasoning and scriptural authority for the difference in their increase and decrease? Answer: According to the Abhidharma, hatred (*dveṣa*) does not function in the higher realms because there is no mutual harm, because there is wholesome desire (*kuśala-chanda*), because their nature is tranquil, and because their minds are moistened with compassion. Nevertheless, it is merely suppressed and does not cease; thus, it is not something that has been eradicated.
Therefore, in the *Lotus Sūtra*, the centipede serves as a metaphor for hatred, which pervades all three realms. As the *Myōryaku* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), fascicle 6, states: (32).
In the Hīnayāna it is said that there is no anger (*vyāpāda*) in the upper realms; however, this does not exhaust the full principle.

[Commentary] This passage discriminates the four truths (*catuḥsatya*), determining for each whether they exist or do not exist. Here, first, the *Abhidharma* is cited to prove that it is taught that there is no hatred (*dveṣa*) in the upper realms, and that when practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one does not cause harm.

In the lower realm of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there is no hatred, yet there are the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*). In the lower realm of origination (*samudaya-satya*), there is no hatred.

When there is meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one’s nature is tranquil; thus, the lower [level] is free from anger. When one possesses concentration and, moreover, approaches the Buddha and the Sangha to hear the Dharma, the mind becomes moistened;
thus, the lower [level] is free from anger. This is because the water of equanimity and concentration of the higher realms is tranquil and moistening.
However, by remaining still and not proceeding downward, one relies on the Mahāyāna to sever anger throughout the three realms. This is as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
It says: "Centipedes, millipedes, and species of venomous snakes, scorched by fire, scramble to exit their burrows. The *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) states:

"Just as those in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) weary of that state and emerge toward the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), like the species of venomous snakes exiting their burrows when burned by fire, so too is hatred (*dveṣa*) pervasive throughout the three realms.
The *Jujì* (Phrase Record) explains: "The realm of form is like a burrow; wearying of the lower [realm] is like being burned; and aspiring to the higher [realm] is like emerging."
It is like emerging from a hole. Previously, in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), anger (*dveṣa*) was compared to a centipede; here, by analogy, it is not separately distinguished.

Since it is called a "centipede" and is furthermore formless (*arūpa*), it serves as a metaphor for that anger. In the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it is called a "poisonous insect," which includes the centipede.
Thus, while in the higher realms the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) of anger does not arise, it is not that the seed (*bīja*) of anger is absent.
[This is] the child. [Note: Regarding the four lines on "Emerging from the Hole by the Lotus Fire," the topical outline (*ke*) determines that this refers to the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
therefore, it is used as a metaphor for the formless, as it shares the same [nature of] desire and anger as the realm of desire.]

[Note] Question: Why do the views of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) exist only with respect to suffering? Answer: These views rely upon the body; therefore, they are called the "view of the body" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Based upon this view of the body, the view of extremes arises. Since the other three [noble truths] are not the body, these two views do not exist there. Furthermore, because they are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), they are absent in the other truths.
Therefore, regarding the passage "In the past... and below: although those in the four formless attainments (*ārūpyadhātu*) lack coarse form, they still possess subtle form;

since their grasping has not yet been extinguished, this constitutes the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). The meaning of the eight sufferings in the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) can be understood accordingly.

[Commentary] The Abhidharma states: The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are confused only with respect to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). This is because ordinary beings all grasp at suffering as being a self; thus, the view of a self-identity arises from the Truth of Suffering.

Because one calculates [the self] as either annihilated or eternal based upon the body, which is a retribution of suffering, the view of extremes likewise arises from confusion regarding the Truth of Suffering.

The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* asks: "For what reason are the views of a self-identity and extremes abandoned through the realization of suffering? It answers: "Because they pertain to the locus of suffering."

Because it functions [in relation to] the fruit, it functions at the locus of the fruit. Therefore, upon seeing that [fruit], its abandonment is not distant; it follows until the root. This view does not follow the sense-faculties (*indriya*);
therefore, it is abandoned immediately upon the initial vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*). [Supplement: The body is the root of all suffering.

Since the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises based on the body, it functions at the locus of suffering and functions at the locus of the fruit. Upon seeing that Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), its abandonment is not distant; it follows until the root.
Fundamentally, ignorance [is the cause]. The eight sufferings of the non-percipient realm appear before one. [Appendix] Bian’e says:

Regarding the phrases "the four formless [attainments]," "form-body," and "view of self," it seems as though it is being claimed that there is no form in the formless realm and thus no view of self; yet this fails to recognize the existence of the other four aggregates.
There is also the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) in the other aggregates; it is not found in the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) alone.

I privately surmise that the Master of Jade was not unaware that the view of a self exists within the four [other] aggregates, yet he singled out the aggregate of form among the four emptinesses because it is that which people most easily overlook.

[□ Note] Question: Why does the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) exist only within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)? Answer: Because it arises only therein. Question: The attachment to precepts conceives of a cause, whereas the Truth of Suffering is an effect.
Why, then, is it included under Suffering? Answer: Because one conceives of many ascetic practices as being the true cause [of liberation], it is placed under Suffering.

Furthermore, because it is not the supramundane path yet is falsely claimed to be the path to liberation, it can also arise in relation to the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*). It differs from the Truths of Origination (*samudaya*) and Cessation (*nirodha*).

Therefore, there is no view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Because there is no view of a self-identity, there is also no view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). One does not give rise to attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) regarding that which is neither the origin nor the cessation [of suffering].

Furthermore, as for attachment to precepts and rituals that falls under the two truths of suffering and the path: those that originally belong to the inner path (Buddhism) are abandoned through the vision of suffering;
those that originally belong to the outer paths (non-Buddhist traditions) are abandoned through the vision of the path. Thus, it exists only in these two.

[Supplement] Regarding the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*): those who originally belonged to the inner path (Buddhists) do not give rise to attachment to precepts at the time they realize suffering;

therefore, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*). Those who originally belonged to the outer paths (non-Buddhists) have already given rise to attachment to precepts; they must abandon the afflictions through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Only then is the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) severed; therefore, it is abandoned through the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). [Supplementary Note] Bian’uo states:

Furthermore, regarding the passage on the attachment to precepts and so forth, this section clarifies that the increase and decrease of the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) differ according to each of the Four Noble Truths. These Four Truths are the Dharma proclaimed by the Buddha.

One should not, conversely, cite non-Buddhist outsiders (tīrthika) as the subject here. In my humble opinion, the term "clinging to precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is generally established in contrast to non-Buddhists.
This section represents Master Yu’s supplementary intention; the preceding interpretation should be taken as the correct judgment.
[□ Note] This possesses the sense of being near or distant. Gu-shan provides an interpretation consisting of sixty-four phrases (as follows).
[■ Record] The explanation is found below.
△ Third, the formation of the total number:
the two realms combined constitute fifty-six; together with the previous thirty-two, they total eighty-eight *anuśayas* (proclivities).

[Note] Regarding the eighty-eight *anuśayas*, this is based solely on the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that the ninety-eight *anuśayas* include these along with the ten [delusions of ignorance].

This is because of [the inclusion of] the "thoughts" (vitarka). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 5, Part 2, states: "The ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) constitute the ninety-eight [afflictions].
[Commentary: Regarding the "ten thoughts," the *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* says there are four in the desire realm—namely, greed, anger, delusion, and pride—and three each in the form and formless realms.

Excluding the latent tendencies of anger (*pratighānuśaya*), there are ten [secondary afflictions]. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the treatise as saying: "The eight envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), parsimony (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and lethargy (*styāna*).
Alternatively, there are ten when adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*). Regarding the enumeration of dharmas, it states: "Regret refers to the transgression of what was done."
One cannot find peace within oneself, and thus the "cover" (āvaraṇa) of regret is formed. "Covering" refers to concealing one's committed transgressions, fearing that others might discover them.
The rest is understandable.

[Note] The explanations provided in various treatises differ. Some name these the "three fetters" (*trisaṃyojana*). The *Zhiguan* states that they are abandoned upon attaining the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), just as a river is exhausted.

The water [of the afflictions] extends forty *li*; the effort required to exhaust it is immense. Fearing that those who hear this might give rise to doubt, I shall briefly sever the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*). (Text) These are:
the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*), as illustrated in the diagram below.
[Commentary] "Treatise" refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. At times, for those of dull faculties, it merely speaks of the severance of three [fetters]; this is the case here.

Regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, they are based on the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*’s "Questions of Kāśyapa": "The Tathāgata says that a *srotāpanna* severs afflictions as if draining forty *li* of water."

What is meant by "severing the three fetters"? First, the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi); second, regarding what is not a cause as a cause (mithyādhimokṣa); and third, the net of doubt (vicikitsā). The Buddha said:
Because these three are heavy, they also encompass the person of the srotāpanna, for they include all the fetters that must be severed.

The *Fuxing* quotes the *Śāstra*, saying: "The three fetters give rise to delusions with predominance: the view of a self gives rise to the sixty-two [wrong views], and the attachment to precepts and rituals gives rise to all [other delusions]."

Asceticism and doubt: one harbors hesitation regarding all things of the past. Furthermore, when the World-Honored One says that one who has severed the eighty-eight *āśravas* (outflows) and immeasurable sufferings is called a *srotāpanna*, those being converted feel distress, thinking:
"How can one uproot eighty-eight great trees and cross over eighty-eight great rivers? If the Buddha were to say that one severs three...

"Knots" (*saṃyojana*) refers to the joy of those being transformed. Regarding the characteristics of severing these knots, according to the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, it is said: "Neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end. The treatise states that this is the characteristic of severing the knots.
This means that the power of the wisdom that exhausts outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*) constitutes the beginning; the wisdom of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) constitutes the middle and the end. Answer:

It is not that the wisdom of abandonment occurs only at the beginning, nor is it only in the middle or at the end. It is like the flame of a lamp, which does not exist solely at its beginning, middle, or end.

Because of grasping at the beginning, middle, and end. That is to say, if one were to grasp [the object] at a single moment, one could not effect its cessation. Only by grasping all three moments together can one speak of cessation.

If cessation is thus contingent upon three moments, then it possesses no fixed nature (*niyata-svabhāva*). Why? If the first moment were capable of cessation, it would not require the middle and the last;
if the last moment were capable of cessation, it would not require the first and the middle. Since it depends upon three moments, we know that it has no inherent nature. (1)
First, regarding the logical inference: all three [phases] are uninterrupted. Therefore, the Sūtra states: "It is neither at the beginning, nor in the middle, nor at the end.

It is only by virtue of being uninterrupted throughout these three times that one is able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Thus, the Śāstra says: "Because of grasping [them] in the prior, middle, and posterior [phases].

The Master [Vasubandhu] takes all three times collectively to manifest that there is no interruption across the three times. While the Sūtra and the Śāstra appear to speak in opposition, their intent is actually complementary; the Sūtra speaks in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*).

The treatises, however, focus on characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Only when nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics are without obstruction can one truly sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Although the sūtras and treatises clarify the manner of severing the fetters according to the Mahāyāna, the principles may also be understood by extension to apply to the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary] A citation from the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "In general, when one conceives that 'sin and merit are what I have created,' one does not take wholesome or unwholesome karma as being the self.
Therefore, the view of a self (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) does not rely upon origination (*samudaya*). Knowing that origination is not the self is not called being deluded regarding origination.

The view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) relies upon the body and likewise does not rely upon origination; it also does not take cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as the self. It conceives of either annihilation or permanence."

The same applies here. Therefore, the body and its sensations are exclusively suffering. As for the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it is a delusion regarding both suffering and the path.

When fools hear it said that diligent asceticism is necessary, they immediately claim that the physical suffering involved in these practices is itself the path. They do not realize that one must diligently contemplate suffering and emptiness in order to sever birth and death;

physical suffering is not the path. Thus, the attachment to precepts and observances arises from delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering. Alternatively, it may not take physical suffering as [the means].
The Path: To take the meritorious practices of observing the precepts and so forth as the path is to mistake the cause for the path.

In this way, such attachment to precepts is called delusion regarding the Truth of the Path. In reality, ordinary fools do not recognize the cause of origination; they falsely grasp it as the path, which should properly be considered delusion regarding the Truth of Origination.
However, because their deluded minds do not consider these meritorious practices to be the cause of origination, they instead regard them as the path.

Therefore, it is not called "delusion regarding origination" (*samudaya*). This differs from one who calculates suffering to be the path and takes suffering as the path; thus, it is called "delusion regarding suffering" (*duḥkha*).

Consequently, the attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is delusion regarding suffering and delusion regarding the path, but it is not delusion regarding origination. Cessation (*nirodha*) is the noble fruit sought by sentient beings;
since one does not grasp the cessation of afflictions as a causal practice for the path, the attachment to precepts is not called "delusion regarding cessation. If...

Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*): these three universally delude one regarding the Four Truths. Wrong view deludes by denying cause and effect;

because it encompasses both ordinary beings and noble ones, it is a universal delusion. Adherence to views takes one's own personal retribution to be supreme; this is delusion regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha*).

To regard worldly wholesome karma as supreme is called delusion regarding origination (*samudaya*). To take rebirth in heavens such as those of Brahmā or the non-percipient beings as *nirvāṇa* is called delusion regarding cessation (*nirodha*).
To take the path described by those who hold to precepts and rituals as supreme is called delusion regarding the path (*mārga*). Thus, these constitute general delusion.
As for doubt, it is the state of not knowing whether or not the causes and effects of ordinary beings and sages exist, giving rise to uncertainty.

It is certain. Thus, doubt (*vicikitsā*) is also fourfold. The five views and doubt explained above are confused only regarding the principle of the Truths (*satya-naya*), and are not termed confusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

Because they are confused regarding the principle, they are severed by seeing that very principle. The *Essentials of Consciousness-Only* (*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-hṛdaya*) states: "Confusion regarding the Truths is both general and specific.

The general refers to the ten [afflictions], all of which are confused regarding the Four Truths; this is because Suffering (*duḥkha*) and Accumulation (*samudaya*) are the causal basis for those six realms of existence."

Because cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are objects of fear for them. Specifically, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are deluded only regarding suffering (*duḥkha*); the other eight [afflictions] are deluded regarding all four truths. The view of a self-identity and the view of extremes arise only with respect to the fruit (the truth of suffering);
they are countered by the specific cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*), as these belong to the truth of suffering.

Doubt (*vicikitsā*), along with the three views—the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, and wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—are directly deluded regarding the principle of suffering. As for the two grasps—the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)—they cling to...
Those three views and the precepts-and-vows (śīlavrataparāmarśa), together with the aggregates upon which they depend, are regarded as supreme and capable of purification.
