Regarding one's own and others' views and their attendants, greed, hatred, and pride arise respectively as appropriate; the associated ignorance shares delusion with the nine [other afflictions], while the non-associated ignorance directly deludes regarding the principle of suffering.
Doubt and false view directly delude regarding the origin [of suffering] and so forth; the two types of grasping, greed, and so on [arise in relation to them].

It should be understood that this is analogous to suffering (*duḥkha*). Furthermore, hatred (*dveṣa*) can also directly obscure the cessation and the path; for one gives rise to aversion and envy out of fear.

Such is the coarse characteristic regarding the direct and indirect obscuration of the truths (*satya*). This is largely the same as the preceding [discussion on ignorance], with only minor differences; they may be identified by comparing them.

[Supplement] Regarding the sixty-four phrases of Mount Gu: The *Xianju bian* states that while the ten *anuśayas* (proclivities) are fully present within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) arises only by taking the object of suffering as its condition.
The Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*) consists of ignorance, karma, and tainted causes; the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) consists of unconditioned and untainted fruits.

Neither of these are objects of the view of a self-identity. As for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), these two follow the [view of a self-identity].

Nor do they arise. Therefore, the three views are eliminated through the cessation of their accumulation. Since the Truth of the Path is fundamentally the cause for the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the views of self and extremes (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi* and *antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) likewise do not arise.
Since false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) negates the existence of the Noble Path, the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) arises from that false view.

To grasp what is not the path as being the true path is the fetter of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Within the Four Noble Truths, there is a distinction between the remote and the proximate: regarding the truth of suffering, three are remote and seven are proximate.

To grasp at "self" and "what belongs to self" is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). From this view of identity, one calculates either annihilation or permanence, which constitutes the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

The view of negation (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) repudiates the existence of cause, effect, and phenomena. The view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) clings to that which is inferior as being superior. [The fetter of] adherence to prohibitions...
To grasp at what is not a cause as being a cause is "wrong view"; to doubt is to be hesitant and indecisive; and ignorance is delusion and darkness that fails to understand.
These all arise based on the Truth of Suffering and the other truths. Therefore, these seven afflictions are called "direct delusions.

As for the three types of afflictions—greed, hatred, and pride—they do not arise from the objective sphere of the Truth of Suffering; rather, they arise by taking the aforementioned seven as their basis. For this reason:

Third, regarding the acquisition of the names for the distant [afflictions]: among the seven [afflictions], four are proximate and three are distant. Wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) consists of denial and doubt; view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists of clinging to the inferior;
and delusion (*moha*) consists of ignorance and darkness. The designations for these three distant ones are also as previously stated.

Greed and the others arise based solely on the four [noble] truths; when they cease, three are proximate and four are distant. As for the distant ones, the previous three are augmented by view-grasping. This refers to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
To grasp what is inferior as superior is therefore called "adherence to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*). Now, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is a supreme and sublime dharma;

it cannot be further described as inferior being superior. It arises merely from the back of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); grasping the inferior as superior is named adherence to views. Therefore, the Truth of Cessation is distantly related in four ways.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) regarding the distant and the proximate are entirely as previously stated. Regarding the Eightfold Path, three are proximately related.

There are five types of remote [factors]. As for the immediate ones, they are delusion, doubt, and false view. To the remote factors, one adds the grasping at rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) to those preceding them.

Regarding the truth of suffering, the grasping at rules and observances serves as the cause; it is a contaminated fruit and not the uncontaminated path. This is because one falsely clings to it as being the cause and the fruit.

Thus, there is the proximate condition of precept-and-vow attachment (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Because the Truth of the Path is the true cause and the true path, that which is not a cause or a path cannot be its proximate condition;
rather, it arises from false views as a non-path. Therefore, precept-and-vow attachment is categorized among the remote factors.

Since both the Path and Cessation are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas, this is not a case of grasping at what is inferior as superior. Furthermore, view-attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) also belongs to the remote category based on the preceding [analysis]. However—

The grasping arises from wrong view; this is explained in general according to the *Abhidharmakośa* as above. Regarding the four lines omitted here, the transcriber has deleted those that were not essential.

Furthermore, in the *Xianju biansong yan*, it is said: "Those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) arising from the Truths are called 'intimate'; those latent dispositions arising from other latent dispositions are called 'distant.
Latent dispositions such as greed, hatred, and pride are all distant with respect to the Four Truths; [only] those arising from the Truths themselves are intimate."

The [afflictions] of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), delusion (*moha*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—as well as the [view of] self and what belongs to self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—are exclusively "intimate" (*sāmanta*) to the Truth of Suffering. The [view of] precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is intimate to the Truth of Suffering but remote from the Truth of the Path.

The [clinging to] views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is intimate to the Truth of Origin but remote from the lower [Truth of Cessation]. Such is the meaning of intimacy and remoteness with respect to the Truths. Regarding the final two phrases, they should be revised to state:

"There are four [afflictions] that are intimate to the Truth of Origin and four that are remote from the Truth of Cessation. This is more concise and clear when adding the clinging to views to the previous three. Furthermore, there are seven [afflictions] regarding the Truth of Suffering.

Regarding those who are "intimate with the three" yet alienated from the [true] distant [truth]: they take the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and conceive of them as a self.

Based on this body, they give rise to views such as annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*). They regard ascetic practices as the true cause and conceive of the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi*) as *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, they negate worldly fruits, declaring them to be non-existent. Thus, they are all deluded and ignorant, remaining in hesitation and indecision; for this reason, they are "intimate for seven days."
Greed, hatred, and pride arise from what is near to one’s person; because they are separated by one layer, these three are called "distant.

The aggregate [of afflictions] is formed through views and grasping, which misapprehend causes as being causes. As for the "erroneous," it negates the causes of the world, reducing them to non-existence.

Delusion and doubt may be understood accordingly; thus, these four are called "intimate. The meaning of the three "distant" ones is the same as before. Cessation occurs through wrong view, which [negates] that which transcends the world...
They deny the fruits [of karma] as being non-existent; being deluded and ignorant, they remain in doubt and indecision—therefore, the third is called "intimate.
When one takes false views as the Way, one denies the causes for transcending the world as being non-existent; their ignorance and doubt are evident—therefore, the third is called "intimate."

The five loosenesses arise from being deluded regarding the true Path; one consequently clings to the view of attachment to precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) as the Path. Thus, together with greed, anger, and pride, they constitute the five loosenesses.
△ Second, the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*), in three parts: first, the title and enumeration.
Second, regarding the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*): there are eighty-one categories.

[Commentary: These are the thoughts bound to this realm; they are also called "thoughts deluded regarding phenomena" (*vastu-mūḍha-vitarka*) and "the actual three poisons. They differ from both the innate thoughts (*sahaja-vitarka*) and the thoughts of calculation (*tarka-vitarka*).

[Commentary] Regarding "bound to the realms" (*dhātu-bandhana*): by means of this affliction of volition (*cetanā-kleśa*), one is bound to the three realms. "Delusion regarding phenomena" (*vastu-moha*) refers to the obstruction of phenomena;
it arises as hatred, attachment, and so forth in relation to the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Thus, the delusion resides in the phenomena themselves. Regarding the "three primary poisons":

the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states that there are four types of volitional afflictions; since pride (*māna*) is subsumed under delusion (*moha*), they constitute three. They are termed "primary" because they are neither derivative propensities (*anuśaya*) nor habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). These are innate (*sahaja*).
[The faculty of] investigation (*vitarka*) returns to [the category of] views (*dṛṣṭi*). As for the dullness of investigation that follows upon sharpness (*tīkṣṇa-anu-vitarka*):

when the sharpness that is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*) has departed, the dullness of investigation that follows upon it also departs. Therefore, this is examined [here]. The co-arising investigation and sharpness have been explained previously.

Investigation is based upon the thoughts associated with views. [Supplement: One who has attained the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) by abandoning views, although there may be [wisdom] that is solitary regarding phenomena (*vastu*), [is not yet liberated from the bonds of existence].

The Head Correspondence: Understanding that dharmas arise from conditions and not reckoning them as having a real nature, one remains without deviance regarding the three poisons; therefore, it is called "Right.
△ Second, showing the essence by way of the realms, in two parts. First, a general indication of the nine stages.

This means that the three realms are divided into nine stages (*bhūmi*). The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is combined into one stage; the four dhyānas and the four concentrations (*samādhi*) constitute eight stages, making nine in total.
[Note] These nine stages are named after their respective bases of support. Because the desire realm is a single stage of distraction (*vikṣepa-bhūmi*), it is combined into one.
△ Second, the section on the classification of stages (bhūmi-vibhāga), in two parts. First, the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu).

Within this single stage of the Desire Realm, there are nine grades of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride. Regarding these "nine grades," they are: the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra), the high-middle (adhimātra-madhya), [and so forth].
Upper-upper, upper-middle, upper-lower; middle-upper, middle-middle, middle-lower; lower-upper, lower-middle, lower-lower.
△ Second, the higher realms:
each of the eight stages has nine grades, excluding the latent tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*).
△ Third, the total number is established.
Thus, there are eighty-one.
[Note] Within the nine stages (*bhūmi*), each possesses nine grades of greed, hatred, delusion, and pride; however, in the upper eight stages, hatred is absent.
[Commentary] Master Zhiyi’s *Fuxing* says: "One uses wisdom to sever delusions; as wisdom becomes increasingly distinct, delusions gradually come to an end. How could there be fewer than nine stages?
In establishing the teachings and judging the fruits, they are provisionally set forth as nine for the sake of brevity."
[Commentary] It is not mentioned that doubt [remains], because it has already been severed upon seeing the Path; logically, there should be no doubt.
[Record] Although the obstacles of phenomena still exist, right faith is necessarily complete.

[Note] When severing these delusions, one may either directly take the single True Truth (*satyadharma*) as the object of focus, or take any one of the Four Truths as the object of focus according to one's inclination.
[Commentary] The *Shiqian* states: "Within the Four Truths, one contemplates any one truth according to one's thought, or contemplates only the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
By severing the various grades of delusions belonging to the three realms differently, one attains the latter three fruits [of the path]."
[Note] Therefore, it is said in the *Zhiguan*: "The delusions of view are like forty *li* of water; the delusions of thought are like ten *li* of water. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"That which is severed by the first fruit is like forty *li* of water; that which remains is like a single drop from a hair."

[Commentary] Although there are eighty-one grades of volition (*cetanā*), they arise only in relation to their respective objects. This is because they differ from the views (*dṛṣṭi*) that arise indiscriminately toward the mental object (*dharmadhātu*).
△ Third, the summary and collection of the truths (*satya*).

The distinctions between the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*vitarka*) discussed above all belong to the "real existence" (*satya*) of the *saṃghāṭa* (Tripitaka) teaching’s Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
[Note] These afflictions are the cause of conditioned and out-flowing (*sāsrava*) phenomena; therefore, they are said to be "real existences.

Above, the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of views and the eighty-one grades of the delusions of thought were explained, which constitutes the simultaneous opening of both categories. If one speaks of the ninety-eight proclivities, this refers to the opening [of the delusions of views alone].

Regarding the combination of *dṛṣṭi* (view) and *kleśa* (affliction): if one speaks of the "four abodes" (*catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ*), this opens up *kleśa* while combining *dṛṣṭi*; it simply means that both *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa* are combined. Alternatively, they are called the "three outflows" (*traya āsravāḥ*:

desire, existence, and ignorance); or the "four currents" (*catasra oghāḥ*: view, desire, existence, and ignorance); or the "five parts of the upper and lower realms. As the *Myōryaku-ki* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 7, states:

"Within the five parts of the upper realm, the defilements of the form realm and the formless realm are exclusively of the upper [realms], as are the three [factors] beginning with restlessness (*auddhatya*)."

Although restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*) extend downward, they cannot pull one down [to rebirth] in the desire realm; therefore, they are called "upper fetters" (*ūrdhva-bhāgīya*). As for the "lower fetters" (*avarabhāgīya*):

although craving (*rāga*) extends upward, it is not exclusively an upper-fettering factor. Hatred (*pratigha*) is exclusively lower, as it does not extend to the upper realms. The remaining three [fetters] encompass all [realms].
Although the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) extend upward, they are able to pull one down; therefore, they are named "lower. Thus says the *Abhidharmakośa*.

It is said: "By means of two [afflictions, namely greed and hatred], one does not transcend the desire realm; by means of three [afflictions, namely the view of a self-identity, extreme views, and adherence to precepts and rituals], one returns once more to the lower realms.

Even if one has severed greed and the others—[which is termed 'suppression' as a form of 'severance']—up to the sphere of nothingness, where greed is also severed and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained, one still returns to the desire realm due to the view of a self-identity and the like" (text).

[Commentary] This clarifies the opening and closing of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*), as well as their specific designations. To "leak" into the three realms is called a "leak" (*āsrava*). There are four flows (*ogha*):
the *Subcommentary* (Fuxing) states that the "view-flow" refers to the views of the three realms; the "desire-flow" refers to the various delusions of the desire realm, excluding views and ignorance;
the "existence-flow" refers to the various delusions of the two upper realms, excluding views and ignorance; and the "ignorance-flow" refers to the ignorance of the three realms.
To drift incessantly is called "flowing" (*srotas*); it signifies being stained by greed. (The Verse says:
The body is comprised of extreme views, while precepts are grasped [by them]; False views fundamentally arise from doubt.

The four dull faculties all arise from the sharp proclivities; Therefore, the three fetters encompass the exhaustion of views. Delusion gives rise to greed and hatred, while the two give rise to pride.
The two [factors] subsume the two, forming desire and volition; Ignorance is delusion, and defilement is greed; Excitement pervades all three, while craving is associated with concentration.
[Commentary Note: The verse states: The body subsumes the view of extremes, and the precepts subsume the grasping of rules and rituals.

[Supplement] Since [these views] arise from the extremes regarding the self, they are not the "clinging to precepts and observances" (śīlavrataparāmarśa) which takes what is not a cause to be a cause. Within these [extremes], there must necessarily be something grasped;
this is precisely the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
[Boxed Note] Wrong views fundamentally arise from doubt.
[Commentary] First there is hesitation and indecision; subsequently, one denies the existence of cause and effect.
[Note] The four dull [defilements] all arise from the sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*). Therefore, the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*) encompass the entirety of the views (*dṛṣṭi*).

[Supplement] The three fetters are: self-view (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). This verse explains the views of the lower fivefold division (*pañcavarga-dṛṣṭi*).

[Commentary] Ignorance (*moha*) gives rise to greed (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*), while from these two, pride (*māna*) arises. By citing two [factors], two others are subsumed, thereby forming the "desire-thought" (*kāma-cetanā*).
[Record] This verse refers to the "desire-thought" of the lower five parts. "Citing two" indicates greed and hatred; "subsuming two" indicates ignorance and pride.

[Note] Ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion (*moha*); defilement (*saṃkleśa*) is greed (*rāga*). Restlessness (*auddhatya*) pervades all three and is associated with craving for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

[Commentary] This verse concerns the five factors of the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the higher realms. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* asks: "Restlessness is termed a 'fetter' (*saṃyojana*) in the higher realms;

why is it not so stated for the desire realm? The answer is: "Because that realm lacks coarse afflictions, restlessness and frivolity (*pralāpa*) are manifest there. Furthermore, it disrupts meditative concentration."
Because there is power within the body, it constitutes a fetter (*saṃyojana*). By severing these higher fetters, one attains liberation.
