[Note] Third, causing unarisen wholesome states to arise: when practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the five types of wholesome faculties, such as faith, have not yet arisen.
In order to cause them to arise, one applies oneself with single-minded diligence and exerts skillful means in cultivation so that these wholesome faculties may emerge.
[Commentary] Regarding the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), they are called "the abandonment through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Abandonment through cultivation refers to the fact that, regarding wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, by repeatedly cultivating those wholesome dharmas, one is able to bring before oneself what was previously unattained."
One is able to effect what must be severed.

[Note] Fourth, causing those wholesome states already arisen to increase. When practicing the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the five kinds of wholesome roots—faith and the others—have already arisen.
In order to cause them to increase, one applies oneself with single-minded diligence and exerts skillful means in cultivation so that they do not decline or be lost, but rather increase.
The long-term accomplishment.
[Commentary] Among the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), this is called "abandonment through protection" (*ārakṣaṇaprahāṇa*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"Abandonment through protection refers to the fact that, regarding already arisen wholesome dharmas, because they have already been attained and are currently manifest, one remains far removed from negligence (*pramāda*) within those wholesome dharmas."
It is able to generate wholesome dharmas, abide in them without forgetting, cultivate them to perfection, and guard those already arisen;

it is also able to abandon that which is to be abandoned. Question: Why are these four called the "Right Efforts" (*samyak-prahāṇa*), and why are the subsequent eight called the "Right Path" (*samyak-mārga*)?
Why are the others not so named? Answer: Because the mind must exert vigor with diligence, fearing errors and mistakes, it is so described.
"Correct. It is called "correct" because one practices the Path out of fear of falling into heterodox teachings.
△ Third, the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*):
the four bases of psychic power (desire, thought, energy, and wisdom).

【□Note】The *Fajie Cidian* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm), section thirteen, states: "Because one obtains whatever is wished for through the power of wisdom, meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and so forth, they are called the bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*)."
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Dharmadhātu": it refers to the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness and the diligence of the four right efforts.

Because wisdom and diligence increase while concentration-power is slight and weak, one attains the four types of meditative absorptions that collect the mind; these are the equalities of wisdom and concentration.
Thus, they are collectively termed "as desired" (ruci). Because the equality of wisdom and concentration can sever the fetters and latent tendencies, the practice of abandonment is accomplished.
[Note]: These four belong to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the power of the body (*kāya-ṛddhipāda*) is manifested by means of them.
Furthermore, since the supernormal powers arise from concentration, it may also be said that all six supernormal powers are simultaneously activated by means of them.

[Commentary] There are three types of bodily *ṛddhi* (supernormal power): namely, *gamana-ṛddhi* (the power of movement), *pariṇāma-ṛddhi* (the power of transformation), and *ārya-ṛddhi* (noble power).
Regarding *gamana-ṛddhi*, there are four further varieties: first, flying through the air like a bird without obstruction; second, making the distant near so that one arrives without having traveled;

third, vanishing from here and appearing there; and fourth, reaching a destination in a single thought-moment. As for *pariṇāma-ṛddhi*, it consists of making the large small and the small large, or making the one many.

It is likewise so. All manner of various objects can be transformed. While the transformations of the non-Buddhists do not exceed seven days, the Buddha and his disciples possess mastery over transformation such that there is no limit to its duration.

As for the "Noble Power of Wish-Fulfilling" (ārya-ṛddhi), one is able to contemplate unlovely and impure things among the six external sense objects and make them pure, or contemplate lovely and pure things and [make them otherwise].
This causes impurity. Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) that arise on this basis: as for the power of mastery (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), it is as described above.
As for the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*): the eye attains the pure matter (*rūpa*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

It can illuminate all things belonging to the six realms of sentient beings across its own level and lower levels—whether near or far, coarse or subtle—without anything remaining unseen. This [power] is of two kinds: first, that obtained through karmic retribution (*vipākaja*); second, [that obtained through cultivation].

It is acquired through cultivation. Among the five destinies, the divine eye is acquired through cultivation; it is not acquired as a result of karmic retribution (*vipāka*), because it is obtained by constantly recollecting various kinds of light.
As for the supernormal power of the divine ear, one is able to hear all sounds: celestial sounds, human sounds, and the sounds of the three evil realms.
How is the divine ear acquired through cultivation? By constantly recollecting various kinds of sounds. [The supernormal power of] knowing past lives...

Regarding the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*): one constantly recollects past events, from months, days, years, and the period within the womb, up to one past life, ten, a hundred, a thousand, ten million, or a hundred billion lifetimes, and even as far back as the great Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, who know eighty thousand great kalpas;
while Bodhisattvas and Buddhas know immeasurable kalpas. Regarding the power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*): one knows the minds of others, whether they possess defilements or not.
It is stainless. One attains it by constantly recollecting when one observes for oneself the arising, abiding, and ceasing of the mind.
Furthermore, by observing the signs of joy, anger, and fear in others, and having seen these signs, one subsequently knows their minds; this is the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding the untainted supernormal power (*anāsrava-abhijñā*), it is an adornment of the Tathāgata, as stated in the *Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra*: "There is no..."
"Outflows" (*āsrava*) refers to being free from the four outflows; because one does not grasp at those four kinds of outflows, it is called "the wisdom that is far removed from all outflows.

[Commentary] The four right efforts are wisdom; if there is no diligent observation through wisdom, the foundations of mindfulness will not be established, and instead they will invite distraction, like a lamp in the wind.

Now, by cultivating the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), it is as if entering a sealed chamber; concentration and wisdom are balanced. "Desire" (*chanda*) means aspiration, longing, and joyful inclination.

One adorns that dharma. By "that dharma," it is meant the objects of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). By "adorning," it is meant cultivating a mind of aspiration so that the dharma becomes upright and beautiful.
Regarding all dharmas that are practiced and established, if there is no joyful desire (*chanda*), the task will inevitably be neglected.

*Smṛti* (mindfulness) means focusing one's attention on that object, dwelling with single-mindedness and correctness; if there is no single-mindedness, the contemplation of phenomena will be interrupted.
*Vīrya* (diligence) means focusing exclusively on contemplating the principle so as to prevent any intermingling. Because it is unmixed, it is refined; because it is uninterrupted, it is diligent.

Regarding all dharmas practiced and established, if there is no diligence, the task will certainly not be accomplished. *Prajñā* (wisdom) refers to the sequential order of the dharma-realm within śamatha and vipaśyanā.

All are termed "contemplation" (*cintā*). One contemplates that principle so that the mind does not wander or scatter; one should know that these four dharmas are the skillful means for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The four and five faculties (*śraddhā*, *vīrya*, *smṛti*, *samādhi*, *prajñā*).

(Text) Regarding faith: it is faith in the principle of the Truths (*satya*), which is able to give rise to all the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), samādhis, and so forth.

△ Five Powers (the names of the five powers are the same as those of the five faculties).
[Note] Because they did not enter [the path] previously, one advances to cultivate the five powers (*pañcabala*), causing the faculties (*indriya*) to increase so that one can eliminate obstacles.

Regarding those whose names are the same as the faculties, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 7, part 1 (13), states: Question: Since their names are the same as the faculties, why is it necessary to establish them again?

Answer: Although the wholesome roots have arisen, evil has not yet been destroyed. One must further practice and cultivate them to cause the faculties to increase; therefore, these five are again received [as distinct powers].
Regarding the name "Power" (*bala*): because they accomplish what is wholesome and destroy what is unwholesome, they are called powers. (Text) *Fanyi chiqian* 1.9 states: The *Xinyue pin* says:
"There is no deception, indolence, anger, or resentment. Deception is an obstacle to faith; indolence is an obstacle to diligence; anger is an obstacle to mindfulness.

Regret is an obstacle to concentration (*samādhi*); resentment is an obstacle to wisdom (*prajñā*). If the faculties (*indriya*) increase, they can destroy these five obstacles; therefore, they are called "powers" (*bala*).

[Commentary] This explanation cites the scriptural passage from the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fmen*) to clarify the five obstacles. Deception consists of negligence, agitation, superficiality, and doubt.
An inability to deeply endure and take delight in [the Dharma] obstructs faith. Laziness prevents one from being courageous and reaching profound realization, thereby obstructing diligence.
Anger results in a preponderance of unwholesome states of mind, such that one cannot clearly remember the path of the primary and auxiliary practices; this obstructs mindfulness.

Resentment causes the mind and spirit to become stifled and constricted, preventing one from merging into and withdrawing into the foundations of mindfulness; this obstructs concentration. Enmity harbors...
The matter of poison is profound; because one cannot discern the principle of reality, it obstructs wisdom.
[Note] The power of faith is to believe in the truths, remaining unmoved by the various doubts of heterodox outsiders.

[Commentary: Although there are many kinds of doubt, they do not necessarily obstruct meditative concentration (*samādhi*). According to the treatise, there are three types that obstruct concentration:

First, doubt regarding oneself: One thinks to oneself, "My faculties are dull and dark; my sins and defilements are deep and heavy. Am I not unfit for this? By harboring such self-doubt, concentration and wisdom do not arise. Second, doubt regarding the teacher:
One thinks, "That person’s deportment and physical appearance are like this, yet he himself does not possess the Way. [By doubting the teacher in this way, one's own practice is hindered.]
"How can you teach me? When such doubts arise, they immediately become an obstacle to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Third, regarding doubt concerning the Dharma:

as worldly people often cling to their own preconceived notions, they fail to receive, revere, or practice the teachings they have received with faith. If such hesitation arises, the Dharma will not permeate the mind.
Now, when this faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) grows and becomes powerful, one will not be moved by such [doubts]. [Appendix] Three Doubts.

This is a universal malady throughout all ages. Within the Teachings it is said: regarding those who doubt themselves, they should reflect on the boundless roots of goodness from their past lives and diligently apply themselves to repentance to break through that doubt.
Regarding those who doubt the teacher, they should simply follow the Dharma without judging the person;
it is like traveling at night with a lamp held by an ignoble person—one does not discard the light because of the person. Regarding those who doubt the Dharma, the Buddha never speaks deceptively.
It is appropriate to practice with sincere faith and diligent effort.

[Commentary] Advance with vigor to contemplate the Truths (satya), with a mind free from distraction or confusion. Originally seeking the fruit of the Path, do not cease until realization is attained.

Maintain the Truths through the power of mindfulness (*smṛti-bala*), destroying biased and heterodox conceptions so that they cannot be destroyed by the afflictions (*kleśa*). If the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*) is perfected, one can destroy desire.
All distractions throughout the realms can be overcome such that the various dhyānas do not obstruct one another; this is unlike the characteristics of practicing the fundamental stages in isolation.

[Commentary] If the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is perfected, it not only destroys the distractions of the desire realm, but also differs from the practice of the higher stages in isolation.

Samādhi. This is because within the various dhyāna-samādhis, there is no mutual obstruction. As stated in the *Fǔxíng* (The Practice of the Ancients): "Although one employs the linguistic methods of the desire realm, they do not obstruct the constituent factors (*aṅga*) of the first dhyāna;
or, while abiding in the factors of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna, they do not obstruct the internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) of the second dhyāna;
or, while abiding in the second dhyāna associated with joy (*prīti*), they do not obstruct the pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*) of the third dhyāna. Or...

The fourth dhyāna is associated with equanimity and feeling, yet it is capable of teaching and transforming all sentient beings. Even if it obstructs the [specific states of] the fourth dhyāna, it does not obstruct other meditative concentrations.

"Obstructs" (fáng) means to hinder; "hinders" (ài) means to block or prevent. Thus, even if there are causes and conditions that prevent one from entering the fourth dhyāna, it does not impede other samādhis.
This does not hinder the mastery of all dhyānas. [Appendix] Bian’uo says: “The various dhyānas do not obstruct one another.

This text on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* follows the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), whereas the present explanation concerns the Tripitaka Teachings (*zangjiao*). One should weigh these points when interpreting them.”
[Note] The power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*). It can shatter all erroneous and heterodox forms of wisdom; it can shatter all attachments such as views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
△ 67. Factors of Enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The Seven Factors of Enlightenment (mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity).

[Commentary] One who previously failed to enter [the path] due to an imbalance between concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) employs these seven factors of enlightenment to bring them into equilibrium.

[Commentary] Mindfulness and diligence are wisdom; the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) are concentration. Furthermore, although one has attained the faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*), thereby accomplishing the good and destroying evil, one who has not yet entered into the principle does so because concentration and wisdom are not harmonized;
therefore, one balances them by means of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

[Note] "Awakening" (jue) means to fully comprehend. "Limbs" (zhi) refers to constituent parts. The *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), section 14, states: "The true awakening of one beyond training."
The seven factors that lead to arrival (text).

[Commentary] "Actual awakening" refers to the wisdom that awakens according to reality (*yathābhūta*). Regarding the *Dharmadhātu-śāstra*: first is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), which is well able to discriminate between the true and the false, because it does not erroneously grasp at various deceptive phenomena.
Second is the awakening factor of vigor (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), which is well able to bring about clear realization.
3. The awakening of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): Because one constantly exerts oneself with the mind dwelling in the true Dharma, one practices without engaging in fruitless asceticism.
One attains the joy of the Dharma; awakening to this joy, one does not give rise to joy based on inverted dharmas, but dwells in the joy of the true Dharma.
4. The awakening of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): When severing all views and afflictions, one awakens to the removal of all falsehoods, without causing harm.

1. The awakening factor of true roots of goodness (*samyak-saṃkalpa*): because one is truly able to awaken to and understand that the objects being relinquished are false and unreal, never again to pursue them with recollection. 2. The awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one is well able to awaken to and understand the objects of relinquishment as deceptive and unsubstantial, never again to recall them.

3. The awakening factor of investigation (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one is well able to awaken to and understand, constantly ensuring that concentration and wisdom remain balanced. 4. The awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one is well able to awaken to and understand, constantly ensuring that concentration and wisdom remain balanced. 5. The awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one is well able to awaken to and understand, constantly ensuring that concentration and wisdom remain balanced. 6. The awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one gives rise to various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and awakens to the fact that all such absorptions are deceptive, thereby not giving rise to views, attachments, or deluded thoughts. 7. The awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): because one is well able to awaken to and understand, constantly ensuring that concentration and wisdom remain balanced.
If the mind is sunken, arouse it through investigation, exertion, and joy; if the mind is agitated, settle it through equanimity, relinquishment, and concentration.
Thus, one brings it to a state of balanced harmony.
[Boxed Note] *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (7.9) states: "When the mind is floating and restless, one eliminates coarse [disturbances] of body and speech through the elimination of *vitarka*.

[Commentary] "Lightness-and-ease" (*praśrabdhi*) is precisely the elimination of *vitarka*, also termed the "elimination of *vitarka*" (*vitarka-prahāṇa*). It refers to a state of mental ease, relaxation, and mastery.

The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) are the essential means for entering the Path. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one abandons the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*) and exclusively cultivates the seven factors of enlightenment, yet fails to enter meditative absorption (*dhyāna*)."
Such a thing is impossible.

[Commentary] One abandons contemplative wisdom through the awakening-factor of equanimity (*upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga*), and enters dhyāna with a concentrated mind. When the mind becomes sunken, one arouses it by means of diligence (*vīriya*) and the discernment of joy (*pītisampassa*).
"Mindfulness" (*sati*) refers to the passage concerning both locations.
[Commentary] To gather the distracted and stimulate the dull, so as not to fall into the extremes of dullness or distraction—this is the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

While it was previously stated that the even balance of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) is the reason for employing the seven factors of awakening, this present discussion concerns the essential nature of the awakening factor of mindfulness itself.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), fascicle 7, part 1, page 13, states: "There are three aspects each for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). One employs whichever is appropriate for each; once the benefit is obtained, one stops.

There is no need to practice them all exhaustively. Only if there is no benefit at all does one proceed to the subsequent category. Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is able to universally sustain the six factors of both concentration and wisdom;
therefore, the category of mindfulness applies to both places [in the text]. (Text)
[Commentary: The Buddha taught the instructions so that one might practice them. It is like a physician who prescribes medicine according to a prescription;

if the illness does not subside after taking a single dose, he adds a subsequent medicine. If the previous remedy provided no benefit, he then employs the next stage of awakening. Although the Dharma is received from the physician, its practice depends upon oneself.
One should stop once the benefit has been obtained.
△ 7–8. The Eightfold Right Path (right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right effort, right concentration, right mindfulness, and right livelihood).

[Commentary] Right mindfulness and right concentration constitute *samādhi*. Right view, right thought, and right effort constitute *prajñā*. Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are collectively termed *śīla*.
Furthermore, the first seven factors of enlightenment are analytical, while these eight constitute the correct practice of the Eightfold Noble Path.
[Note] "Right" (samyak) has the meaning of being non-deviant. Because it can lead one to reach Nirvana, it is called the "Path" (mārga).
[Commentary] The Eightfold Right Path is also called the Eightfold Noble Path; this appears in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
[Square Note] Right View: Because one cultivates the sixteen aspects of the untainted (*anāsrava*), one clearly perceives the Four Noble Truths.
[Bullet Point Note] The explanation of the sixteen aspects is found in Volume Five.

【□Note】Right Thought: By means of right thought, one initiates this contemplation. Right Speech: By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one eliminates the four types of wrong livelihood and constantly restrains the vocal karma, abiding within right speech.
[Supplement] The *Aṣṭagranthaka-śāstra* states: "Engaging in the four types of verbal misconduct through wrong livelihood is termed 'wrong speech' and 'wrong livelihood.

Engaging in the three types of bodily misconduct through wrong livelihood is termed 'wrong action' and 'wrong livelihood. Furthermore, among the five types of wrong [livelihood], the latter four are all vocal actions;
they do not necessarily refer exclusively to the greedy pursuit of gain and offerings, but include all such things as frivolous play and the like, which belong to wrong livelihood."

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that watching elephant fights and the like, the Buddha also established as wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*), because one improperly receives external objects and thus vainly prolongs life.

[Supplement] Bian’e says: It is likely unnecessary to point specifically to the latter four [of the ten unwholesome paths] here, for those four are termed the "four wrong actions" (*catur-mithyākarma*) in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.
Thus, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "Among bodily and vocal actions, if they are originated by greed (*lobha*), they are all termed wrong livelihood."
[Square Note] Right Action: By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one eliminates the bodily wrong livelihood and abides in purity within right bodily action.
[Bullet Point Note] Bodily wrong [livelihood] refers to manifesting wonders and the like.

【□Note】 Right Effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*): Diligently cultivating *nirvāṇa*, skillfully entering the True Truths (*saddharma*). Right Concentration (*samyak-samādhi*): Correctly abiding in principle, remaining resolute and unshakable.
Right Mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*): The mind is not moved or lost; it is upright and free from forgetfulness. Right Livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*):

By means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), one thoroughly eliminates the five kinds of wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*) within the three types of action (*trikarma*). When seeing others obtain benefit, the mind does not become feverish or distressed; rather, regarding one's own benefit...
Always knowing contentment and sufficiency, one dwells in pure right livelihood.
[Commentary] Four types are specific to verbal karma; five types pertain to all three karmas.
△ Third, the conclusion and dedication.
The seven categories above constitute the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) within the *śrāvaka* teachings, characterized by arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).
[Note] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Vol. 1, Part 1 (11), states: "Enlightenment (*bodhi*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) overturn one another; therefore, they are called 'arising and ceasing.'"

△ Second, a general discussion of the Four Noble Truths, in two parts. First, a discussion on how the teaching is adapted to the capacities of beings, resulting in differences of superiority and inferiority.
However, regarding the names and enumerations of the Four Noble Truths as previously listed, these apply throughout the three lower teachings;

they differ only in that the scope of each teaching is broad or narrow, superior or inferior, and in their respective designations as *samskrta* (arising and ceasing), *anupapatti* (non-arising), *apramāṇa* (immeasurable), and *anabhisaṃskāra* (unconditioned). Therefore, their names and enumerations will not be listed again below.

[Commentary on the *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra-ṭīkā*, Fascicle 3 (8): It says: Question: For what reason are the distinctions of the four kinds of Four Noble Truths established? Answer: The Truths originally do not consist of four.
The Truth is simply the Principle (*li*). Since even the Principle does not exist as a single entity, how could there be four?

Thus we know that, based upon the Tathāgatagarbha’s identity of the provisional and the real, and by the power of Great Compassion and unconditioned vows, [the Buddha] employs these means when struck by the capacities of sentient beings, having no choice but to act.

Because capacities and circumstances differ, the Dharma manifests in varying degrees of excellence. From the single principle of ultimate reality (*tattva*), there is the provisional principle (*upāya*) that is deployed;

since these two principles—the provisional and the real—differ in their verbal expressions (*deśanā*), four types of distinct teachings arise. Following the realization of the ultimate *Nirvāṇa*, the three provisional [vehicles] are temporarily employed to assist the Perfect [teaching].

Therefore, it is necessary to employ both the partial and the perfect, as well as both phenomena and principle. Thus, they are cited here to serve as corroborating evidence. The third is the partial...
One circle. Within the realm and outside the realm; each has its own principle and phenomenon, thus forming four kinds (text).
[Commentary] "That which is struck by the capacities of beings" explains the aforementioned reliance on the power of great compassion and unconditioned vows.

Because the faculties and vessels of sentient beings differ in a thousand ways, the Tathāgata’s vocal teachings are ten thousandfold. As it is said, the Tathāgata acts for the sake of sentient beings according to their respective capacities.

This is spoken according to the measure [of the teaching]. From "one true principle" and so forth, the preceding [categories] are explained: the principle of phenomena within and outside the *dharmadhātu* refers to the *Hīnayāna* (Treasury) for phenomena, the *Mahāyāna* (Pervasion) for principles, the *Separate Teachings* (Distinction) for phenomena, and the *Perfect Teaching* (Round) for principles.

[Note] Regarding "broad and narrow" and so forth: the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) [teachings] establish six truths, and are therefore narrow; the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) [teachings] establish ten truths, and are therefore broad.

Because the *Zang* and *Bie* do not speak of identity (*ji*), they are inferior; because the *Tong* and *Yuan* speak of identity, they are superior. When discussing superiority and inferiority within these broad and narrow objects, four types of Four Noble Truths are formed.

Since there are degrees of gravity in delusion regarding True Suchness (*zhenyou*), one discusses the "Arising and Ceasing" (*shengmie*) and "Non-arising" (*wusheng*). Since there are likewise degrees of gravity in delusion regarding the Middle Way (*zhongdao*), [one discusses the "Suffering of Suffering" and the "Suffering of Pervasive Conditioning"].
Therefore, regarding the immeasurable and the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*), one should not engage in ordinary, reciprocal debates concerning their relative superiority or inferiority.

[Commentary] This means that one should discuss their respective superiority and inferiority by contrasting the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) with the *Sūtra* (Pāramitā), and the *Vaipulya* (Separate) with the *Vimalakīrti* (Perfect).
[Note on "Arising and Ceasing"]: The *Miaoxuan* (20) states: "Because delusion regarding the Truth is profound, one receives the name based on phenomena (*dharma*), as explained previously."

[Commentary on the preceding explanation: Regarding "suffering," it refers to the shifting of the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*) and so forth. Whether mundane or supramundane, all four [truths] are subject to transformation.

[Sub-commentary on "Non-arising" (*anutpāda*): The *Miaoxuan* (20) states: Because delusion regarding the Truth is slight, [this name] is derived from the Principle. Suffering lacks the characteristic of oppression.
The origin of suffering has the characteristic of non-conjunction; the path has the characteristic of non-duality; cessation has the characteristic of non-arising. [Commentary:
That suffering is without oppression means that the five aggregates are all empty. How could emptiness oppress emptiness?
That the origin is without conjunction means that cause and effect are both empty. How could the emptiness of the cause conjoin with the emptiness of the effect? Thus it applies to all things.
Greed, hatred, and delusion are also like this. "The Way is non-dual" means there is neither that which treats nor that which is treated.
Since even emptiness does not possess even one [duality], how could there be two? "Cessation is non-arising" means that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen; they do not arise now, nor do they cease.
This non-arising and non-ceasing is called true non-arising.

[Note] "Immeasurable. The *Miaoxuan* states: Because they are heavy within the state of delusion, they are designated according to their phenomena (*dharma*). Suffering has immeasurable aspects, because the ten dharma-realms are not identical.
Accumulation (*samudaya*) has immeasurable aspects, because the afflictions of the five abodes (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are not identical.

The Path (*mārga*) has immeasurable aspects, because the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are not identical. Cessation (*nirodha*) has immeasurable aspects, because the various pāramitās are not identical.

Therefore (the text). [Commentary] Regarding "suffering is immeasurable": this means that even the suffering within a single dharma-realm is already manifold; how much more so for the ten dharma-realms?

This is not something known by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). That is to say, the various forms of flaying, burning, boiling, and hacking in the hells are beyond calculation; how much more so [for the rest]?
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s eye of wisdom thoroughly penetrates the various characteristics of suffering within the other realms.
"Immeasurable accumulation" refers to the manifold afflictions such as ignorance, the sands of dust-like views, and the delusions of thought.

"Immeasurable path" refers to the analytical and substantial methods—whether crude or skillful, provisional or real, primary or auxiliary. "Immeasurable cessation" refers to how such skillful means can extinguish the delusions of views and thoughts, and so forth.
Only those who are Bodhisattvas are able to understand this clearly. Furthermore, it is emptiness itself;
though there are various skillful means, they are all without variety. Although there is no variety, one discriminates among varieties without error or confusion. Such are these skillful means.
It can extinguish the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). By such skillful means, it can extinguish the dust-like and river-sand-like ignorance (*avidyā*).

Furthermore, while there are various distinctions among the three *siddhāntas*, the *paramārtha-siddhānta* has no such distinctions. Although it has no distinctions, when discussed from the perspective of its vastness, it is called "immeasurable."

[Note on "Non-action" (Amala-karma): The *Miaoxuan* states: "Because it is slight within delusion, it derives its name from principle. The *Zhi guan* (1.3) says: "The aggregates and sense bases are all suchness;
there is no suffering to be abandoned. Ignorance and afflictions are themselves bodhi; there is no accumulation to be severed. Extremes and deviance are all the Middle Way;
there is no path to be cultivated. Birth-and-death is itself nirvana; there is no cessation to be realized" (text).
[Commentary: There is no creator; all are the inconceivable true aspect (*dharmatā*). The commentary on the Four Mindfulnesses regarding the Four Truths of Non-action states:
"A single thought-moment possesses the suffering of the ten realms—this is called the Truth of Suffering. It possesses the delusions of the ten realms—this is called the Truth of Origination.

Suffering itself is *nirvāṇa*—this is called the Truth of Cessation. Delusion itself is *bodhi*—this is called the Truth of the Path. This is what is meant by 'the very phenomenon is the Middle Way.'"
Without thought and without recollection, and with no one who performs the creation, it is called "non-action.
△ Second, showing that there is a difference between the coarse and the subtle regarding the causes and effects of the two periods. First, clarifying the distinctions between cause and effect.

Nevertheless, within the Four Noble Truths, there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane: the first two truths constitute mundane cause and effect (the fruit of suffering and the cause of its accumulation), while the latter two truths constitute supramundane cause and effect (the fruit of cessation and the cause of the path).

[Commentary] The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Jieshenmi Jing*), fascicle 3, part 8, states: "Suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are merely all mundane phenomena (*laukika-dharma*). The path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*) are merely the single supramundane phenomenon (*lokottara-dharma*).
While the causal natures of mundane and supramundane phenomena differ, a cause must necessarily lead to its fruit; yet the categories of cause and fruit are distinct."
Therefore, four distinctions are established.
△ Second, explaining the reason for these distinctions.

Question: For what reason are the worldly and world-transcending paths presented with the former as fruit and the latter as cause? Answer: Because the faculties of the śrāvakas are dull; they first realize suffering and then sever the origin [of suffering].
One cultivates the cause out of a longing for the fruit; it is for this reason that it is so.

[Commentary] For those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, whose faculties are dull, suffering is the initial gateway. For Pratyekabuddhas, it is origination. For Bodhisattvas, it is the path. For Bodhisattvas of the general category, it is cessation.
For Bodhisattvas of the distinct category, it is the path beyond the realms. For Bodhisattvas of the perfect category, it is cessation beyond the realms.

[Commentary] The commentary further clarifies the initial gateways practiced by the four teachings. That is to say: those of the Śrāvaka vehicle have dull faculties and take the suffering within the realm (*dhātu*) as their initial gateway;
Pratyekabuddhas take the origin (*samudaya*) within the realm; and Bodhisattvas take the path (*mārga*) within the realm.

These three vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zàngjiào) cultivate the truth of conditioned arising and cessation (*utpādanirodha-satya*), distinguishing between sharp and dull faculties. The Shared Teaching (Tōngjiào) cultivates the principle of non-arising emptiness; therefore, it takes the realm... [text truncated].
The internal extinction refers to the separate cultivation of immeasurable and inconceivable phenomena; therefore, it is the extinction within the realm.
The external-to-the-realm extinction refers to the perfect cultivation of the unconditioned and inconceivable principle; therefore, it is the extinction beyond the realm.

[Commentary] Aspiring to the fruit while cultivating the cause, this refers for now to the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). If one has attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), it is said that "one practices the cause while carrying the fruit.
Since the Pratyekabuddha does not establish partial fruits, it is said that "one practices the cause while looking toward the fruit."
[Commentary] This clarifies the phrase "cultivating the cause out of aspiration for the fruit," which refers specifically to the stage of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) among the Śrāvakas.
[Sub-commentary] In the Four Noble Truths, the fruit comes first and the cause follows; this is merely one perspective, as other sequences are not fixed.
[Commentary] The indeterminate [positions] are as shown below.

[Commentary] The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "Some say that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) refers to suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), while ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) refers to the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Others say that conventional truth refers to suffering, its origin, and cessation, while ultimate truth refers to the path. The critic says: "All four are conventional truths; they are also..."

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*): just as suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are conventional truths (*saṃvṛtisatya*), the fact that suffering is empty (*śūnya*), impermanent (*anitya*), and that its origin arises from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the ultimate truth.

As for cessation (*nirodha*) being a conventional truth, the Buddha taught it as being like a city, a garden, or a grove; whereas [the aforementioned nature of suffering and its origin] is the ultimate truth.

Exhaustion, cessation, the wondrous, and detachment—these are the Path as conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The Buddha has taught that [conventional truth] is like a raft, a mountain, a ladder, or a tower.

As for ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the Path is like a track or a vehicle. If the Four Truths were exclusively ultimate truth, then while conventional truth speaks of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), ultimate truth would likewise speak of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

Part Two: Practice and Stages. First, a general heading:
A brief clarification of the practice of the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao), including persons and stages.
[Note] Regarding the practitioner who cultivates the one teaching of the Path and the stages of the Three Vehicles, the *Miaoxuan* (4.32) states:
"It is to shatter the practitioner's mind of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), and to eliminate [obstacles] so that people may be inspired to aspire toward it.
The *Shiqian* (5.21) states: "If there were no stages, by what means would one contemplate the worthy and seek to equal them? By what means would one transcend overweening pride?"
The Transgression of Arrogance (Text).

[Commentary] This explanation generally identifies the stages of the practitioners. As for "stages," it is intended to clarify that there are gradations in the cultivation of causes and the attainment of fruits by those practicing the Three Vehicles.
The *Zhou Yi* states: "The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life-giving. The Sage—
The Great Treasure says it is a "position" (*wei*). Thus we know that if it were not a position, there would be no means to lead practitioners toward their aspirations.
As the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) states: "The superior positions of the various sages cannot be fathomed by ordinary beings; how could one dare to speak of them recklessly?

Those who have a rough understanding of the general meaning do so for two purposes: to shatter the practitioner's pride (*adhimāna*) and to clarify the scriptural text in order to inspire aspiration in others.
"Upon seeing the virtuous, one thinks of becoming equal to them.
(From the *Lunyu*). △ Second, the detailed explanation has three parts. First, the Śrāvakas have three sections. First, the designation of the stages and the division of the categories.

First, clarifying the stage of the Śrāvaka, which is divided into two: first, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); second, the noble one (*ārya*). The ordinary person is further divided into two: the outer ordinary person and the inner ordinary person.

[Commentary] Generally, there are four gates that clarify the stages [of spiritual cultivation]: first, the *Abhidharma* gate of existence (*astitva*), which clarifies the seven types of worthies and the seven types of sages;

Because the gate of existence (*yu-men*) serves as the foundation. Regarding the three points that accord with the purport of the teaching: this means that the intent of the holy teachings is in full agreement with the gate of existence.
As for the passage beginning "The fundamental basis of the Buddha-dharma," this separately explains the second point.

It means that the various phenomena (*dharma*)—the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—expounded by the gate of existence, are produced through the direct causes and conditions of ignorance; that is, they take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as [their ultimate ground].
With ignorance as the condition and ignorance as the cause, and with objective realms as the condition, the various phenomena of the world arise.
This is not the same as the false, causeless arising asserted by non-Buddhists, for those non-Buddhists may reckon that all phenomena arise from Brahmā, empty space, or other such sources.

This is the root of the Buddha-dharma. In the third fascicle, it is asked: "Since the two gates do not lead [to the same result], one cannot judge them definitively.

Regarding the "one-seeded" (ekabījī): if one does not pass away before advancing to sever one further grade [of affliction], one immediately realizes the third fruit (*phala*). As for those heading toward the first fruit (*srotāpanna*):

during the sixteen moments of mind, it refers to the time of the fifteen preceding moments of the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), when the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have not yet been fully severed.
One who has attained the first fruit is fully endowed with the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), having completely severed the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
This refers to the realization of the Truths. One who is "heading toward the second fruit" has already abandoned five grades of the afflictions of the desire realm.

When a person dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they may attain the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) and enter *parinirvāṇa* during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) before actually arriving at that realm;

One who attains *parinirvāṇa* through application (*sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin*) is one who, having been born in the form realm, further exerts effort (*prayoga*).

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa through practice (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*): they exhaust all seventy-one categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) pertaining to the higher realms and then attain parinirvāṇa.

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa without practice (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*): having been born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they attain the manifestation of the noble path and attain parinirvāṇa naturally, without applying further effort.
Regarding "those who flow upward" (*ūrdhvasrotas*): this carries the sense of "flowing upward," as they gradually ascend through the form realm.
The various devas of the realms receive birth; only when they have severed seventy-one grades of afflictions and exhausted them do they enter parinirvāṇa.
