Since the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) clarifies the path of the teachings, it follows the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* in listing the stages; thus, there is the name "body-witness.

The present text follows this and lists twenty-seven types of noble persons (āryapudgala). However, since the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the Great Calming and Contemplation) clarifies the gates of contemplation, it follows the *Abhidharmakośa*.

Venerable sirs, there is no such designation as "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*). As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "The Sūtra speaks of eighteen types of those in training (*śaikṣa*);
for what reason is 'one who has realized through the body' not mentioned therein? The explanation says: it is because the necessary basis (*āśraya*) is absent. What is meant by "basis"?

It refers to the various untainted (*anāsrava*) three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) and the fruits of the noble ones (*āryaphala*); it is based on these distinctions that one is established as being in training. [This applies to] the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

It is not "training" (*śaikṣa*), because it is not the fruit of training. Regarding the statement "the three trainings": untainted ethical discipline (*anāsrava-śīla*) refers to the unmanifested [karma] of the śrāvakas;

untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) refers to the fundamental pure dhyānas, which are cultivated through contemplation, refinement, and perfuming; untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) refers to the principle of the Four Noble Truths.
Only by possessing these three trainings is one capable of entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*); this is the cause of being a noble one.

Regarding what is called "Nirvana": this corresponds to the principle wherein, once the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-kleśa*) are completely severed, one realizes the *nirvāṇa* of true emptiness.

This is the fruit of the noble ones (*ārya*), and it does not depend on the body as a basis or take the out-flowing (*sāsrava*) as its cause. Therefore, the realization by means of the body is not included among these [categories].

[Supplement] Regarding the "out-flowing" of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*): this is the mundane meditative absorption (*vastu-samādhi*) of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), consisting of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*).
When the mind ceases, although it resembles *nirvāṇa*, compared to the four fruits [of the śramaṇa], it is still considered "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Since it belongs to the category of the "outflowing," it is not the cause upon which the first three fruits rely; therefore, it is not included among those counted as persons in training (*śaikṣa*).

However, the reason the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) makes such a distinction is that those who wish to train must take the principle as their object to sever the fetters and rely on the cultivation of the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), rather than entering through mundane meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).

Furthermore, if one cultivates the meditative concentration on phenomenal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-samādhi*) with an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), there is no entry [into this state] that is not attained;

however, that is not the subject of this treatise. Moreover, in the case of a body-witness *anāgāmin* (*kāyasākṣin-anāgāmin*), the afflictions of thought and perception (*saṃjñā-vitarka-kleśa*) have not yet been entirely severed.

Precisely at the moment of entering this meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the six preceding consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta*) do not manifest at all; thus, they do not [function as] the... [uncontaminated mind].

It is associated with the wisdom of observing outflows (*āsrava*), yet it lacks the efficacy of severing afflictions or realizing the principle; therefore, it belongs to the outflowed (*sāsrava*) category and is not based on causes.

*Pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) has been explained previously. Furthermore, according to the "Resonant Response" (*Hexiangyan*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) resembles the dharma of *nirvāṇa*;
thus, it is not subsumed under the category of those in training (*śaikṣa*). Since it is not true *nirvāṇa*, it is also not subsumed under the category of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
[Note] The Madhyama Āgama (31) states: A householder asked the Buddha, "How many kinds of fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) are there? The Buddha’s answer is the same as that in the Abhidharmakośa.

Furthermore, according to this, the twenty-seven types of persons—those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—are identical. However, while the *Puṇyavastu-sūtra* lists the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*), the *Abhidharmakośa* does not.

[Commentary] In the *Puṇyavastu-sūtra*, the Buddha said: "In the world, there are two kinds of fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). There are eighteen types of persons in training and [nine] types of persons beyond training."

There are nine types of persons and eighteen learners (*śaikṣa*). These are: those who follow by faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those who follow by dharma (*dharmānusārin*), those liberated by faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*), those who go from family to family (*kulaṅkula*), those with one more seed (*ekavīcika*), those proceeding toward stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*), those who have attained stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), those proceeding toward once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), those who have attained once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), those proceeding toward non-returning (*anāgāmi-pratipannaka*), those who have attained non-returning (*anāgāmin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), those who attain parinirvāṇa with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who attain parinirvāṇa without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*). Above these...

The stream [of those] proceeding to the Akaniṣṭha heaven. There are nine types of non-learners (*aśaikṣa*): namely, the one who contemplates the dharma (*cintā-dharman*), the one who advances (*prativedhanā-dharman*), the immovable one (*akopya-dharman*), the one liable to fall away (*parihāṇa-dharman*), the one not liable to fall away (*aparihāṇa-dharman*), the one who guards the dharma (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*)—who, if guarding, does not fall away, but if not guarding, falls away—the one who abides in the actual state (*sthitākampya-dharman*), and the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*).

"Both-liberated" (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta) refers to the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) listed in the sūtras. As for why this term does not appear in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the text of that treatise states:

"Learners (śaikṣas) refer to the four candidates (pratipannaka), the three fruits (phala), the faith-follower (śraddhānusārin), the dharma-follower (dharmānusārin), the one liberated by faith (śraddhādhimukta), the one attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), the one who goes from family to family (kulaṃkula), the one with only one interval remaining (ekavīcika), and the intermediate [arahant] (antarāparinirvāyin)."

The "born," the "practitioner," the "non-practitioner," and the "one who flows upward" constitute the nine types of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*): namely, the regressive, the protective, the reflective, the abiding, the advancing, and the immovable.
The non-retrogressive, the one liberated by wisdom, and the one liberated both ways—these are what the *Śāstra* mentions; it does not list the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*). [Note:

Regarding the statement that twenty-seven are the same, this is said based on the number twenty-seven; their numerical count is identical, but as for whether the body-witness exists or not, they differ.

[Commentary] "Ordinary" (fán) means constant; it is also termed "worthy" (xián). A "worthy" is one who is good and upright, and is also said to be "adjacent to the sages. Regarding the distinction between internal and external:
those whose realization of principle is similar [to that of the sages] are called internal; those who have not yet attained such a similar understanding are called external.

[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: These seven stages are all neither of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) nor of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). They consist of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), equalizing knowledge (*samatā-jñāna*), and semblance-understanding (*pratirūpa-adhimukti*).

Because they can suppress the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and because this semblance-understanding can give rise to the true illumination of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), they are called "Worthy Ones" (*bhadra*) as they neighbor the state of holiness (*ārya*).
According to our current interpretation, their name signifies "virtuous rectitude. All celestial Māras and ordinary worldlings possess minds of attachment and craving.
Cultivation. All non-Buddhists cultivate with minds of false views; being hypocritical and crooked, it is not called "straight.

The seven types of disciples of the Buddha clearly understand the principle of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing, and they know that both the theory of craving and the theory of views are all crooked.
By subduing this crooked mind of views and craving, they employ a mind of right faith and rectitude to cultivate all wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is so named.

Excellent and direct! Furthermore, all that is expounded by the theory of craving contains the principle of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing, which neither the hosts of celestial Māras nor ordinary worldlings can perceive; therefore, they wander through birth and death.
Moreover, all that is expounded by the theory of views contains the principle of the four noble truths of arising and ceasing, which none of the six heretical teachers can [perceive].
Because they have seen [the truths], they transmigrate through birth and death. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "In the past, I and you did not see the Four Noble Truths;

for this reason, we have long transmigrated in the great ocean of suffering of birth and death. Now, through the seven kinds of understanding born of hearing, we clearly recognize these two kinds of arising and ceasing within the Four Noble Truths;
thus, we attain upright faith, which is precisely what is called 'wholesome uprightness.'"
He is a worthy one (*bhadra*). Furthermore, there are four criteria for discernment: first, one who breaks the precepts while following craving and views is neither upright nor virtuous;

second, one who maintains the precepts and practices meditative concentration yet gives rise to false views is virtuous but not upright; third, one who possesses sincere faith and upright views but breaks the precepts and has a distracted mind is upright but not virtuous—none of these are called "worthy.
Fourth, one whose faith and understanding are authentic and who grasps the intent of the Buddha's teaching is truly worthy.
Maintaining pure ethical discipline and cultivating contemplations such as *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) and the meditation on impurity, one’s mind attains stability;

this is termed "skillful and upright," the stage of the initial noble one (*ārya*), or the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This refers to having a vague, approximate understanding of the principles of the Four Noble Truths, yet not yet seeing them clearly;
such a person is called an outer ordinary person.

△ Second, the explanation of the Dharma received, in two parts. First, the ordinary person (pṛthagjana), in two parts. First, clarifying the outer ordinary person, in two parts. First, the division of sections.
Within the explanation of the outer ordinary person, there are three self-divisions.
△ Second, the enumeration of the dharmas has two parts. First, the dharmas for counteracting the mind; this has two parts. First, the indication of the number.

First, the five *sthāpanā* (stopping the mind). [Note] *Sthāpanā* means "to stop" or "to abide. By practicing these five dharmas, one stops and abides from the five faults. As for the "mind," there are four kinds.
First, grasses and trees; second, the mass of flesh; third, the accumulation of essential elements; fourth, deliberative cognition. Here, it refers to the mind of deliberative cognition.
[Commentary] Grasses and trees are called "mind" because they are able to grow and fall according to the seasons. The mass of flesh is comprised within the category of form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).

Regarding the "accumulation of essential elements," this refers to the *Heart Sūtra*, which contains the essential purport of the Prajñāpāramitā section. The *Prātimokṣa* is called the "mind of precepts" (*śīla-citta*). This is...
The essential text for the formulation of the precepts, as well as Jingxi’s *Ten Gates of Non-duality*, are included among the categories of the "mind of contemplation" (*wénxīn*).
Regarding the "mind of deliberative thought" (*lǜzhī xīn*): while non-Buddhists mostly reckon this as the "self," Buddhism classifies it as the "mind of deliberative thought.
Although the teachings enumerate eight consciousnesses, here it refers specifically to the sixth consciousness as the mind for the contemplative methods of current practice.

[Note] These five *sthāpanā-citta* (stopping the mind) practices apply across all four teachings, as is clearly explained in the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness*. In the fifth fascicle of the *Miaoxuan*, it is stated that the five *sthāpanā-citta* correspond to the five grades of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

In the third fascicle of the *Chanmen*, they are termed the "Five-Gate Meditation" (*pañca-dvāra-dhyāna*), a meaning that encompasses both the Great and Small Vehicles, applies to both ordinary persons and sages, and is practiced by Bodhisattvas and others alike. Currently, however, these are the aids to the path for the Śrāvakas of the Tripitaka teaching.
[Commentary] The five methods of *sthāpanā* (calming the mind) according to the Hīnayāna teachings are as follows. Regarding the method for calming the mind according to the Mahāyāna:

if one has an excess of vitarka and vicāra (applied and sustained thought), one should contemplate that the inhalation does not arise and the exhalation does not cease. Being neither arising nor ceasing, breath is itself emptiness. There is neither a subject who contemplates nor an object of contemplation;
all are unattainable. This unattainability is the truth (*tathatā*). This truth is the stilling of the mind. [This applies to those with] excessive desire...
One should contemplate that desire is neither defilement nor is non-desire purity. Because it is not defilement, it does not arise; because it is not purity, it does not cease.
That which neither arises nor ceases is emptiness. Emptiness is the Real. Because it is the Real, the mind comes to rest. As for those with much anger and resentment:
One should contemplate loving-kindness (*maitrī*) toward loving-kindness; then hatred will neither arise nor cease, as described above.

For one who is deeply attached to a self, one should contemplate the body as being like a butcher’s four quarters of an ox, seeing only the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), and the twelve sense fields (*dvādaśāyatana*).

By asking "In which of the eighteen realms is there a self? one immediately destroys the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*). For the foolish, by contemplating the three periods of time in relation to causes and conditions, one destroys [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism;

by [contemplating] two periods of time, one destroys the self as a recipient of retribution; and by [contemplating] one period of time, one destroys the self as an inherently real entity. Thus, one skillfully employs the five remedies.
The mind then abides in peace; one attains the contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*). Regarding the distinct methods of settling the mind:

the three preceding methods—the counting of breaths (*ānāpāna*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and so forth—settle the mind through matters that are remote and conventional. This method universally settles the mind by contemplating that the breath neither arises nor ceases;

thus, it takes phenomena as they are, approaching the principle closely, intimately, and truly. Now, the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) takes the observance of precepts as its foundation. If I were to remain in the world... [text fragment] ...there would be none.
It is different from this. That which is the Buddha abides in reliance upon this, which is the Sangha. Although this is so, when viewed in relation to the Tripiṭaka, it is esoteric and true;
yet when viewed in relation to the ultimate reality (dharmatā), it is neither proximate nor esoteric, neither true nor rational. It is distinct from what precedes and distinct from what follows.
To dwell between the positions of the youngest and the middle son—this meaning can be understood thereby.

One who is able to uphold the five branches of the various precepts and the ten kinds of precepts explained in the *Śāstra*, possessing within each individual precept such a multitude of dharma-gates, is one who has separately attained *śamatha* (calm abiding).

Since the precepts are the foundation of the Dharma and the source of the Path, one takes the precepts as the basis for *śamatha*. Thus, [the text] correlates the five *śamatha*-abidings with [the five precepts].

The five grades are explained in detail below in the nine-fascicle *Complete Teaching* (Yuanjiao). Regarding the statement that the Chan school designates the "stilling of the mind" as the Five Gates of Chan and so forth, the text says:
"Although the five gates are few, their practice extends through all forms of dhyāna. First is the gate of ānāpāna."

1. This [contemplation] extends to the fundamental dhyānas, the special dhyānas (*viśeṣa-dhyāna*), the dhyānas of universal clarity (*samantaprabhāsa*), and various other meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).

It also encompasses the two gates of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): namely, the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the serial attainments (*abhibhvāyatana*). It further extends to all such meditative absorptions. 2. The third is the gate of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*).

This extends to the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) and all such meditative absorptions. 3. The fourth is the gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This extends as far as the twelve links of dependent origination.

The practice of wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths and so forth, the various *dhyānas* and *samādhis*, and the five gates of mindfulness of the Buddha—these extend to the nine grades of *dhyāna* and the one hundred and eight *samādhis*.
Furthermore, first, the gate of counting the breaths is the mundane *dhyāna* of ordinary worldlings;
next, the gate of impurity is the supramundane *dhyāna* practiced by *śrāvakas*; next, the gate of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) pertains to both the ordinary and the holy.

These two constitute great merit and virtue; by cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they enter the immeasurable states of mind. Next is the gate of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-mukha*); this is the practice of the *pratyekabuddhas*.
Next is the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti-mukha*); its merit is vast and great, and it is the practice of the multitude of *bodhisattvas*.
This briefly clarifies the sequence and the relative depth of these five gates.

[Note] Greed and so forth are the objects; impurity is the contemplation. The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), fascicle 2, part 4, states: "Once the mind is stabilized, one may then practice contemplation.
It is like a lamp in a sealed room; there is nothing that surpasses these five dharmas as the foundation for entering the Path" (text).

[Commentary] This contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is called an effective antidote (*pratipakṣa-dharma*) for desire (*rāga*). However, regarding the affliction of hatred (*dveṣa*), it is not called an effective antidote.

Because observing the defects of the body is termed the "contemplation of impurity," if one observes the defects of the body while afflicted by hatred, it will instead increase that hatred. Other objects of observation should be understood by this same principle. [The four teachings.]

The Commentary states: There are three stages in the cultivation of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing): first, the initial practice; second, the practiced stage; and third, the stage of having transcended through contemplation.
First, counting (*gaṇanā*) is the initial practice. Second, following (*anugama*) is the practiced stage. Third, observing (*upalakṣaṇā*) is the stage of having transcended.

Furthermore, counting, following, and observing are all termed "initial practice. Attaining the three types of *anāgamya-samādhi* (threshold concentration) of the desire realm is termed "the practiced stage."
The arising of the various first dhyānas is called "having crossed over. The remaining impurity contemplations (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth are also to be distinguished in this same way.
Once the mind is properly balanced, one may then practice contemplation, like a lamp in a sealed room. There is no method for entering the Path that surpasses these five dharmas.

【□Note】 Some say that the five *sthāpanā-cittas* (stopping the mind) derive from wisdom (*prajñā*), while others say they derive from concentration (*samādhi*). Because concentration and wisdom are balanced and harmonized, they are called "stopping the mind" (*sthāpanā*).

[Commentary] However, regarding the sequence listed above, *Xixuan* places the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) first; this is based on the order of the three unwholesome roots (*akuśala-mūla*).
The fourth section, which clarifies the contemplation of analyzing the elements (*dhātu-vibhanga*), is explained after the unwholesome roots.
The fifth section, which clarifies counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), is explained after the afflictions (*kleśa*), because distraction (*vikṣepa*) is a secondary affliction (*upakleśa*).

[Commentary] There are three unwholesome [roots]. This is because they rely upon the three fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*) of greed, hatred, and delusion. First is impurity; second is loving-kindness and compassion;

third is the causal conditions. Furthermore, since the attachment to a self is distinguished by means of the three unwholesome roots, the analysis of the elements (*dhātuvibhaṅga*) is established as the fourth.
Since distraction (*vikṣepa*) is an secondary affliction (*upakleśa*), the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) treats it after the fundamental delusions.
[Regarding this:

In texts such as the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings), the practice of counting the breath (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) is placed at the beginning because those who cultivate meditation must first restrain their scattered thoughts and enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
The second fascicle of the *Sìjiàoyì* states: "Now, following the *Chánmén* (Gate of Meditation), I shall distinguish the sequence; for illness [arises] first..."
The subsequent sequence follows the person; it is not necessary to rigidly adhere to a fixed order of priority.
[Commentary] Question: Why does one not rely on the Sāṃkhya school’s teaching that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) comes first? Answer:
Here, we follow the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate) to distinguish the sequence.

[Note] Furthermore, regarding why various texts specifically place the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) at the beginning, the *Myōryaku-ki* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 6, citing the *Abhidharmakośa*, states:
"There are two essential gateways for entering the Path: the meditation on impurity and mindfulness of breathing."

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "There are two essential gateways for entering cultivation: the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Those in whom desire (*rāga*) or discursive thought (*vitarka*) predominates should practice accordingly.
The prose commentary explains: "The essentials for correctly entering the gateway of cultivation are twofold: first, the contemplation of impurity; second, mindfulness of breathing.
Whichever gateway one follows that enables correct entry into cultivation, it should be understood according to the sequence [of the respective afflictions], such as desire..."
Regarding "increasing vitarka": this refers to when greed is intense and frequently manifests before one. A sentient being in such a state is called a "greed-practitioner" (*rāga-carita*);
they can correctly enter into cultivation by contemplating the foul (*aśubha*). One whose mind is greatly distracted by vitarka is called a "vitarka-practitioner" (*vitarka-carita*);

they can correctly enter into cultivation by relying on mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). Thus, one should know that in various texts, either the contemplation of the foul or mindfulness of breathing is taken as the primary method.
This means administering medicine according to the illness.

[Commentary] Regarding the mutual presence and absence of the analysis of the realms (*dhātu*) and the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*): In the second (fourth) question of the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings), it asks:

"Why is the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* not explained here as being of five kinds? The answer is: "Because the analysis of the realms serves as a skillful means (*upāya*) that replaces [the samādhi], emerging from the context of causes and conditions. Realm.
The skillful means (*upāya*) is identical to the mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) of the Hīnayāna. It also destroys the obstacle of the compulsion of the objective realm (*viṣaya*).

(Because both the causes and conditions of the two periods and the skillful means regarding the realms [all serve to] destroy attachment to a self; although the means of destruction differ, that which is destroyed is the same. Therefore, by hearing the causes and conditions of the two periods, one destroys attachment to the self and departs from the realm; thus, this serves as a substitute for mindfulness of the Buddha.

Furthermore, how can the skillful means regarding the realms serve as a substitute for mindfulness of the Buddha? Therefore, the text immediately explains below: because the characteristics of what is destroyed by the skillful means regarding the realms are identical to the characteristics of the objective realm destroyed by mindfulness of the Buddha; since both do not transcend the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*) and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), mindfulness of the Buddha destroys the compulsion of the objective realm.
[This refers to] the obstruction of compulsion; the "expedient means of analyzing the realms" (*dhātu-pravicaya-upāya*) likewise involves deconstruction.

[Supplement] This section analyzes and distinguishes between the two contemplations of analyzing the realms and mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). It intends to show that by employing one, the other may be set aside. First, I shall clarify the meaning of the Four Teachings.
Regarding the use of the expedient means of analyzing the realms to destroy attachment to the self: "analyzing the realms" means dividing them into the six realms (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*).
The characteristics of the eighteen realms are presented to reveal non-self (*anātman*). In the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), the response to a question states:

"By means of the causes and conditions of the two periods [past and future], one breaks attachment to a self. This is the expedient for transcending the realms. By breaking the obstructive barriers of oppression, one replaces mindfulness of the Buddha;
therefore, mindfulness of the Buddha is not employed. Thus, it is known that the analysis of the realms can destroy attachment to a self and can destroy oppression, as is the case today.

The opening of the text: [The practitioner] uses the causes and conditions of the two periods to destroy attachment to the self, and uses mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*) to destroy oppression; therefore, there is no need for the skillful means (*upāya*) of the realms (*dhātu*).

One may observe the skillful means of the realms, which, when regressing, can substitute for the causes and conditions of the two periods, and when progressing, can substitute for mindfulness of the Buddha.

Thus, in the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) and the *Sìniànchù* (Four Foundations of Mindfulness), the skillful means of the realms are retained while mindfulness of the Buddha is omitted. In the *Míxuán* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), it is simply "stopping" (*śamatha*).
In the current text, while the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (nienfo) is preserved, the "expedient means regarding realms" (jie fangbian) is omitted.

Furthermore, the reason why the expedient means regarding realms is identical to the mindfulness of the Buddha in the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is that when one contemplates the true emptiness of the Dharmakāya according to the Lesser Vehicle, it is quiescent and unconditioned;

thus, there are no characteristics of the six ordinary realms to be apprehended. When analyzing the realms, one contemplates the triad of sense organs, objects, and consciousness, which ultimately do not exist.

In essence, since no characteristic of a self (*ātman*) can be found within the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), it is said that their characteristics are identical. [Appendix] Regarding the two periods of destroying attachment to the self:
below the section on "contemplating the Buddha to destroy and suppress obstacles," this is explained in detail within the contemplation of mindfulness through causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

One must know that for those whose attachment to the self is heavy, one should specifically employ the skillful means of opening up the realms (*dhātu*) as the remedy, which concurrently treats the suppression of obstacles. If, however, the suppression of obstacles is heavy while attachment to the self is light...

For those of lesser capacity, the specific remedy is exclusively the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*). Within the context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the two temporal conditions destroy attachment to a self;
thus, attachment to a self is subsumed within the contemplation of dependent origination and thereby shattered. All of these are applied according to what is appropriate for each individual.

[Note] Furthermore, regarding the single question on the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*): why does this section not mention "stabilizing the mind by recollecting the Buddha" (*buddhānusmṛti*)?

Answer: It is not required when operating through the gateway of the five perfections (*pañca-pāramitā*); it is required when operating through the gateway of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). This is because the causal conditions naturally correspond to the [four] equal parts (*catur-vibhāga*): [the natures of] reality, annihilationism, eternalism, and attachment to self.
All three of these possess [these qualities]; therefore, they are called "equal parts" (*sabhāga*). Regarding the text "Mindfulness of the Buddha counters the obstacle of oppression":

this clarifies that while the *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundations of mindfulness) exist as skillful means within the realms, the intent of mindfulness of the Buddha is submerged. The original note states "equal parts. The *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) says:
"Delusion is countered by the contemplation of causes and conditions; one lifetime breaks through the nature of reality, and two lifetimes break through retribution."
The self (*ātman*) is the destruction of the three periods of time and the severance of permanence and annihilation; therefore, it is said to be "co-existent with its own category" (*sabhāga*).

[Supplement] This refers to delusion as the co-existent category. Since these three—clinging to a self, permanence, and annihilation—are all essentially delusion, they constitute the causal conditions for the practice of the Six Perfections.
Because the illness involves all three types simultaneously, it is called "co-existent"; thus, causal conditions are indispensable.

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan* (7.17) states: "The *Abhidharma* uses the skillful means of the *dhātus* to dismantle the notion of self (that is, observing and dismantling the six and eighteen *dhātus*)," as explained in the *Fuxing* (7a).
[Commentary] Master Zhiyi’s *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: Regarding the *Abhidharma*’s use of the analysis of the *dhātus* (elements) to refute the self (*ātman*):

the self, the views of annihilationism and eternalism, and the notion of an intrinsic nature—these three are all categorized under delusion (*moha*). First, concerning the refutation of the self, the various sūtras and śāstras differ in their explanations; the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: [text follows].

For one who practices by means of views, through the method of the elements (*dhātu*), the fool fails to understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are accumulated through past karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the conditions, he conceives of a self within his own person. By means of the method of the elements, he contemplates the various natures, various karmas, and various characteristics—namely, the six elements such as earth and so forth.
The earth element is moistened by the water element, yet they are not separate from one another. Water...
Because it is sustained by the element of earth, it does not disperse; because of the element of fire, it is matured, and thus does not decay;
because of the element of wind, it moves and attains growth; because of the element of space, food can enter and exit; and because of the element of consciousness, there is volitional activity.
Through these various conditions, one knows that there is no self. Furthermore, one contemplates this body as being filled with impurities, like a bellows being blown.

One scatters the accumulated sand. Regarding formless phenomena (*ārūpya-dharma*) that continue in succession from before to after, one who contemplates in this way obtains the seed of the liberation door of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
Becoming weary of them, one obtains the seed of the liberation door of wishlessness (*apranihita-vimokṣamukha*) and proceeds directly toward nirvāṇa.
Obtaining the seeds for the gate of liberation through signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is called the skillful means regarding the elements (*dhātu-upāya*).

As stated in the Mahāyāna sūtras, for those who are excessively attached to a self, the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are analyzed. This [analysis] distinguishes between the general and specific aspects of the six elements and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The discussion of the ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) accounts for half of them; the discussion of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) accounts for half of the seven mental elements (*citta-dhātu*). Thus, matter is merely combined [into a single category].

Fourth: combining the mind into one and further adding the element of space (*ākāśa*). These teachings vary in their inclusion or exclusion according to the capacities of sentient beings (*yathābhavyatā*).

Now, following the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, the self is refuted through causes and conditions; the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* likewise refutes the self through two periods. To distinguish between these, both are listed and explained here.
[Note] The antidotes differ; they are now illustrated in a diagram.

[Commentary] Regarding the six types of antidotes for *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: first, as for the "antidote," this refers to a portion of afflictions (*kleśa*). There are three such portions, which together constitute twelve.
Corresponding to these, there are likewise twelve antidotes. This is called an "antidote" because it is like setting up a military formation to confront an enemy.

Second, regarding "transformative treatment" (*parivṛtti-pratipakṣa*): for example, while the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is an antidote to sensual desire (*rāga*), it is not appropriate [for everyone]; one should instead attain liberation through the contemplation of purity (*śubha-bhāvanā*).

One should transform the practice by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), mindful that one is to be settled in the bliss of pure dharmas; how could one further subject them to defilement and humiliation? This is called transformative treatment.

If one teaches the contemplation of impurity to a person prone to anger, or teaches the meditation on the finite and infinite to a person prone to delusion (*moha*), or teaches the application [of mindfulness] to one who is agitated and distracted—[these are examples of inappropriate application].
Through the discernment of wisdom, one understands that while this illness changes, the treatment does not change; both are termed "changing treatment.

If both the medicine and the illness change, this is also called "changing treatment," and it is likewise a form of counteractive therapy (*pratipakṣa*). Regarding the three types of "unchanging treatment": although the illness changes, the treatment never changes.
One simply applies this specific method and cultivates this specific treatment; because the treatment remains unchanging even as the illness changes, it is called "unchanging."

1. Treatment by a single method; 2. Treatment by two methods; 3. Treatment by three methods; 4. Treatment by four combined methods; 5. Treatment by all five methods combined. Regarding the fourth, "treatment by four combined methods": when a disease is combined with a remedy, both are combined.

For example, if greed is combined with anger, one must employ the meditation on impurity while simultaneously maintaining a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). When the diseases are combined in pairs or threes, the remedies are likewise combined in pairs or threes; this is called "combined treatment. Fifth is "treatment by all [five] methods combined."

Employing the aforementioned methods together to treat a single ailment is called the "Small Vehicle" (Hīnayāna) approach, which first employs the five remedies and subsequently uses the knowledge of the Truths (satya-jñāna) to enter the Real.
The "Great Vehicle" (Mahāyāna) approach treats the illness by means of that which is neither dualistic nor cumulative;

this is termed the "Remedy of the Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha-cikitsā), like the Agada medicine, which translates as "removing what has adhered," for it removes all manner of ailments. The Small Vehicle primarily employs three [remedies].

The *siddhānta* serves as the remedy. In the Mahāyāna, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is most frequently employed as the remedy. Regarding the five remedies according to the meaning of the four teachings (*catur-yāna-artha*), it is asked:

"Do these five gates of contemplation correspond to five types of persons, or do they correspond to a single person? The answer is: "Horizontally, they correspond to five persons; vertically, they constitute a single person.
Depending on the extent of the afflictions, the correspondence is not fixed. These five kinds of contemplative methods serve as remedies for the five [afflictions].

Regarding unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*), there are five points: first, pairing; second, turning away; third, not turning away; fourth, combining; and fifth, both pairing, turning away, and not turning away, as well as combining. First, regarding "pairing" (*pratipakṣa*):

when discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are excessive, one practices mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*). When sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is excessive, one practices the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

When ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is excessive, one practices loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*). When delusion (*moha*) is excessive, one practices the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). [One also practices this] when attached to a self (*ātman*).

Much. One should cultivate the skillful means of the elements (*dhātu*). If a practitioner’s discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are in equal measure, and their afflictions (*kleśa*) predominate such that they cannot remain focused, they should practice counting the breaths (*gaṇanā*).
By practicing mindfulness of the breath (*ānāpānasmṛti*) in accordance with the appropriate remedy, the three types of afflictions associated with discursive thought and investigation will cease.

The mind will no longer be agitated or distracted, and various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) will arise. Sustained by these methods of concentration, the mind will enter and emerge from them with stability and ease; therefore—
This is called the "stopping of the mind" (*cittasthāpana*). The *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) states: "These five gates of stopping further have five meanings:

namely, 'confronting' (*pratipakṣa*), 'turning away' (*parāvṛtti*), 'not turning away,' 'combined,' and 'both confronting and turning away,' 'both not turning away and combined. Regarding "confronting": counting the breath confronts discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*);

likewise, the application of means (*upāya*) confronts the self; and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) confronts ignorance (*moha*). When the remedy (*pratipakṣa*) is perfected, the afflictions (*kleśa*) do not arise. Furthermore, it gives rise to...

Dhyāna-concentration. One maintains the mind through dhyāna-concentration, entering and emerging from it with composure. Once the mind is thus balanced and settled, one may then practice contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

If the application of the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) has not yet brought benefit, one must further employ the latter four types of remedies. The practitioner skillfully employs the four kinds of "following" (*anuvartana*).
Skillfully cultivating the five remedies, afflictions cannot create obstacles. When the observation of the mind comes to rest, one immediately enters the stage of the first noble person (*ārya*).

This is explained in detail in the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Dhyāna). Furthermore, the two-fascicle [version] states: "If one skillfully employs the five remedies to govern the mind, the mind will then abide in peace."

One attains the contemplation of non-arising; when non-arising manifests before one, one immediately destroys the afflictions. Being straightforward and virtuous, this is called the first stage of the noble ones (ārya).
The three types of understanding and vision are explained below.
△ Second, the five methods for enumerating the teachings. First, the method for subduing greed through contemplation:
1. The contemplation of impurity for sentient beings with excessive greed.
[Note] Because the deluded mind of the six consciousnesses gives rise to insatiability toward objects that accord with its desires, they are said to have "excessive greed. (From the *Chanmen*)
Fourth, the explanation of the three types of craving: first, external craving, which is the mutual attachment to the physical bodies of men and women;

this is treated by means of the nine contemplations (contemplating the bodies of others). The nine contemplations are: (1) bloated, (2) livid, (3) putrefied, (4) blood-stained, (5) festering, (6) devoured, (7) scattered, (8) bleached bones, and (9) burned.

[Commentary] The Chan Gate clarifies: When a practitioner is cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if thoughts of greed arise—whether a man takes a woman as his object or a woman takes a man as her object, grasping at their physical appearance, features, deportment, and speech—then the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the mind arise, remaining unsettled from moment to moment.
This is the manifestation of the external fetter of lustful greed. To treat this with the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*), [one contemplates] the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

The sequence is as follows: First is the visualization of the bloated corpse. One contemplates a dead person’s bloated body, which is like a leather bag filled with wind, having changed from its original appearance.
Second is the visualization of the livid corpse. One contemplates the skin and flesh of a dead person, which has become yellowish-red, mottled black, or bluish-green.

3. The perception of disintegration (*vibhava-saṃjñā*): One contemplates a dead person being blown by the wind and scorched by the sun, until they become increasingly torn and broken, lying upon the ground.
4. The perception of blood-stained spreading (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*): One contemplates a dead person with pus and blood flowing everywhere, overflowing and spreading as a foul stain over the ground.

5. The perception of festering (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*): One contemplates a corpse from which worms and blood flow out, the skin and flesh rotting away and pooling upon the ground. 6. [The perception of worm-infested (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*)...]

7. The Contemplation of Devouring (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*): One contemplates a corpse being devoured by worms and maggots; its eyes pecked at by birds; and it chewed upon by foxes and dogs, while tigers and wolves tear it apart with their claws. 8. The Contemplation of Dispersal (*vidhūta-saṃjñā*):
One contemplates a corpse torn apart by birds and beasts, its physical form shattered and mangled, its tendons severed and bones separated, with head and hands scattered in all directions.
9. The Contemplation of the Skeleton (*asthi-saṃjñā*): One contemplates a dead person whose skin and flesh have completely vanished, leaving only the white [bones].
The bones and sinews remain connected, or they are scattered and strewn about like shells or white jade.

Ninth is the contemplation of burning: one observes a corpse being consumed by fire, crackling and emitting smoke and stench; when the fuel is exhausted, the form is extinguished, becoming identical to ashes and dust.

Even if it were not burned, it would likewise return to extinction. Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "These nine [contemplations] generally remedy the afflictions of the six desire realms; if applied specifically, [they remedy specific objects]."

[The first] is the contemplation of the corpse as a treatment for the desire for deportment and speech. [The next three—] bloated, festering, and being devoured—are treatments for the desire for form.
[The next three—] blood-stained, pus-filled and putrid, and livid—are treatments for the desire for color. [The next two—] skeletal and cremated—are treatments for the desire for smoothness.
Furthermore, the nine visualizations collectively treat the desire for the person one is attached to; they disperse the desire for human characteristics and can move the ninety-eight [afflictions].
The "Mountain" (Śaila) Samādhi is therefore the most powerful among those to be cultivated.

[Commentary] Second, internal and external greed: one gives rise to craving and attachment toward others and toward one's own body. This is countered by means of the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*). (First, because one contemplates the skeleton-chain of the internal body, one is able to counteract internal [greed]).

[Commentary] The *Chanmen* (Gate of Meditation) states: When a practitioner is cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if the desire-mind is stirred—whether by taking as an object the physical forms, appearances, gestures, or deportment of external men or women, thereby giving rise to greedy attachment;

or again, by taking as an object one's own physical form and appearance, such as stroking the head or wiping the neck, becoming stained and attached in every thought, thereby giving rise to greedy craving that obstructs all meditative concentrations—this is the internal [obstruction].

Regarding the manifestation of external desire for sensual pleasure and its treatment through the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the *Fajie Cidi* states: First, "possessing internal forms while perceiving external forms.

This means that "possessing internal forms" refers to not destroying or extinguishing the internal perception of form, and "perceiving external forms" refers to not destroying or extinguishing the external perception of form. By means of this mind of impurity, one contemplates external forms.
This being so, because the practitioner is cultivating the radiance of light, they should not destroy the internal skeleton within the first liberation (aśubha-vimokṣa).
Since the fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm are difficult to sever, it is necessary to contemplate external forms with a mind focused on impurity.
This is the first liberation (*vimokṣa*). Its stage is the first dhyāna. Because it is able to relinquish both self and others, as well as the lower stages, it is called "liberation.
Second is "internally having no perception of form, one perceives forms externally. "Internally having no perception of form" means the destruction of internal perceptions of form.
"Perceives forms externally" means not destroying external perceptions of form. One contemplates the external with this mind of impurity.

Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): The reason for this is that because the practitioner, in order to enter the internal purity of the second dhyāna, has destroyed the perception of the internal skeleton-person (*asthika-puruṣa*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the desire realm are difficult to sever;
therefore, they still contemplate the signs of external impurity. The third liberation through purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*) is realized by the body.
This is called "purity" because it takes purity as its object; thus, the practitioner sets aside the signs of external impurity and [contemplates only]...

Within meditative concentration, one refines the eightfold light of form, which is pure, brilliant, and like the color of a wondrous jewel; this is called the "perfection of purity" (*śubha-vimokṣa*).
One who realizes it with the body experiences the pervasive bliss of the third dhyāna with a mind free from attachment.

The fourth is the "liberation of the sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*), which refers to the cessation of the fundamental fourth dhyāna, as well as the [preceding] three liberations and the four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Entering into the sphere of all-pervading form, one focuses the mind on infinite space and enters meditative absorption.
One then contemplates this absorption as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self by virtue of its dependence upon the aggregates, bases, and elements;

seeing it as deceptive and unreal, the mind develops revulsion and detachment, neither grasping nor clinging, entering deeply and without regression. This is the liberation through turning away from the sphere of the five consciousnesses. If one relinquishes space, [one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness].

With a single mind taking consciousness as its object, at the moment of entering meditative absorption, one contemplates this very absorption as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, based upon the aggregates, bases, and elements;
it is deceptive and unreal. Thus, the mind gives rise to revulsion and turns away from it, neither grasping nor clinging, entering deeply without regression.
This is the liberation through turning away from the sphere of nothingness. If one relinquishes consciousness, with a single mind taking "nothingness" as the object, one enters meditative absorption.
At that time, one contemplates this meditative absorption (samādhi) by way of the aggregates (skandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).

Seeing it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, as deceptive and unreal, the mind gives rise to revulsion and turns away from it, neither grasping nor clinging to it. One enters deeply and does not turn back. This is the seventh liberation (vimokṣa):

the liberation of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Having relinquished the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), one single-mindedly takes the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as one's object.

When entering meditative absorption, one contemplates this very absorption as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self by way of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Seeing it as deceptive and unreal, the mind gives rise to revulsion and detachment, neither grasping nor clinging to it, entering deeply without turning back. Eighth is the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*);
by turning away from sensation, perception, and all mental states and their concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), this is called the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception.

"Relinquishment. Why is this? Because the disciples of the Buddhas loathe a distracted mind and desire to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*) for rest, taking the dharma of *nirvāṇa* and fixing it within their minds;
therefore, it is said that they "realize it with the body" and that "feeling and perception cease. [Supplement] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"To turn one's back on these pure five desires and to relinquish this attached mind is called 'turning away' (*vairāgya*)."

[Note] Third, greed for all places and objects of livelihood, such as the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). This is treated by means of the Great Impurity Meditation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which is equivalent to the Eight Stages of Mastery (*aṣṭa-abhibhv-āyatana*).

Because one gradually perceives the environment and its inhabitants in the ten directions based on the visualization of the skeleton of one's own body, one is able to treat the greed of both oneself and others.
[Commentary] The Chan Gate says: This person is attached to internal and external things as previously described.

Furthermore, regarding all objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*), material goods, and so forth, they give rise to craving and attachment; or they crave fields, gardens, houses, clothing, food, and drink.
Regarding the manifestation of greed arising in all places, its remedy is the contemplation of great impurity (*mahā-aśubha-bhāvanā*).
As the *Mahā-śāstra* explains the treatment for greed regarding food and drink: "Contemplate this food as arising from impure causes and conditions;

just as meat arises from semen, blood, and the urinary tract, it is called the dwelling place of pus and worms. Like ghee, milk, and curd, it is formed by the transformation of blood and is like putrid pus."
There is no difference. The kitchen staff's sweat and various impurities, if they enter the mouth, mix with the putrid saliva in the brain that flows down through the channels;
this combines with the spittle and then forms flavor. Its appearance is like vomit as it enters through the gateway of the abdomen.
The earth supports it, water softens it, wind moves it, and fire cooks it, like rice being boiled in a cauldron until it becomes a thick mash. The dregs and turbidity sink to the bottom;
the turbid portion becomes feces, and the clear portion becomes urine. There are three apertures at the waist through which the wind blows the oily essence, dispersing it into the hundred vessels.
This combines with the prior blood, coagulating and transforming into flesh. From this new flesh, fat, marrow, and bone are produced; from within these, the body arises.
Roots: From the union of new and old flesh, the five sense organs arise. From these five organs, the five consciousnesses arise.

Following the sequence of the five consciousnesses, the mental consciousness arises, which discriminates and grasps at signs, deliberates upon the beautiful and the ugly, and subsequently gives rise to the notions of "I" and "mine," as well as various afflictions and sinful karmas.
Thus one contemplates the fundamental and derivative causes and conditions of food. This is the first seed.
It is of various impurities. One knows that the four internal elements are no different from the four external elements;
it is only because of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) that one forcibly claims them as "mine. Furthermore, contemplate this food:

it is produced through the heavy labor of plowing, sowing, weeding, harvesting, threshing, grinding, winnowing, cooking, and boiling. Calculating for even a single bowl of rice, it is the sweat of many laborers.
Gathered together in measure, food is little while sweat is much; thus the labor expended in producing it is great.
Yet, once it enters the mouth and is consumed, it immediately becomes impure and is of no value whatsoever. Within a single night, it transforms into excrement and urine.
Originally a delicious food, it was something people relished; now transformed into impurity, it is loathsome and one does not wish to see it.
The practitioner reflects: "If I were to crave such vile food, I would fall into hell and have to swallow glowing iron balls.
Emerging from hell, I would become an animal—a cow, sheep, camel, or perhaps a pig or dog—to repay my past debts. Constantly...
"Eating excrement" removes [the craving for food]. By contemplating food in this way, one gives rise to the perception of revulsion; thus, one becomes weary of all five desires.

Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭau abhibhvāyatanāni*), the *Dharmadhātu-śāstra* states: "First, internally perceiving forms, one externally perceives forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called 'mastery of knowledge and mastery of vision. As for 'internally perceiving forms, one externally perceives forms that are few,' it is so named because the objects of focus are few."

"Less. If one's contemplation of the path has not yet increased, it is necessary to contemplate the causes and conditions of the "less. Contemplating the "many" involves fear and difficulty in maintaining focus;

the transformation does not accord with the mind. It is like contemplating the "less": among beautiful and ugly phenomena, one contemplates impurity, attaining mastery over transformation, penetrating without obstruction, having no grasping or rejecting in the mind, and giving rise to neither love nor hatred. Second, internally perceiving the sign of form while externally contemplating [form].

Forms are manifold—whether beautiful or ugly—this is called superior knowledge and superior vision. Regarding the phrase "having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as manifold":

they are called "manifold" because one contemplates their manifold causes and conditions. Once the mind has been disciplined through contemplation, there is no hindrance to contemplating the manifold.

If, amidst many beautiful or ugly impure objects, one transforms them with mastery, attains unimpeded penetration, and the mind neither grasps nor rejects, giving rise to neither attachment nor aversion—this is it.
Third, being internally without the perception of form, one perceives forms externally as limited, whether beautiful or ugly;
this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision. This refers to being internally without the perception of form, as in the second liberation, while perceiving externally.
The forms are few, whether beautiful or ugly; all are as in the first *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery). Fourth:
internally perceiving no sign of form, one externally perceives many forms, whether beautiful or ugly; this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.

That is to say, internally perceiving no sign of form—just as in the two *vimokṣas* (liberations)—one externally perceives many forms, whether beautiful or ugly; all are as in the second *abhibhvāyatana*. Fifth.
The Blue Sphere of Mastery (*nīlābhivimokṣa*). This refers to when one contemplates blue, up to its radiance, which surpasses what is seen in the [blue] liberation (*vimokṣa*);

furthermore, one does not give rise to craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*) regarding the perceived sign of blue. It is the mastery of transformation, wherein the few can become many and the many can become few;
this luminous color is called the Blue Sphere of Mastery. The six Yellow Spheres of Mastery, the seven Red Spheres of Mastery, and the eight White Spheres of Mastery are all analogous.
As analyzed in the section on the "Blue Excellent Object" (*nīla-uddeśa*), four colors are now employed as the excellent objects (*abhibhvāyatana*). This is based on the *Mahā-śāstra*.

However, in the *Ratna-ketu-pariṇāma-sūtra*, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are taken as the four excellent objects. Regarding the phrase "due to one's own body and so forth," the *Mahā-śāstra* states:
"For example, it is like a master of illusions who, observing the illusory objects created by himself, knows they have issued from him and thus no attachment arises in his mind."
When one is able not to follow after the objects of perception, at that time the "liberation" (vimokṣa) changes its name to "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
Although it is superior to the pure contemplation (*śubha-vipaśyanā*), it has not yet become vast. At this time, the practitioner again takes up the sign of purity;

by means of the power of liberation and the power of the spheres of mastery, they take up the sign of the pure earth, which gradually fills the empty space of the ten directions, as do water, fire, and wind.
Thus, one takes the mark of blue and gradually causes it to expand until it pervades the empty space of the ten directions. Yellow and white are treated in the same manner.

Second, the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion for sentient beings with excessive anger.

[Note] When one harbors persistent resentment toward objects that provoke aversion, this is termed "excessive anger. The Buddha instructed that one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion.
This can be countered. [Commentary:

Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is able to bestow happiness; compassion (*karuṇā*) is able to extract suffering. Since one still desires to bestow happiness and extract suffering, how could one cause others to fall into suffering and affliction?
[Commentary] If one follows the second of the four meanings of the Chan Gate that apply to the Mahāyāna, there are three types of object-contemplation (*ālambana-vipaśyanā*):

first, irrational anger (sudden outbursts of anger regardless of the circumstances). One should cultivate the *maitrī* based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), regarding all sentient beings as one's own kinsmen.

[Commentary] Regarding the Zen tradition’s clarification of anger arising from irrationality: When a practitioner is cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if a thought of anger suddenly arises—regardless of whether it is justified or not, and irrespective of whether another has committed an offense or not—one becomes angry without cause. This is the characteristic of the manifestation of irrational, deviant anger.

As for one who cultivates the "compassion based on sentient beings" (*sattvālambanā maitrī*), they contemplate all sentient beings with the thought that they are like their own parents, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding the compassion that takes sentient beings as its object (*sattvālambana-maitrī*): one regards the sentient beings of the five destinies throughout the ten directions with a single mind of loving-kindness, as if they were one's parents, brothers, children, nephews, or close friends, constantly seeking what is good for them and desiring to bring them benefit, profit, and peace.

Such compassion is called "taking sentient beings as its object" and is mostly practiced by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) or by those in training (*śaikṣa*) who have not yet exhausted their outflows (*āsrava*).

[Commentary] Second, anger that accords with principle (*yoniśas-krodha*). (When a person actually comes to disturb me,) one practices the "object-conditioned loving-kindness" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), seeing that all phenomena arise from conditions.

[Commentary] Regarding the Chan school’s clarification that anger arises from following [deluded] principles: when a practitioner is cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if an external person actually comes to provoke or disturb them,
and they give rise to a thought of anger that continues without ceasing— just as a person who upholds the precepts may give rise to hatred upon seeing one who acts contrary to the Dharma—
the Mahāyāna teaches that although there are no false [perceptions] in the pure Buddha-lands...

Regarding "poisons," there are indeed the three primary poisons. As for "compassion with respect to phenomena" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that one perceives all phenomena as arising from conditions.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that Arhats who have exhausted all outflows (*āsrava*) and Pratyekabuddhas have destroyed the mark of a self (*ātman*).
Having extinguished the characteristics of identity and difference, one contemplates only the continuity from causes and conditions.
When various desirous thoughts arise, one observes that they are produced from the continuity of combined causes and conditions; it is merely the five aggregates that constitute a "sentient being.

One contemplates these five aggregates with loving-kindness toward sentient beings, yet remains unaware that the five skandhas are empty of self-nature, maintaining this single-minded focus at all times.

When sentient beings desire to obtain happiness, the Noble Ones take pity on them and cause them to obtain happiness according to their wishes; because this pertains to worldly dharmas, it is called "compassion with a dharma-object" (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

[Note] Third, regarding anger arising from disputes (clinging to one's own understanding as correct and asserting that the actions of others are wrong): one cultivates "unconditioned compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*)—the compassion in which subject and object are of one essence is precisely unconditioned.

[Commentary] Regarding those who provoke disputes through anger as clarified in the Chan Gate: If a practitioner, while practicing meditation, becomes attached to the doctrines they themselves understand, deeming them correct and asserting that the practices and teachings of others are incorrect, they will give rise to a mind of resentment whenever these views do not accord with their own.

There are people in the world who, even when their wealth and possessions are encroached upon, are still able to remain patient; yet over a slight matter of doctrinal principle, they immediately engage in dispute.
This immediately gives rise to great resentment; this is called the characteristic of anger arising from contentious debate.

Regarding "objectless compassion" (*apratihata-maitrī*), the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies that it does not dwell upon the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) nor the characteristics of sentient beings (*sattva-lakṣaṇa*). The *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that this compassion exists only in the Buddhas.

Why is this? Because the Buddhas do not dwell within the nature of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), they do not rely upon the three periods of time, and they know that all conditions are unreal.

Because it is inverted and deceptive, the mind has no object of focus. Since sentient beings do not know the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena and thus wander through the five realms of existence, their minds become attached to phenomena, engaging in discrimination, grasping, and rejecting. Therefore, by means of this true reality of all phenomena, the Buddha causes sentient beings to attain it;
hence, it is called "objectless compassion" (*anālambana-maitrī*).
[Note] This is now the auxiliary contemplation of the Hīnayāna, corresponding to the first of those [four immeasurables], the "compassion based on sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).

If following the *Fajie Cidian* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm), it would fully clarify all four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; here, however, only loving-kindness and compassion are treated.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Dharmadhātu" (the realm of phenomena): these four are collectively termed "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) because they derive their name from their objects.

Since the sentient beings who are the objects of focus (*ālambana*) are immeasurable, the minds that take them as objects are likewise immeasurable; therefore, they all receive the name "immeasurable minds. Compassion (*karuṇā*) and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) have already been explained previously.

As for joy (*muditā*): it is the arising of a mind of delight upon celebrating the happiness attained by others; thus it is called "joy. As for equanimity (*upekṣā*): [it is the state of impartiality].

If one takes others as the object [of meditation], being free from both hatred and attachment, and realizing it as if it were *nirvāṇa*, this is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). For a detailed explanation, see the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).

Neutral persons constitute a single category. Enemies are also divided into three: inferior, middling, and superior. This results in seven categories in total. Having thus distinguished the categories, first...

[Note] Regarding "first the relatives, then the enemies": this proceeds from the easy to the difficult, allowing the contemplation to be established in accordance with the mind.
