second, because this follows the sequence of the seven cycles, wherein each cycle employs the contemplation by first bestowing pleasure upon the upper [beings], while the middle and lower are not essential and thus remain for later. Although [pleasure] is bestowed [upon them later],...
Before and after, for every object, there are three [types of beings]. One should treat enemies and kin with equality in order to destroy the obstacle of anger.
[Commentary] This specifically clarifies the sixth contemplation of the *Vibhaṅga-samādhi*, concerning the giving of happiness to objects. There are two intended meanings.
First, according to the sequential cultivation of contemplation, one should, within the initial contemplation, give superior happiness to superior kin, middle [happiness] to middle [kin], and so on.
One gives superior happiness to superior friends; middling happiness to middling friends; and inferior happiness to inferior friends.

Continuing thus up to the seventh contemplation, one gives superior happiness to superior enemies, middling happiness to superior friends, and inferior happiness to middling friends, as explained in the preceding diagram.

Therefore, according to the sequential cultivation of the contemplation, it should occur within the sixth or seventh cycles, wherein one gives inferior happiness to the objects of superior friends and middling friends.
This is the lower form of happiness. Second, it refers to following the sequence of the seven rounds, in which one bestows the highest happiness upon others.

Thus, in the first round, one should bestow the highest happiness upon close relatives; in the second round, the highest happiness upon middle relatives; in the third round, the highest happiness upon distant relatives;
and so on, until in the seventh round, one bestows the highest happiness upon close enemies. This is also as shown in the preceding diagram.

It is said that these two, the intermediate and the inferior joys, are not essential. Therefore, within the six or seven cycles, by means of the inferior joy, the inferior joy is applied to the superior, the intermediate, and the intermediate objects.
Although there is a sequence between the [bestowal of] joy, all seven objects obtain the three types of joy.
For instance, regarding the superior object, one obtains the superior joy during the first cycle, and this continues until the sixth cycle.
They obtain the lower pleasure. In the seventh cycle, they obtain the middle pleasure, and so on up to the superior enemies.
Regarding the superior enemies, they obtain the lower pleasure in the fifth cycle, the middle pleasure in the sixth cycle, and the superior pleasure in the seventh cycle.

Those who are superior kinsmen or enemies all obtain these three pleasures; those who are middling or inferior kinsmen or enemies, as well as neutral persons, all likewise obtain these three pleasures. It is thus.
Practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) enables one to treat enemies and kin with equality, thereby destroying the obstacle of anger.

[Note] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) expands this into nine cycles: first, proceeding from kin to enemies in sequence to bestow happiness, without waiting for the sixth or seventh cycle, one then returns to the previous kin.

[Commentary] This section specifically clarifies the nine cycles of practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*) as explained in the *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice). That is to say, one follows the sequence from relatives to enemies, bestowing happiness in successive stages.

Thus, in the first cycle, one bestows superior happiness upon lower relatives; in the second cycle, one bestows middling happiness upon superior relatives; in the third cycle, one bestows superior happiness upon superior relatives;
and so on, until the seventh cycle, where one bestows inferior happiness upon superior enemies, and the eighth cycle, where one bestows middling happiness upon superior enemies.

Regarding "joy": the ninth [week] corresponds to the superior joy of the superior enemy. This constitutes the first, second, and third cycles, which correspond to the three grades of joy for the superior relatives.
Why wait for the sixth and seventh cycles before, based on the previously mentioned objects of superior and middling relatives, one finally grants the inferior, middling, and lower joys?
Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) follows the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* in opening this up into nine cycles.
[Commentary] Furthermore, as for the preceding object—whether it is attained or not—it is merely a mental cultivation undertaken to destroy obstacles.

In reality, the person before one has not actually obtained happiness. Therefore, the *Xiyuan* (Analysis of the Profound) states: "Question: If one possesses happiness within oneself, it can be bestowed upon others;

but if one suddenly lacks happiness within oneself, with what will one bestow it? Answer: If there is no happiness within oneself that can be bestowed, then one should cultivate the mind [of giving]."
One bestows upon the remaining devas, bodhisattvas, and others the pleasures one enjoys, wishing that enemies and kin may be equalized so that sentient beings may receive such happiness.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-śūtra* states: "Though one wishes to uproot suffering, in reality, one has not yet uprooted it."
All these are empty words. Although they desire to bestow happiness, they have not actually attained happiness; this is merely a provisional designation.
[Appendix] Bian’e says: Furthermore, from the section on Nirvāṇa down to "this is a provisional designation," it seems unnecessary to cite [these as the primary meaning];
one should know that the central intent here lies in exercising a mind of compassion and equanimity, whose power is inconceivable.
[Commentary: That passage from the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* is a text that employs reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).

Its intent is to mean that although those of the Two Vehicles cultivate compassion, it is merely for their own sake—to free themselves from suffering and attain happiness—and they are unable to benefit others.

Therefore, it says, "This is a provisional designation" and "merely empty words," precisely to show that only Bodhisattvas are capable of benefiting others. [My private opinion: I fear that later generations, not understanding this, might...
This means that because compassion might otherwise be established in vain, it is clarified here.

[Commentary] Furthermore, when a practitioner employs contemplation, they must regard their enemies as having been their parents in the past; only then can they achieve equanimity toward both enemies and kin and bestow happiness upon them.
This is explained in detail in the *Xixuan* (Analysis of the Profundities), Part One, etc. (as cited).
△ Third, the method for curing excessive distraction through the contemplation of counting breaths (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).

【□ Note】 When discursive thoughts and mental preoccupations conflict with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is termed "excessive distraction. There are four characteristics of the breath, and eight [aspects] of śamatha and vipaśyanā.

(17) Regarding sound: that which has sound is called *vāyu* (wind). If one holds onto it, it disperses. That which is congealed and obstructed is called *prāṇa* (vital energy). If one holds onto it, it becomes further congealed.

When inhalation and exhalation are not complete, it is called *śvāsa* (labored breathing). If one holds onto it, it leads to exhaustion. That which is neither sounding nor obstructed, where inhalation and exhalation are both complete, is called *ānāpāna* (breath).

If one holds onto this, the mind becomes settled. (Text) As for counting: from one to ten, neither more nor less, so as to prevent the mind from scattering. This is the first stage of the Dhyāna-gate.

There are five [methods], of which there are four teachers. The first teacher counts the exhalation; when it is neither hurried nor distended, the body becomes light and agile, and one easily enters samādhi.

The second teacher counts the inhalation; following the breath inward, he draws it within. The third teacher has no fixed preference for either inhalation or exhalation, but simply counts whichever is most convenient.
[Supplement] If the mind is flighty, bind it to the *dantian* (elixir field) and count the inhalations. If there is drowsiness, bind the mind to the tip of the nose and count the exhalations.
[Commentary] The four masters employ counting according to these four stages.
[Supplement] During spring and summer, when things emerge and flourish, one counts the exhalations. During autumn and winter, when things contract and withdraw, one counts the inhalations.
[Commentary] Our school primarily follows the third master. Furthermore, we do not permit counting both inhalations and exhalations together, for fear that it may give rise to illness.
[Commentary] In the Chan school, there are four masters who clarify the method of counting the breath (*ānāpāna*). One master teaches that one should fix the mind on counting the exhalation;
thus, the breath will not be forced, the body will not feel distended, and the body and mind will become light and agile, making it easy to enter *samādhi*.

Another master teaches counting the inhalation for five reasons: first, it is easier to enter meditative concentration because the mind follows the breath inwardly; second, it cuts off external objects [of distraction]; third...

First, because it is easy to perceive the thirty-six impure substances within; second, because the four bodily powers become light and vigorous; third, because greed and anger are truly stilled within.
Such are the benefits. One should practice counting the inhalations. Some masters teach that one may count either the inhalation or the exhalation, taking whichever is convenient without restriction;
one must not apply only one method. By following whatever brings peace to the mind, one enters meditative concentration without fault.
Regarding the application [of counting breaths], the discourses of the three masters all do not permit counting inhalation and exhalation as a single unit at one time. Why is this?
Because there is a disease that obstructs the breath; it arises in the throat like a blade of grass, such that when one exhales it does not come out, and when one inhales it does not go in.
Because this affliction arises, other masters rely on counting according to the four periods [of inhalation, retention, exhalation, and pause]. This is not yet fully detailed here. Now, we rely on...
This is the third method of the Teacher.
[Note] In the Sanskrit language, it is *ānāpāna*; here it is translated as "sending forth and sending away," referring to inhalation and exhalation.
This is the initial gateway for entering the Path for all Buddhas of the three periods of time, and it is common to the Three Vehicles and the Four Teachings.
[Commentary] The *Fanyi mingyi* (Explanation of Terms in Translation) states: *Āna* is also called *ānā*; this is translated as "sending in," which refers to the inhalation of breath.
*Prāṇa* is translated as "sending out," which refers to the exhalation of breath. The *Anban shouyi jing* (Sutra on Mindfulness of Breathing) says: "Āna is the body; prāṇa is the breath.
Āna is birth; prāṇa is cessation. Āna is mindfulness of the Path; prāṇa is the unraveling of knots. This is why one begins with counting.

Regarding "entry": externally there are seven evils and internally there are three evils; because these [evils] are numerous and cannot be overcome by a small [amount of merit], one first practices counting the breaths (*gaṇanā*).
As for the "initial gateway to entering the Path," Deva said: "The Buddha taught the Gate of Ambrosia (*amṛta-dvāra*), which is named *ānāpāna*."
Among all dharma-gates, this is the foremost path of peace and security.
[Commentary] Furthermore, one employs the six subtle gates of clarity through breath: namely, counting, following, stopping, contemplating, returning, and purification.
Focusing the mind upon the breath, from one to ten, is called "counting. With a subtle mind relying on the breath, knowing its entry and exit is called "following. As for the breath...
The stillness of the mind is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). The analytical investigation of phenomena is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
Turning the mind back to reflect upon itself is called "returning" (*pratyāhāra*). When the mind has no point of dependence and the waves of delusion do not arise, it is called "purity.
As stated in the *Dharmadhātusthāna-sūtra*, this is currently the auxiliary path of the Hīnayāna, which is simply termed "counting the breaths" (*ānāpānasmṛti*).
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Dharmadhātu": the six dharmas follow one another in sequence and can lead to the truly wondrous *nirvāṇa*;

therefore, they are called "wondrous gates. According to what is elucidated by this school, there are ten kinds of six wondrous gates; here, however, we shall briefly present only the section on their sequential arising.
As for why these six gates are arranged in this order: these six gates are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*).

Dhyāna. Among the other dhyānas that are both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), this is shallow and limited; therefore, it is placed next [in the sequence]. First is the gate of counting the breaths (ānāpānasmṛti).
Focusing the mind on the count from one to ten is called "counting" (gaṇanā). To cultivate the outflow-free true Dharma, one must first regulate the mind and enter meditative concentration (samādhi).
Because the mind of the desire realm is coarse and distracted, it is difficult to control; it cannot be pacified except through counting. Therefore, one must...
Skillfully regulating the body and breath from one to ten, coarse agitation is stilled and the mind dwells in purity;

this is the essential method for entering meditative concentration (samādhi), and thus counting is designated as the gate. Second is the gate of following the breath: with a subtle mind, one relies on the breath, knowing its entry and knowing its exit.
It is called "following" (*anugama*). Although the mind abides by means of counting the breaths, meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) has not yet arisen.

If one continues to maintain the count, there will be the fault of the mind giving rise to discursive thoughts; therefore, one relinquishes the count and cultivates following. The mind relies upon the breath: when entering, one knows it enters;
when exiting, one knows it exits. One fully knows its length, its coldness, and its warmth. If the mind becomes peaceful, luminous, and pure, then the various dhyānas will arise spontaneously.
Therefore, it is established as a gateway. Third is the gateway of *śamatha* (calm abiding). To still the mind and contemplate in tranquility is called *śamatha*.

Although the mind becomes clear and pure by following the breath, concentration (*samādhi*) has not yet been aroused. If the mind follows [the breath], there is a slight disturbance of arising conceptualization.

For clarity, purity, and peaceful stability, nothing compares to *śamatha*. Therefore, one abandons following and cultivates *śamatha*, primarily employing the "concentrating the mind" (*cittasamkṣepa*) method of *śamatha*. Concentrating the mind...
When the mind is stilled and free from fluctuation, the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) will spontaneously unfold; therefore, *śamatha* (calm abiding) serves as the gateway.

As for the four gateways of *vipaśyanā* (insight), "observation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the analytical discernment and investigation of phenomena. Although one realizes the various meditative concentrations through *śamatha*, liberating wisdom has not yet been generated.

If one dwells in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there may still be the discordance of attachment to the flavor of ignorance; thus, one must investigate, examine, and analyze to realize the various dhyānas and samādhis.

One should frequently employ the actual contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). When the observation of the mind becomes clear, one will know that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty and deceptive.
One destroys the four inversions as well as the sixteen views of self and so forth. Since the inversions are no longer present, the untainted (anāsrava) skillful means are thereby developed;
therefore, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is regarded as the gate. Regarding the five gates of returning: "returning" refers to turning the mind back to reflect upon itself.

Although one practices contemplative observation, true illumination has not yet been manifested. If one calculates that there is a self capable of observing and analyzing, thereby destroying the inversions, then...
The delusion of conceiving a self still clings to the contemplation of arising, making it identical to the views of non-Buddhists;

therefore, it is said that non-Buddhists who cling to the contemplation of emptiness and the wisdom of contemplation do not attain liberation. If one awakens to this affliction, one should immediately turn the light back to illuminate the contemplating mind itself.
If one knows that the contemplating mind is empty, deceptive, and without reality, then the inversion of clinging to a self through attachment to contemplation will perish of its own accord.

Because this untainted (*anāsrava*) skillful means is spontaneously luminous, it serves as a gateway once again—the sixth gateway of purity. When the mind has no basis of reliance and the waves of delusion do not arise, it is called "purity.

At the time of returning through cultivation, although one has destroyed the inversions of contemplation, if true illumination has not yet emerged, abiding in a state where neither subject nor object exists is precisely the mindfulness of sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Therefore, it causes the mind and its cognitive faculties to be turbid and defiled; this is what is known as "awareness" (*saṃjñā*).

This being so, one does not dwell and does not cling; all things merge into a state of pure clarity. Through this, true illumination is developed, whereby the fetters of the three realms are severed and the paths of the Three Vehicles are realized;
thus it is said that through purity, one attains single-mindedness (*ekacitta*), whereby the ten thousand evils are extinguished.
To take purity as the gateway—this is the intended meaning. [Appendix] Bian’e says: This is now the auxiliary teaching of the Hīnayāna.

The two phrases regarding the Path may seem restrictive; one should know that within the Six Sublime Methods (ṣaḍ-anupūrva-samāpatti), the first three are the skillful means for concentration (samādhi), while the latter three are the skillful means for wisdom (prajñā).

Once one has attained concentration by practicing up to the third stage, one then contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni). Thus, the latter three may also be subsumed under the four foundations of mindfulness.
Since they belong to both concentration and wisdom, they cannot be described merely as the "counting of breaths" (ānāpānasmṛti) as an auxiliary to the Path. My personal view is as follows:
This is the method for settling the mind, which focuses exclusively on counting the breaths;
it may also be categorized as an auxiliary practice for the Path. *Tiantai sijiao yi zhu huibu fu hong ji*, Fascicle 5, Part 1;
*Tiantai sijiao yi zhu huibu fu hong ji*, Fascicle 5, Part 2.

△ Four. The Contemplation Method for Treating Ignorance.
4. Contemplation on the Conditions for Foolish Sentient Beings.

[Commentary] They are deluded and lack understanding; they deny cause and effect, and are thus called "foolish. It should be known that attachment to a self (*ātman*), the calculation of annihilationism or eternalism (*uccheda-śāśvata*), and the grasping at intrinsic reality—these three are all forms of delusion.
[Commentary] There are three kinds of delusion, which the Chan school refers to as the "three delusions. First is the calculation of existence and non-existence:

one wonders whether the self and the aggregates (skandhas), etc., exist or do not exist, and so on, even to the point of wondering whether they neither exist nor do not exist. This is attachment to the self.
Second is the calculation of annihilationism and eternalism: one wonders whether past phenomena cease to exist or continue to exist, and whether present phenomena do not cease.

And yet, [they ask] whether it exists. When they investigate the three periods of time, if they perceive cessation, they fall into nihilism; if they do not perceive cessation, they grasp at permanence. This is the reckoning of annihilation and permanence.
Third is the reckoning of the nature of the world, which claims that because of the existence of subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), there exist real dharmas and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*);
and because of the existence of the four great elements, there exist conventionally designated sentient beings and the world. Based on these reflections, they proceed upon false paths. This...
"Grasping at intrinsic nature" means it is real.

[□ Note] Regarding "causes and conditions," the *Dharmadhātu-krama* (The Sequence of the Dharma Realm), fascicle 17, states: "That which successively brings about the fruition is the cause; that which mutually relies upon one another is the condition.
(Text) For example, ignorance acts as the cause and serves as the condition for the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), continuing in this manner up to the link of birth (*jāti*).
The cause is able to serve as a condition for old age and death.

[Commentary] Regarding the term "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu), herein the three matters of affliction, karma, and suffering are briefly explained; these act as mutual causes and conditions for one another.

These are the causes and conditions for afflictions and karma; the causes and conditions for karma and suffering; the causes and conditions for the suffering of suffering; and the causes and conditions for suffering and afflictions;

as well as the causes and conditions for afflictions and karma, karma and suffering, and the suffering of suffering. This constitutes their mutual functioning as causes and conditions for one another.
As illustrated by the example of ignorance (*avidyā*) below, one should know that there are two types of dharmas regarding causes and conditions, such as when it is said: "the cause..."
The direct condition is proximate, while the causal factor is like a seed and the conditional factor is like rain and dew;

therefore, that which is capable of directly producing a fruit is designated as the cause, whereas that which is distal and assists in its manifestation is designated as the condition. Here, we discuss cause and condition with respect to a single branch of the dharma.

[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 2 (18), states: "The twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) have three different types. First, the twelve links across the three periods of time:
two links of the past are causes; five links of the present are effects; three links of the present are causes; and two links of the future are effects.
Second, the twelve links across two periods of time: there are ten links in the present and two links in the future."

Third: "The twelve links of dependent origination in a single thought-moment. This refers to the present; as soon as a single thought arises, it is already complete with the twelve links of dependent origination.

The three periods [of time] refute the views of annihilationism and eternalism; the two periods refute attachment to a self; and the single thought-moment refutes the notion of a substantial nature (*svabhāva*). (Text)
[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states: The two causes of the past are ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

The five fruits of the present are consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*). The three causes of the present are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).

The two fruits of the future are birth (*jāti*) and old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and distress (*jarāmaraṇa-śoka-parideva-duḥkha-daurmanasyopāyāsa*). These constitute the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) explained collectively across the three periods of time. From [ignorance]...

From its beginning until now, birth and death have continued without end; if one does not cultivate contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), one will continue to transmigrate in the future without limit.

If one cultivates contemplative wisdom, then ignorance (*avidyā*) is extinguished, and even up to old age, death, sorrow, and affliction, all are extinguished; this is called the awakening through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Regarding the dependent origination of two lifetimes, it is fully contained in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, where the Buddha spoke it for those seeking the state of a *pratyekabuddha*. It is manifested here.
Regarding the ten [factors]: there are two in the future. Some explain that there are nine in the present and three in the future; others say ten in the present, one of which is ignorance (*avidyā*).
The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* asks: "What is meant by contemplating ignorance? It first contemplates how the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) enters the parents' presence.

First, there is the mind of craving and attachment. Due to the conditions of this craving, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) harmonize. The two drops of semen and blood combine to form a single drop.
It is called *kalala*. This consists of three factors: first, life; second, consciousness; and third, warmth. From the causes and conditions of karma in past lives, the fruit is induced;
there is neither an agent nor a recipient. The initial inhalation and exhalation of breath is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

There are three kinds of paths: namely, following the mother’s breath as it ascends and descends; changing once every seven days; and the inhalation and exhalation of breath, which is called "life-span.

This is called the path of wind (*vāyu-mārga*). That which is neither foul-smelling nor putrid is called "warmth" (*uṣman*). That which is within this [body] is the mind, called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

Regarding these two practices, one further contemplates the causes and conditions of the three feelings, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*). What are they?

Contemplation: Following the mindful mind, one contemplates the inhalation and exhalation of the breath. One contemplates the skin, muscles, tendons, bones, marrow, and brain within the internal body as being like clouds in the sky;

the winds within this body are likewise so. There are winds that can move upward, winds that can move downward, winds that can fill [the body], winds that can cause desiccation, and winds that increase [growth]. Thus, there is the inhalation and exhalation of the breath.

The formations of name (*nāma-kāya-saṃskāra*) arise from vitarka and vicāra by means of inhalation and exhalation; these are called the formations of mind (*mano-saṃskāra*). The production of sound through their conjunction is called the formations of speech (*vāk-saṃskāra*).
Third is consciousness (*vijñāna*): when the three formations serve as causes and conditions, consciousness arises; this is called consciousness. Fourth is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*):

due to the attachment to the conditions of consciousness, there are the four aggregates (*skandha*) along with the aggregate of form; these are called name-and-form. Fifth and sixth are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
The five aggregates are the conditions for consciousness to operate within the six bases; these are called the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍāyatana*). As for the six contacts (*ṣaṭsparśa*):

the mutual encounter of the eye and forms is called contact, and so on up to the mind and mental objects (*dharmas*), which are likewise. As for the seven feelings (*saptavedanā*): due to the condition of contact, one perceives forms through to mental objects.
The eighth is sensation (*vedanā*). The ninth, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), refers to the desire for forms, up to and including mental phenomena (*dharma*); this is called craving.

The tenth, grasping (*upādāna*), refers to seeking and searching in the four directions due to the condition of craving; this is called grasping. The eleventh, existence (*bhava*), refers to receiving a future body due to the condition of grasping;
this is called existence. These latter two conditions belong to the future. The twelfth, birth (*jāti*), refers to [arising] due to the condition of existence.
Birth is called "birth. The twelfth [link] is old age and death. Because birth is the condition, there are old age, death, and various forms of suffering.

These are called the great tree of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). If one hears this and gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they are also called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer) through dependent origination.
As for "dependent origination in a single thought-moment," it refers to the present: as soon as a single thought arises, it is already complete.

The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination also appear in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, where they are taught for the sake of *pratyekabuddhas*. The sūtra states: "When the eye sees a form and gives rise to craving, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).

To perform karma for the sake of craving is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). To focus the mind with single-minded attention is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). The co-arising of consciousness and form is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The arising of greed through the six sense bases is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Seeking craving because of the sense bases is called contact (*sparśa*). To dwell upon form..."
The arrival at phenomena is called "feeling" (*vedanā*). If the mind becomes greedily attached to them, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Seeking such phenomena is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).

The arising of these phenomena is called "existence" (*bhava*). Their continuous succession is called "birth" (*jāti*). Because this succession is severed, it is called "death" (*maraṇa*). These are the causes and conditions of birth and death.
Being oppressed by manifold sufferings is called "affliction" (*nirvedha*). This applies likewise even to the arising of craving toward mental objects (*dharmas*) through the mind.
If, upon hearing this, one’s mind attains liberation and gives rise to untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*), such a person is also called a "Pratyekabuddha by means of causes and conditions."

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), fascicle 7, part 1 (end), states: "Regarding the refutation of annihilationism and eternalism across the three periods of time:

because the three periods are continuous, there is no annihilation; because the three periods successively pass away, there is no eternity. Furthermore, the past refutes eternity, the future refutes annihilation, and the present refutes both annihilation and eternity.

Regarding the refutation of the self across two periods: in the two periods of the present and the future, the twelve links of dependent origination are complete, whereby one gives rise to attachment toward the father."
To give rise to anger toward one’s mother is called ignorance (*avidyā*). When the father’s physical remains are regarded as one’s own, this is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

From the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to the link of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), these correspond to the three periods of time. (Text) The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Fascicle 8, Part 1, section 11, states:

"As for the term 'one thought-moment' (*ekakṣaṇa*), it does not refer to an extremely brief instant of a single moment. Rather, it refers to the completion of wholesome or unwholesome karma, which is termed 'one thought-moment.'"
Because it differs from the three periods of time, the two periods, and characteristics such as continuous binding (*saṃbandha*), it is called a "single thought-moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*).
Since all [dharmas] are impermanent, they lack substantial intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). (Text: *Miaoxuan* 2, *Chanmen* 3).

[Commentary] Regarding the refutation of annihilationism and eternalism concerning the three times: this means that the past draws forth the present, and the present draws forth the future, such that their continuity is uninterrupted.
Furthermore, the past has already ceased, the future has not yet arisen, and the present perishes moment by moment; thus, phenomena are not eternally constant.

This constitutes the general refutation of annihilationism and eternalism regarding the three times. As for the specific treatment of each of the three times: it refers to the cessation of each preceding [moment].
Therefore, the conception of permanence is refuted. Some say that because the past has already passed and does not reach the present, permanence is refuted;

yet because there is a successive continuity from one moment to the next, annihilationism is refuted. Others say that although [the past] has not yet arrived, it still awaits connection [with the present], and thus the conception of annihilationism is refuted.
Since the present is not the past, the conception of annihilationism is refuted; since it is not the future, the conception of permanence is refuted. This is...
This is to simultaneously refute [the views of] annihilationism and eternalism regarding the present. Regarding the refutation of the self across the two time periods:

by inferring through the twelve links of the two time periods, it is seen that in neither case is there a real, substantial self-entity. This constitutes the destruction of attachment to the self across the two time periods.

As for the term "a single moment" (*ekakṣaṇa*): it refers to the completion of wholesome and unwholesome karma; this precisely demonstrates the single moment in which the twelve factors of dependent origination are fully present. As...

This refers to the saying: "As soon as a wholesome thought arises, the jeweled palaces of the celestial realms are formed; as soon as an evil intention begins to sprout, the fiery wheels of hell are already complete.

Regarding the characteristics of "continuous binding" (*prabandha*) and so forth, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the various stages (*avasthā*) and the long-term continuity [of the causal process].

As stated in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary): "The *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā* treatises explain that there are four types of twelvefold dependent origination: first, the momentary (*kṣaṇika*); second,..."

"Continuous binding" (saṃyojana) refers to the three stages [of karma], which are discussed in relation to the year. "Distant succession" (dūre-anubandha) is as in the case of a Pratyekabuddha observing hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes;
for example, if one commits evil in this life, the retribution may not necessarily be received in the next life, but only after subsequent future lives—this is why it is so named.
The latter three are merely the causes and conditions of the three periods of time, as they are categorized according to their capacity to accord [with the result].

Because they experience [the results] equally after birth and so forth, three [types of continuity] are distinguished. Furthermore, the treatise states: "As for 'continuous bondage' (*saṃbandha*), it is as explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
all five aggregates existing throughout the twelve stages of the dependent origination factors are subsumed under the category of 'stages' (*avasthā*).
This very uninterrupted succession from beginningless time is called 'continuous bondage. The *Huayan-chao* says: 'Continuous bondage requires that cause and effect be without interval.'"
They arise in continuous succession. Whether sentient or insentient, all things possess arising and ceasing that continue moment by moment;
thus, they are bound together in each *kṣaṇa*, pervading all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Regarding the conditions of states (*avasthā-pratyaya*):

this refers primarily to karma conducive to birth-experience and indeterminate karma, as well as the twelve links of existence across the three times and the states of the five aggregates. As for distant continuity, it refers to the preceding portion.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that they are merely distant continuations. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* says: "Distant continuity as a condition" refers to the prior and subsequent limits;
it refers to karma to be experienced in a later life (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*) and indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karma*), which have flowed without beginning.

The "predominant cause" (*adhipati-hetu*) is precisely the "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*). The reason the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) clarifies this is that it now explains how phenomena relate to one another through their respective functions and obscurations, and how good and evil mutually trigger one another. Among the six causes, these are subsumed under four; among the four conditions (*pratyaya*), there are differences in their applicability. Therefore, it briefly explains the four conditions as well as the six causes. As for the names and meanings of the six causes and four conditions: 1. **Simultaneous Cause** (*sahabhū-hetu*): Refers to dharmas that arise together and function simultaneously, such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives (*upādāya-rūpa*), or the mental factors (*caitta*) and the mind (*citta*). 2. **Associated Cause** (*samprayuktaka-hetu*): Refers to the mutual functioning of the mind and its associated mental factors. 3. **Homogeneous Cause** (*sabhāga-hetu*): Refers to dharmas of the same category that produce subsequent dharmas of the same kind, such as wholesome dharmas producing wholesome dharmas. 4. **Universal Cause** (*sarvatraga-hetu*): Refers to defiled dharmas that act as a pervasive cause for other defiled dharmas within the same continuum. 5. **Repaying Cause** (*vipāka-hetu*): Refers to the cause that produces a result of maturation (*vipāka-phala*), specifically the unwholesome and the obscured-neutral. 6. **Efficient Cause** (*kāraṇa-hetu*): This refers to all dharmas that do not obstruct the arising of others; it is the most extensive, encompassing everything. Regarding the four conditions: 1. **Condition as Object** (*ālambana-pratyaya*): All dharmas can serve as objects for the mind and its mental factors.

2. **Dominant Condition** (*adhipati-pratyaya*): All dharmas can act as a dominant influence upon others. 3. **Immediate Condition** (*samanantara-pratyaya*): Refers to the preceding moment of consciousness and its mental factors that give way to the immediately succeeding ones. 4. **Causal Condition** (*hetu-pratyaya*): This refers to the five causes (excluding the efficient cause) that function as conditions for the arising of dharmas. Thus, the relationship between the six causes and four conditions is established through their respective definitions and applications.

It seems inappropriate to claim that a wholesome action (*śubha-karma*) invites the maturation (*vipāka*) of a subsequent consciousness; thus, wholesome actions should be considered partial universal causes. This leads us to the discussion of universal causes, specifically those associated with views and doubt.
Ignorance (*moha*) and so forth—indeed, all defiled and wholesome dharmas—are fully present in both ordinary people and non-Buddhists. These shall be retained here for determination at a later time.
[Note] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Fascicle 8, Part 1 (11), states: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "The Buddha has taught that dependent origination is extremely difficult to understand;

how can it be made for ignorant people to contemplate? The answer is: "It is not like [the case of] oxen, horses, and the like. The *Chanmen* (Dhyāna Gate) simply speaks of those who are intelligent and of keen faculties.
To discriminate and deliberate without attaining right wisdom, and to grasp the principle with a deviant mind, is called ignorance (*moha*).
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Ignorance is not like the stupidity of oxen or horses.

It refers to a person who, while seeking the true path, gives rise to various false views because they contemplate with a deviant mind; such a person is an ignorant one. One should observe dependent origination. This is what is meant.
The Skillful Method for Cultivation. Under the Zen Gate: Reaffirmation.

[Commentary] How does this contemplation of causes and conditions differ from that of the Pratyekabuddhas? Herein, it serves as an aid to the Path for breaking through obstacles; thus, the three periods of time are discussed briefly.

The Pratyekabuddha’s correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) for destroying delusions must rely on both the "inverse" and "concordant" conditions, such as the causes and conditions spanning hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes.
[Note] Regarding the Pratyekabuddha’s reliance on both inverse and concordant conditions across hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes, the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states:

"First is the contemplation belonging to the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) associated with craving; second is the contemplation belonging to the twelve links associated with views. As for the former:
This constitutes two meanings: first, analytical investigation; second, contemplative deconstruction. Regarding the first, analytical investigation:

if one hears the teaching on the laws of arising and ceasing through correct causes and conditions, one understands and discerns them with faith, realizing that all things belonging to craving and affliction are entirely comprised within the twelve links of dependent origination.

Observing causes and conditions, he enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Desiring to still the mind and reach the fundamental source, he seeks spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and delights in solitary tranquility.
Cultivating a concentrated mind, he attains various *dhyānas*. Abiding within these concentrations, he recognizes that the afflictions belonging to craving are none other than ignorance (*avidyā*).

By investigating them both in reverse and in direct order, he perceives the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). How does he investigate in reverse? This craving has as its cause...

What gives rise to birth? One knows it is due to clinging (*upādāna*). Clinging is due to craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Craving is due to feeling (*vedanā*). Feeling is due to contact (*sparśa*). Contact is due to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).

The six sense bases are due to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Name-and-form is due to consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness is due to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Volitional formations are due to ignorance (*avidyā*); these are all the afflictions of the past.

Furthermore, by tracing this craving in reverse order: craving can give rise to grasping (*upādāna*). Due to grasping, there is becoming (*bhava*). Due to becoming, there is birth (*jāti*). Due to birth... [the rest of the chain follows].
Birth gives rise to the mass of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and suffering; thus one revolves without end.
If, by means of stabilizing the mind through contemplation, one enters deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one may thus trace back in reverse order.

At times, one sees the *kalala* stage of initial conception, and even sees past bodies generating karma and afflictions (*kleśa*), extending back through two births, a hundred births, or a thousand births. One continues this tracing in forward order as well.
There is. If, through the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one sees one future life, two lives, or even up to hundreds of thousands of lives;
or if, seeing past and future events, one’s mind is moved by compassion and the resolve for the Way (*bodhicitta*) increases further. Regarding the second, the contemplation that breaks [delusion]:

this refers to the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* (the application of mindfulness to phenomena), which involves the sequential and distinct contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). The contemplation of *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* is briefly as explained previously.
Why is this? If one contemplates craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding the nature of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as defiled.

If one contemplates craving, contact (*sparśa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), it is the application of mindfulness regarding the nature of the five aggregates as neutral (*avyākṛta*) karmic results.

If one contemplates formations (*saṃskāra*), it is the application of mindfulness regarding the nature of the five aggregates as wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*). If one contemplates ignorance (*avidyā*), it is the past [defiled...].

The four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) have the nature of the five aggregates (skandha) of defiled afflictions. If one contemplates grasping, it is the four foundations of mindfulness of the nature of the presently defiled five aggregates.
If one contemplates existence, it is the four foundations of mindfulness of the nature of the wholesome and unwholesome five aggregates.

If one contemplates future birth, aging, and death, it is the four foundations of mindfulness of the nature of the resultant rebirth (vipākaja) which is indeterminate (avyākṛta). This is the application of the foundations of mindfulness.
One contemplates [the aggregates] in both reverse and direct order, thereby destroying the four perversions. When the perversions are extinguished, ignorance and all afflictions are extinguished.

Because ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations are extinguished, and so on, up to the extinction of old age and death. This is called the *dharmatā-smṛtyupasthāna* (the four foundations of mindfulness of intrinsic nature).

The sequential and distinct contemplations belong to the contemplation of the causes and conditions of afflictions associated with craving. Regarding the subsequent [contemplations], there are also two aspects:

first, analytical investigation; second, contemplative refutation. First, as for analytical investigation: if one perceives a self (*ātman*) and the world as permanent, impermanent, both permanent and impermanent, or neither permanent nor impermanent, these constitute the four views regarding the self and the body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) arising in the present life. It is because of this [that they arise].

The four views regarding the self and its possessions give rise to the fourteen difficult questions and the sixty-two views. These four views regarding the self and its possessions are themselves the four graspings (*upādāna*).

By tracing them backward and forward, these graspings are caused by the four cravings (*tṛṣṇā*); craving is caused by the four feelings (*vedanā*), and so on, down to the four formations (*saṃskāra*), which are caused by the four ignorances (*avidyā*).
Furthermore, tracing the four graspings forward, they are able to produce the four existences (*bhava*). This existence is precisely the reception of all two [types of suffering].

The fifteen modes of existence consist of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction. If, by means of stabilizing the mind through contemplation, one attains deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one may perceive the events of past and future births, as fully described previously.
One contemplates the two types of destruction through the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding the nature of causes.
One contemplates the four graspings (*upādāna*) and the four views concerning the self and extremes (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). Following this sequence down to ignorance (*avidyā*), one destroys the past.

Whether it be "going as such," "not going as such," "both going as such and not going as such," "neither going as such nor not going as such"—these are the two views of self and body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which defile the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Furthermore, one should subsequently contemplate the four graspings (*catvāry upādānāni*) and their existence, extending even unto birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
One destroys [the views of] the future: that it is finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite.

These are the two views of self and of the extremes, which defile the five aggregates. If one can thus employ the application of mindfulness to the nature of phenomena to destroy these four views of self and extremes throughout the three periods of time, one immediately destroys the fourteen difficult questions, the sixty-two views, and all [erroneous views].

The afflictions associated with views are extinguished all at once; this is called the extinction of ignorance, which is the extinction of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and so on, up to the extinction of old age and death.

When the afflictions associated with views are extinguished, one again employs the aforementioned contemplation of the mindfulness of the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination regarding craving (*tṛṣṇā*) to destroy craving for the realms of desire, form, and formlessness; these are then all extinguished. This constitutes the afflictions, karma, and paths of the three realms.
"Cessation" refers to *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana with remainder). If the path of suffering is extinguished, that is *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder).
This is called the wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness as causal nature (*hetu-bhūta-smṛtyupasthāna*). By contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one enters nirvana.

This applies even to what is termed the "shared foundations of mindfulness" (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*) and the "foundations of mindfulness as objects" (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*); their assistance in contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
△ Five: The Method for Contemplating the Subduing of Obstacles. Fifth:
The Contemplation of Mindfulness of the Buddha for Sentient Beings with Many Obstacles.

[□ Note] The *Zhiguan* states: "Sleep obstructs the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)," which it further refers to as "the obstacle of oppression. The fourth section of the *Chanmen* clarifies three types [of obstacles].

Obstacles. The remedy is mindfulness of the three bodies (*trikāya*). (While those [remedies] generally pertain to the Mahāyāna, for now we shall clarify those that assist the path in the Hīnayāna. Obstacles are, namely, evil karma. As for the three types:

first, the obstacle of dullness and mental obstruction (*styānamiddha-āvaraṇa*)—[characterized by] drowsiness and non-defined states (*avyākṛta*)—is remedied by mindfulness of the thirty-two marks of the Response Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Second, the obstacle of evil thoughts and reflections.

(When one intends to commit the five heinous crimes, the ten evil deeds, and so forth,) one should apply the remedies of mindfulness of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*), its powers (*bala*), and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). Third, the obstacle of environmental oppression: (the body suddenly suffers acute pain.)

Or one may see [visions] such as being without hands or feet, or being burned by fire or drowned in water. This is the contemplation of the Dharma-body as empty, quiescent, and unconditioned, serving as an antidote (as explained in the text). Now, we clarify the auxiliary practices of the Hīnayāna.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "the hindrance of sleep": as for "oppression," the Abhidharma school (Lakṣaṇavāda) clarifies that sleep has dullness and brevity as its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and its function (*karman*) is to obstruct contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) has clarity and non-forgetfulness as its intrinsic nature, and its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Since sleep and mindfulness are diametrically opposed in both essence and function, mindfulness destroys sleep; yet when sleep is powerful, it obstructs mindfulness. One should know that when drowsiness and sleep are predominant, they are like...
The mountain-like grossness weighs down and oppresses the body and mind; because one undergoes such oppressive hardship, it is called the "obstruction of oppression.

Now, it is treated by means of the contemplation of Buddha-recitation (*nienfo*). The Chan school employs the method of treating the three obstructions with the Three Bodies (*trikāya*); this is now recorded in full as follows:

To contemplate the Response-Buddha (*nirmāṇakāya*), one takes up any one of the thirty-two marks, or first takes up the mark of the ūrṇā-kośa (the tuft of hair between the eyebrows), and closes [the eyes].
Observe with your eyes. If you cannot achieve success while visualizing [the image] as if suspended before you, you should face a single, majestic physical image.
With a single-minded focus, grasp its characteristics and take them as the object of meditation to enter samādhi. If it is not clear, open your eyes and observe again; then close them once more.

In this way, grasp one characteristic until it is clearly manifest, and then gradually observe all characteristics in succession, causing the eye of the mind to open and become bright, thereby shattering dullness and darkness.

Regarding "mindfulness of repaying the Buddha": one uses right mindfulness to take as an object the Buddha’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, eighteen unique qualities, and the omniscience that perfectly illuminates the dharma-realm;
which is eternally quiescent and immovable, yet universally manifests form-bodies to benefit all beings with immeasurable merit.
When one is mindful in this way, it serves as an antidote. Regarding "mindfulness of the Dharma-Buddha," one contemplates:
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal; it is neither born nor extinguished, devoid of form or color, empty, quiescent, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Within the unconditioned, since there are no objective spheres (*viṣaya*), what could possibly be a characteristic of oppression? To know that objective spheres are empty is itself the antidote.
If one contemplates the thirty-two marks, this is not the antidote. Why is this? Because even before such a person has taken those marks as an object, [they have already...]
If one is disturbed by external objects and yet further grasps at their characteristics, one will frequently fall under the influence of demons and become deranged due to this attachment.

This principle applies generally to Mahayana contemplation; however, the present practice is an auxiliary contemplation of the Hinayana, which consists solely of mindfulness of the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.

[□ Note] According to the *Sìjiào yì* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), it says: "It destroys the obstacle of the oppression of objective realms and unites mindfulness with the Dharma-body of true emptiness (*zhēnkōng fǎshēn*).

[■ Record] This passage from the *Sìjiào yì* concerns the practice of Buddha-recollection for destroying the obstacle of oppression; however, its underlying intent differs from that of the *Chánmén* (Chan Gate).
[■ Supplement] "The Dharma-body of true emptiness" refers to the fivefold Dharma-body of true emptiness realized by the Hīnayāna. Ā...

He said: "The Buddha's Dharma-body is emptiness. Therefore, speaking according to the specific perspective of the Hīnayāna, the physical form of sixteen feet is taken as the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), the fruit realized through causes as the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), and the five aggregates as the *dharmakāya*."
[Commentary] If one contemplates the body in relation to the teachings, as stated in the first volume, part seven, of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary):

"In the preceding three teachings, each contemplates a single body—namely, the birth-body, the response-body, and the retribution-body; in the Perfect [Teaching], one contemplates the Dharma-body, wherein all bodies are fully present. (Text)

[Commentary] *Zang* (Treasure/Store): Recollecting the inferior transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). *Tong* (Pervasive): Recollecting the superior transformation body (*saṃbhogakāya*). *Bie* (Distinct): Recollecting the reward body (*vipākakāya*).

*Yuan* (Perfect/Round): Recollecting the Dharma body (*dharmakāya*). Because the essence of the Dharma-Buddha is perfect and fully possesses all bodies, recollecting the Dharma body is itself the full possession of the transformation, reward, and response bodies.
△ Second, establishing the method for the meditative object of contemplation has two parts:
first, the general [classification]; second, the specific applications of mindfulness (as in the four applications of mindfulness mentioned previously).
【□ Note】 *Miaoxuan* 4 (23) states: "Once the five hindrances have been removed, the wisdom of contemplation becomes precise and accurate, enabling one to contemplate the Four Noble Truths."

Precisely because the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) serves as the initial gateway, one practices the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to destroy the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
[Commentary] Because the faculties of the Śrāvakas are dull, the Truth of Suffering is precisely taken as the initial gateway; they contemplate impurity, suffering, impermanence, and non-self.

[Commentary on the *Xuanzan* (20): "Distinct" (*bie*) means individual; it refers to the fact that body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are each different. "Characteristics" (*xiang*) refers to the modes of activity (*ākāra*);

it means observing these four dharmas by forming modes of activity such as impurity and so forth. Regarding the term "contemplation through mindfulness" (*nian guan*): however, the essence of contemplation is not mindfulness.
Contemplation is wisdom (*prajñā*), for it investigates and examines to know [them as] impure and so forth. "Even unto the bases" (*chu*): this refers to the locations (*sthāna*).
That is to say: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena (*kāya*, *vedanā*, *citta*, *dharma*). These are the objects of mindfulness and the bases for its abiding (text).
[Commentary]: "Body" has the meaning of accumulation. "Sensation" has the meaning of experiencing. "Mind" has the meaning of discerning. Regarding "phenomena," there are two types:

perception (*saṃjñā*), which has the meaning of grasping signs; and formations (*saṃskāra*), which have the meaning of flux. They are called "mindfulness" here because they are designated as the "four foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) at the outset.

In training, one employs mindfulness (*smṛti*), maintenance (*dhāraṇā*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). One does not erroneously accept other conditions; since mindfulness is predominant, it is named after mindfulness.

[Commentary] Regarding the objects of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛty-upasthānāni*) in order to destroy the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). The five are combined into four; as for "reception" (*vedanā*), there are six.

The sense faculties (*indriya*) face the six objects (*viṣaya*); since their meaning encompasses both the internal and external, they are treated as a single category. Perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) reside exclusively within; therefore, they are combined into one.

[Commentary] The *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states: "A person gives rise to the inversion of purity regarding form (*rūpa*), the inversion of pleasure regarding sensation (*vedanā*), and the inversions of self and permanence regarding perception and mental formations."
Inversion. The mind gives rise to the inversion of permanence; because it subverts the four inversions, the five are combined into four.

If the mental faculty (*manas*) experiences mental objects (*dharma*), it is called internal feeling (*ādhyātmika-vedanā*); if the five faculties, such as the eye, experience form and so forth, it is called external feeling (*bāhya-vedanā*).

Although the objects are either internal or external, the act of experiencing them is not twofold; therefore, feeling alone constitutes a single category. As for perception (*saṃjñā*), it grasps characteristics within the mind. As for formations (*saṃskāra*)...
Thus, moment by moment it does not abide, but dwells exclusively within, merging into one.

[Commentary] Furthermore, this *smṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness) is specifically designated as wisdom (*prajñā*). Generally, it also includes concentration (*samādhi*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 3, Part 2, p. 17, states:
"Because the mind is stilled upon the four objects, it is called concentration" (text).
△ Second, the general [classification].

Third, the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) of general characteristics: 1. Contemplating the body as impure; one contemplates that sensation, mind, and dharmas are all impure, and so on until contemplating that dharmas are selfless;

one contemplates that body, sensation, and mind are also selfless. The intermediate cases are to be understood by analogy. (The above three sections are called the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), and are also termed the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).)

[Commentary] This consists of four propositions. Regarding the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni): (1) When the object is distinct and the contemplation is distinct, this is precisely the foundation of mindfulness of specific characteristics (lakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna).

(2) When the object is distinct and the contemplation is general; (3) when the object is general and the contemplation is distinct—these two are the skillful means for the foundation of mindfulness of general characteristics (sāmānyalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna).

(4) When both object and contemplation are general, this is the foundation of mindfulness of general characteristics. (Text) The first [proposition] applies one medicine to one perversion; the middle two...
Verse: When the contemplation of the mind gradually matures, one may apply all four contemplations to a single object, or apply a single contemplation to all four objects.
Once the contemplation of the fourth object has become thoroughly matured, by taking up any one of them, all are attained simultaneously.
[Commentary] One uses the contemplation of impurity to remedy the inversion regarding the body, and so on, up to using the contemplation of non-self to destroy the inversion regarding the self.

As explained above in the individual mindfulnesses, this constitutes the distinction of objects and the distinction of contemplations. Alternatively, when one takes a single object and employs all four contemplations in total—such as contemplating the body as impure, and so on, up to [contemplating it] as suffering, impermanent, and non-self—this is the second case: the distinction of objects with the totality of contemplations.
Alternatively, there is the case where one specific contemplation is used to contemplate four objects collectively.

For example, when one contemplates a single *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity), one contemplates not only the body, but also feelings (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and phenomena (*dharma*), all as being impure. This is the third type: the collective contemplation of individual objects.
The fourth is the case where by taking up one, both are attained. For instance, by taking up the single object of the mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), [one attains the others].
Feeling, mind, and phenomena are all included therein. If one contemplates impurity as a single object, suffering, impermanence, and non-self are all included within it.
This constitutes the fourth [type], wherein both the object and the contemplation are comprehensive.

[Commentary] If one analyzes this according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā*, the first three [of the four types of objects] are all distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), while the fourth phrase alone constitutes the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
[Record] The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā* translated by Paramārtha states: "Among the four, three types have only non-mixed objects; the object of the fourth..."
These encompass both the mixed and the unmixed. If one contemplates only phenomena (*dharma*), it is called "unmixed object.

If one observes two, three, or four [of the aggregates], such as the body and so forth, by taking them collectively as an object, it is called "mixed object. The reference here is intended to exclude [the latter].
[Note] Now, based on the "Four Mindfulnesses" (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) in the *Miaoxuan*, the first phrase is specific (*bié*), while the latter three are all general (*zǒng*).
Here, it precisely corresponds to the general observation of the object (*jìng zǒngguān bié*). That is to say, one employs a single observation specifically to generally observe four objects.
[Commentary] Now, following the *Miaoxuan*, the first [section] is judged to be specific (*bie*), while the latter three are all general (*zong*). From "Now, this...
below, the formal text is correctly judged to be the third category. For example, it says: "Contemplate that the body is impure; feeling, mind, and dharmas are all impure. This is it.

[Note] Furthermore, while the preceding stage of "stopping the mind" (tingxin) and the "four foundations of mindfulness" (sīti-paṭṭhāna) involve contemplating only the Truth of Suffering, it is only upon reaching the stage of the "inner ordinary person" (antara-pudgala) that one contemplates all four truths.
The *Miaoxuan* (4.33) states: "The persons in the stage of the seven worthies clearly recognize the four truths. This is explained from the perspective of theoretical understanding.

[Commentary] "Contemplating only the Truth of Suffering" refers to the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena as they are observed through the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
This is restricted solely to the Truth of Suffering; it is as if one were taking the Truth of Suffering as the primary gateway. As the *Miaoxuan* states:

"The heavenly Māras and non-Buddhists wander in transmigration due to craving and views, failing to recognize the Four Truths. Those who clearly recognize the Four Truths across the seven stages [of the Bodhisattva path] do so by way of understanding. This refers to realization (*adhimukti*).
It is said as follows in the Mahāyāna Sūtra: "In the past, I and you did not see the Four Noble Truths.
Those who see the Four Noble Truths—whether their consciousness is attached to the Truth of Craving or their consciousness is attached to the Truth of Seeing—are all able to understand them clearly.

If one understands the Four Noble Truths, then what is seen is true and correct, without any deviation or crookedness. Thus, it is known that the seven types of noble persons (*saptakṣāntika*) are defined solely in terms of understanding. *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) states:

To claim that one contemplates only the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya) is too restrictive. If one says that the Truth of Suffering serves as the initial gateway, then it follows that the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—which are the objects of contemplation in the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna)—are themselves suffering; that which is countered by them, namely permanence, bliss, self, and purity, is the origin (samudaya);

the contemplation of the applications of mindfulness itself is the path (mārga); and that which is extinguished is the cessation (nirodha). Thus, it is incorrect to restrict this to contemplating only suffering. My personal view is that...
"Contemplating" means focusing one's attention specifically on suffering; it does not mean that one contemplates only the Truth of Suffering while failing to contemplate the other three truths.
A detailed discussion of this may be found in the diagram below.

[Commentary] When mental activity transcends the [conventional] principle, one is called an "external ordinary person" (bāhyapṛthagjana). As for "provisions" (sambhāra), it is a metaphorical designation; desiring to transcend the three realms of existence, these serve as the provisions.

[Commentary] Zhuangzi says: "One traveling a hundred *li* must stay overnight and grind grain for provisions; one traveling a thousand *li* must gather provisions for three months. If one's provisions are insufficient, one cannot advance.
To transcend the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), nothing short of these [provisions] can enable one to set out and move forward;

therefore, they are called "provisions" (*sambhāra*). [Supplement] The *Miaoxuan* states: Previously, through the distinct contemplation of characteristics, the four inversions were destroyed. Now, [the contemplation is] profound...

Through careful observation and wisdom, one comprehensively breaks [delusions], giving rise to right diligence, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), and the path (*mārga*), thereby swiftly entering the subsequent dharmas.
II. Explaining the Inner Worldlings (*adhyātma-prthagjana*).

There are four stages for explaining the inner worldlings: namely, Heat (*ūṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*). (These four stages constitute the inner worldlings; they are also called the stage of application [*prayoga-avasthā*]. Furthermore...)
[This refers to] the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).

[Commentary: Gradually perceiving the *dharmatā*, the mind dwells within the principle while the body remains amidst outflows (*sāsrava*); because the Noble Path has not yet arisen, they are called "inner ordinary persons" (*adhyātma-prthagjana*).
Because they employ meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to support wisdom (*prajñā*) and apply effortful cultivation, it is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*).
[Note] "Dharmatā" refers to the principle of universal emptiness. [Commentary] If either concentration or wisdom is lacking, one cannot advance.

While those at the stage of external worthies possess a degree of contemplation and some concentration, those at the stage of internal worthies now progress with vigor; they further augment their contemplative wisdom by means of meditative concentration.
This is called "preparatory application" (*prayoga*). [Note] It is the root of the noble path (*āryamārga*), and is also termed "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).
[Commentary] "Root" carries the sense of "giving birth. These four are able to bring forth the flowers of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the fruit of the noble path.
The wholesome dharmas of the four fruits arise from this; they are also called "wholesome roots" (*kuśalamūla*).

[Note] Regarding "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) as a metaphor, the *Miaoxuan* (4.24) states: "By means of the specific and general applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one contemplates the objects of the Four Truths."

It is able to give rise to a semblance of understanding, subdue the afflictions and delusions, and attain a portion of the Buddha-dharma’s essence, like smoke preceding fire when drilling for kindling, or the emergence of warmth in springtime.
By using the drill of wisdom upon the object, one gives rise to a semblance of understanding; this "understanding" is a metaphor for "warmth" (this metaphor refers to the practice of wisdom).

Furthermore, it is like flowers and grasses accumulated in spring and summer that naturally produce warmth; by means of the wisdom of the Four Truths, one cultivates various wholesome dharmas, and these wholesome dharmas become accumulated through perfuming.
Because the understanding through wisdom (*prajñā*) arises, it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). (This is a metaphor for the practice of practice.
[Commentary] This same text and its meaning also appear in the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra-ṭīkā*. It explains the name "Heat."

[Note on *Mūrdhan* (The Summit): The *Miaoxuan* (4.24) states: "As semblance-understanding increases, one attains the four *ṛddhipāda* concentrations (*ṛddhipāda-samādhi*). The sixteenfold contemplation of the truths becomes even more distinct.
Being above the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat), it is like ascending a mountain peak; one surveys the four directions and sees them all with complete clarity.
Therefore, it is called the Dharma of the Summit (*mūrdha-dharma*). (Text)
[Commentary] The wisdom of understanding increases; furthermore, by adding the sustenance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one reaches the ultimate stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

This is why it is likened to ascending a mountain peak: the wisdom of awakening is clear and distinct. The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning) further states: "It is like the path to a mountain peak; a person does not stay there long.

If no obstacles arise, they will certainly pass beyond this and reach that [other side]. The practitioner who dwells on the peak does not remain for long; if no obstacles arise, they will certainly..."
Upon reaching *kṣānti* (patience), if there is an obstacle, one regresses back to *uṣmagata* (warmth).

[Commentary] Regarding *kṣānti*, the *Miaoxuan* (4.24) states: "This is also the further growth of semblance-understanding (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). The five kinds of wholesome dharmas increase and become faculties (*indriya*).
Within the Four Noble Truths, one is capable of enduring and possesses a joyful aspiration. (Text) It also carries the meaning of "acceptance" (*kṣama*).
[Commentary: In the stage of *kṣānti* (receptivity), there is further the increase of faculties resembling those of understanding.

Thus, the five kinds of wholesome dharmas—faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—which were previously accumulated in the stage of *uṣmagata* (heat), advance to become faculties (*indriya*). Consequently, one becomes capable of enduring and desiring the objects of the Four Noble Truths;
for this reason, it is named *kṣānti*. Furthermore, "receptivity" (*kṣānti*) means that one accepts the objects of the Four Noble Truths within the mind.
To have clarity within the mind yet be unable to express it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

[Commentary] Regarding the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*), fascicle 5, part 4, states: "This is with outflows (*sāsrava*), and therefore it is called 'worldly' (*laukika*).
Because it is the most excellent among them, it is called 'supreme' (*agra')" (text).
[Commentary] The *Xuánwén* states: "These mental states and their associated mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are the most, the superior, the honored, and the highest among all other phenomena;
they are both partially superior and entirely superior. That is to say, they are partially superior to the stages of *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti*;

and they are partially superior to all the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*) attained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). As for the spheres of mastery, they are indeed superior."
Furthermore, regarding "supreme" (*agra*), it does not mean supreme among all activities; rather, it is because it can open the gateway to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).

Those [factors] such as the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) cannot open the gateway to the Noble Path; it is the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) that opens the gateway to the Noble Path.

Those factors such as the vision of the truths are cultivated through attainment (*bhāvanāpratilambha*). As for those factors such as the vision of the truths being cultivated through attainment, they are all [preceded by] the Supreme Worldly Dharma.
"The efficacy of this single dharma" means that its name is established based on its functional capacity. Regarding the meaning of the name of this foremost dharma:
it is the most supreme meaning; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). It attains the wondrous fruit; it is the ultimate truth.
Like the summit of a lofty banner, there is nothing superior above it—this is the ultimate truth.

[Note on the Four Stages]: Regarding these four stages for the practitioner of contemplation, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "From this arise the factors of Heat" (from the subsequent [contemplation] of general characteristics, the wholesome root of Heat arises).

[Commentary] The treatise explains: One cultivates the mindfulness-establishment on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) by taking general characteristics as its object, gradually bringing it to maturity until it reaches the highest of the high degrees.
Following this mindfulness-establishment, the first root of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) arises. This stage is like "heat" (*uṣmagata*);
thus it is given the name "Heat. It is capable of burning the fuel of the afflictions and serves as the precursor to the fire of the Noble Path, just as heat precedes fire.

Because it possesses the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects of observation (wherein the Four Truths are the objects of cognition and the sixteen aspects are the cognitive faculties;

the *Shiqian* states that "Warmth" consists of eight truths and sixteen aspects—some interpret the character "eight" as an error, perhaps because the essence of the Four Truths is the same across the two upper realms and thus they are collectively referred to as "eight," though in reality one contemplates only the Four Truths of the Desire Realm), this stage is called "Warmth. [This stage comprises three grades. [Note: The character □ appears in the source text.]

[Commentary] The *Śāstra* states: Because this stage of the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) root of goodness is extensive, it is able to fully investigate the objects of the Four Noble Truths and fully cultivate the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*). The sixteen aspects will be explained later. Regarding the three grades:
The *Miaoxuan* states: "There are three levels of 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*): namely, the lower-of-the-lower, the middle-of-the-lower, and the upper-of-the-lower. [Supplementary Note] The *Bian'e* says:
