"Because one contemplates all four truths throughout their entirety, it is said that they are 'contemplated completely. Furthermore, the *Shiqian* states there are eight truths;

it is not the case that external ordinary people (*bāwài-fán*) contemplate only suffering, and only upon reaching the stage of Heat do they contemplate them completely. Therefore, Jingxi specifically mentions the 'eight truths,' as seen in the detailed discussion."
[Below. [Note] Next, the arising of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is likewise (the application of contemplation is the same as before, and it also has three grades).

[Commentary] The treatise says: These roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), through their gradual increase in the lower, middle, and upper grades, reach the stage of full completion.
The arising of roots of goodness is called "Summits" (*mūrdhan*). Because these are superior to the preceding stage, they are given a distinct name.

Among the fluctuating roots of goodness, the Summits are the most excellent, for they are like the crown of a person's head. Alternatively, because this stage marks the boundary between advancing and retreating, it is like the summit of a mountain.
This is called the "Summit" (mūrdhan). Like the "Heat" stage, it fully contemplates the Four Noble Truths and is able to fully cultivate the sixteen aspects (ākāra).
The *Miaoxuan* states: "The Summit has three types: namely, medium-low, medium-medium, and medium-high. This is what is meant.

[Commentary] The lower and middle stages of patience are the same as the "Summit" stage (the lower patience universally contemplates the eight truths; the middle patience contracts its contemplation to focus on cessation, path, and formations. Here, both are said to be the same as the Summit because, although the lower patience universally contemplates the upper and lower [truths], it does not transcend the four truths;
the middle patience’s difficult-to-eliminate formations are explained according to its initial contemplation).
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* states: These roots of goodness of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) stage increase gradually through their lower, middle, and upper grades.

When they reach the point of full completion, a root of goodness arises called "Patience" (*kṣānti*). Because it is the most excellent among those capable of patient acceptance (*kṣamaṇa*) regarding the principle of the Truths (*satya*), it is named "Patience.

Furthermore, because there is no falling back or regression at this stage of Patience, it is called "Patience. This root of goodness of Patience is firmly established and further advanced; all of these are dharmas.

The foundations of mindfulness differ from those mentioned previously. However, these consist of lower, middle, and superior levels. The lower and middle levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are identical to the "summit" (*mūrdhan*);
that is, they involve the complete contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and the complete cultivation of the sixteen aspects (*ākāra*). The superior level differs.
One contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm; because it is immediately adjacent to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), this principle holds.

By analogy with the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth, which are all capable of taking the suffering and other truths of the three realms as their objects, this meaning is already established, as there is no distinction made.

That is to say, for the practitioner of yoga, regarding each aspect (*ākāra*) and object (*ālambana*) of the noble truths—such as the paths of antidote (*pratipakṣa-mārga*) pertaining to the form and formless realms—their cultivation proceeds gradually.
It decreases; it gradually decreases until there are only two moments of mental attention (*manasikāra*) directed toward the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the Desire Realm.
Up to this point, it is called the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*). [Supplement] The *Śūchí* states: "In this stage of medium patience, the Path has not yet been reduced."
Although the aspects (*ākāra*) are reduced, because the path (*mārga*) has not yet been reduced, one is able to fully contemplate all four truths. The verse states:
"The lower and middle levels of patience (*kṣānti*) are the same as the Peak (*mūrdhan*). This is said with reference to this stage.

If, at this stage of middle patience, the truth of the path is reduced, one cultivates only twelve aspects. Since the mind no longer takes delight in that path once it has been reduced, those four aspects of the lower path are also not attained.

Arising. By this principle, when the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is being reduced, one cultivates only eight aspects (*ākāra*), because four aspects each are excluded from the Truths of the Path (*mārga*) and Cessation (*nirodha*).

When the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) is being reduced, one cultivates only four aspects. Thus, during Middle Patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*), one fully cultivates sixteen, twelve, eight, and four aspects of the aspects of truth; this is what is meant.

[Note] Above, one contemplates only the suffering of the desire realm. One aspect and one moment (this "one moment" refers to the culmination; although this stage of Supreme Patience [kṣānti] consists of two moments within one aspect, it is described here according to its completion).

[Commentary] The *Śāstra* explains: Immediately following this stage, one gives rise to superior roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). A single practice for a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*) is called "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).

Because these roots of goodness arise without continuity, they are so designated. [Supplementary Note] The *Jian* states that "superior patience" refers exclusively to the contemplation of the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and that it is termed "superior patience" because it consists of a single practice for a single moment.
Furthermore, it says that within superior patience, one also cultivates the four [noble truths].

[The practitioner] practices. Although they give rise to a single mode of activity within a single moment of mind, because it arises through the contemplation of suffering, they are able to cultivate the four modes of activity belonging to that suffering.
Question: At the stage of "supreme patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), those three modes of activity are reduced;

why then does one cultivate those very modes that have been reduced? Answer: Although those modes of activity are reduced, the Truths themselves are not reduced. Because of a mind of longing and aspiration, one is thus able to cultivate them.
Regarding the aspects of the practice that are diminished therein: the practice diminished during the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) may be understood by analogy.
One retains the lower level of suffering as a single aspect because one intends to enter the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); therefore, it must be retained.

[Commentary] The Supreme Worldly Dharma is likewise. (In the stage of Superior Patience, there are two moments. When one moment has ended and one moment remains, it is called "the fulfillment of the superior mind," at which point one enters the Supreme Worldly Dharma.
Now, as this single moment introduces the outflow-free state, it is said to be "likewise.")
[Commentary] The *Śāstra* states: Immediately following the highest degree of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) arises.

Like the highest degree of patience, it takes the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm as its object and cultivates a single aspect (*ākāra*). It lasts for only one moment. Because it is contaminated (*sāsrava*), it is called "worldly" (*laukika*);

because it is the most excellent, it is called "supreme" (*agra*). Through the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra-bala*), it is produced apart from a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and leads to the Noble Path (*ārya-mārga*).
Because it gives rise to the Path, it is named "Most Supreme.
[Supplementary Note] Bian’e says: In the diagram, the observation of only the aspect of suffering in the Desire Realm appears to be restrictive.

For instance, when practicing the Six Sublime Gates, if one develops the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the Form Realm, one takes that very concentration of the Form Realm as the object of observation; how could this be restricted to the Desire Realm? Furthermore, in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-six...

The four applications of mindfulness clearly encompass all ten knowledges; how could they be restricted to the contemplation of suffering alone? Furthermore, to contemplate only the four truths of the desire realm would also seem too narrow.

As the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (New Vibhāṣā) explains in the seventh fascicle regarding the stage of the preparatory practice of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*), one contemplates all eight truths of the upper and lower realms.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twenty-three, states: "The roots of goodness such as Heat, etc., are all able to fully take the three [realms] as their object."

Regarding the passage on the "suffering of the realms" (*dhātu-duḥkha*) and so forth: for the time being, the *uṣmagata* roots of goodness mostly arise from the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpa-dhyāna*).

Since the afflictions of the lower realms have already been suppressed, one is born in the upper realms; once the higher absorptions have arisen, the afflictions of those upper realms subsequently emerge. How could it be that there is a disease but no medicine? The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 4, states:
"From the *uṣmagata* roots of goodness up until the attainment of the *laukikāgra-dharma*, one may either universally contemplate both the upper and lower realms, or [one may] abandon..."
The upper [levels] take the lower as their object; it is not merely the observation of the desire realm. I privately remark that the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

within the application of mindfulness on the composite and miscellaneous phenomena (*sambhinna-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*), one observes the four objects—the body and so forth—collectively and cultivates the four aspects (*ākāra*), namely: impermanence (*anitya*).

"Suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Having cultivated this contemplation, one gives rise to the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) root of goodness. It is further stated: "Therefore, there are only four [foundations], neither more nor less.

Based on this, the *Jizhu* (Compendium of Notes) judges that those at the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) contemplate only the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*). The treatise also says:

"It is traditionally taught that while in meditative concentration, one contemplates the body individually through its atoms (*paramāṇu*) and moments (*kṣaṇa*); this is called the fulfillment of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*). Although...

It specifies the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). However, since ordinary outsiders (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) do not even have the leisure to contemplate the origin (*samudaya*) and other aspects of the desire realm, it seems they fall short [of this requirement].

Regarding the statement in the *Commentary on the Suffering and Origin [Truths]* (*Duḥkhasamudayavibhāṣā*), it is not without reason. As for the citation in the *Discerning Errors* (*Bian'e*) regarding the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) being subsumed by mindfulness (*smṛti*), it seems unnecessary to cite;
the underlying intent differs. As for the fact that the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) can take the three realms as their objects, Master Yu was certainly not unaware of this.
Thus it is judged that one observes the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) of the desire realm. Speaking from the perspective of the majority, this shall be reserved for future determination.
[Commentary] *Miaoxuan*: Question: Are there three grades of the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)? Answer: For a single person, there are none; for many people, there are.
Śāriputra was superior, Maudgalyāyana was middling, and the rest were all inferior. In terms of the Buddha, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka, these constitute the three grades.

[Commentary] Regarding the practitioner who reduces the objects of focus during the stage of medium patience (*madhyamā kṣānti*): if they contemplate all eight truths and cultivate thirty-two aspects (*ākāra*), this is termed the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*).

If, first relying on the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they cultivate four aspects, and subsequently, by analogy, contemplate the suffering of the two upper realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), likewise cultivating four aspects for each; [this constitutes the progression].
Furthermore, one contemplates the four aspects of the origin of desire. Next, one contemplates the four aspects of the origin of the two higher realms.
Continuing in this manner down to the path of the two higher realms, omitting the final single aspect of the vehicle, is called "one cycle of reducing by one aspect."
[Commentary] This explains one cycle. One eliminates one aspect of the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) of the lower vehicle from the upper realms.
[Sub-commentary] Furthermore, observing from the preceding stage, one eliminates from the end until the fourth round, eliminating one aspect of the Path within the Path Truth of the two upper realms.

Reaching this point, since the aspect of the path that acts as the subjective condition (*ālambaka*) no longer exists, the Truth that serves as the objective condition (*ālambana*) is also eliminated. This is the practice of the Path.

They share the same name as the conditions for the Path (*mārga-pratyaya*), and they likewise diminish together with those conditions. Therefore it is said: "If the conditions diminish, the practice (*caryā*) necessarily diminishes" (based on the first line);
however, "the practice may diminish without the conditions necessarily diminishing" (based on the latter three lines).
[Commentary] This clarifies that [the practice] reaches the four surrounding edges and is equally diminished. The *Shiqian* states:
"Under each of the Truths (*satya*), there is one practice whose name is identical to that of the object (*ālambana*), and it is likewise diminished in the same manner as the object. This is correct.

When it says "the object and practice are equally diminished," if this refers to the first practice, it points to the "diminishment of the Path" (*mārga-prahāṇa*); if it refers to the latter three practices, it points to the "correct [practice]."
This is the stage of the *yicheng* (trace-vehicle).

[Note] The fifth round involves the reduction of the practice of the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) within the Desire Realm, down to the initial practice of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) within the Suffering Truth (*duḥkhasatya*) of the Desire Realm.
Altogether, there are thirty-one rounds of reducing the objects and reducing the practices; all these are termed "Middle Patience" (*madhyakṣānti*). Only one practice remains.
Together with the object of observation, which is the realm of suffering (*duḥkha-viṣaya*), one enters the stage of "Supreme Patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).

[Commentary] The *Shiqian* states: "Both the objects and the modes of practice (*ākāra*) are reduced from the end. Consequently, for the final [stage] of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the mode of practice regarding suffering (*duḥkhākāra*) alone remains.
In total, there are thirty-one cycles; by reducing both the objects and the modes of practice, at the end there remain only one mode of practice and two moments."
That mind which contemplates the suffering of the desire realm is called the fulfillment of medium patience (*madhyā-kṣānti*).

That which, for a single moment of mind and a single mode of activity, contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, is called the accomplishment of superior patience (*adhimātrā-kṣānti*). This is because the subject that perceives (*ālambaka*) and the object perceived (*ālambana*) share the same name, "suffering";

therefore, they are retained together as one, and one enters the stage of superior patience. (The single mode of activity retained in this stage is according to what is appropriate for the practitioner, as stated in the fourth fascicle of the *Shiqian*, etc. [Commentary] Explanation:

The divination slip says: "Following conditions, each single practice does not abide for even a single kṣaṇa; thus it resembles the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga). Why is this so? There are two types of practitioners:
first, those who act out of craving (tṛṣṇā-carita), and second, those who act out of views (dṛṣṭi-carita). Craving is of two kinds: first, self-conceit (asmimāna), and second, indolence (kausīdya).
Views are also of two kinds: namely, 'I' (ātman) and 'mine' (ātmīya). Those who are attached to self-conceit cultivate impermanence (anityatā) to enter the mundane [path]."
Regarding the first dharma: for those in whom laziness increases, one cultivates the entrance of suffering; for those attached to a self, one cultivates the entrance of non-self;
for those attached to "mine," one cultivates the entrance of emptiness. Thus, one should know that the single practice retained need not be fixed to one specific type;
rather, whichever type is suitable for the practitioner should be retained in order to enter the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

[Note] This refers to the four superior and twenty-eight inferior conditions (*pratyaya*). These share the same name as the initial practice (*caryā*), yet because the practices and conditions are equally reduced, the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), fascicle 4, states:
"The seven cycles reduce the conditions; the twenty-four cycles reduce the practices."

[Commentary] Therefore, in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*), it is shown that there are reductions in both objects (*ālambana*) and modes of activity (*ākāra*). That is to say, the eight truths of the upper and lower realms are called "objects" because they are the objects of cognition;
each has sixteen modes of activity, thus totaling thirty-two, which are called "modes of activity" because they are the cognitive activities directed toward those objects.

One should know that there are seven cycles of reduction in objects and twenty-four cycles of reduction in modes of activity. This means that beneath each individual truth, there are three modes of activity.

The names [of the aspects] differ from their objects, yet they do not diminish along with the objects. Because they are named after the activities (*ākāra*), there are eight [aspects] for each of the three [truths], totaling twenty-four, which diminish according to the activities;

this is called "twenty-fourfold diminution of activity. Furthermore, beneath each of the four truths, there is one aspect whose name is identical to its object, and it diminishes along with the object.
Since these are named solely after their objects, they are called the "sevenfold diminution of objects. Thus, in the upper realms, there are four...

[The practitioner contemplates] the Truths. In the lower realm, suffering remains; only three conditions are reduced. [Specifically,] four in the upper realms and three in the lower are called the "seven cycles.

[Appendix: *Bian'e* (Discerning Errors) states: Regarding the listing of "impurity" (*aśubha*) beneath "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*) in the diagram, according to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, all list "emptiness" and do not include the name "impurity.
Therefore, one knows that this is not a discrepancy arising from different translations. In the *Fuxingji* (Record of Aiding Practice), Jingxi...
At one time, it was simply transcribed. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is the initial gateway.
Because it overturns the perversion of purity, which gives rise to lustful desire, one speaks of "impurity" in order to destroy that notion of purity; this leads to liberation.

However, as it is not a contemplation of reality, it is [merely] impure and does not enter into the enumeration of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*). This should be examined. [Commentary: Fearing that people might not understand how to proceed from the preceding to the following, [the author] provides this [explanation].

From the beginning to the end, one contemplates the Four Truths in direct order; then, returning from the top back down, one proceeds from the end to the beginning, gradually reducing the objects and modes of contemplation in reverse order.
Therefore, this is illustrated by a diagram to facilitate easy understanding. [Supplement] The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is like carrying a heavy burden."

Therefore, it is suffering (*duḥkha*). Because it is internally devoid of a person (*puruṣa*), it is empty (*śūnya*). Because it is not ultimate, it is impermanent (*anitya*). Because it lacks sovereignty, it is non-self (*anātman*).

Furthermore, because it appears equally, it is the origin (*samudaya*). Because it is like the principle of a seed, it is the cause (*hetu*). Because it is the principle of accomplishment, it is the condition (*pratyaya*). Because it is the principle of continuity, it is arising (*jāti*).
Just as a jar and other objects are accomplished through the combination of various conditions such as a lump of clay, a wheel, a string, and wood; and furthermore—

It is a "cause" (*hetu*) in the sense of drawing forth; a "collection" (*samudaya*) in the sense of appearing; an "origination" (*jāti*) in the sense of producing; and a "condition" (*pratyaya*) in the sense of being a basis.

Furthermore, it is "cessation" (*nirodha*) because it is the non-continuation of what was continuous and the severance [of the stream]; "tranquility" (*śānta*) because it is free from the three conditioned characteristics; and "excellent" (*praṇīta*) in the sense of being sublime and wholesome.

Therefore it is "sublime" (*praṇīta*). Because it is supremely secure, it is "detached" (*viveka*). Furthermore, because it signifies a "universal path," it is the "path" (*mārga*). Because it accords with correct principle, it is "right" (*nyāya*).
Because it correctly leads toward [liberation], it is the "practice" (*pratipad*). Because it can transcend forever, it is the "deliverance" (*nairyāṇika*).

[Note] The meaning of the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) is fully explained in Fascicle 3, Part 2 (17) of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*) and in the first fascicle of the *Xixuan* (Analysis of the Profundities).

[Record] This explains the meaning of the sixteen aspects as stated in the *Fuxing*: "The four aspects under 'suffering' are impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
Because one contemplates that which arises from causes and conditions as arising and ceasing moment by moment, it is impermanent; being oppressed by impermanence, it is suffering."

Therefore it is suffering (*duḥkha*). Because neither a single characteristic nor distinct characteristics can be apprehended, it is empty (*śūnya*). Because "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*) cannot be apprehended, it is non-self (*anātman*).

Regarding the four lines concerning origination (*samudaya*): that which arises from causes and conditions, the combination of outflows (*āsrava*) capable of inviting the fruit of suffering, is called origination.

To contemplate the six causes that can produce the fruit of suffering is called "cause" (*hetu*). To contemplate the four conditions that can produce the fruit of suffering is called "condition" (*pratyaya*).

To undergo further existence and suffering again is called "arising" (*utpāda*). The cessation of the four lower aspects, the cessation, extinction, and sublime detachment through which all afflictions are extinguished, is called "cessation" (*nirodha*).
The exhaustion of all suffering is called "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*). Being supreme among all things is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*). To transcend birth and death is [the meaning of] "transcendence."

It is called "leaving" (*niḥsaraṇa*). The four aspects of the lower path are the "path" (*mārga*), the "right track" (*pratipad*), and the "vehicle" (*yāna*). That which can lead to *nirvāṇa* is called the "path. That which is not a perverted dharma is called "right" (*samyak*).
That which is the sphere of activity for the noble ones (*ārya*) is called the "track. That which conveys one to the three liberations is called the "vehicle."

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the merging of the two upper realms into a single set of the Four Noble Truths: because they share the same stage of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-bhūmi*), one contemplates them by analogy with what is manifest in the desire realm.
This is explained exhaustively through five meanings in the *Xie Xuan* (Analysis of the Profundities), etc.

Thus, when the afflictions underlying the Four Noble Truths of the three realms are suppressed, at the time of realizing the truth, the two upper realms are likewise designated as "inferential patience and knowledge" (*anvaya-dharma-kṣānti-jñāna*, etc.).

[Supplement] *Píxuán* (Analysis of the Profound) states: The Four Truths of the two upper realms share five points of similarity; therefore, they may be contemplated together. First, they are identical in being the realm of gods (*deva-gati*).

Second, they are identical in their meditative stage (*dhyāna-bhūmi*). Third, they are identical in being born by transformation (*upapāduka*). Fourth, they are identical in the nature of their afflictions (*kleśa*).
Fifth, they are identical in their ability to induce the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state.

[Note] Furthermore, the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) are simply gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanāmukha*). In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, they are termed the "sixteen truths" (*ṣoḍaśasatya*), because they take the sense of "truthfully and minutely observing" as their meaning.
[Commentary] The *Nirvāṇa-kāśyapa-parivarta* states that the "sixteen practices" are the sixteen truths (*satya*).

These are also the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), and so forth. Since the afflictions have not yet been abandoned at this stage, it is known that these still take the sense of "thoroughly examining" and "thoroughly observing" the truths as their object.

[Note] Furthermore, regarding these reduced stages of contemplation (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the *Miaoxuan* (3.8) groups them into eight cycles by following the practice according to the objects of contemplation;

this constitutes eight rounds based solely on the Eight Truths (*aṣṭasatya*). The *Sijiaoyi* (2.12) states: "The middle stage of patience (*madhyakṣānti*) involves ten cycles of abbreviated contemplation.

This refers to the latter seven truths, where the practice follows the objects of contemplation to form seven rounds, while opening up the three [objects] to be reduced from the suffering of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The practice consists of three cycles, totaling ten sections. The *Miaoxuan* (8.8) states: "The three cycles of abbreviated contemplation advance one toward the stage of 'Patience for Superiority' (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
Since the three realms are not outside the Four Noble Truths, and since practice follows conditions, the latter three truths are reduced; hence they are called the 'three cycles.
The various texts differ in their detail and brevity, as these are merely adaptations to different capacities."

[Commentary] Regarding the eight stages mentioned in the *Miaoxuan*: the text states that "the contemplation of the stage of patience (*kṣānti-dharma*) consists of correctly contemplating the suffering of the desire realm and the suffering of the form and formless realms;

the origin of formations in the desire realm and the origin of formations in the form and formless realms; the cessation of formations in the desire realm and the cessation of formations in the form and formless realms;
and the path leading to the abandonment of the desire realm and the path leading to the abandonment of the form and formless realms. These thirty-two moments of mind are called..."

This constitutes the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). At a later time, the practitioner gradually diminishes both the mental applications (*prayoga*) and their objects (*ālambana*), and further rectifies the correct contemplation of suffering in the desire, form, and formless realms, continuing until the contemplation of the path for abandoning [defilements] in the desire realm—excluding the contemplation of the path for abandoning [defilements] in the form and formless realms.

From this point, it is called middle patience (*madhya-kṣānti*). Thereafter, one again rectifies the correct contemplation of suffering in the desire realm and contemplates suffering in the form and formless realms.
...up to contemplating the cessation of formations of the form and formless realms, excluding the path and all paths.

Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, the suffering of the form and formless realms, up to contemplating the cessation of formations of the desire realm, excluding the cessation of formations of the form and formless realms.

Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the desire realm, up to contemplating the origination of formations of the form and formless realms, excluding all cessations, as well as excluding the desire realm.

The elements cease. Furthermore, one correctly contemplates the suffering of desire, up to contemplating the origination of formations within the realm of desire, excluding the origination of formations in the realms of form and formlessness.
Again, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the realms of form and formlessness within the realm of desire, excluding all origination.

Again, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the realm of desire, excluding the suffering of the realms of form and formlessness. Again, one correctly contemplates the suffering of the realm of desire as being constant, continuous, and uninterrupted.

[The practitioner] distances [themselves from them]. When observing in this way, they develop a deep sense of weary aversion (*nirveda*) and further diminish [their afflictions], contemplating only two moments of mind regarding a single category [of suffering].

Such patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), observed in this intermediate manner, is called "intermediate patience" (*madhyamā kṣānti*).

Furthermore, contemplating the suffering of the desire realm with a single moment of mind is called "superior patience" (*adhimātrā kṣānti*). Next, after the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) have arisen, immediately thereafter—
The "Dharma-patience regarding the suffering of birth" (jō-kuhō-nin) is now explained by following its practice according to its conditions; this constitutes the intent of eight sections.

Regarding the "ten-fold contraction of contemplation" (jū-ban-shuku-kan) in the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), the text states: "In the lower patience (*ge-nin*), one performs the contemplation of the Truths of Phenomena (*hō-tai*) across sixteen aspects;

in the middle patience (*chū-nin*), one performs the ten-fold contraction of contemplation; in the upper patience (*jō-nin*), one contemplates only the lower four aspects of the suffering of the desire realm. Here, we clarify only [the latter].

This refers to the Middle Patience (*madhyā-kṣānti*). Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* (Exquisite Profundity) clarifies that the Middle Patience involves three successive stages of contraction in contemplation (*guan*).
Here, too, the practice is explained in terms of following conditions (*pratyaya*), which elucidates the meaning of these three stages.
[Note on the Benefits of the Four Roots of Goodness]: The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) necessarily leads to Nirvāṇa;

the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*) never severs the roots of goodness. (The *Shiqian* [Sub-commentary] Vol. 4 says: "The stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) is advancing; the stage of Heat is retreating; the stage of Summits is the boundary of both advancing and retreating, like the peak of a mountain. (Text). The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) Vol. 2 asks: "If one who has attained the stages of Heat and Summits can regress, why is it called the 'Stage of Nature' (*gotrabhūmi*)? Answer:

Although such a person may commit evil and fall into hell, once they have entered and received their retribution, they do not enter again. Because they possess the roots of goodness of the Stage of Nature, they are able to attain the fruit of the Sages. (Text). Now, what is the difference between "necessarily leading to Nirvāṇa" and "never severing the roots of goodness"? It is because although the stage of Heat...

Having committed evil and entered hell, one will not remain there for long; later, one will certainly be reborn among humans or devas and realize the fruit of nirvana. Even if one reaches the "peak stage" (*mūrdhan*) and subsequently regresses to enter the evil realms, one will certainly not give rise to great wrong views, because the roots of goodness have not been severed. There is only a distinction between clarity and obscurity, or depth and shallowness;
the roots of goodness themselves remain the same.

[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* states: "If one discusses the four roots of goodness in general, they are also called the 'four patiences' (*kṣānti*). However, because the stage of patience (*kṣānti-dharma*) does not regress, it alone receives the specific name 'patience.

As for the stage of 'warmth' (*uṣmagata*), if one encounters adverse conditions and regresses, one may commit the five heinous crimes, slander the Vaipulya sutras, become an icchantika, and fall into the Avīci Hell.
As for the stage of 'summit' (*mūrdhan*), even if one encounters adverse conditions and regresses, although..."
They do not sever their roots of goodness; yet, because they still commit the five heinous crimes and the like, this question is raised once more.

The intent of the answer clarifies that although one may create evil and fall into suffering, once the retribution for the sin is exhausted and one is liberated from suffering, not only does one no longer commit evil, but one can furthermore uphold goodness and realize the state of a sage.

Furthermore, below, the distinct characteristics of the roots of goodness of *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit) are distinguished. The answer clarifies that although those in these two stages equally fall into suffering due to having committed evil...
Regarding suffering, there are views of its arising and non-arising, as well as differences between severing and not severing the roots of goodness. The commentary explains:

among the four roots of goodness, if one attains the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), although there may be regression—such as severing the roots of goodness, committing acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), or falling into the evil destinies—one will not wander for long, as one is certain to reach Nirvana. If this is so, what need is there for the "Aids to Liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*)?
If there are no obstacles, one is close to the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*), for this is identical in its mode of activity to the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).

If one attains the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*), although there may be regression and the increase of unwholesome states, one ultimately never severs the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). [Appendix] The stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summits" belong to the internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the Abhidharma treasury;

the stage of "Nature" (*gotrabhū*) belongs to the internal ordinary beings who have transcended [the lower stages]. Because these internal ordinary stages are equivalent, "Heat" and "Summits" are classified as the "stage of nature. Nature...
The *bhūmi* (ground) is explained in the seventh fascicle.

[Note] Patience prevents falling into the evil realms. (*Sijiao yi*, Fascicle 22, states: "Although the lower and middle levels of patience may give rise to afflictions and evil karma, one does not undergo rebirth in the three miserable paths; rather, one is born among humans and devas for hundreds of thousands of millions of lifetimes.
If the upper level of patience is perfected, there remain only seven more births as humans or devas.")
[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: To be capable of enduring and desiring [the truth] regarding the Four Noble Truths is called the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).
In the stage of the Peak Dharma (*mūrdhan*), one employs correct means to diligently cultivate and advance the roots of goodness of the Peak Dharma, relying on the concentrations of the six stages.

If the roots of goodness of the Peak Dharma advance, one then gives rise to the Patience of Accordance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), which likewise takes the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths as its object. At that time, there is faith...
These five kinds of wholesome dharmas all attain the status of faculties (*indriya*). Because of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), one is able to endure and aspire toward the Four Noble Truths;
this is called the stage of patience (*kṣānti-dharma*). Now, because this wisdom is strong and delusion is weak, one cannot be moved by any evils.
Due to the greatness of the power of patience, all evil thoughts undergo non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). It is like the lion king, whom other beasts avoid from afar.

Therefore, one does not fall into the evil destinies. The commentary explains: When one attains *kṣānti* (receptivity), although at the end of life one abandons the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and passes away, one progresses without regression;
one does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*) and does not fall into the evil realms.

However, while the verse mentions only that one does not fall into the destinies, it is understood by implication that one does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution. This is because those who commit the deeds of immediate retribution necessarily fall into the evil destinies.

Therefore, as previously established, there is no falling back from the stage of *kṣānti*. One does not fall into the various evil destinies (*durgati*) at this stage because one has already distanced oneself from the karma and afflictions that lead to them.
If one reaches the stage of *kṣānti*, one will take birth in only a limited number of places; for among the afflictions, one has attained the quality of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma*).
"Destinies" refers to the various evil destinies. "Births" refers to egg-born and moisture-born births. "Places" refers to the realm of non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva*) and Uttarakuru.

Regarding the Great Brahmā realm: as for the body, it refers to the bodies of *śaṇḍha*, *paṇḍaka*, and those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*). As for existence, it refers to the eighth [birth] and so forth.

As for the afflictions, they refer to the afflictions abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*). These are obtained according to what is appropriate during the stages of Patience (*kṣānti*) in the lower and upper realms;
that is, through lower Patience, one obtains non-arising in the miserable destinies, while the remaining non-arising is obtained only upon reaching upper Patience. [Supplement]: Regarding *śaṇḍha*:
Born with an incomplete male organ; a paṇḍaka (eunuch); one who undergoes transformation; one whose gender changes in this life; excluded from the categories of the Dharma.

[Note] First, entering the state beyond birth (*janma-vivikta*): (Because this single moment is the entry into the Path of Seeing, it is identical to the Path of Seeing in that one leaves behind birth in the four miserable realms.)

[Commentary: The treatise states that although the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) abide within the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they are capable of entering the state of correct nature free from outflows (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Although the verse does not explicitly mention the relinquishing [of these dharmas] at the end of life, since one enters the state of correct nature free from outflows immediately thereafter, it follows by implication that there is no relinquishing at the end of life.
For what reason is it only this [state] that can enter the state free from outflows? [For one has already attained the status of an ordinary person.]

Because it is a non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), one is able to know the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) and abandon the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Therefore, these four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) each have three grades, due to the differences in the lineages (*gotra*) of the śrāvakas and others. [Supplement] The *Mahāvibhāṣā* states: "The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*)."
It acts as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
There is no phenomenon more swift in its revolution than the mind that could act as an obstacle at that time, preventing one from entering the clear realization (*abhisamaya*) of the Noble Truths.
Thus one knows that this dharma is definitively non-retrogressive; having entered the state of rightness (*samyaktva*), one is freed from birth in the four miserable destinies.
[Question: In the section on "Middle Patience" (*madhya-kṣānti*) in the *Xuánwén*, it says: "One merely gives rise to two moments of mind (*citta*) and contemplates a single aspect (*eka-ākāra*).

Why, then, does the *Shìqiàn* say that those four moments of mind share the same aspect and the same object (*ālambana*)? [Answer: The two moments of mind in Middle Patience resemble the two [stages] of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).

It is the mind. Because it is attained through the two minds of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), even though true realization arises after the mind of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*);
since this semblance-understanding exists at the present stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*), it is called "resembling. This is stated in reference to a single practice (*ekākāra*).

Since there are only two minds involved, it says "only performing two minds. Regarding the contemplation of a single practice, if the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) speaks of "four minds," it refers to two for each [of the two] objects and practices (*ālambana* and *ākāra*).
Therefore, it is said that those four minds share the same practice and the same object.
[Commentary] This section of analysis concerns the contemplative mind within the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*). Question:

The *Xuánwén* (Profound Text) speaks of two minds contemplating one practice, whereas the *Shìqiàn* (Sub-commentary) asks how four minds can share the same object and practice. In the answer, first the meaning of what is stated in the *Xuánwén* is clarified.
Just as with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna), one contemplates in this manner;

this is called the meaning of "intermediate patience" (madhya-kṣānti). Therefore, the *Miaoxuan* directly uses the two moments of mind—patience and knowledge—which resemble the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma), to provide the answer.
The full text of this section is found on page sixty of the original volume. From the phrase "because of the following," the reason for this resemblance is set forth. Within this question:

This was not explicitly stated [in the question], but is supplemented in the answer. Regarding the phrase "explained by way of a single practice" (*yī xíng*), this indicates the meaning of the "two minds" in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Words).

As for the passage in the *Shìqiǎn* (Explanatory Notes), it refers to two [minds] each regarding conditions (*yuán*) and practice (*xíng*), based on the principle that the four minds are identical in their practice and their object (*yuán*).
[Supplement] Regarding the four minds being identical in practice and object: the *Póshā* (Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra) states that they decrease down to [the mind of] suffering (*kū*).
Following the mind of dharma-patience (dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti), one attains right determination (samyaktva-niyāma). Those four minds share the same mode of activity and the same object;

that is to say, they are like the supreme worldly dharma (laukikāgra-dharma), wherein the two minds of the dharma-patience of suffering (duḥkha-dharmanidhyāna-kṣānti) and the dharma-knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-dharmajñāna) share the same object.

This is so. Furthermore, although the two minds of *kṣānti* (patience) and *jñāna* (wisdom) can only be induced to arise as untainted (*anāsrava*) and produce true realization after the mind of the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), in the present stage of "Middle Patience" (*madhyama-kṣānti*), there exists a semblance of these two minds—*kṣānti* and *jñāna*.
Therefore, the *Xuánwén* states: "It is like the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* and *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*. [Appendix] *Biànyuē* says: "The objects and the practices are each..."
These two phrases appear to be separated [from the main text] as if they were impossible [to connect].

One should know that the mention of "four minds" in the *Śāstra* (the *Jian*) refers to the two minds of "semblance patience" (*sārūpya-kṣānti*) within the stage of medium patience (*madhyama-kṣānti*), the single momentary mind of the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), and the single momentary mind of the "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). This remains for further investigation.

[Commentary on the *Sub-commentary* (Jieshan), Vol. 4]: The *Śāstra* cited in this passage clarifies that those who cultivate the "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) stage range from the Desire Realm up to the Sphere of Nothingness—eight stages in total—with nine grades each, plus one person who is still bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*). This makes a total of seventy-three persons. Thus, the Heat stage extends throughout the three realms.
How then can the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* say, "Such a Heat stage is a dharma of the Form Realm and does not exist in the Desire Realm"? One must understand that [the sūtra] refers to... [text truncated].

The practitioner who cultivates this penetrates the three realms (*tridhātu*). The "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharma that is generated is based on the meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

The *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) quotes the *Pingjia* (Critique School), stating: "All of these are dharmas of the form realm, abiding in the stages of meditative concentration" (text). The *Niepan Shu* (Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) provides an explanation in three senses, saying:

first, because the generation of the "Heat" dharma through observation primarily relies on meditative concentration, it is spoken of in terms of what is predominant; second, according to the intermediate [view], all three realms [possess it].

One is able to give rise to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Since the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) occupies the central position, it is called "form-existence" (*rūpabhava*). These three [realms] are spoken of in terms of their locations;
it is easier to give rise to the stage of Heat in the form realm than it is in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). (Text)
[Commentary] This clarifies the selection of seventy-three individuals regarding the *uṣmagata* (Heat) stage. The *Nirvāṇa-śūtra* explains three interpretations. First, *Zhuāngyán* states:

"The mind associated with the ten wholesome actions of the desire realm is called the 'Lightning Flash Samādhi' (*vidyut-pradīpa-samādhi*). Because it is attained at times and lost at other times, these individuals are said to possess the nature of afflictions (*kleśa-dharmatā*);
their specific categories are not differentiated. However, if one discusses the method [of cultivation], there are certainly nine grades of samādhi and afflictions."

There are likewise nine grades. By means of the nine concentrations (*dhyāna*), one abandons the nine delusions. Including the single individual of "Lightning Flash" (*vidyut-prabhā*), they total ten.

Within the four *dhyānas* of the Form Realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) and the three *śūnyatās* of the Formless Realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*), there are likewise nine grades of delusion and nine grades of concentration. Seven times nine makes sixty-three;
adding the previous ten individuals, the total is seventy-three. Second, Kai-shan says: "There is no separate method distinct from 'Lightning Flash,' nor is there..."

The method differs from the "Lightning" (vidyut-prabhā) concentration. In the Lightning concentration alone, nine concentrations are established in opposition to the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*).

The first grade of concentration consists solely of real dharmas (*dravyadharma*) and does not yet rely on the conventional (*prajñapti*); it is still a state where afflictions are being resisted, but has not yet been able to subdue them.

The second grade of concentration, acting together with the first grade as a continuous conventional entity (*santati-prajñapti*), only then exerts its power to subdue the afflictions of the first grade.
Regarding the third grade of afflictions: one suppresses the second grade of afflictions, and so on up to the ninth grade of meditative absorption, suppressing the eighth grade of afflictions.
With only the single remaining grade of the ninth affliction of the desire realm left, it draws forth the single grade of the first dhyāna absorption to arise and suppress it together with it.

This applies likewise to the four dhyānas and the three formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*); for each, there are nine grades of afflictions and nine grades of absorption, continuing thus up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

The nine grades of concentration suppress eight grades of afflictions; the remaining ninth grade of affliction still persists. One further employs the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to suppress the ninth grade of affliction of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Eight times nine is seventy-two; one then adds the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception to complete it.

In total, there are seventy-three. Regarding the three types of persons who possess analytical knowledge (*pratisaṃvid*), there are two different views. First, concerning those whose obstacles to the future are severed: their analytical knowledge is divided into nine grades.

One grade of analytical knowledge corresponds to the abandonment of one grade of afflictions. Furthermore, for a person who possesses the nature of afflictions, there is a mind associated with the ten wholesome paths of action;
added to the preceding, this makes ten. Such a person possessing afflictions [attains] the first grade of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Together...

When one grade of affliction is abandoned, the liberation from that grade follows. Corresponding to the abandonment of each grade of affliction, there are nine meditative attainments (dhyānas and formless absorptions) for each of the four dhyānas and three formless absorptions;

thus, there are seventy-three [attainments]. Regarding those who possess both natures as fundamental obstacles: this refers to the nine grades of concentration in the *anāgāmya* (preparatory stage), which abandon the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm.
This includes taking one person of the desire realm who possesses the nature of full affliction and adding them to this.
The nine grades become ten. These ten persons all possess the future-dhyāna (anāgāmya) of the first dhyāna, which severs the nine grades of afflictions of the first dhyāna;
the future-nine-grade concentration of the second dhyāna, which severs the nine grades of afflictions of the second dhyāna;

and so on, up to the future concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), which severs the nine grades of afflictions of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana). There are likewise seventy-three [types], as stated in the Commentary.

Question: It was previously explained that "heat" (*uṣmagata*) is a phenomenon belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). How can it be said to extend throughout all three realms and constitute seventy-three types of persons?
Answer: For a beginner, one must rely upon the four dhyānas. However, according to later stages of proficiency, it extends throughout the three realms.

Furthermore, while formerly in the state of an ordinary person outside the Buddha's teaching, one had already attained these seventy-three concentrations; now, having entered the Buddha-dharma, one practices the contemplation of the stage of heat. This is so.

Furthermore, in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, Kāśyapa says: "The Buddha taught that the three factors of life-force (*āyu*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—their conjunction is called a sentient being (*sattva*).
If this principle were followed, a sentient being should first possess warmth. Why, then, do you say that the factor of warmth arises because of a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)?"
The Buddha said: "Just as I have now explained the *uṣmagata* (heat) stage, it must be attained through skillful means; it was originally non-existent and now exists.

Such a *uṣmagata* is a dharma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and does not exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Regarding 'due to a virtuous friend,' it is only by relying on the instructions of a virtuous friend and practicing accordingly that one first attains it.
Now, this commentary is provided specifically to clarify the realms and stages to which the *uṣmagata* extends; therefore, it is cited here."

The question within the divination text (śāstra) is the inquiry; the answer states that, based on the person capable of cultivating the stage of Heat (uṣmagata), it is said that Heat pervades the three realms.
However, the Heat being cultivated must necessarily arise in dependence upon the meditative concentration of the form realm (rūpadhātu). This is cited as the critique of the opposing school.

[The *Shu*] states: Regarding the passage in the *Xuanwen* [of Jizang], it says: "The Dharma of the Summit (*mūrdhan*) consists of the wholesome roots of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). There are those that are mobile and those that are immobile; those that abide and those that do not abide; those that are difficult and those that are not difficult;

those that are subject to severance and those that are not; those that involve falling back and those that do not. Within the category from 'mobile' to 'falling back,' there are two: the lower is 'Heat' (*uṣmagata*), and the upper is 'Summit.
Within the category from 'immobile' to 'not falling back,' there are two: the lower is 'Patience' (*kṣānti*), and the upper is 'Supreme Worldly Dharmas' (*laukikāgradharma*). [End of] *Shiqian*.
It says: This passage is the same as the *Śāstra*. For the *Śāstra* states: "Some say that there are two types of wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) in the desire realm:

the lower is Heat (*uṣmagata*), and the higher is Summits (*mūrdhan*). There are two types of wholesome roots in the form realm: the lower is Patience (*kṣānti*), and the higher is the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

The Master of Evaluation (*viniścayakāra*) says: "One should not speak thus. It should be said: All of these are dharmas of the form realm; they are dharmas abiding in the stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*); they are the practice of the noble ones (*āryacaryā*)."

This is correct. Now, following the *Píngjiā* (Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa), it says "the realm of form" (*rūpadhātu*). These [terms] merely distinguish the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) based on their differences, such as being "shakable" (*cala*) and so forth, in contrast to the four distinct types.
From the "shakable" up to the "partially shakable" (*heya*) there are two; from the "unshakable" (*acala*) up to the "non-regressing" (*anivartana*) there are two.
Although they all reside within the realm of form, because of the differences in the depth and shallowness of the roots of goodness, they result in [these distinctions].

The distinctions between these states are not uniform. "Movement" (*dong*) refers to being moved by external conditions. "Abiding" (*zhu*) refers to dwelling for a long time in the stages of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit).

"Difficulty" (*nan*) refers to encountering obstacles within the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*. "Severance" (*duan*) refers to cutting off the roots of goodness. "Retreat" (*tui*) refers to falling back into the commission of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*). "Non-movement" and so forth are the opposites of these.
The above commentary from the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* provides a threefold interpretation, which may be understood according to the text.

[Supplement] The *Vibhāṣā* states: In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten types of persons: namely, first, the ordinary person bound by all fetters; second, those who have eliminated one grade of the fetters, up to those who have eliminated all nine grades.
In the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*), there are nine types: those who have eliminated one grade of the fetters, up to those who have eliminated all nine grades.

There are no persons bound by all fetters in the first dhyāna, because this is being discussed specifically in reference to the desire realm. This continues in the same manner up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

In some places there are nine; although this is also the case for the Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma), there are seventy-three persons in total.

Some say that because the Non-Perception Sphere (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) is characterized by the deepest attachment to meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), one cannot cultivate the Heat-dharma (uṣmagata);
therefore, they exclude that single stage. The Master of Evaluation (pūrvapakṣa-viniścaya) states: the *Vibhāṣā* was compiled by various Arhats, yet it contains four great [divisions].
The Arhats provide the correct interpretation for the school: first, Śrīlāta; second, Ghoṣaka; third, Dharmatrāta; and fourth, Buddhadeva.

The "Noble Practices" (ārya-caryā) refer to the stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and so forth, as these are not the practices of ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana). [Supplementary Note: Bian’eo states:

Regarding those capable of cultivating the supernormal powers (abhijñā) throughout the three realms and so forth, it is generally the case that when the Dharma of Heat (uṣmagata-dharma) arises, it occurs for the most part while one has attained meditative absorption (dhyāna-samādhi) of a higher stage within the Desire Realm.

The commentary cites the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* as stating that warmth (*uṣman*) is a phenomenon belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). One should understand that this refers to the Buddha’s refutation of Kāśyapa’s objection regarding the three factors of life-force, warmth, and consciousness.
Because [Kāśyapa] had spoken of sentient beings possessing warmth, the Buddha replied with the words, “Such warmth and so forth.

Later it says that it is easy to produce the factor of warmth in the form realm, whereas it is difficult in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). This clearly demonstrates that it is difficult to produce the factor of warmth while practicing the meditative concentration of the desire realm.
One must cultivate the dhyāna-concentration of the form realm; only then will it become easy to give rise to the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*). Please examine this carefully.
△ Third, the conclusion revealing alternative names:

The aforementioned stages of the inner ordinary person (*adhyātma-prthagjana*) and the outer ordinary person (*bāhya-prthagjana*) are collectively termed the "stage of the ordinary person" (*prthagjana-bhūmi*), and are also called the "seven stages of skillful means" (*saptavidha-upāya-bhūmi*).
[Commentary] These seven stages serve as the expedient means for entering the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). In various texts, some refer to them as the "five expedients" (*pañca-upāya*);

this is because the stages of stabilizing the mind (*sthiti-citta*) and breaking through hindrances (*vighna-bheda*) are not counted. Thus, the general and specific applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are simply combined into one. (Text)
[Supplementary Note] Because the stabilization of the mind is not correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*).
