△ Part Two: The Two Sages and Three [Patriarchs]. First, the headings and the arrangement of sections.

Next, the stages of the noble ones (ārya-bhūmi) are explained, also divided into three: first, the path of seeing (darśana-mārga), which is the first fruit; second, the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), which comprises the second and third fruits; and third, the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa-mārga), which is the fourth fruit.

[□ Note] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: "The common name for these is 'sage' (*ārya*). 'Sage' takes 'correctness' as its meaning. One abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and enters the nature of correctness.

[■ Record] The *Sijiaoyi* states: "Through the true illumination of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), one abandons the nature of an ordinary person and attains entry into the nature of a sage.
Because true wisdom perceives the principle and severs the causes of the same category, they are called 'sages'."

[Note] The first fruit (*srotāpanna*) involves seeing the principle and destroying delusions; this is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). The second and third fruits involve repeatedly contemplating the Truth;

this is called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). When the delusions of the fourth fruit are exhausted, it is called "Beyond Training" (*aśaikṣa*). The *Wenju* (8.4) states: "To investigate the Truth and sever delusions is called 'Training' (*śaikṣa*);
when the Truth is fully realized and delusions are exhausted, it is called 'Beyond Training' (*aśaikṣa*). (Text)

[Commentary] This clarifies the meaning of the four fruits and the three paths. The first fruit is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) because those who have attained the first fruit destroy the eighty-eight latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of seeing;
they first perceive the principle of true reality as exclusively emptiness. Therefore, it is called the Path of Seeing.
The second and third fruits are called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) because those who have attained the second and third fruits again give rise to mental objects of contemplation.

Taking as an object the Truth previously perceived, one exhausts all afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through the abandonment of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). One then proceeds to abandon the afflictions of the higher realms;

this is "cultivating the cause while carrying the fruit," and is therefore called the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). As for the four fruits being called the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*):
it means that those who have attained the four fruits have exhausted all afflictions of the three realms and have nothing further to learn regarding any of their activities. Thus, they are so named.
This is called the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). Under the following text, it explains and verifies "No-More-Learning.

This means that while one is precisely engaged in the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to investigate the Real, one uses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) to sever delusions; "severing" here refers specifically to severing the false. "False" (*wang*) is synonymous with "delusion" (*huo*).

When there remains something of the Real or the False that has not yet been fully exhausted, this is termed "Learning" (*śaikṣa*), which refers to the three preceding fruits [of the path]. If that which is investigated—the Real—is already fully exhausted...

The afflictions to be abandoned have been completely exhausted, and regarding all matters of training, there is nothing further to be learned; therefore, they are called "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
However, this is explained according to the present teaching; if one looks toward subsequent teachings, the distance is indeed far.

[Note] However, regarding the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*): following the mind-moment of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), there arises the true clarity of "suffering-acceptance" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).

(Alternatively, it is said that "suffering-acceptance" is the arising of clarity; this refers to the "dharma-acceptance of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) within the truth of suffering in the desire realm. "Arising of clarity" refers to the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), meaning the arising of true wisdom. Within the eight truths, one gives rise to eight acceptances and eight knowledges, totaling sixteen moments of mind.

The "Gate of Existence" (*yōmon*) designates fifteen moments of mind as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) for the candidate for the first fruit (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*); the sixteenth moment is...

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) subsumes the first fruit (*prathamaphala*). By analyzing the gate of profound emptiness, the sixteen moments of mind are termed the "path of seeing" (*darśanamārga*), which constitutes the first fruit.
From the second fruit onward, one then belongs to the path of cultivation. Since the tenets of various schools differ, there is no need to reconcile them here.

Although our own school primarily employs the gate of existence (*sattvadvāra*), the Korean master, wishing to facilitate understanding, provisionally follows the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatādvāra*) by annotating that the path of seeing is the first fruit.

[Commentary] This clarifies the meaning of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) in relation to the [four] truths (*satya*). The first three sentences clarify the truths from which the first fruit arises and the development of the sixteen moments of mind (*citta-kṣaṇa*).

Regarding this, there are two explanations. The first states that "the true insight of the patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti-bhūta-prajñā*) refers specifically to the dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) within the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The second states that "the arising of the insight of the patience regarding suffering" refers to the truth of suffering of the desire realm.

This refers to the subsequent dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*). However, while "patience" (*kṣānti*) serves as the cause and "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as the fruit, this section speaks of them in terms of the causal relationship between patience and knowledge.
That is to say, immediately following the mind of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), true knowledge clearly arises. [Appendix] Bian’e states:

The two fruits [of the path of seeing] belong to the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). One should know that the two schools—the Madhyamaka and the Yogācāra—dispute only over the duration of a single moment. And...

Although the Śūnyavāda school takes the sixteen moments of mind as the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one should know that beyond these sixteen moments, they still belong to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
How could it be that from the second fruit onward they belong to the path of cultivation? I privately maintain that the commentaries are fundamentally the same;

it was only because the characters for "from the second fruit onward" (*èrguòqù*) were somewhat obscure that I have clarified them. Furthermore, the *Biànyuó* states: "Moreover, this accords with the phrasing of the Śūnyavāda school."

It should be understood that the Master [Zhiyi], for the time being, makes a provisional judgment based on the fruits [of the path]: he identifies the first fruit as the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga), and from the second fruit onwards as the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
This is not according to the Gate of Emptiness (śūnyatā-dvāra). Personally, I maintain that since this judgment is identical to that of the Gate of Emptiness, [it must be so].
It may also be said that this conforms to emptiness.

[Note] Regarding the eight patiences and eight knowledges, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The first fifteen moments constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because one sees what has never been seen before."

Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one produces the Dharma-Patience (*dharmakṣānti*) which is untainted (*anāsrava*) and takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object. Following that Patience, one produces Dharma-Knowledge (*dharmajñāna*).

Next, taking the suffering of the remaining realms as its object, one produces Subsequent Patience (*anvayakṣānti*) and Subsequent Knowledge (*anvayajñāna*). It is likewise for each of the truths of origin, cessation, and the path, with two [moments] arising for each.
This clarifies that the fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). It is called "never before seen" because it refers to the principle perceived by the path of seeing;
since this has never been seen from the outset and is only now being seen for the first time, it is so designated.

If one were practicing the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) regarding the principle already seen, it could be said that one had previously seen it within the process of seeing. Regarding the term "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*), there are two [meanings].
Regarding the meaning: first, because one enters the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) in a single *kṣaṇa*.
Second, because one focuses exclusively on the principle of untainted emptiness (*anāsrava-śūnyatā-tattva*), not allowing other thoughts to intervene; thus it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).

As for the statement that "patience (*kṣānti*) is followed by the arising of knowledge (*jñāna*"), these sixteen moments of mind originally arise simultaneously. How could there be any sequence? Now...
Regarding the phrase "in succession": this refers to discussing a sequence within that which has no sequence. [Appendix] Bian’e states: "The same applies to each producing two.
According to the two characters of the treatise, there should be four characters; for under the Truth of Suffering, there are both Dharma-patience (dharma-kṣānti) and Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna).

The two—receptivity (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*)—are likewise fourfold under each of the three truths of origin, cessation, and the path. I [the author] say: although the two sets of four differ in their terminology, their meaning is the same.

Regarding the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the treatise explains that it begins with the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñānakṣānti*) and ends with the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*). Within this, there are fifteen moments in total, all of which constitute the path of seeing.

It is subsumed [under the path of cultivation]. Because one sees truths not yet seen, when reaching the sixteenth moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*), there is not a single principle of truth that has not been seen;
seeing it now is like practicing what was previously seen. Therefore, it is subsumed under the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). These two lines of verse originally appeared later.

The verses on the sequence of the "Worldly Supreme Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) and its immediate successor follow below; they were originally placed earlier. Regarding "immediate succession" (*anantara*), the treatise states:

"Immediately following the worldly supreme roots of goodness, there arises the 'receptivity to the knowledge of phenomena' (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) which is comprised within the untainted (*anāsrava*), taking as its object the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm.
It further states: "Immediately following this receptivity, there arises the 'knowledge of phenomena' (*dharma-jñāna*) taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, immediately following the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there arises an acceptance of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñānakṣānti*) taking the suffering of the remaining realms as its object.

Because it is the first realization of the true reality of the Dharma, it is called "knowledge of phenomena. Subsequent objects and cognitions resemble those preceding them; therefore, they receive the name "subsequent" (*anvaya*).
The same applies to each of the four [acceptances and knowledges] regarding the remaining three truths. The above is all from the treatise (*śāstra*).

The mind immediately following the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) spontaneously takes the Four Truths as its object and gives rise to Patience (kṣānti) and Knowledge (jñāna). This differs from the mental application (manasikāra) directed toward the Four Truths during the preceding stage of Patience.

Although the sixteen moments of mind arise all at once, it is Patience that is able to sever the afflictions (kleśa), while Knowledge is able to realize the principle; furthermore, both must necessarily take the Four Truths as their objects in a spontaneous manner. [Supplement] Regarding the term "Patience": *Note:

This passage explains the transition from the final worldly stage to the supramundane path of seeing (darśanamārga). It clarifies that while the cognitive process unfolds rapidly through sixteen distinct moments, the specific functions of severing delusions and realizing truth are attributed respectively to the stages of Patience and Knowledge, both of which operate by naturally apprehending the Four Noble Truths.*
Regarding "the fruit of wisdom": this means that while *kṣānti* (receptivity) is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*), *jñāna* (wisdom) is able to realize the principle (*tattva*).

Since the principle is only manifested through the severing of the afflictions, *kṣānti* is the cause and *jñāna* is the fruit. It is also called "unimpeded" (*anantarya*), which refers to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).

This means that the first fruit (*prathamaphala*) relies upon the eight *kṣāntis* to sever the delusions regarding the principle found within the four noble truths; these eight *kṣāntis* are not [obstructed].
That which is interrupted by the delusions of view is called the Path of Uninterruptedness (*ānantarya-mārga*).

As for the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it refers to the initial fruit [of the stream-enterer] relying on the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) to realize the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the eight truths; because these eight knowledges have already abandoned the bonds of delusion, they are called the Path of Liberation.

(From the *Chuxuan ji*). [Supplementary Note]: Regarding "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*): "Suffering" refers to the suffering of birth and death within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
*Dharma* refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness). *Kṣānti* (patience) means acceptance, which also carries the sense of verification or certification.

This means that within the stages of *ūṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*, by contemplating the suffering of birth and death in the desire realm, the principle of *tathatā* becomes manifest at the final moment of the stage of *laukikāgradharma*.

The arising of untainted (*anāsrava*) *dharma-kṣānti* is called "Dharma-patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). As for "subsequent patience regarding suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), it pertains to the form and...
Form is suffering; this is a category of the desire realm. Furthermore, one contemplates the suffering of the two higher realms as being a category of the desire realm.

Moreover, contemplating the suffering of the two higher realms also gives rise to the untainted dharma-patience, which is called "patience with the subsequent knowledge of suffering" (duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti). As for "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna):

Wisdom (*jñāna*) is the wisdom capable of realizing *tathatā* (suchness). That is to say, when the suffering of birth and death in the desire realm is clearly illuminated by true wisdom, one realizes the principle of *tathatā*;

this is called the "dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*). As for the "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), one further contemplates the truths of the two higher realms.
When true wisdom clearly arises, it is a derivative of the Dharma-knowledge of suffering within the desire realm; this is termed "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
The other three truths—origin, cessation, and the path—may be understood in the same manner. [From] *The Enumeration of Dharmas in the Tripiṭaka*:

Regarding the "patience regarding the Dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*), it is when the practitioner turns the light inward to reflect and specifically investigates the locus of suffering; seeing only its emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, one abides [therein].

There is a characteristic of suffering that can be apprehended; by means of the principle of non-apprehensibility, one brings this into acceptance within the mind, and thus it is called "patience regarding the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for "knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), when one investigates with the contemplation of emptiness until it is profound, the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) spontaneously manifests clearly before one; thus it is called "knowledge of the dharma of suffering.

The same applies to the higher realms, with the corresponding terms being "patience regarding the category [of suffering]" (*anvaya-kṣānti*) and "knowledge regarding the category [of suffering]" (*anvaya-jñāna*).

"Category" (lei) means "analogy" (bi). This means that when a practitioner wishes to contemplate the suffering of the higher realms, they must know it by means of analogy with the phenomena of suffering in the desire realm.

[Note] Regarding the seven stages of the noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*), their sequence relative to the three paths and four fruits—including those who are candidates for the fruits, those who abide in the fruits, and those who progress toward higher attainments—is explained in detail in the *Miaoxuan* and the *Sijiaoyi*.
I shall now illustrate them here in a diagram.

[Commentary: Below, the stages, names, and meanings of the four fruits will be examined in detail, as well as their functional efficacy in entering the Path. Since these are now intended to be made easily understood, they are first presented here by means of a diagram.
[Commentary] This chart merely provides a brief indication of the corresponding names and meanings.

If one wishes to know them in full detail, one should consult the fourth volume, part two, of the *Xuanyiwen* (Profound Meaning) and the third volume of the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings). Here, I shall briefly transcribe the text from the *Sijiaoyi* to clarify this.

As the *Sijiaoyi* states: "The seven stages of the noble ones are: first, the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, the one resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*); fourth..."
One attains [the fruits]. There are five types of bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*), six types of liberation by time (*samayavimukta*), and seven types of non-time liberation (*asamayavimukta*).

These seven noble stages are divided into three paths: namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*). First, regarding the path of seeing:

this refers to the realization of principle through the Eightfold Noble Path, whereby one severs the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) up to the fifteenth moment of mind, like the skillful means of breaking a stone.

Second, the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) consists of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). It involves contemplating each truth (*satya*) in succession and severing discursive thought (*vitarka*), much like the skillful means used to cut lotus fibers.

Third, the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*): as previously distinguished, when true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*) has reached its ultimate limit regarding the realization of principle, the active afflictions (*anuśaya*) of the three realms are already exhausted. Since there are no further delusions to be remedied, there is no need for further training. This is the first clarification.

The stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-pratipannaka*) is a designation for those of dull faculties who enter the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*). "Dull" means that their understanding is not produced by the熏 (*vāsanā*, perfuming) of their own wisdom, but rather relies upon others.

This stage belongs to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*); although they previously possessed faith, because they have not yet given rise to true insight (*tattva-jñāna*), it is not called "practice.
"Practice" (*pratipatti*) takes the sense of advancing toward [the goal]. From the attainment of the true illumination of *duḥkha-kṣānti* (receptivity to suffering), fifteen... [moments follow].

Advancing for a single *kṣaṇa* toward the vision of reality is called "following through faith" (*śraddhānusārin*). This extends to what is termed the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the follower by faith, consisting of fifteen moments of mind;

it is also called the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*). Having fully attained the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and being deficient by one part of the knowledges (*jñāna*), this is the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattipratipannaka*), also known as the "stream-enterer-in-training. Second, regarding the stage of the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*): this refers to those who are sharp-witted...

The "Root Entry" (*mūla-praveśa*) is a name for the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*). It is called "sharp" (*tīkṣṇa*) because one personally utilizes wisdom to penetrate the principles and sever the fetters.

Originally situated within the Path of Expedient Means (*prayoga-mārga*), one is able to employ contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to contemplate the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths; however, as long as true [realization] has not yet arisen, it is not termed "practice" (*caryā*).
By means of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*), the true illumination of the Patience toward Suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) arises, lasting for fifteen moments (*kṣaṇa*).

Advancing toward the vision of reality, it is called "Dharma-practice" (*dharmānusārin*). It continues: "However, those of dull faculties rely on others to produce understanding and possess little analytical wisdom;
those of sharp faculties differ in that they possess much of their own wisdom through analytical observation. Regarding the third, the "one who practices through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*):

this refers to one who enters the path of cultivation through faith and is subsequently termed a "one resolved through faith. Those of dull faculties give rise to faith by relying on others and advance [in practice].

Because it is true understanding, it is called "faith-understanding" (śraddhādhimukta). For such a person of faith-understanding, there are three ways of realizing the fruit. First, regarding the realization of the fruit of Srotāpanna:

at the sixteenth moment of the path, through the corresponding subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), one realizes it. If the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the view-division are severed—briefly stated, the exhaustion of the three fetters (saṃyojana);
more extensively stated, the exhaustion of the eighty-eight latent tendencies—one is named a Srotāpanna. One undergoes seven [more] births and deaths.

Returning, one will ultimately not undergo eight more births. Second, regarding those who realize the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner), there are two types: those who are "bound by one more birth" (*ekavīcika*) and those who have attained the fruit.
As for the "bound by one more birth," from the moment after the mind of the first fruit, they further cultivate the contemplation of the sixteen truths;

the seven factors of enlightenment and the practice of awakening manifest before them, and in this very life, through untainted wisdom, they sever the afflictions, becoming unimpeded in the severance of even a single grade of desire.

Regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the realms: when one has eliminated one grade or two grades without obstruction, and is severing the second through the fifth grades of affliction, these are all the stage of the candidate for the fruit of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmi-pratipannaka*), also called the "superiorly progressing stream-enterer" (*viśeṣa-srotāpanna*). It is with reference to this that the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner is described. As for the second fruit:
if one has completely severed six grades and realizes the liberation from the sixth grade of the desire realm, one is then a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Regarding the fruit: those who realize the stage of *anāgāmin* are also of two types: first, the candidate (*pratipannaka*), and second, the fruit (*phala*). As for the candidate:
if one has abandoned seven or eight categories of afflictions of the desire realm, they are called a candidate for *anāgāmin*, and are also termed a "superiorly progressing *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Based on this, it is described as being of "one seed" (*ekabījī*). Second, regarding the fruit: by means of the ninth path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons the fetters of the desire realm and realizes the [third] fruit.
The nine liberations are the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Furthermore, there are three types of *srotāpanna*:
first, the *srotāpanna* in the course of practice, which is the candidate for the fruit of *srotāpanna*; second, the one abiding in the fruit, who is the actual fruit of *srotāpanna*;
and third, the one of superior progress, who is the *srotāpanna* of superior progress, also called *kulaṅkula*, and who is the candidate for the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The Sakṛdāgāmin has only two types: first, those abiding in the fruit; second, those who have progressed further.
The Sakṛdāgāmin who has progressed further is also called "One-seed" (Ekabījī). The Anāgāmin also has two types: first, those abiding in the fruit; second, those who have progressed further.

Those who have progressed further advance to sever the five higher fetters; they are the candidates for Arhatship (Arhattva-pratipannaka). The Arhat has only one type: those abiding in the fruit. If...

According to the Abhidharma, one who attains the fruit through "leap-over" (vyutkrāntaka) refers to one who, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), has severed the six grades up to the eight grades of the desire realm and then enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Subsequently, they give rise to the true illumination of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe-dharmakṣānti*). During the fifteen moments of mind, this is the stage of being a candidate for the second fruit;
at the sixteenth moment of mind, they realize the second fruit itself. If, while still an ordinary person, they previously...
Having severed the ninth grade of the desire realm up to the exhaustion of the sphere of nothingness, one subsequently enters the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing;
this is called the practice of an Anāgāmin. In the sixteenth moment of mind, one realizes the third fruit. This is the person of "leap-over" attainment.

They do not realize the first two fruits. Fourth, regarding those who "attain through vision": when one who practices according to the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this is called "attainment through vision.
Such a person, within the path of contemplation (*bhāvanāmārga*), realizes the three fruits in succession or attains the two fruits by means of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*).

This is also as distinguished in the section on "Resolute Understanding" (adhimokṣa). The difference is that one with sharp faculties is able to perceive the Dharma and realize the principle by oneself, without relying on hearing the Dharma or external requisites.

Fifth, regarding the "Body-Witness" (kāyasākṣin): this refers to the same two types of persons—those of Resolute Understanding and those who have attained through vision—who enter the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and, employing untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna), sever the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana). Thus, they give rise to the four [fruits].

Regarding the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*): one employs the common foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to cultivate the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

One enters the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) and the three concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatāsamādhi*). Having already completely severed both the obstacles of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*) and the obstacles of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*), one further severs the obstacle of phenomena within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
By extinguishing the mind and mental factors that take principles as their objects, one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and attains this concentration.

Therefore, he is called a "body-witness Anāgāmin. Why is this? Because by entering the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which resembles the dharma of nirvāṇa, he establishes it within his body, bringing to rest all the labors of the three realms.
Since he has personally realized the cessation of sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha*) with his own body, he is called a "body-witness.
If one explains the "body-witness" in relation to the first fruit [of the path], it is simply because he previously, while still an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), employed...

Through conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), one abandons the fetters. After attaining the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), one attains the sixteenth moment of mind that perceives the truths (*satyadarśana*) and realizes the third fruit [of stream-entry].

Thereupon, one cultivates the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in common; subsequently, one again cultivates the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) starting from the desire realm.
In all places, one enters the nine successive meditative attainments (navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti) and achieves the realization through bodily witness (kāyasākṣin). There are two types of Anāgāmin:
first, those who abide in the fruit, who are merely Anāgāmins; second, those who practice while carrying the fruit toward the next stage, which are the superior-progressing Anāgāmins.

Because they are still termed "Anāgāmin practicing toward [the fruit]," they are subsumed under the category of the candidate for Arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka). Thus, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* says:
That [category] contains eleven types. Five of these are precisely *anāgāmins*; six are subsumed under those who are candidates for *arhatship* (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).

It should be understood that this "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*) *anāgāmin* is precisely the superior-progressing (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) *anāgāmin*, and is subsumed under those who are candidates for *arhatship*.

As for the five types of *parinirvāyin* *anāgāmins* and the seven types of *parinirvāyin* [in general], they all consist solely of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the upward stream (*ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin*). Eight.
Regarding the types of *anāgāmins*, there are only those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain it in the formless realm (*ārūpya-parinirvāyin*).

Thus, according to the Abhidharma, when categorized by way of the distinction between those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those liberated through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they number as many as twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty types.

To refute the original intent [of this teaching] would require no further elaboration. Sixth, regarding the arhat liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*): this refers to those of dull faculties who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*).
Because they attain liberation only when waiting for the proper time and when all necessary conditions are assembled, they are called "liberated by time. Furthermore, there are five distinct types:

namely, those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇa-dharman*), those of the nature of reflecting (*cetana-dharman*), those of the nature of guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*), those of the nature of abiding (*sthiti-dharman*), and those of the nature of certain progress (*prativedhana-dharman*). These possess two [qualities].
Wisdom refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), which is the vision of the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*).

When the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*) is employed, once the ninth grade of afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has been exhausted, in the immediately following moment, one realizes the ninth liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and achieves the knowledge of exhaustion.

Next, in a single moment, one attains the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Because such a person may occasionally regress, it is not said that they have attained the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
These five types of arhats belong to the lineage of faith (*śraddhāgotra*); their faculties are dull.

While practicing the path during the causal stage, they necessarily depend upon clothing, food, bedding, dwellings, the preaching of the Dharma, and the compliance of others for their roots of goodness to increase; they are unable [to progress otherwise].
These are the five types of arhats who are to be further developed at all times. Each of these five has two varieties:

those who have not attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*); those who have attained the meditative absorption of cessation are "doubly liberated" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

If one has not attained the meditative absorption of cessation, such a person, during the causal stage, has cultivated the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertaining to their own nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), but has not cultivated the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness shared with others (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*). If [one] has attained...

Regarding the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): this person cultivates the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) pertaining to their own nature during the stage of practice, as well as the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness shared with others.

When they realize the fruit, the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) are attained simultaneously; therefore, they are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).

Seventh, regarding the Arhat of "liberation not dependent on time" (*asamayavimukta*): this refers to one of the "dharma-practitioner" type with sharp faculties, who is termed "unshakable" (*akopyadharman*).
They are Arhats. Regarding those who are "not liberated at specific times," these are persons of immovable dharma who possess exclusively sharp faculties.
Having cultivated the path during the causal stage, they are able at all times to advance in the cultivation of wholesome deeds according to their desires, without depending on external requisites.
Therefore, he is called one liberated at any time (asamaya-vimukta). This person is not moved by afflictions; thus, he is called "immovable" (akopya), which means non-retrogression.

Because he has accomplished the three knowledges—namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna), and the vision of the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣa-jñāna)—he is so designated.
He is able to employ the profound samādhi of emptiness to strike at the noble and wholesome dharmas; because he uses concentration to relinquish concentration, it is said that he "is able to strike.
[Supplement] This Immovable Arhat also has two types of differences: first, there is one who does not attain the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
One is called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*). Second, one who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*).

If, upon hearing the Buddha’s teaching of the Tripiṭaka, one cultivates the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and thereby gives rise to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), this is called "liberation through the absence of doubt" (*akopya-vimukti*).
These are termed *pāramitā* śrāvakas; they are capable of ultimately fulfilling all the functional capacities of an arhat. Question: Is it not the case that...?
Question: At that time, the two individuals differ in their faculties—some being sharp and others dull. How can they both attain simultaneous liberation? Answer:

This [distinction] merely clarifies the difference between difficulty and ease in attainment based on whether one’s faculties are dull or sharp; it has nothing to do with whether one attains it or not.
These seven types of noble ones are designated as *śramaṇas*. There are two kinds of *śramaṇas*: first, the *śramaṇa* in name only, which refers to the cause.

The second is *śramaṇatva*, which is the fruit. There are eighty-nine types of *śramaṇa*: namely, the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) of the vision of the truths (*darśanamārga*), the eighty [moments] of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and one unimpeded [knowledge]. *Śramaṇatva* also consists of eighty-nine:

namely, the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) of the vision of the truths, the eighty [moments] of cultivation, and one liberation (*vimukti*). Furthermore, *śramaṇatva* is of two kinds: first, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Regarding the fruits: there are eighty-nine conditioned fruits and two unconditioned bodies; these are the eighty-nine unconditioned fruits.
These two are discussed in terms of wisdom and abandonment. In terms of the virtue of wisdom, it clarifies the eighty-nine conditioned fruits.
Regarding the virtue of abandonment, this clarifies the eighty-nine unconditioned fruits.
△ Second, the stages for abandoning delusions, in four parts. First, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).

One: *Srotāpanna*. This is translated as "entering the stream. In this stage, one abandons the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) across the three realms. Regarding views:
Because it is the ultimate truth, it is called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and it is also termed the Stage of the Noble Ones (*ārya-bhūmi*).

[Note] One who has "entered the stream" (*srotāpanna*) has entered the flow of the Dharma of the Noble Path. As the *Vajra* [Sūtra] says, "entering the stream," or alternatively, "flowing against the current," meaning to go against the current of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
In the eighth fascicle of the *Xi xu* (*Xixuan*), this is termed "discharging a debt," because one no longer receives the karmic debts of the three miserable realms (*trāya-patha*).
[Commentary] This explains the meaning of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer). Regarding the phrase "severing the three realms," this refers to flowing against the current;
specifically, it is flowing against the stream of views (*dṛṣṭi-srotas*) among the four streams. Regarding the phrase "attaining the fruit and realization," this refers to entering the stream;
specifically, it is entering the stream of the Eightfold Noble Path. Thus, there are two meanings. First, regarding the stream of birth and death, the person who is a *srotāpanna*...

Sentient beings go against this flow; only they follow it. Second, regarding the flow of the Way: those who have attained the stage of *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) follow and enter this flow, whereas sentient beings go against it and have not yet entered.
To analyze the term "emerging from the profound" (*xíxuán*), it refers to those called "debtors.
For example, an Arhat has first directly attained the Way but has not yet had the leisure to repay their karmic debts; therefore, they are called "debtors. As the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* says: "If..."

If a person who has incurred a debt to the Triple Gem is correctly engaged in the practice of the Way and seeks the stage of *srotāpanna* up to that of *arhat*, they need not repay it. However, if they do not study the Way, they must repay it immediately.

Based on this principle, one knows that for a noble one (*ārya*) who has seen the Way, the karmic debt is fundamentally empty; since its point of repayment cannot be found upon investigation, it is termed "nullified" (*di*).
[This refers to] the debt.

[Note: Regarding the severance of the eighty-eight *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) of the three realms, why does the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* state that twenty-eight *anuśayas* are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the remaining sixty *anuśayas* are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)? Former masters have said: There are two types of root-natures (*indriya-gotra*). If they are equal...
Regarding those who contemplate the Four Noble Truths: they eliminate eighty proclivities (*anuśaya*) through the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

If one does not contemplate the Four Noble Truths equally, then within the Path of Seeing, one eliminates only twenty-eight proclivities under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) of the three realms; the remaining [proclivities] under the other three truths are eliminated according to the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This refers to those of dull faculties.
[Commentary] This explains that there are two different ways of severing the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya*).
The reason the note cites the *Mahāvibhāṣā* (Póshālùn) as the source for the question is that the *Vibhāṣā* asks: "For what reason did Pūrṇa make such a statement? [Namely, that it takes eighty...]"
Eight are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and ten are abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). He answers thus:

twenty-eight are definitely abandoned by the path of seeing, and ten are abandoned by the path of cultivation. Regarding the sixty that are indeterminate, there is a distinction within the path of seeing;
because the *Paryāya* explains them in sequence, it states that eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned by the path of seeing.
"Ten are abandoned through the path of cultivation. This refers to the fact that the commentary raises the essential meaning of the answer as the opening of the question.
Now, to provide the answer, it cites the ancient teaching that there are two types of root-natures (*indriya*): namely, the two types of root-natures.

According to the intent of the *Śāstra*, those with dull faculties abandon the remaining delusions of view (*darśana-heya*) under the three other truths in accordance with the path of cultivation; whereas for those with sharp faculties and so forth...
"Contemplating the Four Truths" explains the passage concerning the severance of the eighty-eight *āśravas* (defilements) of the three realms through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
[Appendix] Bian'e states: The predecessors cited this section based on the end of volume forty of the old *Mahāvibhāṣā*, which lists ninety-eight *āśravas*.

Twenty-eight *āśravas* are severed by the path of seeing; ten are severed by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); as for the remainder, they are severed by the path of cultivation either by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) or...
The disciples of the Inner Teaching [believe] that these are abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*). Furthermore, the four fascicles state:
"Twenty-eight dharmas are definitely abandoned through the Path of Seeing; sixty are indefinite. Regarding those that are indefinite, there are distinctions within the Path of Seeing.

Since this is explained in contrast to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and the disciples of the Buddha, it follows that for the disciples of the Buddha, eighty-eight [defilements] are abandoned instantaneously during the Path of Seeing.

The "messenger" (dūta) refers to the path of cultivation that abandons the remaining sixty [defilements]. The *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra* (Old *Vibhāṣā*) points to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) when explaining this; there is no doubt regarding their faith.
△ Second, the fruit of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Second is the Sakṛdāgāmin, which here is translated as "Once-returner. In this stage, one has abandoned the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm;
having completely severed the first six grades among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, the final three grades still remain. Therefore, one returns once more.
[Commentary] This fruit involves the abandonment of the first six of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Between the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and this fruit, one must discuss the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner. Here, we shall first clarify how the afflictions of the desire realm moisten seven cycles of birth and death;
next, we will generally demonstrate the faculties and natures that transcend the sequence; and finally, we will specifically explain the meaning of "family-to-family."
[Commentary] This clarifies the meritorious practice regarding what is abandoned through the second fruit. Because the names and their meanings do not correspond, it is necessary to discuss them.
First, the three points are established as in the *Vajrasamādhi-śāstra*. Regarding the explanation of this person’s name as "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*):

it means that after dying from here, one goes once to the heavens and returns once to the human realm to bring an end to all suffering. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to this as *sakkadāgāmī*.

*Mī* (彌) means "to cease"; *xījì* (息忌) means "one. *Gāmī* (伽彌) means "to come. In the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings), it is translated as "thin" (*bó*). Because much has already been severed previously and what remains unsevered is little, it is called "thin.
The current text explains this term in the same way as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dàlùn), and its meaning accords with the Four Teachings. The *Yízhù* (Commentary on the Ritual) states:
"This fruit [of the Once-returner] consists of having severed the first six of the nine grades of afflictions within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). If one follows the perspective of emptiness...

Regarding the sequence of the stages [of the spiritual path]: it should be after the abandonment of the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa) in the first fruit (srotāpanna), and before the abandonment of the sixth grade of the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-kleśa) in the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin).

Alternatively, after abandoning four grades, one becomes a "three-birth" (tri-jāti) or "two-birth" (dvi-jāti) practitioner, or a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner. Although the ritual text is brief, I have now supplemented it with these notes.
Therefore, we shall first explain in general terms the nine grades of the afflictions of cultivation in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), which collectively moisten seven cycles of rebirth.
"Death. Next, this provides a general indication of the four fruits and the Buddha, noting that there are root-natures (indriya) characterized by either skipping stages or proceeding sequentially;

thereafter, it specifically sets forth the meanings of "two-birth," "three-birth," and "family-to-family" practitioners. This is a brief preliminary outline; the subsequent text explains each point in detail.

[Note] Afflictions (*kleśa*) have coarse and subtle degrees; therefore, they are divided into nine grades. Because of the power of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one passes through seven births.
As for why seven births are required, as cited in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Siddhi*) from the *Śāstra*: "Within these seven lifetimes, untainted wisdom reaches maturity.

It is like the method of taking clarified butter (*ghṛta*), where the illness is eliminated in seven days; like the *kalala* stage of embryonic development, which transforms once every seven days; and like the law of kinship, which is limited to..."
"Seven generations" is like the seven-step snake: by virtue of its four great powers, it travels seven steps; yet by virtue of the power of its venom, it does not reach an eighth step.

The power of delusion reaches seven, while the power of the Path does not reach eight. The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "One should say fourteen; for what reason is it said to be seven? The answer is:

because the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) do not exceed the number seven, it is therefore simply called seven. This applies even when discussing birth in its entirety.

One should say there are seven persons, seven heavens, and fourteen intermediate states (*antarābhava*), totaling twenty-eight births. However, following the previous explanation, since no more than seven [realms] are established, it is simply said that there are seven.
