It continues until it says, "These five grades are the same as the four grades," thereby explaining the entire passage concerning small transcendence according to the number of grades of fundamental abandonment and so forth. How could one possibly divide and match these [grades] individually?
[Commentary] This section of "Recorded Explanations" (*Ji*) corresponds to the sequential and non-sequential [treatments] of the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue* (*Fuxing*).

In the question, one stubbornly adheres to their own view by dividing the *Fuxing* to correspond to the sequential and non-sequential aspects of the *Zhi guan*. In the answer, there is both concession (*zong*) and refutation (*duo*).

By way of concession, it clarifies that the *Zhi guan* distinguishes them through the sequential and non-sequential; by way of refutation, it reveals that the *Fuxing* only points to the "minor" non-sequential, as stated in the passage beginning with "As it says below."

The *Sub-commentary* (*Fuxing*) merely cites the passage concerning "leaping over" (*chao*) in the *Śrāvaka-bhūmi*. How could it be appropriate to conclude by criticizing that the text should not be divided into corresponding sections?

[Appendix] Regarding the sequential versus leaping comparison in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, the text states: "Now, for the sake of illustration, suppose one relies on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to abandon the first grade of desire-delusion, proceeding sequentially until the fifth grade is exhausted;
all these are termed 'candidates for the stage of Once-returner' (*sakṛdāgāmin-patipannaka*). If, however, one abandons them by leaping..."
The fifth stage is called *Kulaputra* (Family-to-Family). Next, when the sixth grade of defilements is completely abandoned, it is called the fruit of *Sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-Returner).

When one transcends [the lower stages] and abandons up to the sixth grade, it is called *Ekavīcika* (One-Interval). Next, from the abandonment of the seventh grade up to the eighth grade, it is called the candidate for *Anāgāmin* (Non-Returner).
When one transcends [the lower stages] and abandons up to the eighth grade, it is called *Ekabījī* (One-Seed). Next, when the ninth grade is completely abandoned, it is called *Anāgāmin*...

The fruit of anāgāmin: one never again returns to the desire realm. Subsequently, from the abandonment of the first category of the first dhyāna up to the eighth category of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these seventy-one categories are all termed the stage of the arhat-pṛthagjana (the candidate for arhatship). There are six types of anāgāmins.

He occupies the middle position. When the ninth affliction of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is exhausted through the ninth path of non-obstruction, its realization via the ninth path of liberation is called the fruit of Arhatship.
This is it. Regarding those who attain the stage of "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) through the fulfillment of three conditions, as explained in the treatises:
The *Fuxing* commentary states: "What is here called 'transcendent abandonment' refers to the person of 'small transcendence' mentioned below.

Originally situated in the stage of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), they have not yet attained the meditative absorptions of the form realm (*rūpadhyāna*). Alternatively, having cultivated the meditative absorptions of the desire realm, their afflictions of the desire realm remain unextinguished.

When such a person reaches the sixteenth moment of mind, they transcendently abandon five grades [of afflictions] and are termed a 'family-to-family' (*kulaṃkula*) practitioner. These five grades are identical to the four grades [previously discussed]."

According to the number of categories of fundamental abandonment, they receive the names "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*), "seed," and so forth, as well as the designations for those "heading toward the fruit of no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa-phala-pratipannaka*) and the like. *Bian'e* states: "This is a statement from the *Jiyao*; its explanation is fundamentally correct."

It should not be refuted. Personally, I consider this to be a passage of "small transcendence" (xiao-chao). How could it be appropriate to split it apart and force it to correspond to two distinct statements?
The *Jizhu* (Collected Annotations) determines its meaning based on the text itself, without any forced manipulation; thus, it may be followed.

We, who have not yet attained even a hair’s breadth of cultivation, can only look up to it with sincere faith when it comes to the determination of stages. We do not dare to engage in contentious debate.
This refers to the "seeing of length.

[Commentary] Question: Since *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are distinguished by their progressive and leaping sequences, why does the "small leap" (*xiǎochuāo*) extend only to the stage of the "one-seed" (*yīzhǒngzǐ*)? Answer:
Before the small leap reaches the one-seed stage, it differs from the gradual severance (*cìduàn*).

[Supplement] Regarding the one seed [grade] and below: subsequently, the abandonment must occur after having attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), following which one initiates the preparatory application (*prayoga*).

In abandoning two, one necessarily abandons three; in abandoning five, one necessarily abandons six, and so forth. If there is a minor "leap-over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), the afflictions of the views (*dṛṣṭi*) and the thoughts (*vicāra*) are abandoned simultaneously.
Thus, it differs when leaping over to the fifth grade and so on.
[□ Note] If it occurs after the third fruit, it is identical to the subsequent abandonment; therefore, it is not discussed in the context of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
[■ Supplement] This is intended to distinguish between the sequential and the transcendent (*vyutkrāntaka*) modes of practice regarding *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

That is to say, when the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm are completely abandoned—whether sequentially or transcendently—it is termed the "third fruit. One then proceeds to abandon the seventy-one grades of *saṃyojana* (fetters) belonging to the eight higher stages.

Whether progressing by successive stages (*anupūrva*) or by skipping stages (*vyutkrānta*), these are collectively termed the "four paths" (*catur-yogācāra*). When the seventy-two grades of defilements are completely exhausted, they are uniformly termed "those beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary] In the response, there are both similarities and differences. Because the former [the four paths] differ, they are distinguished according to whether one proceeds by succession or by skipping.
Because the latter [the state of being beyond training] is uniform, there is no discussion regarding a minor skipping that leads directly to the path toward the fruit of being beyond training.

[Note] Question: Some claim that after the sixteen moments of mind, one who leaps directly to the fruit of Anāgāmin belongs to the "leap over the fundamental abandonments" (ben-duan-chao), while one who leaps directly to Arhatship belongs to the "great leap" (da-chao).
If so, why is the "lesser leap" (xiao-chao) not included? Answer: Does the person who leaps over the fundamental abandonments stop merely at Anāgāmin? No.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement "one who has fundamentally severed [the defilements] and transcended existence to reach the stage of the candidate for the fourth fruit": this does not exclude the *anāgāmin* (Non-returner).

[Supplement] There are those who are merely designated as candidates for the *anāgāmin* fruit; likewise, there are those who have severed three or four grades of desire and are merely designated as being in the first fruit.

How could it be that the term "candidate" applies only to the *anāgāmin*? [Appendix] *Bian'e* states: Since it is said to be after the sixteen moments of mind, one does not abide in the four types of transcendence (*cātus-krama*).
[This] is included within the intermediate [category]. If one wishes to include it, when it transcends to the stage of *anāgāmin*, it may be subsumed under the "Small Leap" (*kṣudra-saṃdhāna*).

If it reaches the stage of *arhat*, it may perhaps be appended to the "Great Leap" (*mahā-saṃdhāna*). However, this is not equivalent to those who, upon hearing the proclamation "Welcome," attain [realization].

One should know that all that is called "leaping" (*saṃdhāna*) pertains to the discourse on the ten minds (*daśa-citta-śāstra*), and does not occur after the sixteen [moments of mind]. Personally, I say that the word "after" (*paścāt*) must be understood flexibly.
Now, it is said that "one thought-moment" (ekakṣaṇa) is an extremely brief duration; it is not necessarily the case that realization occurs only after a long time has passed.

Furthermore, since these types of transcendental attainments (abhisamaya) are neither included among the four types of transcendence nor discussed separately thereafter, there is an omission in the meaning.
Since this differs from the common ground regarding those who hear the proclamation, it would not be entirely appropriate to include it within the "Great Leap" (mahā-vīthi).

It would be more suitable, as in the current commentary, to categorize it under the "Small Leap" (paritta-vīthi) based on the explanation of the continuous sequence from the stage of training toward the fruit of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa).

As for the claim that the leap occurs within the theory of the sixteen moments of mind: for those of the type who realize the truth upon hearing the proclamation, how could they have ever passed through [those stages]?

Whether [these stages] correspond to the levels of *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), etc., shall be reserved for later determination. Furthermore, regarding the "original abandonment" (*mūlaccheda*) and "leaping over" (*vyutkrāntaka*), these pertain to non-Buddhists who abandon thought (*vitarka*) but do not abandon views (*dṛṣṭi*);

thus, reaching as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), they should be termed candidates for Arhatship (*arhattvapratipannaka*). Alternatively, suppressing one stage, they belong to the Anāgāmin and stop there.
This interpretation is consistent with the records.
[Commentary] If one is a Great Arhat, upon hearing the cry of "Welcome" while still on the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), they immediately realize arhatship.

How, then, can it be said that this occurs after the sixteen moments of mind? This analysis concerns those who attain the fruit of transcendence (*abhisamaya*) after the sixteen moments; this is the "lesser transcendence. It is because there were teachers who erroneously [applied] the *śamatha*...

In the commentary, it is stated that after the sixteen moments of mind, if one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* by transcending in a single moment, this is judged to belong to "transcendence of the fundamental abandonment" (*mūlaccheda-saṃkrama*).
If one transcends further to attain the state of an *arhat*, this is judged to belong to "great transcendence" (*mahā-saṃkrama*).

Therefore, in the present question, the fact that the attainment of the fruit following the sixteen moments of mind belongs to [the category of] transcendence is cited to ask why the "minor transcendence" (*parīttasaṃkrama*) is not included among those who attain the fruit of transcendence. However, the intent of this question is as follows: since...
There are masters who make such a judgment, yet they do not include the "lesser leap" (kṣudra-saṃkrānti) within the category of the "leap after the sixteen moments" (ṣoḍaśa-citta-pṛṣṭha-saṃkrānti).
How then can the previously cited "leap after the sixteen moments" be used as proof for the "lesser leap"? [The meaning of the answer is clear:
It clarifies what is stated in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*: that the "leap after the sixteen moments" refers to a single moment of leaping to the fruit of Anāgāmin. It is only...
If Xiao Chao has not yet attained dhyāna, he may reach the stage of Arhat;
however, if Xiao Chao has already attained dhyāna, this specifically pertains to the uncertainty regarding Xiao Chao’s realization of the fruit, and does not pertain to Ben-duan or Tai-chao.
[Question]: Since the "lesser leaper" (*kṣudra-saṃkrāntin*) has already reached the stage of Arhatship, how does he differ from the "greater leaper" (*mahā-saṃkrāntin*)? [Answer]:

Because the lesser leaper cultivates contemplation while still at the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), he merely suppresses the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*). Upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind, his leap to the fruit is not yet definitive.
In contrast, when a greater leaper is called "Welcome" (*svāgata*) while still an ordinary person, he directly leaps to the fourth fruit; thus, he is not comparable to the lesser leaper.
[Commentary] This section distinguishes between the two types of "leap-over" (*vyutkrānta*)—the Small and the Great—which are vastly different.

In the question, it is asked how the Small Leap-over, which leaps as far as the stage of Arhat, differs from the Great Leap-over, which reaches the stage of Arhat directly. In the answer, it is clarified that the Small Leap-over occurs while one is still at the level of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
at the time of practicing the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one has already attained the suppression of afflictions (*kleśa*), and this continues until after the sixteenth moment of mind (*citta*).

Some were able to transcend directly to the stage of Arhat; yet, when [the Buddha] addressed them with the great transcendence by calling out "Welcome" (*ehi-bhadrika*), they immediately realized Arhatship—this is what distinguishes this case as being far superior.
Regarding the statement that realization occurs upon a single call, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) says:
When the Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu," he naturally attained full ordination. At that very moment, his hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and the *kāṣāya* robe appeared upon him.
With body and almsbowl in hand, appearing as if five years of age, such is the Dharma-knowing bhikṣu, like Bādarapālaṅka.
The above explains the thorough discernment of those with transcendent faculties beyond the sequential order.

[Commentary] Next, the meaning of *kulaṃkula* (family-to-family) is explained. "Family-to-family" means that the places of rebirth are not uniform. Among humans, there are differences in the three continents (*tri-dvīpa*), with varying rulers and kings.

In the heavens, among the six classes of desire-realm deities (*ṣaḍ-kāma-deva*), there are distinctions such as different palaces and abodes. Therefore, the treatise distinguishes between heavenly *kulaṃkula* and human *kulaṃkula*.

Regarding "not-equal household-to-household" (不等家家) and "equal household-to-household" (平等家家), the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 6, part 1, states: "As for 'household-to-household' (家家), there are two differences:

namely, among devas and among humans. Regarding devas, this refers to being born in three or two households among the desire-realm devas and then realizing parinirvāṇa (this is the deva-household-to-household). Regarding humans..."

This refers to one who attains parinirvāṇa after being reborn in three or two families among humans, or in three or two continents [as a human]. (These individuals are "family-to-family" [kulaṃkula]; those above are all "equal family-to-family").
If it concerns the heavens, there are three births in heaven and two in the human realm, or two births in heaven and one in the human realm (these are "unequal family-to-family").

The cases of humans being born three or twice [in heaven] are to be understood by reversing this (these are "unequal family-to-family"). Therefore, those of the heavenly family-to-family first attain [the fruit] among humans.
Having seen the Path, whether by leaping over or following the sequence, one proceeds to abandon three or four [fetters] and is subsequently reborn in two or three places among the gods;

for those among humans, it is the reverse. Regarding the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) among the gods: in their final birth among the gods, they abandon the remaining fetters and are said to attain parinirvāṇa.
The "family-to-family" among humans should be understood according to this same principle.
[Supplement] This citation from the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains the "upper [stream-enterers]" and "gods-and-men" as referring to the *kulankula* (one who goes from family to family).
It means that those who attain parinirvāṇa after being born three times have already severed the third grade of the afflictions of the desire realm;

thus, they diminish four births, leaving three births remaining, and therefore attain parinirvāṇa after three births. Those who attain parinirvāṇa after being born two times, however, are those regarding the afflictions of the desire realm...
Having already abandoned four grades [of defilements], one diminishes five births; since two births remain, one realizes [nirvana] in those two births.
These are either exclusively among the gods or exclusively among humans; this is what is meant by "equality.
Thus, one who is a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) deity first gives rise to birth after having seen the Path among humans, and finally realizes parinirvāṇa among the gods.
Regarding the "family-to-family" (*kulaṃkula*) among humans: first, they attain the vision of the Path in the heavens, and finally, they realize *parinirvāṇa* among humans.

As for *parinirvāṇa*, it is the principle of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) of the Lesser Vehicle’s *nirvāṇa*; it is the complete seeing [of the truths] and the stilling of the delusions of affliction and views.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "The family-to-family among gods refers to those who go from one family to another within the heavens. If...

"Whether going or coming, one realizes the end of suffering. "From house to house among humans" means that among human beings, one goes from one household to another, whether going or coming, until realizing the end of suffering. Furthermore, regarding "the gods' lack of equality":
this refers to being born in the heavens—three for the gods and two for humans—and finally attaining parinirvāṇa in the heavenly realms. Among humans, it is the reverse of this.

(However, the *Fuxing* [Commentary on the Meaning of the Text] states: "To realize parinirvāṇa after three or two births refers to the fruit of arhatship. This is the lineage of 'going from family to family' (*kulaṃkula*). It cannot be explained as the ordinary attainment of the third fruit through the severance of the nine grades of afflictions.")

[Commentary] This is the standard explanation: one who has severed the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm can only attain the third fruit (*anāgāmin*). That they now realize *parinirvāṇa* refers to the fourth fruit (*arhat*).
[Supplementary Note] Bian’e states: Master Yu’s intention is that because [these practitioners] belong to the *kula-kula* (family-to-family) lineage, they are not reborn in the higher realms.

And thus they attain the four fruits. If one were to follow the ordinary sequence of abandoning the nine grades of afflictions, one would have to be reborn in the two higher realms before realizing the four fruits;
therefore, it is said that one cannot proceed by the ordinary method and so forth. This is because [the sūtra] does not refer to noble ones who undergo rebirth within the desire realm.
They will certainly not be reborn in the form or formless realms again. This is because those two higher realms also possess long-term suffering that is identical to that of the desire realm.
Personally, I remark that the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "If one is in the stage of an Arya and undergoes birth in the desire realm..."
They will certainly not be reborn in the form or formless realms, because having realized the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*), they will definitely attain parinirvāṇa in their present body.
While for a noble one (*ārya*) who has undergone rebirth in the form realm, there is the possibility of being reborn in the formless realm,
the two terms "accumulation" (*ji*) and "usual" (*zhùng*) in the *Jízhù* refer specifically to the severing of the nine grades of afflictions, whereby one attains only the third fruit.
This is the explanation. It clarifies that the present realization of parinirvāṇa constitutes the fourth fruit [of Arhatship]. [Note] The *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states:

"To sever the third or fourth categories of afflictions in the desire realm is to become a 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula) practitioner; [this occurs after] two or three births. (These two lines specifically define the family-to-family practitioner. Regarding the severing of the three categories...)

Then four births are reduced; the remaining three births persist, which are discussed as the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) of three births. If one abandons four categories [of afflictions], then five births are reduced; the remaining two births persist, which are discussed as the "family-to-family" of two births.
[Commentary] These two lines of sub-commentary explain the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) according to the *Śāstra*. However, the root treatise (*Mūlaśāstra*) explains:
"Furthermore, one should speak of those who undergo three or two births, because there is further progress; regarding the births they undergo, they may be fewer, or none at all, or more than this.
For what reason is it that one who has not abandoned five categories [of afflictions] does not become such? Because if the fifth category is abandoned, the sixth must necessarily be abandoned.
A single grade of affliction cannot obstruct the attainment of the fruit, just as one who has only one interval remaining has not yet transcended the realm.
[Note] From the abandonment of the fifth grade up to the second stage of the candidate (abandoning up to the fifth grade is called the candidate for the second fruit).

[Commentary] The treatise states: "That is to say, the stream-enterer who proceeds to abandon from one grade up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm—should be known as being designated by the names 'candidate for the fruit of once-returner' (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka) and 'fruit of once-returner' (sakṛdāgāmiphala)."
[Boxed Annotation] Abandoning six [fetters], one attains the fruit of a Once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
[Commentary] The treatise states: "If one abandons the sixth [fetter], one becomes a Once-returner; having been in the heavenly realms, they return once more to the human realm."
And having entered parinirvāṇa, this is called the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*).

Because there is no further birth after this point, these afflictions are termed "thin greed, hatred, and delusion" (*tanu-rāga-dveṣa-moha*), for only the inferior grades of greed, hatred, and delusion remain.

[Commentary] Having abandoned seven or eight grades [of defilements], one who has only one birth remaining is called an *ekavīcika* (one-intervener). (This refers to one who has abandoned up to the seventh or eighth grade and still has one birth as an interval remaining, based on those who will pass away from this life.)
[Commentary] The treatise states: "That is to say, the Once-returner who further abandons the remaining afflictions is termed an 'Ekavīcika' (One-interval) if three conditions are met:

first, by the abandonment of afflictions, because they have abandoned seven or eight grades of the cultivated afflictions of the desire realm; second, by the attainment of faculties, because they have acquired the untainted faculties capable of counteracting those [afflictions];
and third, by the taking of birth, because they will undergo one more birth in the desire realm. Thus it is said in the verse.

However, only the two conditions for abandoning afflictions and taking rebirth—namely, the initial and the final stages—are mentioned; the condition for the formation of the faculties (*indriya*) is not discussed.

How is it that a single grade of affliction obstructs the attainment of the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*)? It is because once those [afflictions] are abandoned, one transcends the realm (*dhātu*).

As previously stated, karma at its most extreme acts as an obstruction during the three periods; one should know that afflictions function in the same way as karma, for they transcend both the outflowing (*niṣyanda*) and the retributive (*vipāka*) stages.
"Interval" (antara) means separation. Because that remaining single birth acts as a separation, one cannot avoid [attaining] the fruit of non-returning;
thus, one who has one interval is called "One-Interval" (Ekābhisamaya). The *Huayan shu* states: "When three conditions are fulfilled, one is named 'One-Interval.
The first two phrases above constitute two of these conditions; there is a third as well: obtaining the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) to serve as the antidote."
It is not mentioned because it is easily understood, being the same as the previously discussed *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).

Because the three lower grades [of defilements] together moisten a single lifetime, one abandons seven or eight [grades], while the ninth remains; thus, there is still one lifetime remaining as an interval, and for this reason they are called *ekavīcika* (those with one interval).

Because one grade of delusion remains, one does not realize the state of *anāgāmin* (non-returner); because one lifetime remains, one does not realize parinirvāṇa. All such cases are termed *ekavīcika*.
[Note] This refers to the third candidate (this is based on one who does not die [in the interim] but proceeds toward the third fruit). [Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:
"One who has abandoned seven or eight categories of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation should be known as a candidate for the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmī-phala-pratipannaka*).

It should be understood that those who previously abandoned three, four, seven, or eight categories of afflictions and entered the vision of the truths, when they subsequently attain the fruit, [are likewise candidates]. Even until...
If one has not yet cultivated the subsequent path of superior fruit, one is still not called a *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family).

This is because the stage of *ekavīcika* (one-intervener) has not yet been accomplished, as it requires the cultivation of those untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "This very *ekavīcika* is the candidate for the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin-pṛthagjana*). [Supplementary Note] Bian'e says:

The original commentary distinguishes between "having reached the end" and "not reaching the end. However, according to the treatise (*śāstra*), there is no such intention. If [the term] refers to reaching the end of life...
Regarding the *ekavīcika* (one-intervener): should the designation "not dying" not be applied here as it was for those attaining the second fruit, termed "once-returner"?

Should this also be discussed in terms of whether one dies or does not die? Since the two fruits can be said to exist in the present, the *ekavīcika* must necessarily be restricted to referring to death.
Furthermore, the root verse expresses a single meaning; it should not be divided into two distinct meanings.
[Note] The abandonment of the ninth [defilement] constitutes the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

[Commentary] The treatise explains: if one abandons the ninth [defilement], one attains the fruit of non-returner; such a person will certainly not return to be born again in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Therefore, these afflictions are called the "five lower fetters" (*pañca avarabhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāni*). Although they may have been severed previously—either two or three at a time—they are here collectively severed at this stage;
thus, with reference to the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), various sūtras establish their distinctions through diverse methods.
The *Huayan shu* states: "Because the nine grades are completely severed and one is never again reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is so called."
This is the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

[□ Note] The above is the verse of the treatise. It correctly praises the sequence of preparatory application (*prayoga*) followed by abandonment, which is fully endowed with nine types of faculties (*indriya*).

[■ Record] Regarding the "nine types of faculties," this refers to the nine types of parinirvāṇa in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); that is, within the parinirvāṇa in the realm of form, there are five combined.

There are three [types], namely: those who attain parinirvāṇa with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), those who attain it without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), and those who attain it upon being born (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*). Together with those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarā-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa by ascending to higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin*), these constitute three groups.

By further subdividing these three into nine, one obtains the nine types of parinirvāṇa as illustrated in the diagram below. [Supplement] Regarding the nine types of spiritual faculties (*indriya-gotra*):

first, those who attain parinirvāṇa after three births (*tri-jāti-kulaṅkula*); second, those who attain parinirvāṇa after two births (*dvi-jāti-kulaṅkula*); third, those who are candidates for the second fruit (*dvitīya-phala-pratipannaka*); fourth, those who have attained the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*); fifth...

1. One who has abandoned seven categories [of afflictions] and is a "one-interval" (ekavīcika) practitioner; 2. [One who has abandoned six]; 3. One who has abandoned eight categories and is a "one-interval" practitioner; 4. [One who has abandoned seven]; 5. One who has abandoned seven categories and is a candidate for the third fruit; 6.

Regarding those of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are four distinctions. That is to say, having been in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and become free from craving for the form realm, they pass away from there and are born in the formless realm.
Within this category, there are only four types, due to the distinctions among those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*).
Together with the five previously mentioned, these constitute the six non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Furthermore, there are those who do not go to either the form or formless realms.

Abiding right here, one is able to attain parinirvāṇa; this is called "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin). Together with the six preceding types, these constitute seven.

(The *Fuxing* [Sub-commentary], fascicle 6, part 1, provides a detailed explanation. The verses of the treatise list seven types: first those of the form realm, then those of the formless realm, and finally those who attain parinirvāṇa in the desire realm. The present diagram follows the sequential order of the three realms.)

[Commentary] This brief note refers to the text to explain the verse. As stated in the *Fǔxíng* (The Practice of the Assistants): 1. *Antarāparinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state):

this refers to one who, having passed away from the desire realm, attains parinirvāṇa within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm. 2. *Upapadyaparinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa upon rebirth):

having been born into the form realm, one attains parinirvāṇa. 3. *Sābhisaṃskāra* (one with exertion): having been born into the form realm, one attains parinirvāṇa only after practicing for a long time; there is merely diligence.

5. One who practices [the path] without rapid progress (*anabhisampāra-mārga*). There are four types: one who, having been born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), attains *parinirvāṇa* without long cultivation and without effortful application (*anābhoga-prayoga*).
One who diligently cultivates and possesses rapid progress. One who lacks both paths. 5. The "Upstreamer" (*ūrdhvasrotas*):

within the form realm, one must pass through the various levels of the four *dhyāna* heavens before attaining *parinirvāṇa*. Furthermore, there are two types of Upstreamers: first, the "Mixed" (*miśra*).

Cultivation is precisely the delight in wisdom. Second is non-mixed cultivation, which is the delight in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Those who practice mixed cultivation proceed to Akaniṣṭha;
those who practice non-mixed cultivation proceed to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). The remaining words in the verse refer to this non-mixed cultivation. Furthermore, there are three types:
first, the "complete leaper," meaning one who, while in the desire realm, has already practiced mixed cultivation throughout all four dhyānas.

Falling away due to conditions, they pass away from the Brahmakāyika heaven and are reborn in Akaniṣṭha, completely bypassing all intermediate stages; this is called "Total Leaping" (sakalābhisambheda).

Second is "Half-Leaping" (ardhapluta): having passed away from the Brahmakāyika heaven, they gradually experience fourteen heavenly abodes in the intermediate stages—leaping over one or two, up to thirteen—and only thereafter are born in Akaniṣṭha heaven; all such cases are termed "Half-Leaping. It is not...
Because they leap entirely, they are collectively given the name "Half-Leapers" (ardhapluta). Those who cannot leap at all are called "Universal Descenters" (sarvasthānacyuta).
As for those who do not practice mixed meditation (vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā), they are born in the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu); however, they are unable to be born in the Five Pure Abodes (śuddhāvāsa).

Having passed away from the Vast Fruit Heaven (Bṛhatphala), they are born in the three Formless Heavens, and only after being born in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) do they finally attain parinirvāṇa. Therefore, these Anāgāmins, even if they are born in the Formless Realm, still belong to [this category].

It is subsumed under form (*rūpa*). If one dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is then subsumed under the formless. As for the analysis and profound explanation [of this], it has not been fully detailed.
Below the verse of the treatise, the sequence of the three realms is clarified; the present diagram differs slightly from that.

[Commentary] Regarding "intermittent cultivation" (*miśra-bhāvanā*): because at times one cultivates the wisdom of the first *dhyāna*, and at other times one cultivates the wisdom of the fourth *dhyāna*, they are cultivated alternately;

thus, this refers to the nature of the faculty of joy-wisdom (*prīti-prajñendriya*). Question: What dharma does the "upward-streamer who practices intermittent cultivation" (*ūrdhva-srotas miśra-bhāvaka*) cultivate?

Answer: He cultivates the "interlaced perfuming *dhyāna*" (*vyavakīrṇa-vāsanā-dhyāna*). First, he takes one moment of outflow-free (*anāsrava*) [wisdom], one moment of outflowing (*sāsrava*), and again one moment of outflow-free [wisdom].
The two moments of outflow-free (anāsrava) consciousness before and after permeate this single moment of outflowing (sāsrava) consciousness; together, these three moments constitute the root.
In the second turn, the preceding three moments serve as the preparatory application (prayoga), further inducing three more moments, resulting in six moments.
Continuing in this manner up to the fifth heaven, Akaniṣṭha, there are fifteen moments of mind. From this, [the distinction between] outflowing and outflow-free [consciousness arises].
To cultivate by interspersing with outflows (*āsrava*) is called "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*), and it is also termed "intermingled perfuming meditation" (*miśra-vāsana-dhyāna*).

Those who do not practice mixed cultivation are not reborn in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). Because those who practice mixed cultivation cultivate this intermingled perfuming meditation, they are able to be born among the gods of the Pure Abodes.
Those who do not practice mixed cultivation do not cultivate this meditation; therefore, they are not reborn there. Since that [meditation] is absent...
Regarding the cause: how can there be a fruit? It is not only those who have completely transcended who do not take birth; even those who have "half-transcended" do not take birth.

Furthermore, even those who have gone to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti) and are of the nature of one who attains parinirvāṇa within the form realm (rūpa-bhava) do not take birth. As the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: [text follows].
Regarding those who do not practice mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*), they are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). They are simply unable to be born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Having passed away from the Fruit of Vastness (*Bṛhatphala*), they are born in the three formless realms and subsequently in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), where they finally attain parinirvāṇa. This still belongs to the category of "passing away in the form realm" (*rūpopaga-parinirvāṇa*).

[Appendix] Discerning Errors states: Although it is said that they "perish everywhere," it does not necessarily mean they are reborn everywhere. This is taught so as to cause people to feel weary of and detach from cyclic existence by means of the possibility of such rebirth.
Furthermore, this statement merely implies that one who has fully traversed all four dhyānas may be said to have "perished everywhere."

Therefore, the *Mahā-sūtra* clarifies that among those who "proceed upward" (*ūrdhva-srotas*), if they receive two births, they are called those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya`); if they receive four births, they are called those of dull faculties (*mṛdu-indriya`).
[Note] The seven types in the *Mahā-śāstra* have the same names as in the *Abhidharma-kośa*, though their order differs slightly, as shown in the diagram below. *Abhidharma-kośa-śāstra*.

It is said: There are four distinctions regarding those who practice the formless realm (*ārūpya*). That is to say, there are those who, while in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), become free from craving for the form realm;
at the end of their life there, they are reborn in the formless realm. These, together with the five previously mentioned, constitute six types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).

Furthermore, there are those who do not go to either the form or formless realms, but rather remain right here in this [desire realm] until their afflictions are exhausted and they attain parinirvāṇa in the present life. Together with the previous six, these make seven. This is the "complete leaping over" (*atyantābhisambhedaka*).
This refers to one who, having already practiced the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) throughout the four dhyānas within the desire realm, is capable of being reborn in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

However, due to falling away from that state because of encountering certain conditions, they are reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas. Only after passing away from the Brahmakāyika realm can they subsequently be born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Because they completely bypass all intermediate stages, this is called "Total Leaping" (*sakalābhisambhinna*).
[Supplement] This refers to a person who, taking the relish of the first dhyāna as a condition, is reborn among the Brahmakāyika devas at the end of their life.

Furthermore, by the power of habitual practice from previous lives, they are able to perform the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna; thus, passing away from the Brahmakāyika realm, they are reborn in Akaniṣṭha.

This is called "complete leaping" (*ūrdhvaṃsrotas*). [Appendix] Questions and Answers from the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries). Question: How can one who has fallen away [from a higher state] subsequently attain "complete leaping"?

Why is this? The answer is: according to the intent of the *Abhidharmakośa*, one who encounters adverse conditions and falls back from their attainment gives rise to fear and exerts great application (*prayoga*).

How much more so for one in the desire realm who has already practiced extensively; thus, they are able to leap entirely beyond [the stages] without falling back. It is not so for those who do not fall back.
Therefore, there are only two types: the Half-Leaper (*ardhapluta*) and the One Who Dies Everywhere (*sarvacyuta*).

[Commentary] As for the Half-Leaper: having passed away from the Brahmakāyika heaven, one gradually undergoes rebirth through the intermediate heavens—such as the Brahmapurohita and Parīttābha—in an indefinite order.
Within these fourteen heavens, one may leap over one, two, or even thirteen levels before finally being born in the Akaniṣṭha heaven; all such cases are termed [Half-Leapers].
This is the "Half-Transcender" (*ardhapluta*), so called because it is not a "Full-Transcender" (*sarvacyuta*); thus, it is collectively designated by the name "half.

[Supplement] Within the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*), there are eighteen heavens in total. The Brahmakāyika is the first place where one passes away, while the Akaniṣṭha is the final heaven of rebirth.
As for the intermediate Mahābrahmā, the Ābhāsvara (associated with the pride of *asmimāna*), and the Asaṃjñisattva—heavenly abodes of these two types are not [inhabited by] noble ones (*ārya*).
Therefore, it is said there are fourteen. Within these, if one transcends one heaven, one transcends the Heaven of Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita).

If one transcends two heavens, one transcends both the Heaven of Ministers of Brahmā and the Heaven of Limited Radiance (Parīttābha), and so on, up to the thirteenth, which is the transcendence up to the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudarśana).
If one reaches the fourteenth, this constitutes a complete transcendence; therefore, it is not discussed [as a partial leap]. It can be seen that among the fourteen heavens, as if there were one...
If one does not transcend even to the heavens, all such cases are termed "half-transcending" (*ardhapluta*).

[Note] "Universal descent" (*sarvasthānacyuta*) refers to those who are entirely unable to transcend; this is called universal descent. Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are sixteen heavens.

Mahābrahmā is the abode of the conceit of being a lord of gods (*īśvara-māna*); the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) is where non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*) dwell. Noble ones (*ārya*) are never born in these two heavens.
[Note] In the Avataṃsaka, the Great Brahmā King is assigned to the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi). Regarding the statement that "the noble ones are not born," how should this be reconciled?

One must understand that while those who manifest through the clear aspiration of the Mahāyāna may likewise be considered "born" [into these stages], the śrāvakas of the Small Vehicle who practice according to the reality [of their path] are not born [therein].

[Commentary] In the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are further nine types. That is, within the "attainment of nirvāṇa in the form realm" (*rūpadhātu-saṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), the five [types] are combined into three:

those with exertion (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and those without exertion (*anabhisaṃskāra*), both of which are subsumed under "attainment of nirvāṇa upon rebirth" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*). Thus, the three are expanded into nine. The verse says: "There are nine in the form realm, meaning each of the three is divided into three;
due to differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties, the distinction between the three and the nine is established."

[Commentary] This indicates the nine types [of non-returners] in the *Abhidharmakośa*. By combining the single type of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin)—which consists of both those with effort (*sābhisamskāra*) and those without effort (*anabhisamskāra*)—with the aforementioned "attaining parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarā-parinirvāyin) and the subsequent "ascending to the highest" (ūrdhvasrotas), these five are consolidated into three. The treatise states:

"That is, the five types of non-returners who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are collectively established as three; since each is further divided into three, they constitute nine types. What are these?

Third, there are three types, distinguished as those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain it upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who ascend to higher realms (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

How are these three each further divided into three? First, those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state are divided into three: those who attain it quickly, those who do not attain it quickly, and those who attain it after a long duration.

This is illustrated by the analogy of the three sparks. Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth are likewise divided into three: those who attain it with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and so forth. Parinirvāṇa...

Because they attain parinirvāṇa after being born, these are all "attainers of parinirvāṇa upon birth. Therefore, they should all be designated as "attainers of parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadya-parinirvāyin).
Within the category of those who go upstream (ūrdhva-srotas), there are also three types distinguished by the differences of "leaping over" (pluta), "half-leaping" (ardha-pluta), and so forth.
Nevertheless, all three types attain parinirvāṇa—whether quickly, not quickly, or after a long duration—therefore, when compared with one another...
Because they are free from confusion, these three types and nine types of non-returners (anāgāmin) differ according to their karma, afflictions (kleśa), and faculties (indriya).
Consequently, there are distinctions such as being swift, not swift, or taking a long time; thus, they are collectively categorized into three groups.

Furthermore, due to the differences in the performance and accumulation of subsequent karma that leads to rebirth, there is the manifestation of lower, middling, and superior afflictions respectively.
Due to their distinctions, and due to the distinctions among the superior, middling, and inferior faculties, each of these three is further divided according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, because there are distinctions in both karma and faculties, with three factors for each, nine types are formed; namely, the first two sets of three.

Due to differences in afflictions (*kleśa*), faculties (*indriya*), and [the timing of] karma, each [type of non-returner] is established as threefold. The latter three are not differentiated by differences in karma alone;

they are also divided into three types due to distinctions in karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*). Thus, it is said that these non-returners who proceed to the form realm (*rūpaga-anāgāmin*) are distinguished into nine types based on the differences in their karma, afflictions, and faculties.

[■ Record] This chart illustrates the seven types [of *anāgāmin*] from the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*. Their names are identical to those in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, though their order differs slightly.

[■ Supplement] Regarding the statement that "the six types of *anāgāmin* are included therein," the intended meaning is that the six types of *anāgāmin* according to the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (the treatise on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*) are identical to the seven types in the two aforementioned treatises (*Kośa* and *Vibhāṣā*).
Why? Because when the six types are explained according to the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, they correspond to the "one who takes birth twice in one realm" (*ekavīcika*) within the sevenfold classification.

Up to the sixth, the "attaining parinirvāṇa in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*). Among the seven types, the "attaining parinirvāṇa in the formless realm" (*ārūpya-dhātu-parinirvāyin*) is missing.

If one follows the *Abhidharmakośa* in clarifying six types, this consists of the "two births in one [life]" (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) up to the sixth, the "attaining parinirvāṇa in the formless realm"; thus, the seven types are complete.
Therefore, Jingxi [Zhiyi] established one and did not establish another, specifically pointing to the sixth to correspond with *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, thereby making it manifest.
Although *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are said to be of six kinds, they are actually seven.

[Commentary] This diagram illustrates the nine types of *parinirvāṇa* according to the *Abhidharmakośa*. The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing zhuanhong jue*) quotes the treatise, stating that there are three types of *antarāparinirvāyin*:

namely, the swift (*kṣipra*), the non-swift (*akṣipra*), and the long-dwelling (*cirasthitika*). According to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, these constitute nine types in total, as each of the three is further divided.
Third is the "one who attains parinirvāṇa after having been born" (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), which refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa only after being born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

This includes both those with effort (*sābhisaṃskāra*) and those without effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*). These are all subsumed under the category of "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth. Regarding the three types within this middle category, they are: the swift, the non-swift, and the long-delayed.

These three meanings are illustrated by the analogy of a flying spark; reflect on this and it will be understood. All of these are discussed in terms of "swift," "non-swift," and so forth, regarding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). There are three types of birth.

Regarding these: first, the "one-birth" (ekajāti) is established based on speed; second, the "with-effort" (sābhisaṃskāra) is established based on non-speed; third, the "without-effort" (anabhisaṃskāra) is established based on duration.

These all refer to the speed and so forth once one has already been born in the form realm. Regarding the three types of "up-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas): first, the "complete leaper" (pluta) is established based on speed;
second, the "half-leaper" (ardhapluta) is established based on non-speed; third, the "all-perishing" (sarvasthānacyuta) is established based on duration. From the initial form realm...

Śrīlāta: From beginning to end, these three types of persons differ. Thus there are three groups of nine. These differences arise from the distinctions in karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the difference in karma: one who performs karma conducive to the present life becomes an *antarāparinirvāyin*; one who performs karma conducive to the next birth becomes a *upapadyaparinirvāyin*;

and one who performs karma conducive to a subsequent life becomes an *ūrdhvasrotas*. Regarding the three types of afflictions: one with weak afflictions becomes an *antarāparinirvāyin*; one with middling [afflictions]...

Those with weak afflictions attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; those with strong afflictions attain parinirvāṁṇa by going upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Regarding the distinction of faculties: those of superior faculties attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyī*);

those of middling faculties attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth; and those of inferior faculties attain parinirvāṇa by going upstream. [Supplement] Those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state quickly do so before abandoning the body while still within the desire realm.
Those who are not quick do so after having left the desire realm. Those who take a long time do so until reaching the edge of the form realm. Those who attain parinirvāṇa upon rebirth do so quickly.
"Those who attain parinirvāṇa immediately upon birth in the form realm; those who are not swift, who are born in one of the four or five heavens with varying intervals;
those who take a long time, reaching up to Akaniṣṭha; those with a swift upward flow, who leap entirely across; those who are not swift, who leap halfway; and those who take a long time."

"Universal extinction. Regarding those who attain [nirvana] in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*): this person’s revulsion toward suffering is so intense that they regard the three realms as a prison; they attain nirvana while still remaining in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Regarding those who attain it in the next life (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*): their minds are more lax, and they reach the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Regarding those who attain it in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-parinirvāyin*): these are even more lax;

reaching the Akaniṣṭha heaven (the highest point of the form realm), those with inferior-grade afflictions reach the form realm; those with medium-grade afflictions reach the third or fourth dhyāna heavens; and those with superior-grade afflictions [reach higher].

Furthermore, it is heavy. Reaching up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven: "up" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); "middle" refers to the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); and "down" reaches the Akaniṣṭha.
This is the explanation based on the *Mahāsūtra*. [Appendix] Bian’e says: "The 'intermediate parinirvāṇa' is the 'subsequent-to-arising' [attainment] according to the treatise."

What is called "arising through eating fragrance" refers to the arising of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Since the intermediate state takes fragrance as its food, it is said to "arise by eating fragrance.

It is also the intermediate state itself; therefore, it is called "arising in accordance [with its nature]. Master Jingxi, fearing that people might not understand this, changed the character for "manifest" (*xian*) to [the character for] "arise" (*qi*).
[Note] Various texts state that there are either five types, referring exclusively to the *rūpa-parinirvāyin* (one who attains parinirvāṇa in the form realm), or eight types.

These consist of the seven [types] within the three realms, with the addition of the *aniyata-parinirvāyin* (one of indefinite attainment). (Supplementary Note: As cited at the beginning of section 14 from the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, this category includes those who, among the parinirvāyins of the three realms, possess an indefinite nature.

It demonstrates the characteristics of the indefinite type: having set their intention for the desire realm, they attain parinirvāṇa; or, failing to achieve it, they are reborn in the upper realms where they realize the fruit. Alternatively, those who intend to be reborn in the upper realms may suddenly activate past habitual tendencies and realize the fruit immediately in the desire realm. The cases of the form and formless realms should be understood by analogy.)
[Commentary] This explains the one who attains parinirvāṇa without fixed timing (*aniyata-parinirvāyin*). Regarding the statement that "the form and formless realms are explained by analogy":

this means that having set one's intention for the form realm, one either attains parinirvāṇa immediately, or fails to achieve it and instead takes birth in the formless realm to realize realization; or, having set one's intention for the formless realm, one realizes realization while still in the form realm.
Furthermore, having set one's intention for the formless realm, one may attain parinirvāṇa in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), or fail to achieve it.

[They] are reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). The various heavens above this take [this] as their realization; or, those who aspire to be born in the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) realize it at the very moment they reach the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
[Supplement]: "Old Master Jin" (*Jinlao*) is a personal title. During the Song dynasty, there was Dharma Master Chongjin, whose *Yingjing ji* (Collection of Elite Works) is still extant.

Because his age and spiritual attainment were similar [to the author], he was addressed as "Old Master Jin. In the *Shunjiang jiyao* (Essentials of the Shunjiang Region), the name Jin appears frequently.
Regarding the designation "old":

[Note] The *Abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* (Zaxin lun) enumerates seven types. Those employed in the *Miaoxuan* consist of five from the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), where the first is divided into three—namely, "quick," "not quick," and "long duration"—to which the latter four are added to form seven.

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmahṛdaya* lists seven types of parinirvāṇa: namely, one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly, one who does not attain it quickly, one who attains it after a long duration, one who attains it upon rebirth (*upapadya-parinirvāyin*), one who attains it through exertion (*sābhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*), one who attains it without exertion (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*), and one who flows upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas-parinirvāyin*).
[Note] The *Abhidharma* contains twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty types of *anāgāmin*. This is fully demonstrated in the fifth fascicle of the *Shiqian*.
[Record] The *Shiqian* cites the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma* as saying: "The *anāgāmin* may be of five, seven, or eight types."

Five [types] refer to those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), with effort (*sābhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), without effort (*anabhisaṃskāraparinirvāyin*), and those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*). Seven [types] refer to dividing the intermediate-state attainers into three, according to the analogy of a spark of fire.

Eight [types] refer to the five as mentioned above, plus those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmaparinirvāyin*), those in the formless realm (*ārūpyaga*), and those who are indeterminate (*aniyata*); for now, they are explained according to these five categories.
That is to say, there are five kinds of form (*rūpa*). From the perspective of the faculties (*indriya*), there are fifteen, because each of the three—superior, middling, and inferior—is fivefold.

In terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), they become twenty, because there are five in each of the four dhyānas. In terms of lineage (*gotra*), there are thirty, because each of the six lineages—those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), those who reflect (*cetana-dharman*), those who protect (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those who abide (*sthita-ākampya*), those who advance (*prativedhanādharman*), and the immovable (*akopyadharman*)—is fivefold.
In terms of locations (*sthāna*), there are eighty, from the Brahmakāyika heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, which comprise sixteen locations.
Because there are five for each. For each type of *anāgāmin*, there are two thousand five hundred and ninety-two. Why?
Based on the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), sixteen persons are formed. Based on the six spiritual lineages (*gotra*), this is multiplied by six, resulting in ninety-six.
Based on the faculties (*indriya*), there are three types; multiplying these by three results in two hundred and eighty-eight.
Further multiplying this by nine—the number of persons who have abandoned desire—results in two thousand five hundred and ninety-two persons.
Since this is the case for one type, when the five kinds of *anāgāmin* are likewise multiplied in succession, they become twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty types. Nine.
Regarding those who have abandoned desire (*vītarāga*): this refers to nine types of persons based on their abandonment of the nine grades of afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

[Commentary] As for those who attain *parinirvāṇa* in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*): immediately upon leaving the desire realm and being born into the form realm, their revulsion and mental distress are so acute that they attain *parinirvāṇa* while still in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*). Therefore, they are categorized as belonging to the form realm.
[Supplement] This briefly clarifies the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the parinirvāṇa therein. As in the Mahā-sūtra’s *Kāśyapa-paripṛcchā*:

"For what reason is there parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? The Buddha said: 'Good son, this person contemplates that the causes and conditions of the afflictions (*kleśa*) in the desire realm are twofold:
first, internal; second, external. In the form realm, there are no such internal or external causes and conditions. Regarding the desire realm...
Furthermore, there are two kinds of craving: first, sensual desire; second, craving for food. One contemplates these two cravings and rebukes them with a sincere heart.
Having thus rebuked them, one attains entry into nirvāṇa. Within this realm of desire, one is thus able to rebuke all coarse afflictions.
That is to say, through stinginess, greed, jealousy, lack of shame, and lack of remorse—by these causes and conditions—one is able to attain parinirvāṇa.

Furthermore, because the path of the desire realm is courageous and vigorous, one attains the fruit of the direction [toward liberation]; therefore, there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) within the desire realm, but not within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Good son, there are three kinds of nirvāṇa. The superior kind is when, having cast off the body but not yet being free from the desire realm, one immediately...
Parinirvāṇa. The intermediate type attains nirvāṇa having just departed from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) but not yet reached the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The inferior type attains nirvāṇa only after departing from the desire realm and reaching the edge of the form realm. Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* asks:

"If there is parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state in the form realm, is there also such in the desire realm? The answer is: "No. The desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is [characterized by] much..."

When one dwells in the state of the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*), it is already difficult to attain the fruit due to various faults and obstacles; how much more so when dwelling in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) with its subtle and inferior body?
Yet, the *Mahāsāṃghika-āgama* states that there is "attainment of parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyī*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Why is this different from the *Vibhāṣā*, which says there is no such attainment in the desire realm? It is likely because the Sūtra refers to those who, upon the end of their life in the desire realm, immediately undergo the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); thus, it speaks of the desire realm.

Regarding "existence in the realm" (*dhātu-bhava*): this treatise bases its argument on the defilement of desire (*kāmarāga*). Since one must necessarily proceed toward the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) before attaining parinirvāṇa, it speaks of "existence in the form realm.
Although the terminology differs, their meaning is identical. Therefore, the mention here of "intermediate existence" (*antarābhava*) is included within the category of the form realm.
[Note] If one reaches the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and is reborn in a higher heaven, although there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one cannot be said to attain parinirvāṇa therein;
this is because one lacks the power of prior habituation to cultivate revulsion toward suffering, as explained in the *Xuanzong* (Section on the Lower).
[Commentary] The details regarding the analysis of the *Xuán* (Mysterious) are not yet clear.

[Note] Regarding why the intermediate parinirvāṇa (*antarāparinirvāyin*) is not established for those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), the *Zhǐguī Chão* (Notes on the Pointing Back), fascicle 18, states: "The Sūtra says: 'Sentient beings of the formless realm...'"

Regarding those who maintain that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*): according to the teachings of the Abhidharma, with the exception of the four formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), an intermediate state definitely exists in all other places;
this is because the formless realm lacks a physical location (text).

[Commentary] This passage briefly clarifies that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) does not establish the existence of one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*). However, in the *Chao* (the Sub-commentary), it cites a treatise explaining a sutra:

"In the formless realm, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*). As the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states: "The five types of intermediate beings consist of the five aggregates of the intermediate state;
they possess coming and going, and thus are not 'mixed' in color. Because they possess coming and going, the intermediate state exists in the desire and form realms."
It is not the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because form (*rūpa*) is not a constituent part [there]. Therefore, one knows that there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm;

thus, "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (*antarāparinirvāyī*) is not established [there]. [Supplement] Master Jingjue composed a commentary on the *Amitābha-sūtra* titled the *Zhíguīchāo*.

Regarding the fact that the formless realm has no location, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states: "The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) dwells below, the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) dwells above, and the formless realm has no [location]."

Regarding location: the *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) has no location. This is because when one attains that meditative absorption, one is reborn in that very place immediately upon the end of life;
furthermore, when one passes away from there and is born into the desire or form realms, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises in that very same place.
Since the formless realm lacks a location, when one dies and is born there, "that place" is simply where one was at the moment of death.
Therefore, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) for those who later fall back and are reborn in the realms of desire or form; it is only at that time that the intermediate state manifests.

Furthermore, this explains why there is no intermediate state in the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). This is because the intermediate state belongs to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*);

taking conception in a womb necessarily requires a physical location. Since the four formless heavens lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), they rely solely on space and so forth as their locus, being supported by the environment of emptiness.
Since form (*rūpa*) is absent, how could there be the substance of a primary retribution? Therefore, in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that wherever one attains the formless meditative absorption (*ārūpyasamādhi*), at the time of death, one is immediately reborn in the Formless Realm.
[Commentary] This refers to the treatise’s clarification intended to resolve potential objections. Fearing that there might be an objection stating:

"If there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how can it be known that one attains birth there?"—this [passage] explains it by clarifying that taking the attainment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in each respective place as the cause results in birth in the formless realm immediately upon the end of life as the effect.

[Note] The diagram cites the "five distinctions" (referring to the five *anāgāmin* heavens; there are five types of distinctions within the causal stage). These are: lower, middle, upper, superior-upper, and supreme-upper.

The *Fuxing* (Vol. 6, Part 1) and the *Poxuan* (Vol. 13, Part 2) provide detailed explanations of their characteristics. By means of these five dhyānas, one is born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
[Commentary] This concise diagram cites five distinctions. The first phrase indicates the heading; the subsequent part points to the explanation of the modes of practice (*ākāra*).
The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Regarding the generation of the five containments: however, due to the cultivation of perfumed dhyāna, there are five stages of gradation.

While the nine concentrations in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* universally perfume the nine stages, herein one perfumes only the stage of the fourth dhyāna. Having first cultivated and attained it, one further uses many moments of thought..."
The untainted (anāsrava) continuity arises; from this, many moments of the tainted (sāsrava) are induced; from this, again, many moments of the untainted arise.
In this manner, they gradually decrease in each subsequent stage until finally there are two moments of the untainted.

Next, two moments of contaminated [thought] are induced; immediately thereafter, two moments of uncontaminated [thought] arise. This is called the "perfuming of the preparatory stage" (*prayoga-saṃskāra*).
Next, there is one moment of uncontaminated [thought], followed by one moment of contaminated [thought]; immediately thereafter, one moment of uncontaminated [thought] arises again.
This is called the "fundamental stage" (*maula*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Completion occurs through a single moment of intermingling."

Regarding the "five distinctions," these refer to: inferior, middling, superior, superior-excellent, and supreme. Each grade consists of three levels, and each subsequent grade incorporates those preceding it;
thus, the fifth grade comprises fifteen levels in total. These five grades, following their respective order—namely three, six, nine, and so forth—give rise to the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
This concludes the explanation by summarizing the intent of the citation. [Supplement] The diagram cited herein illustrates the five distinctions.
This refers to the aforementioned diagram of the seven types of *anāgāmin* within the three realms of the *Abhidharmakośa*. "Difference" (*chā*) refers to the gradations;
it specifically points to those who practice mixed cultivation through the joy of wisdom (*prajñā*), who are born in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

Since the characteristics of the five grades of mixed cultivation have not yet been clarified, this is now explained: practicing mixed cultivation at the lower level results in birth in the *Avṛha* heaven, and so forth.

The highest grade of the mixed cultivation leads to rebirth in the Akaniṣṭha heaven. The *Lengyan wenju* states: "The first is the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Avṛha*), which corresponds to the lowest grade of mixed cultivation.

This means that after the practitioner has first refined the four dhyānas of the human realm, within these meditative concentrations, they first give rise to a continuous succession of many moments of untainted (*anāsrava*) mind manifesting before them, followed by a continuous succession of many moments of tainted (*sāsrava*) mind."
It manifests before one. Furthermore, many moments of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind arise and manifest in succession.

In this manner, gradually reducing them until there are two moments of uncontaminated mind followed by two moments of contaminated (*sāsrava*) mind, and then again two moments of uncontaminated mind—at that time, it is called the completion of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of mixed cultivation.
Next, one moment of uncontaminated mind, one moment of contaminated mind, and one moment of uncontaminated mind arise; reaching this point is called [the completion of the actual mixed cultivation].

This serves to bring the fundamental [attainments] to completion. Because these are interspersed with both outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states, they are called "mixed cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*).

They are also termed "interlaced perfuming meditation" (*miśra-vāsana-dhyāna*), because by using the outflow-free to interlace and perfume the outflow-tainted, the form-sphere concentrations become increasingly clear and their karmic fruition becomes increasingly superior.
By means of this, they sustain their prior karma; thus, they pass away from the Bṛhatphala heaven and are born in the Avṛha heaven.
Next, in the Atapa heaven, one practices the intermediate degree of mixed cultivation (*miśrabhāvanā*). This involves six moments of mind:

using the three lower grades of the aforementioned [moments] as the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), one further induces three moments of mind—one untainted (*anāsrava*), one tainted (*sāsrava*), and one untainted—as the fundamental stage (*maula*). By sustaining their prior karma through this, they pass from the Bṛhatphala...

Upon passing away from the Fruit of Great Reward (*Bṛhatphala*), one is able to arise in the Heaven Free from Affliction (*Avṛha*) and the Heaven Free from Heat (*Atapa*). Third is the Heaven of Good Vision (*Sudṛśa*):

this refers to those who have practiced the superior degree of mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*). There are nine moments of mind; the first six serve as the preparatory application (*prayoga*), while three further moments of mind are produced as the fundamental (*maula*).

By means of these, they support their prior karma and, passing away from the Fruit of Great Reward, are born in the Heaven of Good Vision. Fourth is the Heaven of Good Appearance (*Sudarśana*): this refers to those who have practiced the superior-superior degree of mixed cultivation.

In this stage, there are twelve moments of mind. One employs the first nine moments as the preliminary application (*prayoga*), further inducing three moments as the fundamental (*maula*) to support the previous karma, thereby enabling one to transcend the three heavens and be born in the Sudarśana (Good Appearance) Heaven.

This is the highest grade of the fivefold mixed cultivation (*pañcavidha-vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*). There are fifteen moments of mind; one employs the preceding twelve moments as the preliminary application, further inducing three [moments].
The mind is the root. Supported by past karma, it is able to transcend the four dhyāna heavens and be born in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven. Regarding the outflow-free and the outflowing:
it is like contemplating all phenomena as lacking a real self and lacking real dharmas, observing them directly in accordance with the principle.
This very [practice] can serve as the condition for perfuming the inherently existent untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) so that they are activated; this is called "untainted" (*anāsrava*).
If, however, it arises without observing the principle and involves a mind mixed with grasping, it is called "tainted" (*sāsrava*). The same applies to mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*).
First, many moments of the outflow-free (anāsrava) arise; next, many moments of the outflow-possessing (sāsrava) arise; and finally, again many moments of the outflow-free arise.

This remains the case even down to a single moment. This discussion, however, is made solely with reference to the state of meditative concentration (samādhi), regarding what is outflow-possessing and what is outflow-free.
As for the claim that while one is in meditative absorption it is untainted (*anāsrava*), but upon emerging from absorption it becomes tainted (*sāsrava*): this is incorrect.
What is meant by "arousing a tainted thought within concentration" is precisely this: becoming greedily attached to the state of concentration, thinking, "This is sublime. This is what is meant.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding those who delight in discussion (*vāda*), this is said in fear that they might practice contemplation while in the lower realms;
it does not mean that there is discussion among those born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*). This is because from the Second Dhyāna upward, there is no speech (text).

[Commentary] This briefly clarifies that there is no discursive debate in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. As the Abhidharma school states: "The three faculties of eye, ear, and body reside in two stages [of dhyāna];
thus, even in the first dhyāna, gustatory consciousness does not arise, let alone in the second dhyāna. In the second dhyāna, even speech is not required, let alone in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Therefore, one knows that there is certainly no discursive debate in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. Some say that the Anāgāmin...
The statement regarding those who delight in discursive debate refers only to the time when they practice contemplation in the lower stages. [Supplement] The Mahāyāna Sūtra states:

"There are two types of those who attain parinirvāṇa by ascending to the higher realms: first, those who delight in wisdom; second, those who delight in meditative concentration. Those who delight in wisdom enter the five Pure Abodes."

Regarding those who delight in concentration: they enter the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Thus there are two types of persons: one who delights in discursive discussion (*saṃkathya*) and one who delights in tranquility (*śamatha*).
The one who delights in tranquility enters the formless realm; the one who delights in discursive discussion is born in the Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).
