Section Four, The Fruit of Non-arising. Four:

Arhat (*arhan*). This is translated as "One Beyond Training" (*aśaikṣa*), also called "Non-arising," also called "Slayer of Thieves" (*vadhaka-ghāta*), and also called "Worthy of Offerings" (*dakṣiṇīya*).
In this stage, both the views and the afflictions (*kleśa*) are completely severed. While the fetters of the cause have been eliminated, the fetters of the fruit still remain;
this is called *nirvāṇa with remainder*. If the body is reduced to ashes and consciousness is extinguished, it is called *nirvāṇa without remainder*, also known as "solitary liberation."

[Note] In this stage, the eighty-four defilements of the eight upper stages are severed, and the four wisdoms (*jñāna*) are perfected: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established;

what was to be done has been accomplished; there is no further state of existence. Since there is no further dharma to be learned, it is called the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and it is also termed the ultimate. This is as explained in the lower section of the *Jieshenmi* (Analysis of the Profound).

[Commentary] Regarding the eight stages of the form and formless realms, each has nine grades of volitional thought (*cetanā*). Thus, there are seventy-two grades of afflictions of volitional thought (*cetanā-kleśa*) in total.
At this stage, these are completely purified and exhausted without remainder. As for the phrase "perfection of knowledge" (*jñāna-pāramitā*), it is as stated in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*:

First, "My births are ended"—the Arhat has severed the afflictions of views and volitional thought (*dṛṣṭi-cetanā-kleśa*) and will no longer undergo birth and death within the three realms. Second, "The holy life (*brahmacarya*)..."

"Already established," O Brahmā, refers to pure conduct; that is to say, an Arhat achieves this fruit through the perfection of the practices of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Third, "that which was to be done has been accomplished": this means that while the Arhat originally sought liberation from the three realms, now that birth and death have been exhausted, they will no longer receive a future body of existence.
Furthermore, the Preceptor said: "The cycle of birth and death spanning vast eons has, at this present moment—"
Birth has come to an end; thus my births are exhausted. Having ascended the stages of the untainted path-factors (*anāsrava-mārga-pakṣya*), the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is established.

The four fruits of the śramaṇa have now been realized; thus what was to be done is accomplished. With the dissolution of the physical body and the cessation of cognition, there shall be no further rebirth.

Therefore, there is no further existence. Furthermore, the *Vibhāṣā* states: "My births are exhausted" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*). "The holy life is established" refers to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
"What was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). "There is no further existence" refers to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

Furthermore, "my births are exhausted" is said to be the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). "The holy life is established" is said to be the knowledge of the path. "What was to be done has been accomplished" is said to be the knowledge of cessation. There is no further existence... [text continues].

There is no further existence. This is the teaching on the knowledge of suffering; thus, the four knowledges are perfected. Furthermore, these four phrases are also called the "four applications of the lower [stages] to the Four Truths. As the *Vibhāṣā* states:

"My births are exhausted" refers to the four applications of the lower [stages] to the Truth of Origination (*samudaya*). "The holy life is established" refers to the four applications of the lower [stages] to the Truth of the Path (*mārga*).

"What was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the four applications of the lower [stages] to the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha*). "No further existence will be received" refers to two applications of the lower [stages] to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha*), namely: [the application of the aspect of] emptiness and [the application of the aspect of] non-self.
[They are] impermanent and suffering. Furthermore, according to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, among the two kinds of death, there is no "death by fragmentation" (*vibhava-maraṇa*).
Therefore, it is said that for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, "birth has been exhausted," and they have attained the realization of the fruit with remainder;

thus it is said that "the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established. This is something that ordinary persons, gods, and humans cannot accomplish, nor was it previously [attained] by the seven types of trainees (*śaikṣa*).
That which has not yet been done is the severing of false and delusive afflictions; this is called "having completed what was to be done.
Because the afflictions severed by Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas can never again lead to future existence, it is said that they "will not undergo further existence.

Thus, their names are now explained based on the perfection of their wisdom and the fulfillment of their practice: investigating the Truth and severing delusions constitutes the stage of "those still in training" (śaikṣa); when the Truth is fully realized and delusions exhausted...

Exhaustion is called "no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*). Furthermore, this state of no-more-learning is termed "ultimate" because the four knowledges are perfected and complete therein, and the two types of delusion are ultimately exhausted.

The *Bie xuan* does not elaborate on this. [Appendix] Bian’e says: In this ritual text, "no-more-learning" should be "non-attachment" (*asaṅga*), for "no-more-learning" refers to a stage of practice rather than a literal translation of the term. This remains to be examined.

[Commentary] Regarding the term *arhat*: according to one passage in the *Wenju* (Textual Explanations), it is said that there is no direct equivalent translation because it encompasses three meanings.

The *Jingming shu* (Vimalakīrti Commentary), fascicle 10, citing the *Zhilun* (Treatise on Wisdom), explains: first, "slayer of thieves" (*vadhaka*), so named from the destruction of evil; second, "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), so titled from the terrifying of Māras;

third, "worthy of offerings" (*arhat*), a virtue established through the mendicant’s life. (This is an explanation based on the correspondence between cause and effect. Because it contains many meanings, it is not translated [into a single Chinese character].
Now, the Master [Jizang] rectifies the original intent and translates it according to three meanings; this merely accords with ancient usage.

[Commentary] This clarifies that the translation is based on three meanings: first, because the husk of ignorance has been shed, one will not receive the retribution of birth and death in the fields of future lives, and is thus called "Unborn" (A-janma).
Second, because the ninety-eight types of afflictions (*anuśaya*) have been exhausted, one is named "Slayer of Thieves" (Arhat).
Possessing the merits of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*), he is worthy of being a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for humans and devas; thus, he is called "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*).
Because it encompasses these three meanings, the Sanskrit name is retained and said to be "untranslatable. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Arha means 'thief' and han means 'to destroy.
Because all thieves of the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been destroyed, he is an Arhat. Furthermore, because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, he is an Arhat. He should attain [the fruit].
He is honored by all the devas and humans of the entire world. Furthermore, "A" is named "Non-," and "Arhat" is named "Birth.

Because he will not be born again in future lives, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā* quotes this to provide a definitive explanation. This is a phrase explained through the correspondence of cause and effect.
To further explain the meaning:
[Note] When explaining the etymological names for bhikṣus, such as "mendicant" (*yācanaka*), one cites these names based on their results.
This is intended to manifest the rank of a *mahābhikṣu* (as seen in the *Fahua wenju* and the *Guanjing shu*).

[Commentary] This clarifies the intent behind various commentaries explaining the cause by reference to the fruit. The first two phrases directly explain the cause by reference to the fruit. The passage beginning with "It is because...
expresses the underlying meaning; that is to say, as in the various commentaries, the name of the *bhikṣu* (mendicant) is explained by reference to the cause of being a "beggar" (*yācanaka*).
He terrifies Māra, destroys evil, and—necessarily corresponding to the name of the fruit—is called an Arhat (Worthy of Offerings). He is "Unborn" and a "Slayer of Thieves.
These names are used because one wishes to reveal that the rank of a Great Bhikṣu is precisely that of an Arhat; thus, by referring to the fruit, the cause is explained. The *Wenju* states:
regarding "Bhikṣu," Master Sengzhao says it means "Pure Life" (*śuddhājīva*) in the Qin language, [attained through] begging for food, and it signifies the destruction of afflictions (*kleśa*).

"Being able to uphold the precepts," "frightening Māra," and so forth—these four meanings are contained within a single name in India. Since there was no corresponding term in the Qin language to translate it, the original designation was retained.
Master Kumārajīva said: "At the beginning, when one leaves the household of wife and children, one should sustain oneself by begging for alms to maintain a pure livelihood;
at the end, when one leaves the household of the triple world, one must destroy the afflictions and maintain the precepts to guard oneself. One must possess these two."
Regarding the meaning: the celestial Māras fear that he has transcended their realm. The *Śāstra* states: "Frightening the Māras" and "Destroying evil.

As for the "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*): Māra delights in birth and death; since [the practitioner] has left the household life and further transforms others so that they all depart from the three realms, this runs counter to Māra’s intent.
When Māra attempted to subdue him with force, he was instead bound by the five fetters; thus, being filled only with sorrow and fear, he is called "Terrifier of Māra" (Bhumagha).

Those who have left the household life must destroy the seven evils of body and speech; therefore, they are said to "destroy evil. Now, for those living at home, there are three ways of acting in accordance with the Dharma:

first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service—these are used to sustain one's physical life. For those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit these; they may only beg for themselves.

"Ji" (to rescue/salvage). When the person is at ease, the Way exists; this brings benefit and merit to the donor (*dānapati*). These three meanings mutually support one another, which is precisely the meaning of a *bhikṣu*.

In the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* and the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*, those who destroy evil are all designated as *bhikṣus*, yet these [three] meanings were not fully explained there. Now, to clarify these three meanings, they should apply throughout both the beginning and the end.

For example, at the time of initial ordination, through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations), the power of the unmanifest precept (*avijñapti-śīla*) pervades...

Regarding all objects, one reverses non-action and evil. When first practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one gives rise to the precepts concomitant with concentration (*samādhi-sahagata-śīla*), which restrains and subdues the mental ground so that greed and anger do not arise.

When first practicing insight (*vipaśyanā*), one gives rise to the precepts concomitant with the path of semblance (*sambhāra-mārga-sahagata-śīla*), which is able to subdue the initial moments of the afflictions (*kleśa*);
this is also called "destroying evil. Why should it apply only to the final moment? As for "terrifying Māra," this occurs when one first shaves the hair and receives the precepts.

They cause Māra to grieve. One cultivates concentration (*samādhi*) with the desire to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*); one cultivates wisdom (*prajñā*) with the desire to destroy the afflictions. Even the initial mind causes Māra to fear; why speak only of the final mind?
As for the "mendicant" (*bhikṣu*), from the very beginning they abandon wrong livelihood and sustain themselves by begging;

in cultivating meditation, they seek concentration amidst the various sensory objects; in cultivating wisdom, they seek the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state by taking principle as their object—all these are mendicants. How much more so when [the characteristics] are present?
One who is worthy but not a mendicant—because he possesses this meaning, he is universally termed a *bhikṣu*. According to the Sūtra masters, they all praise the latter mind;

however, the meaning of *bhikṣu* necessarily extends to the beginning, while the realization of faith must come later. Therefore, it is praised here because it encompasses both the beginning and the end.

All of these reflect the intent of the Tripiṭaka. Having concluded the citation from the *Wénjù*, the *Guānjīng Shū* states: "Regarding the term 'bhikṣu' (monk), there are six meanings based on cause and effect.
As for the causes: 'beggar' (*kṣānti*), 'frightener of Māras,' and 'destroyer of evil. As for the effects: 'worthy of offerings' (*arhat*), 'slayer of thieves,' and 'non-arising' (*anutpāda*).

Furthermore, the *Shū* explains that the name "beggar" refers to pure food. The *Chão* says: "One who constantly practices begging for alms is called a beggar; this applies up until the attainment of the fruit."

This constitutes the attainment of the virtue of being worthy of offerings (*arhat*). The Commentary states: Regarding "frightening Māra," if one resolves to leave the household life, the terrestrial *yakṣas* proclaim it;
this is relayed through the air-dwelling [yakṣas] up to the six heavens of the desire realm. When the King of Māras hears this, he fears losing his retinue. The Sub-commentary says:
Because leaving the household life entails freedom from defilement and an orientation toward the unborn (*anutpāda*), when the King of Māra hears of this, his mind...

Giving rise to a sense of dread, one diligently cultivates the three trainings and realizes the fruit of non-arising (*anutpāda*). The *Sū* (Commentary) states that "destroying evil" means that all ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) are completely shattered and severed.

The *Chao* (Excerpts) says: "To investigate and exhaustively analyze through the cultivation of contemplation is called 'destroying evil'; when realized wisdom has brought them to total cessation, it is called 'severing'."
This is called "slaying the thief. [Supplement] It is translated as "one who refrains from committing evil. The objects are the five desires and the six sense-fields.
If one indulges excessively in lust and killing, then lust and killing manifest at all times; this is called "committing evil.
Now, by receiving the precepts, one turns away from lust, killing, and so forth toward the mind that upholds the precepts; thus, the characteristics of the precepts manifest.
[Note] Furthermore, while the preceding reference to "śrāvakas" encompasses both ordinary and noble stages, the term "arhat" is restricted to the fourth fruit.

The samādhis cultivated at this stage are threefold: first, the Vajra; second, the Double Emptiness; and third, the Lightning Flash (the former two names are as in the fourth fascicle of the *Miaoxuan*;

the Lightning Flash is as in the ninth fascicle of the *Zhiguan*; the meaning of the Lightning Flash applies generally to the first fruit, while the Vajra applies to all five types of arhats; the Double Emptiness specifically pertains to that practiced by the Immovable Arhat).

[Commentary] This explains the samādhis cultivated by an arhat. First, the names are listed; next, they are explained; finally, the names are concluded as applying to the general stage. As the *Xuánwén* says:
"The arhat liberated by time (samayavimukta) attains the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the insight of one beyond training (aśaikṣadṛṣṭi) in five ways.

If he employs the vajra-samādhi, the nine grades of delusion in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) are exhausted. Immediately thereafter, in a single kṣaṇa..."

Then, having realized the ninth liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). In the subsequent moment, one acquires the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
Alternatively, because such a person may encounter adverse conditions and occasionally regress, it is not said that they attain the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).

Furthermore, it is said that an Arhat who is liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*) is called one of immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*); such a person accomplishes three knowledges, namely: the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, and [the right view].
Wisdom. It is the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samyagjñāna*) that is able to use the "repeated emptiness samādhi" (*guru-śūnyatā-samādhi*) to strike at the noble and wholesome dharmas.

Because it uses concentration to relinquish concentration, it is said to be "able to strike. The commentary states: "The samādhi of 'emptiness of emptiness' (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), the samādhi of 'signlessness of signlessness' (*animitta-animitta*), and the samādhi of 'wishlessness of wishlessness' (*apraṇihita-apraṇihita*):
emptiness is itself a noble dharma; to further cultivate emptiness and strike at those prior noble dharmas is called 'repeated emptiness. However, gold..."
The *khaṅkha* (vajra) samādhi is common to the first five types of arhats, whereas the *śūnyatā-viśeṣa* (repeated emptiness) samādhi is cultivated specifically by the immovable (*akopya*) arhat.

The *Zhi guan* states: "Regarding that which is called 'lightning-flash' (*vidyut-prabhā*), the aforementioned treatise asks: Apart from the seven bases of concentration (*saptāśraya-samādhi*), is there further concentration that gives rise to the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state?

The answer is: Yes; there is the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) that can give rise to the outflow-free state, appearing as sudden as a lightning flash. (From the *Yizu jiaojie jing*).

The Sūtra says: "If one sees a flash of lightning, one may momentarily attain the vision of the Path. This is like Ānanda, who, exerting his mind and not allowing it to relax, reached for his pillow and immediately entered the lightning-flash state.

The meaning of this "vision" extends to the first fruit [of the path]. [Supplement: Because it can sever the difficult-to-sever delusions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called "Vajra" (the Diamond-like Samādhi).

[Note] This is the specific designation for the fruit. There are two kinds, three kinds, six kinds, and nine kinds; furthermore, there is the meaning of the nature of the fruit being subject to regression or non-regression.
These shall now be demonstrated in detail. First, the two kinds are clarified.

[Supplement] Regarding *prajñā-vimukti* (liberation through wisdom): although it is said that one enters directly by taking emptiness as the object, it is also connected with the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight recollections (*aṣṭasmṛti*), and the ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*).

As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The nine perceptions are the contemplation for attaining liberation. Because fear arises from practicing the nine perceptions, one further practices the eight recollections to eliminate it.
Since the mind is then peaceful and free from hindrances, one further practices the ten perceptions to transform the mind."

Contemplation (*saṃjñā*). Taking these as conditions, one opens the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*); taking the thirty-seven factors as conditions, one opens the gate to *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, although one cultivates the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) and so forth, this is nonetheless a direct entry into emptiness (*śūnyatā*) by means of conditions.

As for "liberation through both [aspects] that involves phenomena and combined cultivation," this refers to the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight spheres of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten spheres of totality (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*), which constitute "phenomena."
Regarding "the non-decaying dharma comes to dwell in the perception of bones," the *Yishu ji* (Commentary on the Meaning) states:

this refers to the eighth stage within the nine perceptions (*navasaṃjñā*), where one cultivates the "eight-colored radiant light" upon the white bones of the eighth [perception]. As for the "eight colors":

one perceives the color of earth, like a ground that is yellowish-white, pure, and clean; one perceives the color of water, like the clear, limpid water of a deep abyss; one perceives the color of fire, like...
It is like smokeless and pure fire; seeing the color of wind, it is like dustless and swirling pure wind. Seeing blue, it is like Mount Kanakamuni (Golden Essence Mountain).
Seeing yellow, it is like a *campaka* flower. Seeing red, it is like the morning glow of spring. Seeing white, it is like jade, conch, or snow.
It is the state where colors are clearly perceived yet lack substantiality or obstruction. [Note] The analysis in the *Xuán* (Mysteries) section below is not detailed. In the diagram:
The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mysteries), fascicle 4, states: "One liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) is a practitioner of faith with dull faculties;

because they attain liberation only when the time and conditions are complete, they are called 'timely. One liberated not by time (*asamayavimukta*) is a practitioner of the Dharma with sharp faculties.

Such a person, having cultivated the path during their causal stage, is able at all times to advance in the cultivation of wholesome deeds according to their desire, without depending on external conditions."

Therefore, they are called "those liberated at improper times" (*asamaya-vimukta*). Furthermore, it is said that those who do not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) are merely those liberated by wisdom at specific times (*samaya-prajñā-vimukta*), whereas those who do attain the meditative absorption of cessation are those liberated both ways at all times (*asamaya-ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*). The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Regarding those in whom the meditation on impurity arises: first, there are those who follow the 'Dharma of Destruction' (*vināśa-dharma*) and cultivate the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*); such persons seek only to sever suffering and burn it away."
Regarding the skeleton: one should urgently attain the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and take no pleasure in the contemplation of conditioned phenomena.

Since there is no skeleton to be contemplated, there will be no supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transformations, the "wishing-knowledge" (*praṇidhijñāna*), or the "summit-dhyāna" (*mūrdha-dhyāna*). Nevertheless, although the body perishes, the actual body still exists. It continues until it is said:

"This is precisely the person of wisdom who severs delusions through worldly knowledge; if they are not a person who destroys the dharmas, they cultivate the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), beginning with the bloated."
Contemplation. One comes to dwell in the eighth contemplation of the skeleton, but does not advance to the ninth contemplation of burning.

One attains the possession of radiant light, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), refinement, perfuming, cultivation, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transformations, and all other merits in their entirety, thereby becoming a person liberated-in-both-ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*).
Now, according to the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), the explanation of the nine contemplations states: "The Six Subtle Gates and the Special Victories..."
The "clear comprehensions" (*abhiññā*) and so forth are merely contemplations of reality (*bhūta-vipaśyanā*); they are not yet contemplations that have attained liberation (*vimokṣa*).

From the "nine perceptions" (*navasaṃjñā*) onward, these are contemplations that have attained liberation; they possess powerful efficacy in counteracting the grave illness of the afflictions (*kleśa*).

These nine are called "perceptions" (*saṃjñā*) because they can transform the mind and transform perception—that is, they can transform the inverted perception of impurity. Therefore, these nine dharmas are all termed [perceptions].

This is the contemplation. A detailed explanation can be found in the fifth fascicle of the *Aśubhabhāvanā* (Contemplation of Impurity). Regarding the "Eight Recollections" (*aṣṭau smṛtyupasthānāni*), the text states:

"If, while practicing the nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*), one contemplates a corpse as loathsome and thereby becomes startled and terrified—so much so that the hair stands on end—the evil Māra will cause agitation and distress, and one's anxiety and fear will only increase.
If, however, one maintains the mind upon the eight recollections, such dread and fear will immediately be eliminated. As for what is meant by "recollection," it refers internally to...
The mind dwells upon recollecting various names; by focusing the mind exclusively on recollecting the eight kinds of merit, they are called the "eight recollections.

What are the eight recollections? They are: first, recollection of the Buddha; second, recollection of the Dharma; third, recollection of the Saṃgha; fourth, recollection of the precepts; fifth, recollection of relinquishment.

Sixth is the recollection of the devas; seventh is the recollection of non-returning (*anāgāmin*); eighth is the recollection of death. Regarding the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*), the text states: "The nine perceptions are like binding a thief;
the tenth perception is like killing a thief. The Great Master said: "If that were so, then the ninth perception should follow immediately after the preceding [set];
why is it placed after the eight recollections? It is simply because when practicing the nine perceptions, obstacles such as fear may arise; once the eight [recollections] have been practiced...

Contemplation. Being free from all terrors, the mind becomes peaceful and unobstructed. Therefore, following the eight recollections (*aṣṭa-anusmṛti*), one should employ the ten perceptions (*daśa-saṃjñā*).

Generally speaking, "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to that which can transform the mind and transform perceptions; it is called perception because it can transform and overturn various inverted perceptions, such as those of permanence and bliss.
The first three perceptions are taught for the purpose of severing the delusions regarding the truths (*satya-kleśa*). The middle...

There are four perceptions taught for the purpose of severing the afflictions associated with discursive thought. The latter three perceptions are taught for those practicing the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).

Therefore, by cultivating these ten perceptions, one who destroys [the defilements] can sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms and realize the fruit of untainted holiness (*anāsrava-āryaphala*).
What are the ten perceptions? They are: first, the perception of impermanence; second, suffering; third, non-self; fourth, the perception of the foulness of food...
1. Purity; 2. the five worldly things that are not to be delighted in; 3. death; 4. impurity; 5. severance; 6. the perception of detachment; 7. the perception of exhaustion.
Regarding the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), the text states: "The preceding nine perceptions and the tenth perception are mental states that involve the disintegration of phenomena.

As counteractive contemplative methods, they are restricted horizontally and short vertically; none of them are fully complete. If one realizes the fruit of sainthood, these three [liberations] do not exist."

This explains the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*). When one cultivates these contemplations to refine the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and realizes the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), one becomes a powerful Arhat, endowed with the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the eight liberations, and other such merits.

Regarding why these eight are collectively termed "back-turning abandonments" (*prātikūlyavimokṣa*), the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "To turn one's back on these pure five desires is 'back-turning' (*prātikūlya*); to abandon the mind of attachment is 'abandonment' (*vimokṣa*). Thus it is called "back-turning abandonment."

It is called "liberation" (*vimokṣa*). If one gives rise to true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) and exhausts the fetters and karma of the three realms, it is then called "deliverance" (*vimukti*).

For a detailed explanation, see the fifth fascicle on the Meditation on Impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and the Eight Bases of Mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), which are also called the Eight Spheres of Totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*);

these are also found in the fifth fascicle. Regarding the Ten Spheres of Totality (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), the text states that they are named after the objects of observation; they are also called the Eleven [Spheres].
The entry points are: first, the sphere of all-blue; second, yellow; third, red; fourth, white; fifth, earth; sixth, water; seventh, fire; eighth, wind; ninth, space;
and up to the tenth, the sphere of all-consciousness. Regarding the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the text says:

When entering dhyāna, because one’s profound resolve and wisdom are deep and sharp, one can enter from one dhyāna into another with each moment of mind succeeding the next, uninterrupted by any other thought;
therefore, it is called "successive. Regarding the successive concentration of the first dhyāna:

having abandoned all desires, unwholesome states, and evil dharmas, and possessing applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one enters the first dhyāna concentration born of seclusion, characterized by joy and bliss. At the time of entering this first dhyāna concentration:
In this regard, the meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*) of the first dhyāna is balanced and even. One recognizes one's own mind, and the mind enters [the state] sequentially;
there is not a single moment of distracted thought intervening before entering the first dhyāna. This is called the sequential attainment (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) of the first dhyāna.
As for the sequential attainment of the second dhyāna: when one enters the second dhyāna from the first dhyāna, the meditative observation of that second dhyāna is likewise balanced and even.
Equanimity (*śamatha*). One recognizes one's own mind, and the mind enters sequentially, without a single moment of intervening discursive thought, entering the second *dhyāna* absorption.

This is the sequential concentration of the second *dhyāna*. The sequential concentrations of the third and fourth *dhyānas* are to be understood by analogy with the explanations given for the first two *dhyānas*.

[The same applies to] the fifth, the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); the sixth, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); the seventh, the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); and the eighth, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The successive attainments (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are both explained as above in the first two dhyānas.
Regarding the ninth successive attainment, the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha*):

when entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one first recognizes one’s own mind prior to this attainment, resolves with a sharp mind, and enters it stage by stage, mind following upon mind.

Without a single moment of distracted thought intervening, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception; this is the sequential concentration of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Regarding the "lion," the text states that the bodhisattva, relying on the nine sequential concentrations, enters the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi* (the lion’s stretch samādhi).
The term "lion’s stretch" is used as a metaphor to reveal the Dharma, just as a worldly lion stretches.
"Swift. This is for two reasons: first, to shake off and cast away the dust; second, to be able to run forward and run back with a speed that surpasses all other beasts.
This samādhi is likewise: first, it shakes off and removes the subtle, ignorant delusions that obstruct concentration;
second, it is able to enter and emerge with such swift, uninterrupted agility that it differs from the meditative concentrations previously attained. Furthermore, there is...
There are two meanings. First, regarding "the lion’s leap into meditative absorption" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*):

having abandoned sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, one enters the first dhyāna; proceeding in this manner, one enters the second and third dhyānas.

The four dhyānas, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—these constitute the "leaping entry.
Second is the "leaping emergence from dhyāna. Regarding the "lion’s leaping emergence":
one arises from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling and re-enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the sphere of neither-perception...
It is not that the perception of nothingness does not arise; rather, one returns to the sphere of nothingness.

In this same manner, one proceeds through the spheres of consciousness, space, and the fourth, third, second, and first dhyānas, even down to emerging into the distracted mind. This is called "emergence by mastery" (*vikrīḍita*). Regarding "transcending," the text says:
The Bodhisattva, relying upon the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, enters the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* and is thus called a "transcender" (*vyutkrāntaka*).
Because they are able to transcend the various stages (*bhūmi*) and enter and emerge from them with mastery, it is named "transcending. Furthermore, there are three meanings.
First is the "transcendent entry into samādhi. What is meant by the transcendent entry into samādhi? It is to be free from all desires, evil, and unwholesome states. There is...

Perceiving with directed thought, he enters the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss. Arising from the first dhyāna, he leaps directly into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he returns to the first dhyāna. Arising from the first dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling...

Emerging from concentration, he enters the second dhyāna. Emerging from the second dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the third dhyāna.

Emerging from the third dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the fourth dhyāna.

Emerging from the fourth dhyāna, he enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling. Emerging from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, he enters the sphere of infinite space. Emerging from the sphere of infinite space, he enters...
He enters the cessation of perception and feeling; from the cessation of perception and feeling he arises. He enters the sphere of consciousness; from the sphere of consciousness he arises.

He enters the cessation of perception and feeling; from the cessation of perception and feeling he arises. He enters the sphere of nothingness; from the sphere of nothingness he arises. He enters the cessation of perception and feeling; from the cessation of perception and feeling he arises.
He enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception he arises. He enters...
The attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*). This constitutes the characteristic of a bodhisattva’s transcendent entry into samādhi.
If a śrāvaka can only enter one [of these] transcendentally and cannot enter two, how much less could they achieve the sovereign transcendence explained above?

Within this, three types of transcendent entry are clarified: first, transcendent entry in forward order; second, transcendent entry in reverse order; and third, transcendent entry in both forward and reverse order.
The subtle mind, in terms of its meaning, can be understood by oneself. Second is the "transcending samādhi. What is called transcending samādhi?

It is when one arises from the cessation of perception and feeling and enters into a state of distracted consciousness; then, arising from that distracted consciousness, one enters the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one dwells again in a distracted state of mind. Arising from that distracted state of mind, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one dwells in a distracted state of mind. Arising from that distracted state of mind, one enters the sphere of nothingness.

Arising from the sphere of nothingness, one dwells in a distracted state of mind. Arising from that distracted state of mind, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness. The sphere of infinite consciousness...

He arises. He dwells in a distracted state of mind. From the distracted state of mind, he arises and enters the sphere of infinite space. From the sphere of infinite space, he arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind.

From the distracted state of mind, he arises and enters the fourth dhyāna. From the fourth dhyāna, he arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind. From the distracted state of mind, he arises and enters the third dhyāna. From the third dhyāna, he arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind.
From the distracted state of mind, he arises and enters the second dhyāna. From the second dhyāna, he arises and dwells in a distracted state of mind.
Rising from a distracted state of mind, one enters the first dhyāna; this is the mark of the samādhi-superiority of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If Śrāvakas can only emerge from one dhyāna and cannot emerge from a second, how much less could they emerge with mastery?
Within this, there are three types of transcendence: first, progressive transcendence; second, regressive transcendence; and third, both progressive and regressive transcendence.
Together with the three preceding types of transcendent entry, these constitute the six types of the *vyutkrāntaka-samādhi* (transcendental samādhi).
It is through these six types of samādhi that the Tathāgata enters nirvāṇa. This concludes the explanation of the shared meditative practices of the three vehicles.

Regarding "contemplation, refinement, perfuming, and cultivation," the *Zhiguan* states: "Contemplation" refers to the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhvāyatana*), and the ten totalities (*daśakṛtsnāyatana*).
These are collectively termed the contemplative meditations (*vipaśyanādhyāna*). The nine notions are established to destroy the fire of lust in the practitioner;

they require the cultivation of increased mental imagery until it is thoroughly matured, so as to eliminate worldly craving and destroy the six kinds of desire. Once these nine have removed desire, [the subsequent stages follow].

Furthermore, anger and delusion are attenuated, and the mountain of the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is shaken. The characteristics are fully detailed in the *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate). Regarding the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni*):

These three types of contemplative fulfillment constitute the accomplishment of the essential body of the contemplation-dhyāna, as detailed in the *Dhyanamukha*. As for "refining," it refers to the nine successive stages.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the phrase "named according to conditions": this means that liberation is attained only when one awaits the proper time and the requisite conditions; thus it is called "timely.

[Note] Alternatively, according to the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, it is because it is associated with wisdom that is either timely or untimely as its opposing factor.

If the five faculties are progressively inferior, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*).
One should know that the treatise states: those with sharp faculties are called "simultaneous" (kū), which refers to the "non-timed" (apratītya) in contrast to the "simultaneous" person;

Those who are both [concentrated and wise] are those liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*), who are practitioners of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) with sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇendriya*), and are called "immovable arhats" (*akopya-arhat*). "One should know that the one liberated through wisdom does not attain the absorption of cessation; if one attains the absorption of cessation, one should know them as liberated both ways.

Question: Since the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are said to consist solely of the mental factor of wisdom (prajñā), which is weak, how can they sever the fetters (saṃyojana)?

Answer: The mental factor of wisdom does not arise in isolation; how could it not be able to sever the fetters? Question: If these various factors arise together, this would mean they share a common nature (sādhāraṇa). Answer: [As follows:]
The various enumerations (*gaṇanā*) arise accordingly; there are three types. First, when the wisdom that contemplates the principle arises, the various enumerations arise spontaneously;

this is called the "foundational mindfulness of nature" (*dharmatā-smṛtyupasthāna*). Second, by cultivating the various enumerations as auxiliary wholesome dharmas for the path, one severs the fetters;
therefore, the Buddha taught that the accumulation of wholesome dharmas belongs to the "shared mindfulness" (*sābhisaṃskāra-smṛtyupasthāna*). These are the auxiliary path and the direct path.

Because they sever the fetters in common, the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* specifically states that the universal foundations of mindfulness (*sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna*) can sever the fetters. However, for those of sharp or dull faculties who employ the specific foundations of mindfulness (*svabhāvasmṛtyupasthāna*), it is not the case that they do not sever the fetters.

[Note] Third: In terms of phenomena and principle, directly taking the true principle as the object of focus is called "liberation through wisdom" (prajñā-vimukti). Practicing with both phenomena and principle concurrently is called "double liberation" (ubhaya-vimukti).

(Text) By this it is known that those who possess both [powers] are fully endowed with the three clear knowledges.

[Commentary] This section specifically clarifies the distinctions regarding the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). As for the "three types of clear knowledge," they are: the clear knowledge of the divine eye, the clear knowledge of past lives, and the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*).
While these are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, what is presented here is the Hīnayāna version of the three clear knowledges, which differs from the Mahāyāna.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Although those of the three vehicles attain the three clear knowledges, their clarity is not fully perfected; the Buddha alone has perfected them all. This is the distinction."

Regarding the eight liberations: first, the liberation of one who possesses internal perception of forms while observing external forms; second, the liberation of one who lacks internal perception of forms while observing external forms.

These two involve turning away from and abandoning attachment to form. Third, the liberation of the body through the realization of the sublime resolve of purity, wherein one dwells having fully attained it;

this one involves turning away from and abandoning the mind of impurity. Fourth, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, and not... [the text continues].
Reflecting on various perceptions, he enters and dwells in the sphere of infinite space; this is the first turning away.

Abandoning the factors of the lower stage, fifth, he transcends the entire sphere of infinite space and enters and dwells in the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is the sixth.
7. Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one enters and dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters and dwells in the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. These three constitute the turning away.

One abandons the dharmas of the lower stages. Eighth: transcending all spheres of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters and dwells in the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling;
this is the eighth liberation. This constitutes the abandonment of all minds that take existence as their object. These are the eight liberations.

Now, by means of these three knowledges (*vidyā*) and eight liberations, one distinguishes and determines whether wisdom (*prajñā*) is conjoined with other factors. That is to say, those who possess them [the knowledges] are necessarily endowed with [the liberations], because they were already present within the causal stage.

Regarding the simultaneous attainment of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) as both cultivated and innate, and the simultaneous realization of the three knowledges (vidyā) and eight liberations (vimokṣa) at the stage of fruition:

the reason why those of "wisdom" (prajñā) do not possess them is that during the causal stage they cultivate only the innate foundations of mindfulness, and at the stage of fruition they realize only the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).

If one were to fear that those of wisdom lack the three knowledges, how could the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) speak of the three knowledges? [The answer is that it refers to the three knowledges attained through cultivation.]
Regarding the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*): do all arhats possess them? Therefore, this [passage] addresses the distinction between being complete and incomplete.

The intention is that those who possess the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are "persons of both" (i.e., possessing both wisdom and supernormal powers), whereas those who lack them are merely "persons of wisdom. (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, Vol. [lower]).
There is a deficiency in the wisdom of separate realization. Furthermore, there are three schools that praise both concentration and wisdom. The first school, which praises wisdom, speaks as follows:
"If one possesses the three types of higher knowledge (*trividyā*) but does not possess the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), they are called 'one with the three knowledges.

If one possesses the three types of higher knowledge and also possesses the eight liberations, they are likewise called 'one with the three knowledges. One who possesses the eight liberations but lacks the three types of higher knowledge is called..."
Both are liberated. If there are those who possess one or two types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*), they are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*).

Why is this? Because their wisdom is superior to the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). The second school, which praises meditative absorption, speaks as follows: "If one possesses all eight liberations..."

One who lacks the three types of higher knowledge (*traividya*) is called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*). If one possesses the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and has the three types of higher knowledge, they are also called "liberated in both ways.
If one has the three types of higher knowledge but does not possess the liberations, they are called "one with the three types of higher knowledge" (*traividyaka*).

If one possesses only one or two types of higher knowledge, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñāvimukta*). Why is this? Because the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is superior to wisdom. This is the third school of thought.

It is said: These two explanations are both futile in their effort and offer no benefit regarding the meaning of the text, because among those with the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*), some have attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) while others have not.
If one has attained it, they are called "liberated in both ways" (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) and possess the three knowledges;

if one has not attained it, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (*prajñā-vimukta*) and possess the three knowledges. Now, the commentary cites the second passage as a praise of those who have attained this meditative absorption.

Regarding those who have realized the three knowledges (*vidyā*) but possess deficiencies, these are "persons of wisdom" (*prajñā-pudgala*). By analogy, one should understand that those who are fully endowed with the three knowledges are "persons of both" (*ubhaya-pudgala*).

This is precisely what is meant by the statement that there are "persons of wisdom who lack the three knowledges," which is also based on the initial intent of the *Jñānaprasthāna* (or *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*).

However, the supplementary explanatory text cited above states: "The 'penetrations' (*abhisamaya*) apply to all six [knowledges], whereas the 'knowledges' (*vidyā*) are restricted solely to the three. This is because...

This reveals that there is a difference in the application of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the clear knowledges (*vidyā*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is the difference between the supernormal powers and the clear knowledges? It answers:

"To directly know past lives is called the supernormal power of recollecting past existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*). To know past causes, conditions, and karmic actions in addition to that is called a clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

To directly know dying here and being born there is called the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*). To know the causal conditions and limits of those births in addition to that is [the clear knowledge of death and rebirth]."

The assembly does not fail; this is called "clarity" (*vidyā*). To directly know the exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) but not yet know whether there will be further rebirth or no further rebirth is called the supernormal power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).

If one knows the destruction of outflows and that there will be no further rebirth, it is called "clarity. Thus, there is a distinction between shallow and deep within the supernormal powers and the clarities.

Furthermore, regarding why three of the six supernormal powers are established as "clarities" while the remaining three are not, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The supernormal power of the body..."
These are the methods of skillful means. The divine ear hears sounds only; the knowledge of others' minds perceives distinct characteristics of phenomena.

These three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) accord with the dharma of wearying detachment, enable the abandonment of birth and death, accord with wholesome dharmas, and lead to nirvana. Why is this?

By means of the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, one realizes the wisdom of previous existences; through higher knowledge, one sees the events of the past and gives rise to great wearying detachment.

The supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is the realization of the knowledge of birth and death; it clearly perceives the affairs of future lives and engenders great wearying detachment (*nirveda*).

Because of this wearying detachment, one realizes the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), whereby one is able to practice correct contemplation and sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, while the supernormal power of the divine eye merely knows that sentient beings die here and are born there, "clarity" (*vidyā*) additionally knows the distinctions of the karma they have created, as does the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*).

The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-abhijñā*) consists merely in knowing past births; the corresponding clear knowledge (*vidyā*) additionally knows the distinctions of names and surnames.

The supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-abhijñā*) consists merely in knowing that the afflictions have been severed and exhausted; the corresponding clear knowledge additionally knows that they will never arise again.

The Four Foundations of Mindfulness (1). Regarding the two meanings of the Four Teachings (*sijiao*), the *Abhidharmakośa* also speaks of three types of Arhats, each discussing three foundations of mindfulness.

[Supplement] "Those who sever the fetters by taking principle as their object" refers to those who take the principle of non-arising emptiness as their object, giving rise to true untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to sever the fetters and delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
"Eliminating inherent defects" refers to eliminating [defects] within the body, sensation, mind, and dharmas.
"Permanence, bliss, self, and purity" are the defects of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena are by their very nature originally impermanent, suffering, empty, non-self, and impure; they cannot be altered, and therefore they are called "nature. [Commentary] The *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna*) states:

The Abhidharma explains three kinds of foundations of mindfulness—namely, nature (*svabhāva*), association (*sahabhū*), and object (*ālambana*). These are established to counteract the three types of non-Buddhist paths. There is...

Regarding the "nature mindfulness-establishment" (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna): observing the shallowness of non-arising is called "arising. they give rise to the true [path] and sever the fetters, attaining the state of an Arhat liberated by wisdom. This serves to refute false causes and conditions. There is no...

Those who hold inverted views regarding causes and conditions and the nature of all-knowledge are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). As for the "shared application of mindfulness" (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*):

by employing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) as an auxiliary to the Path, one practices the union of the primary and the auxiliary; this is also called the "contemplation of both phenomena and principle.

Through this, one brings forth and attains the untainted (*anāsrava*) three knowledges (*vidyā*), six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), becoming an Arhat liberated in both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*). This stands in contrast to those outside [the Buddhist path] who, having destroyed fundamental craving and pride, attain only the five supernormal powers.

This is the Way. As for those who take the foundations of mindfulness as their object: they take as their objects the words and phrases of the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures, as well as all worldly names and designations;

thus, the scope of their objects is vast. They thoroughly understand the faculties and natures [of beings], are skilled in the four analytical knowledges, and are capable of compiling the Dharma-treasury.
He attained the state of a Great Arhat free from doubt. He refuted the worldly Vedas, astrology, and geomancy; their scriptural texts are base and narrow.
One should know the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, the true and the false, just as gold is compared to iron. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "Among all conceptualizations..."
Impermanence is supreme. Among all types of plowing, autumn plowing is supreme. Among all tracks, the elephant’s footprint is supreme.
Impermanence is like the nature [of the field], plowing is like supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the track is like written characters. The Sūtra says:

"O upāsakas, you are well-versed in the gateways of the counteractive methods (*pratipakṣa*) of all phenomena, namely permanence, impermanence, and so forth. Therefore, one knows the activity of the mind.
"Outside of principle" means not yet having entered into the true and correct [path]. The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states:

Regarding the three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* that result in the three kinds of *arhat*, the "nature *smṛtyupasthāna*" (*xing nianchu*) is precisely the wisdom that takes principle as its object. When this *smṛtyupasthāna* is associated with it, one gives rise to the true outflow-free [wisdom].

One becomes an Arhat liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*). Through the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the wholesome five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the accomplishment of the liberations (*vimokṣa*), up to the samādhi of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*), the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), and the summit dhyāna (*mūrdha-dhyāna*)—such aids to the path unite with the right path (*samyag-mārga*) to give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*).

One attains the three knowledges (*vidyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and being endowed with the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), one becomes an Arhat liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*). If one contemplates...

As for the "bases" (*sthāna*): they consist of the Buddha’s teachings as the conditions, and all that is expressed therein—the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—as well as the two kinds of mindfulness of the nature [of phenomena] (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*).
When one contemplates these names and meanings while in meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one gives rise to the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*);

such a person is called a Great Arhat with the liberation of non-doubt (*aniśrita-vimokṣa*). Furthermore, it is said: "That which is called the 'mindfulness of self-nature' (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna')..."
This refers to non-erroneous wisdom (*aviparīta-prajñā*). As the Buddha taught the cultivation of the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*): this "contemplation of the body" is wisdom.

Regarding the "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), because one does not falsely grasp at objects in whatever task is undertaken, and because one eliminates the faults of intrinsic nature, they are called "foundations of mindfulness.

Nanyue said: They are also called the "practice of wisdom" (*prajñā-caryā*) and the "contemplation of reality" (*bhūta-darśana*); they are the essential method for severing the fetters by taking principle as the object. Thus it is said:

Regarding the "shared foundations of mindfulness" (sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna): they are dharmas that accompany wisdom. As the Buddha said, "This bhikṣu is an accumulation of wholesome dharmas," referring to the four foundations of mindfulness;
this is the correct teaching. Nanyue says: They are also called "practices of practice" and "attaining liberation.
They are wholesome dharmas among the objects of counteraction that, together with the Right Path, sever the fetters—namely, form and the various categories of phenomena.

Furthermore, one can also give rise to the various dhyānas and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). That which is called the "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) refers to all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
As the Buddha has said: "O Bhikṣus, all phenomena are the four foundations of mindfulness; this constitutes their correct gathering and fulfillment."

Furthermore, regarding the abbreviated conditions, Nanyue said: "These are still the two types of *smṛtyupasthāna*—the intrinsic and the concomitant—which, through the union of the observing wisdom and the observed objects, fully establish the meaning of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
If one can analyze and observe them, one will immediately give rise to the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*).
He further stated: "The Buddha’s teaching on the four *smṛtyupasthānas* transcends the [teachings of] the three groups of six heretical masters."
Thus, he is able to refute all non-Buddhists. Regarding the six teachers of "all-knowledge," they first perceive principles through their initial resolve, yet they give rise to false wisdom;
their eloquence is unimpeded. Regarding the six teachers of "supernatural powers," they have attained mundane meditative concentrations.

They have developed the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and possess the power of compassion and patience. Whether their bodies are cut with knives or smeared with fragrant incense, their minds harbor neither hatred nor attachment;
all of this is the functional power of the twelve gates of fundamental dhyāna.

As for the six teachers of the Vedas, they were extensively learned and well-informed, mastering the four Vedas, the eighteen great scriptures, worldly auspiciousness and misfortune, astronomy, geography, and medicine.

He was currently engaged in divination and physiognomy, knowing nothing that he did not know. These six teachers were such that, internally, they possessed the manifestation of all-encompassing wisdom;
externally, they were able to perform supernatural transformations and discern the auspiciousness and misfortune of the world.

They were thoroughly proficient in the four Vedas and the eighteen great scriptures, understanding them all without exception. The sixteen great kingdoms revered them as Buddhas. [The Buddha thought: "I wish to destroy these..."

Because there are three kinds of six teachers, three kinds of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are taught. First, the foundation of mindfulness regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*) refutes those who claim to possess "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*).

These outsiders all rely upon the two views of self and body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) to give rise to their claim of all-knowledge, asserting that they have attained *nirvāṇa* characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
This is like an insect boring through wood and accidentally forming characters; the insect itself does not know whether these are characters or not.

Furthermore, the present contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) destroys these two views—the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)—so that the four views, the sixty-two views, and other such inversions do not arise.
For this reason, it destroys all the six teachers who claim omniscience. Second, the shared foundations of mindfulness destroy those with supernatural powers (abhijñā).

Non-Buddhists (bāhyaka) merely develop the five supernatural powers based on the four fundamental dhyānas; since their concentration is shallow and limited, [it cannot withstand the power of this contemplation].
There is no lack of the contemplation of impurity. As for the transformations of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), they need not even be mentioned.

Now, through the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is immediately able to give rise to the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the lion’s bound and leaping samādhis (*siṃhavijṛmbhitātikrāntasamādhi*).

He manifested various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Since his meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) was profound and the power of his contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) was great, the supernormal powers he manifested were unimpeded and sovereign, with transformations beyond limit.

He crushed all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) as easily as turning over one's hand. Thus, it was through the power of the common mindfulness foundations (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*) that Śāriputra subdued Raudrākṣa and Maudgalyāyana transformed the river to drown the non-Buddhists. All these were accomplished by means of the contemplation of the common mindfulness foundations.
This is supernormal power (*abhijñā*). Next, regarding the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that destroys the Vedic non-Buddhists:
the four Vedas and the eighteen great scriptures all clarify worldly discourses on the love of humans and devas, as well as views and shallow, mundane theories.
The Buddha’s teaching of the supramundane Tripiṭaka—both in name and in meaning—is not recorded in those scriptures. Thus, the Buddha taught the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): by taking as an object the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) of teachings spoken by the Buddha—the supramundane names, meanings, and principles of the Dharma—one compares and contrasts them.
How could these be what outsiders have heard or seen? Therefore, by means of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness, one refutes the Vedas and the non-Buddhist paths.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmakośa* also speaks of three kinds of Arhats, each discussing the three foundations of mindfulness; this refers precisely to that treatise.
In the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* on the essence of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it says:

"The essence of these four foundations of mindfulness each has three types, distinguished by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), their association (*saṃsarga*), and their object (*ālambana*). The foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence.

This wisdom is of three kinds, namely that which is produced through hearing, reflection, and cultivation; these are also called the three types of foundation of mindfulness. The foundation of mindfulness as association [has wisdom as its essence]..."

The remaining [factors] have co-existent [dharmas] as their substance. As for the object-condition mindfulness-establishment (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), it has the various dharmas that are the objects of wisdom (*prajñā*) as its substance.

How is it known that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is wisdom and nothing else? A sutra states: "Abiding in the body while contemplating the body is called the mindfulness-establishment of the body."

The same applies to the other three [foundations]. The term "contemplation" (*anupaśyanā*) refers exclusively to wisdom (*prajñā*); it does not refer to that which is not wisdom, because such things lack the function of contemplation.
For what reason is the name "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) established for wisdom? The Vaibhāṣika masters say: "Because mindfulness is predominant in this category;
it is by the sustaining power of mindfulness that wisdom is able to proceed, just as an axe cuts wood by the sustaining power of a wedge. In truth, however, one should say:

Wisdom causes mindfulness to abide; therefore, the name "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is established for wisdom. This is because, in accordance with what wisdom contemplates, it is able to clearly retain [the object] in memory.

For this reason, Aniruddha spoke thus: "If one is able to abide in the body while practicing the contemplation of the body (*kāyānupaśyanā*), mindfulness conditioned by the body will become established," and so forth at length.
The Blessed One also said: "If one abides in the body while practicing the contemplation of the body..."

As for the practitioner of contemplation, mindfulness abides without error. However, there is a sutra that says: "By what cause do these four foundations of mindfulness arise? By what cause do they cease?
They arise because of the arising of nutriment, contact, name-and-form, and attention; respectively, they cause the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena to arise.
They cease because of the cessation of nutriment, contact, name-and-form, and attention; respectively, they cause the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena to cease. This should be understood.
That [tradition] explains it as the application of mindfulness with respect to the object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), because mindfulness abides therein.

Furthermore, the specific names of the applications of mindfulness vary according to their respective objects, due to the differences between one's own, another's, and both's continuums (*saṃtāna*). Each individual application of mindfulness has three types.

[Supplementary Note] The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* explains the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely: body, sensation, mind, and phenomena. Within a single moment of thought, these further possess three types:
intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), association (*saṃsarga*), and object (*ālambana*). What constitutes the foundation of mindfulness by intrinsic nature?

"Contemplation" (*cintā*) refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) arising from reflection. Why is it called the "application of mindfulness associated with intermingling"? For example, when one contemplates the impurity of the body, this is the primary wisdom;

Why is it called the "application of mindfulness with respect to the object"? It refers precisely to the objects of focus—the body and sensations.
The mental factors (citta-dharma) constitute its essence; it is nourished by contact (sparśa) and name-and-form (nāmarūpa). This is an analytical exposition of all phenomena.

Why are the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) distinguished by their respective objects? Because they differ according to whether they take themselves as the object, others as the object, or both self and others in their continuity.

Liberation; it is liberation through the absence of doubt. (Text) Since this is extracted from the *Mahāśāstra* (*Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*), it was included among the teachings during the Buddha’s lifetime.

[Commentary] Regarding the first point, "The *Ji* [sub-commentary] says: 'The *Xiyuan*' (Analysis of the Profound) states... although the text lacks detail, the intended meaning explains why the state of "regression" (*parihāṇi*) receives its name.

Having attained liberation through occasion (*samayavimukti*), he personally realized it and took his own life with a blade. Question:

Was that Venerable Ghoṭamukha of a nature prone to regression (*parihāṇadharman*), or was he of a nature prone to recollection (*cetayitadharman*)? If he were of a regressive nature, why did he take his own life with a blade?

Because he was afflicted by the thought of falling away from his state, he took his own life with a blade. If one who has not fallen away were to take his own life in this manner, it would be because he is mindful of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Furthermore, the new translation asks: "Is he one who falls away, or is it the intention regarding the blade? If he is one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), for what reason does he take his own life?

He commits suicide. Furthermore, he was one of those subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*); having refined himself into one of the "thought-dharma" type (*cetana-dharman*), he still feared falling back, and thus committed suicide with a blade.
Therefore, it is known that committing suicide with a blade applies to both types. Regarding the passage "below the thought-dharma type," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* also states this;

It is harmful. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* refers to the "dharma of death" (*maraṇadharma*), explaining it as follows: This characteristic of death involves a slight degree of superiority in the faculties and a deep revulsion toward all states of existence (*bhava*).
Because such a person has not attained meditative concentration (*samādhi*), untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) is difficult to manifest;

even if it is attained, it is easily lost. Therefore, they seek death. What the treatise calls the "characteristic of death" is what is meant here by the "dharma of death. [This is from] the old *Vibhāṣā*.

The term "one who recollects the Dharma" (yìfǎ) is the name used in the translations of the Northern Liáng period. The old *Abhidharmakośa* calls this "one who harms himself through the Dharma" (zìhài fǎ), which corresponds to the Chen dynasty translation of the *Kośa-bhāṣya*.
This treatise explains six types of arhats, the second of which is called "one who harms himself through the Dharma.

The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* calls him "one who recollects the Dharma" (niàn fǎ); examining the six types of arhats in the Tang dynasty translation of that treatise, he is also called "one who contemplates the Dharma" (sī fǎ).

It is not termed "mindfulness of the Dharma" (*dharmānusmṛti*). Alternatively, there are older translations that refer to it as "mindfulness of the Dharma," though this cannot be definitively determined.

Nevertheless, although the names differ across various texts, their meaning is one and the same. Regarding "guarding the Dharma" (*dharmarakṣa*) below, the older *Abhidharmakośa* translations refer to it as "protecting the Dharma."
In the Chen version of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā*, the third among the six types [of noble persons] is called "one who guards the Dharma" (*anurakṣaṇadharman*).
Regarding "one who dwells in the Dharma" (*sthitākampya*) below: in the old *Abhidharmakośa*, this is called the fourth among the six types, "one who dwells immovably in the Dharma.

As for what is stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (*Xianyang lun*), it refers to the fourth type mentioned within the section explaining the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣaphala*) in the third fascicle. It is called "one who dwells immovably."
"Moving" (*cala*) refers to one who has accomplished such roots of goodness that, although they do not intentionally harm themselves nor practice negligence, they nonetheless do not regress;

The term "者" (zhě) is from the Tang translation. Regarding the title *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Jí lùn), the Tang version lacks this name; among the six types [of individuals], the fifth is called *Abhimukta*.
Alternatively, this may be a rendering based on the old translation. Below the term *Akopyadharman*, the old *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* uses the term *Abhedya-dharman*;

From the outset, this person possesses naturally sharp faculties. Regarding all roots of goodness, they are not shaken by the quality of retrogression (*parihāṇadharma*), nor are they moved by the arousal of superior qualities or the refinement of faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*). Therefore, they are called "one of immovable dharma" (*akopyadharman*).
Thus, the commentary stating that this refers to "one of non-retrogressive dharma" (*aparihāṇadharman*) is an error. This is as named in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
Regarding the "one of no-doubt" (*aniyata-dharma*): in the Tang edition, there are six types, yet this specific name does not appear there;

[Supplement] These six types all involve first destroying seventy-one categories of afflictions through cultivation, and subsequently severing the final remaining category. This section clarifies the "Gate of Double Profundity" (*chongxuan-men*), as well as the fruit.

[Commentary] The *Vibhāṣā* translated during the Northern Liang period clarifies these six types: namely, the one of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), the one of the nature of recollection (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one of the nature of guarding (*sthitākampyadharman*), the one of the nature of abiding equally (*prativedhanādharman*), the one of the nature of advancing (*akopyadharman*), and the one of the nature of being immovable. Regarding the sixth, the Arhat of immovable nature, it is said that there are two kinds.
This refers to those who proceed from the *samayavimukta* (liberated by occasion) to the *akopya* (unshakable), and those whose nature is inherently unshakable (*prakṛty-akopya*).

Those who proceed from the *samayavimukta* to the *akopya* are of medium or superior capacity; those whose nature is inherently unshakable are of inferior or superior capacity. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (Treatise on Correct Reasoning) states:

"The lineage of the *parihāṇadharman* (one subject to retrogression) must necessarily have existed previously; the other five, such as the *cetana-dharman* (one capable of volition), may also be acquired later. That is to say, there are those who have been of the *cetana-dharman* type from the very beginning."

Regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), up to and including the "immovable" (*akopya*): there are those who initially possess the quality of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), yet by refining their faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) achieve the "thought-bound" (*cetana*) stage, reaching up to the immovable and so forth. There are many such distinctions which should be contemplated according to reason.

Since both the *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* treat the immovable as being divided into two types, they complete the total of seven kinds. Therefore, this is explained here to clarify that the seven do not exceed the six; they are not treated separately.
This is merely shown by way of clarification.

The mark of guarding, the mark of death, the mark of abiding, the mark of progress, the mark of non-destruction, the mark of liberation through wisdom, the mark of double liberation, and the mark of non-retrogression.

the mark of progress is annotated as "reflection" (*sī*). Thus, while there are minor differences in the names, reflection and death are fundamentally two distinct things. Or...
