[Supplement] "Regressing" means falling away from samādhi, whereby wisdom finds it difficult to manifest. "Guarding" means that because one's faculties are somewhat superior, one protects the samādhi so as not to fall away;
thus, this is superior to the "regressive" type. Although one guards it, even such a person may still regress; therefore, [the guarding type is distinct].
"Guarding" refers to those who, because the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is difficult to bring before them and they fear losing it even if attained, seek death.
"Abiding" refers to those who, having attained samādhi, neither advance nor regress. "Advancing" refers to those who, having attained samādhi, further deepen and increase it.
"Indestructible" refers to those who, having attained samādhi, cannot be defeated or destroyed. "Accompanied by wisdom" refers to [the attainment] through the cessation of [defilements].
Because they are fixed, there are two types of persons who both obtain the name "attainment of cessation," yet have not yet obtained the name "wisdom.
As for those who do not regress, it is because the meritorious deeds they have performed are never lost.

[Commentary] The six types are categorized according to the nature of the faculties (*indriya*). The nine types are categorized according to meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, these [nine] present both the nature of the faculties and meditative practice together.

[Commentary] Regarding the six types categorized by faculty-nature (*indriya-gotra*): The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states: "The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) has five types;

the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) has only one type, namely the immovable (*akopya*). This is based on the faculties. It further states: "Because there are five types of nature, there are [five kinds of] Arhats."
The six types include the Dharma-practitioner (*dharmacārin*), which is designated as "Immovable" (*acala*); thus there are six types in total.

Regarding the distinction between those who possess wisdom (*prajñā*) and those who possess both [wisdom and concentration], it is as explained previously: the person of wisdom enters directly by taking emptiness as their object, whereas the person who possesses both practices while still retaining phenomenal phenomena.
These nine types can be understood by applying both meanings to each category.
[Note] Furthermore, nine of these are the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the twenty-seven noble ones (*āryapudgala*), constituting the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

This is to answer the inquiry of the Elder Kṣetra (Field of Merit) and to manifest the vastness of the field of merit, thereby generating wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*) in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.

Moreover, six types clarify the distinctions between the two preparatory practices (*prayoga*): as explained in the *Xuánmén* (Gate of Profundity), fascicle 29, part 1: (1) Constant preparatory practice, which is diligent cultivation; (2) Reverential preparatory practice, which is intense and sharp cultivation. Six.

Regarding the types of Arhats: the first two types both lack applied effort (*prayoga*); the third, the Protector of the Dharma (*dharmapāla*), possesses only constant application but lacks reverence; the fourth, the Abider in the Dharma (*dharmaniviṣṭa*), possesses only reverence but lacks constancy; and the fifth and sixth possess both types of applied effort.

[Supplement] The *Nyāyānusāra* states: "The first two [types of practitioners] lack constant respect; however, upon reaching the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), those who protect their dharma through reflection (*cintā-dharman*) possess slight diligence, while those who protect their dharma through guarding (*anurakṣaṇā-dharman*) possess only constant application.

Those who abide in their dharma (*sthitākampya-dharman*) possess only the application of respect, while those capable of attaining [a higher state] (*prativedhanādharman*) possess both, yet they are of dull faculties.
Those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*) possess both and are of sharp faculties."

[Commentary] This refers to two types of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) to distinguish and categorize six kinds [of Arhats]. The first phrase provides the heading; the second phrase points to the source.
In the *Xiaozhu* (Small Commentary), the six kinds of Arhats are first listed and then correlated with the two types of preparatory practice.
Following this, a fourfold analysis is conducted: the first two and the last two are each treated as one phrase, while the middle two types are each treated as one [phrase].
This is a phrase.

[Commentary] Regarding whether the nature of the fruit can regress, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "There are six types of Arhats, from those subject to regression (parihāṇadharman) up to the immovable (akopyadharman)."

The first five arise from *śraddhādhimukta* (the stage of faith-practice that enters the path of cultivation is called *śraddhādhimukta*). They are collectively termed *samayavimukta*. The latter is *asamayavimukta*.

These arise from the preceding *dṛṣṭiprāpta* (one who has attained through vision; this is also a name for one who has attained through vision, and it is likewise a designation for the transition from *dharmānusārin* into the path of cultivation).

[Commentary] The treatise explains: The Sūtra states that there are six types of Arhats. First, the *parihāṇadharman* (one liable to fall away), because they fall away from what has been attained upon encountering even slight adverse conditions.

Second, the *cetayitadharman* (one intent on self-harm), because they constantly contemplate suicide out of fear of falling away. Third, the *anurakṣaṇādharman* (one who guards), because they personally guard the wholesome qualities they have attained.
Fourth, the *sthitākampya* (one who remains steadfast), because they do not fall away even without personal guarding, provided no superior adverse conditions arise.

Furthermore, they are also non-retrogressive because there is no superior application of effort and no further increase [in their faculties]. Fifth are those of the "attainable" nature (*kāmada-dharman*), who are capable of skillfully cultivating the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*) and swiftly reaching the state of non-retrogression.
Sixth are those of the "immovable" nature (*akopya-dharman*), who cannot be shaken or retrogressed by afflictions (*kleśa*).

The first five possess a movable nature; arising from the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) within the category of those resolved through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), they are collectively termed "liberated by time" (*samaya-vimukta*). This is because...
One must wait for the proper conditions before being able to enter meditative absorption and achieve liberation of mind. There are six such conditions that must be awaited:
first, clothing; second, food; third, bedding; fourth, a suitable location; fifth, a teacher who excels at preaching the Dharma; and sixth, virtuous companions in study.

Those of later immovable nature are called "those liberated regardless of time" (asamayavimukta); this refers to those of sharp faculties who, because they do not depend on these conditions, are able [to attain liberation] immediately.
Because they have entered meditative absorption and attained liberation of mind, they arise from the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) as those who have "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

Regarding the designations "liberated by faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "attained through vision," the treatise states: "The sixteenth moment of mind, according to whether one abides in one of the three paths, is called 'liberated by faith' or 'attained through vision.
This distinction is also due to the difference between dull and sharp faculties. The commentator explains: "They are so named because they abide in accordance with the persons of the three paths."

Regarding the fruit, there are two faculties—dull and sharp—and thus their designations differ. If one has a dull faculty, they are called "resolved through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*); if one has a sharp faculty, they are called "attained through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
The former "follower by faith" is now termed "resolved through faith," meaning that because of faith, the characteristic of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) becomes manifest.
The former "follower by dharma" is now termed "attained through vision," meaning that by tending toward vision, one attains the vision of the fruit. These two types of noble ones—
Because faith and wisdom mutually increase, there are the distinct designations of "one liberated by faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*) and "one who has attained vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

[Commentary: Some possess this as their original lineage (*gotra*), while others acquire it later through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*). (Regarding the six types of arhats: some possess a fixed lineage from previous lives;

others later cultivate and refine their faculties so that an inferior nature is transformed into a superior one—for instance, one originally of the "regressive type" (*parihāṇadharman*) refines themselves into the "reflective type" (*cetanādharman*), up to the "immovable type" (*akopyadharman*); or the "reflective type" refines themselves into the "guardian type" (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), up to the "progressive type" refining themselves into the "immovable type. Only the initial "regressive type" is of a naturally unstable nature and lacks the capacity for the refinement of faculties.

Furthermore, the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) relies upon both the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) and the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), excluding only the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), because its duration is so rapid that it cannot effect a transformation of the faculties.
[Commentary] This explains the two meanings of "prior" and "subsequent. In the text, the first two phrases indicate these two types—prior and subsequent.

The phrase "as in the original" (*yathā mūla*) explains the refinement of the faculties. The phrase "only the first" (*kevalam ādau*) explains the prior [cultivation]. The phrase "furthermore, the refinement of the faculties" (*api cendriya-saṃcāra*) clarifies...

Regarding the stages accessible through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), only those below [the stage of the path of seeing] are excluded; this clarifies that the refinement of the faculties does not apply to the stages of the path of seeing.
This is because the sixteenth moment of mind—the final moment of the path of seeing—is too swift to transform an inferior nature into a superior one.

However, there is a difference in how the treatise (*śāstra*) explains the verse. For the commentary states: "The lineage of the one subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) must necessarily have existed previously as the lineage of the one who reflects (*cetayitṛdharman*) and so forth."

5. There are also those who attain [the higher faculties] subsequently. This means that there may have been one who was originally of the nature of a "thought-dweller" (*cetanā-dharman*) or of the nature of one subject to falling away (*parihāṇa-dharman*), but later, through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvaraṇa*), becomes a "thought-dweller," and so on, up to the "immovable" (*akopya*). These will be explained according to the text; here they are recorded in full. Furthermore, it is said:

"The lineage of one subject to falling away does not necessarily entail falling away," and so on, up to "one capable of reaching [the goal]" (*prativedhana-bhavya*) does not necessarily reach it; this is merely stated in terms of what is possible.
Because this designation is established, the six types of *arhats* exist throughout all three realms.

If one maintains that those who are subject to regression (*parihāṇadharman*) must necessarily regress, and so on up to those who are capable of reaching [the goal] (*prativedhanādharman*) who must necessarily reach it, then according to that position, all six exist fully in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

However, within the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), there are only those who are immovable (*akopyadharman*), for they lack regression, self-harm, self-protection, and cultivation.

[Commentary] Generally speaking, those who practice through faith and are liberated by wisdom do not cultivate the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) based on formal objects, nor do they attain the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

thus, there is regression.

(Adverse conditions are: first, chronic illness; second, long-distance travel; third, disputes arising from admonition; fourth, involvement in administrative affairs; fifth, excessive recitation and study. One attains the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary: Some say: "In the preceding cases of 'timely' and 'untimely' liberation, each is accompanied by wisdom (*prajñā-samprayukta*). [Commentary] The intent of this question is as follows: since both timely (*sāmayika*) and untimely (*asāmayika*) wisdom are subject to regression, and since each of these two possesses both wisdom and liberation, then among the untimely, those who are liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) should also be subject to regression.

Furthermore, since the immovable [attainer] (*akopyadharman*) arises from the timely liberated, they too should not be exempt from regression. Is it not the case, then, that all six types [of noble ones] possess the possibility of regression?

[□ Commentary] Answer: It is not necessarily the case that those of wisdom invariably fall back. One fears only that those of dull faculties, whose outflow-tainted knowledge has been severed, might fall back upon encountering adverse conditions.

[■ Record] This section distinguishes those of sharp faculties from those who do not fall back. The question cites the previous principle to inquire whether the sixth [type of person] will necessarily fall back.
[The interlocutor] withdraws. [The Master] replies: "It is said that those of dull faculties may regress when encountering adverse conditions;

As it is said in the Āgamas, Ānanda asked the Buddha: 'Venerable Sir, does one in training (śaikṣa) fall away?
Does one beyond training (aśaikṣa) fall away? The Buddha replied: 'One beyond training falls away. From this, we know that [the regression spoken of] refers to the abandonment of mundane wisdom."

Because those who have attained liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*) still possess afflictions, they are subject to regression. It is not the case that one who has abandoned even a single grade of affliction through untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and has advanced to the next grade would then undergo regression.

when they refine their faculties from the state of regression and achieve the immovable, they likewise become those liberated by occasion. Since the former five already possess wisdom...

There is also regression. Therefore, based on this, the question is asked: "In the case of those of immovable faculties who have refined their faculties, does the person of wisdom (prajñā-pudgala) possess the possibility of regression?

Indeed, how could there be a person of immovable wisdom who would still be subject to regression? This definitively establishes the meaning of being immovable and non-regressive.

[Commentary] In the diagram, the distinction between those who are "timely" (*akālika*) and "untimely" (*sakālika*) based on sharpness or dullness of faculty is merely a provisional explanation. In reality, these qualities exist interchangeably among them.

Regarding sharpness and dullness of faculties, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "If one discusses the sharpness or dullness of faculties: those who practice through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) are sharp, because they internally contemplate the Dharma for themselves;

those who practice through faith (*śraddhānusārin*) are dull, because they rely on hearing the Dharma from others. Furthermore, those who practice through faith may be sharp, because they awaken immediately upon hearing;

those who practice through the Dharma may be dull, because they observe by traversing the various phenomena. Alternatively, both may be sharp or both dull: those who practice through faith are sharp in the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) but dull in the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)."
The practitioner of the Dharma (dharmacārin) has sharp wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā), whereas the practitioner of learning (śrutamayī-prajñā) has dull wisdom;

this is what is meant. [Note on the Sixfold Treatise: Regarding the six types of falling back (parihāṇi), the restriction applies specifically to the fourth fruit (arhatship). To comprehensively distinguish whether the four fruits are subject to falling back or not, the *Xiyuan* (Analysis of the Profound) cites three schools of thought:
1. The Sarvāstivādins maintain that the first fruit does not fall back, while the latter three fruits may fall back. 2. The Mahāsāṃghikas maintain that... [text continues]

One may fall away from the first three fruits, but not from the fourth. Thirdly, the Sautrāntika school maintains that one does not fall away from the first two fruits, whereas one may fall away from the middle two fruits (as detailed in their texts).

[Commentary] This section generally clarifies the meaning of the four fruits of the śrāvaka path regarding falling back (*parihāṇi*) or not falling back. The *Xie xuán* (Analysis of the Profound) below points out that the tenets cited by various masters differ.
[Note] That work merely notes: "The three masters find it difficult to determine [the position]; fearing that this might lead to dispute, I have now briefly harmonized them. (Fǔ xíng, Scroll 9).
The fifteenth [section] above cites the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, which says: "When an Arhat falls away, he is pulled down to the second or third fruit, just like sand in a well.
There are bricks above and below, with only sand in between. If the upper brick collapses, how could the sand in between not collapse from top to bottom?
The fourth fruit is like the upper brick; the second and third fruits are like the middle sand; and the first fruit is like the bottom. And so forth.

Prior to the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), there is no further falling away. If one were to fall away at that time, there would be no place to abide. (Text: It is impossible for a noble one to regress to the state of an ordinary person.

This accords with the first master’s view; however, since the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) does not involve an equal contemplation of the four truths, as the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:

"Twenty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through the path of seeing, while the remaining sixty proclivities are abandoned through the path of cultivation" (first abandoning the suffering of the three realms below).

Regarding the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*): once these views are exhausted, the principle of the fruit is not yet perfected. This is illustrated by the fact that even Śāriputra, while at the sixth stage, was still subject to regression.

Furthermore, among the latter three fruits, the wisdom that abandons delusions is both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). Thus, regarding the four fruits, there are cases of both regression and non-regression;
the assertions of the three masters are all without contradiction.

[Commentary] This refers to the harmonious integration of the three schools according to their meaning. The first two phrases cite the wording from the *Xuánzhù* (Profound Commentary). The following two phrases clarify the present harmonization.
In the lower section of the *Fǔxíng* (Aids to Practice), the cited passages are raised to demonstrate the synthesis. However, here only the cited passages are briefly presented.
I shall now record this in full. It is asked in the *Vibhāṣā*: "If an Arhat falls away, it should not be that he also falls away from the second or third fruits.
The answer says: "When an Arhat falls away, he drags along a fall from the two [lower] fruits. It is like a sand well with bricks at the top and bottom and only sand in between.
If the upper brick collapses, then from the top down to the bottom, how could the sand in between fail to collapse?"
The fruit of the fourth [arahantship] is like the uppermost brick; the fruit of the second [sakadāgāmi] is like the middle sand; the fruit of the first [sotāpanna] is like the bottom layer.
If one reaches the very bottom, one can never go further. Question: If one has reached the first fruit, should it not also be said that there is falling back from the second and third fruits?
Answer: It is like a person who falls from a three-story house; it is the same in this case. Although one does not speak of falling back from the second or third, [the principle applies].
Indeed, there is falling away. Furthermore, two or three [fruits] are the fourth cause; since their fruit has already fallen away, their cause also falls away.
If this were so, then the first fruit would also be the cause of the fourth fruit, and it should likewise be said that it falls away. Answer: Prior to the first fruit, there is no further fruit.
If one were to fall away from it, there would be no place to abide. To allow for the falling away of the first fruit would entail many contradictions. This is because...

[One who] previously saw the truths (dṛṣṭasatya) is not now seeing the truths; previously they had attained the fruit (phalaprāpta), but now they have not attained the fruit; previously they were certain (niyata), but now they are not certain;
previously they were noble ones (ārya), but now they are not noble ones. Because such faults have been eliminated, it is said that there is no falling away (parihāṇi).
In short, one cannot claim that a noble one (ārya) can regress to the state of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Just as gold extracted from ore can never again become ore, it should be understood that this treatise accords with the teachings of the Sarvāstivāda school.

However, regarding the statement in the *Vibhāṣā* that there is the possibility of regression even for those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) after the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the aforementioned commentary states: "The predecessors say that there is [such a case]."
There are two types of root-natures. If one contemplates the Four Truths equally, one abandons eighty-eight *anuśayas* through the Path of Seeing.
If one does not contemplate the Four Truths equally, one abandons only twenty-eight *anuśayas* belonging to the Truth of Suffering within the Three Realms during the Path of Seeing.
The views remaining under the other three Truths are abandoned through the path of cultivation; these belong to those of dull faculties.
Although their views are exhausted, the fruit and principle are not yet perfected, just as when the tarnish on a mirror has not been entirely removed, its light does not manifest fully.

This is illustrated by the case of Śāriputra, who still regressed even at the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭha-bhūmi*). For sixty kalpas, Śāriputra practiced the bodhisattva path and realized the six [perfections] of the *pratyekabuddha* vehicle.
While he was dwelling there, as he was about to cross the river of giving, someone begged for his eyes. Śāriputra said, "The eyes are of no use; why do you seek them?
If you require my body or my wealth, I shall give them to you. The man replied, "I have no need for your body or your wealth;

"Please give it. At that time, Śāriputra plucked out one eye and gave it to him.

"This eye is truly of no use, yet he demanded it by force. Having obtained it, he has discarded it and even stepped on it. How can his depravity be so extreme?"

"Such people as these cannot be saved. It is better to discipline oneself and quickly escape birth and death. Having reflected thus, they retreat from the bodhisattva path and turn toward the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

[Commentary] This passage explains the essence of the two types of nirvāṇa: with remainder and without remainder. However, within the Śrāvaka schools themselves, there are two interpretations.
First, the Sarvāstivādins say: "The essence of nirvāṇa is one; it receives two names based on differences in time."
Regarding the statement that "the essence is one": within this school, the afflictions, karma, and volition—due to the power of the Path—should arise but do not;

this cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is the essence of *nirvāṇa*. This essence is one, yet it receives two names based on its relation to the body and wisdom (*jñāna*).

When body and wisdom are not yet exhausted, the former *nirvāṇa* is said to be "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). When body and wisdom are completely exhausted... [toward]... [it is called] "without remainder" (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
The former *nirvāṇa* is renamed "without remainder" (*anupadhiśeṣa*). It is not that the extinction of body and wisdom is itself called *nirvāṇa*.

Because this body and wisdom have arisen and then ceased, they are impermanent. Furthermore, because the causes [of rebirth] have been severed, preventing them from arising again, this is "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*);

Since the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—and the fruits of birth and death are not directly severed by the Path, they are not included [in this category].

According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, because the remaining [defilements] do not arise once the afflictions have been severed, and because they are severed by the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*), they also attain analytical cessation.

Therefore it is called *nirvāṇa*. This now accords with the tenets of the Sarvāstivāda school. [□ Note] Bodhisattva (pú-sà): the full term is *bodhisattva* (*móhē-sàtuó*). It was formerly translated as "sentient beings with the mind for the Great Way" (*dà-dào-xīn zhòngshēng*).

They also accomplish the Great Way for the sake of sentient beings; the new translation calls them "Awakened Beings" (bodhisattva), because they seek the Buddha-way above and transform sentient beings below.
Within this teaching, these bodhisattvas are also termed Mahāyāna.
[Commentary] This explains the etymological meaning of the term "Bodhisattva" in both its Indic and Chinese forms. First, the complete Sanskrit term is presented;
next, two lines provide the old Chinese translation. Regarding the old translation "sentient beings with the mind of the Great Way," the *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states:
"Bodhi is named 'Way' (mārga); sattva is named 'mind' (citta); mahā means 'great. Thus, it is the 'mind of the Great Way. This appears to be [the case].
This is a translation of the name based on its own meaning (*svārtha*). Regarding "one who accomplishes sentient beings through the Great Way" (*mahāsattva*):
as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states, *bodhi* is translated as "Buddha-way" (*buddhamārga*), *sattva* is translated as "accomplishing sentient beings," and *mahā* is translated as "great.

This means that such a person uses the Great Way of all Buddhas to bring sentient beings to fulfillment. This appears to be a translation of the name based on its function for others (*parārtha*). This refers to the old translations.
This refers to the states of Qin and Jin. Regarding the frequent mention of "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" in various sūtras, Master Kumārajīva noted that the Indic language is prolix;
since two phrases constitute eight characters when naming a title, he abbreviated three and retained five, merging two into one to say "bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The following two sentences explain the new translation. However, there are three interpretations in the Tang translation. First: [The text continues with the specific interpretations.]
First: "Awakening" (jue) refers to the path of bodhi; "sentient beings" (youqing) refers to the state of having objects of thought and concern.
This means that while one is personally able to awaken to the path of bodhi, one still possesses the state of having objects of thought and concern.

It is called "Awakened Sentient Being" (bodhisattva) because it addresses those sentient beings who are deluded. Second: "Awakening" refers to the practice of bodhi; "sentient beings" refers to ordinary beings of the vast ground.
This means that such a person not only practices the path to the Bodhi of all Buddhas themselves, but is also able to awaken all sentient beings.
That is to say: "I shall, by means of this path, awaken these people. Therefore, they are called "Awakeners of Sentient Beings" (Bodhisattvas).
Thirdly, "Awakening" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood, Bodhi, which is sought; "sentient beings" refers to the vast multitude of living beings who are to be saved. Thus it is said:
This person seeks supreme enlightenment above and transforms sentient beings below; because they benefit both themselves and others, they are called "enlightened sentient beings" (*bodhisattva*).

This is an explanation based on the single principle of seeking enlightenment above and transforming beings below. Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* (*Qixin lun shu*) also provides three explanations.

First, regarding the objective realm: there is that which is sought and that which is delivered. "Enlightened" (*bodhi*) refers to the fruit of Buddhahood, the Bodhi that is sought; "sentient beings" (*sattva*)... [refers to those who are delivered].

This refers to the great multitude of sentient beings to be saved. It means that this person seeks the awakening of a Buddha through wisdom above, while transforming sentient beings below through compassion;
because they benefit both themselves and others, they are called "Awakened Sentient Beings" (*bodhisattva*). Second, regarding the mind:
there is the wisdom of awakening and the consciousness of other emotional deliberations. This means that while this person is able to awaken to the path of Bodhi by themselves, they still possess...
Regarding the mental state of seeking: because it is directed toward sentient beings who are entirely deluded, one is called a "Bodhisattva" (Awakened Being).
Third, in terms of the subject and object, there is that which seeks and that which is sought. "Awakening" (bodhi) refers to the path of enlightenment that is sought;

"sentient being" (sattva) refers to the person who seeks the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, one is called a "Bodhisattva. The current commentary’s mention of "seeking upward," etc., is based on this first meaning.

This is the explanation. How could there then be such matters as subduing afflictions for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* or a hundred eons?
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise was able to use the real to refute the provisional and the Great to destroy the Small. The original commentary at the end of the passage clearly identifies this.

[Commentary] This section is an original annotation explaining Miaole’s intention in citing the *Śāstra* to refute provisional [teachings].

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan Sanmei* (36) states: "The fat of afflictions being eliminated" refers to their suppression being termed "elimination. Therefore, the *Bie xing zhuang* (Treatise on Separate Practices), lower section 3, says:
"Merely suppressing the delusions without severing them is like a fat sheep without its fat. Taking worldly wisdom as *prajñā* is precisely this meaning.
[Commentary] This explains the meaning of the melting away of the fat of afflictions through the samatha-vipaśyanā of this assembly. First, the text is cited and directly interpreted;
second, the *Separate Practice Commentary* (*Bie xing shu*) is quoted to provide proof. As stated in the *Avalokana-ṭīkā*: "A fat sheep without fat. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Although this bodhisattva possesses the five supreme sensual desires, he does not give rise to greedy attachment, because he possesses contemplations such as impermanence. This is used as an analogy.
Suppose there is a king who has a minister that conceals his own crimes. When the king wishes to punish him for his offense, he says to the minister:
"If you can obtain a fat sheep that is devoid of fat, I shall grant you a partial pardon. The minister is wise; he ties a rope around the sheep's neck and nourishes it with water and grass.
Three times every day, he terrifies it with a wolf. Although the sheep is well-fed, it becomes fat yet remains without fat. By this means—
He presented it to the King. Upon seeing it, the King asked, "How did you achieve this? He answered with the aforementioned matters. The Bodhisattva is also like this:
seeing the wolves of impermanence and emptiness, he causes the fat of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be consumed, so that the body of merit becomes plump.
This is taking worldly knowledge as *prajñā*; it is precisely by means of this that "subduing" is intended to mean "consuming. [Supplement] Regarding "taking worldly knowledge": by means of...
As long as afflictions have not been severed, true wisdom cannot manifest. Although one may practice the six perfections, one takes tainted worldly knowledge as prajñā;
this is precisely the sense of suppressing [the afflictions] without severing them.
[Note] Furthermore, the intention of the *Abhidharmakośa* and *Vibhāṣā* is that the afflictions of the eight lower stages have already been severed previously at the time of first practicing dhyāna.
This severance of outflows also carries the meaning of "subduing" (as explained in the *Fuxing* [Commentary on the Mohe Zhiguan], Vol. 3, Part 2, etc.).
[Commentary] This section explains the abandonment of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower eight stages according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Vibhāṣā*.
Because contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*) is weak, although it is said that they are "abandoned," in reality this is termed "suppression" (*vighāta*). As stated in the *Fǔxíng yùjì*:

regarding the "thirty-four moments of mind," following the intent of the treatise, this differs slightly from the explanations of abandonment found in various sūtras and śāstras. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The various afflictions of the lower stages, at the time of [their arising as] causes..."

They have not yet been severed. When [the practitioner] reaches the foot of the tree, the nine grades of afflictions of the realm of thought (bhāvanā-heya) belonging to the nine stages are collectively termed "one group of nine";

therefore, it is said that the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka [Vehicle] are in status equal to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). The nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberations (*vimukti-jñāna*) together constitute eighteen;
the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) together constitute sixteen; when combined with the preceding, they total thirty-four.
Regarding the mind: the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the afflictions of the lower eight stages have already been completely severed when one first cultivates the First Dhyāna.
Only the nine grades of both the views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thoughts (*saṃjñā*) pertaining to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception remain in their entirety.

By means of the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation, because his faculties are superior, he no longer further cultivates the meditative concentrations of the lower eight stages. This is unlike the Śrāvakas and differs from the Pratyekabuddhas.

It continues by stating that this differs from the *Abhidharmakośa*. It suggests that since Master Kumārajīva’s translation and the intent of Nāgārjuna differ from the *Abhidharmakośa*, the latter must be erroneous.
For now, let us resolve this through a single interpretation: the principles of these two treatises are identical.

The *Abhidharmakośa* maintains that when one has already severed the afflictions (*kleśas*) during the time of practicing dhyāna, they are not severed again. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, however, relies on other schools (nikāyas). Although...
The abandonment of outflows (*āsrava*) is not yet called "abandonment" [in this context]; it is only at the foot of the Bodhi tree that one abandons non-perception (*asaṃjñā*).

The eight stages are both termed "without outflows" (*anāsrava*), yet they differ in how they derive their names from their respective categories; thus, the application of these meanings differs between the two treatises.

[Note] However, while not severing the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*), does one still sever the *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions? Answer: One must know that throughout the three great eons (*tri-kalpa*) and one hundred kalpas, these [rajas-afflictions] are merely suppressed and not severed.

Therefore, when one reaches the foot of the King of Trees (*vṛkṣarāja*) and severs the afflictions of views and thought, one realizes the Four Noble Truths (*catuḥ-āryasatya*) regarding the dharmas of the *rajas*-afflictions, and only then does one sever them.

[Commentary] This section examines the Bodhisattva’s severance and subduing of the *rajas* (dust-like afflictions). Regarding the question, which follows the discussion on not severing *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-āsrava* (afflictions of cultivation) to inquire about the severance of *rajas*:
it is because *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava* obstruct emptiness and quiescence (*śūnyatā-vivikta*), whereas *rajas* obstructs transformative guidance (*parinirvāṇa*).
Thus, while it is permissible for a Bodhisattva not to sever *dṛṣṭi-āsrava* and *bhāvanā-āsrava*, it is not permissible for them not to sever *rajas*; therefore, this question is posed.

The answer clarifies that while practicing the causes, [the afflictions] are suppressed but not severed; it is only upon attaining enlightenment that they are severed together with the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃskāra-kleśa*).

The *Bie xing xuanyi* states: "Regarding the simultaneous exhaustion of both the fundamental and residual habits through thirty-four moments of mind, this refers to those who suddenly realize the stage of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha, also attaining it in the uninterrupted sequence of thirty-four moments of mind; however, they do not thereby suddenly exhaust both the fundamental and residual habits."

Regarding "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) in a single word: there are the habitual tendencies of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-vāsanā*), and the habitual tendencies of the *rajas-śata* (dust-like sands).

When a Bodhisattva cultivates and studies the *dharmamukhas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they remedy their inferior wisdom. Within each and every *dharmamukha*, they employ the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*) to subdue the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*).

Within each and every *dharmamukha*, they practice the conduct of the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to permeate and purify the habitual tendencies of view and thought. Therefore, beneath the King of Trees (*pippala-vṛkṣa-rāja*), through thirty-four moments of mind, [they overcome] the dust...
In the stage of the *śaikṣa*, one realizes the Four Noble Truths; thus, the active afflictions (*anuśaya*) as well as the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted simultaneously.

Consequently, one is able to reach the ultimate realization of both truths. This distinguishes [the Bodhisattva] from the disciples of the Two Vehicles, who remain partially obstructed from the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom.

[Note] As stated in the *Zhiguan Sanmei* (The Three Samādhis of Stopping and Contemplation), volume 36: "One attains the Dharma-eye, which illuminates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). [Commentary]: This refers to attaining a semblance of the Dharma-eye;
it is merely the illumination of outflow-tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*).

[Commentary] This explanation clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye illuminates the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) through the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. First, the text is cited; second, it is formally explained.

That is to say, when a Bodhisattva cultivates the causal stage, the Dharma-eye attained therein is neither a conceptualized contemplative practice (*nāma-vipaśyanā*) nor a partial realization of the ultimate;
rather, it is a "concordant" Dharma-eye (*pratirūpa-dharmacakṣus*). Regarding the objects of conventional truth, it can only perceive them in a vague and indistinct manner.

One sees them as if in a faint semblance; this is merely the illumination of tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-jñāna*). Therefore, regarding the *rajas-reṇu* (dust-like afflictions), it is said that they are only suppressed and not severed.
△ Second, clarifying the Dharma has two parts. First, the heading.

From the initial generation of the mind of enlightenment, one takes the objects of the Four Noble Truths as one's focus, gives rise to the Four Great Vows, and cultivates the practices of the Six Perfections.
[Note] The Four Noble Truths of arising and ceasing serve as the objective basis. "Great" (弘) means vast. To restrain the mind and resolve to seek fulfillment is termed a "vow" (誓願).
[Commentary] This explains the four noble truths as objects of perception (*ālambana*). As stated in the preceding note: suffering (*duḥkha*) involves the shifting of the three characteristics;

origination (*samudaya*) involves the flowing of the four minds; cessation (*nirodha*) involves the extinction of existence and its return to non-existence; and the path (*mārga*) involves being easily supplanted by counteractive measures. These are called the four noble truths of arising and ceasing.
It was based on these that the Bodhisattva Tripiṭaka-vinaya (Sanzang Pusa) formulated his great vows. Essential. Seek.
Furthermore, among all mundane and supramundane aspirations, none surpass these four; therefore, they are called "vast.
To add a vow to these aspirations is the means by which their fulfillment is made firm.
[Square Note]: "To cross over" means to transcend the flow of birth and death and reach the other shore. If one's vows have no objective scope, they are called "mad aspirations.

If one does not practice the six *pāramitās*, those vows will be empty. Furthermore, this universal study of the four gates for transforming others differs from the single-gate self-cultivation of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
[Commentary] This clarifies the breadth and narrowness of the three vehicles (*triyāna*) and their differences in practice.

That is to say, because the mind of one belonging to the Bodhisattva vehicle is vast, they study each of the four gates—existence and so forth—comprehensively and universally. They do not act for their own benefit, but solely delight in benefiting others.

As for those of the Two Vehicles, their minds are already narrow and inferior, and their practice is likewise solitary and limited. They rely solely upon the dharma of emptiness to realize the fruits of the path;
they seek only their own liberation and have no desire to deliver others. It is for these reasons that they differ from this [Mahayana] approach.

[Note] Furthermore, although those of the Two Vehicles do not break the precepts, and so forth, even if they are free from folly, their actions that do not benefit sentient beings cannot be called the Six Perfections;
this is stated by way of exclusion.
[Commentary] This clarifies that the practice of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) does not consist of the six perfections.

That is to say, if one observes them superficially, the Two Vehicles are seen to be earnestly guarding the precepts, which appears similar to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); even up to their "conduct free from delusion," which appears similar to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

However, to speak according to reality, since these are practices for one's own private benefit rather than for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they are merely called "self-cultivation" and are not [called perfections].
The Six Perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). As for the Six Perfections, they are that which deliver others from the six obscurations. Thus, to bestow [these perfections] is right;
to withhold them is wrong.
[Commentary: Specifically corresponding to the Truths and Conditions over three great aeons and one hundred kalpas, this is called the four stages of attaining the Way.
[Commentary] These are called the four stages (*catur-vīthi*) based on the objects of the truths (*satya*). That is to say: Śrāvakas cultivate the practice of the Four Truths;
Pratyekabuddhas cultivate the practice of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*); and Bodhisattvas cultivate the practice of the four stages.

Furthermore, the attainment of the Way through these four stages is called "Emerging from Laṅkā" (*laṅkā-niryāṇa*), as stated in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. This refers to: the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, the second asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa, and the planting of the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) during the hundred kalpas.
Excellent. △ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the vow and practice has two parts. First, the vow: 1.
To cause those not yet crossed over to cross over; this is the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. This takes the realm of the Truth of Suffering as its object. 2. [The second part follows.]
1. Those who have not yet attained understanding, I shall cause to understand; this is the vow to sever countless afflictions, which takes the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) as its object.
2. Those who have not yet found peace, I shall cause to find peace; this is the vow to study immeasurable Dharma-gates, which takes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) as its object.
3. Those who have not yet attained Nirvana, I shall cause to attain Nirvana; this is the vow to realize the unsurpassed Buddha-way, which takes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) as its object.

【□ Note】The first part of the *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states: First, "to cause those who have not crossed over to cross over" means to cause those in the six realms of existence—those bound by craving and views—to cross over from the suffering of the triple-world house of fire, which they have not yet crossed, so that they may attain liberation.
Second, "to cause those who have not understood to understand" refers to these same two types of beings, who have not yet understood [the truth regarding] craving and views.
Fifteenth, there is karma that brings about liberation. Third, those who are not yet at peace are brought to peace;

this refers to the two types of sentient beings—those driven by craving and those driven by views—who are not yet established in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all other paths, and are thus brought to rest in the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

Fourth, those who have not attained *nirvāṇa* are made to attain *nirvāṇa*; this refers to the two types of sentient beings—those driven by craving and those driven by views—who have not yet extinguished the twenty-five [existences].
There are causes and effects of birth and death; [the teaching] enables all to attain the extinction-truth (*nirvāṇa*).
[■ Commentary] The above may be understood according to the text.
△ Second, the practice has two parts. First, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows.
Having already resolved the mind, one must practice deeds to fulfill that vow.
[Note] The *Mysterious Record of Avalokiteśvara*, Volume One (7), states: "If it were not for the mountain of practice, one could not fill the ocean of vows. (Text)
[Commentary] This explanation fills the vows with practice. This is because the *Mysterious Meaning of Guanyin* states: "To fulfill these vows, one must necessarily engage in cultivation.
Cultivation does not go beyond merit and wisdom. Wisdom is *prajñā*; merit consists of the [other] five perfections (*pāramitā*). These mutually support and guide one another;

thus, through practice, one accords with the vow, and both phenomena and principle become perfectly fulfilled. Therefore, the commentary says: "If it were not for the mountain of practice, there would be nothing to fill [the vows]."

The ocean of vows consists of practice, which is both merit and wisdom; in meaning, this corresponds to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). Five of these provide the support for wisdom, while wisdom guides the five; they are like eyes and feet, neither of which can be lacking.

The five remove the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*), while wisdom removes the obstacles of principle (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*); when the efficacy of these two is perfected, [enlightenment is attained].
Having realized the principle, one attains the phenomena.
△ Second, the actual explanation of cultivation has two parts. First, the general heading:
Over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, one cultivates the practices of the six perfections; during a hundred kalpas, one plants the seeds for the marks and signs of excellence.
[Supplement] For one who practices the Six Perfections: in practicing giving, they exhaust their life and pour out their wealth; in maintaining precepts, they guard and protect their nature;

in practicing patience, they submit even to being cut by knives or cast into water; in practicing diligence, they act as if their hair were on fire; in practicing dhyāna, the four modes of conduct are serene and still;
and in practicing wisdom, a single thought is perfectly luminous. Their great vow-purifying mind universally covers all, and their conditioned activities...
The Path consists of universal giving; it crosses the stream of birth and death and ascends to the shore of Nirvana. Therefore, they are called the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
The first is named the Perfection of Giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). In Sanskrit it is *dāna*; in the language of Qin (Chinese) it is "universal giving" (*biànshī*).

If there is internal faith, external fields of merit, and material wealth—when these three factors converge, the mind gives rise to the dharma of relinquishment, which is able to destroy stinginess and greed. This is *dāna*. It is distributed...

There are two kinds of giving. First is the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*), which refers to food, drink, clothing, fields, houses, livestock, slaves, servants, precious jewels, and all other means of livelihood that one possesses, as well as one's wife and children, even up to one’s own body and life.
Since these are entirely subject to others and become the property of others, they are still classified as the gift of material wealth. One is able to give whatever is required.
To give these is all called the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*). Second is the giving of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*):

if one hears the teachings on mundane and supramundane dharmas from the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), and then expounds them for others with a pure mind, all such acts are called the giving of the Dharma.
The second [perfection] is named the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīlapāramitā*). In Sanskrit it is *śīla*, which here is translated as "precept" (*jie*). Precepts serve to prevent wrongdoing.

The meaning of *śīla* (precept) is the cessation of evil; that is, it is able to prevent the non-manifestation of improper conduct and to stop the evils arising from the three karmas of body, speech, and mind.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "What is precept? It is when evil has ceased and is no longer committed, even if such thoughts arise in the mind."
If one speaks with the mouth or receives [precepts] from another, ceasing evil in body and speech, this is called *śīla* (precept). Furthermore, *śīla* means "to admonish" (*xùn jǐng*);

it refers to the exhortation and discipline of the three types of action (*trikarma*) to remain far removed from faults and transgressions. Moreover, *śīla* is termed "restraint" (*zhì*), for it is able to restrain all unwholesome dharmas.
The third is called patience (*kṣānti*). In the Sanskrit language, it is *kṣānti*; here it is translated as "patience. This refers to the internal...

The mind is able to remain at peace. Because one endures external circumstances of insult, it is called "patience" (kṣānti). There are two types of patience: first, patience toward living beings (janma-kṣānti);
second, patience regarding phenomena (dharma-kṣānti). Patience toward living beings is further divided into two: first, being able to endure without attachment amidst respect and offerings.
Thus, one does not give rise to arrogance or negligence. Second, one is able to endure being reviled, struck, or harmed;
thus, one does not give rise to anger, resentment, or distress. Patience regarding phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*) is also twofold:

first, those that are non-mental phenomena (*acaitasika*), namely cold, heat, wind, rain, hunger, thirst, old age, sickness, death, and so forth; second, mental phenomena (*caitasika*), namely anger, sorrow, lust, and pride.
Regarding various wrong views and such, the bodhisattva is able to endure both of these dharmas without wavering; this is called the patience regarding arising dharmas (*utpatti-dharma-kṣānti*).
The fourth is diligence (*vīrya*); in the Sanskrit it is *vīrya*, which here is translated as "diligence.
To desire, delight in, and energetically practice wholesome dharmas without self-indulgence is termed diligence. There are two types of diligence: first, physical diligence...

Advancing: if one diligently cultivates wholesome dharmas with the body, such as practicing the Way, prostrating, preaching, exhorting, and transforming others, this is called physical diligence (*kāya-vīrya*).
Second, mental diligence: diligently cultivating patience, meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and so forth;

this is called mental diligence (*citta-vīrya*). The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* states that there are two kinds of diligence: first, the diligence of initial undertaking; second, the diligence of completion.
He accomplishes diligence. By initiating diligence at its outset, the bodhisattva practices and perfects all wholesome dharmas;
by completing diligence at its conclusion, he discerns that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature. The fifth is called the perfection of dhyāna (*dhyānapāramitā*);
in Sanskrit it is *dhyāna*, which means "meditative concentration" (*samādhi*). There are two kinds of dhyāna: first, mundane dhyāna, which refers to the four fundamental [dhyānas]...

Dhyāna, the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), and so forth—these are called the dhyāna practiced by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).

Second, supramundane dhyāna (*lokottara-dhyāna*) is further divided into two. First, as for supramundane dhyāna, it refers to the six subtle gates (*ṣaḍ-sūkṣma-mukha*) and the sixteen special excellences (*ṣoḍaśa-viśeṣa*).

[The first category consists of] contemplation, training, perfuming, cultivation, and so forth. The second is the supramundane, supreme dhyāna, which refers to the nine kinds of great dhyānas, such as the *svabhāva-dhyāna* (self-nature dhyāna) and others;
the present [category] is the dhyāna of phenomena (*vastu-dhyāna*), not the supramundane, supreme dhyāna. The sixth is named Prajñāpāramitā;
in Sanskrit it is *prajñā*, which here is translated as "wisdom. It is the wisdom possessed by the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka, which illuminates only arising and ceasing.
This is the principle of partial emptiness.

"Among gods and humans, those who are capable of calculating numbers reach a point where they can no longer know the limit; this is called one *asaṃkhyeya*. It is like ten thousand being called 'ten-thousand' (*wan*)."
One hundred thousand is called a *koṭi*. One million is called a *nayuta*. Ten million *nayutas* is called a *vibhūta*.
One million *vibhūtas* is called a *kaṭāha*. Beyond *kaṭāha* is called an *asaṃkhyeya*, which is also translated as *asaṃkhyeya*;

Regarding the differentiation of time periods, the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: The shortest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*. One hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*. Sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*. Thirty *lavas* constitute one *muhūrta*. Fifty *muhūrtas* constitute one period (*yāma*). Two such periods constitute one day and night (*ahorātra*). Six such days and nights constitute one month. Two such months constitute one season (*ṛtu*). Three such seasons constitute one half-year. Two such half-years constitute one year. Five such years constitute one *yuga*. Twenty such *yugas* constitute one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Four such intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). Twenty small kalpas constitute one intermediate kalpa. Four intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa. One thousand great kalpas constitute one incalculable kalpa (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*). Three incalculable kalpas constitute the lifespan of a Buddha. Furthermore, there are three types of kalpas: first, the kalpa of formation; second, the kalpa of abiding; third, the kalpa of destruction. Each of these consists of twenty small kalpas. The kalpa of formation refers to the period when the world is being created from emptiness until it reaches completion. The kalpa of abiding refers to the period from the completion of the world’s creation until its destruction. The kalpa of destruction refers to the period from the commencement of destruction until the world has been completely annihilated. The kalpa of destruction is further divided into seven stages: first, destruction by fire; second, destruction by water; third, destruction by wind; fourth, destruction by fire; fifth, destruction by water; sixth, destruction by fire; seventh, destruction by wind. After the seventh destruction by wind, the world remains empty for twenty small kalpas. This is called the kalpa of emptiness. Thus, the kalpa of formation, the kalpa of abiding, the kalpa of destruction, and the kalpa of emptiness each consist of twenty small kalpas. These four together constitute eighty small kalpas, which is one great kalpa. A great kalpa is also termed a "long kalpa" (*dīrghakalpa*). It is said that the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha was eighty great kalpas. The lifespan of Maitreya Buddha will be eighty-four great kalpas. This explains the number of the three *asaṃkhyeyas*, up to the designation "three *asaṃkhyeyas*. According to the numerical system of this region, there are only ten levels and so forth;

as stated in the *Huangdi suanshu jing* (The Yellow Emperor’s Classic of Calculation): *yì* (billion), *zhào* (ten billion), *jīng* (hundred billion), *zǐ* (trillion), *yì* (quadrillion), *rǎng* (quintillion), *gōu* (sexillion), and so on.
*Jian*. *Zheng*. *Zai*. The *Fengsu tong* states: "A thousand gives birth to ten thousand; ten thousand gives birth to a hundred million (*yi*); and so on until *zheng* gives birth to *zai*.
Even the earth cannot support a *zai*. A *yi* is divided into four grades: first, one hundred thousand is a *yi*; second, one million is a *yi*; third, ten million is a *yi*;

[Commentary] The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* asks: "Since they have been accumulated in incalculable numbers, why speak further of 'three'? The answer is: "It is not that they are 'incalculable' (asaṃkhyeya) in the sense of being beyond counting;
rather, it reveals that they cannot be counted. (Text)
[Commentary] The treatise states: The *Vimokṣa-sūtra* says that among the sixty numerical units, *asaṃkhyeya* is one such number.
What are these sixty? As that sūtra says: There is "one" and nothing beyond it; this is the beginning of numbering as one. Ten ones make ten; ten tens make a hundred;
ten hundreds make a thousand; ten thousands make ten thousand (*ayuta*); and one hundred thousand makes a *lakṣa*.
Up to the *mahābalaṃcana*, it constitutes an *asaṃkhyeya*. Here, eight of the sixty numerical units have been omitted.
When the counting of great eons (*mahākalpa*) reaches this number of *asaṃkhyeya*, it is called an "incalculable eon" (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*).
When these incalculable eons are further accumulated to three, they are described in the sūtras as "three incalculable eons" (*tri-asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); they cannot be reached by any calculation.
Because one is able to calculate and know [the duration], it can be said that there are "three incalculable eons" (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, stating: "A Brahmā deity possesses a celestial robe weighing three *zhu*. Once every three years, he brushes it once.

When this robe has completely worn away a square stone forty *li* on each side, that constitutes a small kalpa (*antarakalpa*). When it has worn away a stone eighty *li* on each side, that constitutes a middle kalpa (*madhyakalpa*).

When it has worn away a stone one hundred and twenty *li* on each side, that constitutes a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*). If one does not cultivate and study for such kalpas, it cannot be called [true practice]."

Because the World-Honored One Śākyamuni first planted the seeds for his marks and signs under the Buddha Vipaśyin, he was the foremost of the seven Buddhas.
Furthermore, because he praised the power of Puṣya’s diligence, he transcended nine great eons and has thus reached the present. [He has passed] nine...
"Eleven great kalpas. [Supplement] Vipaśyin, the first of the Seven Buddhas, lived at the end of the Kalpa of Adornment (Bhadrakalpa), separated from him by only one kalpa.
How could there be ninety-one kalpas? Inferring from this principle, he must not be among the Seven Buddhas.
This may be understood by reference to Śikhin Buddha.
[Note] The *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* states that one completes three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* under Kāśyapa Buddha; this is merely a different explanation according to the capacities of beings.
[Commentary] This clarifies the differences in the fulfillment of the practices of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
In the first chapter of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, "The Chapter on Cultivating the Karma for the Thirty-two Marks," the Buddha said to Sujāta:

"Good son, in the past, at the place of the Buddha Ratnaśikhin, I fulfilled the first *asaṃkhyeya*; at the place of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, I fulfilled the second *asaṃkhyeya*; [and at the place of] Kāśyapa..."
"At the Buddha's place, the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa was fulfilled. One should know that this passage is spoken according to the capacities of sentient beings.

[Supplement] The *Tongji* states: "According to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, the Buddha said: 'I first resolved my mind for enlightenment under Śākyamuni; under Kāśyapa Buddha, I fulfilled the three asaṃkhyeyas.
Examining this in detail, the time when the three asaṃkhyeyas were fulfilled was actually during the era of Vipaśyin Buddha. That it is now stated to be Kāśyapa is [due to the capacities of beings]."
This refers to the statement that [the Buddha] cultivated the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over a hundred *kalpas*.
[Note: These meanings concerning the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and so forth all appear in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, and the *Vibhāṣā*.
[Commentary: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that from the past Śākyamuni Buddha up to the Buddha Kanakamuni (罽那尸棄佛) constitutes the first [period].
From the time [the Bodhisattva] reached the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, it was the second asaṃkhyeya; from the time he reached the Buddha Vipaśyin, it was the third asaṃkhyeya.
During this period, the Bodhisattva cultivated the karmic causes and conditions for the thirty-two marks. As the Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya states:

At the completion of the first asaṃkhyeya, he encountered the Buddha Ratnaśikhin. At the completion of the second, he encountered the Buddha Dīpaṃkara. At the completion of the third, he encountered the Buddha Abhibhū.

Thus, it should be understood that the name *Kāśyapa* (罽那) found in the *Mahā-śāstra* [the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*] refers to *Viśvabhū*; the difference between these names is merely a matter of phonetic variation.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "at this time, one knows for oneself," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), Part 3, states:

"At this time, the inner mind is clearly aware that one will become a Buddha, and one speaks these words of one's own accord. According to the stages, one is situated within the stage of the *mūrdhan* (Summit).

One practices the six *pāramitās* and has a clear understanding of the Four Noble Truths, like ascending a mountain peak and seeing clearly in all four directions; therefore, one speaks to others" (text).
[Commentary] The *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: "At this time, the Bodhisattva clearly understands within his own mind that he shall become a Buddha;
he speaks these words himself without any fear or hesitation: 'In a future age, I shall attain Buddhahood. This is now called the stage of the *mūrdha-dharma* (the Peak Dharma).
Practicing the six perfections and the four truths, his contemplative understanding is as clear as reaching the summit of a mountain and looking out in all four directions."
He clearly and fully knows for himself that he will become a Buddha, and he also speaks of this to others.

[Note] The *Xuánjì* on the *Guānyīn* (Avalokiteśvara), Part 4, states: "The śrāvakas cultivate the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth only within a single object and a single gateway."
Therefore, it is easily accomplished. The Bodhisattva pervades all realms; within each of the four gates, they further apply the six perfections.

Through long-term cultivation and refinement, they cause every single practice to gather in all sentient beings, leading them through the stages of planting seeds, maturing, and liberation. Thus, within three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas—
In all, how many people have been transformed? Having transcended the mundane and entered the sacred, he has himself crossed from this shore to ferry others to the other shore;
thus, even after long kalpas, his realized rank remains as yet lowly.

[Commentary] This explanation refers to the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) of the Śrāvakas. However, the cited passage from the *Recorded Texts* (*Shuji*) is actually a response to a prior question.
That question stated: "The faculties of Śrāvakas are dull, yet they can swiftly enter the seven stages of worthiness and the four noble fruits;

why is it that Bodhisattvas, whose wisdom is sharp, still remain at the stage of the 'Summit' for three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*? Therefore, the present text cites the Śrāvaka as an example, noting that he [remains] at a single object of focus.
This is the response concerning the "single gate" and so forth, which clarifies that the Bodhisattva’s stage of aspiration surpasses the stages of the Śrāvaka and the Peak Dharma (mūrdha-dharma).
△ Second, the cultivation of the causes for the marks and signs over two hundred kalpas. First, concluding the preceding section and introducing the subsequent one.

After such a period of time, having completed the cultivation of the six perfections, he further dwells for a hundred kalpas planting the causes for the marks and signs and cultivating a hundred merits to produce each single mark.

[Fǔxíng (Subcommentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) Vol. 3, Part 2 (3) states: "Having passed the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one plants the marks with a hundred merits. Here, 'planting' means cultivation. At this point...

In the desire realm, among human beings, in Jambudvīpa, with a male body, and at a time when a Buddha has appeared in the world—one is able to plant the karma for the [major] marks; there are no restrictions regarding the preceding or succeeding moments (as stated in the text).
[Commentary] Question: At what time does a bodhisattva plant the seeds for the thirty-two marks? Answer: At the quickest, ninety-one *kalpas*; at the slowest, one hundred *kalpas*.
As for the statement that this occurs "among humans in the desire realm," this is discussed from the perspective of the *Kātyāyanīputra* school of the Hīnayāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* records its question as follows: "Regarding the karma for the thirty-two marks..."
"In what place can it be planted? He replied, "It is planted within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form or formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
Within the five destinies (*gati*) of the desire realm, it is planted in the human destiny. Among the four continents (*caturdvīpa*), it is planted in the southern continent (*Jambudvīpa*).

Within the human destiny, it is planted in a male body. Regarding time, it is planted during the period when a Buddha has appeared in the world. Why? Because it is planted by virtue of the Buddha’s body as its condition. Again, he asked:

Among the three types of karma, which type of karma is the seed? Answer: It is the karma of the mind (*manas-karma*). Why? Because the karma of the mind is sharp. The karma of the mind consists of the six consciousnesses;
among these, which consciousness is the seed? Answer: It is the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). Why? Because the five [sensory] consciousnesses lack the capacity for discrimination.
Regarding that which is not restricted by preceding or succeeding moments, the *Mahā-śāstra* asks: "What are the characteristics of the initial seed? Answer: Some say it is beneath the feet.
The mark of the well-established eyes is planted first. Why? Because it is established first, and subsequently the other marks can be planted.
Some say that the mark of the deep blue eyes is planted first; one attains this mark of the eyes because of observing sentient beings with great compassion.
Now it is said: although these words exist, they are not necessarily so. If the conditions and causes are in harmony and conjoined, that itself constitutes the initial planting of the seed.

[Supplement] Those in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are addicted to pleasure, while those in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) abide in meditative absorption; therefore, they cannot plant the seed.

In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), suffering is abundant and pleasure is scarce, which enables the arousal of the great resolve and the practice of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*). Among the remaining three continents, the merit and reward are most excellent; [only there...]

In the Southern Continent (Jambudvīpa), both merit and lifespan are meager, yet wholesome minds arise easily; therefore, when sages transform and guide others, they are necessarily born in the Southern Continent.
Women have many obstacles and lack wisdom, so [the marks] require a male body. If it were not the time of a Buddha’s appearance, there would be no object of focus;
thus, it is only when a Buddha appears in the world that one can plant the karma for the marks.

[Note] Regarding "one hundred merits forming one mark," the *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 3, part 2, states: "By practicing the six perfections, one accomplishes one hundred merits;
using these one hundred merits to form one mark serves as the karmic cause for the thirty-two marks" (text).
[Commentary] This explains the marks formed by the hundred merits; it concerns the causal conditions for the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Furthermore, there are those who practice giving; this is the causal condition for the thirty-two marks. Why is this so?

Because at the time of giving, one’s resolve is firm, one obtains the mark of the feet being firmly planted on the ground (*supratiṣṭhita-pāda*). At the time of giving, one is surrounded by the five [requisites], and the recipient is one’s retinue."
Due to the causal conditions of his past karma, he obtained the mark of wheels on the soles of his feet. Because he bestowed great heroic power, he obtained the mark of broad and level heels.
Because he gathered people through generosity, he obtained the mark of webbed fingers and toes. Because he bestowed delicious food and drink, [he obtained the mark of a soft and tender skin].
One attains the marks of soft and supple hands and feet and the seven parts of the body being full because of giving that benefits life.

One attains the marks of long fingers, a straight body without curvature, and great uprightness because at the time of giving, one says, "I shall give this to you," and thus the intention to give increases further.

One attains the mark of high ankles and body hair pointing upward because at the time of giving, when the recipient requests it, one listens attentively with a single mind and issues instructions with earnest diligence.

Because he caused [others] to necessarily attain them quickly, he obtained the mark of the *iṇiyā* (ūrṇā) tuft between the eyebrows. Because he was neither angry nor contemptuous toward those who requested [gifts], he obtained the mark of arms extending past the knees.
Because he gave according to the wishes of the requester without waiting for words, he obtained the mark of the concealed organ (*kośagata-vasti-guhya*).
Because he gave fine clothing, bedding, gold, silver, and precious jewels, he obtained the mark of a golden-colored body and the mark of thin skin. He spread...

At the time of giving, because he acted in accordance with the wishes of others and gave rise to the causal conditions for sovereign karma, he obtained the mark of a single hair growing from each pore and the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows.
When a beggar requested something, he would immediately say, "I shall give it to you. By virtue of this karma, [he attained these marks].

He attains the mark of the upper body being like that of a lion with rounded shoulders because he provided medicine to the sick and gave food and drink to those who were hungry and thirsty, thereby creating the karmic causes and conditions for having little illness.

He attains the mark of the fullness of both armpits and the mark of the supreme sense of taste because, when giving, he exhorted others to practice generosity and comforted them, thereby opening the path of giving. He attains the mark of the *uṣṇīṣa* (cranial protuberance) and a well-rounded body [because...].

Because, like a *mṛduguluka* (soft clay ball), when there is a petitioner and one intends to give, one speaks with gentle and truthful words, giving certainly and without falsehood, one obtains the mark of a broad and long tongue and the mark of the Brahma-voice.

Because, at the time of giving, one speaks according to reality and beneficial words, such as the voice of the *kalaviṅka* bird, one obtains the mark of lion-like jaws. At the time of giving, one makes offerings...

Because the recipient’s mind was pure, he obtained the marks of white teeth and even teeth. Because he spoke truthful and harmonious words at the time of giving, he obtained the mark of closely set teeth and the mark of forty teeth.

Because at the time of giving he was free from anger and attachment, and regarded the recipient with an impartial mind, he obtained the mark of blue eyes and the mark of eyelashes like those of a bull king. These are the causes for planting the seeds of the thirty-two marks.

This is the condition (*pratyaya*). However, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* mentions only "giving" (*dāna*); yet, with respect to its underlying intention, it encompasses all six perfections, because the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) is able to subsume the other five.
That is to say, the meaning of "giving" (*dāna*) subsumes the six: material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma; among these, there are one, two, and three [types respectively].
This is called the stage of abiding in cultivation. Question: What is meant by practicing the six perfections to accomplish the hundred merits?
Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: First, abstaining from killing and so forth up to wrong views to a small degree constitutes one merit;

second, abstaining from killing and so forth to a great degree; third, abstaining from killing and so forth completely; fourth, abstaining for a short time; fifth, abstaining for a long time; sixth, abstaining for the duration of one's life.
7. One refrains from it oneself; 8. one teaches others to refrain from it; 9. one extols and praises its abstention with immeasurable words; 10.

upon seeing others refrain from killing and so forth, one rejoices with a profound mind and gives rise to great joy. Each of these ten gates contains ten [factors], which collectively are called the hundredfold meritorious practices (*śatapuṇyakriyā*).
The *Huayan chao* states: "As for 'a small portion,' the Sūtra school permits that one may receive [the merit] partially, whether in part or in full."
Based on those faculties, there are distinctions of inferior, middling, and superior; and as for time, there is a distinction between a short duration and a long duration.
A short duration ranges from one day to ten days; a long duration refers to one year up until the end of life.

Furthermore, these ten types are divided into four categories: the first thirty are distinguished according to their objective basis (*vastu*), while the subsequent thirty are distinguished according to their temporal duration (*kāla*).
The first twenty [marks] are explained in terms of oneself and others; the latter twenty are established in terms of praise and description.

When correctly applied to the time of practice, they are called the "one hundred deeds" (*śata-karman*); when applied to the merit produced, they are called the "one hundred merits" (*śata-puṇya*). Based on these one hundred merits, one mark is formed.
△ Second, the specific exposition of the characteristics of merit.

The meaning of "merit" has many pathways and is difficult to define with certainty. Some say that curing a single person of blindness within a great trichiliocosm constitutes one unit of merit, and so forth.
【□Note】 Regarding the phrase "the meaning of merit has many paths," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 3, Part 2, states: "Question: How much constitutes one unit of merit? ...
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva cultivates the ten wholesome paths of action, each has five mental states: namely, inferior, middling, superior, superior-superior, and supreme-middling-superior.
From the first arising of these five minds up to the full completion of the five minds—these hundred minds are called the 'hundred merits' that constitute one [unit of merit]."
[The marks] continue in this manner up to the thirty-second, which is called the purity of the body (text).

[Commentary: This explains the meaning of "merit" (*puṇya*). However, according to the text, it refers to a detailed demonstration of specific instances; yet the intention of the commentary seems to clarify the measure of merit in a general sense.
Now, as for the many paths regarding the meaning of merit: the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks, "How much is defined as one unit of merit?"
