The Venerable replied: "Some say that the karmic retribution of a Cakravartin King, who enjoys sovereign bliss over the four continents, constitutes one merit.

One hundred such merits form one mark (*lakṣaṇa*). Others say that becoming Śakra Devānām Indra, who attains sovereignty over two heavens, constitutes one merit. Others say that becoming the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven..."

Attaining mastery within the desire realm is called one unit of merit. Some say that the meritorious retribution obtained by all sentient beings, with the exception of Bodhisattvas in their final birth before Buddhahood, constitutes one unit of merit.

Others say that when a kalpa of heaven and earth comes to an end, the retribution of the trichiliocosm is established through the collective merit of all sentient beings; this is called one unit of merit. There is...
It is said that this merit is immeasurable and cannot be known through analogy. Suppose all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm were blind and sightless;
if someone could cure them all so that they were healed, this would constitute one unit of merit. Or suppose all people were afflicted by lethal poison;
if one person could cure them all so that they were healed—whereas otherwise all people would have died—[this would likewise constitute one unit of merit].

One who is able to rescue and liberate all those people who have broken their precepts and correct views, and who can teach a single person so that they attain pure precepts and correct views—such acts together constitute a single merit. Furthermore, some say that this merit is immeasurable.
It cannot be illustrated by analogy. This Bodhisattva has entered the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa and, with his mind intent on great practices, plants the causal conditions for the thirty-two marks.
Therefore, one should know that this merit is immeasurable; only a Buddha can fully know it.
Thus, the meaning of "merit" has many paths and is difficult to definitively judge. For now, this ritual text cites but one type.
And so it is. The commentary states: "Up to the cultivation of the ten wholesome paths of action, there are five types of mind," and so forth.
This explains the meaning of the "hundred blessings" by means of a hundred minds, based on the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, Chapter on the Noble Virtuous King (*Gao-gui-de-wang-pin*), which says:
"Regarding the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of a pure body, the Bodhisattva cultivates the precept against killing with five kinds of mind: namely, inferior, middling, superior, supreme, and ultimate."
From the middle and superior [levels] up to right view, it is likewise. These fifty moments of mind are called the fulfillment of the initial resolve.
When these fifty moments of mind are definitively accomplished, this is called "fulfillment. These one hundred moments of mind are called the "one hundred merits.
Possessing these one hundred merits, one accomplishes one mark. In this manner, proceeding successively and becoming fully endowed with them, one achieves the thirty-two marks.
This is called the "Pure Body. Furthermore, these one hundred mental states (*citta*) are precisely one hundred volitions (*cetana*).

That is to say, the Bodhisattva first employs fifty volitions to purify the body—meaning that by practicing each of the ten wholesome paths of action with five volitions, fifty volitions are accomplished. Subsequently, the mind further gives rise to another fifty volitions, causing the hundred merits (*puṇya*) to be fully perfected.
Regarding these five volitions, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: [they consist of] the volition to abstain from killing, the volition to exhort others [to do so], and so forth.
[It consists of] reflection, reflection on what is excellent, sympathetic joy, and dedication. [Note:
*Guanyin xuán* (Mysterious Commentary on Avalokiteśvara), Part 2, states: "In general, by employing three thousand two hundred merits, one cultivates and perfects the thirty-two marks of a Great Man.
Only when these appear in the present does one truly receive the title of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva."
[Commentary] The "three thousand two hundred merits" refers to the accumulation of hundreds of merits that constitute the causal nature.
The "thirty-two marks" refer to the resultant characteristics achieved. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 4, asks: "Does the Cakravartin King possess the thirty-two marks?"

The Bodhisattva likewise possesses the thirty-two marks. What is the distinction between them? Answer: The Bodhisattva’s marks are superior to those of a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) in seven respects:
first, they are pure and beautiful; second, they are distinct; third, they do not deviate from their proper locations; fourth, they are complete.
Five: profound penetration. Six: acting in accordance with wisdom and not following the ways of the world. Seven: acting in accordance with detachment.

The marks of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*) are not like this. Again, it was asked: "For what reason does a bodhisattva possess exactly thirty-two marks, neither more nor less? The answer is:
Some say that the Buddha adorns his body with thirty-two marks so that he is upright and not disordered; if there were fewer, the body would not be [complete].
It is upright. If there were more [marks], the physical characteristics of the Buddha’s body would become disordered; these thirty-two marks are upright and not disordered.
They cannot be increased and cannot be decreased, just as the Buddha-dharma cannot be increased or decreased. The physical characteristics are also like this. Again, he asked:
For what reason does a bodhisattva adorn his body with the marks of a great man? Answer: When people see the Buddha’s physical marks, they attain pure faith;
for this reason, he adorns his body with the marks. Furthermore, because all Buddhas are supreme in every respect, [they possess] the color of their bodies.
Regarding majesty, physical characteristics, lineage, wisdom, meditative concentration, liberation, and all such matters, he is supreme.
If the Buddha did not adorn his physical form, these qualities would be diminished. It is said that Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi dwells within this body;
if the physical characteristics were not upright and majestic, Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi would not dwell within this body. For this reason, the Bodhisattva practices [the perfection of form].
He adorns his body with the thirty-two marks for the sake of attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Question: The Buddha’s wisdom is immeasurable;
his physical marks should likewise be immeasurable. Why, then, are they limited to the same thirty-two marks as those of a *cakravartin* wheel-turning sage king?
Answer: They are neither more nor less. The meaning is as previously explained. Furthermore, some say that the marks of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—
It is indeterminate. As it is said, [the Buddha] manifests appearances according to what sentient beings prefer, so as to be able to guide their minds.

If sentient beings do not value gold but value other colors, such as lapis lazuli, crystal, diamond, and so forth—as is the case with the people of this land—then the Buddha does not manifest a golden color. Rather, observing what they prefer, he manifests that particular color.

If sentient beings do not prize long, slender fingers or webbed hands—since long fingers with sharp claws are the mark of a rākṣasa, and webbed hands are the mark of a water bird—and since such features make one's activities inconvenient, like wearing gloves, what use are they?
For example, the Bodhisattva Maitreya of Kaśmīra had webbed hands; his father disapproved of this.
Some considered it a deformity and cut it with a knife. Some said, "For what reason does my son resemble a bird? His shoulders are not well-formed and appear swollen.

Others said, "His abdomen is not visible; he has no belly like a hungry ghost. Some considered blue eyes to be unattractive, whereas they held that the distinction between black and white [of the eyes] was what was truly beautiful.
Therefore, the Buddha manifests physical characteristics in accordance with what sentient beings find pleasing.

In this way, there is no fixed certainty. Some say that these thirty-two marks are indeed fixed, yet by means of the power of supernormal abilities (*abhijñā*), the Buddha manifests a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to the preferences of sentient beings to display these marks.

Others say that while the Buddha sometimes manifests through supernormal transformations, at other times he is born into a specific location within a world; in such cases of birth, one cannot say it is a supernormal transformation.
Furthermore, within the trichiliocosm, he takes birth wherever there are sentient beings who can be delivered, manifesting signs accordingly.
As stated in the Guhyakapada Sūtra, he may manifest a golden color, a silver color, or the colors of the sun, moon, and stars;
he may appear tall or short. He manifests these signs according to what is necessary to guide sentient beings, just as one discerns the characteristics of a person.
The *Madhyama Āgama* states: "Five features are considered excellent when they are long: namely, the eyes, the nose, the tongue, the arms, and the fingers and thighs.
These characteristics—whether like wheels, lotuses, conch shells, or the sun and moon—are thus present.

Therefore, the Buddha’s hands and feet possess wheels with a thousand spokes, his fingers are slender and long, his nose is high and well-formed, and his tongue is broad, long, and thin. All such qualities surpass those previously esteemed."
To inspire a mind of reverence, the Buddha manifests ten million marks, or immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* marks,
or five, six, four, or three; he thus manifests the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics according to what is favored in India.
△ III. Specifically Indicating the Characteristics of the Fulfillment of the Six Perfections (2). First, the general summary:
In the practice of the six perfections, each has its own time of fulfillment.

[□ Note] Regarding the textual passage on the fulfillment of the six perfections appearing after the section on the characteristics of the seeds (*bīja-lakṣaṇa*): this is because at the stage of the characteristics of the seeds, one also practices the six perfections.
△ Second, the demonstration of the signs:
such as King Śibi’s fulfillment of the perfection of generosity by substituting himself for a dove; King Samantaprabha’s fulfillment of the perfection of the body by relinquishing his kingdom;

the seer Kṣāntivādin’s fulfillment of the perfection of patience through enduring mutilation without resentment at the hands of King Kaliṅga; and Prince Mahātyāga’s draining of the ocean and standing on one foot for seven days.
In praising Puṣya Buddha, his progress reached fulfillment; while practicing dhyāna atop the crow’s nest of his preceptor Sañjaya, his meditative concentration reached fulfillment;

and when the minister Gopaka divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts to quell strife, his wisdom reached fulfillment. Looking toward the initial stage of a śrāvaka, this is the stage of "lower patience" (mṛdu-kṣānti).

[Note] The *Xuánjì* (Mysterious Record) on Avalokiteśvara, Part 3, states: "He cut pieces from his own flesh and traded it for a dove with a hawk; even until his entire body was exhausted, he felt neither distress nor despair.
Because his self-vow was true and sincere, his body was miraculously restored to its original state. This is the mark of the perfection of *dāna* (generosity). *Śibi* is translated as 'to give'."
*Dāna* (檀) is translated as "giving" (施).

[Commentary: When Śākyamuni was practicing the path as a bodhisattva, he was a king named Śibi. He attained the *dhāraṇī* for protection through taking refuge and looked upon all sentient beings as a mother loves her child.
At that time, the Lord of Devas, knowing that [the King's] life was about to end, sought out the Buddha to inquire about his doubts.

Having searched everywhere without success, he returned to his celestial palace, filled with grief, anxiety, and distress. At that time, the celestial master artisan named Viśvakarman asked the Lord of Heaven, "Why are you so sorrowful and distressed?
He replied, "I have sought a person of all-knowledge (sarvajña), yet I have been unable to find one.
Viśvakarman said, "There is a Great Bodhisattva who has fulfilled the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā); before long, he will attain Buddhahood. The Deva—

The Lord replied with a verse: "When Bodhisattvas resolve upon the Great Mind, it is like fish eggs or mango blossoms—of these three things, many exist within the cause, yet when it comes to the fruit, they are few.
"You became a pigeon and I became a hawk; you then feigned fear and entered beneath the King's armpit.
We shall go to test him: is he truly a Bodhisattva? Viśvakarman said, "He is a great Bodhisattva. How could this be otherwise?"
This matter distressed him. Śakra said, "I have no ill intent. Gold must be tested. Then, just as he had described, [the pigeon] transformed and entered the king's armpit.
His entire body trembled with fear; his eyes darted about and he made sounds. The people said, "This king is most compassionate; he should protect all beings.
Even such a small bird as this has come to him for refuge, as if entering its own home. This was a mark of a Bodhisattva.
"It is so. It will not be long before you become a Buddha. A hawk, perched on a nearby tree, spoke to the king, saying, "Give me back my dove!
The king said, "I accepted this dove first; it was not you who accepted it first. I previously made a vow to deliver all sentient beings.
The hawk said, "If you wish to deliver all sentient beings, am I not also a sentient being? Why..."
"You have taken away my food. The king asked, "What food do you require? He replied, "I require fresh meat and warm blood.
The king said, "There is no way to obtain these without killing. I have previously made a vow that if any sentient being comes to me for refuge, I must protect them.
How can I kill one to give to another? Having reflected thus, his mind became firm, and he spoke this verse: "This is my..."
"My physical body constantly undergoes old age, sickness, and death; it will soon become putrid and decayed. You require it, and I shall give it to you.
He took a knife and cut flesh from his own thigh, offering it to him. The hawk said, "You must act according to principle;
do not deceive me. Make the weights equal. The king said, "Hold the scales and weigh them. As the dove’s body became heavier, the king’s body became lighter, and so it continued until—
The King’s body was completely cut away. The ministers and retinue cleared away the onlookers, saying, "The King is now in such a state that he can no longer be viewed.
The King said, "View me as you please; if I am to attain the Way of Buddhahood, I shall endure this great matter.
The King smeared his hands with blood and, grasping the scale, attempted to ascend until he was level with the pigeon. The hawk said, "Why do you act thus? Return the pigeon to me."
The King said: "Since the beginningless kalpas of the past, I have lost my body countless times. Now is the time to seek the Buddha-way with ease.

Though my flesh is exhausted and my sinews severed, and I wish to ascend but fall back, I rebuke myself, saying: 'You must remain firm and resolute; do not allow yourself to become confused or despondent.'"
Sentient beings have fallen into the ocean of sorrow; you ought to rescue and protect them. Why are you indolent?
[Their suffering] does not even equal one-sixteenth part of the suffering of hell. I am especially diligent, yet I still suffer from this [present] pain; how much more so in the midst of hell?

Those without wisdom [should reflect thus]. The devas praised him, saying: "If a small bird can act in this way, how much more so its larger counterparts? At that time, the great earth shook in six ways.
The earth shook; the waters of the ocean surged with waves; flowers bloomed upon withered trees; celestial perfumed water rained down; and all the Buddhas came to offer praise.
"He shall certainly attain Buddhahood," said the hawk to the pigeon. "You are a true Bodhisattva," said Viśvakarman. "O Lord of Devas, you possess divine power."
He caused him to recover. Śakra said, "I do not need it. Let the King himself make a vow; it shall move all beings.
He then asked the King, "Is your mind not troubled? The King replied, "My heart is joyful; it is neither troubled nor despondent.
Śakra said, "Who will believe you? The King made this oath: "If my mind is not troubled and I seek the path of the Buddha, [may my body be restored as it was]."

He restored [the body] to its former state. As soon as he had spoken, it was restored. When humans and devas saw this, they were all filled with great joy and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence, saying, "This one will surely become a Buddha; we shall provide him with offerings."

[Note] For example, King Sudāma met his death by surrendering his body, yet he maintained the precept of non-falsehood. This is the mark of *śīla* (translated as "goodness" or "virtue," referring specifically to the goodness of the precepts).
[Commentary] King Śūdraka possessed great diligence and always relied upon truthful speech.
Desiring to enter a garden for recreation, he had just passed through the city gate when a brahmin approached him and begged, saying, "O King, you are a man of merit;
have compassion for my poverty. The King said, "Wait until I return. Just as he reached the garden, there was a king of birds with two wings named...
He replied, "Mṛgapada. Previously, he made a vow with the mountain deity to capture one thousand kings;
he has already obtained nine hundred and ninety-nine, lacking only King Śūdraka. He flew through the air, seized the king, and took him away.
The women wept piteously, their cries shaking the entire grove. Mṛgapada took the king to his dwelling and placed him among the other kings. Śūdra—
King Māndhātṛ shed tears like falling rain. Mṛgāra said, "Great Kṣatriya, why do you weep like a small child?
All who are born must die; those who meet must eventually part. Sūta replied, "I do not fear death.
I regret that from birth until now, I have never uttered a falsehood, yet now I have broken my word. For this reason, I am distressed. I wish to give [this] to the brāhmaṇa..."
"I have practiced giving, yet I have betrayed my former resolve and brought upon myself the sin of deception. Mṛgāra said, "I release you to go back.

When you have finished practicing giving for seven days, come at once to face death. If you do not come, I have the power to seize you. The king returned and gave generously according to his heart's desire.
He installed his crown prince as king, assembled the great multitude of the people, and then offered this apology: "My wisdom was insufficient..."
[Zhou] was young and did not act according to the Dharma; he would immediately become angry. "My present body is not my own; I must depart.
When the people tried to detain him, they said, "We pray that Your Majesty will take heed and continue to provide your protection to this land; do not worry about the ghost-king Ruru."
One should station an iron-clad vanguard to provide protection; even the Divine Deer-Foot (Mṛgāra) would not fear them.
The King spoke in verse: "Truthful speech is the foremost precept; truthful speech is the ladder to heaven. Truthful speech makes a man great;
false speech leads one to hell. I now uphold truthful speech; I would rather lose my body and life. Thereupon he set out and arrived at the place of the Deer-Foot.
Seeing him arrive, he was filled with joy. "You are a man of truthful speech; you have not violated your solemn pledge.
All people cherish their own lives; why did the King release you and allow you to return? You are a great man. At that time, King Śūdraka extensively praised truthful speech and rebuked false speech.
Hearing this, Mṛgāra’s faith became pure, and he said to Śūdraka: "Since you are able to speak thus, I shall now [grant you my daughter]."

"Relinquish [your claims] and each return to your own kingdom. After these words were spoken, at that time the kings, each cherishing the grace of the non-killing [edict], could not bear to part with one another.
They dwelt together here and jointly established a city, which is the present-day city of Rājagṛha.

This is the mark of the perfection of the precepts (*śīla*). [Note] Bian’e says: "Goodness" should be read as "innate goodness. As for "innate" (*xing*), it refers to that which has been formed through habitual practice.
Because one upholds and maintains the dharma of the precepts, allowing them to function spontaneously, it is called "innate goodness."

[Note] For example, when the Rishi Kṣāntivādin was subjected to the mutilation of his body by King Kali (a corruption of "evil world" and "unrighteous"), he remained unmoved in his compassionate forbearance.
By making a vow, he immediately caused the blood to transform into milk. This is the mark of the fulfillment of kṣānti (kṣānti is translated as "forbearance").
[Commentary] As in the past, when the Seer Kṣāntivādin was dwelling in the forest practicing patience, King Kali entered the garden with his court ladies to sport.
After they had finished eating and drinking, the king slept for a short while.
While the ladies were gathering flowers in the forest, they saw this seer; they paid him respectful homage and stood to one side. At that time...

The rishi praised loving-kindness and patience for the sake of the court ladies; his words were so exquisite that those who heard them forgot their weariness and remained for a long time without leaving.
When the king awoke from his sleep, he did not see the ladies. Drawing his sword, he followed their tracks and saw the women standing before the rishi.
His jealousy flared up intensely; with eyes blazing with rage, he brandished his sword at the rishi and asked, "What have you done?"
[The King] asked, “What is your practice? He replied, “I cultivate loving-kindness and patience. The King said, “I shall now test you.
I will cut off your hands, feet, ears, and nose with a sharp sword; if you do not become angry, I shall know that you truly cultivate patience. The Rishi said, “Do as you wish.
The King immediately drew his sword and tested him as described above, then asked, “Has your mind wavered? He replied, “My mind has not wavered. The King—
He said, "You are alone here; you have no power. Though you say you will not move, who would believe it? The seer made a vow:
"If I have truly cultivated loving-kindness and patience, let my blood turn to milk. Once the vow was made, it immediately turned into milk.
The king was greatly terrified and fled, taking his court ladies with him. At that time, the nāga deity of the forest, for the sake of this seer—

A man encountered rain, thunder, lightning, and a thunderbolt, which brought him grievous harm. Consequently, he did not return to the palace; this is the mark of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti*).
*Kṣānti* is pronounced "chǎn.

[Commentary] It is like the Crown Prince Mahādāna, who sought the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) to rain down treasures and relieve the poor. Having obtained the jewel, it fell into the ocean; he then attempted to drain the sea.

He took it up. (The pronunciation of "shu" is *ru*; it means to scoop and take. Though his tendons and bones were broken and damaged, he never slackened or desisted. The devas asked him why, and he replied, "I shall not cease my efforts throughout my lifetimes;
therefore, I assist in scooping the ocean. When the seawater had decreased by half, the dragon, fearing the ocean would dry up, presented him with a pearl.
This is the mark of the fulfillment of *vīrya* (diligence).

[Commentary]: As in the case of Prince Sudatta, who sought the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "As for the obtaining of the jewel and its falling into the sea:
the Sea God, being envious of the jewel, stole it while [the prince] was asleep. After the Prince awoke, he began to bale out the great ocean;

even though his sinews and bones were worn away to exhaustion, he never slackened or desisted. He vowed to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel in order to provide for sentient beings and save their bodies."

It was painful. The devas questioned him, and he replied, "I shall continue to draw water without ceasing. Seeing his diligence, the devas assisted him in bailing out the ocean until the water had decreased by half.
Fearing that the ocean would run dry, the nāgas presented him with a jewel. This constitutes the mark of the perfection of diligence.

[Note] Śāṇakavāsin (the name of a śramaṇa with a conch-shell-shaped topknot) attained the fourth dhyāna, wherein inhalation and exhalation ceased. A bird mistook him for a tree and laid its eggs in his topknot.
When he arose from meditative absorption and wished to depart, fearing that the mother bird would not return, he immediately entered dhyāna once more; only when the bird flew away did he rise.
This is the mark of one perfected in dhyāna.
[Commentary] For example, there was a śramaṇa named Śaṅkara who was a ṛṣi with a conch-shell topknot. It is incorrect for anyone to depict his image in the form of a monk.
Having attained the fourth dhyāna, his inhalation and exhalation ceased. Sitting beneath a tree, he remained silent and motionless.
A bird, seeing him unmoving, mistook him for a tree and laid an egg upon the rishi’s topknot. When the rishi arose from his meditative absorption, he realized there was an egg upon his head.
He then reflected: "If I move away, the mother bird will never return. [The bird's egg...]
It will surely collapse. He then re-enters dhyāna, and only when it is time for it to fly away does he arise and walk; this is the mark of the fulfillment of dhyāna.
[Note] When the minister Gupila divided Jambudvīpa into seven parts, he distributed the cities, towns, mountains, and rivers equally so as to quell disputes;
this is the mark of the fulfillment of prajñā.
[Commentary] It is like the minister Gopī, who divided the land of Jambudvīpa into seven parts, making the cities and villages all equal.
He divided the large and small cities, as well as the people, into seven portions, so that the seven kingdoms were without dispute.
This is the mark of the perfection of Prajñā. [Supplementary Note] The *Jieyi* states: The fifth fascicle of the *Dīrgha Āgama* says that Śākya...
King Maitrībala had a son of a great minister named Mahāgovinda, who succeeded his father as prime minister. At that time, the king had six Kṣatriya kings;
Govinda divided the land and waters of Jambudvīpa into seven equal portions, enfeoffing the six Kṣatriyas and the Great King himself as the lords of seven great nations.
Some teachers say that this constitutes the mark of perfection by means of worldly knowledge.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refutes this, stating: "Even a Bodhisattva on the first stage (*bhūmi*) does not yet know its boundaries; only one on the tenth stage can know them.
How can you say that the great ground (*mahābhūmi*) is divided into seven parts to constitute the complete characteristic of *prajñā*?"
[Note] Regarding what is called "fulfillment": the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) were originally practiced to remedy the obscurations; their practice was intended to fulfill one's vows.

Now that the obscurations have been abandoned, and [beings] have been delivered and their hearts' desires fulfilled, it is known that the merit of the six perfections has reached its full completion. (Text) Regarding "standing on tiptoe for seven days," the *Xuánjì* (Profound Record) on the *Guānyīn* (Avalokiteśvara), Part 4, states:
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* says: At that time there was a Buddha named Tiṣya, who had two disciples. One was named... [text continues].
Śākyamuni delights in practicing deeds for the benefit of others, while the second, named Maitreya, delights in practicing deeds for his own benefit.
Since the sentient beings to be converted by him would ripen only later, that Buddha thought to himself: "It is difficult for many to approach one person, but it is easy for one to approach many.
Desiring to cause Śākyamuni to attain enlightenment first, he then left his two disciples behind and entered the mountains. At that time, Śākyamuni...
The Bodhisattva followed him into the mountains to seek his original teacher, but found no trace of him.

While he was walking uprightly, he suddenly saw that Buddha within a jeweled niche, having entered the fire-element samādhi; his majestic radiance was so brilliant as to be extraordinary compared to ordinary times.
As he walked, he forgot to set down one foot for seven days, during which time he recited a single verse in praise of that World-Honored One, saying: "Heaven and earth..."
In the many halls of learning, in the palaces of the departed, and throughout the celestial realms of the ten directions—nowhere was there a peer to this Great Śramaṇa, the Bull-King among men.
Having searched the earth, mountains, and forests, he found no equal. By virtue of this diligence, he surpassed nine kalpas and attained Buddhahood before Maitreya. (Text)

[Supplement] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When Puṣya Buddha wished to observe whether the mind of Śākyamuni Bodhisattva was pure and mature, he immediately perceived it and knew that his mind was not yet pure and mature, whereas the minds of his disciples were all pure and mature.
Furthermore, the mind of Maitreya Bodhisattva was already pure and mature, yet his disciples were not yet pure and mature. At that time, Puṣya Buddha reflected in this way:
He reflected: "The mind of a single person is easily and swiftly transformed; the minds of many people are difficult to treat rapidly.

Having completed his contemplation, desiring to cause Śākyamuni to quickly attain Buddhahood, he ascended Mount Himavat and entered the *jyotisprabha-samādhi* (fire-light samādhi) within a jeweled cave.
It is further said that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was at that time a non-Buddhist *ṛṣi*; while ascending the mountain to gather medicinal herbs, [the Buddha] appeared.
This was Buddha Puṣya, who sat within a jeweled cave and entered the fire-light samādhi, emitting a great radiance. Having seen this, his heart was filled with joy, faith, and reverence;
he stood upon one foot, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and gazed at him with single-minded concentration, his eyes never blinking for even a moment.
For seven days and seven nights, he praised the Buddha with a single verse: "In the heavens above and the world below, there is none like the Buddha;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer. Of all that exists in the world, I have seen it all, yet there is nothing at all equal to the Buddha.
By this, he transcended nine kalpas; thus, after ninety-one kalpas, he attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

[Commentary] Regarding "this stage of lower patience," the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts), Volume 3, states: "If one has passed through three asaṃkhyeya kalpas and planted the karma for the thirty-two marks, by comparison, this corresponds to the stage of lower patience" (text).
[Commentary] Regarding the thirty-two marks (*lakṣaṇa*): one should verify them through the numerical categories of the Dharma and know them for oneself.
These thirty-two are collectively called "marks" (*xiàng*) because they signify something; when observed, they can be distinguished, and thus they are termed "marks.

The Tathāgata’s manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) displays these thirty-two marks to signify that the manifold virtues of the *dharmakāya* are perfectly complete, causing those who see them to feel love and reverence, and thereby come to know [the Buddha].
Possessing supreme virtues worthy of veneration, the Honored One among humans and devas, the King among all sages, thus manifests the thirty-two marks.
The karma for these various marks is as described above. Regarding the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), according to the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 4, it states:
"These are all the wisdom of lower patience, which can subdue the faculties and fulfill the six perfections. This is why—
Why is this? It is because at the stage of lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*), the power of wisdom is strong while the power of afflictions is weak.

By employing this wisdom to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), one is able to endure the six obscurations and, being without regard for body or life, fulfills the six perfections. The fulfillment of the first four perfections is due to the power of the foundations of mindfulness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*);

this reaches up to the stage of lower patience. The fulfillment of the perfection of meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*) is mostly due to the power of the common foundations of mindfulness (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*); this reaches up to the stage of lower...

This is patience (*kṣānti*). When the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is fulfilled, this power of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) reaches the stage of "lower patience" (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). Question:

Even Arhats are unable to practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) without regard for their own bodies or lives; how then can the power of wisdom at the stage of lower patience accomplish the six perfections? Answer:
Without the power of compassion (*karuṇā*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), and the force of cultivation over accumulated kalpas, the wisdom of an Arhat [cannot do so].
If even wisdom cannot achieve this, how much less so can the lower stage of patience (*kṣānti*)? Now, because external conditions— compassion and vows— have been long cultivated and refined,
and because internally there is the power of the patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*) and wisdom to assist in breaking through the six obscurations,
the Bodhisattva, when compared to that Śrāvaka, is at the stage of the lower patience.
[Note] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The six *pāramitās* throughout the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* refer to the fulfillment of the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* of the stage of phenomena (*vastu*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "Prior to the Bodhi tree, four *pāramitās* are fulfilled; upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood, two *pāramitās* are fulfilled.
This is based on the fact that the *dhyāna* and *prajñā* which take principle (*tattva*) as their object begin to be fulfilled [at that point].

[Supplement] In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), the character "wu" (without) is missing from the section on the lower stage of dhyāna. [Record] This commentary explains how the two treatises (*Abhidharmakośa* and *Yogācārabhūmi*) are consistent regarding the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
The *Fuxing* states: "The explanation here of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred kalpas differs slightly from that of the *Abhidharmakośa*.

According to the *Kośa*, the first four perfections are fulfilled prior to the Bodhi-tree, while the final two perfections are fulfilled upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood. As the verse says: 'It is solely through compassion...'"
Viśvantara, having had his body mangled, was free from resentment and praised Buddha Tiṣya, supreme enlightenment, and the six pāramitās.
Regarding these four stages, he cultivated and perfected them in pairs, one by one, and again two by two, in their respective order:
the first refers to generosity; the next two refer to ethical discipline and patience; the next one refers to diligence; and the final two refer to meditative concentration and wisdom.
These correspond respectively to the four propositions. Because he was praised by Tiṣya, he transcended nine *kalpas*;

thus, from the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, he fulfilled the two *pāramitās* of dhyāna and prajñā over ninety-one *kalpas*. If one follows the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the six *pāramitās* were fulfilled over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, which is likewise not contradictory.
According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, during those three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, he merely practiced the matter of dhyāna.

"Wisdom is fulfilled. If one arrives beneath the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree), it is also because the wisdom of *prajñā* based on principle (*li*) has begun to be fulfilled through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

[Commentary] The *Guan-yin xuan* (Mysterious Meaning of Avalokiteśvara), Part 3, states: Question: According to the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, Śākyamuni and Maitreya conceived the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) simultaneously.
"By skipping one [kalpa], nine kalpas are bypassed. For what reason do both Buddhas become Buddhas within the Bhadrakalpa?
Answer: Śākyamuni encountered Puṣya and shortened a hundred kalpas; Maitreya encounters various Buddhas—why should he not likewise shorten ninety-one kalpas?
(The *Commentary on the Abhidharmakośa*, Vol. 4, states: "Maitreya must certainly skip kalpas when encountering a Buddha; it is feared that the Sanskrit original has not yet reached us.")
[Commentary] This citation serves to examine and distinguish how two Buddhas equally achieve enlightenment within the same Bhadrakalpa.
Specifically, it addresses the doubt that while Śākyamuni Buddha transcended kalpas, Maitreya does not; how, then, can they both achieve Buddhahood in the same single kalpa?

In the response, the example of Śākyamuni’s past life—where he encountered Puṣya and was able to condense a hundred kalpas—is cited as a precedent for Maitreya’s encounters with various Buddhas. It also...
It should be understood that [the duration] is reduced to ninety-one kalpas. The record below clarifies that Maitreya will certainly transcend these kalpas;
thus, he is able to attain enlightenment together with [Śākyamuni] within the Bhadrakalpa.
△ Second, the fulfillment of the fruit and the realization of the vow, in four parts. First, the time of attaining the Way.

Next, he enters the stage of the candidate for Buddhahood (*abhiṣikta*). He is born in Tuṣita; he takes birth in a womb; he emerges from the womb; he leaves the household life; he subdues Māra; and he sits unmoving.

This constitutes the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*). Then, in the next single moment (*kṣaṇa*), he enters the stage of superior patience (*adhimātrakṣānti*). In the subsequent single moment, he enters the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
[Commentary] Regarding the "one who fills the place" (*kṣetra-pūraṇa*): since the previous Buddha has already entered extinction, this Bodhisattva immediately fills that position;

therefore, he is called one who "fills the place. (Text) Below this, the eight phases [of a Buddha's life] are fully detailed: 1. descending from Tuṣita Heaven; 2. entering the womb; 3. birth; 4. renunciation; 5.
subduing Māra; 6. attaining enlightenment; 7. turning the wheel of Dharma; 8. entering *nirvāṇa*. However, these eight phases generally...

Regarding the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna: traditionally, it was said that the Mahāyāna lacks the subduing of Māra because one realizes that Māra is itself the Dharma-realm, whereas the Hīnayāna lacks dwelling in the womb because it does not discuss eternal abiding.
However, since the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* enumerates the manifestations of subduing Māra, how could it be of the Hīnayāna? Therefore, the former masters said:

One who attains enlightenment must necessarily subdue Māra; one who takes conception must necessarily abide in the womb. If one were to expand upon "abiding in the womb," then "subduing Māra" would logically be included within "attaining enlightenment.
If one were to expand upon "subduing Māra," then "abiding in the womb" would logically be included within "taking conception. It is merely a matter of what is emphasized or omitted.
[Commentary: Regarding the Bodhisattva who dwells in Tuṣita as the successor to the position [of Buddhahood]:

it is like a crown prince who, when about to succeed to the throne of the Nine-and-Five (the imperial seat), must first reside temporarily in the Eastern Palace. The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: "Under the Bodhi tree, he sat cross-legged."
The hosts of the Māra king were infinite in number, possessing various extraordinary forms that were most terrifying.

Among sentient beings, there was none who, upon seeing them, did not become struck with awe and terror; they all fell into madness and confusion, and some even met their deaths. Such demonic hordes filled the entirety of space.
Yet when the Tathāgata beheld them, his mind was free from fear, his countenance remained unchanged, and not a single hair on his body stood on end.
Unwavering in movement, free from conceptual discrimination, serene and pure, he dwells where the Buddhas dwell.
Endowed with the power of compassion, his faculties are thoroughly subdued; his mind is fearless and cannot be shaken by any host of Māras.
He is able to crush and subdue all the armies of Māra, causing them all to turn their hearts toward him, prostrate themselves, and take refuge. Thereafter, he further employs the three wheels...
He teaches and transforms them, causing them to resolve upon the Way and never again to regress. One should know that this passage describes the signs of subduing Māra.

Furthermore, there are also passages concerning the subduing of Māra in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokadhātuparivarta*). If one were to say that the Mahāyāna lacks [passages on] subduing Māra while the Hīnayāna possesses them, [that would be incorrect].

Furthermore, how could the texts listed in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra be the teachings of the Hīnayāna? Thus, when the ancients clarified the differences between the eight manifestations (aṣṭākāra) of the Great and Small Vehicles, they were merely distinguishing between their different modes of expansion and condensation.

[Commentary] Regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, they are differentiated based on the True [Dharmadhātu]. This is because the eight phases of enlightenment (*aṣṭa-mahābhijñā*) listed in the *Avataṃsaka* belong to the Mahāyāna;
thus, while the eight phases of the Small Vehicle are all inferior, the eight phases of the Mahāyāna are inconceivable. If this is so, are the individual characteristics also inconceivable?
Since they equally express the Middle Way and their realization of the Path is identical to that of the Perfect [Vehicle], these are now the eight phases of the Small Vehicle.
[Commentary] This clarifies the distinction between the eight phases (*aṣṭākāra*) of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

That is to say, the eight phases of the Mahāyāna are manifested based on the wondrous principle of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), whereas the eight phases of the Hīnayāna are manifested based on the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*). Therefore, there is a difference between them in terms of superiority and inferiority.

The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary) states: "In the provisional teaching of the Tripiṭaka Buddha, one speaks only of the eight phases; yet each phase is inferior. [This contrasts with] the Mahāyāna eight..."

Regarding the "phases" (*lakṣaṇa*): within each of these, all eight phases are fully present. Question: If it is said that the eight phases of the Mahāyāna are inconceivable, then are the eight phases of the Buddha according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*) also inconceivable?
Answer: That which is elucidated by the Separate Teaching is merely the "Middle" (*madhyama*). That which is elucidated by the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-śāsana*) is not merely the Middle.
Although the "merely" and "not merely" differ, the "Middle" that is elucidated does not differ. Furthermore, regarding the Separate Teaching’s entry into...

Since the ground and the circle are identical, the Buddha’s manifestation of the eight phases is likewise inconceivable. The final phrase concludes the present discussion on the eight phases of the Hīnayāna.
Among these eight phases of the Hīnayāna, the first four have already been seen in the first fascicle, while the latter four will be explained in the subsequent text.
For a full understanding, one should consult the *Sijiaoyi* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings). [Supplement] The One Phase of the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the possession of the eight phases: as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, these are the Bodhisattva’s manifestation of dwelling in Tuṣita, his initial birth within the mother’s womb,
his childhood, his renunciation, his ascetic practices, his attainment of enlightenment, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, and his parinirvāṇa.

【□Note】 Regarding "subduing Māra," the *Sijiaoyi* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 3, section 5, states: "That is to say, beneath the Bodhi tree, he shattered eighteen trillion demonic armies and hosts.
The Demon King suffered defeat; his demonic forces retreated and dispersed" (text).
[Commentary] This explains the fifth phase, the subduing of Māra. As stated in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*: "The Tripiṭaka Master first subdued the four Māras.

Sitting at the site of enlightenment, he attained the path of Bodhi; he destroyed the Māra of afflictions (*kleśa-māra*) and obtained the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). He destroyed the Māra of the aggregates and sense-bases (*skandhāyatana-māra*); these two together destroy the Māra of death (*mṛtyu-māra*).
Beneath the Bodhi tree, he attained the Samādhi of Immovability (*akampya-samādhi*), transformed the three jade maidens, and destroyed the eight [Māras]."

That the crowns and swords of ten thousand billion soldiers all fell was the work of the Māra of the Heavenly Son (*devaputra-māra*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, which says:
"The Lord of Heaven first commanded his armies; next he dispatched his crown prince; then he sent his three consorts; yet none could destroy [the Buddha].
Finally, he led the great army himself, but was subdued by the Buddha. The great army retreated in dispersal, and the King fell headlong. His crown, parasol, and sword—these three—each..."
In one place, according to the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Ruiying jing*), it is further stated that when the Māra King saw that the three jade maidens were unable to disturb the Bodhisattva,
he transformed himself into an old woman who could not return to her original form. Increasingly enraged,
he summoned a host of spirits and ghosts numbering one hundred and eighty million, causing them all to transform into lions, bears, badgers, tigers, rhinoceroses, and elephants.
There were those in the forms of dragons, oxen, horses, dogs, pigs, and monkeys, beyond description. Some had the heads of insects with human bodies, or the bodies of vipers and snakes;
some had the heads of soft-shelled turtles with six eyes; others had a single neck with many heads.

With teeth, fangs, claws, and talons, they carried mountains and spat fire, surrounded by thunder and lightning, and brandished spears and halberds. Yet the Bodhisattva, with a heart of compassion, was neither startled nor afraid.
Not even a single hair moved; his radiant countenance became even more serene. The ghostly soldiers retreated and dispersed, unable to approach him. [Note:

Regarding "sitting peacefully without moving," etc., the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), fascicle 3, states: "After the host of Māras had dispersed, he gathered his mind and sat upright."]

Abiding in the middle stage of patience (*madhyā-kṣānti*) within the fourth dhyāna, one completes the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*). Middle patience lasts for one moment; supreme patience (*adhimātrā-kṣānti*) lasts for one moment;
and the highest mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) last for one moment (text).
[Commentary: This explains that by sitting firmly and remaining unmoving, one accomplishes the *agradharma* (the supreme mundane dharma). The *Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
When the Māra King saw the Bodhisattva sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, his body upright and motionless, having vowed to attain enlightenment, he immediately departed from his palace.
He went to where the Bodhisattva was and said to him, "O son of the Kṣatriya caste, you may rise from this seat. In this present age of the five turbidities, sentient beings are stubborn and fierce;
you will certainly be unable to realize unexcelled bodhi. For now, you should instead accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King."
"I shall offer you my seven treasures as a gift. The Bodhisattva said, "What you have just said is like trying to lure a child.
One might cause the sun, moon, and stars to fall; one might make the mountains, forests, and great earth ascend into the void.
But for me to fail to attain Great Enlightenment and rise from this seat—such a thing is absolutely impossible. Later, Māra led thirty-six...

A *koṭi* of māra armies, each manifesting various terrifying forms and wielding weapons of infinite varieties, rushed simultaneously toward the foot of the Bodhi tree across an area spanning thirty-six *yojanas* in order to disturb the Bodhisattva;
yet they were unable to do so, for his body and mind remained unmoved, like Mount Sumeru. This was because...

It is immovable, and thus the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is accomplished. [Supplement] After the practitioner of insight has universally contemplated the eight truths of the upper and lower realms, they contract their contemplation, reducing both objects and modes of activity. By sitting upright and practicing insight in this manner, they achieve the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
[Appendix] *Biandong* (Discerning Errors) states: "The phrase 'accomplishing middle patience' (*chūng zhōng rěn*) is the concluding text.

To speak again of 'one moment of superior patience' (*shàng rěn*) and 'one moment of the supreme mundane dharma' (*shì dì yī fǎ*)—according to the *Sìjiào yì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), it is said that one moment gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*zhēn wú lóu*).
Since true outflow-free wisdom has now arisen, the three characters 'last one moment' (*zuì hòu yī chà nà*) are redundant. This appears to be the case in the printed edition."

Read by breaking the sentence. [Commentary] Regarding the term "kṣaṇa" (instant): the *Zhiguan Sanmei* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 36, states: "The Sūtra says that in one thought-moment there are six hundred arisings and ceasings.

The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* say that one thought-moment consists of sixty kṣaṇas. (*Text*) The *Abhidharmakośa* says: "In the time it takes a strong man to snap his fingers, there are sixty-five..."

*Kṣaṇa* (text). [Commentary] "The words of the Sūtra" refers to the discourse of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Furthermore, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "Within one thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*;
one *kṣaṇa* passes through nine hundred births and cessations. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "It is the minimum unit of time."
This is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Second, severing the fetters to attain Buddhahood:

giving rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), one suddenly severs the views, afflictions, and habitual tendencies through thirty-four moments of mind while sitting beneath the Bodhi tree made of wood.
He takes a seat of living grass and manifests as the Inferior Response-body Buddha of sixteen feet.

[Note] Regarding "arousing true outflow-free wisdom" and so forth, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 3, Part 2, cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "The various afflictions of the lower eight stages have not yet been severed during the causal period;
it is only upon reaching the time beneath the King of Trees that the nine grades of afflictions of the ninth stage are collectively termed 'one'."

Nine. By combining the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*) and the nine liberations (*vimukti-jñāna*), they form eighteen. Within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) together constitute sixteen moments of mind.
When combined with the preceding, these total thirty-four moments of mind.

[Supplement] Regarding the *Zhiguan*’s explanation of the thirty-four moments of mind (*citta*), it states that by entering from the conventional into emptiness within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), one attains the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), and thereby achieves Buddhahood.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) quotes a sutra stating that "within a single thought-moment there are six hundred arisings and ceasings," etc., to clarify that a single thought-moment inherently possesses many moments;
however, this is insufficient as proof for the uninterrupted sequence of the thirty-four moments of mind.
[This is] an obstacle.

[Commentary: For the Śrāvakas, the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are severed separately, one before the other. Although the Pratyekabuddhas sever the afflictions of views and thought instantaneously, their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted;

therefore, neither of them can be said to possess the thirty-four moments of mind. As for the *Tripiṭaka* Bodhisattvas, when they reach the foot of the King of Trees (*pārijāta*), both the active habits and the latent tendencies are simultaneously...
Only when [the afflictions] are exhausted can one discuss [this matter].
[Note: The *Xuánjì* on the *Guānyīn* states: "Those who suddenly realize the stage of Arhat or Pratyekabuddha likewise possess thirty-four moments of mind."
They are attained without interval; however, they do not eradicate the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) all at once.

Regarding the term "tendencies," there are the tendencies of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-vāsanā*), as well as the tendencies of the *rajas-saṃkhyeya* [dharmas]. The Bodhisattva cultivates and studies the *rajas-saṃkhyeya* Dharma-gates to remedy his inferior wisdom.

Within each and every gate, he employs the contemplation of the Four Truths (*catur-ārya-satya*) to subdue the active afflictions (*kleśa*). Within each and every gate, he practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to permeate and transform the tendencies of view and thought.
Therefore, beneath the King of Trees (the Bodhi tree), through thirty-four moments of mind, one realizes the Four Noble Truths regarding dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Consequently, the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and the two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are simultaneously exhausted. Thus, one is able to bring both truths to ultimate perfection.

Only then does one differ from the disciples of the Two Vehicles, uniquely manifesting the Buddha-eye and Buddha-wisdom. [Supplement] Regarding the eight patiences and eight knowledges: by means of desire...

Within each of the four truths of the [desire] realm, there is one patience (*kṣānti*) and one knowledge (*jñāna*), namely, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and so forth.

Within each of the four truths of the two upper realms, there is likewise one patience and one knowledge, namely, the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), and so forth.

Taken together, these constitute the eight patiences and eight knowledges. As for "patience," it refers to untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-dhyāna-samādhi*); "knowledge" refers to untainted...

The wisdom that contemplates the outflows (*āsrava*) is as follows: within the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that severs delusions is called "patience" (*kṣānti*); this is the concentration inherent in wisdom.

Within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), the wisdom that contemplates and realizes the principle is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*); this is the wisdom inherent in concentration. When these patiences and knowledges are fully possessed, one severs the delusions of views and directly perceives the true reality;
therefore, it is said that within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) there are eight patiences and eight knowledges. This concludes the synthesis.

Regarding the accomplishment of thirty-four moments of mind: the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*jñāna*) of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are called the sixteen moments of mind.

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), categorized according to the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms, consists of one moment of non-obstruction (*anantarya*) and one moment of liberation (*vimukti*) for each stage, totaling eighteen moments of mind.

When the paths of seeing and cultivation are combined, they collectively constitute thirty-four moments of mind. This concentration and wisdom are both fundamentally and primordially possessed from beginningless time.

The manifest active states (*saṃskāra*) emerge from the seeds of outflows (*āsrava-bīja*). Through these active states, one is able to realize the true reality (*tattva*), the True Suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of self.
Therefore, it is said that "the thirty-four moments of mind that give rise to the true outflow-free state" occur.

The merit and wisdom cultivated over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), while the beginningless, natural outflow-free seeds serve as the immediate causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); thus, [realization] is attained.

It is sudden in its arousal, sudden in its severance, and sudden in its realization. Nevertheless, in terms of the categories of afflictions to be severed, it is divided into thirty-four moments of mind;
yet, in terms of that which severs and realizes, it consists solely of untainted concentration and wisdom. That which is realized is precisely the true suchness of the emptiness of self.

It is also called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). It is the unconditioned *tathatā* (suchness), which does not fall within the categories of numerical reckoning;
yet, because it possesses distinctions within its unconditioned nature, it is termed the "thirty-four minds. The *Mahā-śāstra* asks: "By attaining what merit is one named a Buddha?"
Answer: Because he has attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), he is called a Buddha.

Some say it is because he has attained the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇikadharma*), the three types of unhindered penetration (*trividha-pratisaṃvid*), and the three bases of mindfulness (*trīṇi smṛtyupasthānāni*). Regarding the three bases of mindfulness: first, receiving instruction with reverence yet feeling no elation;
second, receiving instruction without reverence yet feeling no sorrow; third, [remaining equanimous] whether instruction is received with reverence or without reverence.

The mind is without differentiation. Possessing great kindness and great compassion, one thoroughly knows the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all phenomena, both their general characteristics and their specific characteristics; therefore, one is called a Buddha.
△ Third, preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings.
Accepting the invitation of the Brahma King, he turned the Wheel of the Dharma three times and delivered those of the three root-natures.
[□ Note] Regarding "accepting the invitation of the Brahma King," the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states: In the past, there was a king who had two consorts. The first...
The first lady gave birth to one thousand sons. To test their sequence for attaining Buddhahood in the future, Śākyamuni drew lots and found himself fourth in order.
The second lady gave birth to two sons. The first son vowed to become a Brahmā King and requested his elder brother to be the master who turns the wheel of Dharma;
the younger vowed to become the Vajrapāṇi of Secret Footsteps to protect his elder brother’s teaching. (Text) The Brahmā King shall generally preside over one kalpa.
I request the Lord who turns the Wheel of Dharma to now turn it separately for those of lesser capacity.

[Commentary] The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: After the Tathāgata had attained the Way, Brahmā King exhorted him, saying, "I only pray that the Tathāgata will, for the sake of sentient beings, extensively open the gate of ambrosia and preach the unsurpassed Dharma. The Buddha said, "Brahmā King, all sentient beings..."
They are constantly shrouded and obstructed by afflictions, and thus are unable to receive my words of the True Dharma. The Brahma King spoke again:
"World-Honored One, all sentient beings generally fall into three categories: those of sharp faculties, those of middling faculties, and those of dull faculties."
"Those of sharp faculties are able to receive it; I pray that you will explain it for me. The Buddha said, "Brahmā King, I shall now open the gate of ambrosia for all sentient beings.

Thus, at Vārāṇasī, I turned the Wheel of the True Dharma. Guhyapada-vajra (Secret Trace Vajra) is so named because he secretly conceals [his nature] while manifesting externally, grasping the vajra-pestle.
It is not as the worldly tradition claims—that he is the Buddha Ruci. [Thus ends the] Sūtra."
Originally there was but one person. That there are now two images at the temple gate may be because the fulfillment of vows knows no fixed method;

thus, even if there are many, there is no fault. A certain master marked [the figures] as follows: first, Qingyu, with his hair and beard; second, Loutide. Bian’e said: [The text continues with the critique of these identifications.]
Having accepted the invitation of Brahmā, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* is not clear; it should be understood according to the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*.
[Note] Regarding the "three turnings of the wheel of Dharma," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "He turned the wheel of Dharma three times throughout the great trichiliocosm;

that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. (Text) As for the "wheel": because the Buddha’s realization of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths possesses the sense of being something that can be turned, it is called a "wheel."

The wheel. Furthermore, because it can destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called a wheel. As for the "three turnings": first, the turning of demonstration, which means "This is suffering," and so forth;
second, the turning of exhortation, which means "This is suffering; you should know it," and so forth; third, the turning of realization, which means "This is suffering;
I have known it, and shall not know it again," and so on, up to "This is the path; I have cultivated it, and shall not cultivate it again. (1)

First, there is the arising of the eye, knowledge, clarity, and awakening; through three turnings, this constitutes the Wheel of Dharma with twelve aspects, as explained in the text and its commentary in the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter (etc.).
[Commentary] This explains the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma. The first line indicates this;
it is the verse spoken by Ratnākara, the son of a householder, expressing joy in the Tathāgata’s pure gift of Dharma. It says: "The Wheel of Dharma is turned throughout the great trichiliocosm;
that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. That gods and humans attain the Way serves as its witness; thus the Three Jewels appear in the world. Next...
One line and a half. There are two meanings for the term *dharmacakra* (wheel of the Dharma). First is the meaning of "turning" (*pravartana*). As the *Wenju* states:

"To take the methods for transforming others from within the Buddha’s own mind and cause them to enter the minds of others is called turning the wheel of the Dharma. Second is the meaning of "crushing" (*mathana*). As the *Fuxing* says:

"By means of the wheel of the Four Truths, one delivers [the truth] to the minds of others, thereby crushing and grinding away their fetters and afflictions. Below this, the "three turnings" [are explained].
This clearly explains the three turnings of the Wheel of Dharma. Each section below concludes by establishing the benefit as the wheel.
As indicated in the *Wénjù* (Textual Commentary), the following provides a complete record of the explicit explanation. The *Wénjù* states:

"To turn this Dharma and cause it to enter the minds of others, enabling them to attain awakening and shatter the sixty-two views—this is what is called 'turning the Wheel of Dharma. All worldly phenomena do not transcend craving."
[The Buddha] saw that this present Wheel of Dharma is called "pure" because it transcends craving and views. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:

"The wheel possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of revolving; second, the meaning of crushing and grinding. By means of the Wheel of the Four Truths, one revolves to deliver others and crushes their fetters and delusions.
Just as the King’s Wheel-Treasure can both destroy and bring peace, so too does the Wheel of Dharma destroy the enemies of affliction and establish [beings in peace]."
Abiding in the principle of the Truths, he turns this Wheel of Dharma throughout the great trichiliocosm. This principle of the Four Truths is, in its essence, free from fetters and delusions;
thus it is called the "Fourfold Original Purity" (*prakṛti-vyavadāna*). Furthermore, because it is fundamentally inexpressible, it is termed "Original Purity.

It is only out of necessity, to destroy the delusions of others, that he turns [the wheel]. As for the term "to show," it means to demonstrate its characteristics. "To exhort" means to urge one toward cultivation. "To realize" means...
To cite oneself as proof for others regarding the twelve aspects of practice (*dvādaśākāra*) consists of: first, concerning the teaching (*deśanā*); second, concerning the practice (*pratipatti*).

The twelve aspects of the teaching refer to the demonstration, the exhortation, and the realization. The twelve aspects of practice refer to the arising of vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening through each of the three turnings.
The twelve teachings constitute the "turner," while the twelve practices constitute the "turned. These twelve practices are the wheel; the twelve teachings are not.
Regarding the wheel: if one explains it according to the meaning of two wheels, then with respect to the forty-eight factors, these four minds are expanded into sixteen moments of mind.

Taking the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) as "eye," the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) as "wisdom," the subsequent patience (*anvaya-kṣānti*) as "clarity," and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) as "awakening.
The same applies to the remaining three truths, each forming sixteen moments of mind. Individuals of the three faculties each attain [these].

The sixteen moments of mind constitute forty-eight modes of activity. The twelve truths are the wheel of teaching (*śāsana-cakra*), and the twelve modes of activity are the wheel of practice (*caryā-cakra*).
The wheel of teaching is able to turn the single, unique provisional wisdom; that which is turned by it consists of the twelve teachings.

The Wheel of Practice. There are twelve teachings that can turn it, and there are also twelve practices that are turned. These may apply to three types of persons collectively, or they may be considered individually.
Now, within the three paths, we focus specifically on the three types of persons within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

Those of sharp faculties, upon hearing the turning of the demonstration, immediately give rise to vision, knowledge, clarity, and awakening. Since these three types of persons are mentioned together, it is said that there are "twelve aspects of practice" (*dvādaśākāra*). [Record]

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "the twelve aspects" in the initial passage, each of the Four Truths employs [the functions of] showing and so forth as the teaching (*deśanā*), while each revolution gives rise to the eye and so forth as the practice (*pratipatti*).
As for the terms "agent" and "object": the fact that all four are spoken by the Buddha constitutes the agent; their being understood and entered into by the minds of others constitutes the object.
Regarding the statement "this is a wheel, not a non-wheel": a wheel (*cakra*) has the meaning of crushing and grinding; this applies only to the teaching, and not...
How could one possibly destroy delusions? If delusions are not destroyed, it cannot even be called a "wheel. The Buddha knows the capacities [of beings] and knows the timing;
thus, he does not turn the wheel in vain without practice. What is meant here by "not" is that the teaching follows the master of transformation, while the practice follows the recipient.

Therefore, the wheel of practice is obtained from the recipient, while the merit returns to the master of transformation; thus, it is obtained from the Buddha. Because the principle has not yet been fully exhausted, this is explained again:
if the two wheels of teaching and practice revolve in mutual succession, they together can destroy delusions; how much more so when both teaching and practice proceed from the Buddha?
Therefore, both teaching and practice are designated as "wheels. However, [the terms] "eye," "wisdom," and so forth do not [apply here].

Because they are distinct entities, [the text] again refers to patience (*kṣānti*) and so forth. Thus, the mental applications (*manasikāra*) regarding the eye and so forth, when categorized according to the teachings on the Truths (*satya*), become sixteen.

Therefore, for individuals possessing the three faculties (*indriya*), upon hearing the teaching of the three turnings, each gives rise to the eye and so forth, resulting in forty-eight [applications]. This is the distinction between the broad and the narrow.
Regarding the phrase "the wheel of teaching" (*dharmacakra*) and so forth: this is the wisdom for transforming others (*parārtha-jñāna*), which pertains solely to skillful means (*upāya*).

Consequently, that which is able to turn [the wheel] is singular, while that which is turned is twelvefold. Thus, the name of that which turns is narrow while its substance is broad; the name of that which is turned is broad while its substance is narrow. Regarding the "wheel of practice" (*pratipatti-cakra*):
the teaching is the signifier (*vācaka*), and practice is the signified (*vācya*). Therefore, because practice follows the benefit of the teaching, there are twelve types. Although both are...

Twelfth: While they differ in breadth and narrowness, the teaching is fixed at twelve [turns]. These give rise to the eye and so forth. If one were to demonstrate them as equal, they would give rise to the eye and so forth;
thus, while the number is the same, the names differ. Next, in distinguishing between the general and the specific, the word "or" (*vā*) is used as an indefinite term.
It means that either three people each hear three turns, or one person hears the three [turns] sequentially. Although they were initially distinguished separately, [the meaning remains as stated].

Now, following the preceding section, we provide the formal explanation. Regarding the first turning of the Wheel of Dharma, those of the three vehicles who attain the realization of the Truths (dṛṣṭi-prativedha) then possess these twelve [faculties].

[Supplement] In the desire realm, the direct objects of perception are termed "vision" (cakṣus) and "knowledge" (jñāna); in the higher realms, they are inferred through analogy and termed "clarity" (vidyā) and "awakening" (buddhi). This is because clarity arises dependent on vision, and awakening arises dependent on knowledge.
Just as one has clarity by means of the eye, so too does one have awakening by means of knowledge.
[Commentary] Regarding the three types of root-capacities: the *Wenju* (7.17) states, "For the Śrāvakas, there are three turnings; for the Pratyekabuddhas, there are two turnings."
It is turned once for the bodhisattvas. Why is this so? It is because of the sharpness or dullness of their faculties; this is merely a general statement.

In principle, it is said that all [turnings] consist of three revolutions. This is the dharma-speech of the Buddhas; the dharma reaches up to three [turnings] because sentient beings possess three types of faculties (text).
[Commentary] The commentary states: Regarding the statement that there are three faculties among sentient beings, these three exist inherently within the Śrāvaka vehicle;
therefore, their realizations at the Deer Park differed. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* also speak of these three faculties:

those of superior faculty attained realization upon hearing the first turning of the wheel, while those of middling and inferior faculties may be inferred accordingly. The *Wenju* (Textual Explanations) asks: "If he initially taught the five bhikṣus, how can they be categorized as having three faculties? Furthermore...
There are eighty thousand devas. For what reason do they lack the three faculties? It is for the sake of generating the three types of wisdom, the three faculties, and the three paths.

The commentary explains: Regarding the question "Why, at the beginning, [is it] equal?"—since it is said that *śrāvakas* themselves possess the three faculties, and the five persons are all of the *śrāvaka* faculty-nature, and thus already possess the three faculties, what is the intention behind the fact that the various devas lack these three? It is for the sake of generating...

[The Master] replied: "Humans and devas alike share three meanings, namely: wisdom (*prajñā*), faculties (*indriya*), and the path (*mārga*). These correspond respectively to the differences in the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation;

the sequence of awakening, which constitutes the three faculties; and the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, which constitute the three paths. This also includes the attainments of cessation in the realms of form and formlessness."
In principle, there are also [other cases], but they do not attain it through the Wheel of Dharma.
△ Fourth, the entry into extinction upon the exhaustion of conditions:
Having remained in the world for eighty years, manifesting the appearance of an aged bhikṣu, when the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, he enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the fruit of Buddhahood according to the Tripiṭaka.
[Commentary] He dwelt in the world for eighty years. The *Guangju* (Volume 21) states: "The lifespan of the world has three grades: the lower grade is forty years; the middle grade is eighty years;
and the upper grade is one hundred and twenty years. In the lower grade, there is premature death; in the upper grade, one is excessively old; and the middle grade is [the ideal]."
Neither old nor young, he manifests permanence; furthermore, he is "central" (fang), which signifies the Middle Way.
Because the Buddha delights in the Middle Way for this reason, he remains for eighty years (text).
[Commentary] "Below" refers to the "lower grade. This explains that [the Buddha] dwelt in the world for eighty years. The first line clarifies that there are three grades of lifespan;
the following two lines clarify that the Buddha adopted a middle-grade lifespan. Generally speaking, the lifespan manifested by various Buddhas is indefinite as to its length or brevity.
As stated in the seventh fascicle of the *Buddhanāmasūtra*: "The lifespan of the Buddha Brahmaghoṣa was one billion years; the Buddha Candrānana..."
The cultivation of the life-span lasts for one day and one night. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that the Buddha Susīma appeared in the morning and became silent by evening;
whereas the lifespan of Amitābha is immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, yet the lifespan of our Śākyamuni Tathāgata does not exceed a hundred years.
Nevertheless, as the World-Honored One is a human being, his lifespan should have been a full hundred years; as for why it is not so now—
As for his dissatisfaction: it was in order to set aside twenty years of his merit to protect the disciples of the Final Dharma.

As stated in the tenth fascicle of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, "Moon Store" (*Candragarbha-parivarta*): "He relinquished his lifespan out of compassion for sentient beings. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* states: "He saw their arrogance and self-indulgence."
He manifested the trace of entering nirvana, leaving behind his remaining merit and teachings to rescue those in peril and suffering. Thus,

the World-Honored One’s manifestation over eighty years not only demonstrated the abiding in the Middle Way and the Heaven of the Supreme Ultimate Meaning, but also left behind blessings to protect the disciples of the Final Dharma.
[Note] Regarding "the elderly bhikṣu," the *Miaole* (vol. 1, p. 24) states: "The 'elderly bhikṣu' is so called because he is distinct from those who follow [him]" (text).
[Commentary] Each of the four teachings has its own physical form. The *Tripiṭaka* (Śrāvaka) teaching features a body sixteen feet tall, which differs from the latter three;
thus, the term "old" is used to distinguish it. The *Āgama* states: "When the Buddha was approaching nirvana, he appeared like an old bhikṣu and went to the house of Cunda.

[Supplement] Regarding the differences mentioned later: the *Shared Teaching* (Tongjiao) manifests in the form of a bhikṣu, whereas the *Distinct Teaching* (Biejiao) manifests as the *Vaiśvāsika* (Exalted) body.
The term "old" is used here for the purpose of discernment.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished": the Buddha’s body is called the fuel, and his wisdom is called the fire. When the body ceases and wisdom perishes, it is termed *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana without remainder).
In the Mahayana, it is said that once the fuel of the sentient beings' capacities (*indriya*) is exhausted, the responding fire likewise perishes.

[Commentary] The Buddha entered the *tejo-dhātu-samādhi* (fire-element samādhi) at the city of Kuśinagara, incinerating his body to enter *parinirvāṇa*, leaving behind only the *śarīra* (relics) as a field of merit for humans and devas.
Although both body and wisdom have ceased, this is the mark of *nirupadhi-śeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvana without remainder) according to the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
As for the Great Vehicle (*Mahāyāna*), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra Commentary* states: "The Buddha appears in the world when moved by four conditions."
When the four capacities for instruction have ceased, the Buddha then proclaims his extinction.
△ Third, concluding by returning to the Tripitaka Teaching:
