Although the three types of persons explained above differ in their cultivation of practice and realization of the fruit, they are alike in severing the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa), and alike...
They emerge from the triple world and equally realize the limited truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*); they have traveled only three hundred *yojanas* and entered the "transformed city" (*nirmita-pura*).

This concludes the brief explanation of the Tripitaka Teachings (*zàngjiào*). [Note] The *Miaoxuan* (1.5) states: "The three causes are greatly different; the three fruits are slightly the same. (Text). The *Shiqian* (1.15) states: [same as above].

The truths (*satya*), conditions (*pratyaya*), and perfections (*pāramitā*) differ; therefore, the causes are greatly distinct. Both sever the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), yet there is a slight difference among the three vehicles; thus, their fruits are largely the same.

[Text] [Commentary] Śrāvakas sever the afflictions of views and thought sequentially, one after the other. Pratyekabuddhas sever the afflictions of views and thought all at once, yet their residual habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted.
Because the Bodhisattvas have exhausted both their correct practice and their residual habits, the fruits they realize are largely the same.

[Note] This is because it is explained from the perspective of the partial truth in contrast to the Great [Vehicle]. Regarding the "three hundred yojanas," the *Wenju* (7.27) clarifies this through three meanings.
1. In terms of the locus of birth and death, the resultant states of the three realms are taken as the three hundred. 2. In terms of afflictions, namely view-delusion and thought-delusion.
3. In terms of contemplative wisdom, namely the contemplation of emptiness.

[Commentary] The *Wenju* states: "The realms of retribution within the triple world constitute three hundred; the remaining lands constitute four hundred; the land of true retribution constitutes five hundred.
The delusions of view constitute one hundred; the five lower fetters constitute two hundred; the five upper fetters constitute three hundred;
the delusions as numerous as dust motes constitute four hundred; and ignorance constitutes five hundred. One is able to enter the contemplation of emptiness [through these]."
Passing three hundred [yojanas], one provisionally contemplates; passing four hundred, one enters middle contemplation;

and passing five hundred, one realizes that the Hīnayāna teachings, when compared to the Middle Way of the Mahāyāna, are five hundred yojanas away—yet they speak of only three hundred. [Supplement] To sever the fetters (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm constitutes one hundred;
to sever the fetters of the form realm constitutes two hundred; and to sever the fetters of the formless realm constitutes three hundred.
[Note] *Yojana* is the same as *yojana*. This is translated here as "measured limit" (*xiàngliáng*). It is like a postal station in this region.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that there are three distinctions of *yojana*: the large is eighty *li*, the medium is sixty *li*, and the small is forty *li* (text).
[Commentary] This explains the measurement of the *yojana*. The first two lines clarify the Sanskrit name for "flower" (*puṣpa*). The next line provides a comparison.

The lower section of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites scriptural evidence to elucidate the specific measurements, noting that there are differences between large, medium, and small units. This concludes the brief explanation of the Tripitaka teachings.

△ Second, the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). Part one: the heading. Part two:
the explanation of the Shared Teaching.

[Commentary] The *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 1, part 2, states: "This teaching clarifies that causes and conditions are themselves emptiness, the principle of the four noble truths of non-arising.

It is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna (for it leads far to the permanent abiding). It is primarily for Bodhisattvas, while secondarily extending to the two vehicles (as it accommodates all capacities).
Therefore, among the various Mahāyāna Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā scriptures, those who attain the Way through the two vehicles do so because they have equally received this [teaching]."
"Teaching" (the Universal Section).

[Commentary] This explains the meaning of what is universally taught by the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). As it is said: "Of those dharmas arisen through causes and conditions, I say they are empty."
Its essence is non-arising, yet it universally penetrates the principles of both the "exclusive" and "inclusive" [teachings]; this is the far-reaching penetration of this teaching.
As for the distinction between Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles as being "lateral" and "primary," these are the capacities to whom this teaching is addressed.

This teaching primarily intends for Bodhisattvas to study Prajñā until reaching the stage of Buddhahood; while it far-reachingly penetrates the *Bie* (Separate) and *Yuan* (Perfect) [vehicles], there are also Pratyekabuddhas who have already completed their task.

Because it addresses the capacities of those of the Two Vehicles, it is called "ancillary. As for the Vaipulya Prajñāpāramitā, there are those of the Two Vehicles who receive its teachings and attain the Way;
this refers to the section of the teaching that is accessible to them. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Those who wish to attain the Śrāvaka vehicle should study Prajñā;
those who wish to attain the Pratyekabuddha vehicle should study Prajñā; those who wish to attain the Bodhisattva vehicle should study Prajñā."

As it is said, "The three vehicles equally receive the *prajñā* [teachings]"; this refers to the categories through which this teaching is transmitted. Some masters designate them as follows: the *Avataṃsaka* is unique;
the *Āgama* belongs exclusively to the *piṭaka*; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is the revelation and manifestation; and only the Vaipulya and *Prajñā* are common to all.
Jieyi said: "The 'causes and conditions are empty' phrase is a reflection of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The 'unborn Four Noble Truths' phrase is a reflection of the *Mahāyāna sūtras*.
All four teachings first present this fundamental principle."
[Note] Question: Why is it not called "Shared Teaching" (sādhāraṇa-deśanā)? Answer: The name "Shared" applies only to the proximate stage of the Two Vehicles, but not to the remote stage.

If one establishes the general term [“Shared”], it is convenient for both the remote and the proximate. To say it is "convenient for the remote" means it encompasses both the Separate (pratyekabuddha) and the Perfect (yuan).
[Commentary] This is also from the *Fourfold Teaching* (*Sishijiao yi*). It provides a detailed analysis of the reasons for establishing the name "Shared Teaching" (*Tongjiao*).
In the question, it is asked why the name "Shared" (*Gong*) is not established, given that this teaching is studied in common by the three vehicles.

In the answer, it first clarifies that establishing the name "Shared" is inappropriate, and subsequently clarifies that establishing the name "Shared" (*Tong*) is appropriate for both [the Mahayana and Hinayana].
△ Second, the explanation of the four [teachings] has four parts. First, the explanation of the name has two parts. First, the mutual interpenetration of preceding and succeeding [stages]:

because it is common to the preceding *pitaka* teachings and common to the subsequent *Pratyekabuddha* and *Vimalakīrti* (Distinct and Perfect) teachings, it is called the "Common Teaching" (*Tongjiao*).
[Note] This refers back to what preceded and forward to what follows; it explains the name of the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao) specifically from the perspective of the Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary] This indicates the establishment of the name "Shared Teaching. It is established by taking the Bodhisattvas alone as the primary focus, because they connect with what precedes and also connect with what follows.
Although the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) possess the sense of connecting with what precedes, they do not connect with what follows, and thus [the name would] have no basis [for them].
[As for] "expectation" (*mōng*): therefore, it cannot be said that [the teaching] universally applies to what precedes it.
[Note]: The *Shiqian*, fascicle 9 (20), states: "Universally applying to the near is the same as the Tripiṭaka; universally applying to the distant is like the Separate Teaching."

[Supplement] However, since the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) universally reaches back to the Constant Abiding [of the Buddha], it should be said that the Shared reaches as far as the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Yet, the present commentary (*Shuji*) states, "as in the Distinct Teaching" (*biejiao*), because the Path of Realization (*zhengdao*) of the Distinct Teaching is identical to the Perfect, and their essence is the same.

Some masters mark this by stating that the Shared Teaching includes the preceding three vehicles along with the Tripitaka; why, then, is the name also explained from the perspective of the Bodhisattva? The answer is: it specifically refers to the Buddha of that particular teaching.

Furthermore, according to the Tripiṭaka, the Buddha returns to the state of annihilation in ashes. Yet, how could this Buddha be one accomplished by the Two Vehicles? Therefore, it is explained from the perspective of the Bodhisattva.

[Commentary] Regarding the two phrases on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness, there are three ways in which they are "comprehensive" (tong): first, they are comprehensive in both cause and fruit; being comprehensive within their own specific teaching is one such case. Second...

To have penetration as the cause but not penetration as the fruit refers to those who are "received" [into the path]. Regarding the three types—distinct, general, and perfect—this refers to those who rely on penetration to guide others;
that is, using the distinct and perfect [teachings] as skillful means, they become individuals who achieve the causes and fruits of the distinct and perfect stages.
These three meanings of "thorough" (tong) apply exclusively to Bodhisattvas.
[Commentary] This citation explains the reason why this name is established solely with respect to Bodhisattvas. As it says in the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catur-smṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*):

There are eight general meanings: namely, teaching, principle, wisdom, severance, practice, stage, cause, and fruit. "Teaching" refers to the shared reception of the discourse on non-arising (*anutpāda*).
"Principle" refers to the shared contemplation that form itself is emptiness (*rūpaṃ eva śūnyatā*). "Wisdom" refers to the arising of *prajñā* through the non-arising of all phenomena.
Regarding "severance": whether it be the severance of a *srotāpanna* or that of others, they are equally identical to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Regarding "practice": they equally ride the Mahāyāna vehicle. Regarding "stages": they equally occupy the stages from the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) up to the Buddha-stage.

Regarding "cause": they equally study the *prajñā-pāramitā*. Regarding "fruit": they equally reach the ocean of *sarvajñatā*. Because these three persons and eight meanings are not distinct, they are so named.
It is "penetration" (*tong*). Furthermore, there are three meanings of penetration: First, that both cause and effect are penetrating:

as in the aforementioned eight meanings, this refers to the near-penetration of the partial truth (*pratyekabuddha*), which is the fourfold "withered" and clumsy means of deliverance. Second, that the cause is penetrating while the fruit is not:

this refers to the distinct fruit (*vyutkrāntaka*) coming to connect with the penetrating cause, whereby one attains the vision of Buddha-nature and achieves the fourfold "flourishing" at the twin trees. Third, that the distinct and the common penetrate the perfect: the distinct...
The Perfect (Vyūha) cause and fruit both differ from the Shared (Sādhāraṇa). By relying on the Shared to provide guidance and opening, one attains entry into the Distinct (Vaiśeṣika) and the Perfect.

Thus, the causal stage achieves a fruit that is neither withered nor flourishing—the fruit of the twin trees. However, the meaning of the three types of penetration (*samantamukha*) is discussed solely in relation to the Bodhisattva.

[Supplement] For example, although the single principle of the Shared applies to both cause and fruit, it should also apply to the Two Vehicles; yet, the reason it pertains only to the Bodhisattva is that the Two Vehicles...
Although the first of the aforementioned meanings exists, the latter two meanings are absent; therefore, it does not even receive the names of "cause" and "effect.

[Note] Regarding the current text’s inclusion of the subsequent Distinct and Complete Teachings, this will be explained below. Although it is only applied to those who are "received" [into the higher stages], its intent also encompasses [the other teachings].
"Relying on the Shared [Teaching] for guidance.

[Commentary: This is because those with the capacities of the Shared Teaching are diverse. If they are to be received by the Distinct or Complete Teachings and transformed into persons of the Distinct or Complete Vehicles, they must necessarily rely on the Shared Teaching for guidance.
Although those of the Shared Teaching may be received by the Distinct or Complete Teachings, the Distinct and Complete themselves also rely upon the Shared.
The teaching was intended to provide preliminary guidance; thus, it is truly for this reason that the *Sūtra of General Penetration* serves as the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.
Regarding what is meant by "relying on general penetration for guidance," the *Shiyiji* (Record of Supplementary Omissions) states:

"Within the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and the stage of Nature (*dharmatā-bhūmi*), one hears that the essence of phenomena is empty—not only is the twenty-five realms of existence empty, but even Nirvāṇa itself is empty. This person...
One must rely on the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) to discuss emptiness and guide the mind; yet, one realizes that the essence of this emptiness is the Middle Way.

Thereupon, through the contemplations of the outer and inner ordinary beings of the Distinct and Complete Teachings, which are identical to those of the Two Vehicles, one passes through the Stage of Dry Wisdom and all subsequent stages up to the tenth stage.
Thus, one becomes a Buddha of the eight aspects at the first stage or the first dwelling of the Distinct and Complete Teachings. This is the Shared [Teaching].

This explains the meaning of the provisional, distinct, and perfect teachings. Thus, one should know that although the subsequent passage mentions those who are to be "received and transformed," its intent must necessarily encompass those who rely on the provisional teachings for guidance.
△ Second, the teaching by which they receive their name.

Furthermore, they receive their name from the teaching they are to follow. That is to say, these three types of persons equally enter into emptiness through the body of the Dharma (dharmakāya) by means of the path of non-verbalization; therefore, it is called the Shared Teaching (Pāryāyika-yāna).

[Note] This section explains the name "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao) by way of the three vehicles. In the Tripiṭaka [Teaching], the three vehicles are distinguished based on the three categories of the Truths, the Conditions, and the Perfections.

In the present Shared Teaching, however, the three vehicles are identical in that they all contemplate the four truths as non-arising, equally realize the entry into emptiness through the provisional nature of phenomena, contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination, and equally contemplate the six pāramitās to perceive the ultimate truth (paramārtha). As for what distinguishes the three vehicles from one another, it is merely...

The wisdoms of general characteristics and specific characteristics sever the fetters and attenuate the habitual tendencies; they differ only in their capacity for self-cultivation and the transformation of others.
Such verbal explanations are themselves empty and thus non-existent.

[Commentary] The three individuals all share the same path of wordless discourse. Regarding the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings), there is a detailed explanation in the *Sìjiàoyì Wèn* (Questions on the Meaning of the Four Teachings).

[Question: While it is appropriate for Bodhisattvas to cultivate the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), how can the followers of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) likewise contemplate and cultivate the six perfections?
[Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Adornment through merit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and tainted (*sāsrava*); this is the Dharma of the Śrāvakas. How...
Are there among the śrāvakas those who possess stinginess and greed? Or among arhats and pratyekabuddhas those who break the precepts, harbor anger, are negligent, distracted, or deluded?
It is only that the followers of the two vehicles are unable to universally carry out these deeds to bring sentient beings to maturity;
for when have they not likewise cultivated the six perfections, the ultimate truth, and the path of ineffable speech to sever their fetters? As for what is currently...

Regarding the distinction between the three vehicles: the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states that the three vehicles equally uphold the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), equally perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha-satya*), equally sever the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the triple world, and equally attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). They equally seek the nirvana with remainder and without remainder.

Since these meanings are identical, what distinguishes the three vehicles? It is that the Śrāvaka enters emptiness by means of the "total-characteristic realization of dharmas" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-dharma-bhāva-praveśa*).
The power of their wisdom is weak; they merely sever the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*). Because their root dispositions differ, there are also two kinds of liberation:

those accompanied by wisdom and those accompanied by both [wisdom and concentration], as distinguished in the previous Tripiṭaka teachings. Pratyekabuddhas possess merit and sharp faculties; they are able to slightly discern characteristics and enter emptiness by realizing the nature of phenomena.
They are born in a world where no Buddha exists and do not rely on hearing the Dharma. When the time arrives and the path matures, they attain it spontaneously.

To awaken to and perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), to sever all fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms, and to eliminate even the residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)—this is called the Pratyekabuddhayāna.
Because their root dispositions (*indriya-gotra*) differ, there are also two types: first, the *kṣudra-pratyekabuddha*;

second, the *mahā-pratyekabuddha*, as already explained previously. As for the Bodhisattva, they fully cultivate both the general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Wisdom realizes that the essence of causes and conditions is emptiness. It gives rise to the vow of great compassion to cultivate all practices and perceive the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It severs the afflictions within the realms and, supported by its vows, returns to birth within the three realms to employ the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*).
He sports with supernatural powers, purifies Buddha-fields, and brings sentient beings to maturity.

When the roots of goodness of the three vehicles have fully ripened, he immediately sits at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and, by means of the wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment, severs the habitual tendencies of afflictions entirely and attains all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).

He is named Buddha because he turns the two kinds of Dharma wheels—those of arising-and-ceasing and non-arising—and transforms sentient beings of the three vehicles so that they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

This is the Mahāyāna. Thus, one should know that the distinction between the three vehicles is made merely by way of their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), equalizing wisdom (*samatā-jñāna*), severing of fetters (*saṃyojana-prahāṇa*), subduing of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), self-cultivation (*svārtha*), and transformation of others (*parārtha*), due to differences in their faculties and natures (*indriya-gotra*).

Furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* states: "In the Śrāvakas of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), through the single gate of universal characteristics (*sōngxiàng*), they realize that the conventional is identical to the ultimate.
The Pratyekabuddhas are able, within the single gate of both universal and particular characteristics, to realize that the conventional is identical to the ultimate.

The Bodhisattvas are able, within all four gates of universal and particular characteristics, to realize that the conventional is identical to the ultimate; furthermore, they can universally emerge from the four gates into the provisional (*chujia*) to teach and transform sentient beings. The *Shiqian* says:

Regarding the general and specific characteristics of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas within a single gate: "General" refers to merely practicing the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
"Specific" refers to contemplating the seven branches of suffering and the five branches of its origin, because they rely on only one gate due to their practice for their own sake.

However, because Bodhisattvas act for the sake of transforming others, they rely on all four gates; yet, prior to the seventh stage, even from the perspective of their own practice, they likewise rely on only one.

This refers to the gate of entering the provisional through skillful means, which must also be practiced universally; this is precisely the intended meaning. Regarding what is called the wisdom of the general and specific characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa* and *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the Sūtra states:
"First, one uses the wisdom that discriminates all phenomena; subsequently, one employs the wisdom of *nirvāṇa* to discriminate all phenomena.

Here, the discrimination of all phenomena constitutes the specific characteristics, while the wisdom of *nirvāṇa* constitutes the general characteristic. Thus, the three types of persons [the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and bodhisattva] act according to their respective capacities.
[Application]. The final two phrases explain the path of wordless discourse.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Vol. 6, Part 1, Section 16) states: "The person of comprehensive realization has already observed that all phenomena are like illusions; since the illusion is fundamentally unarisen, there is now nothing to be extinguished.

This is termed the 'essence' (*tǐ*). [Text] This means that the essence of the six classes of ordinary beings—their physical bodies and their environments—is like an illusion and like a transformation."
The very substance is emptiness; thus one enters the True Principle.

[Commentary] Regarding "the substance of form entering emptiness," the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings) states: "Now, concerning the Four Truths of Non-arising (*anutpāda*), one who believes in the Truth of Suffering of Non-arising believes that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) do not arise.
They are like dreams, illusions, echoes, transformations, the moon in water, and reflections in a mirror."

Ultimately empty and non-existent. Understanding that suffering is without suffering, one is not afflicted by suffering; yet there is the True Dharma. There is no arising or accumulation [of suffering].
One realizes that all afflictions, karma, and volitional formations are like dreams and illusions—empty and non-existent, lacking the characteristic of combination.
Knowing them to be non-existent, one does not circulate through the flow of fetters and karma. Understanding that accumulation is without accumulation, yet there is...
The True Meaning: Regarding "no arising or ceasing," it means knowing that all phenomena of arising and ceasing are unattainable.
Even if there were a phenomenon that surpassed nirvāṇa, it would still be like a dream or an illusion; fundamentally it has never arisen, and now it likewise does not cease.

If one does not know this non-arising and non-ceasing, arising and ceasing will ultimately never cease of themselves. If one knows non-arising and non-ceasing, arising and ceasing cease of themselves.

It is extinguished, yet there is the True Dharma. As for those who cultivate the path of non-arising, they believe that all paths leading to nirvana are like dreams and illusions, devoid of dualistic characteristics.
If one perceives duality—distinguishing between what is permeable and what is not—then obstruction arises.
If one knows non-duality, one does not perceive permeability or obstruction; things proceed spontaneously and with unimpeded openness, entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). This is then...
Knowing this, there are the True Realities (*satya*). This concludes the section on the establishment of names according to the specific teaching.

From the stage of Thinness onward, one learns the playful exercise of supernatural powers and extensively cultivates the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness.

"detachment from desire" refers to the sixth stage, where the nine categories of afflictions of the realm of desire are abandoned; and "having accomplished" refers to the seventh stage, where the [afflictions] of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) are abandoned.

The volitions of the formless realm are exhausted. For a Pratyekabuddha, this occurs from the eighth stage through the tenth stage as they sever the habitual tendencies of ignorance. *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) asks:
"Regarding the correspondence between the first through seventh stages and their respective fruits, which sūtras or śāstras provide this? Answer: It is not that sūtras and śāstras do not correspond;

rather, there are differences in their levels of depth, and thus teachers have differing interpretations. Some use the stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*) to correspond only to the first stage, as for example...

Regarding what is currently used [in various systems]: some take the first three stages and combine them with the first stage; the *Renwang jing* clarifies four stages and likewise combines them with the first stage.

This is difficult to determine definitively. However, the "stage of seeing" (*darśana-bhūmi*) in the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) is fundamentally the path of uninterrupted realization (*anantarya-mārga*).

Since one does not emerge from contemplation to realize the fruit of *srotāpanna*, how could it be that the first stage alone severs the delusions of view? Or perhaps even up to the third or fourth stage?
Is it so? If one speaks of severing specific delusions that are not shared with the Two Vehicles, this principle does exist.
Furthermore, some say that the severance of fetters up to the sixth stage is equal to that of an Arhat, while others say it is the seventh stage. These are fixed attachments.

Regarding the two fruits mentioned above and below, both the sutras and treatises state they are indeterminate; the intermediate stages can be understood through reasoning. Now, following this reasoning, one must not hold fixed attachments. [Appendix]

Citation from the *Fourfold Teachings* (*Sijiaoyi*). [Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*); in the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, it is the Patience of Subjugation (*vinaya-kṣānti*).

In the Śrāvakas, it is the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*); in the Bodhisattvas, it is the Patience of Accordance (*anuloma-kṣānti*). In the Śrāvakas, it is the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*)."

The Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) corresponds to the Śrāvaka’s stage of insight (*darśana-bhūmi*). The Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena also corresponds to the Śrāvaka’s stage of refinement (*tanu-bhūmi*).

The Bodhisattva’s playful mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*) corresponds to the Śrāvaka’s stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*). What is called the Bodhisattva’s stage of purity through freedom from desire corresponds to the Arhat stage;
within the Śrāvaka teachings, this is precisely the Buddha stage. Thus, in the Tripiṭaka, the Buddha [is described as] thirty-four...

When the mind gives rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava*), and the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the three realms are completely severed, one is equal to an Arhat. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to an Arhat is the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*);

even whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a Pratyekabuddha is the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena. This corresponds to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) of the bodhisattva, wherein habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are eroded and eliminated.
Regarding "qi" (spiritual energy): passing nine times beyond the stage of the Pratyekabuddha and entering the rank of a Bodhisattva refers precisely to the ninth and tenth stages (*bhūmi*).

One should know that a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is equivalent to a Buddha. The *Xuánwén* states: "Initially, within the common rank shared by the three vehicles, the name 'patience' (*kṣānti*) is established specifically for the Bodhisattva;

yet its meaning extends to both [the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha]. Using the terminology of the Separate Teaching (*bīejiao*), the name is distinct while the meaning is pervasive. Thus, it is pervasive.

The meaning has already been explained as before. Regarding the separate establishment [of these stages]: this refers to the separate designation of the names "patience of submission" (*kṣānti-avaivartika*), "patience of compliance" (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), and "patience of non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) specifically for Bodhisattvas.

Although the three types of persons on the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) equally suppress the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*), the Bodhisattva is further granted the name "patience of submission" because he believes that dependent origination is itself emptiness and has descended into the Four Noble Truths of non-arising.
He subdues his mind and gives rise to the four great vows. Although he knows that sentient beings are like empty space, he resolves to deliver all sentient beings.
Thus, when a bodhisattva wishes to deliver sentient beings, it is as if he wished to deliver empty space.
Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: "A bodhisattva thus subdues his mind, which is to say, he brings immeasurable sentient beings to parinirvāṇa."
In truth, there are no sentient beings who attain parinirvāṇa. The subsequent three vows to subdue the mind are likewise.

This constitutes the stage of the Bodhisattva on the Ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*). When practicing the contemplation of the distinct and general characteristics of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) while stabilizing the mind, this differs from that of the Two Vehicles;
therefore, it is specifically termed "subduing patience" (*kṣānti*). Furthermore, the persons of the Three Vehicles equally give rise to the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) five [faculties].
The aggregates (skandhas) give rise to similar conceptualizations; all these subdue the delusions of view and accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha).

Yet, it is the Bodhisattva alone who receives the name "Patience of Accordance" (anulomikī-kṣānti), because the Bodhisattva not only subdues the fetters and accords with principle, but is also able to act for the sake of all sentient beings.
Subduing the mind, they practice the six perfections universally. In all matters, they bring both merit and wisdom to ultimate completion.

Just as the *piṭaka* bodhisattvas practiced the six perfections throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* during the stage of "patience toward the middle" (*madhyā-kṣānti*), not sparing even their own bodies or lives, so too does this present bodhisattva.
By means of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they subdue the sense faculties; for the sake of sentient beings, they fulfill the six [perfections].

Because it transcends [them], it is called "compliant patience" (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*). Furthermore, although practitioners of the three vehicles equally give rise to true outflow-free wisdom and abandonment, which are both termed "non-arising," the Bodhisattva alone receives the name "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

This is because, upon seeing the principle of the truths and severing the fetters and proclivities, he does not give rise to a mind that seeks to grasp or realize them; therefore, he specifically receives the name "patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas."
This is merely a name. Why is this so? If one gives rise to a mind that seeks realization, one immediately falls to the level of the Two Vehicles and cannot enter the ninth stage of a Bodhisattva;
thus, there is a profound reason for establishing the specific name "Patience" (kṣānti).

Furthermore, while those of the Three Vehicles equally attain supernormal powers (abhijñā), those of the Two Vehicles cannot employ these powers to bring sentient beings to fulfillment or purify [the realms].

Because they have not yet attained a Buddha-land, they do not receive the name of "sporting. Although an Anāgāmin has severed the five lower fetters, he cannot relinquish his profound meditative concentrations;
thus, he returns to be born in the desire realm to harmonize with others and benefit sentient beings, yet he does not mingle with worldly dust.
Therefore, they do not attain the name of "purity through detachment from desire. Question:

Since the wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*) of those in the three vehicles are equal, why is it that for the two vehicles these are termed "wisdom and abandonment," while for the Bodhisattvas they are termed "Dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*)? Answer: Patience (*kṣānti*) is the cause; wisdom (*jñāna*) is the fruit.

Thus, the fifteen moments of mind are termed patience, and the sixteenth moment of mind is termed wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the realization attained by the two vehicles, it is appropriate to judge them thus.
Regarding "wisdom and abandonment": although a Bodhisattva looks toward the Buddha, they still abide in the stage of a cause and thus receive only the name of "patience" (kṣānti).

Furthermore, when a single grade of a Bodhisattva’s volitional thought is exhausted, a corresponding portion of mastery arises; thus, with each grade there is death and with each grade there is birth.
Because they are able to endure the toil and suffering of such birth and death without entering nirvāṇa, it is called "patience."

[Supplementary Note] This brief commentary originally followed the phrase "the stage of dry wisdom" (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) in the ritual text. Because the main commentary is extensive, it was not convenient to provide an explanation there;

Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*’s explanation of the first stage as "burning the wick," the *Gambhīra-parivarta* (Deep and Profound Chapter) states: Subhūti addressed [the Buddha], saying...
The Buddha said: "World-Honored One, does a bodhisattva attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment by means of the initial mind, or by means of the subsequent mind?

World-Honored One, since these mental states and mental factors do not coexist in this way, how can roots of goodness increase? If the roots of goodness do not increase, how could one [attain enlightenment]?"
[They] attain enlightenment. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "For example, when a lamp is lit, is the wick consumed by the initial flame, or is it consumed by the final flame?
Subhūti replied: "World-Honored One, the wick is not consumed by the initial flame, nor is it apart from the initial flame;
it is not consumed by the final flame, nor is it apart from the final flame. The Buddha said to Subhūti: "What do you think?"
"How is it? Is the wick burned? "World-Honored One, the wick is indeed burned. The Buddha told Subhūti:
"In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not attain awakening by means of the initial mind, yet he is not separate from the initial mind;
he does not attain awakening by means of the final mind, yet he is not separate from the final mind. From the moment a bodhisattva first resolves his mind, he practices the *prajñāpāramitā*..."

Esoteric. [The Buddha] was fully endowed with the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "The lamp" is a metaphor for the bodhisattva path;
"the wick" symbolizes ignorance and afflictions (*kleśa*); and "the flame" represents the wisdom associated with the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Even up to the wisdom associated with the Vajra-samādhi, which burns away the wick of afflictions such as ignorance—this occurs neither by the flame of the initial wisdom nor by the flame of the final wisdom; yet, the wick of afflictions such as ignorance is completely consumed.

One attains unsurpassed *bodhi*. This is thus an explanation of the sūtra by means of the śāstra; it is thereby known that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies the meaning of the wick being consumed at the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Regarding the "first flame" in three locations as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: the *Catuḥsmṛtyupasthāna* states that the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, in its commentary on the "Chapter on the Lamp Wick," says:
"Some say that dry wisdom (*śuklavidarśana*) is the first flame, and the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*) is the final flame. There is...

To say that the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) is the initial flame and the Buddha-ground (*buddha-bhūmi*) is the final flame—such differing explanations likely stem from various Mahāyāna masters interpreting the gateway of the *pūrṇa-akṣara* (complete letter) teachings.

Since the names and stages of the three teachings differ, each took this meaning to explain the initial and final flames. If it is said that the second ground is the path of abandonment for Bodhisattvas, this...
Taking the stage of nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*) as the path of abandonment, one becomes equal to an Arhat upon reaching the sixth stage;

alternatively, taking the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) as the path of abandonment, one uses these three stages as the path of abandonment, becoming equal to an Arhat at the seventh stage.

Now, not taking the second or third stages, but rather taking the stage of dry wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*), we know that this marks the beginning for all three types of persons, serving as a semblance-path (*pratirūpa-mārga*).
First, regarding "Flame-Ear" (Jvalanāśrotra): some say that "joy" constitutes the initial flame and the "Buddha-ground" constitutes the final flame.

This refers to the path of abandonment at the first stage (*bhūmi*) according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekavyavasthāna-śāsana*), which is designated as the initial flame; it is because upon entering the stages of the Separate Teaching, one perceives the principle of eternal abiding and abandons ignorance (*avidyā*).

Because one perceives the Middle Way, joy constitutes the initial flame. As for the statement that the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is the initial flame and the Buddha-ground (*buddhabhūmi*) is the final flame—this is the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*).
According to the Perfect Teaching, ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) is the Middle Way Buddha-nature.
Because one severs a single grade of ignorance, this is the meaning of the Shared (Tongjiao), the Distinct (Biejiao), and the Perfect (Yuanjiao) teachings.

[Note] For now, let us speak generally of the initial flame of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna*). As for what kind of faculty-nature it is, one must know that the treatise explains it as the burning of the wick.

Although it is common to all three teachings, the initial flame of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-jñāna) constitutes its own distinct path; it need not be subsumed within the three [teachings], because the capacities of those for whom the Shared Teaching (sāmānya-dharma) is intended are mixed.
[■ Record] This selection clarifies that dry wisdom is not common to the three [vehicles]. First the question, then the answer, as can be understood from the text. Three.

Regarding "penetration" (*tong*): this refers to what was stated above concerning the simultaneous penetration of both cause and fruit—namely, the categories of penetration in the causal stage (*yintong*), non-penetration in the resultant stage (*guifentong*), as well as the distinct (*bie*) and universal (*yuan*) forms of penetration.

The statement that "it is not necessarily the case that all three types of penetration are subsumed" means that for those whose faculties involve the simultaneous penetration of cause and fruit, they cannot sever the fetters at the first stage (*bhūmi*).
For those whose faculties involve penetration in the causal stage but not in the resultant stage, it is only at the third or fourth stage that they are able to sever the fetters.
Relying on the faculty of penetration to provide guidance is not yet capable of severing the fetters at the initial stage of the mind;
therefore, the first flame of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-jñāna) is simply one path within the specific teaching of the faculty of penetration, and need not be subsumed under all three faculties.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the initial flame of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-vipaśyanā), at what stage are the afflictions suppressed? For example, as in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*), it may be said that those of sharp faculties suppress and sever them simultaneously, as if merely borrowing the framework of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).

[Commentary] This section distinguishes how the initial flame of "dry wisdom" (śuṣka-prajñā) subdues afflictions. Question: Since the initial flame of dry wisdom already functions to sever afflictions, by what stage are afflictions then said to be "subdued"?
This question asks about the stage of subduing afflictions. In the answer, the single and borrowed stages of the ten bhūmis are cited;

the intent is to clarify that if dry wisdom—like the stage of "Joy" (pramuditā-bhūmi) in the Separate Teaching (bhedavyavasthāna)—severs the delusions of views (dṛṣṭi-heya), then it is by means of the [first] bhūmi...

The preceding refers to the stage of suppressing delusions (*vibhāvanā-avasthā*). As in the "Supplementary Practitioner" (*pho-hsing-hang*), this can be understood from the cited text in the diagram above.

The phrase "or it is said below" further indicates another interpretation. [Supplement] However, regarding the stage of suppressing delusions mentioned here, if one says it accommodates various types of faculties (*indriya*) and inclusively takes the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) as the initial flame, then its meaning is broad; thus, it may be treated as analogous to the preceding.
Borrowing from the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*): the stages prior to the [first] stage are established as the positions for subduing delusions (*vītarāga*).

If one speaks of those of dull faculties, the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) and the stage of vision (*darśanabhūmi*) constitute the first flame; for those of sharp faculties, they are able to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*) at the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*), which is itself the first flame.

Thus, it is unnecessary to establish further stages prior to the [first] stage. Why? Because the stage of dry wisdom is fundamentally the position for subduing delusions; however, for those of sharp faculties...

Such a person suppresses and then cuts off [the afflictions] immediately; therefore, this is designated as the "first flame. If one were to further establish a stage for the suppression of afflictions, it could no longer be called "dry wisdom" (śuklavidarśana) as the first flame.
This is truly because the preceding text merely borrowed the framework of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) without considering whether the practitioner's faculties are sharp or dull;
since one does not enter the formal stages until the afflictions are severed, a stage must be established prior to those stages—thus, another stage is established.
In the stage of subduing afflictions, this is not the case; therefore, whether [the stage] is established or not is intended to encompass both perspectives.

[Commentary] This explains the scriptural statement that Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are "like the Buddha. The first phrase cites the preceding text to indicate the subject.
As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "One should know that when a bodhisattva dwells within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), he is like a Buddha.

That is to say, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva is fully endowed with the six *pāramitās*, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to and including the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) and all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), and has completely perfected these while severing all afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their residual tendencies (*vāsanā*), this is what constitutes a bodhisattva mahāsattva."
"One should know that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwelling in the tenth stage is like a Buddha. The commentary explains:

"One should know that he is like a Buddha" means that when a Bodhisattva sits beneath such a tree and enters the tenth stage, called the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā bhūmi*), it is like a great cloud pouring down rain continuously and without interval;
from his mind, there naturally arise immeasurable and boundless pure qualities of all Buddhas. He remains mindful [of them].
Immediately upon this thought, the Bodhisattva reflected: "The Māra of the desire realm has not yet been subdued.
He then emitted light from between his eyebrows, causing the billion demonic palaces to be shrouded in darkness and rendered invisible. Māra became enraged and distressed;
he gathered his hosts of soldiers and came to press upon the Bodhisattva. Once the Bodhisattva had subdued Māra, the Buddhas of the ten directions celebrated his meritorious achievement.
All emitted light from between their eyebrows, which entered the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head. At that time, the merit attained through the ten stages was transformed into the Buddha-dharma;
all habitual tendencies of affliction were severed, and he attained unimpeded liberation.

He became fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four types of unimpeded knowledge, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, and other immeasurable virtues.
The Buddha-dharma caused the earth to quake in six ways; the heavens rained down flowers and incense; and all the bodhisattvas, devas, and humans joined their palms in praise.
At that time, a great radiance was emitted, illuminating immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.

The Buddhas, bodhisattvas, devas, and humans of the ten directions cried out in a loud voice: "In such-and-such a direction, in such-and-such a land, a bodhisattva named so-and-so sits upon the path."
The site where the Buddha’s work is fully accomplished—this is its radiance; this is called the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), which should be understood as being like that of a Buddha.

In the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), the lower volume, Jingxi cites two types of "being like a Buddha" according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) to explain the passage in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* regarding the ten stages being like those of a Buddha.

The first type is easily understood. Regarding the second type, the text states: "As for those who have been 'received' (*pratigṛhīta*), once they reach this point, [their delusions] are already destroyed."
A single grade of ignorance can also manifest the eight aspects; because it is like those eight aspects, it is said to be "like a Buddha.

This corresponds to the phrase "common with the Buddha-ground," meaning that in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the tenth ground is called the Buddha-ground. It is said to be "like" [a Buddha] in contrast to this common Buddha-ground of the three vehicles.

Regarding the phrase "resembling the Buddha of the Shared [Teaching]," this refers to those who have been grafted [into the higher teaching], who are able to shatter ignorance. There is no... [text ends].
The clarification of "pervasion" (*tong*) has been completed. As with those who pervade the Buddhas, they equally attain the eight aspects; therefore, they are called "like" (*ru*).

In the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua Wenju*), Volume Lower, it clarifies that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) also possesses two kinds of being "like the Buddha. The text states: "If one enters the Perfect Teaching, even if one is still prior to the stage of 'abiding' (*zhuzhuan*), one may also receive the provisional name of 'sitting at the site of enlightenment' (*daochang*).
This refers to being 'like the Buddha' through semblance (*xiangsi*) and 'like the Buddha' through contemplative practice (*guanhxing*). However, as for those...

The meaning of the text is as follows: this is merely a distinct designation for the path of teaching according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), and it does not refer to the "Tathatā" (Suchness) discussed here in the context of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).

II. Detailed Explanation [of the Ten Stages] has two parts. First, listing the names of the stages while on the ground of causes; there are eight. The first is named the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).

First is the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*). It receives this name because it has not yet attained the water of principle; it corresponds to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and is equivalent to the three stages of the five *sthāpana-citta* (stabilizing the mind) and the general and specific [contemplations] in the Tripiṭaka Teaching.

[Commentary] At the beginning of the three vehicles, they are all equally termed "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). Although one has not yet attained the water-like principle of the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage through practices such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) that take phenomena as their substance, the wisdom of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is profoundly sharp; therefore, it is called "Dry Wisdom."
[Commentary] This explains why it is called the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*).

It means that although there is the wisdom capable of contemplation, the fire of the delusions to be illuminated has not yet been extinguished, and the water of the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) has not yet appeared. Since the water of principle is as yet absent, its wisdom exists in a dry state;
thus, it receives the name "Dry Wisdom. One should know that delusion is metaphorically likened to fire, while principle is likened to water.

When delusion perishes, principle is revealed; it is like water extinguishing fire. In the *Miaoxuan*, it is clarified that the three vehicles share the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The first is named the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*);

this is the beginning of the three vehicles, and thus they are all equally termed "Dry Wisdom. This refers to the contemplation of the five stopping-minds (*pañca-nīvaraṇa-pratipakṣa*) through the realization of dharmas (*dharmatā*), as well as the general and specific characteristics of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). In terms of phenomenal characteristics, these do not differ from those of the Tripiṭaka; these constitute the first stage.

The Dharma-gate: realizing that the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are like illusions and transformations, thereby comprehensively destroying the eight inversions of views and craving, is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*).

Feeling, mind, and phenomena are likewise. Abiding within this contemplation, one cultivates the right efforts, the bases of power, the faculties, the powers, the factors of enlightenment, and the path.

Although one has not yet attained the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage—the water-like principle that resembles the truth—because the wisdom of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is profound and sharp, one realizes the essence.
The *Dharma-sthiti-citta-vibhaṅga-sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna-bhāvanā* is explained in detail in the second fascicle of the *Sijiao yi*; those who require it should consult that text.
△ Second, the explanation of the stage of the nature-ground (*gotra-bhūmi*).
Second is the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*). Having attained a semblance of the water of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), one subdues the afflictions of views and thought (*darśana-bhāvanā-kleśa*);

this is the stage of the internal ordinary person (*antarapudgala*) and is equivalent to the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*) of the Tripiṭaka Teaching. [Note] Within the Stage of Nature, the skillful means regarding non-arising and the dexterity of liberating wisdom are superior to the preceding stages; one attains a semblance of the unconditioned.
Because its nature is to leak like water, it is called the "Stage of Nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary] The *Miaoxuan* states: Regarding the "Stage of Nature," once one has attained the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) stage and surpassed the "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*), one is able to advance through the initial, middle, and final stages of mind, entering the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) dharma and even up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). All these are termed the Stage of Nature. Within the Stage of Nature, there is no...
The wisdom of skillful means arising from birth becomes increasingly superior to what preceded it. Regarding what is called "superior to the former":

it is like understanding that although suffering is non-existent, there is nevertheless a true reality (*satya*). This is because the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) do not arise;

they are all like dreams, illusions, echoes, transformations, the moon in water, and reflections in a mirror, being ultimately empty and non-existent. Likewise, one understands that although accumulation (*samudaya*) is non-existent, there is nevertheless a true reality, because...

Because one realizes that all afflictions, karma, and volitional formations are like dreams and illusions, one understands that cessation is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning and is likewise without cessation now;

yet there is the True Truth (*satyadharma*). Because one knows that all phenomena of arising and ceasing are unattainable, there exists a Dharma that transcends even *nirvāṇa*, for it too is like a dream or an illusion. Thus, one knows the Path and the existence of the Path.

Yet there is the True Truth (*satyadharma*). When one believes that all paths leading to nirvāṇa are like dreams and illusions, being without dual characteristics, then one spontaneously becomes empty and pervasive, entering the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
One thereby attains the water of the nature of semblance-anāsrava; hence it is called the "Stage of Nature" (*gotrabhūmi*).

△ Third, the two stages are explained together. To say they are "explained together" means that these two positions both enter the *anantarya-samādhi* (uninterrupted samādhi) and both sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*); therefore, they are explained together as an illumination.

The thirty-eighth person is the stage of the four stages of seeing (*catur-darśana-bhūmi*). These two positions enter the *ānantarya-samādhi*, severing the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the three realms and exhausting all views.
They give rise to true outflow-free wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and perceive the principle of the True Truth (*satya-artha*), which is equal to the first fruit of the Tripitaka Teaching.
[Commentary] The two practices of faith and dharma of the three vehicles take the realization of the provisional as the substance to trigger the realization of the true and sever delusions.

Within the Uninterrupted Samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*), the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are fully perfected, while wisdom is still lacking one part; therefore, it is called the stage of the Eight Persons (which refers to the eight patiences).
The three vehicles equally perceive the principle of the first meaning—the Four Noble Truths of non-arising—and equally sever the eighty-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view.

[Supplement] This clarifies the attainment of the name "Eight Persons" (aṣṭamaka) and the stage of vision (darśana-bhūmi). The first section, "The Three Vehicles Below," explains the stage of the Eight Persons;

the subsequent section, "The Three Vehicles Below," explains the stage of vision. Within the rank of the Eight Persons, one possesses only the eight patiences (kṣānti) and seven knowledges (jñāna), totaling only fifteen moments of mind.
Because they lack one moment of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), it is said that while the eight patiences are complete, the knowledges are deficient by one part. That is to say:

Because they are established by way of their full completion, it is called the Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*). Upon reaching the fulfillment of the sixteenth moment of mind, one immediately enters the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), which is called the Stage of Seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).
[Note] Regarding "the samādhi of the uninterrupted" and so forth: the *Zhiguan* (Mohe Zhiguan), fascicle 6, part 6, states: "If one speaks of three stages, this is based on the severance of views."
First, regarding the statement "the fourth stage": this refers to the period after the abandonment of [wrong] views, wherein one never again emerges from meditative contemplation (*samādhi*).

[Commentary]: This explains that the uninterrupted samādhi (*ānantarya-samādhi*) of these two stages abandons [wrong] views. The *Zhiguan* states: "Regarding the common designation for the shared stage of the 'Universal Householder' (*Vaiśvāsika*):
formerly it was said that wrong views are abandoned at the third stage, or that they are abandoned at the fourth stage, or it was said [they are abandoned at] the sixth."
"The stages of the path exhaust the afflictions of contemplation," or as some say, "the seven stages exhaust the afflictions of contemplation. Now, let us examine these statements.

If it is claimed that both the third and fourth stages exhaust the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi*), then this master does not understand the meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). In the common stage of the three vehicles, they all enter the *anantarya-samādhi* together;
they exhaust the afflictions of views without emerging from or entering the meditative observation. Why, then, would one suddenly claim that the third and fourth stages exhaust them?
Is this seen? If one takes only the three stages as those where views are abandoned, then the fourth stage should abandon [only] latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
If one takes only the four stages as those where views are abandoned, then the third stage would have views not yet abandoned.

If two stages are used for the abandonment of views, does this constitute entering and emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), or not entering and emerging from it? If there is no entering and emerging from absorption, then there are not two stages. If two stages are used...

The view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) constitutes the entry into and emergence from contemplation; it is not the stage of the view of annihilation itself. A teacher of men attempts to defend this by claiming that the sutra speaks thus.

This is because that teacher does not understand the intent of the sutra. What is said here is that the sutra borrows the meaning of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyākaraṇa*) to reveal the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇavyākaraṇa*).

However, the meaning of the view in the Distinct Teaching is extensive, as it discusses the third and fourth stages; the meaning of the view in the Shared Teaching is brief, as it does not involve entry into or emergence from contemplation.
However, while names may be applied specifically, their meaning must necessarily rely on a general application.

If one were to provide an interpretation based on the view that there is no "entering" or "emerging" from meditative absorption—for instance, stating that "the third stage" refers to the initial severance of views, and "the fourth stage" refers to the period following the severance of views—in both cases, one does not emerge from the absorption.
For example, regarding the sixteen moments of mind, some say they constitute the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), while others say they constitute the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
As for the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*), it refers to the third and fourth stages; these two stages are divided by the initial and final points of the abandonment of views.
Although they are divided into two stages, the wisdom of contemplation is without interruption; therefore, it is called "uninterrupted."

【□Note】The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 6, Part 1, Section 7, states: "Although [the stages] are common to both levels, the duration of severance remains brief because they are shared by the Three Vehicles.
Yet, despite being brief, they are also long; therefore, although they are divided into three stages and four stages..."

[Commentary] This explanation clarifies that the severance of views in the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) must be distinguished across two stages: the third and the fourth. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) asks:

"Within the Shared Teaching, when determining the stage of severing views, one distinguishes these two stages oneself; why then is it necessary to refute others by borrowing from the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) to establish the stage of severing views, only to end up being the same as the Shared Teaching?
Answer: It is precisely because they are the same as the Shared Teaching that they are named "Shared. Although there are two [aspects], they are nonetheless shared.
The stage (*bhūmi*) is brief at the time of its initial severance because it is shared by the three vehicles (*triyāna*). Although brief, it is nonetheless extensive;

therefore, even though it is divided into three stages or four stages, or sometimes borrowed from the distinct [vehicle], the vision within the distinct [vehicle] is further extended. There are two perspectives here: if explained according to principle (*tattva*), it extends through to the Buddha-stage (*buddhabhūmi*);
if explained according to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), it is called the third or fourth stage. Although these two perspectives differ, the meaning of "vision" is equally extensive in both.
Because of the distinction regarding their specific length, there is no error in using the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) to determine the meaning of the abandonment of views across two stages.
If one follows the general sense, it is said that one does not emerge from meditative absorption; if one follows the specific sense, each stage is capable of destroying views.

This constitutes the difference. Because of the distinction regarding their specific length, the latter two instances universally employ all four stages as the state of abandoning views. Many people...
It is not seen. This means that the general definition is sufficient; why must one borrow from the specific?
△ Fourth, the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi).

Fifth, the Stage of Thinness severs the first six of the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm through cultivation; it is equal to the second fruit in the Treasury Teaching (Tripiṭaka-vinaya).

[Note] The essence of craving is that the provisional is identical to the real. One gives rise to the six grades of unimpeded knowledge, abandons the six grades [of afflictions] of the desire realm, and realizes the sixth liberation;
thus, the afflictions of the desire realm become light and thin.
[Commentary] This clarifies that it is called the "Thin Ground" (*tanubhūmi*). To say "thin" is to refer to its counterpart, "thick.

In the preceding three and four stages, one has severed only the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) remain entirely intact, like ice that is hard and thick.

Upon reaching this fifth stage, one not only severs the delusions of views but is further able to advance and sever the first [portion] of the nine grades of delusions of thought within the desire realm.
These six stages are equivalent to the second fruit stage of the Śrāvaka vehicle within the Tripiṭaka teachings.
Because the afflictions of the desire realm are slight and thin, like ice that is barely formed, they are called the "Stage of Thinness" (Tanubhūmi).
△ Fifth, the Stage of Departure from Desire (*vairāgya-bhūmi*).
Sixth, the Stage of Departure from Desire: having exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is equivalent to the third fruit in the Tripiṭaka teachings.

[Note] Worshiping and loving the provisional is itself the real. Having exhausted the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*) of the desire realm, one is free from the afflictions of the desire realm.

[Commentary] This clarifies that the name [of this stage] is derived from being free from desire. Regarding the "five lower-tier fetters" (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*): first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*);

third, the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*); fourth, the latent tendency of greed (*rāga-anuśaya*); and fifth, the latent tendency of hatred (*pratigha-anuśaya*). These are explained in detail in the fourth fascicle.
△ Sixth, the stage of having already accomplished (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*).

Seventh, the stage of having already accomplished (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*). Having exhausted all afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the three realms, one merely severs the manifest outflows (*paryavasthāna*) but cannot yet eradicate their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
This is like burning wood into charcoal. It is equal to the four fruits of the Treasury Teaching (*piṭaka*). The stages of the Śrāvaka are coextensive with this.

[Note] For those of the three vehicles, when the craving for the realm of form and the formless realm is realized as suchness, the fifty-two grades of the five higher fetters (*pañca-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*) are exhausted.
Because the delusions regarding the phenomena of the three realms have been completely severed, it is called the "Stage of Having Accomplished" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*). (Text)

[Supplement] This concludes the explanation of how [the stage] is named. Regarding the phrase "already accomplished" (*kṛtakṛtya*): it means that because the afflictions of the three realms have been completely severed, there is no further effort required, as it is said, "that which was to be done has been done.

Afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-heya*) are called "afflictive obstructions" (*vastu-āvaraṇa*), while ignorance (*avidyā*) is called the "obstruction to the principle" (*tattva-āvaraṇa*).
Because ignorance, the obstruction to the principle, is contrasted with the afflictions of view and thought, the latter are termed "afflictive obstructions. As for these "afflictive obstructions":
These are the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīyāni*). The five higher fetters are: first, restlessness; second, conceit; third, ignorance; fourth, attachment to the realm of form;
and fifth, attachment to the formless realm. When these are completely severed, it is called "having done what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*).

[Commentary] Burning wood produces charcoal. In the third section (twelfth item) of the *Sijiaoyi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings), it quotes the *Jilun* (Treatise on Wisdom): "The power of the wisdom of the Śrāvakas is weak;
it is like a small fire burning wood. Nevertheless, there remains charcoal."

[Commentary] This explains that while the primary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) have been severed, they cannot yet invade the residual tendencies (*vāsanā*). What are called "residual tendencies" are the remaining traces of the afflictions.
It is like the clothing of a wet-nurse: though it has been washed clean with ash until no visible stain remains, the odor of the stain persists.
The clothing is like the mind of the Noble One; the stains are like the various afflictions. Although one washes it with the water of wisdom, the fragrance of the afflictions...

The habit-energy of vexation still remains, as in the case of Nanda. Because his habitual practice of lust was so heavy, although he attained the path of Arhatship, when sitting among a great assembly of men and women, his eyes would first look toward the women and he would converse with them while preaching the Dharma.
Śāriputra, because his habitual practice of anger was so heavy, when he heard the Buddha say, "Śāriputra, you have eaten impure food," he immediately vomited the food.

He never again accepted invitations. Because Mahākāśyapa’s habituation to anger was so heavy, at the time when the Dharma was being compiled after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he ordered Ānanda to enter and repent for his *duṣkṛta* offense;
furthermore, he personally took Ānanda by the hand and led him out, refusing to dwell with him, saying:
"Your outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted; you must not participate in the compilation of the Buddha's teachings as one who is impure."
The Dharma [states]: Pindola Bharadvaja insulted a river deity, calling her a "little slave"; this was due to the heavy habituation of arrogance.
Madhuvāsiṣṭha would sometimes leap from a clothes rack onto a beam, or from a beam to a loft, or from a loft to a pavilion, and so forth.
Restlessness and frivolity are heavy habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Such noble ones (*ārya*), although their outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, still possess these remaining habits;
it is like fire burning wood, where the embers still remain.

[Note] Regarding the statement that "the stages of the Śrāvakas are equal to this," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 6, Part 1, states: "In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the two vehicles [Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas] from before the seventh stage are common to the Bodhisattvas;
thus they are called 'Shared Śrāvakas. If this is so, since the eighth stage and above transcend the levels of the two vehicles, why are they also called 'common to the Bodhisattvas'?

Answer: This is because the initial name is applied to the subsequent stages; the name is established based on the original state. This is not the case for the Distinct (*bie*) and Complete (*yuan*) Teachings."
"Because their beginnings and ends are distinct.
[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) further asks: "The *Zangjiao* (Tripitaka Teaching) is also shared with the Śrāvakas; why is it not established as having the name 'shared'? It answers:

"Within the Tripitaka Teaching, although there are three vehicles, the Bodhisattva practice is remote; from beginning to end, they suppress the afflictions and are forever distinct from the two vehicles."

It is not called "shared," yet one does not hear of a distinct principle; nor is it "unshared. This reveals that the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching exhaust the primary afflictions (*āsrava*) and are thus equal to the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, upon hearing the distinct principle, they receive the special reception; thus, there is both the shared and the unshared.
All of these can be explained; they differ from the Tripiṭaka.
△ Seventh, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha.
Eighth, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha further subdues habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), like burning charcoal until it becomes ash.
[Commentary] The Pratyekabuddha has awakened to the true, outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). Because the power of his merit is great, he is able to erode and eliminate the residual habits (*vāsanā*).
[Record] "Erode" means to diminish. Since the residual habits have not yet been exhausted, it is said only that he "erodes" and "diminishes" them, thereby causing them to reach their end.

[Note] Regarding "burning charcoal until it becomes ash," the *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 3, section 12, quotes the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, stating: "The power of the pratyekabuddha’s wisdom is superior;
it is like a great fire burning wood. When the wood has burned and the charcoal is exhausted, some ash remains."

[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "For example, it is like a poor man who owes another money. Although his debt is nearly paid off, because a small portion remains unpaid, he is still bound in prison and cannot escape. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are also like this;
because they possess the residual traces of the habit-energies of craving, they are unable to achieve Bodhi."
△ Eighth, clarifying the Bodhisattva-bhūmi.

Ninth, the Bodhisattva-bhūmi: even if one were to exhaustively sever [afflictions], such that they are identical to those of the Two Vehicles, one sustains residual habits to moisten rebirth, so that the path and contemplation flow together as a dual stream.

They sport with supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*), purify Buddha-lands, [enter the provisional from the ultimate], and the paths of contemplation flow as one. Deeply contemplating the two truths, they advance to sever the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and the ignorance regarding form and mind.

They attain the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) and the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārga-jñatā*). They sport with supernatural powers, purify Buddha-lands, and bring sentient beings to maturity. They study...
The Buddha’s ten powers and four fearlessnesses indicate that the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are about to be exhausted.

[Commentary] This clarifies that the Bodhisattva cultivates and studies the Buddha-way, eliminating both active afflictions and their latent habits simultaneously, thereby manifesting a form that transcends those of the two vehicles.
They are the preeminent figures among the three vehicles, truly those who stand out from the crowd. As for the statement "proceeding from emptiness" (*śūnyatā*):

the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) of the two vehicles perceives emptiness and contemplates only the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*) of the Bodhisattvas illuminates the provisional and is able to contemplate the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, while proceeding from emptiness, they are also able to enter into the provisional. "Way" (*mārga*) refers to the path of transformation, which is to say, compassion and benefit for others.

"Observing things" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); this is the realization of principle for one's own benefit. It is what is called the simultaneous integration of compassion and wisdom, and the concurrent operation of the ultimate and conventional truths.

That "form and mind are without cognition" refers to the habitual tendencies of the obstacles as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Among the five eyes, it is the Dharma-eye that is able to observe the conventional.

Among the three types of wisdom, the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*) is able to illuminate the conventional. This is explained below within the stages of abiding, practice, and heading toward [enlightenment] in the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).

Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyavyavasthāna*) and the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching, there is a vast difference in depth and subtlety concerning their severance of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and their attainment of the eye of wisdom.

Nevertheless, contemplating emptiness serves one’s own benefit, while contemplating the conventional benefits others; furthermore, they are able to progressively sever the "dust and sand" [of afflictions] and attain the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*).

This is the realization of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). "Bringing sentient beings to maturity" refers to the subsequent passage on gathering sentient beings through giving so that they may be born in his land, and so forth.
Regarding the "Ten Powers of a Buddha," the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states:

These ten are collectively termed "powers" because they are the functional application of the Tathāgatas' realized wisdom of reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), which penetrates all things with perfect clarity and cannot be destroyed by anything.

Because there is nothing that can surpass it, it is called a "power" (*bala*). Great Bodhisattvas also partially attain this power of wisdom; however, as it is slightly inferior to that of a Buddha, they do not receive the title.

The ten powers are: the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*); the power of karma; the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); the power of the faculties (*indriya*);

the power of aspiration (*chanda*); the power of disposition (*dhātu*); the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad*); the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*); the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); and the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). (4)

Regarding the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the obstacles to the path;

and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path leading to the end of suffering. These four are collectively termed "fearlessness" because, when one extensively proclaims within the great assembly one's own and others' knowledge and abandonment, being certain and free from error, there is no appearance of dread; therefore, they are called "fearless."
This is what is feared. Regarding the statement that "the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) will be exhausted," the word "will" (*jāng*) indicates that they have not yet been entirely exhausted.
