The wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*): the essence of the jewel is originally empty, which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); yet its ability to rain down treasures is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The jewel is used as a metaphor for the ultimate, and its function as a metaphor for the conventional. Thus, the jewel is the function, and the function is the jewel. They are non-dual, yet dual;
they are distinguished only as the ultimate and the conventional. The above is a summary of the text from the *Miaoxuan*, constituting the seven types of the two truths.
The fourth is the correct [view]. The three treatises provide the connection.
[Commentary] Among the twenty-three schools of antiquity that elucidated the two truths, only the Zhuangyan (Zhuangyan Temple) and Kaishan schools possessed a reputation for elegance.

Zhuangyan held that the Buddha-fruit transcends the two truths (this refers to those currently being "received" [into the higher stage]); Kaishan held that the Buddha-fruit does not transcend the two truths.

[The Master] said: (Regarding the teachings of the Buddha as a whole,) my patriarch [Zhiyi] has fully elucidated the manner in which the Tathāgata adapted his teachings to the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, when clearly understood through this reception [of the teachings], there shall be no further obstructions regarding any of the sūtras.

[Commentary] This demonstrates that while the various masters of past and present have elucidated the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*), there remains something that has not yet reached full perfection.

The first phrase provides a general indication; the second phrase offers a specific praise. The section beginning with "Zhuangyan" (Sthiramati) reveals the ultimate destination of the doctrines of these two masters.
However, the position established by Zhuangyan is based on those of sharp faculties—namely, those who are currently being "received" [into the higher teaching]. Kaishan...
The establishment of the doctrine is based on those of dull faculties; therefore, this is the Buddha-fruit of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).

From "Our Patriarch" onwards, it clarifies that the Tiantai wisdom-eye is preeminent throughout antiquity and modernity, standing alone as the peerless authority for the classification of teachings. For this reason, the Two Truths serve as the point of transition.

This accords with the meaning of the Buddhist sutras. As stated in the third fascicle of the *Zhiguan*: "In the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), the three vehicles [bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas] take the conventional as their substance and enter emptiness;

however, the two vehicles [śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] enter only 'bare emptiness' (*dankong*) and cannot proceed from bare emptiness into the conventional, as they lack the capacity to transform and benefit others.

Bodhisattvas take the conventional as their substance and enter bare emptiness, yet they are able to proceed from bare emptiness back into the conventional to transform and deliver sentient beings. Bodhisattvas of superior faculties take the conventional as their substance..."

Entering emptiness: first one enters mere emptiness; next one enters "not merely emptiness," whereby ignorance is shattered and the Buddha-nature is seen. This is eternally distinct from the previous [state of] reality;

how could it be used as the same single Truth? Master Zhuangyan says that the *satyasamudaya* (truth of origination) of the triple world is the outflowing, mundane condition for the material and mental aggregates of the environment and its inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*), whereas the fruition of Buddhahood is non-outflowing and does not engender such conditions.
Form and mind transcend the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), yet there exists an ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Once seen, it is not seen again; therefore, it lies outside the two truths.
Now, you say that this meaning merely captures a fragment of the intent, yet the argument is not established.

One does not know what distinct realm the Buddha’s wisdom illuminates, nor what distinct delusions it severs. If one grasps the present meaning, the intention to transcend [the two truths] is established. This is the opening.
The "virtuous teacher" refers to the conventional reality of the substance of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi* and *saṃjñā*), which is the truth of emptiness within that very conventionality.

Therefore, the fruit of Buddhahood does not transcend the two truths. If one cannot move toward this meaning now, then it differs from the mental application of the Two Vehicles, and furthermore, it will not be accomplished.
If one grasps this intent, the principle of "not transcending" is also established. This has been known as the "Wind" since ancient times.
The two truths flow [into one]. The meaning lies herein: it is emptiness, yet not merely emptiness. When combined, they are simply the One True Truth;
when separated, they instead become two True Truths. This differs from the Tripiṭaka school.

In that Tripiṭaka system, the third truth has only the name "Middle Way" but possesses no distinct essence; there is no separate vision for the eye and no separate cognition for wisdom. Now, it is not so.

However, the three truths are also called the True Truth (*satyadharma*) and are also called the Middle Way Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*). They possess distinct essences, distinct views, and distinct cognitions;
this constitutes the characteristic of the convergence and divergence of the two truths and three truths in the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*). The *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary) states:

Zhuangyan says [the Buddha-fruit] emerges; Kaishan says it does not emerge. This arises because among those who study the Bodhisattva path shared by the Three Vehicles, there are those with the "but" (exclusive) and "not-but" (inclusive) capacities.
The ancients did not understand the distinction between the two faculties of sharp and dull, but merely debated whether the Buddha-fruit emerges or does not emerge.

Ultimately, they failed to perceive the intent behind the present opening and closing [of the gates], which allowed each of the two schools to clarify their own respective positions. The current text refutes both.

Therefore, it is said that in all cases, mental attention (*manasikāra*) is not established. Thus we know that both schools have each grasped only one side of the current text—either the sharp or the dull faculty—and for this reason they are described as having "partial intent.
Furthermore, they are unable to understand that which transcends these to separately illuminate the realm of the Middle Way.
By employing the wisdom of the Middle Way, one advances to shatter ignorance; hence it is called "a partial meaning.

If one is unable to understand and, being of dull faculties, relies on the teachings to realize the True Truth (satyadharma) in common with the Two Vehicles, this too is merely obtaining a partial meaning. If one fully grasps the present meaning, [one attains the complete sense].
The meanings of both "emerging" and "not emerging" are fully established. For this reason, the ancients praised both schools equally, referring to these two truths as "fengliu" (refined elegance).
To speak of fengliu means that one’s movements and stillness accord with propriety, and whether entering or departing, there is no error.

If one relies on the two truths of the "containing the middle" as employed today, then whether advancing or retreating, all is beautiful and refined elegance abounds; thus it was said by my ancestors.

That [this work] exhaustively captures the manner in which the Tathāgata adapts his teachings to the capacities of sentient beings is indeed for good reason. As the *Nirvāṇa Xuányún* states regarding "adornment":
the fruit of Buddhahood transcends the two truths and is not subsumed under either the ultimate or the conventional.

Ordinary beings experience fruits induced by deluded causes; this is the insubstantial conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Because its provisional substance is empty, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The fruit of Buddhahood, however, is not produced by delusion.
Because it is produced by causes and conditions, it is not the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); because it cannot be further negated as empty, it is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

As the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "Transcending both the conventional truth and the ultimate truth, one abides in the eleventh stage, the stage of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). This is precisely what that means.
Kaishan said: "The fruit of Buddhahood does not transcend the two truths. The nirvana of the Buddha's fruit is likewise subsumed within the two truths.

Its essence consists of the two provisional designations of continuity and dependence; therefore, it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Since these two provisional designations can be emptied, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The numinous wisdom of the Buddha’s fruit likewise merges with the ultimate."

[Commentary] The ancient masters’ explanations of the reception [of the provisional into the real] do not exceed three meanings: taking the inclusion of the Middle Way as the source, the pointing-out as the essential pivot, and the awakening of practice as the fundamental nature.

Because the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is skillful, within the one truth there is the inclusion of two truths. When a bodhisattva of sharp faculties realizes the true emptiness, it is immediately pointed out for them.
This is as explained in the *Miaoxuan* regarding the connection between the Distinct and Shared Teachings, where the three dharmas are employed to demonstrate it.

The three faculties resolve the source; that is to say, they are neither out-flowing (*āsrava*) nor non-out-flowing, neither empty nor non-empty, and are the destination of all dharmas, as fully explained in Fascicle 39 of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning).
However, it is only by means of sharp faculties awakening what was previously practiced that one can be pointed out [to this truth].
If a Bodhisattva of dull faculties is like those of the Two Vehicles, they will only be gathered into the assembly at the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.

[Commentary] This indicates that the ancient masters explained the process of "being grafted" (being received into the higher stage) as having three meanings. The first sentence provides a general heading for these three meanings. The next three sentences list the three meanings individually.
The subsequent five lines provide a comprehensive explanation of these three meanings. Regarding the phrase "the one true [nature] containing the two middle [natures]":
it is as when it is said that illusory existence is itself emptiness, and emptiness and non-emptiness together constitute the True. This "True" contains only the "Middle."
That which exists as an illusion is itself empty, yet not empty. That all phenomena tend toward emptiness and non-emptiness is the truth. This truth contains not only the Middle Way;

it serves as the source for the Single Truth containing the Two Truths within it, which characterizes the Shared Teaching. For those of sharp faculties who have merely realized true emptiness, this constitutes the "pointing-out instruction.
This explanation takes the pointing-out instruction to be the essential pivot, ensuring that those of sharp faculties do not become mired in attachment.

By abiding in true emptiness, one causes [the practitioner] to become a sage of the Distinct or Perfect teachings. This is as demonstrated by the citations and indications in the lower volume of the *Miaoxuan*.
The *Miaoxuan* states: "When the one conventional truth follows the three truths of reality, it becomes threefold. What are their characteristics?

As clarified in the *Dapin* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra), there is that which is neither outflowing (*sāsrava*) nor non-outflowing (*anāsrava*). Regarding this, the first person considers 'neither outflowing' to be the negation of the conventional; 'nor non-outflowing' is..."

It is said that one abandons attachment. Why? Because attachment arises conditioned by the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); just as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) arise conditioned by cessation (*nirodha*), one destroys attachment and returns to the outflow-free.
This is one set of the two truths. Next, another person hears [the teaching] that it is neither outflow nor outflow-free, and says:
"This is not the two extremes, but separately reveals the Middle Way; this Middle Way is the truth. This is yet another set of the two truths. Then, another person hears...
It is neither outflow (*āsrava*) nor non-outflow; thus one knows the "double negation," which directly reveals the Middle Way.
The power and function of the Middle Way Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) are vast and great, equal to empty space. All phenomena (*dharma*) tend toward that which is neither outflow nor non-outflow.

This, moreover, constitutes another instance of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). The first instance refers to the single ultimate and the single conventional, encompassing the two truths in general. The second instance refers to the specific [distinction].
The "connection through inclusion" (tongjiao han) refers to entering the two truths of the ultimate (zhen) and the conventional (chu) within the middle [truth].

The three grades [of the connection through inclusion] refer to the perfect (yuan) connection through inclusion, which enters the two truths of the ultimate and the inconceivable middle. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The śrāvaka sees only emptiness, but does not see non-emptiness."
The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness; this is precisely that meaning. Those of the Two Vehicles claim to be attached to this emptiness;
to shatter their attachment to emptiness, it is called "non-empty. Once attachment to emptiness is shattered, they see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness.
Those of superior capacity regard non-emptiness as wondrous existence, and thus speak of "non-emptiness. When those of the most superior capacity hear of "non-emptiness," they consider it to be...
The *tathāgatagarbha*. All phenomena (*dharma*) tend toward the *tathāgatagarbha*. Again, with respect to the empty and the non-empty, there are three types.
Furthermore, regarding how all phenomena tend toward that which is neither outflowing (*āsava*) nor non-outflowing, to reveal the distinctions between these three types:
first, when a person hears that all phenomena tend toward that which is neither outflowing nor non-outflowing, they say that all phenomena do not depart from emptiness and circulate universally.
The spaces of the ten directions are just like the space within a jar. The jar serves as a metaphor for a person;

the emptiness within a person is no different from the emptiness of the ten directions, and the emptiness of the ten directions is no different from the emptiness within a jar. Therefore, the emptiness of the ten directions all converges into the emptiness of the jar.
Next, having heard of this convergence, one understands the principle herein: that all practices must come forth and converge toward its realization.

"All practices" refers to the emptiness and provisional nature of skillful means. One must understand the practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) in order to proceed toward the arousal of this Middle Way;

this is "conditioned cultivation" (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*), which serves to manifest "true cultivation" (*tattva-bhāvanā*). That is to say, when conditioned cultivation is perfected, true cultivation manifests of itself.
When later practitioners hear that all phenomena (*dharma*) proceed toward [the ultimate], they realize it is neither outflowing (*āsava*) nor non-outflowing, and is endowed with the one [vehicle].

This refers to all dharmas. As explained in detail in the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning), the text states: "The three dharmas are universally employed as a basis to distinguish their characteristics.
'Outflowing' (*āsrava*) and 'outflow-free' (*anāsrava*) are fundamentally universal dharmas; however, in order to establish the meaning of 'reception,' the 'neither-nor' is established.

'Empty' (*śūnya*) and 'not-empty' are fundamentally distinct dharmas. 'All dharmas tending toward [the One Vehicle]' is fundamentally the Perfect Dharma. Within each of these dharmas, there are respectively three types of persons."
The difference in their comprehension arises precisely because the awakening of their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) varies; thus, what they hear differs accordingly.
This extends even to the distinct and perfect capacities, which, when contrasted with those of dull faculties abiding in emptiness, result in three distinct types.

Therefore, in explaining the latter two forms of "reception" (*pratigraha*), one must consider them in relation to the common and dull faculties, whereby three types of persons together listen to the same teaching yet hear it differently. This statement serves as proof. How can it be said that they "hear"? It is because...
Because those of sharp faculties realize [the truth] immediately upon hearing it, the source of understanding is demonstrated by means of the outflows (*āsrava*) and so forth.
If one grasps this intent, one will attain mastery and non-obstruction regarding all phenomena; this is the essential point revealed for the sake of the practitioner. Now, from the passage below:

The commentary explains that the arousal of practice constitutes the nature of the faculties. The *Shu* (Sub-commentary) states: "Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching differ in their arousal of practice according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull.
If they arouse the distinct understanding practiced in previous lives and are able to understand the 'mere Middle' (*but zhong*), they may then be pointed out and received by the Distinct Teaching.
Alternatively, if they arouse the perfect understanding practiced in previous lives and are able to understand the 'not merely Middle' (*bu dan zhong*), they may then be pointed out."
This indicates the reception of the Perfect Teaching (Ekanaya). Although those of sharp faculties likewise contemplate the conventional as illusory existence, their realization of the Truth differs;
therefore, they are received into the Middle Way beforehand. Those of dull faculties, however, are identical to the Two Vehicles and are only brought into this assembly at the Lotus Sutra gathering.
This is because their spiritual capacity is defined by the nature of their past practice and present awakening.

[Note] Regarding the phrase "not only seeing emptiness, etc.": The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (Dà jīng), cited in the *Zhǐguān sānshíliù* (Treatise on the Thirty-Six Topics of Stopping and Contemplation), states:
"Those of the Two Vehicles see only emptiness and do not see non-emptiness. The wise person, however, not only sees emptiness but is also able to see non-emptiness.
This 'non-emptiness' is precisely Great Nirvāṇa. (Source text).
[Commentary] Master Zhixu states: "The 'Wise One' refers to those of sharp faculties. 'Seeing the Middle' is called seeing that it is not empty;
'not empty' means it is not merely empty. The perfection of the three virtues is termed Great Nirvana."
[Commentary] To be "separate from extremes" is called "only"; to be "identical with extremes" is called "not only.

[Record] This explains the distinction between "only-middle" and "not-only-middle. Regarding "only-middle," it necessarily refers to emptiness and existence that are free from the two extremes, manifesting the single middle alone.
To illustrate this through a metaphor: it is like setting aside empty space and pointing specifically to the moon.
As for the statement that it is "not merely the middle": one need not depart from the two extremes of emptiness and existence to separately manifest the Middle Way;

rather, one must point out that the extremes themselves are the middle. Apart from the extremes of emptiness and existence, the middle cannot be found, just as [the nature of space cannot be found] apart from space itself.

Where else could there be a moon to point out? This clarifies that those of the Separate Teaching enter into this [Middle Way] by understanding only the intrinsically pure *tathatā* as being devoid of all phenomena;
hence it is called "merely the Middle. It is not so for those of the Perfect Teaching.

They realize that mind, Buddha, and sentient beings are non-different in their threefold nature, such that every form and every fragrance is none other than the Middle Way. It is like eating honey: [every part is sweet].
The edges are all sweet; therefore, it is said that it is not only sweet in the center.
△ Second, distinguishing the stages has two parts. First, the question: Question:
At what stage is one received? Into what stage is one received?
[□ Note] First, he asks about that which is received; next, he asks about that which receives.
[■ Record] This explains the intent of the questions. "That which is received" refers to those of sharp faculties in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). "That which receives" refers to...

This indicates that the Tathāgata uses the two dharmas of the Perfect (yuan) and the Distinct (bie) to guide and lead those of the two types of superior capacity within the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).
Regarding "at what stage": the meaning is that one simply does not know at what stage a person may be received through the guidance of these two higher teachings;
nor, even if they are granted entry, does one know which position they may occupy within those two teachings.
△ Second, the response in two parts. First, the response concerning the three faculties common to both [the general and specific] concentrations.
Response: The three faculties of the persons who receive the transition differ. If they are of superior faculty, they are received in the third or fourth stage;
those of middling faculty, in the fifth or sixth stage; and those of inferior faculty, in the seventh or eighth stage.
[Note] In the response, the three faculties are discussed in terms of the speed with which they develop their practice upon being received by the Buddha’s transformative power.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) identifies the fourth stage as superior, the sixth and seventh as middling, and the eighth and ninth as inferior. Here, advancing one stage refers to the ease of the teaching’s position, as the text may sometimes advance or retreat. This answers the first question.

[Supplement] This clarifies the response to the first question. The first three phrases explain the meaning of the three faculties (*indriya*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), lower section, correlates these with the three faculties in the present text.
The final phrase provides the concluding answer. "The third and fourth stages" refers to the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*) and the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).
In this stage, one exhausts the delusions of views and perceives the principle of true emptiness.

However, those of sharp faculties attain the Path of Vision (darśana-mārga) at the fifteenth moment of mind, whereas those of dull faculties must wait until the sixteenth moment is complete before they can perceive the Path. Thus, two positions are established.
Furthermore, the reason these two stages are joined is that those of superior capacity see all by seeing one; they do not merely see emptiness.

They also perceive non-emptiness. Having perceived non-emptiness, they are thus able to be received [into the path]. In the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), one abandons the six grades of afflictions of the desire realm;

in the sixth stage, one completely abandons the nine grades of lower afflictions. Having abandoned the afflictions of the desire realm, one may for the first time perceive non-emptiness and receive the empowerment.

Therefore, this is judged to belong to those of middling faculties. In the seventh stage, one completely abandons the afflictions; in the eighth stage, one attacks the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). This...

Since one must wait until both the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and thought (*saṃjñā*) are exhausted before the non-empty is realized, this refers to those of inferior capacity. The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Only when the delusions of views and thought have been destroyed and one has reached the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) is the true 'within' then explained. Therefore, it is said that the wise perceive emptiness.

As for those who are not yet empty [of afflictions], they hear [the teaching] only upon being received. Regarding the statement in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) that "one is received at the eighth stage," this refers to those of inferior capacity.
Question: Why must one know that reception occurs specifically at the eighth stage? Answer: It is because one wishes to demonstrate the midst within the true [nature].
Therefore, one must wait for the realization of emptiness before it can be pointed out, so that one may deeply contemplate emptiness and thereby perceive that which is not empty.

If this is so, what is the meaning regarding those of medium and superior faculties? The answer is: for those of medium and superior faculties as well, the true nature is revealed only after they have already seen it;
however, because their realization of the ultimate emptiness is still shallow, the teachings are mostly directed toward those of inferior faculties.

△ Second, the answer concerning the true and semblance stages of entry and the teachings received therein differs according to whether they are true or semblance. If one is received into the semblance stage, it corresponds to the distinct [Vehicle]’s ten *pariṇāmanā* (dedications) and the round [Vehicle]’s ten *śraddhā* (faith) positions.
If one is received into the true stage, it corresponds to the distinct [Vehicle]’s first *bhūmi* and the round [Vehicle]’s first *vihāra*.
[□ Note] Regarding the phrase "the teaching received," etc., this answers the subsequent question. The character "suǒ" (所) is merely a particle.

[■ Record] This clarifies that it is an answer to the following question. However, the single character "shàng" (上) above is a grammatical particle (*yu-zhùcí*); it does not refer to the "object" (*suǒ*) in the sense of "subject-object" (*néng-suǒ*).

[Note] "Distinct dedication" (*biexiang*) refers to the connection with the stage of Perfect Faith (*yuanxin*). "Distinct ground" (*biedi*) refers to the connection with the stage of Superior Progression (*shengjin*).
[Supplement] This clarifies the teachings that are connected; there is a distinction between "semblance stages" (*siliwei*) and "true stages" (*zhenwei*). A semblance stage is a stage of resemblance;

it refers to those who have partially severed *dṛṣṭi-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* afflictions and are thus connected by the ten distinct dedications (*bie shixiang*), up to the cultivation of the Middle Way.

The Path: Those who have subdued ignorance and are received by the ten stages of the Perfect Teaching’s faith (*śraddhā*)—namely, the ten transferences of the Distinct Teaching and the ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching—are both considered "conformable" (*sādṛśya*), as they all occupy the stage of severing the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*).

Now, because one wishes to receive those who have severed the afflictions of views and thought, the teachings of the Distinct Transferences and the Perfect Faith are employed to cover them; thus, those so received are established in their respective positions according to the Distinct Teaching.
They are among those within the Perfect Teaching (Yuan); hence it is said, "to receive them according to their station. "True station" refers to the station of partial realization (fenzhen).

This means that while the teaching of the Shared Vehicle (Tongjiao) eliminates afflictions by severing only the delusions of views and thought (jian-si), when compared with the latter two teachings [the Distinct and the Perfect], this is merely a state of semblance (xiangsi).

Because its faculties are sharp, one is able to perceive non-emptiness; now, wishing to guide and lead such practitioners, one employs the stages of the Distinct Teaching (Biedi) and the dwellings of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzhu).
When these teachings are spread and encompassed, those who encounter them will, according to their respective progress, become practitioners of either the Distinct or the Perfect [Vehicles].

Generally, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward in the Distinct Teaching, and from the first *vihāra* onward in the Perfect Teaching, all belong to the stage of "partial realization" (*pratilambha-satya*), as they are all positions where ignorance (*avidyā*) is being shattered.
Thus, by means of this profound stage of shattering ignorance, one connects with the severing of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
This refers to a shallow stage; hence it is said that there is "reception upon superior progress.

[Note]: According to the preceding, it appears that one at a provisional stage is received and one at a true stage undergoes reception; thus, the character "bei" (to be) should be used. This is because the active agent follows the passive object.

[Commentary] This explains the character "receive" (*shou*) in the phrase "receiving the transition" (*shouchie*) regarding the true stage (*zhenwei*). In accordance with the meaning, it would be more appropriate to use the character "cover" (*bei*).
Why? It is because the "being received" (*beicheng*) in the aforementioned stage of semblance (*sili*) refers to being covered (*fubei*), acting as the agent of reception;

therefore, the character "receive" (*shou*) in "receiving the transition" at the subsequent true stage should also be read as the character "cover" (*bei*), so that both may equally function as the agent.

Regarding the phrase "receiving the reception" (*jiejie*) in the ritual text: it is because the position of the one who receives (*nengjie*) follows the sequence of the three faculties (*san-gen*) of the one being received (*suo-jie*). [Note: *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), Vol.

3, Part 2 (8), states: "If 'receiving the reception' is entered into the Path of Teaching (*jiaodao*), it occurs within the stage of Dedication (*huixiang*); if it is entered into the Path of Realization (*zhengdao*)," etc.]
The Path exists within the First Stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). If one enters the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), it is likewise divided into the Path of Teaching and the Path of Realization;

this can be understood from what follows (text). [Commentary] Regarding the "Path of Teaching" and the "Path of Realization": the teaching that expresses [the truth] constitutes the Path of Teaching, because verbal expression proceeds in a sequential order.
The principle that is realized constitutes the Path of Realization, because the True Reality is non-dual. [This refers to] the Three Preliminary Stages (*trayaḥ kṣānti*) of the Separate Teaching.

While within these stages, one has not yet shattered ignorance and must still practice and realize; such practice necessarily proceeds through successive stages, and such realization necessarily proceeds through successive stages.

Therefore, this belongs to the Path of Teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). Once one ascends to the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), ignorance has already been shattered and True Suchness (*tathatā*) is directly realized;

therefore, this belongs to the Path of Realization (*adhigama-mārga*). If one were to further subdivide the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*) into teaching and realization, it is because the Perfect Teaching fundamentally possesses no distinction between teaching and realization.
It is distinct. If one wishes to differentiate it, the explanation of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) may serve as an analogy.

That is to say, entry into the Path of Cultivation occurs within the stage of the Six Organs’ Purity; entry into the Path of Realization occurs at the First Abode (Prathama-bhūmi). Therefore, it is said that "the explanation may be known by analogy."

[Note] Furthermore, regarding the interfusion of the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles]: it connects the Noble but does not connect the Worthy; it connects the Real but does not connect the Conventional.
If the Perfect connects with the Separate, it connects the Conventional but does not connect the Real; it connects the Worthy but does not connect the Noble.

[Commentary] This section distinguishes between the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) and the Shared, Connecting, and Separate Teachings (Tong, Jie, and Bie), each having its own specific cases regarding whether they are "connected" or "not connected.
For instance, in the Shared Teaching, from the third and fourth stages (*bhūmi*) onward, one has already attained the severance of delusions and is therefore termed a "sage" (*ārya*).

In the first and second stages, one does not sever delusions at all and can only be termed a "worthy" (*bhadra*). Since even the [delusions of] views are not severed, how could it be discussed that they are "connected"? Therefore, it is said:

It is that one is received [into the higher realms] as a Sage, not as an Ordinary Person (*bhadra*). The first two stages are considered conventional (*saṃvṛti*); the latter seven stages are considered real (*tattva*), with the exception of the Buddha-stage.
Since the first two are not received [into the higher realms], it is said that "one is received into the Real, not the Conventional.

In the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), the forty preceding positions where ignorance (*avidyā*) has not yet been shattered are collectively termed "conventional. From the attainment of the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) onward, ignorance is progressively shattered. All...

It is called a "mantra. Regarding the phrase "connecting with the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) but not connecting with the real (*tattva*"): because the Real is the realization of the Way where [conventional and ultimate] are equally perfected (*pariniṣpanna*), there is no need to connect with it.

Therefore, that which is connected is only the conventional. The conventional is the level of the worthy (*ārya-pudgala*), while the Real is the level of the sage (*ārya*). Within the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) as well, there are three different faculties.

Those of superior faculty can be connected as soon as they reach the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*). Those of middling faculty [are connected] only upon reaching the ten stages of practice (*daśa-pratipatti*).

Those of inferior capacity can be grafted; they must wait until the tenth stage (*daśamī-bhūmi*) before they can be grafted. This is according to the delimitations of the teachings, whereby the principle of receiving a graft is established.
Thus, while those who come from the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) may be grafted, as for those in the noble true stages (*sheng zhen wei*), they are like those at the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*):

having already shattered ignorance (*avidyā*) and having already perfected the true cause, they flow into [the ultimate] spontaneously. Why would they need further grafting? Therefore, they are not grafted by the Perfect Teaching.

Furthermore, in the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning), following the teachings that express [the truth], it fully explains the "three receptions" from the perspective of the path of teaching (*jiao-dao*). In the *Zhi-guan* (Calming and Contemplation), because the purpose is to accomplish contemplation,
it explains only the "one reception" from the perspective of the path of realization (*zheng-dao*), based on the principle that is expressed.
[Commentary] This clarifies the connection between the two divisions of the teachings (*dvividha-dharma-paryāya*), and how their three aspects differ. Regarding the question:

"Why is it said that the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*) connects to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), rather than being said to connect to the Tripitaka (*piṭaka*)? The answer is: Because in the Separate Teaching, one first cultivates the two contemplations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the provisional (*prajñapti*).

Only when the delusions regarding the two truths of the real (*satya*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) are exhausted does one hear of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Nevertheless, one must still cultivate contemplation to destroy ignorance (*avidyā*) and manifest the eight aspects of Buddhahood (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa-buddhatva*).
"Buddha" refers to this fruit. It still requires the preceding contemplations to serve as its cause; therefore, it is said that "the Separate [Vehicle] connects to the Shared [Vehicle].

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) explains the meaning of the question as follows: "Why is it said only that the Separate connects to the Shared, rather than saying the Separate connects to the Storehouse [Teaching]?

Why is it said only that the Separate connects [to the Shared], rather than saying the Separate connects to the Perfect [Vehicle]? The answer means: The Shared must be connected by the Separate because the capacities of sentient beings differ. If the beginning and the end were not...

If one hears [the teaching] at the very beginning, it belongs entirely to the former two stages. If one hears it upon reaching the eighth stage after having exhausted the two delusions, then it belongs entirely to the latter two stages.

Furthermore, there is another person who, having completely destroyed the two delusions and reached the eighth stage, hears [the teaching] while practicing contemplation therein; they subsequently destroy ignorance and attain the essence of the Dharma-body.

Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases: although one may perceive the Middle Way, one must necessarily rely on the two contemplations of emptiness and provisionality from the Shared Teaching (*p’ung-gyo*) as a preliminary expedient for advancement;
furthermore, one must await the principle of the Distinct Teaching (*byeol-gyo*) to receive the "distinct reception" (*byeol-jeop*). As for what is now termed "distinct reception":

It should possess two meanings: first, the distinct teaching (*biejiao*), because it teaches what is proximate; second, the distinct principle (*bili*), because its principle differs from the ultimate truth (*zhen*).

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* states: "In the *Xuanyan*, the connection between the Perfect and the Distinct is divided into 'teaching' and 'realization,' because their stages of practice and positions are distinct."
The reason it is not mentioned now is because it pertains to the path of realization (*darśana-mārga*) and concerns only the perspective of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). As the *Shiqian* states:

"Within the context of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, in order to establish the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), one merely uses the principle beyond the realm [of desire] to connect with the principle within the realm. This applies to both the Shared and Distinct Teachings;
thus, this clarifies the intersection of these two principles, and so it is said that the Distinct Teaching connects to the Shared. Now, the first six stages of the *Xuanyu* still maintain this.

Regarding the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*), there are two perspectives: the perfect (*pariniṣpanna*) connecting with the provisional (*neyārtha*), and the distinct (*vibhinna*) connecting with the provisional.

Since the path of reality (*tattva-mārga*) connects the provisional with the principle of the perfect alone, the commentary on this passage must rely upon the path of teaching. Furthermore, it is the perfect within the middle [truth] that connects with the mere middle.

As for the six stages: first, the *āgama* (Tripitaka); second, the *sāmānya* (Shared); third, the distinct connecting with the shared; fourth, the perfect connecting with the shared; fifth, the distinct; and sixth, the perfect connecting with the distinct. — *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation).

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) combines these three. Furthermore, there are passages clarifying that the Perfect [Teaching] does not admit of "receiving" (*jie*) from other vehicles; those who require them should examine them in detail. [Note:

Nevertheless, the Perfect and Sudden *Zhiguan* also clarifies the subject of "being received," so that one may know the points of penetration and obstruction, and further manifest this through the use of conceptual thought.
How inconceivable! As stated in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), fascicle 3, section 17:
"This point indicates the clear connection of the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. It has another meaning that cannot be discussed as being on the same level as the preceding section.
For this Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* has already been revealed through the *Lotus Sūtra*; it is solely this [one vehicle]."
This is the reality; the other two are not true. What "connection" or "non-connection" could there be? For the three previous teachings involve obstructions, acceptance, and rejection;
whereas this present Dharma-gate observes only the single thought-moment of our own minds, transcending both subject and object.
It is absolute dependence; subject and object are non-dual, and principle and wisdom are one and the same.

When one looks back upon the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, they are like the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. To have that which is produced by one's own mind [unimpededly manifest] is called "penetration" (*tong*).

If there is even the slightest trace of obstruction within the inner mind, it is called "blockage" (*sai*). Therefore, this dharma-gate is inconceivable; this single thought-moment is originally endowed with it.

The nature and characteristics of the three thousand realms, and the thousand suchnesses of the hundred worlds: above, they are equal to those of the Buddhas; below, they are of one suchness with sentient beings.
Suchness is likewise so for the mind, and suchness is likewise so for Buddhas and sentient beings; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.

Furthermore, when practicing *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, to become attached to the names of the true and the arising is called "obstruction"; to be able to penetrate that which is between them is called "penetration. True suchness is the realm.
The internal provisional principle is called "conceivable. The middle [principle], which is the true principle outside the realm [of delusion], is called "inconceivable.

*Fuxing* asks: The *Xuanyiwen* states that "connecting" (*jie*) does not have the same meaning as "uniting" (*hui*). Now, regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, one should only discuss "uniting. Why, then, do you discuss "connecting"? Answer:

In the various preceding and subsequent texts, the meaning of "uniting" is not uniform. Since we are now discussing the cultivation of contemplation (*guan*), it is also permissible to speak of "connecting" again.
In describing the teachings prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, I have used them as examples to illustrate the signs of progress and obstruction in the practitioner's path.

Since the gateways of teaching themselves possess these characteristics of penetration and blockage, they must be clarified. Clarifying the process of "reception" (*jiejie*) in this manner does not hinder the ultimate "convergence" (*huihe*); moreover, such reception occurs specifically within the stage of the bodhisattva.

The context of the assembly is no different [from what precedes]. Furthermore, throughout the preceding and following passages, it is consistently clarified that [the dharmas] are "conceivable" and so forth;

however, this is merely for the purpose of manifesting the "inconceivable. Thus, the former depends upon the latter to reach its cessation, and such a sequence is naturally appropriate. Why, then, must one ask whether they should not be joined in discussion?
△ Third, distinguishing [the Separate Teaching] from the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings. First, the question: Question:
These two teachings, the Tripitaka and the Shared, are both for the three vehicles; both sever the four abidings; both merely exit the triple world; both realize partial truth;
both practice for three hundred *yojanas*; and both enter the illusory city. For what reason are they divided into two?
△ Second, the response, which has two parts. First, granting the premise, the response: "Truly as you have asked.
△ Second, the definitive judgment, which has two parts. First, analyzing that there is difference within the same [category].
Nevertheless, they are identical yet not identical. Although that which is realized is the same, the Great and Small Vehicles differ eternally in their skillfulness and crudeness.

These two teachings belong to the teachings within the realm (*dhātu*). II. The Second Part: A Correct Explanation of the Reasons for Their Differences. This has two sections. First, clarifying the crudeness of the *piṭaka* teachings.
The *Zang* (Treasury) school is limited within its own realm and does not penetrate the Great [Vehicle]; therefore, it is "Small. It reduces form into emptiness; therefore, it is "Crude.

Although there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior among the three types of practitioners within this teaching, when viewed in relation to those who have attained penetration, they are all uniformly of dull faculties.
Therefore, it must be analyzed and deconstructed.

[Commentary] However, although the three vehicles of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and *Pratyekabuddha* (Shared) teachings are identical in their severing of delusions, their departure from the realms, and their realization of principle, they differ in their teaching and practice, as well as in their magnitude.

Regarding the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and the Mahāyāna, in terms of skillfulness and clumsiness, and in terms of discussing essence versus analysis, those teachings that correspond to the expedient lands outside the realm are called "teachings within the realm.

These two [vehicles] teach and transform those within the realm; they do not extend to the Great [Vehicle], and are thus termed "Small," because they cannot reach far to communicate with the eternal abiding.
Regarding the analysis of form into emptiness: externalists calculate that the *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom) does not escape the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
Now, by observing the arising and ceasing of form and mind as a whole, one sees they are neither annihilated nor eternal, thereby refuting the non-Buddhists. Your assertion is not correct;
this is as explained in the *Zhi guan* (3.26) and the *Fuxing* (3.4).
[Commentary: This clarifies that for those of dull faculties, the teachings of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) and the *Vaipulya* (Shared) are similar; for those of sharp faculties, they differ greatly.

However, the teaching of the *Āgama* is that of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), while the teaching of the *Vaipulya* is that of non-arising (*anutpāda*). The contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) of the *Āgama* is analytical emptiness (*vibhanga-śūnyatā*), whereas the contemplation of the *Vaipulya* is essential emptiness (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*);

thus it is said that there is a difference in teaching and practice. Regarding the distinction between "Small" and "Great" based on the Small and the Mahāyāna (*vaipulya*), this is a further explanation of the difference in teaching.

This means that the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) is the Hinayana, while the *Vaipulya* is the Mahayana; this constitutes the difference between the Great and Small Vehicles in terms of their teachings (*śāsana*).

Regarding the discussion of skill versus clumsiness in analyzing the essence: this refers to the difference in the practice (*caryā*) of transformation and interpretation. That is to say, those of the *Āgama* school analyze form (*rūpa*) to clarify emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereas those of the *Vaipulya* school realize emptiness within form itself;
this constitutes the difference between skill and clumsiness in practice. To speak of "opposing" refers to the designation of the "beyond-realm" (*dharmadhātu-bāhya*) as the "realm" (*dhātu*).

Regarding the internal teachings, they are spoken of in terms of the four lands. The two teachings of the Tripitaka and the Shared merely transform the six realms of ordinary beings within the land of common residence for both ordinary people and sages.
The two teachings of the Distinctive and the Perfect transform all three lands: the land of expedient means, the land of true retribution, and the land of serene light.

These are the four noble dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Thus, one should know that the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings are designated as "teachings within the realm" (*jiejiaojiao*) in contrast to the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) realms.
Regarding the statement that they cannot reach the eternally abiding (*changzhu*), this "eternally abiding" refers to the wondrous principle of the Middle Way within the Mahāyāna.
It is distant by five hundred *yojanas*, yet because the teachings within the realm of the *Hīnayāna* (Zàngshèng) cannot penetrate it, it is considered "small.

The section on "analyzing form to enter emptiness" specifically clarifies the ineptitude of the contemplative practice of those in the *Hīnayāna*. The first two phrases present the externalist calculations;
from "now, in total" (*jǐn zǒng*) below, it clarifies that although the practice of the *Hīnayāna* is inept, it is nonetheless capable of refuting heterodoxy. The final two phrases [conclude this].
Citing scriptural evidence: As stated in the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) when refuting the external "adjacent atom" (*paramāṇu*):

"Is this dust-atom existent or non-existent? If there is such a color of an ultimate atom, it must possess divisions in the ten directions; if there is no such color of an ultimate atom, it lacks divisions in the ten directions.

If one analyzes the color of the ultimate atom without exhausting it, one falls into the eternalist view of existence; if one exhausts the analysis, one falls into the nihilist view of non-existence."

[The Buddha] saw that these non-Buddhists analyze form (*rūpa*), and they analyze the mind (*citta*) in the same way. Whether [they assert it] exists or does not exist, they all fall into the extremes of nihilism or eternalism.
Regarding the *Tripiṭaka-vibhaṅga-śāstra*, it says: "Whether form is coarse or subtle, when observed as a whole, it is impermanent and without self.
Since form arises from ignorance (*avidyā*), and ignorance is unreal, both the coarse and the subtle are merely provisional (*prajñapti*). Because they are provisional, they do not [truly exist]."

By realizing that all things are eternally devoid of intrinsic nature, one enters into emptiness. Furthermore, the arising of even a fleeting thought necessarily relies upon the sense organs and their objects;
there is not a single dharma that does not arise from conditions. That which arises from conditions is entirely impermanent.

Some say a single thought-moment consists of sixty *kṣaṇas*, while others say it consists of ten billion *kṣaṇas*. Moment by moment there is no abiding; every thought is impermanent. It continues thus until... [it is said]:

"Analysis of form by name" (*ming-xi-se-guan*) refers to the intention [of this contemplation]. "Analyzing names" originated with non-Buddhists; however, in contrast to their heterodox analysis, this is called "correct analysis.
Not only must heterodox views be correctly analyzed, but even the attachments arising from the four gates of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) must likewise be analyzed and shattered.
The *Fuxing* commentary explains: "Spatial divisions" refer to nothing more than atoms (*paramāṇu*). Whatever exists is necessarily form (*rūpa*). Form...
There must be a spatial direction (*diś*). A direction must have divisions; there are the ten spatial divisions.
Next, one analyzes and further dissects the atom (*paramāṇu*). Because it is analyzed, it is exhausted. If a single atom can be exhausted, then all atoms can be exhausted.
If they can be exhausted, how could they combine to form a body? If they cannot be exhausted, then a single atom is permanent, and all atoms are permanent. If...
If this were permanent, the body would not undergo cessation; therefore, this is not the correct analytical characteristic of the Buddha’s Dharma. The analysis of the mind is likewise.
If a single moment of mind could not be exhausted, how could a subsequent moment arise? Yet a subsequent moment does arise.

The preceding mind must necessarily cease. If it were to cease forever, how could a subsequent mind arise? Therefore, one knows that each moment arises and ceases; it is neither annihilated nor eternal.
Now, when the Tripiṭaka masters analyze phenomena (*dharma*), they first contemplate form (*rūpa*) and subsequently contemplate the mind (*citta*).
When contemplating form and mind, they merely observe their coarseness and subtlety, as well as their impermanence and selflessness; there is no need to speak of "exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) or...
Because it is inexhaustible: that is to say, from a single moment of past ignorance, the various formations (*saṃskāra*) arise;
furthermore, upon reaching the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), my ignorant mind again unites with the ignorant minds of the parents to produce the physical body.

Even the environment and its retributions are likewise collectively induced by the karma of shared ignorance. Therefore, there is nothing—neither the primary body nor the secondary environment—that does not arise from ignorance.
It arises; the substance of ignorance exists through causes and conditions, and thus even derived matter (bhautika-rūpa) likewise arises from causes and conditions.
One should know that both cause and effect are impermanent. How can one reckon them as being either exhausted or inexhaustible? The observation of the mind is also like this.
Past moments give rise to the present moment; how much more so does the present moment exist by virtue of external conditions and causes?

Therefore, every thought-moment is entirely impermanent. When investigating in this manner, one sees that it is not only consciousness and form that are impermanent, but even further, one realizes that mental states are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, thereby perceiving the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the dharma-nature as eternally abiding. However...
This analysis of names originated with the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). Now, observing impermanence is also termed "analysis.
The above passages are all from the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practices), which were originally intended to refute the non-Buddhists; your analysis is not correct.
△ Second, explaining the skillfulness of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), in two parts.

First, the formal explanation of the skillfulness of the Great [Vehicle] within the Shared Teaching. "Great" refers to it being the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna. "Skillful" refers to the fact that its substance (the form-aggregate) enters into emptiness.

Although there are distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior among the three types of practitioners within this teaching, when viewed in comparison with the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao), they are all treated as one.
[Commentary]:

This applies to both the Shared and Distinct/Perfect [teachings], and is therefore the initial gateway. One thoroughly understands that all phenomena are like illusions and transformations; their very substance is emptiness.
[Commentary] This clarifies the skillfulness of those who have attained penetration. Therefore, it serves as the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna.

Because one can thoroughly comprehend all phenomena as being like dreams, illusions, bubbles, shadows, reflections in a mirror, or the moon in water—ultimately unobtainable and entirely empty in their very substance—for this reason, the Separate and Perfect [Teachings] rely upon this for guidance.
△ Second, the inclusion of the two vehicles within the comprehensive [teaching]. First, the inquiry.
Question: Since the teaching is already Mahāyāna, why are there persons of the two vehicles?
[Commentary]: The intent of the question is that since this teaching is called the initial gate of the Mahāyāna, the capacities of those for whom it is intended must necessarily be...
He is a Great Being who benefits both [self and others]. Why, then, would there be those of the śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and solitary good [who seek only their own benefit]?
△ Second, the explanation of the answer:
The answer is that within the Vermilion Bird Gate (the South Gate), what prevents commoners from entering and exiting? Therefore, although the person may be small, the teaching is certainly great.
The Mahāyāna incorporates the Hīnayāna, gradually leading beings into the ultimate reality; how ingenious this is!
[Commentary] The southern gate of the Heavenly Son is called Zhuque (the Vermilion Bird). "Gradually leading into the reality" clarifies the Buddha’s intention.
[Commentary] This explains, according to the Buddha’s intention, how one is gradually led into the ultimate reality. It reflects the meaning of the saying:
"First, one is drawn in by the hook of desire; later, one is caused to enter the Buddha-wisdom. As the *Zhi guan* says:

"It is like the Vermilion Bird Gate, established by the Son of Heaven, which primarily facilitates royal affairs yet does not hinder the passage of commoners. Although they are but lowly persons, it remains ultimately the gate of the Son of Heaven."
Now, the Mahāyāna is also like this: it is precisely for the sake of bodhisattvas who realize the nature of phenomena and enter emptiness.

Although there is the Hīnayāna, it is ultimately termed "Great. One should know that when persons of small capacity enter and exit the gateway of the Mahāyāna teachings, it is because they are transforming the small into the great.
As for "gradually leading them into the reality," this refers to guiding them through successive stages, causing them to cultivate [the path].
One enters and arrives at the ground of perfect reality; thus, although it is small, it is great.

Therefore, the practice cultivated by those of the Two Vehicles within the Shared Teaching may also be called "skillful deliverance. Regarding the statement that the South Gate of the Son of Heaven is called Zhuque:
the King is referred to as the "Son of Heaven" (Tianzi) to indicate that he is no ordinary person, for he possesses protective guardianship.

His virtue and his benevolent grace in nurturing the people are truly like those of a Son of Heaven. Thus, the proverb says: "That which all spirits tremble before and protect is the Sage Son of Heaven.
Regarding the capital where he resides, each of its four gates in the four directions has its own name:

the east is called Qinglong (Azure Dragon), the west is called Baihu (White Tiger), the south is called Zhuque (Vermilion Bird), and the north is called Xuanwu (Mysterious Warrior). Now, taking the Gate of Correct Yang...
The Southern Gate. How much more so for the initial gate of the Mahāyāna of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), wherein both the Great and Small Vehicles enter and exit together.
△ Fourth, the conclusion regarding the affiliated texts:
within the Prajñā and Vaipulya divisions, the *Prajñāpāramitā-samaya* and others belong precisely to this teaching.
[Commentary on the *Śūnyatā-saṃgraha* (Shiqian), Fascicle 4, Section 19] states: "The Tripiṭaka and the four Āgamas are distinct from other collections of texts (*bùzhì*).
Here, among the various Vaipulya and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, those that constitute the common practice of the Three Vehicles are judged to belong to the 'Shared' (*tōng*) category. (Text).

In the present passage, the term "Prajñā" broadly refers to the Vaipulya; the subsequent mention of "common Prajñā," etc., likely refers to the Vaipulya’s function of refuting and challenging [other views].
The meaning is somewhat obscure.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase in the ritual text, "the *sādhāraṇa-prajñā* and so forth within the *prajñā* and *vaipulya* sections," this does not restrict the term *sādhāraṇa-prajñā* solely to those teachings heard by the three vehicles within the *prajñā-pāramitā* corpus. Rather, the intent is to include both the *vaipulya* and *prajñā* [sections].
Within that section, those who hear it together across the three vehicles are all termed "Shared Prajñā. As stated in the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning):
"Although there is no separate text for Shared Prajñā, one simply takes passages from within the Vaipulya Prajñā [sūtras] that occur at the same time or in the same assembly."
Chapter One: Clarifying the Shared Meaning Alone. Its manifestations are also many. Now, observing this text, we know that within the Vaipulya (fangděng) division there is also "Shared Prajñā";

this is precisely the passage belonging to this teaching. The commentary cites the *Shiqian* (Exposition of the Profound Meaning) to provide proof, stating that it is "not the same as the Tripiṭaka," because the teachings of the Tripiṭaka consist of the four Āgamas... [text continues].
The *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra* and others constitute distinct sections (*buzhi*). Now, this Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) has no separate section of its own;

therefore, that which was heard together by the three vehicles during the two periods [of the Vaipulya and Prajñā] is judged to belong to the Shared Teaching. Yet, it is not called "Shared Vaipulya," but rather "Shared Prajñā.
This is because the Vaipulya emphasizes censure and rebuke, making the sense of "shared" somewhat remote, whereas the emptiness of the Prajñā...
The Thesis: It is precisely this that constitutes the sublime purport of the teaching. Thus, to say that the "Shared Prajñā" is the ultimate perfection of goodness.
△ Third, the Conclusion:
The brief explanation of the Shared Teaching is complete.
[Commentary] This sentence summarizes the entire text of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). Regarding the phrase "briefly elucidated":

because the preceding and succeeding sections of the Shared Teaching are mutually integrated, and the Great and Small Vehicles do not obstruct one another, how could one possibly exhaustively dissect its profundities? It is merely a matter of providing a brief explanation and clarification.
