The *Miaozong*, fascicle upper (23), states: "When there are delusions yet to be severed, one is called an 'Upward-Bound Person' (you shangshi)" [text].
[Commentary] Regarding the term "one more birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha): because ignorance has not yet been exhausted, there remains one grade of the characteristic of birth.

If one can employ the diamond-like contemplation (*vajropama-samādhi*) to further shatter one grade of ignorance, this is called "having passed one birth," and one may then succeed to the station of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksambuddhatva*).
Regarding the phrase "still like a crown prince": it is like a king’s heir apparent who is about to...
Shao faces south. Because he was first temporarily enshrined in the Eastern Palace, he is called the "Heir Apparent" (Chujun).
As for the "Superior Being with Superiority" (You Shangshi), this refers to Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), which is a stage of cause rather than a stage of fruition.
Since there is still the ultimate fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue) above it, it cannot be called "Unsurpassed"; therefore, it is described as a "Superior Being with Superiority."
△ Second, the clarification of the fruition has two parts. First, the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment:
having further destroyed one grade of ignorance, he enters the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-bodhi*).
Seated beneath the seven-jeweled Bodhi tree on the Great Jewel Flower King Throne in the Lotus Treasury World (*padmagarbha-loka*), he manifests the complete Reward Body (*vipāka-kāya*).
[Note] The *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 4 (15), states: "At the final mind of the Vajra stage, there is the vast and luminous Great Enlightenment.

Wondrous wisdom exhausts the source; the habitual tendencies of ignorance are extinguished, which is called True Liberation. Being carefree and free from all burdens, it is quiescent yet constantly illuminating; this is called the Stage of Wondrous Enlightenment" (text).

[Commentary] This clarifies the characteristics of attaining Buddhahood through the ultimate fruit of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*). The annotation cites the text to explain its fulfillment.

The first three phrases clarify the perfection of the merit of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*); the next three phrases clarify the perfection of the merit of cessation (*prahāṇaguṇa*); and the final two phrases mean that quiescence is itself the wondrous.
"Illumination" means awakening.
[Commentary] "Treasury" (garbha) means that it encompasses the dharma-realm of the ten directions, all of which are contained within it (text).
[Record] The Sūtra says: "In the Flower Treasury World-Ocean, there are worlds as numerous as the atoms in ten unspeakable numbers of Buddha-lands."
Each of these types consists of twenty layers of worlds.

[Commentary] Regarding the Bodhi tree made of the seven treasures: the multiplicity of the seven treasures symbolizes the infinite. Regarding the great jewel-flower king-throne: the *Miaoxuan* (7.12) states:
"Some say it is the site of the path of tranquil extinction (*śānta-mārga-kṣetra*), with a throne of seven-jeweled flowers; the body corresponds to the flower."
Upon each of the thousand petals of the flower pedestal is a bodhisattva; furthermore, there are ten billion bodhisattvas, such that there are thus a thousand times ten billion bodhisattvas.

From the white tuft of hair (*ūrṇā*) and from his emanated bodies, light radiates throughout the ten directions. This light from the white tuft enters the crowns of the heads of the bodhisattvas upon the flower pedestal.
The light from the divided bodies enters the crowns of the Bodhisattvas’ heads; this is called "receiving the rank of Dharma King.

Having thoroughly attained the depths of all Buddha-dharmas, they achieve Buddhahood. The flower pedestal is called the *saṃbhoga*-buddha (reward-buddha), and those upon the flower petals are called the *nirmāṇa*-buddhas (response-buddhas).
The *saṃbhoga* and *nirmāṇa* are merely related to one another; they cannot be identified as identical. This is the appearance of the distinct attainment of the Buddha-fruit (text).
[Commentary] Regarding the "Field of Quiescent Extinction" (*śānti-kṣetra*), see the notes in the first fascicle. As for the "seat of seven-jeweled flowers," the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"Those flowers are vast, equal in measure to a million triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems.

They are adorned with an intermingling of various precious flowers... [and so on], up to: 'with *vaiḍūrya* mani-jewels for their stalks and *candana-rāja* sandalwood for their calyxes. *Maṇi*... [text continues].
Its stamens are made of vaidūrya, and its petals are made of Jāmbūnada gold. This flower constantly emits immeasurable radiance;
its interior is composed of various jewels, and it is completely covered by jeweled nets. It has as many lotus flowers as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms as its retinue.
When a bodhisattva sits upon this lotus seat, their physical form and the dimensions of the seat are perfectly proportioned. Immeasurable...

The Bodhisattva sat upon a remaining lotus flower, with other flowers as his retinue. From the space between the eyebrows of the Buddhas of the ten directions, a pure light issued forth, named "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Supernormal Powers. It was accompanied by countless rays of light as its retinue, universally illuminating all worlds throughout the ten directions.
After circling ten times to the right, it manifested various kinds of magnificent adornments.
They enter through the crown of the Great Bodhisattva’s head; their retinues of light likewise each enter the crowns of those various bodhisattvas.
This bodhisattva attains one million samādhis never before attained, which is called having attained the rank of consecration.
He enters the realm of the Buddha, becomes fully endowed with the ten powers, and is reckoned among the Buddhas. Thus concludes the perfection.
Regarding the *saṃbhogakāya*: it is as if, when one first sits upon the lotus pedestal, the attendant bodhisattvas all sit upon the lotus petals.

The Buddhas of the ten directions emit light from between their eyebrows which enters the crown of the lotus pedestal; the retinues of those Buddhas also emit light from between their eyebrows which enters the crowns of the lotus petals.
The bodhisattva on the lotus pedestal receives his office through samādhi and becomes a *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha, while the bodhisattvas on the petals...
Sakyamuni attained the Sambhogakaya Buddha; because his great conditions and vision were superior, he manifested as the perfect Rupakaya Buddha.
Second, regarding the turning of the Great Dharma Wheel:
for the assembly of Bodhisattvas with pure faculties, he turned the immeasurable wheel of the Four Noble Truths; this refers to this very Buddha.

[Commentary] Bodhisattvas with blunt faculties (puruṣendriya) are so called because their delusion within saṃsāra is profound; they progress through gradual cultivation and realization to reach the precious destination. In contrast to those of the Perfect Teaching (yuan), they are termed "blunt."
[Supplement] At the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to manifest bodies in a hundred worlds and fully turn the wheel of the Dharma of the four teachings.
Here, the term "immeasurable" is used because the delusion regarding the individual person's Middle Way is heavy;

since one practices based on the immeasurable Four Truths during the causal stage, one also turns the immeasurable wheel of the Four Truths at the level of the fruit. This is what is meant by "in terms of the teaching," which pertains from beginning to end.
This is what is meant by "instruction.

△ Third, specifically showing [the teaching] according to capacities has two parts. First, the actual clarification of instruction according to capacities has three parts. First, pointing out and showing the path of instruction:

There are sutras and treatises which state that from the seventh stage downward is called the Path of Effort (*sābhoga-mārga*), and from the eighth stage upward is called the Path Without Effort (*anābhoga-mārga*).

Regarding the "Path of Practice" (*yòng dào*): the statement that those at the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*miào jué*) merely break through one grade of ignorance refers entirely to the Path of Teaching (*jiào dào*).
[Note] The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "When a Bodhisattva has not yet reached the eighth stage, it is like a person riding a boat who wishes to cross the great ocean."

Before reaching the great ocean, much effort and power are required; but once one reaches the eighth stage, proceeding from great skillful means toward the wisdom of the Buddha, there is no need for effortful application of mind, nor does one expend further labor.

[Commentary] The following section provides a detailed analysis of the sutras and treatises regarding the determination of stages (*bhūmi*). There are differences between the Shared (*tong*), Distinct (*bie*), and Perfect (*yuan*) teachings;
the text of this current section belongs to the Distinct Teaching. As the text on the eighth stage in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"For example, suppose there is a person who, in a dream, sees his body falling into a great river. Desiring to cross it, he exerts great courage and employs great skillful means. By means of these...
By the power of courageous skillful means, one immediately awakens; having awakened, all that was to be done comes to rest. It is the same for the Bodhisattva:
seeing sentient beings within the turbulent flow, for the sake of their rescue and deliverance, they give rise to great courage and exert great diligence.
By virtue of such courageous diligence, they reach the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*). Having reached this stage, all...
All functional activities cease without exception.
[Note] It is not yet clear on what textual authority it is said that the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (miao-jue-wei) destroys only one grade of ignorance.
[Supplement] This is the definitive statement of Master Yu; Master Zhao says it is from the *Lengyan Sanmei Jing* (Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra). The text states: "First..."
The *Lengyan* samādhi is not attained from the first stage through the ninth stage; it can only be attained at the tenth stage.
Since it is attained only at the tenth stage, one then enters the Buddha-stage, which involves the destruction of but a single grade of ignorance.
[Note] Various texts merely state that by severing twelve grades [of delusion], one is designated as "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue).

[Commentary] At the stage of the fruit in the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao), it corresponds to the two practices of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). If one advances three stages further, the name is not known;

therefore, we know this is explained in terms of the path of teaching (jiaodao). Beyond the severance of eleven grades of ignorance at the level of Equal Enlightenment (Dengque), one further destroys one grade. This is...
Is it that by severing only twelve grades [of afflictions], one is designated as "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue)?
△ Second, borrowing specific names to apply them generally:

There are places where it is said that the first stage (bhūmi) severs the afflictions of views (dṛṣṭi), while the second through sixth stages sever the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā), thereby being equal to an Arhat. This...
This merely borrows the names of the stages of the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) to designate the stages of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).

[Note] Regarding the statement that "reaching the sixth stage, one cuts off the afflictions of the realm of thought (sīfàn), becoming equal to an Arhat": this takes the meaning of the Ten Perfections (shìdù). It is because one cuts off delusions through the sixth perfection, the wisdom of emptiness (*prajñā*).
This is as explained in the section on "Borrowing Stages" in the sixth fascicle of the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Treatise on Calming and Contemplation), and so forth.

[Commentary] This section properly belongs to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao). The statement that "the first stage (*bhūmi*) severs [delusions of] views" and so forth was cited previously in the seventh fascicle.

Regarding the mention of "taking up the meaning of the ten perfections (*pāramitā*)," this is for the convenience of following the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning). Among the ten perfections, the sixth, Prajñā, is the wisdom that enters into emptiness;
when the severing of delusions is complete, one is equal to an Arhat. Upon reaching the seventh, the Perfection of Skillful Means (*upāya-prajñā*),...

This is because they emerge from the provisional to manifest transformative functions. Regarding the *Zhi guan* (Calming and Contemplation), the text states: "The old [tradition] says that the exhaustion of thought at the sixth stage is equivalent to an Arhat.
[Commentary] As for the ten pāramitās, these are the six pāramitās with the addition of aspiration, power, knowledge, and skillful means.
△ Third, borrowing the names of other teachings to clarify the Perfect [Teaching].
Some say: "The three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood abide in retribution; only the Buddha alone dwells in the Pure Land.
This borrows the names of the Distinct Teaching to clarify the stages of the Perfect Teaching.

[Note] Regarding the "Three Sages": these refer to those dwelling in the stages of Separate Practice (Biezhuxing), Abiding (Zhu), and Approaching (Xiang). While their abiding in the land of retribution belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), this verse from the *Renyang jing* [Sūtra of the Benevolent Kings] pertains to it.

[Commentary] This section clearly belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). The *Renwang jing shu* states: "The three levels of worthiness (sān xián) refer to the thirty minds prior to the stages (dì qián sānshí xīn);

the ten sages (shí shèng) refer to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (shí dì). These forty minds are all born together in the fruition-recompense land (guǒbào tǔ) of the Flower Treasury World (Huāzàng).

This is not the fruition-recompense [land] of the Tripitaka or Shared Teachings (zàng-tōng jiào). If it were the Tripitaka Teaching, it would be the Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages; if it were the Shared Teaching,"

There are only those born in the remaining transformation cities. What is now called "retribution" refers to those of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, who attain non-obstruction and are born in the land of non-obstruction.
Question: Are the three stages of worthiness herein of the Separate or the Perfect Teaching? Answer: They are of the Perfect Teaching. Question:
The Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is conjoined with the Birth [Land] and the Constant Quiescent Light Land (Changjiguang). Why, then, is there birth in the Flower Treasury World (Huazang)? Answer:

Within the Flower Treasury World, the Separate Teaching (Biejiao) and the Perfect Teaching arise together. Because this is a cause rather than a fruit, one cannot yet be born in the Land of Constant Quiescent Light;

therefore, within the Flower Treasury Land, the ten stages (bhūmi) of the Separate Teaching and the forty minds of the Perfect Teaching arise together. This is the ultimate fruit of Wondrous Enlightenment, Vairocana.

Then, only a single person enters the Pure Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*). Question: Within the first three lands there are also pure lands; why is it that Tranquil Light alone bears this name? Answer:
In the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary Beings and Sages, sages are few and ordinary beings are many; thus it is defiled, not pure.

In the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder, although one has eliminated the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhava-kleśa*), one has not yet severed ignorance (*avidyā*); its purity is merely partial truth, not [ultimate purity].

This is the Truly Pure Land. The Flower Treasury World (Huazang) involves residual expedient means and is not yet purely pure; the Land of Tranquil Light (Jiguang) is free from these various defects and alone possesses the name "Pure Land.

Furthermore, the *Yili* states: "Some say this includes both teachings—the three stages of worthiness in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanyiao) and the ten stages of sainthood in the Separate Teaching (Bietao).
The analogy says: that which is called "retributive fruit" refers to the Land of Real Retribution (Shibao). Since one has already been born there...

The "fruit-retribution" [stage] refers precisely to those of the four stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). This master merely sees the names of the worthy and sage [stages] and immediately distinguishes between the Perfect and Separate Teachings.

The titles of "worthy and sage" are actually borrowed from the Separate Teaching to clarify the Perfect; however, being born in the True Reward Land (*sambhoga-kāya*) is what correctly clarifies the stages of the Perfect Teaching.
If one says that the stages of the worthy and sage of the Separate Teaching should not be born there, yet [the text] judges the ten... [the text is truncated].

Regarding the distinctiveness of the stages (*bhūmi*): since all forty positions within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) equally destroy ignorance, for what reason are they divided into ten distinct stages?

Furthermore, from the perspective of the path of realization (*zhengdao*), the stage is itself the dwelling (*zhu*); why then is it necessary to differentiate them? Even if one were to maintain the perspective of the path of teaching (*jiaodao*), the ten stages already encompass both teachings (the Shared and Distinct), and thus there would still be no basis for such differentiation.
△ Second, the exhortation to examine the stages of abandonment and realization.

There are many such categories; one must have detailed knowledge of the stages of abandonment and realization as taught. One must understand up to what stage one abandons which afflictions and realizes which principle.
Thus, when judging the stages of realization across various teachings, there is nothing that will not be thoroughly understood.

[Note] This is the Master Guan’s method for instructing others on the classification of teachings (*jiaopan*). One who can understand this will not only find the separate gates accessible, but will encounter no obstructions regarding any of the teachings whatsoever.

[Commentary] As for "Master Guan," he was the Dharma Master from Goryeo. Master Guan taught people that one must first carefully examine within the fundamental teachings at what stage delusions are severed and the principle realized, at which stage how many delusions are severed, and at which stage what principle is realized;
only then may one proceed to judge the various stages across the various teachings, after which nothing will remain unclear.
△ Three Bonds. The brief explanation of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) is concluded.

[Note] Regarding this teaching’s clarification of the "vertical and horizontal": in the Separate Teaching, it is not that nature is horizontal and practice is vertical; rather, the cause is vertical and the fruit is horizontal. This applies throughout.
Treatise: Cause and effect each possess both the vertical and horizontal dimensions; nature possesses only the horizontal; cultivation possesses both the vertical and horizontal.

[Commentary] This is a general heading for the two distinct treatises—both general and specific—concerning the vertical and horizontal dimensions of cultivation, nature, cause, and effect. Regarding the specific treatise:
there is the pair of nature and cultivation, and the pair of cause and effect. Regarding the general treatise: nature, cultivation, cause, and effect are discussed collectively.

[Commentary] Regarding "the initial nature is horizontal while cultivation is vertical": The *Myōku* (Exquisite Sentences), fascicle 9, states: "If there are only the three Tathāgatas of the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), this is horizontal;

the three Tathāgatas of the cultivation-virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*) are vertical (attained sequentially). First the Dharma-body, next the Reward-body, and finally the Response-body—this is also vertical. (One nature and two cultivations). The *Ki* (Record/Commentary), fascicle 9, states:
"The name 'nature-virtue' applies generally to both the Shared and Distinct Teachings (*pṛthag-dharma*). Although the Distinct Teaching contains the term 'nature-virtue,' [the three...]"

If all [the three natures] exist within the nature (*prakṛti*) yet do not interpenetrate one another, they constitute a distinct meaning. If the three exist within cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and are attained sequentially, the principle becomes vertical. Furthermore, the *Myōshū* (The Subtle Commentary) states:
"Those of the Separate Teaching (*bhadra-yāna*) do not know that the nature of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*) is endowed with defiled and evil qualities.

Therefore, they hold that the defiled and evil are not the two Buddha-natures; they separately cultivate the conditions and the understanding (*pratyaya* and *bodhi*) to manifest the fundamental Dharma-body. This [view of sequential cultivation] is likewise due to ignorance.

The nature of original enlightenment possesses defiled and evil qualities; it cannot give rise to entirely defiled and evil cultivation from that nature, and thus the principle-body inherently and simultaneously possesses these three dharmas (the nature is simultaneous).

[Commentary] This section provides a detailed explanation of the horizontal nature of the *xing* (nature) and the vertical sequence of the *xiu* (cultivation). First, it cites the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) to directly demonstrate that the nature is horizontal while cultivation is vertical.

Next, it cites the *Jujì* (Record of Sentences) to provide an exegesis. Finally, it cites the doctrines of other schools to further clarify that the oneness of the nature constitutes the horizontal, while the duality of cultivation constitutes the vertical.

The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains the Three Virtues (*sande*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), stating: "The Dharma-body of the Separate Teaching is shrouded by afflictions; this is truly because..."

One does not realize that the nature of original enlightenment (benjue) inherently possesses defiled and evil qualities. Therefore, defilement and evil are not two distinct virtues. Consequently, there are the particular delusions and the pervasive delusions;

the consciousness of karma (ye-shi) and the consciousness of phenomena (shi-shi); the afflictions, fetters, and karmic deeds; and the three vehicles and six paths, which are established as distinct categories of transformation.
All such dualistic dharmas within the state of delusion are not the two Buddha-natures. Since they are not the Buddha-nature, they constitute...

There must certainly be delusions that obscure [the nature]. One must therefore return to employing the awakening-nature according to conditions, separately taking the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) as objects, and sequentially and specifically cultivate the two causes of emptiness and provisionality, or the middle and the edge, through the two aspects of object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Alternatively, one may first take them as objects and subsequently realize them, or first realize them and subsequently take them as objects; through these sequential methods, one overturns and destroys all deluded phenomena.
This reveals the nature of the fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) of the Dharma-body. Therefore, the concealment of this principle constitutes the meaning of "vertical" (long) possession.
Furthermore, it is said that although the principle-body of the Separate Teaching (bie-jian) is fully endowed [with all qualities], these do not mutually encompass one another;

this is because they do not know that the nature of fundamental awakening possesses defiled and evil attributes, and thus cannot give rise to defiled and evil cultivation from the entirety of that nature. Consequently, the principle-body is established as possessing the three dharmas in a "horizontal" (heng) manner.

[Note] Regarding the phrase "next, the cause is vertical and the fruit is horizontal," the *Guangming ji* (Record of Radiance) states: "When practice, wisdom, and principle mutually assist and stimulate one another in their threefold sequence, this is 'vertical' during the stage of cultivation (*xiu*).
When the three fruits of Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Response-body are manifested simultaneously within the fruit, this is 'horizontal' at the time of realization (*zheng*)."

[Supplement] The *Guangju ji* states: They are discussed in terms of mutual support. Practice supports wisdom; wisdom supports principle. Because principle is manifested, one is able to exhaust all suffering.
Because suffering is exhausted, the Dharma-body is manifested. Because wisdom is perfected, the Reward-body is manifested. Thus, its merits are unsurpassed.
Therefore, the *saṃbhogakāya* is manifested.

[Commentary] This teaching is like a fertile field where the fundamental *dharmakāya* is covered by afflictions; thus, it is necessary to separately cultivate the merit of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the causes (*hetu*) to support and bring it into manifestation.
Furthermore, because the three dharmas are inherently complete within this teaching yet do not subsume one another, they cause the three...

"Body manifests horizontally" refers to the cultivation of the vertical. This means that while the nature is vertical, it constitutes the horizontal of the fruit; this is a distinct discussion based on the relative relationship between cultivation and nature, cause and fruit.
[Commentary] This is a specific explanation of the verticality of the cause and the horizontality of the fruit. The *Guangming ji* states:

"That which is vertical during cultivation and horizontal upon realization" refers precisely to the present discussion of the verticality of the cause and the horizontality of the fruit. The phrase "Because of this, below" provides the proof. The *Shiqian* states:
"One should understand that the meaning of 'covering' is not like soil covering a hard stone; it covers only the principle of the Buddha-nature within. As...
A good person is oppressed by an evil person and compelled to commit various evils; therefore, it is said that the ground is covered over by an evil person.

Since this original *dharmakāya* is covered by defiled evil and becomes a phenomenon within delusion, one must separately exert the effort of the conditions (*pratyaya*) and the cause (*hetu*) to assist in its manifestation.
Thus, the treatise speaks of "cultivation and fulfillment" in the sense of unfolding. Furthermore, it says: "By means of..."
The three dharmas of the fixed nature all reside within the nature itself; they are all that which is manifested. It is like three people, each claiming to be an emperor—the third;

how could they possibly encompass one another? Therefore, one does not know the three dharmas within the nature. Two of these belong to the practitioner; thus, they constitute a horizontal [arrangement].
This refers to what follows below, concluding by clarifying that cultivation is vertical while nature is horizontal, such that the cause is vertical and the fruit is horizontal.

[Note] Next, regarding the fact that cause and effect each have both vertical and horizontal dimensions: the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle 2, states: "In the distinct school (*biejia*), at the time of the cause, the three dharmas are both vertical and horizontal;

at the time of the fruit, the three dharmas are likewise both vertical and horizontal. Verticality in the cause is as previously explained. Horizontality in the cause refers to the horizontality of the nature (*xing*).

Verticality in the fruit is as stated in the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), fascicle 9: 'The Dharma-body is inherently present; Prajñā is accomplished through cultivation; Liberation is fulfilled at the beginning [of the fruit]. Horizontality in the fruit is also..."

As previously stated, one must understand that regarding these three dharmas of cause and effect within this teaching: their sequential arrangement constitutes the vertical (zòng), while their distinctness constitutes the horizontal (héng).

The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), fascicle 5, states: "The supportive and completing [nature] comes first; the contemplative and illuminating [nature] occupies the second position; and the true nature comes last. These three being distinct in sequence is the vertical;
they being all distinct from one another is the horizontal. Thus, the vertical is not the Mahāyāna, and the horizontal is also not the Mahāyāna.

[Commentary] This explanation clarifies that cause and effect each possess both vertical and horizontal dimensions. First, the text cites a passage from the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) to generally demonstrate the vertical and horizontal aspects of the three dharmas of cause and effect;
however, this is what is to be refuted, as it serves as the basis for what is now being demonstrated. "Verticality of cause" is as previously mentioned:

when practice, wisdom, and principle successively assist and stimulate one another during cultivation, this is verticality. "Horizontality of cause" refers to the horizontality of nature (*xing*): if it were merely nature...
"The three virtues are horizontal, while the fruit is vertical, as in the *Miaoxuan*," means that the intent is to clarify that the three virtues are accomplished in sequence;
therefore, the fruit is vertical. That the fruit is also horizontal is as stated previously. The *Guangming ji* says:
"Furthermore, because of this teaching, the three dharmas are inherently complete yet do not subsume one another; thus, the three bodies are manifested horizontally. This must be understood.
Below, it exhorts [the reader] to understand the meaning of the vertical and horizontal dimensions of the three dharmas of cause and effect in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

*Miaoxuan* (The Wondrous Profundity), Part 5, Lower, provides the proof and commentary on the final four lines, which conclude by establishing that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is entirely different from the Separate Teaching.

This intends to clarify that the three dharmas of cause and effect in the Perfect Teaching are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct. In this Separate Teaching, the three dharmas are "vertical" because they are distinguished sequentially; they are "simultaneous" because they are presented together.
"Differentiation" refers to the horizontal [dimension].

[Commentary] Next, regarding "nature," there is only the horizontal. Regarding "cultivation," it possesses both the vertical and the horizontal. As for the horizontality of nature, as explained above within the section on the three dharmas of nature, since the arising of cultivation has not yet been discussed, there is no sequence;
thus, it lacks the meaning of the vertical. Generally speaking, what is called "cultivation" encompasses both cause and fruit. Regarding the cause...
Since the fruits each possess both vertical and horizontal dimensions, they exist as spontaneous occurrences.
[Supplementary Note] The meaning is explained extensively in the ninth fascicle; it is now illustrated here by means of a diagram.
Diagram of the Vertical and Horizontal Aspects of the Cultivated Nature and Cause and Effect △ Part Four: The Perfect Teaching (3). First, the heading;
second, the explanation of the Perfect Teaching.
[Commentary] The *Sìjiàoyì* (Meanings of the Four Teachings), fascicle 1, section 3, states: "The Perfect [Teaching] takes 'non-partiality' as its meaning.

This teaching elucidates the inconceivable dependent origination, the two truths, and the Middle Way; phenomena and principle are fully present and not distinct. Because it transforms only those of the highest and sharpest faculties, it is called the Perfect Teaching" (text).
[■ Record] This clarifies the reason why the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) receives its name. One phrase from the ritual text serves as the heading;

the commentary cites and explains it. The *Xuanyi* states: "The inconceivable dependent origination of neither-arising-nor-ceasing" refers to the manifestation of principle through phenomena for those of sharp faculties.
[■ Supplement] The three thousand realms in a single thought-moment are empty, provisional, and middle; they are inconceivable.

Regarding the discussion of the two truths, the *Miaoxuan* states: "One simply identifies *dharmatā* as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) and the twelve links of dependent origination as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The *Shiqian* comments: "Ignorance is the beginning of delusion regarding the truth; *dharmatā* refers entirely to ignorance. Since time without beginning, how has it ever not been the truth?
Prior to the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment, there is nothing that is not conventional. One merely points to a single dharma."

The two truths are distinct and clear: the conventional consists of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, while the ultimate is entirely contained within a single thought-moment. Furthermore, there is no true reality outside the three thousand [realms];

thus, the conventional is eternally the ultimate. The phenomenal creation is identical to the inherent principle. There is no three thousand [realms] outside true reality; therefore, the conventional is always the ultimate.

This is precisely the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Principle (li) is inherently complete, which is identical to the phenomenal creation (shi-zao). Therefore, it is said that principle and phenomena, completion and creation, constitute the two layers of the "three thousand realms" (sanqian), all coexisting within a single thought-moment.

[Commentary] It is further stated: In the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), causes and conditions are explained as being identical to the Middle Way—the inconceivable principle of Buddha-nature and Nirvana.
When Bodhisattvas receive this teaching, although its principle is neither shallow nor deep, those who realize it nonetheless possess stages of shallow and deep realization.

Now, in clarifying the entry into the Way, it likewise possesses four gates; however, the intent of the various Mahāyāna sūtras mostly employs the gate of "neither empty nor existent" to clarify these stages (text).

[Commentary] Regarding "the causal conditions are themselves the Middle Way": The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states that when the Buddha-nature is elucidated through causal conditions, ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*) constitute the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).

Afflictions are themselves bodhi; when bodhi is fully realized, there are no afflictions. Since afflictions are absent, this is ultimate purity—the Buddha-nature as the cause of awakening (*bodhi-hetu*).
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) constitute the path of karma (*karma-mārga*); karma itself is liberation (*vimukti*).
Liberation and mastery are the conditional causes of the Buddha-nature. Name-and-form and old age and death constitute the path of suffering; yet suffering is itself the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is neither suffering nor pleasure, and is thus called "Great Bliss. It is neither born nor does it die; it is eternal. This is the direct cause of the Buddha-nature.
Therefore, it is said that between ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) lies the Middle Way. Ignorance is a transgression.
It departs. This craving is the present; whether at its extremes or its center, there is nothing that is not Buddha-nature—constant, blissful, self, and pure.
Ignorance neither arises nor ceases; this is called the inconceivable dependent origination of non-arising and non-ceasing.
As for the varying depths of the Bodhisattvas' realization of principle, the principle itself transcends cultivation and realization; it is their wisdom that appears to have gradations.

[Commentary on the Sub-commentary] Fascicle 5 (20) states: "In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the Bodhisattva takes the *nirodhasatya* (truth of cessation) outside the realms as the initial gate" (text).
△ Second, the explanation of the two [aspects] has two parts. First, the name and its functional utility. First, the explanation of the name and meaning:
it is called the "Perfect Teaching" (*yuanjiao*) because it is perfect, wondrous, complete, fully sufficient, and perfectly sudden; thus it is named the Perfect Teaching (this explains "Perfection").

[Commentary] The perfect fusion of the three truths is inconceivable; this is called "perfectly wondrous" (*yuánmiào*). The identity of the three as one, without deficiency or diminution, is called "perfectly complete" (*yuánmǎn*).

Perfectly perceiving both phenomena and principle, fully endowed within a single thought-moment, is called "perfectly sufficient" (*yuánzú*). Because its essence is not formed gradually, it is called "perfectly sudden" (*yuántùn*).
[■ Record] The perfect fusion of the three truths is called "perfect" (yuan). Its inconceivability is called "wondrous" (miao). The identity of the three and the one constitutes "perfection.
Because there is no deficiency, it is "complete" (man). Perfectly perceiving both phenomena and principle is called "perfect. Being fully endowed within a single thought-moment is "sufficiency" (zu).

The teaching-body being fundamentally pervasive is called "perfect. Because it is not achieved through gradual stages, it is "sudden" (dun). [■ Supplement] Generally speaking, all four names apply to the initial stage.

Regarding "subsequently" (*paścāt*): in a specific sense, "fulfillment" (*pūrṇa*) applies only to the subsequent stage; whereas "wondrous sufficiency" (*samyak-sampad*) and "suddenness" (*sakṛt*) apply to the initial stage.

This is because the essence of form and mind is fundamentally wondrous and all phenomena are inherently complete. Since one suddenly realizes that they are primordially perfected, it is only when delusions are subsequently exhausted that virtues finally reach fulfillment.
△ Second, the explanation of the functional efficacy (*kāritra*).

This refers to: universal subduing, universal faith, universal abandonment, universal practice, universal stages, universal sovereign adornment, and universally establishing sentient beings (this explains the "perfect" [dharmas]).

[Note] It is "sovereign" (*svatantra*) because it perfectly subdues the five abodes [of ignorance], possesses perfect and constant right faith, perfectly severs the five abodes, and perfectly practices—wherein one practice encompasses all practices—and because its perfect stages mutually include one another, adorned with wondrous functions.

It is "established" (*vyavasthāna*) because it universally benefits through the four *siddhāntas*. As stated in the first [volume] of the *Zhiguan* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 3.

[Commentary] *Zhiguan* states: "One of perfect faith believes that all phenomena are simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle; they are neither one, two, nor three, yet they are one, two, and three.
That 'neither one, two, nor three' is the negation (*zhē*), while 'one, two, and three' is the illumination (*zhào*). There is neither negation nor illumination."
All are ultimately pure and sovereign. Hearing the profound, they are not terrified; hearing the vast, they do not doubt;
hearing that which is neither profound nor vast, their minds possess courage—this is called "perfect faith. As for "perfect practice," one single-mindedly seeks unsurpassed bodhi;
by means of the extremes, one reaches the center, without turning toward anything else. One practices the three truths perfectly, so as not to be stilled by the infinite, nor by the finite.
Movement that is neither moving nor still is the direct entry into the Middle Way; this is called Perfect Practice (*pariṇata-caryā*). Regarding the Perfect Stage (*pariṇata-bhūmi*):
upon entering the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*), one is in all stages simultaneously; all are ultimate, all are pure, and all are sovereign—this is called the Perfect Stage.
Regarding the Adornment of Perfect Sovereignty: one may enter meditative absorption (*samādhi*) through this faculty, or arise from it through that faculty.
Regarding emergence and discourse: either one enters and emerges with respect to two [objects] through a single faculty, or one neither enters nor emerges through that same faculty;
the same applies to each of the remaining faculties. Or, one enters meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) with respect to this object, or arises from it with discourse regarding that object;
or one both enters and emerges with respect to a single object, or neither enters nor emerges with respect to that single object; the same applies to each of the remaining objects.
It is so. Even to the extent that one may enter meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in this direction and emerge from it to speak in that direction (and so forth).
To explain in detail: within a single faculty and a single object, one emerges and enters, both enters and emerges, and neither enters nor emerges;
the same applies to the primary retribution (*vipāka*) and the environmental retribution (*niśraya*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "The three truths in a single mind serve as the object."
Adornment: Taking the threefold contemplation within a single mind as the means of adornment, one attains mastery over both the primary and secondary retributions;

thus, one enters into the true reception (*samādhi*). The merit of emptiness issues forth in speech; the merit of the provisional issues forth in manifestation; and the merit of the middle enters and issues forth simultaneously, yet neither enters nor issues forth.

Thus, the middle merit is perfectly established to bring forth sentient beings. Alternatively, by emitting a single ray of light, one can cause sentient beings to obtain the benefits of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. They obtain...

Entering and exiting; entering and exiting simultaneously; the benefit of neither entering nor exiting. This applies likewise throughout walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, as well as speaking, remaining silent, acting, and ceasing.
[Supplement] The Bodhisattva internally realizes the identity of emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Without moving from the *dharmatā*, they cause sentient beings to obtain various benefits and attain various functions; this is called the establishment of sentient beings through the power of the perfect [teachings]. Question: Adornment.

Question: What is the distinction between "establishment" (*pratisthā*) and [the aforementioned]? Answer: Both are the inconceivable threefold wisdom of the one mind (*ekacitta*), which is able to adorn the *dharmakāya*.
This is called "adornment as external benefit. In that [text], it is termed "establishment. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"Adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom, one delivers sentient beings through this. Delivering sentient beings is precisely what is meant by "establishment. [Supplement] Regarding "perfect severance": it is a severance without severing.
Severance. The delusions of the five abodes are severed; one opens the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and dwells in Great Nirvana; therefore, it is called "perfect severance.
△ Second, according to the sutra to manifest the stages, in two parts: first, the general indication.
The various Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras describe the Buddha’s realm as being distinct from the stages of the Three Vehicles; all of these belong to this teaching.

[Note] Within the entirety of the Buddha’s lifetime teachings, with the exception of the Deer Park [teachings], those Mahāyāna sūtras that reveal the Perfect Dharma without omission all pertain to the Buddha’s realm.
Regarding the phrase "distinct from the stages of the Three Vehicles," this distinguishes it from the distinct (biejiao) teaching and its non-shared [stages].
Vehicles. Now, this perfection is the Buddha-vehicle; therefore, it is not shared with the three vehicles.
[Commentary] This teaching states that the realm of the Buddha is not shared with the three vehicles, as the sutra says: "There is only the Single Vehicle Dharma."
"There is neither two nor three. Furthermore, it says: "I shall not allow any single person to attain extinction alone;
rather, I shall cause all to attain extinction through the extinction of the Tathāgata"—this is precisely what is meant.

△ Second, the detailed explanation of the two [sections]. First, the correct manifestation of the stages and positions. This has two parts. First, the general listing of the various scriptures. First, the actual listing:

the four characters of "opening, revealing, awakening, and entering" (*kaishijowu*) from the *Lotus Sūtra* correspond to the forty stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), namely the stages of abiding (*zhu*), practice (*xing*), direction (*xiang*), and ground (*di*).

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one immediately attains perfect awakening. The entire body of wisdom is not realized through another;
this pure and wondrous Dharma-body is profoundly still yet responds to all things. This clarifies the forty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"In the midst of the campaka grove, one does not smell any other fragrance; so it is for those who enter this chamber—they smell only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas.

Furthermore, it is said: "Entering the Gate of Non-duality clarifies the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*); the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies the Most Excellent Vehicle; and the *Nirvāṇa* clarifies the One Mind and its Five Practices."
Furthermore, a sutra says: Suppose there is a person who enters the great ocean to bathe, having already used the waters of all rivers;
again, when the Sāgara Dragon pours down rain as thick as a chariot axle, only the great ocean can receive it, while other lands cannot endure it.
Furthermore, if one pounds ten thousand kinds of incense into pills and burns even a single particle, it fully possesses the fragrance of all of them.
[Note] "Opening, showing, awakening, and entering" are explained as before.

[Commentary] This refers to the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*), wherein one destroys ignorance, opens the Tathāgatagarbha, and perceives the principle of the true mark; this is called "opening. The Ten Practices (*daśacaryā*)...

Once the obstacles of delusion have been removed, the essence of knowledge and vision becomes manifest, and the myriad virtues of the *dharmadhātu* appear with perfect clarity; this is called "manifestation" (*darśana*).

When the obstacles of the tenth stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) are removed, the essence becomes manifest and the *dharmadhātu* is clearly discerned; phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated, and there is no longer any duality; this is called "realization" (*avabodha*).

The Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*). Since phenomena and principle have already been harmonized, one is sovereign and unimpeded; flowing spontaneously and effortlessly from *a* to *ṭa*, one enters the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñā*), which is called "entering."

[Commentary] For one who has first resolved their mind, the nature of the three causes is manifested; this is the stage of the First Abode (*prathamābhūmi*). From the Second Abode onward, it is no different for all.
Therefore, the conclusion states: "the forty-two stages of the Perfect [Teaching]."

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that "the three causal natures arise at the first dwelling": the *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra) states, "The one who partially realizes Buddhahood is the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*).
In one arising, all arise; all merits arise, all wisdoms arise, and all realms arise.

They are neither before nor after, yet they are not simultaneous. The *Chao* (Sub-commentary) states: "The name 'dwelling' signifies the arousal of the mind; it is the arousal of the fundamental [nature]."
It is the awakened mind. It is eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating; quiescence and illumination are fused as one. This is the original perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*).

It is three within oneness, and it issues forth without being issued. Thus, the three modes of issuing forth are established. In all cases, the term "all" is used because the Dharma-realm has no exterior; it encompasses all phenomena without omission.
Buddhas and sentient beings, the material and mental, the environment and its inhabitants—all share the same essence of awakening. The entire body serves as the condition. The entire...

The substance is the cause of illumination (*jñāna-hetu*); the whole substance is the correct cause (*samyag-hetu*). Because the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is activated, both illumination and correctness are activated.

Because the cause of illumination is activated, both the conditional and the correct causes are activated. Because the correct cause is activated, both the conditional and the causes of illumination are activated. Thus, these three factors are perfectly interfused; when they are activated, they are activated simultaneously.

The activation of the conditional cause is termed "merit" (*puṇya*), for it is able to provide support and bring about fulfillment. The activation of the cause of illumination is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*), for it is able to perform contemplation and discernment.

Therefore, it is correctly designated as the "objective realm" (*viṣaya*), because it is that which is manifested. One should know that just as it is with the first dwelling, so it is for all the subsequent forty-one stages;
there are none that are otherwise.

[Note] Regarding "campaka and so forth": *Campaka* is translated as "yellow flower. This refers to the passage in the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" where the celestial maidens rebuke Śāriputra, and the empty room of Vimalakīrti, which symbolizes the *nitya-prabhāsvara-dharmadhātu* (the eternally quiescent light-realm).
[Commentary]: The *campaka* is a tree found near the coasts of the Western Regions (*Sīdavya*). When the *garuḍa* arrives, it perches upon it. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states:
Śāriputra asked the goddess, "Among the three vehicles, which do you aspire to? The goddess replied, "Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of the *śrāvaka*, I am a *śrāvaka*.
Because I transform sentient beings through the Dharma of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*), [I am a pratyekabuddha]."
I am a pratyekabuddha; it is for the sake of transforming sentient beings through the dharma of great compassion that I am a follower of the Mahāyāna.

Śāriputra, just as when a person enters a campaka grove they do not smell any other fragrance, so too, if one enters this room, one smells only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas and does not take pleasure in the fragrance of the merits of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. At the end...
Phrases serve as auxiliary expressions that lead to and manifest the essential meaning of the sutras. As the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states:
"The empty room of Vimalakīrti symbolizes the Constant, Quiescent Light; therefore, those who enter it smell only the Buddha-vehicle."

[Note] Regarding "entering the gate of non-dual dharmas": In that sutra, after thirty-one bodhisattvas had each spoken on entering the gate of non-dual dharmas, they asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the bodhisattva’s entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas? Mañjuśrī replied:
"As it occurs to me, regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is no speech and no discourse, no indication and no cognition;
being free from all questioning and answering—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "We have each spoken for ourselves;
now you, O Benevolent One, should speak: what is this 'entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality' for a bodhisattva? At that time, Vimalakīrti—
Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word. Mañjuśrī sighed and said, "Excellent, excellent!
Even to the point where there are no words or speech—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
(Text) One must know that while the thirty-one bodhisattvas used words to speak of the wordless, Mañjuśrī used wordlessness to speak of the wordless, and Vimalakīrti used wordlessness...
There was silence. Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised this, saying: "This is the true entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.

[Commentary] The *Huayan Shu* states: "However, the intent of this sutra is such that the preceding and succeeding sections complement one another to collectively manifest the core purport of the scripture.
If one were to distinguish their relative excellence, there may be three or four levels. As for the three levels: first, the various bodhisattvas dispel duality by means of non-duality."

First, by means of words, he explains that there appears to be something non-dual that can be spoken of; he clarifies non-duality in contrast to duality, yet this is not a state of absolute transcendence.
Second, Mañjuśrī uses words to dispel words, clarifying that there is no non-duality that can be spoken of, thereby causing one to forget words and realize the ultimate meaning. Third.
Vimalakīrti’s silence reveals the principle; that is, it is fundamentally wordless from the beginning and does not depend on further negation—this is the third point.
Regarding the "fourfold weight," Mañjuśrī uses words to seal that [silence], thereby clarifying that words are themselves non-words.
If one wishes to synthesize these, the three preceding sections mutually reinforce one another, constituting but a single meaning. First, Mañjuśrī used words to reveal...
There is no speech. First, Vimalakīrti uses silence to seal silence; subsequently, Mañjuśrī uses speech to seal silence.
These three sections show how the two individuals together reveal the principle that transcends words.

While the previous thirty-one bodhisattvas eliminate duality by means of non-duality, these final two great beings eliminate speech by means of silence. There are only these two stages. If they were further combined...
The preceding Bodhisattvas dispelled duality through words; yet, where emptiness and existence transcend speech, by what means could the principle be revealed?
Thus, while the preceding Bodhisattvas manifested the principle through provisional words, the latter two Great Beings manifested the principle through wordlessness.
When both speech and wordlessness are forgotten, all are truly non-dual. Therefore, although there are three stages, they are of one consistent essence without contradiction. This is thus...
This is the Dharma-gate for accomplishing the Perfect Teaching.
[Note] Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā clarifying the Supreme Vehicle: the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra* states, "The Tathāgata speaks for those who have set forth upon the Supreme Vehicle.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states, "Furthermore, there is one practice, which is the practice of the Tathāgata; that is to say, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa."
The principle of Buddha-nature.
[Commentary] Regarding the term "Supreme Vehicle" (Agryayāna): this refers to the sixteen gates within the four teachings (*catur-yāna*). Within each gate, there are immeasurable practices.
That which is called the *Zang* (Treasury) is not equal to the *Tong* (Pervasive); the *Tong* is not equal to the *Bie* (Distinctive); and how could the *Bie* compare to the *Yuan* (Perfect)?

Therefore, the Dharma-gate of the Perfect Teaching is the Supreme Vehicle (*Agryayāna*). Regarding the "One Mind and Five Practices," the text of the "Chapter on the Holy Practices" (*Śrīkṣāntiparivarta*) has its commentary (*śāstra*) designate the non-sequential practices as threefold:
first, the designation of the names of the practices, stating, "Furthermore, there is one practice"; second, the persons, namely, the Tathāgata.
The causal practice of the Tathāgata is itself the person who practices it. There are three dharmas: namely, the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra;
"Mahāyāna" refers to the perfect cause, and "Nirvāṇa" refers to the perfect fruit. Thus, through the cause one attains the fruit, complete and without deficiency.

This is what is meant by "one practice encompassing all practices. [Supplement] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "From the first generation of the bodhicitta, one constantly contemplates the practice of Nirvāṇa."
The Way should be understood as not departing from the single mind that illumines the ten dharma realms: namely, emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

When it is emptiness, the holy practices are fully perfected; when it is the provisional, the practices of the Brahma-sickness and the infant are fully perfected; when it is the middle, the heavenly practices are fully perfected.
This is the five practices within the single mind; one practice is all practices.
[Note] Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, the sutra says": The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states, "For example, suppose there is a person bathing in the great ocean;
one should know that this person has already used the waters of all rivers. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 1, Part 1, p. 27, states:

"The principle contains all dharmas, like the water of the ocean; the practitioner of contemplation is like the one bathing. Because practice encompasses all [dharmas], it is called 'having already used' them. (Text).
[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva is also like this. By practicing this Vajra-samādhi, one should know that he has already practiced all other samādhis.

The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Part 2, cites this scriptural analogy to clarify that the practice of the perfect path (*yuanxing*) which is identical to principle (*li*) fully encompasses all practices, just as bathing in the ocean already utilizes [the water of] all its tributaries.
These are the various river waters.
[Commentary] Sāgara is translated here as the "Salt Sea. It is the Tathāgata-dragon king who rains down the Perfect and Sudden Teaching for those of superior faculties.
It does not rain upon the lands of the inferior classes of the three teachings.
[Commentary] This explains by again citing the passage from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* concerning the rain as thick as a chariot axle and so forth; both the dharma and the metaphor are thus understood.

[Commentary] The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "If one pounds ten thousand kinds of incense into pills, even if one burns but a single particle, it will fully possess the fragrance of all [the ingredients].

(Text) The *Fuxing* (Vol. 1, Part 1, p. 27) states: "The principle-nature is like the pill; contemplative practice is like the burning. That all dharmas are suddenly manifested is called 'possessing the fragrance of all. (Text)
[Commentary] This citation of a sutra serves as an analogy for the practice-gate of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao). It refers to the principle that "one practice is all practices;
one cultivation is all cultivations; one realization is all realizations. In the lower volume of the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), the application of the Dharma to this analogy can be understood.
△ Second, the conclusion.
Such categories as these all belong to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
[■ Record] This is the conclusion regarding their respective affiliations. The term "such as this" (*ru shi*) is a word used for precise reference. "Etc. (*deng*)...

"Category" (lei) means, as the term suggests, "to flow together. This refers to how the textual meanings of the preceding *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Vimalakīrti*, *Nirvāṇa*, and *Śūraṅgama* sūtras all ultimately converge within the encompassment of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
△ Second, the specific reliance on two sutras, in two parts. First, the designation of names to clarify the stages.

Now, according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Ratnakuṭa-sūtra*, the stages will be briefly explained as being eightfold: 1. The stage of the five grades of disciples (the outer ordinary person;

from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*); 2. The stage of the ten faiths (the inner ordinary person); 3. The stage of the ten abidings (the first of the noble ones); 4. The ten practices; 5. The ten dedications; 6. [The ten grounds]...
The ten stages (*bhūmi*), the seven stages of equal enlightenment (the end of the causal stage), and the eighth, the stage of wondrous enlightenment (the fruit stage).
[Commentary] The *Lotus Sūtra* mentions only the five grades and the six faculties; the *Yingluo* [Sūtra] clearly elucidates all fifty-two stages.
The *Myōryaku* [Commentary] states: "If one speaks of the Perfect stages, the 'six identities' (*roku-soku*) are sufficient. Why must one further enumerate the forty-two stages? This is because..."

Because the true stages (*bhūmi*) are extensive, the distinct stages (*vyavasthāna-bhūmi*) are borrowed to differentiate their ranks. (Text) Some, based on this, claim that the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) originally has no sequence of stages, but merely borrows those of the Distinct Teaching to manifest the Perfect.
However, the intention of Miaole is that the fifty-two stages, as found in the sutras and treatises, are mostly used by others;
the Patriarch [Zhiyi] employed them to explain the Perfect stages, and thus he said they were "borrowed. Furthermore, some say there are fifty...

Although the names of these two positions differ, they are equally employed within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) to distinguish between shallow and deep levels. How could it be that the Perfect Teaching lacks any stages of progress at all?

Consider, for instance, the forty-two letters in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the eight manifestations (*aṣṭākāra*) in the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, and the five grades and six faculties in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.

All these are the meaning of "round" (perfect). Therefore it is said that when one principle is revealed, there is no duality from beginning to end; yet when preserved within the teachings, cause and effect are clearly distinct.
Since one has received the teachings and practices accordingly, how could there not be stages?
[Commentary] The *Myōgen* states: "In the equal dharma-realm, one does not even discuss awakening or non-awakening; how then could one distinguish between shallow and deep?
Since one does discuss awakening and non-awakening, what prevents one from distinguishing between shallow and deep? The *Shikan* states: "Regarding principle, the realized Dharma is nameless."

In terms of phenomena, it is not that there are no various stages. Thus we know that awakening corresponds to the first stage (*bhūmi*), while non-awakening corresponds to the stage prior to the stages.
Since both awakening and non-awakening are admitted, what prevents us from discussing their relative depth and shallowness and establishing the fifty-two stages?

This means that even in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are levels of depth and shallowness; how then can one say that there are fundamentally no stages? Regarding the forty-two characters: [Supplementary Note].

The verse says: *A-ra-pa-ca-na-ra-dha, bha-ta-śa-dha-ba-ha-ta, ka-sa-ma-ga-ta-ja-pa, dha-śa-kha-cha-ta-ya-ta, bha-cha-ma-hu-ja-ga-ta, na-pha-ka-ca-ca-cha-ta.* The eight aspects of the first stage (*prathama-vihāra*) in the *Avataṃsaka* are explained in the preceding text. [In the] *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, there are five...
Regarding the "Chapter on the Six Faculties": the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" clarifies the five stages of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata;

the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master" clarifies the stage of the purification of the six faculties (*liùgēn qīngjìng*). The meanings of such scriptures all clarify the Perfect Stage (*yuánwèi*).
[Supplement] The *Miaoxuan* states: "Some say that in the Perfect Teaching there is sudden enlightenment; once enlightened, one is immediately a Buddha, with no further stages."
Next, regarding the distinction: those who speak of the ten stages (bhūmis) do so for the sake of those with dull faculties. As the *Siksāsamuccaya* states:
"This study of the sudden realization of the wondrous principle does not proceed from one stage to another. Furthermore, it is said:

"Since the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is characterized by sudden awakening, a single awakening at the initial stage constitutes ultimate perfection. The existence of forty-two stages is intended for those with dull faculties.

These are merely provisional designations established through skillful means (*upāya*) to distinguish between shallow and deep. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The first stage is the second stage; the second stage is the third stage.
In the quiescent true suchness (*tathatā*), what stages or positions can there be? All of the above are partial explanations that fail to understand the equality of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Since even the distinction between awakening and non-awakening is not yet discussed, how could one discuss shallow or deep? Once this is discussed...

Have you awakened? How could one fail to discern this? Upon examining the Mahāyāna sūtras to clarify their ultimate principles, none surpasses the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Although these clarify that the Dharma-realm is equal, without speech and without demonstration.
The stages of the Bodhisattva’s practice are clearly manifest; therefore, we again rely on seven positions to elucidate the stages of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
[Note] Furthermore, when distinguishing among various texts, there are four ways of opening and closing [the categories]:

first, opening the former and closing the latter, as in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the Thirty-three Heavens (where the stages of Dwelling, Practice, and Direction constitute thirty, while the Grounds, Equal Enlightenment, and Subtle Enlightenment constitute three); second, closing the former and opening the latter, as in the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* regarding the fourteen Prajñās (where the three... [text continues]).

The ten minds constitute three; the ten stages constitute ten; and Equal Enlightenment constitutes one. Altogether, these fourteen patiences transform and enter the Buddha-mind, which is termed "Wisdom.

(3) Both the preceding and following are opened, as in the forty-two characters of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (corresponding to forty-two positions). (4) Both the preceding and following are joined, as in the "Opening, Showing, Awakening, and Entering" (*āviṣkaraṇa-darśana-bodhana-praveśana*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and the "Wandering in the Four Directions" (corresponding to forty positions). *Miaozong* Vol. 1, p. 23.

[Commentary] The phrase "opening the former and closing the latter" below refers to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. However, while the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* mentions the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa) in various preceding and succeeding sections, the sub-commentary (*shu*) does not correlate these with specific stages [of the five paths]. Only in the second fascicle it says:

"It is like a person traveling far who, becoming utterly exhausted on the way, takes refuge in another's house. While he is lying down asleep, a great fire suddenly breaks out. He immediately awakens in alarm and thinks to himself..."
He reflects: "I shall certainly die now; there is no doubt. He then passes away and is reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

The commentary explains the meaning of the six relatives as follows: - Traveling a long distance is a metaphor for the contemplation of principle (li-guan). - Being on the road is a metaphor for the contemplation of names and words (ming-tzu guan). - Staying in another's house is a metaphor for the contemplation of practice (guan-xing guan).

- Immediately awakening from a dream is a metaphor for the contemplation of semblance (xiang-si guan). - Being born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven is a metaphor for the contemplation of partial realization (fen-zhen guan).

"Arising. This analogy illustrates two aspects of accomplishment. The thirty-two ministers represent the meaning of partial realization (*vibhāga-satya*). If considered in relation to the single sovereign, it represents the meaning of ultimate fulfillment.
Now, based on this principle, the preceding [stages] are expanded and the subsequent [stages] are combined to correspond with the forty-two positions. However, the *Miaoxuan* states:
"The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that the thirty-three devas partake of the deathless nectar (*amṛta*), which they consume together with their ministers. This is an analogy..."
The various stages prior [to the first bhūmi] are taken as the thirty minds; the ten bhūmis are combined into one; and Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is taken as one.

This is illustrated by the analogy of thirty-two ministers, representing the causal stage, and the Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue), representing the resultant stage. Thus, the sovereign and his ministers together partake of the ambrosia.
Both cause and fruit are realized as eternal bliss. If this is not explained by means of the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*), this passage will be difficult to comprehend.

Second, combining the preceding [section] with the opening of the latter part below, the "Teaching and Transformation" chapter of the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "This is that which all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have fundamentally practiced;

it is the full perfection of the fourteen patiences within the five patiences, namely: the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*), the patience of firmness (*dṛḍha-kṣānti*), and the patience of excellent awakening (*suvibuddha-kṣānti*)."

These are: the patience of forbearance (*kṣānti*), the patience of transcendent realization, the patience of luminous wisdom, the patience of blazing wisdom, the patience of supreme wisdom, the patience of manifestation, the patience of far-reaching realization, the patience of equal enlightenment, the patience of the light of wisdom, the patience of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), and the patience of perfect awakening. It is further said that these five patiences constitute the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas:

the upper, middle, and lower levels of the patience of subduing; the upper, middle, and lower levels of the patience of faith; the upper, middle, and lower levels of the patience of conformity; and the patience of non-arising.

The upper, middle, and lower levels of patience; the upper, middle, and lower levels of the patience of quiescent extinction—these are called the practice of Prajñāpāramitā by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
It continues until it says: "This is what all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have fundamentally practiced. Among the five patiences, there are fourteen patiences.

The commentary states: "Briefly, there are five patiences; extensively, there are fourteen. That is to say, the three stages of the virtuous (śaikṣa) constitute three [patiences], and the ten stages (bhūmi) constitute [the remaining eleven]."

This constitutes the fourteen stages of Buddhahood. Now, combining the former [stages] with these newly opened [stages], they correspond to the forty-two positions of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*).
Third, regarding the section "Opening Both Before and After," it refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*’s exposition of the forty-two letters. It concludes by stating:
"A single letter enters all forty-two letters, and the forty-two letters also enter a single letter. Nanyue used this to represent the forty [positions].

The two positions: the initial letter *A* represents the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), and so on, up to the final letter *Ṭa*, which represents the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Therefore, it is said that "beyond *Ṭa*, there is no further letter to be spoken. Thus, the preceding and following [sections] correspond here to the forty-two stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*).

Regarding the phrase "the four [stages] where the preceding and following are both joined," this refers to the *Lotus Sūtra*, which states: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, desire to cause sentient beings to open, reveal, awaken to, and enter..."

"Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. The *Fangdeng sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Dharma-Door of Luminosity) states: "At that time, the sons were filled with joy and leaped for gladness;

they mounted this precious vehicle and traveled through the four quarters. Regarding these two passages, Tiantai correlates them respectively with the stages of *zhù* (abiding), *xíng* (practice), *xiàng* (orientation), and *dì* (stages).

Now, combining both the preceding and following texts, they correspond to the forty stages [of the Bodhisattva path]. In the lower section of the *Miaozong chao*, he cites and verifies the four phrases, stating: "Using..."

In that great sūtra, the analogy of the moon’s light illustrates how, from the fifteenth day of the month corresponding to the forty-two stages of perfect cause and effect, the light of wisdom increases and the darkness of delusion decreases.
The first three days correspond to the thirty stages of abiding, practicing, and heading toward enlightenment; the first four through the thirteenth days correspond to the ten bhūmis;
the fourteenth day corresponds to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi); and the fifteenth day corresponds to the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (Sugata).

Combining the preceding thirty [stages] and opening up the subsequent ten stages constitutes the forty-two positions. If the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens collectively partake of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), they correspond to all forty-two positions as they equally realize the eternal principle. Opening up the preceding thirty positions and pairing them with the Thirty-three Heavens, while combining the subsequent ten stages to correspond to a single heaven;
likewise, Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) corresponds to one heaven, and the ultimate stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabuddhatva*) corresponds to one.

It is the celestial principle. Just as with the forty-two letters, where each letter mutually contains all forty-two letters, this corresponds to the perfect realization of the forty-two stages, wherein each stage encompasses the others and both the preceding and succeeding ones are opened.

As for "opening, showing, awakening, and entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision," which corresponds to the forty stages of the perfect true cause, the preceding and succeeding ones are both merged. This is thus consistent with the present Great [Perfection].

They are the same in substance but differ slightly. Here, fourteen Prajñās are cited to clarify the synthesis of the preceding and the opening of the subsequent; the citation of the *Miaozong* (Essential Pivot) likewise clarifies the synthesis of the preceding and the opening of the subsequent—this constitutes their slight difference.

[Note] Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* enumerates sixty stages. By adding the three gradual steps (*tri-ānupūrva*) to the previous [forty-nine], establishing the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*),
and subsequently establishing the four preparatory practices (*catvāraḥ prayogāḥ*) prior to the [ten] stages, together with the constant fifty-two stages, they collectively constitute sixty.
[Commentary] The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* asks: "What are called the three gradual stages? First is 'Cultivation,' which eliminates its auxiliary causes.
Second is 'True Cultivation,' which excises its primary nature. Third is 'Advancement,' which opposes its manifest karma. It further states:

"When desire and love are dried up, the faculties and their objects do not encounter one another; the remaining physical form before one no longer continues into rebirth, and the grasping mind becomes empty and luminous."

It is purely wisdom. The nature of this wisdom is perfectly luminous, adorning the realms of the ten directions. When one possesses this wisdom alone, it is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vijñāna-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, it is said: "Next, one accomplishes the four kinds of wondrously perfect preparatory practices (*prayoga*), taking the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind."
If one has emerged from or not yet emerged [from the state of practice], it is like drilling wood with the intent to kindle fire; this is called the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*).

Furthermore, when one’s own mind traverses the path trodden by the Buddhas—whether relying on conditions or not relying on them—it is like ascending a high mountain where the body enters empty space, yet there remains a slight obstruction below;

this is called the Stage of the Summit (*mūrdhan*). When the mind and the Buddha are identical, and one abides in the Middle Way of virtuous qualities, it is like a person who endures all things. It is not...

When one harbors no [dualistic] emergence, it is called the Stage of Patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*). When the numerical quantities of delusion and awakening are extinguished within the Middle Way, such that neither of the two has any objective referent, it is called the World-First Stage (*laukikāgra-dharma-bhūmi*).

These constitute the four stages of preparatory application (*prayoga*). Together with the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) which are constantly elucidated, these are termed the "Identity of Similarity" (*sādṛśya-ekayāna*).

The stages of Abiding, Progressing, and Entering, as well as the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), are termed the "Partial True Identity" (*aṃśika-tattva-ekayāna*). Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbuddha*) is termed the "Ultimate Identity" (*niṣṭhā-ekayāna*). Thus it is said.
This concludes the sixty positions. The brief explanation of designating names and manifesting positions is finished.
