Although one sees them being removed first, the person has not a single thought of joy. Why is this so?
Because it has not yet fulfilled its original purpose.

[Note] The *Biexing xuanyi* (Lower Volume, Part 6) states: "The Perfect [Teaching] is likened to smelting iron to fashion a vessel; the Separate [Teaching] is metaphorically compared to smelting gold to fashion a vessel."

"Smelting" refers to melting and casting. When the state of simplicity and spontaneity suddenly dissolves, coarse impurities fall away first by the force of natural progression. "Refining" refers to forging and tempering;
while the substance remains solid, it is specifically required that coarse dust be removed first, so that the gold may later be melted to eliminate subtle impurities.

In the same way, when the perfect contemplation (*yuan guan*) suddenly exhausts the Dharma-realm, there is no intention to contemplate the two truths (*satya*) beforehand; rather, the two delusions fall away spontaneously first. In contrast, the distinct contemplation (*bie guan*) reveals the Middle Way through a gradual sequence.
[The text] states: "Because one first contemplates the two truths with intention, the two delusions are first eliminated.
[Commentary: This clarifies that perfect cultivation and perfect severance possess a sequence of priority and posteriority as a matter of course.
The first line uses a metaphor to clarify how the severance of delusions occurs without deliberate intent, and the reason why this natural sequence exists is clearly evident. (Note)

The middle section cites the *Vyākhyā* (Commentary) to establish the argument in three initial lines. First, two analogies are established to demonstrate that the cultivation and abandonment of delusions differ between the Perfect and Distinctive Teachings.

Next, two lines apply two contemplations to the dharmas. Although this cites the stages of the Perfect Teaching, it shows that from beginning to end, the sequence of the various delusions is distinguished by the subtle or manifest nature of wisdom;
it specifically clarifies that within the seven levels of faith in the Perfect Teaching, the power of wisdom [overcomes] the delusions of the four abodes.

The attachments are intimate, whereas the delusions of ignorance are subtle and distant; thus, while the thick delusions of ignorance have not yet been eliminated, the thin delusions of the four abodes have already fallen away.
△ Third, the reconciliation of dharmas.

The practitioner of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is also like this. Although it was not their original expectation, they naturally fall [into realization] first. [Commentary on the *Jiyao chao*, Vol. 5, Part 5] states:

"The practitioner of the Perfect Teaching employs non-dual wisdom from beginning to end, suddenly extinguishing all phenomena. Since even the principle and the fruit are extinguished, how could there be any sequence of delusions?
It is solely because the power and efficacy of this wisdom vary in subtlety and prominence that distinctions of 'intimate' and 'distant' arise. By means of this...
Because of the intimacy or distance [between wisdom and delusion], the confusion falls away earlier or later; this is termed the thickness or thinness of delusion.

When wisdom is distant and delusion is thick, when wisdom is intimate and delusion is thin—this is clarified through successive transmission. This, then, is the classification of delusion according to wisdom (text).
[Commentary] This section applies the Dharma to the analogy to further clarify the sequence of severing delusions. This is due to the diligence or indolence of one's effort;
such diligence or indolence causes the wisdom of contemplation to become either proximate or remote, thereby resulting in the thickness or thinness of delusion.

[Supplement] For the wisdom that transcends all dependencies (*atyantānapekṣā-jñāna*), not a single dharma confronts the mind, and one does not even perceive a principle or fruit to be realized—how much less could there be any sequential order?
Is it that the delusions are severed? Furthermore, consider the question raised in the *Supplementary Notes*: "If the power of contemplation is weak, both [the contemplation and its object] are weak;
if it is attached, both are attached. Why then do the delusions to be destroyed not follow the power of the three contemplations and be partially destroyed simultaneously? The answer is as follows:

This question is indeed well-founded. Traditionally, students have found it difficult to reconcile the phenomenal with the Dharma. Now, it is said that for the person of perfect realization and the perfect Dharma, all things are perfectly interfused.

The delusions that are to be shattered are merely biased emotions; because these biased emotions are coarse or subtle, they appear to have a sequence of priority, leading to the artificial distinction of the "three delusions.
[Supplement] The *Ten Gates of Non-duality* states: "It is simply due to the intimacy or distance of wisdom's extinction [of delusion]."
This causes delusion to become either thick or thin; this is the essential instruction for practicing contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). [Note:

Former masters have said that when practicing contemplation, afflictions (*kleśa*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are of one suchness (*tathatā*); whether the falling away of afflictions occurs sooner or later depends on the completion of one's practice.
[Commentary] These two phrases cite ancient authorities as evidence. "The predecessors" refers to those who have already traversed the path.

"Cultivating contemplation such that delusion and wisdom are one" means that the objective realm and wisdom are identical. "Success being achieved and delusion falling away, whether earlier or later" clarifies that when light arises, darkness perishes.
△ Second, citing the *Yongjia ji* (Collection of Yongjia), in two parts. First, the actual citation:

The Great Master Yongjia said, "When the four abodes (*catur-vāsita*) are equally eliminated, this stage is identical. If one merely suppresses ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripiṭaka [teaching] is inferior. This refers to this very stage.

[Commentary] The *Yongjia ji* states: "However, when comparing the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka with one at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), there are points of equality and inferiority.

In that both have eliminated the four abidings (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), they are equal. Yet, regarding the suppression of ignorance (*avidyā*), the Tripiṭaka [Buddha] is inferior. This can likewise be understood for the two vehicles (*dviyāna*)."
This is originally from the "Excellence of the Stages" (*Weimojie jing xuanshu weimojie weishi*) within the *Wenju*. It was merely cited therein from the *Yongjia ji*.

Formerly, it was transmitted that during the late Tang and Five Dynasties periods, the Tiantai teachings had fallen into obscurity. Consequently, when the Qian family encountered this passage while reading the *Yongjia ji*, they could not understand it and questioned National Teacher Shao.
The National Teacher identified it as a phrase from the Tiantai teachings and instructed them to consult Dharma Master Xiji of Luoxi.

The Master reported that [the practice] was flourishing in海东 (Haidong). He subsequently sought it from Goryeo; thus, as the Master brought the scriptural divisions back with him, the tradition began to flourish once more.
That it is now called Yongjia (Perpetual Peace) is indeed for this reason.
[Commentary] This citation of ancient words serves to verify the excellence of the Perfect Stage (*yuanwei*). Yongjia was the name of the capital city of Dong’ou.
The "Great Master" refers to Chan Master Xuangjue, who was posthumously titled Chan Master Dongming Miaozhi by the Imperial Court.
He was originally a native of Yongjia. Having realized the Way and propagated the Dharma, he resided in his home region from beginning to end; he is now known as...

"Yǒngjiā" (Eternal Tranquility) is likely used to honor the location while concealing its specific name. "Those who have equally eliminated the four abidings are equal in this regard" means their rank is the same as that of the Śrāvaka-piṭaka (Tripiṭaka).
"If they suppress ignorance, then the Tripiṭaka [followers] are inferior" means that their practice surpasses that of the Tripiṭaka.
"The two vehicles can be known" means that even the Buddha-stage is still inferior; how much more so the two vehicles? "Their rank is subtle among the middling" refers to...

Within the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text), there are ten kinds of "subtleties," namely: the subtlety of the object, the subtlety of wisdom, the subtlety of practice, the subtlety of stages, the subtlety of the three dharmas, the subtlety of resonance and response, the subtlety of supernatural powers, the subtlety of preaching the Dharma, the subtlety of the retinue, and the subtlety of benefit.
The passage cited here belongs to the section on the "subtlety of stages" within that work; it was quoted by Yongjia. As for the "Qian family," this refers to Qian Zhong of Wuyue.
King Yi. Reading the *Ji yinyuan* (Collection of Causes and Conditions), one sees the ritual texts, the origins of events, and the biographies.
△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, the removal of the afflictions of views and thought is the same [as the previous section].

The commentary states: The "four abodes" (catvāraḥ sthitayaḥ) are simply the afflictions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa). Taking views as one, they are called the "abode-ground of all-pervading views" (sarvatraga-dṛṣṭi-sthiti-bhūmi).

The afflictions of thought are divided into three: first, the "abode-ground of desire-attachment" (kāmarāga-sthiti-bhūmi), which refers to the nine grades of thought-afflictions in the desire realm; second, the "abode-ground of form-attachment" (rūparāga-sthiti-bhūmi), which refers to the nine grades of thought-afflictions in each of the four stages of the form realm;
and third, the "abode-ground of formless-attachment" (ārūpyarāga-sthiti-bhūmi), which refers to the nine grades [of thought-afflictions] in each of the four stages of the formless realm.

[Commentary on] the *Pin* (Chapter/Section): These four abidings (*catur-vāsa*) are severed by the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka and by those who have attained the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddha*). Therefore, it is said that they "equally eliminate the four abidings.

[■ Record: This explains that, in terms of the stages of practice, the severance of afflictions within the realm of desire is precisely equal [for both]. The "four abidings" refer to the two delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).
Furthermore, the delusions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) pervade all three realms; since they cannot be divided, they are treated as one, because they are abandoned simultaneously.
The delusions of thought (bhāvanā-kleśa) also pervade all three realms, but because they cannot be abandoned simultaneously, they must be divided into three.
Bound by these four delusions, one cannot leap out; though wishing to depart, one finds it difficult to attain freedom. Therefore, it is called "abiding" (*zhù*).
As for "stages" (*dì*), this refers to the locations within the triple world (*tridhātu*); when divided, they constitute the nine stages (*navabhūmi*).

Those who have attained the fruits of the Tripitaka sever these four abidings and can thus proceed toward this [state]. Those whose six sense faculties are purified also sever them spontaneously. Hence, it is said that they are "the same."
It is excluded.
△ Second, the suppression of the delusion of ignorance is inferior.

Regarding the statement that "if one suppresses ignorance, the Three Baskets (Tripitaka) are inferior": ignorance refers specifically to the obstacle to the Middle Way that exists beyond the [three] realms.

Regarding delusions: the Tripitaka Teaching discusses only the pervasive delusions within the realm of transmigration (*dhātu*). Since one cannot even know the names of ignorance, let alone subdue or sever it, it is said that the Tripitaka is inferior.
[Commentary on the *Śūramgama-samādhi-sūtra-śāstra*, Fascicle 6, Section 4] states: "Regarding 'equality' and 'inferiority': equality refers to the point where delusions are exhausted;
the practices of contemplation and hearing the teachings are thus considered inferior. Furthermore, they are compared to the stage of Buddhahood because they accord with the path of the teachings."

[Commentary] This clarifies that ignorance outside the realms is such that even the Tripiṭaka masters do not know its name; how then could they subdue and sever it? For this reason, it is considered inferior.
[The author] earnestly wishes to explain this, citing the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) to clarify the reasons for its inferiority.

The Tripiṭaka masters employ only the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) and thus sever only the pervasive delusions within the realms. Those of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), however, utilize the three contemplations in a single mind; therefore, they are able to perfectly subdue [all delusions].
Ignorance. This concludes the explanation of the preceding seven stages of faith.
△ Second, clarifying the latter three stages of faith.

Next, from the eighth faith through the tenth faith, one exhaustively severs the "dust-sand" delusions both within and outside the realms, and the provisional contemplation manifests before one. One sees...

Regarding the principle of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one opens the Dharma-eye and accomplishes the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*). Having traveled four hundred *yojanas*, this is equal to the stages of the eighth and ninth *vihāras* and the stage of the *pratipannaka* (candidate) in the Separate Teaching (*pṛthagvidyā-śāsana*); it is the stage of non-retrogression in practice.
[Note] Although the stages of severance and realization are compared as if they were equivalent, the Perfect and Distinctive [Teachings] are distinct and must not be conflated.
[Record] This clarifies the practice and realization of the final three stages within the Clarifying Faith. The preceding seven stages merely sever the delusions within the realm;
as for the "dust-like" delusions beyond the realm, they are merely suppressed, because provisional contemplation has not yet manifested before one.

Furthermore, for these three classes of persons, because the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*) has manifested before them, they are able to sever all *rajas* (dust-like) delusions and exhaust them completely.
They are able to open the Dharma-eye (*dharmacakṣus*), perceive the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and achieve the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*).

Having traveled four hundred *yojanas*, they arrive at the Land of Real Reward Adornment (*sambhoga-kṣetra*). This corresponds to the lower stage of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*). As the verse says: "Eight."

In the ten faiths, the two delusions are empty; through the provisional establishment of the conventional, the principle is fully realized and becomes pervasive. This is equal to the previous stage of separate dwelling and the subsequent three stages;

furthermore, the stages of practice and the stage of heading toward [enlightenment] are identical. One must not fail to know the four phrases in the commentary, which admonish and demonstrate the principles of the Perfect and Distinctive [teachings] regarding identity and difference.
Miaole states: "The *Qixinlun shu* (Commentary on the Awakening of Faith) explains that within the gate of True Suchness, two meanings are established."
First, the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as unchanging; second, the meaning of arising and ceasing through following conditions (*pratyaya*).
The *Zhijue yaochao* states: "Following conditions" is spoken in contrast to "unchanging. "Unchanging" refers to the meaning of the fundamental, inherent non-alteration of the Middle Way principle.

"Following conditions" refers to the meaning of the total transformation and creative activity of the principle becoming phenomena. This is truly because True Suchness does not cling to its own nature (*svabhāva*), and thus it undergoes [transformation].

Regarding "perfuming and transformation according to conditions": it is called "according to conditions" because it accords with both defiled and pure conditions. As for its essence and characteristics:

in the Separate Teaching (*bhedanaya*), the principle of the *tathāgatagarbha*—the True Suchness as non-changing—is taken as the primary essence, while the differentiation of ignorance is taken as the supporting essence.

In the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇanaya*), non-changing takes the inherent possession of the three thousand realms (*trisahasra*) within the principle as its primary essence; as for "according to conditions," it takes phenomena...
The three thousand [dharmas] are taken as the substance (*tǐ*) of the reality; both take the single thought of deluded mind as their substratum.
In its unchanging aspect, it is the "three thousand inherently possessed" (*xingjù sānqiān*), wherein every characteristic (*xiàng*) is perfectly distinct.

In its aspect of following conditions (*suíyuán*), true suchness (*tathatā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) mutually perfume one another, forming the two functions of defilement and purity as their characteristic. This differs from other schools, which hold that a single principle follows [conditions].

The term "condition" (*pratyaya*) merely signifies conjunction; it does not discuss the principle of inherent completeness (*li-jù*). To speak solely of True Suchness following conditions (*zhenru suiyuan*) still remains a sense of separation.

Our school clarifies that the principle of the three thousand realms follows conditions to give rise to the function of the three thousand realms; yet when not following conditions, the three thousand realms remain perfectly distinct.
Thus, the differentiated phenomena and their essence are non-dual. This is clearly elucidated within both our own and other schools.

Regarding the two meanings of True Suchness—immutable yet conforming to conditions—if one does not clarify them by distinguishing between their being complete or incomplete, then the principles of the Perfect and the Separate Teachings will become confused.
Therefore, I caution you: they must not be conflated as one. Furthermore, the *Yizhu* states:

Although the text describes the stage of the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) as involving the severance of two delusions and the realization of two principles, it characterizes the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*) as "identity" (*samaya*).

This means that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is identical to *nirvāṇa*, afflictions (*kleśa*) are identical to *bodhi*, and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*) are identical.

Here, there is severance without severing and realization without realizing. In contrast, the Distinct Teaching (*bhinnakrama-yāna*) is termed "separation," meaning that one manifests *bodhi* by separating from afflictions.
"Ti. To leave birth-and-death and attain nirvāṇa; to leave the two extremes is the Middle Way. There are delusions that can be severed and principles that can be realized;
therefore, one must not conflate these and remain ignorant. Regarding those whose practice does not regress:

though the sands-of-the-Ganges of obstacles hindered their transformation and guidance, now that the sands-of-the-Ganges are severed, the practice of transformation and guidance is perfected, and they shall naturally become non-regressing Bodhisattvas."
...practice. Hence it is said that there is no retrogression in practice.
[Note] Furthermore, these six faculties clarify that for those of inferior capacity, emerging into the provisional (out-of-the-world) stage surpasses the merit of the ten abodes.

This is the stage of the semblance of the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna*), which differs from the sequential stages of emerging into the provisional. Furthermore, the five grades clarify that for those of middling capacity, the five grades [of faith]... [emerge into the provisional]. The five grades...

At the beginning, for those of superior capacity, one also discusses sitting at the site of enlightenment and saving sentient beings in terms of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). Furthermore, the fifth volume of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:
"The first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) is taken as the position of truly emerging from the provisional."

[Commentary] This section clarifies that within the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there are differences between those of sharp and dull faculties. Consequently, when they emerge into the provisional realm (*shijie*) to deliver sentient beings, there arises a distinction in the speed of their progress based on three grades of capacity.
The first line clarifies that emerging into the provisional realm during the stage of Clarification (*mingwei*) refers to those of the lower grade of capacity within the Perfect Teaching.

Although they are termed "lower grade," their merit surpasses that of the stage of the Ten Practices and Ten Dedications (*shi xiang*) of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), because they possess the threefold contemplation within a single mind.

In the contemplation [of the mind], one perceives the principle of the perfect fusion of the three truths; this is not the same as the stage of successively emerging into the provisional for those of other capacities.

Furthermore, below, it clarifies that for those of middling capacity, they emerge into the provisional at the level of the five grades, whereas for those of superior capacity, they emerge into the provisional from the very first grade.
If one speaks of the discourse on "being immediately Buddha," this can be discussed within the stage of contemplative practice (*kuan-hsing wei*).
"Sitting at the site of enlightenment" means to deliver sentient beings. The ancient saying that "contemplative practice is to be like a Buddha" refers precisely to this meaning.

The above discusses the provisional stage of emerging into the conventional world (*saṃvṛti-niḥsaraṇa*). The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Part II, discusses the true stage of emerging into the conventional world; this may be understood accordingly.
This concludes the section on ordinary persons.

△ Second, the clarification of the two types of sages. First, the stage of the cause (hetu-bhūmi) has three parts. First, the clarification of the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra). Second, the first position is explained individually. First, the direct explanation has two parts.
First, the clarification of internal realization (pratyātma-adhigama).

Next, one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*). One severs one grade of ignorance and realizes one portion of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), namely liberation (*vimukti*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
These three virtues are neither vertical nor horizontal, like the three dots of the world-symbol *i* or the three eyes of the Lord of Devas.
[Note] This clarifies the severing of delusions, the realization of principle, and the arising of function from the whole body.

Regarding the sequence of the three virtues—Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti—they follow the order of the development of the three minds (the causal, conditional, and direct) as they unfold in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*). Thus, this sequence is established accordingly.
[Commentary] This explains the destruction of ignorance, the manifestation of the *dharmatā*, the arrival at the treasure-store, and the opening of the secret treasury.

At the stage of the first resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*), one is able to give rise to all merits. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the merits of the first stage cannot be fully extolled even by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
if they were explained in their entirety, people would become mad upon hearing them. Now, this text clarifies the first stage.
To realize one portion of the three virtues is to cite the essentials that encompass all others. The *Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra* states:

"Regarding the manifold virtues of the stage of fruition, they are spoken of as merely three; this is simply to cite the concise while including all. As for the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*): this body is neither form nor formless.
Because it is not form, it cannot be seen through physical characteristics; because it is not formless, it cannot be known through mental conception. Although...
It is not form, yet it fills the ten directions; the vast and the minute contain one another, being neither broad nor narrow.

Although it is not non-form, it can nevertheless be sought after, for it gives rise to the profound and expansive wisdom of sentient beings. Therefore, it is said that "the form of the Tathāgata is inexhaustible," and so forth;
this is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As for *prajñā* (wisdom), it is neither cognition nor letters. Because it is not cognition, it cannot be moved by discursive thought.

It is discernment because it is not a [mere] character. It cannot be described and is to be inscribed upon the sash; yet it is not a case of ignorance or the absence of characters. Because it is not ignorant, it does not resemble the extinction of ashes.
Because it is not the absence of characters, it does not resemble partial emptiness. Although it is not knowledge, there is nothing it does not know;

the three truths are universally luminous within the ultimate realm of the Buddha. Though it is not a character, both the mundane and the sagely are clearly illuminated throughout the provisional and the perfect.
It is fully endowed with all worldly, world-transcending, and supremely world-transcending syllables.
It completely understands the continuous flow of the Dharma-realm, like a cascading river or a surging ocean, inexhaustible and beyond end. As stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*:

"One can expound the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind; all say, 'The World-Honored One speaks in my own language. This is precisely the Tathāgata.
The indeterminate dharma is the virtue of *prajñā*. As for liberation (*vimukti*): it is neither clamor nor silence; neither bondage nor release.
Because it is not bound, the five abodes cannot fetter it; because it is not released, the ten knowledges cannot render it void.

It is spoken without being spoken, unrestrained by the two extremes, as explained in the "Liberation in One Hundred Phrases. That which is unbound yet appears bound is due to dullness and insensitivity.
Bound by ignorance, icchantikas, and non-Buddhists, they exhibit both diseased and infantile behaviors;

yet, abiding in Śūraṅgama-samādhi, they manifest both good and evil according to the needs of those to be tamed. Even toward the lowly, they must bestow their aid, just as a physician treats the sick.
Like a flower upon water, it is unstained and unattached; this is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).

The inconceivable bodily activity (*kāyakarman*) of the Buddha is subsumed within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The inconceivable verbal activity (*vākkarman*) of the Buddha is subsumed within wisdom (*prajñā*).

The inconceivable mental activity (*manaskarman*) of the Buddha is subsumed within liberation. Thus, one should know that these three virtues encompass all virtues. Form (*rūpa*) contains both the general and the particular.

Encompassing both phenomena and principle, the concise gathers the extensive; it does not exceed the three virtues (*tri-dharma*). Thus, one knows that in the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), the fruit of Buddhahood is partially realized.
In this "realizing all by realizing one," the statement that "one portion of the three virtues is realized" employs the three virtues as a means to encompass all merits.
Regarding the sequence of these three virtues, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) should occupy the first place, followed by Prajñā.
Next, regarding the sequence after liberation: here, the initial stage of liberation—the Dharma-body—is placed first to accord with the First Abode (Prathamā-bhūmi).
The subsequent development of the three causal minds—conditional (*pratyaya*), direct cause (*hetu*), and immediate (*samyak*)—constitutes the following order.

As it is said that the conditional cause arises from a virtuous mind, sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas have lowered their heads and joined their palms, snapped their fingers and scattered flowers, and given rise to the Bodhicitta and compassion.
Vows, giving, precept-keeping, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and all other roots of goodness are simultaneously awakened;

with a single mind, one becomes fully endowed with the myriad practices. As for the awakening of the wisdom-mind of the "enabling cause," it refers to sentient beings who, throughout immeasurable kalpas, have heard Mahāyāna sūtras—even a single phrase or a single verse—and have received, upheld, recited, read, explained, and transcribed them.
Through the cultivation of contemplative practice, all wisdom is simultaneously manifested and becomes truly untainted (*anāsrava*).

Regarding the arising of the mind of the true principle of the direct cause: since beginningless time, the Buddha-nature and true mind of sentient beings have been constantly obscured and covered by ignorance.
Now, through the power of the two causes—the conditional and the enabling—one is able to shatter the dark delusions of ignorance. And...
This causes the true cause to manifest clearly and perfectly. Because these three aspects arise in perfect harmony, it is called "arousing the mind" (*cittotpāda*).

The arising of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) is liberation (*vimukti*); the arising of the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*) is wisdom (*prajñā*); and the arising of the true cause (*hetu-hetu*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Once these three minds have arisen, they form a shape like the world-character *ī*. One who is provisionally named a "practitioner" dwells in these three minds by means of the dharma of non-abiding; this is precisely what it means to dwell [in them].
The Nirvana of the Three Virtues, the inconceivable secret treasury, is called the Stage of the First Resolve.
[Supplement] When the three minds arise, they arise simultaneously; fundamentally there is no beginning or end. Nevertheless, one may discuss their sequence by means of these three dharmas.

The two serve as the manifestors, and the one serves as that which is manifested. Within the manifestors, the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) provides the support for accomplishment, while the revealing condition (vijñapti-pratyaya) performs the contemplative illumination;
thus, it is not contradictory to discuss a sequence within that which is actually without sequence. The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* states: "Neither before nor after."
Nor are they simultaneous; this is correct.

[Note] Regarding the statement "neither vertical nor horizontal": this differs from the Separate Teaching (biejiao), where what is not vertical is immediately horizontal. The *Shiqian*, fascicle 6, states:
"Although a single dot is at the top, it is not like the verticality of dots falling on water. The Three Virtues (sande) are likewise: although the Dharma-body is fundamental..."

There is. This is not the same as the Separate Teaching (biejiao), where one is traversed by delusions. Although the two dots are positioned below, they do not differ from the horizontal arrangement of the fire [in the character for "three"].

The Three Virtues (sande) are likewise: while the two virtues are accomplished through cultivation, they are not like the separate practitioners' view where the principle-body is fully possessed yet the parts do not mutually encompass one another.
As the *Miaozong* says: "Although the three are inherently possessed, the conditions and causes are cultivated; although these two are cultivated, they have not merely come into being now."
If the two [aspects] were not cultivation, the three dharmas would be horizontal; if the two were not nature, the three dharmas would be vertical. [Commentary:
This clarifies that while the names of the three virtues are identical, the realization in the Perfect and Distinctive [vehicles] differs.

The meaning is that for a person of the Perfect [Vehicle], the three contemplations are cultivated perfectly and the three causes are manifested perfectly; therefore, the three virtues are realized perfectly. It is not so for the person of the Distinctive [Vehicle]; as for cultivation, it is threefold...

Regarding the sequence of contemplation: in terms of manifestation, there are the three causes; in terms of realization, there are the three virtues. Both follow this same order. As for the statement that the *dharmakāya* is shrouded by delusions:
it means that one does not know that the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-pratibhāsa*) inherently possesses the virtue of evil.

Therefore, defiled evil is not the two virtues of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the immediate condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). There is only the *dharmakāya* of original enlightenment which, following along with defiled conditions, produces all phenomena within delusion; this is called... [the name].
Being shrouded by delusion, although it is thus obscured, it merely remains within the principle of Buddha-nature. It is like a pure and good person who is incapable of evil;
yet, being coerced by an evil person, they are made to commit various evils. Therefore, it is said to be "shrouded by evil.

This demonstrates that there is certainly the evil capable of obscuring, while the True Suchness (Tathatā) which is obscured remains immutable in its principle, eternally pure from beginning to end. Thus it is said:
Only by not following from concealment (āvaraṇa) can it receive the name "seed" (*bīja*). [Supplement] The *Yizhu* states:

One must further employ the nature of enlightenment that accords with conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya-bodhi-svabhāva*) to separately take true reality (*paramārtha-satya*) and conventional reality (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as objects, sequentially and specifically cultivating emptiness, the provisional, and the conditions for perfect enlightenment (*pratyekabuddha*, *bodhisattva*, and *samyaksaṃbuddha*).

By overturning and destroying all deluded phenomena, one reveals the nature of the fundamental enlightenment of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-mūla-bodhi-svabhāva*). Therefore, when the principle is concealed, it results in "laxity" (*yōng*).

This is the meaning. It is not so for those of the Perfect Teaching (Yuan), because they know that original enlightenment possesses the nature of defilement and evil; by taking the substance of defilement and evil as cultivation, these are themselves the two Buddha-natures.
How could there be a Buddha-nature that further covers another Buddha-nature? It is like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel; he is capable of both good and evil.
If one associates with evil people and commits evil deeds, one’s own capability is revealed; how could there be anything to conceal?

Therefore, these two delusions serve as the conditions and causes for manifesting the correct [nature]. The two virtues of condition and cause obtain their substance through delusion; in meaning, they are that which is manifested.

The original is the cultivation of virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), which can further be manifested. Although they are distinguished as cultivation and nature (*bhāvanā* and *prakṛti*), both are fundamentally inherent;

thus, the meaning does not constitute a vertical succession (*tiryak*). [Commentary] Therefore, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is not vertical, differing from the verticality of the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*). Although the two dots are located at the lowest of the low.
The clarity and perfection [of the Perfect Teaching] do not constitute "horizontal" [defilement], as this differs from the horizontal [defilement] of the Separate Teaching.

However, those who claim that the principle and substance of the Separate Teaching are fully endowed yet mutually exclusive, fail to understand that the nature of original enlightenment (prakṛti) is inherently endowed with defiled and evil qualities; thus, they are unable to give rise to defiled and evil cultivation by fully utilizing the nature.
Thus, the fundamental principle (li-ti) is established as horizontally possessing three dharmas. As for what is meant by "not mutually inclusive":

these three dharmas are all equally present within the nature (xing), and all are that which is manifested. It is like three people, each claiming to be an emperor; how could they possibly encompass one another?

Therefore, one does not realize that within the nature there are three dharmas. Two of them are those to be cultivated (xiu); thus, these two constitute the horizontal aspect. Consequently, the fundamental principle is fully complete.
Yet they do not mutually encompass one another. [Supplement] The *Yizhu* states: "The person of Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanren*) is not like this.

Because he knows that original enlightenment (*benjue*) possesses the nature of defiled evil, all defiled evils within delusion are, in their very place, the *pratyaya-bhāva* and *nirvedha-bhāva* Buddha-natures.

By means of the two cultivated natures (*xiuxing*), the one original nature is manifested—just as with one lord and two ministers: the lord encompasses the ministers, and the ministers return to the lord. Thus, the three virtues (*sande*) mutually encompass one another."
It is likewise so. [Commentary] Therefore, the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) is not horizontal (*heng*), unlike the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), which is horizontal.
As explained in the *Miaozong* (The Sublime Commentary), the first two phrases further clarify that the three dharmas are not horizontal;

that is, the two virtues are accomplished through cultivation, which differs from the followers of the Separate Teaching who hold that the principle-body is fully possessed yet does not encompass one another. The next two phrases further clarify that the three dharmas are not vertical (*zong*).
This means that the Dharma-body is inherently present, which differs from the Separate Teaching (biejiao), where it is obscured by delusions.

The next two phrases clarify that one does not discuss the two types of cultivation (the cultivated and the inherent), as this would result in a horizontal [classification]. This is because, although the Separate Teaching speaks of "inherent virtue" (xingde), all three [aspects] reside within the nature.

Yet they do not mutually integrate; this is due to their horizontal arrangement within the cause. Furthermore, because the three dharmas of inherent possession according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao) do not encompass one another, the three bodies (trikāya) are manifested horizontally at the stage of fruition. All of this results from the fault of not discussing the two types of cultivation.

The final two phrases clarify that if one does not distinguish between the two natures, it results in a logical redundancy (*yōng*). This is because, according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), the Dharmakāya is primordially present within the causal stage yet is shrouded by delusions;
therefore, one must separately cultivate the functions of the conditions (*yuán*) and the wisdom (*liǎo*), which mutually assist one another to manifest [the Buddha-nature] at the stage of fruition.
Thus, the dharmakāya is primordially present, prajñā is accomplished through cultivation, and liberation is fulfilled at the outset;
all of this results from the fault of not discussing the two natures. Therefore, by discussing these two—nature and cultivation—the three virtues are established as neither vertical nor horizontal.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the three dots of the letter *i* and the three eyes of the Lord of Heaven, which manifest this state of being neither vertical nor horizontal.
[Note] The three dots and three eyes appear in the "Chapter on Lamentation" (*Karuṇāparivarta*) of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. In the West (India), there are two traditions of the vowel *i*:
the old *i* is like a vertical stroke of fire trailing through water; the new *i* is like the subscript character in Chinese cursive script (*cǎoshū*), where fine lines intersect one another.
Neither vertical nor horizontal. Maheśvara has three eyes and eight arms.
[Note] This passage clarifies the origin of the metaphor used. The first two phrases point out the source; the following two lines explain the correct meaning.
As the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra says: "What is called the Secret Treasury? It is like the three dots of the letter 'i', which are arranged side by side."
Then it would not be established; even if they were combined, it would still not be established.
It is only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara that it can be established. If the three dots were separate, they too would not be established. I am likewise so.
The dharma of liberation is not nirvāṇa, and the body of the Tathāgata is also not nirvāṇa. I now abide peacefully within these three dharmas as...
Because of sentient beings, it is called "entering nirvāṇa. The commentary consists of three parts: first, an analogy for the three dots; second, an analogy for the three eyes;
third, a correlation with the three virtues (*triguṇa*). Regarding the phrase "entering principle through phenomena": the three dots represent written characters; this refers to the verbal teachings.
The three eyes are the divine eye; this refers to practice. The three virtues are the Teacher of the Buddha; this refers to principle.
Furthermore, they are the seal of the Buddha, which seals both teaching and practice. Whatever is spoken that accords with these constitutes the secret teaching.

Cultivation in accordance [with the principle] is the secret practice; realization in accordance [with the principle] is the secret principle. Thus, one dharma and two metaphors correspond to principle, teaching, and practice.
Next, regarding the explanation of the three dots: the ancient *ī* (the vowel *i*) serves as a metaphor for the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) of the former teachings.
The Dharma-body is inherently present; Prajñā is accomplished through cultivation. Only upon entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is there liberation, wherein neither body nor wisdom remains.

Vertically, it is like a drop falling into water: though released, they are separated. Furthermore, if categorized by body and wisdom, one obtains *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, which exists simultaneously [with the body].
These three dharmas are each distinct, like fires arranged side-by-side; each is unrelated to the others. This is the "new" [interpretation].
For example, as the teaching of the three virtues now instructs: the Dharma-body is simultaneously illumination and simultaneously sovereignty;

thus, one is named as three. Since these three have no separate substance, they are not horizontal. Since they are neither before nor after, they are not vertical. One is precisely three, like the three dots [of the *i*];
three is precisely one, like a fine drawing. They cannot be described as one or three; they cannot be conceived as one or three. This is called the "inconceivable."
Discourse: It is neither three nor one; it is the secret treasury. [Appendix] Bian’e states: The "I" character (*i*) of the West is indicated by this;
its new and old forms are like the cursive and clerical scripts of this land, differing in their transformations. According to the *Zhi guan*, if the three dots are aligned horizontally...

It is like the horizontal stroke of "running fire" (走火) and the vertical stroke of "dotting water" (點水). Later generations arbitrarily wrote the horizontal as "river" (川) and the vertical as "three" (三), subsequently calling them "horizontal river" and "vertical three.
This is incorrect. In the current text, the two characters "horizontal river" should be removed;

it is correct to simply state that the horizontal is "running fire" and the vertical is "dotting water. One should know that the Western *ī* character merely refers to the presence of these fine [strokes].

That which is painted is "new," while that which lacks fine detail is "old. Thus they are distinguished. The arrangement of fire and the dotting of water are merely metaphorical expressions borrowed from Zhiyan;
they are not intended to explain the vertical and horizontal [structures]. This is likewise the case here.
△ Second, clarifying external transformation (*bāhya-nirmāṇa*).
Manifesting bodies throughout the hundred realms (*śata-dhātu*) and attaining enlightenment through the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*), he extensively saves all sentient beings.
[□ Note] Regarding the "eight phases," the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "In some cases one sees him entering the womb," and so forth. The word "in some cases" (*vā*) is used for each individual phase.
Because all [of these] possess the eight phases (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
[Commentary: The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: When a Bodhisattva descends from Tuṣita to be born, various humans and devas may see the Bodhisattva dwelling in Tuṣita Heaven;
or they may see him entering the womb; or they may see his initial birth; or they may see him leaving home; or they may see him attaining [enlightenment].
The Way [is manifested] thus: sometimes it is seen as the subduing of Māra, sometimes as the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and sometimes as entering Nirvāṇa.
Within each of these marks, there are eight aspects. Regarding the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in the womb, there are ten kinds of subtle manifestations;
that is to say, while in the mother’s womb, he manifests everything from the initial generation of the bodhicitta up to the stage of consecration (abhiṣeka). While in the womb...
These include manifesting residence in Tuṣita Heaven; manifesting birth; manifesting the stage of childhood; manifesting dwelling in the royal palace;
manifesting renunciation; manifesting ascetic practice; proceeding to the site of enlightenment; attaining equal and perfect awakening;

manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and manifesting parinirvāṇa, and so forth. Yet, from the very beginning, while abiding in the hundred realms, he manifests his body’s attainment of the Way.

Regarding "benefiting sentient beings," the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "If a Bodhisattva dwells within the lands of a hundred Buddhas, acts as a king of Jambudvīpa, and rules over the four continents, he cultivates the hundred gates of dharma-illumination and the mind of equality regarding the two truths to transform all sentient beings.
The *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) states: "In the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), one vertically shatters a portion of ignorance and attains a portion of the twenty-five kings."
Samādhi reveals a portion of the nature of self and elucidates the locus of ultimate reality; it is inconceivable.

Transversally, throughout a hundred Buddha-worlds, it manifests as emanated bodies and dispersed reflections, assuming the forms of the ten Dharma-realms to guide and benefit sentient beings. This concludes the formal exposition.
△ Second, citing scriptural evidence, which has two parts. First, citing the sutra:
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "At the very moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one immediately attains perfect enlightenment; the entire body of wisdom is not realized through another."
The pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serenely responsive to all things.
[□ Note] The following section cites the sutra to provide an exposition and, by extension, to refute the errors of others.
[■ Record] The sutra says: "If bodhisattvas are able to accord with such contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), regarding all phenomena..."
Without giving rise to dualistic interpretations, all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before one. At the very moment of first resolving for enlightenment, one attains bodhi;
knowing that all dharmas are the self-nature of mind, one accomplishes the body of wisdom, not through awakening by means of another. It is further said:
"Ultimately free from delusion, unstained like space, the pure and wondrous Dharma-body, serenely responding to all"—this is it.
Question: If one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the mind of awakening (*prathamacittotpāda*), why is there further mention of "bodhi at the final mind"?

Answer: It is neither the beginning nor the end, yet it is not separate from the beginning and the end. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one could attain [enlightenment] through the initial mind alone..."
Regarding the "subsequent mind," when a bodhisattva first generates the resolve for awakening, they should already be a Buddha.

If there were no initial resolve, how could there be a second or third resolve? It is with the initial resolve as the fundamental cause and condition; it is not the case that [Buddhahood] depends solely on the subsequent mind.
Furthermore, it is not separate from the final mind; this final mind is also not separate from the initial mind.

The initial mind accumulates various immeasurable merits, which the final mind then brings to fulfillment. Thus, one is able to sever the habitual tendencies of afflictions and attain the Unsurpassed Way.
This refers to the stage of Perfect Abiding and above; it is through the successive transmission of the discussion of beginning and end that one finally attains Bodhi.

△ Second, the explanation has two parts. First, clarifying the initial attainment of perfect enlightenment has two parts. First, indicating the Dharma and determining the stages has two parts. First, the actual explanation. The commentary states:

"The first arousal of the mind" refers to the name of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*). "Immediately attaining perfect enlightenment" means becoming a Buddha through the eight aspects (*aṣṭalakṣaṇa*).
This is the fruit of partial realization; it is precisely the true cause of this teaching.
[Commentary] This text definitively establishes that "the first arousal of the mind" refers to the first *bhūmi* (stage) of the Perfect Teaching.

Those in this stage have begun to shatter ignorance and thereby manifest the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*). If, while practicing the path prior to abiding in this stage, the assembly with whom one has established karmic connections possesses pure faculties and suitability...
When [the practice] is matured, the Bodhisattva may manifest the body of a Buddha and display the marks of attaining perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Throughout hundreds of Buddha-worlds, he extensively expounds all dharmas to deliver and liberate sentient beings; therefore, it is said that he "immediately attains perfect enlightenment.

This is precisely the Buddha who has accomplished the eight phases [of enlightenment]. This fruit of partial realization is the true cause of this teaching; it is what is called the ultimate fruit of another stage. This is...
This is the true cause of our country.
△ Second, the refutation of errors has three parts. First, taking the cause as the fruit:

to claim that this constitutes the attainment of wondrous enlightenment is an error of the utmost degree. If it were so, then all the subsequent stages from the second dwelling onwards would be rendered in vain.

[Commentary] This refutes the error of taking the cause as the fruit. As the *Myōgen* (Miaoxuan) states: "There is a teacher who claims that the initial moment of sudden enlightenment is itself the ultimate, perfect culmination.
The *Shikan* (Jishi) says: "However, within the *Avataṃsaka*, the stages encompass both the Perfect and the Separate Teachings.

People do not understand the meaning of the stages of these two teachings, nor do they grasp the beginning and end of the Perfect stages; thus, they point directly to the initial mind [as the final goal]."

To regard [this] as the stage of wondrous enlightenment and to value only the sudden gate (dunmen) so that Buddhahood may be swiftly attained, thereby rendering the final stages of the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) superfluous—
is this not a confusion between the provisional and the real, or between the initial and the final?
△ Second, citing a defense and then re-examining it with severity:
If one says that [the teaching] is repeated, the Buddha would incur the fault of redundancy.
[■ Record] This refutes the potential error of a shifting argument. The meaning is: if it is claimed that from the second stage (*dvitīya-bhūmi*) onward, [the teaching is still repeated],...
There are forty-one persons in the latter stage, yet this was not taught merely as a dispensation;

rather, it was the Buddha’s exercise of great compassion, teaching again for the sake of those with dull faculties. If it were so, one would still not escape the fault of the Buddha being overly burdensome.
From this we know that to judge according to the old [interpretation] is truly not permissible.
△ Third, citing texts to encourage careful examination:

Although there are statements that each stage encompasses all other stages, and it is further said, "The initial resolve and its ultimate fulfillment are not distinct," one must understand the reasons for such encompassing and clearly recognize the principle of non-duality.
[Note] Although it is said that each [stage] encompasses all positions, one must understand the reason for this encompassing: it is because they are inherently present (*li-jù*) by principle.
Although it is said that the initial aspiration and the ultimate state are not distinct, those who minutely discern the purport of non-duality find its essence in "immediacy" (*jí*).

While the principle of such immediate presence is thus, how could the phenomenal stages (*shì-wèi*) of the shallow and the bridge not be distinguished? Because they are immediate, the beginning and the end are non-dual; because they are six, the beginning... [is non-dual].

"Later, there is no confusion; each stage encompasses all stages. This means that, for example, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, from the initial letter *A* to the final letter *Ḍa*, with forty characters in between—the gateway of the initial letter *A* contains all forty-two letters, and the gateway of the final letter *Ḍa* is likewise so.
It is also like the first bhūmi in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which possesses the merits of all the bhūmis.
[Commentary] This clarifies that there is still a fear of not reaching the source of error, and it cites scriptural passages as proof.
First, it clarifies how each stage encompasses [all phenomena]: as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states, "The letter A-gate: because all dharmas are unarisen; the letter Ra-gate:
because all dharmas are free from defilement; the letter Pa-gate: because all dharmas are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)."
Therefore, up to the letter-gateway *ṭa*, one enters the ultimate limit of all phenomena. Beyond *ṭa*, there is no further letter to be spoken of.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Among the forty-two letters, a single letter completely enters into all other letters;
for example, taking the letter *a* as the fixed basis, it transforms into *ra*, and also transforms into *pa*, thus completely entering into all forty-two letters. Forty...

Regarding "two characters entering one character": the forty-two characters are all subsumed within the syllable *a*; the syllable *a* in turn enters back into the *a*. This constitutes the complete forty-two characters.
The final phrase refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which states that a Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*) accomplishes the dharmas for purifying all stages.
The text says: "In this way, the Bodhisattva accomplishes the ten kinds of dharmas for perfecting the stages."
That is to say: faith, compassion, loving-kindness, and equanimity; being free from weariness and fatigue; knowing all sūtras and śāstras; being skillful in understanding worldly dharmas;
possessing the firm power of shame and remorse; making offerings to all Buddhas; and practicing according to the teachings. It is further said:

"This bodhisattva’s practice of giving is predominant, yet he does not fail to cultivate the others; he simply practices according to his strength and capacity. It is also said: "The bodhisattva purifies and cultivates himself therein."
In the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), that which is performed is without obstruction and is fully perfected without interruption. Thus, the *Qingliang shu* states:
"Within a single stage, all the merits of every stage are fully encompassed."
[Note] The Mahāyāna Sūtra states: "The initial aspiration and the ultimate realization are not two different things; yet between these two states of mind, the former is more difficult.
Here, "initial aspiration" refers to the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), while "ultimate realization" refers to the state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*).

[Commentary] Next, the text correctly cites scriptures as evidence. Regarding this citation, the preceding phrase is the primary proof; however, the reason for the subsequent phrase has not yet been fully understood.

As for the statement that "the two are not distinct," the *Shenbao ji* states: "Although the Initial Abiding of the Mind (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*) and the Ultimate Identity (*niṣṭhā-gati*) are vastly different in their distinctions, they are identical in terms of the Path of Realization (*darśana-mārga*); therefore, it is said that the two are not distinct."
As for the statement that "the preceding mind is difficult": although the principle is one from beginning to end, the initial arousal [of the mind] is not easy;
therefore, the preceding mind is difficult. [Appendix] One stage universally encompasses all stages, and the ultimate arousal of the mind is no different.

The reason these two passages are cited is to explain and establish the perfect dwelling (*yuan-zhu*); it is not a redundant or superfluous application. Do not forget the essential purport of this chapter.
△ Second, the testimony of persons who have realized this stage:
the Dragon Girl immediately attained perfect enlightenment, and the various Śrāvakas received the prediction of their future attainment of Buddhahood;
these are all signs of attaining Buddhahood at this very stage.

[Note] The account of the dragon girl attaining Buddhahood is spoken according to the provisional teaching (*upāya*). It serves to demonstrate the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood in the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-sūtra*).

If actual practice were not swift, the provisional practice would be in vain. Since the meanings of the provisional and the real are equal, the principle is not in vain. As stated in the *Myōraku* (Wondrous Joy), fascicle 8, section 35: [text follows].
[Commentary] This is a testimony provided by a human being, serving as the mark of attaining Buddhahood in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Regarding the passage from the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy), which states that the Dragon Girl attained Buddhahood: it is asked, "Does she attain Buddhahood without abandoning the *pariccheda* (segmented) existence?
If she does not attain Buddhahood immediately, then how are the attainment of Buddhahood by this Dragon Girl and the verse in the *Garbha-sūtra* to be understood?"
Is this so? The *Tāi jīng* (Womb Sūtra) states: "The daughters of Māra, Brahmā, and Śakra all attain Buddhahood in their present bodies, without casting off the current body or receiving another one.
Thus the verse says: "The nature of phenomena is like the great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong. Whether ordinary person or sage, they are equal without high or low.
It depends only on the purity or defilement of the mind; to realize the proof is as easy as turning over one's palm. Answer: [This is so].

The Dragon Girl attaining Buddhahood is spoken of from the perspective of provisional means (*upāya*), in order to demonstrate the swiftness of attaining Buddhahood according to the Perfect Sūtra (*pariniṣpanna-sūtra*).

If one were to attain it through actual practice (*bhūtacara*) without such swiftness, then provisional practice would be in vain. Thus, the meanings of the provisional and the real are equal, and the principle is not in vain;

therefore, the *Garbha-sūtra* also speaks from the standpoint of actual attainment. If it is from actual attainment, then starting from the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), one attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It should be...
That which all beings cherish is the manifestation of spiritual transformations, appearing in bodily form as a Buddha and realizing the Perfect Sūtra.

Having realized non-arising (*anutpāda*), how could one not know that fundamentally there is nothing to be received? What prevents one from relinquishing this state to proceed to other teachings and the stages of ordinary beings?
Upon reaching these stages, advancing to sever ignorance is likewise so. In all such cases, it is essential that the provisional and the real are not [separated].
2. To resolve doubts and obstacles: In the southern region, conditions are ripe; it is appropriate that he attain enlightenment through the eight phases.

In this land, conditions are shallow; he merely transformed the dragon girl to teach her. This is a skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), by which one body becomes all bodies—the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body.
[Supplement] The *Tāizang jīng* (Womb Sūtra) says: "The world-realm is named Flame; the Buddha is named Non-Desire. All the people..."
All received female bodies and fully realized suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.

Seventy million two hundred thousand *koṭis* of women practiced the three gates of liberation and, in a single day and at a single moment, immediately attained the Buddha-way; this is called "attaining Buddhahood by receiving a body without abandoning the female form. Question:

How are actual practice (*shixing*) and provisional practice (*quanxing*) to be distinguished? Answer: Actual practice refers to those who were the primary recipients of the Buddha’s teaching during his lifetime.

Such a person shall realize the perfect principle (pariniṣpanna-tattva) and thereby know that the dragon girl likewise accomplishes the practice of reality (bhūta-caryā). Next, proceeding to the south, one immediately gives rise to function from essence;
this is the practice of expedient means (upāya-caryā).
[□ Note] The various śrāvakas receive the names of kalpas, lands, and titles; they form karmic connections with sentient beings through material gifts (text).

[■ Record] Miaole states: As for the fact that those of the two vehicles are provisionally granted the prediction of the eight marks of enlightenment, it is to cause them to form pure land karmic connections with sentient beings.

[Supplementary Note] The ritual text cites the Dragon Girl’s attainment of Buddhahood and the Śrāvakas’ receiving of predictions as proof of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*).

This is the original intent. Regarding the statement in the commentary that the Dragon Girl’s case is spoken of from the perspective of provisional teaching (*upāya*), this is likely because one might wonder:

"How is it known that the Dragon Girl’s Buddhahood refers to the first stage? And if it is the first stage, why is it described as 'attaining Buddhahood'? Therefore, it is explained through the lens of provisional teaching.
It can also be understood by analogy that the two vehicles [of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] form karmic connections with the Buddha through the eight aspects [of the bodhisattva path].
△ Second, clarifying how the three causes produce the fruit:

the "Wisdom Body" (prajñā-kāya) is the virtue of *prajñā*, which is the development of the nature of the "enabling cause" (*yuan-yin*); the "Sublime Dharma Body" is the virtue of the *dharmakāya*, which is the "direct cause" (*zheng-yin*).
The nature unfolds and responds to all; this is the virtue of liberation. It is the unfolding of the nature of the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).
Since these three bodies are manifested as that which is originally possessed, it is said that they are not realized through another.

[Note] Regarding "attaining that which is originally possessed," the *Myōshū* (Vol. 22, p. 1) states: "In the first stage of abiding, the three dharmas that are manifested are all inherently complete within the nature (*xingju*).
Therefore, when they are manifested, they are manifested simultaneously. From wisdom one realizes the Dharma; from the Dharma one gives rise to the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This is not a matter of sequential timing, yet the three bodies are attained instantaneously; thus there is no before or after. They are neither vertical nor horizontal. Furthermore, this is seen here: from the beginning, one has practiced the Perfect [Teaching] as one."

The three contemplations of the mind are now attained within a single moment of the perfect threefold wisdom (*trividya*). By means of this very wisdom, one realizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The nature of wisdom is itself form;
the three and the one are fused into a single essence, which is called the "wondrous form-body" (*rūpakāya*). This body is profoundly tranquil, like a mirror devoid of sentience;

yet when forms confront it, images arise, such that even a mountain or a hair-tip leaves no gap. It is thus said to "respond to all. The three bodies and the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are in essence free from either vertical or horizontal differentiation. (Text)

[Commentary] This clarifies that the cause overcomes the fruit without the slightest deviation. The first phrase sets forth the inquiry. From "Miaozong" (The Wondrous Commentary) below, the text cites the source to provide the formal explanation.

That is to say, when one now breaks through ignorance and manifests the *dharmatā*, the merits realized upon ascending to the First Abode (*prathamabhūmi*) are all inherently possessed within the self-nature;
they do not come from without. Therefore, it is said: "Because they are all intrinsically complete," and thus they are manifested.

Then they arise together. The two phrases "from wisdom" and "realizing the Dharma" clarify that the three bodies are not attained simultaneously. The phrase "the three bodies are attained all at once" clarifies that the three bodies are not sequential;

this is the meaning of being neither vertical nor horizontal. [Supplement] Previously, it was discussed in terms of the two types of cultivation and the one nature regarding the development of the three minds;
therefore, they are not horizontal. Since both are also inherently present, they are not vertical. Now, it is discussed from the perspective of...

The *Jizheng fadeng lun* (Treatise on the Equal Dharma Realized by Wisdom) is neither horizontal (*heng*) because [the three wisdoms] are attained simultaneously rather than sequentially, nor vertical (*zong*) because they are explained as a single unit.

Furthermore, it is said "seen again here" to indicate that from the section "cultivating perfectly from the beginning" onwards, one refers to the contemplative practices (*guanxing*) of the preceding five stages;

now, the three perfect wisdoms are attained within a single moment of mind, which is precisely the first stage (*chuzhu*). The three fundamental dharmas thus manifested are called the "three wisdoms."

These are: first, the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*), which externally destroys all darkness; second, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*), which is able to reflect back upon itself;

and third, the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is neither internal nor external, neither self nor other. These three knowledges are now attained within a single moment of mind at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
By means of these very knowledges, one proceeds to explain how the Dharma is realized through wisdom. Now, as for this realization of the Dharma:

The body is called the "one body. When wisdom-nature is form, it is called the "three bodies": wisdom is the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), nature is the *dharmakāya* (dharma body), and form is the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
These three and one are fused into a single essence; this is termed the "pure and wondrous form-body. [Supplement] The *Awakening of Faith* asks:
"If the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas is free from form-characteristics, how can it manifest form-characteristics?"
Answer: Because this very *dharmakāya* is the substance of form (*rūpa*), it is able to manifest as form. That is to say, from the very beginning, form and mind have been non-dual;
because the nature of form is itself wisdom, the substance of form is formless and is called the "wisdom-body" (*jñānakāya*).
Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is called the "dharma-body" (*dharmakāya*) that pervades all places.
△ Third, the conclusion:
The Middle Way manifests before one; the Buddha-eye is opened; the knowledge of all modes is accomplished; one travels five hundred yojanas and reaches the place of treasure.
Initially residing in the *sahābhisaṃbuddha* (actual retribution) realm free from hindrances, one dwells in the stage of "non-retrogression in thought.

[Commentary] Regarding "the Middle Way manifesting before one": since the three causes have been developed, the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*) should be perfected and clarified, and the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) should shine through with penetrating illumination.
Now, when it is simply said that the Buddha-eye is the seed-wisdom (*bīja-jñāna*), within this [eye] there must necessarily be the simultaneous illumination of all three wisdoms.

The four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye and are collectively designated as the "Buddha-eye. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Volume 3, Part 1 (25), states: "It is like a river entering the sea and losing its original name as a river. Why is this?
Because the two eyes of flesh and heaven are conditioned by outflows (*āsrava*); the two eyes of wisdom and dharma have not yet exhausted their residual impressions (*vāsanā*)."
Therefore, one abandons the fundamental position and enters the Buddha-eye (text).

[Commentary] "The middle must simultaneously illuminate" means that the middle must simultaneously illuminate both extremes of emptiness and the provisional. The phrase "the three wisdoms are fully present" means that within the middle, there is necessarily the simultaneous illumination of both emptiness and the provisional.
Thus, it is said that the Knowledge of All Modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), the Knowledge of the Paths (*mārgajñatā*), and the Knowledge of All [Phenomena] (*sarvajñatā*) are naturally and fully possessed.
The *Guanyin xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of Avalokiteśvara) states: "The Knowledge of All Modes is able, within a single mode of knowledge, to know all paths and to know all modes.
It is able to know and understand the various categories of practices—the single mark, which is the mark of quiescence—therefore it is named the Knowledge of All Modes."
The Record states: "The wise one of the Madhyamaka school understands that all phenomena are the Middle Way. 'Middle' (madhya) signifies being non-biased and non-relative.
If a single phenomenon is the Middle, then all the Buddha-dharmas planted by sentient beings on the causal ground will, without exception, converge toward it.
If there were even a single external phenomenon, it could not be called the Middle. Since this is true of one phenomenon, it is so for all phenomena."
It is so in all cases. Therefore, it is said that regarding the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), one knows all paths and knows all modes.
As for the phrase "the single characteristic of quiescent cessation, etc.," this concludes what was previously stated, thereby establishing both negation (*niṣedha*) and illumination (*prakāśana*).

When there is simultaneous negation, there is the single characteristic of quiescence; when there is simultaneous illumination, there is the knowing of all various modes. Because negation and illumination occur simultaneously, it is called "all" (*sarva*).
This is precisely the meaning of "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*). Regarding the statement that the four eyes enter into the Buddha-eye, a sutra says:

"Endowed with the five eyes, one attains bodhi and eternally acts as a parent to those within the three realms. As for why the Buddha-eye alone is so designated: it is like various rivers flowing into the ocean and losing their original names;
it is not that the four functions cease to exist. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The fleshly eye, the divine eye, the wisdom eye, the dharma..."
The eye, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, loses its original name and is simply called the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*). Why is this?

Because the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*) is produced from the various afflictions (*kleśa*), outflows (*āsrava*), and karma; it is deceptive and unreal. Only the Buddha-eye is free from the nature of deception.

The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) arises from the conjunction of causes and conditions such as meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); therefore, being deceptive, it cannot perceive things as they truly are. As for the wisdom-eye (*prajñācakṣus*)...
Because the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted within the Dharma-eye, it is not ultimately pure;
therefore, one relinquishes that original stage and enters into the Buddha-eye, where there is no error, for its limits have been fully reached. [Supplement] The *Miaojuji* states:

"If the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* clarifies that at the first stage (*bhūmi*), one attains the Tathāgata’s single body which is infinite bodies and possesses the three non-regressions (*avaivartika*), the commentary explains..."

It says: "Now, from the first stage (bhūmi) onward, one has already perfected the three virtues; therefore, it is said that they are 'perfected. Prajñā is the stage, because one is free from the two deaths.
Vimukti is the practice, because all practices are complete. Dharmakāya is termed 'mindfulness,' because one realizes the true realm.
This concludes the explanation of the first stage.
△ Second, the nine stages are equally clarified.
Next, from the second stage to the tenth stage, one severes one grade of ignorance at each level and increases one portion of the Middle Way;
this is equal to the ten bhūmis of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

[Note] Regarding the phrase "next, from the second dwelling," the *Miaoxuan* (5.5) states: "This refers to the ten successive advancements into the outflow-free [state], wherein one equally perceives the Middle Way Buddha-nature and the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*).
By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep and dwells in the three virtues of the Buddha as well as all Buddha-dharmas;
therefore, it is called the stage of the Ten Dwellings. (Text)

[Commentary: As described above regarding the three contemplations of the first stage (*bhūmi*), through the effortless mental state manifest before one, one severs the immeasurable grades of ignorance within the *dharmadhātu* in every thought-moment.
These are incalculable; for the time being, they are roughly categorized into ten grades of wisdom and severance, which constitute the Ten Abidings (*daśabhūmi*).
The *Renyō-kyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra) states: "The *prajñā* that enters into principle is called 'abiding'"; this refers to the ten successive advancements.
The untainted true illumination equally enters into the principle of the Middle Way, the Buddha-nature, and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
By means of the non-abiding dharma, one proceeds from shallow to deep until dwelling in the principle of the secret treasury of the Buddha’s three virtues.
This is precisely what is called the "ten stages" (*daśa-vihāra*), which abide in all Buddha-dharmas. Regarding the phrase "abiding in all Buddha-dharmas," the *Miaoxuan* states: Furthermore...
Abiding in the pure and perfect bodhicitta, unconditional compassion, and unconditioned vows, one universally covers the entire dharma-realm.
Furthermore, abiding within a single thought-moment, one accomplishes all myriad practices and the various pāramitās.

Moreover, abiding in the knowledge of all modes, one completely severs the ignorance of views and afflictions throughout the dharma-realm. Finally, abiding in the attainment of the Buddha-eye, one perfectly perceives the ten [directions].

The Dharma-realm consists of the dharmas of the three truths. Furthermore, one dwells in the perfect entry into all dharma-gates, namely the twenty-five samādhis, thereby silently benefiting sentient beings.

Moreover, dwelling in the ability to proceed from one stage while fully possessing the merits of all stages, with every thought in a state of quiescent extinction, one flows into the ocean of sarvajñā (all-knowledge). This concludes the explanation of the Ten Abodes.

△ Second, the two practices directed toward the stages (bhūmi). Part one: first, clarifying the similarities and differences between the first two practices and the preceding Separate Teaching (pratyekabuddha-yāna) in three sections.
First, clarifying how these two practices are the same as the Separate Teaching.

Next, entering the first stage of practice, one severs one grade of ignorance and becomes equal to the "Equal Enlightenment" (Sama-sambodhi) of the Distinct Teaching. Next, entering the second stage of practice, one becomes equal to the "Wonderful Enlightenment" (Prativedha-sambodhi) of the Distinct Teaching.
[Note] Regarding "next, the initial practice," etc.: The *Miaoxuan* (5.5) states that this refers to the period following the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*).

Here, through the inconceivable true illumination of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), one further undergoes ten stages of wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) to destroy the ten grades of ignorance (*avidyā*). This constitutes "one practice as all practices."
Moment by moment one progresses, flowing into the ocean of the equal Dharma-realm.

All the *pāramitās* grow spontaneously, and the merit of one's own practice and the transformation of others becomes equal to space; therefore, this is called the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśaprayoga*). (Text)
[Commentary] The verse says: "The two types of enlightenment, equal and wondrous, have their first two practices [as follows].
△ Second, clarifying the distinction from the subsequent stages.
From the third practice onward, those of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) do not even know the names [of these stages], so how could they suppress or sever [the afflictions]? Because of this...
This is because the teaching merely refutes the twelve categories of ignorance.
