[Commentary] The verse says: "Advancing through the three stages of practice while remaining unaware" refers to this.
△ Third, explaining the reason for their commonality has two parts. First, clarifying that the cause is treated as the fruit.
Therefore, that which is the true cause for my house shall be the ultimate fruit for your house.
[Note] Regarding "the true cause of my house" and so forth, the *Miaoxuan* (Vol. 5, p. 12) states: "If the ten stages and ten grades break through ignorance..."
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), the ten stages of abiding (*shizhu*) likewise involve the destruction of ignorance across ten grades.

Even if the ten grounds (*shidi*) were expanded into thirty grades, these would merely correspond to the thirty grades of the ten stages of abiding in the Perfect Teaching. If we discuss them in terms of their correspondence, the Perfect Teaching does not expand the ten stages of abiding;

rather, it takes the thirty minds (*sanshixin*) as its thirty grades. Thus, when compared with the thirty grades of the ten grounds in the Separate Teaching (*biejia*), they are equal. Therefore, [the text says] "ten..."

The stage of the Ground (bhūmi) is equal to the ten stages of Returnings (daśa-pratipatti) of the Perfect Teaching (Vairocana). If we speak in terms of a strict comparison, the Buddha-ground of the Separate Teaching is equal to the first practice of the Perfect Teaching.

[Supplement] If one includes the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-sambodhi), it is equal to the second practice; however, as we do not include the Stage of Equal Enlightenment here, it is only equal to the first practice.
[Commentary] According to the *Yùlùn* (Discourse on Accordance), the distinct [Vehicle] (*biéjiā*) Buddha-ground is equal to the first ground (*chūdì*) of the Perfect [Vehicle] (*yuánjiā*).
[Record] The verse states: "The distinct grounds are entirely equal to the Perfect dwellings; ignorance is partially severed as one realizes the cause of truth. This refers to that very point.
Now, opening the section below, both giving and taking are discussed.
△ Second, clarifying the reason for cause and effect, in three parts. First, the direct clarification of the reason:
It is simply because the more provisional the teaching, the higher the stage; the more real the teaching, the lower the stage.
[Commentary] Therefore, one knows that the provisional teaching of the Separate Vehicle (biejiao) is high when its Buddha is judged; yet, in relation to the Real [Teaching], that Buddha is still low.
[Record] This precisely clarifies the reason for the provisional and the real. Because the provisional teaching is coarse and mixed, although its stages are high, they are not truly high.
Because the real teaching is subtle and pure, although its stages are low, why would one value being low? Hence it is called "provisional."
To speak of it, one is high; yet in actuality, even such words remain low.
△ Second, the illustration clarifies the reason:
It is like when frontier regions have not yet been pacified; one who borrows an office is considered high, but once ranks are fixed and merits are deliberated, his true position is actually low.

[Note] For example, when a frontier region has not yet been pacified, the rank conferred upon appointing an official is high; yet when ranks are fixed and merits are deliberated, the position assigned is low.
The provisional teachings of the Separate Vehicle (Bie-jiao), though high, are coarse; the ultimate teachings of the Perfect Vehicle (Yuan-jiao), though low, are subtle.

"My cause" becomes "your fruit. (Text) *Jue* means to confer a fief. There are five grades of rank: Duke (*gong*), Marquis (*hou*), Earl (*bo*), Viscount (*zi*), and Baron (*nan*). *Xun* refers to merit.
This is the merit.
[Commentary] This section uses a metaphor to clarify why the provisional is high while the real is low. All that precedes is from the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning).
Regarding the term "rank" (*jué*), Master Yushi explains its meaning; each point can be seen as it appears in the text.
△ Third, the result is identical to the cause.
Therefore, although the provisional teaching (kenkyō) refers to it as "Sublime Enlightenment" (Myōgaku), it is merely the second stage of practice within the true teaching (jikyō).
[■ Commentary] As for why the provisional stages of the Separate Teaching (bekkyō) are said to be "high yet not high," it is because of its circularity (en).
In the teachings, those who follow the two practices are the causes for this person. Within the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao), they may abide in the ultimate fruit of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue).
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate fruit of another house is originally the true cause of our own house.
△ Second, after the three practices have been revealed, the twenty-eight stages are explained all at once.
Next, from the three practices onward until the tenth stage (*bhūmi*), one severs one grade of ignorance at each stage and increases one portion of the Middle Way.
This refers to the severing of forty grades of delusion.

[Commentary] Regarding the stage of the Ten Dedications (*daśapariṇāmanā*), the *Miaoxuan* (5.6) states: "It follows immediately after the Ten Practices (*daśabhūmi*) and constitutes the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*)."
Inconceivable true illumination develops all dharma-realms in every thought-moment.

May the practice of vows and the principle of reality naturally harmonize and merge, returning to the ocean of the equal dharma-realm, further realizing the ten stages of wisdom and severance to shatter the ten grades of ignorance.
Therefore, it is called "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*).

[Supplement] Regarding the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*): from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward, it is already the path of non-effort. The reason it is clarified here within the section on "Dedication" is twofold:

first, it is a provisional borrowing of the term "necklace" (*hāra*), which originally has a distinct meaning; thus, it is explained after the section on "Dedication. Second, [it serves to clarify that]...

Although [the practice of] vows is employed from the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), at this point it becomes a point of attachment; therefore, it is clarified here. Regarding "the harmony and integration of vows and practice":
this refers to the bodhisattva’s path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*). Through the perfuming power of vows, wondrous practices are initiated;

these initiated practices arise entirely from the *dharmadhātu* and are, in turn, dedicated back to the *dharmadhātu*. Dedication is itself the vow; this is the harmony and integration of vow and practice. Furthermore, the vow...
All matters of practice are entirely dedicated to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). The Dharma-realm is principle; this is the harmonious fusion of phenomenon and principle.

[Note] As for the stages of the ten grounds (*daśabhūmi*), these are the untainted, true illumination (*anāsrava-bhūtāloka*). Entering the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*), they are like the great earth.
It is able to give birth to all Buddha-dharmas, to bear the burden of sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, and to universally enter the Buddha-stages of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, it realizes ten successive stages of wisdom and severance, destroying ten grades of ignorance; therefore, they are called the "Ten Grounds" (bhūmi). (Text)

[Commentary] This clarifies the sublime meaning of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Following the preceding discussion on ascending through the stages (*vihāra*), one immediately enters the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), wherein every thought is quiescent and every moment increases in clarity.

The phrase "like the great earth" serves as a metaphor to clarify that the great practices of Bodhisattvas on the stages are thus: just as the earth can grow all things, so too can the Bodhisattva propagate [the Dharma].

The Buddha-dharma: just as the earth can bear all things, so too can the Bodhisattva shoulder the burden of sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm, causing them to universally enter the stages of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This concludes the section on the stages of clear practice and progress.
△ The Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Having further destroyed one grade of ignorance, one enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment. This is the stage of "One Birth Remaining" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

[□ Commentary] Regarding "Equal Enlightenment," the *Miaoxuan* (5.6) states: "It is the ultimate wisdom (*paryanta-jñāna*) that penetrates and reaches the source and bottom of beginningless ignorance."
It is full, ultimately pure, and severs the final, root-source subtle ignorance; ascending the peak of the Middle Way Mountain, one parts from the parents of ignorance.
This is called "that which has something to be severed," and such a person is termed a superior person (as the text states).

[Commentary] This clarifies the abandonment through the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-jñāna*). The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "Abiding at the limit of Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*) is called the fulfillment of the wisdom of the limit (*bianji-zhi man*);
alternatively, it may also be termed the fulfillment of the wisdom of the limit by means of the Buddha’s inconceivable function."
[Note] At the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), both active afflictions (*kleśa*) and residual habits (*vāsanā*) are severed together. As the current text states:

"Furthermore, one breaks through one grade of ignorance," which refers to the severance of both the active and the residual as explained in the *Wenju* (Profound Meaning). The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, fascicle 2, part 4, states: "Regarding 'no longer having residual habits':

in the Round Teaching (*yuanjiao*), from the first *bhūmi* up to the *Dharmameghā-bhūmi*, although all views are completely severed, residual habits still remain. Upon entering the [stage of] Equal Enlightenment..."

In the Mysterious Gate (the Way of the Buddhas), for thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, one has repeatedly cultivated the affairs of ordinary beings until the realization of principle is clear and habitual tendencies are attenuated;
these affairs are then like faint smoke. (This text describes the severing of habitual tendencies.)
[Supplement] Regarding "the Profound and the Profound" (Chongxuan): Previously, one has already used inconceivable wondrous wisdom to sever the delusions of ignorance;

this arising [wisdom] that responds to and benefits sentient beings is called "Profound" (Xuan). Upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), one severs the remaining residual habits and re-cultivates the Dharma-gates previously traversed, performing the deeds of ordinary beings in reverse order.
This is "the Profound within the Profound," which is termed "Double" (Chong).

[Note] Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, fascicle 5 (35), states: "Abiding in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyagbodhi-bhūmi*), there remains one final grade [of affliction] as well as residual habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)" (text).
[Commentary] This single category of ignorance is precisely the initial moment of non-enlightenment (*abodhi*). One must sever this before attaining wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "As when a Bodhisattva reaches the end of the stages (*bhūmi*), having perfected all skillful means (*upāya*), there is a single moment of resonance."
When the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic. Because one is far removed from subtle thoughts, one perceives the nature of the mind;
this nature of the mind is eternally abiding, which is called ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).

Furthermore, this grade [of awakening] and its residual habits (*vāsanā*) are like the two delusions and their corresponding coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) described in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. The treatise states: "Although in this stage one has attained mastery over phenomena, there still remains..."

The remaining obstacles are not yet called "ultimate. This means there are innate, subtle cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) as well as seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These are all severed instantaneously and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests before one.

For this reason, it is said that in the stage of Buddhahood, two types of delusion (*moha*) along with their coarse habitual tendencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) are abandoned: first, [the delusion] regarding all objects...
The ignorance of attachment to extremely subtle objects refers to the subtle cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) within this [system].

The ignorance of obstruction by extremely subtle impediments refers to the seeds of spontaneous afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within this [system]. (Text) However, these two treatises do not seem to accord with the intent of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Moreover, it is not established that there is a separate stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Rather, by means of the final mind of the tenth stage, one clearly severs the subtle obstacles and habitual tendencies of the phase of birth (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa*), thereby achieving ultimate enlightenment (*atyanta-bodhi*).

I shall now merely record this so that, by analogy, one may understand that in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), Equal Enlightenment still has one remaining grade and residual habitual tendencies;
these must be severed completely before one achieves Wondrous Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bodhi*). This concludes the explanation of Equal Enlightenment.
△ Second, the stage of fruition has two parts. First, wisdom and abandonment are manifested together:

advancing to break through one final grade of subtle ignorance, one enters the stage of *miao-jue* (wonderful enlightenment). One is forever separated from the parents of ignorance and ultimately ascends to the summit of the mountain of *nirvāṇa*.
All phenomena do not arise; *prajñā* does not arise; non-arising and non-non-arising—this is called Great *Nirvāṇa*.

[Note]: The *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra* (*Guanjing shu*) states: "The ultimate Buddha is one whose Way has reached the pinnacle of wondrous enlightenment (*miaojue*), standing adjacent to the stage of *tathāgata*.

Therefore, only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. With the wisdom of the limit (*prāntajñāna*) fulfilled and the various types of awakening suddenly perfected, [he is] unsurpassed."
A "Śāstṛ" (Teacher) is one for whom there is nothing further to be severed. An "Anuttara-śāstṛ" (Unsurpassed Teacher) is one beyond whom there is no superior.
[Commentary] The *Miaozongchao* states: "The Stage of Equal Enlightenment is already named the 'Stage of Fulfillment of Expedient Means' and the 'Ultimate Stage of the Bodhisattva.'"

The path of initial awakening reaches its consummation, and the principle of original awakening attains its ultimate limit. Since the original and the initial have both merged, there is no name by which to designate it;

yet, for the sake of conventional expression, it is termed "Sublime Awakening" (*miaojue*). [Commentary on the Miaozong] Vol. 1 (23) states: "This present stage of culmination is the ultimate perfection of the merits of all stages. Therefore...

The *Lotus Sūtra* cites that only I, Śākyamuni, together with all Buddhas, are able to exhaustively fathom the provisional means (*upāya*) and the reality (*bhūtārtha*) of all phenomena, reaching the bottom of ignorance and arriving at the limit of all dharmas;
this is called "limit-reaching wisdom" (*paryanta-jñāna*), which is inconceivable wisdom of skillful means.
Now, having reached ultimate consummation, it is termed "fulfilled. Regarding the various dharmas, one realizes the fundamental, perfect, and inconceivable *bodhi*.

It is true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). This awakening is utterly full; it is called "sudden perfection" (*tun-yuan*). Furthermore, the title "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara-puruṣa*) is employed to manifest the ultimate limit of wisdom and abandonment.
When there are delusions yet to be abandoned, it is called the "Stage of Equal Awakening" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) of the "Surpassed Being.

When there are no delusions remaining to be abandoned, it is called the "Unsurpassed Being," which is precisely "Sublime Awakening" (*miao-jué*). The culmination of the virtue of abandonment is termed "Great Nirvāṇa" (*mahā-nirvāṇa*). (And so forth... Ignorance is the father.
Regarding the "mother," the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "Kill the father of ignorance and sever the mother of craving" (text).
[Commentary] The *Laṅkāvatāra-śāstra-vyākhyā* explains the sūtra: What is the mother of sentient beings? It refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) conjoined with delight (*nandī*).
Just as children depend upon their mother to be established, ignorance is the father and deluded craving is the mother; they give rise to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the ten... [bases].
The two locations are the village and the assembly. To sever the two roots of ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called "killing one's father and mother.
The Great Sūtra states: "If one takes craving as the mother and ignorance as the father, and follows them with gravity, one will fall into the Avīci Hell.
The intention is that by slaying and severing these parents, one ultimately attains Buddhahood. The metaphor of the parents refers to craving... [and] ignorance.
The mind is inward-facing, analogous to the mother; ignorance is the external object, analogous to the father. Furthermore, ignorance is the root of receiving a body, analogous to the father;
craving is a secondary affliction, like the mother. Moreover, the father is a remote condition, as is ignorance.
The mother is a kinsman; she is like "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*). "Slaying and severing" explains the severance of afflictions (*kleśa*) to manifest the contemplation of principle.
[Note] The summit of the mountain of *nirvāṇa* is a metaphor for that which is unsurpassed. All phenomena (*dharma*) are the object (*viṣaya*), and *prajñā* is the wisdom (*jñāna*).
The quiescence of both object and wisdom is called Great *Nirvāṇa*.
[Commentary] The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "I have placed my sons within the secret treasury; I, too, shall enter parinirvāṇa within this secret treasury.
This ultimate nirvāṇa is called "the non-arising of non-arising. Prajñā is ultimately neither arising nor non-arising, neither ceasing nor non-ceasing;
there is no further delusion to be extinguished. Here, the various dharmas are used as an analogy for prajñā.

Regarding the designation of "object and wisdom" as *Mahāparinirvāṇa*, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* (*Catur-smṛtyupasthāna*) states: "The wisdom that contemplates is ever-quiescent while illuminating;
the object that is contemplated is ever-illuminating while quiescent. When the object is quiescent, wisdom is also quiescent; when wisdom illuminates, the object is also illuminated.
This single mark of marklessness is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), which is called the unsurpassed *Mahāparinirvāṇa*: perfect, luminous, eternally quiescent, and illuminating."
Thus it is. △ Second, the simultaneous clarification of the environment and the inhabitants.

Taking empty space as one’s seat, one accomplishes the pure Dharma-body and dwells in the land of Constant Quiescent Light; this is the aspect of the Buddha according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
[Note] Regarding "taking empty space as one’s seat": this meaning illustrates that the Dharma-body is omnipresent.
[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "The Dharma-body pervades all places—every sentient being and every land throughout the three periods of time."
All are present without exception, yet no form or characteristic can be apprehended; therefore, it is said that "space is taken as the seat.

[Commentary] The phrase "accomplishing the pure Dharma-body" refers to cultivation being identical to nature (*xing*), spoken of in terms of its increasing excellence. If one discusses the Teacher himself, however...
It is also called "Honored and Distinct" (zūntè) and "Supreme Response" (shèngyìng).
[Commentary] The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The pure and wondrous Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. This refers to cultivation being identical with nature (*xiù jí xìng*).
This is an explanation based on the superior [teachings]. Next, regarding the discussion from the perspective of the masters of the Perfect and Real (Yuan-shi) schools:

in terms of the teaching, the thirty-two marks of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitute the superior, exalted, and distinctive [body]. In terms of the physical marks, the marks and signs of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, numbering as many as motes of dust, are the superior marks and signs.
These are perceived according to the capacity of those with perfect faculties; therefore, they are called the "superior response-body" (*viśeṣa-nirmāṇakāya*).
【□ Note】 *Miaoxuan* 7 (13) states: "Alternatively, it is said that the site of enlightenment (*dojang*) takes empty space as its seat.
Once [the Way] is realized, all is realized. Vairocana pervades all places; Śākyamuni and Sāṃbhogakāya Buddhas realize it, and they likewise pervade all places.
The three Buddhas are complete and without deficiency. The three Buddhas are mutually identical, without any distinction or difference. In the *Lotus Sūtra*, in each of the eight directions..."
Each direction extends for four million billion nayutas of lands, wherein Śākyamuni is established as Vairocana.
The *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana. This is precisely the manifestation of the perfected fruit of the Perfect Buddha (the *vṛtta-buddha-phala*). (Text)

[Commentary] This establishes that the Perfect Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka* possesses the three bodies (*trikāya*) in their full excellence. First, regarding the perfected aspect of the Perfect Buddha of the *Avataṃsaka*: space serves as the seat;
this is the perfection of the *pariṇirmita-nirmāṇa* (the environment or dependent retribution). Vairocana, Vajrasattva, and Śākyamuni represent the three bodies of Dharma, Reward, and Response;

the perfection of one is the perfection of all—this is the perfection of the *upapatti-saṃskāra* (the primary retribution or the embodied being). Next, it clarifies the meaning of the mutual identity and complete fulfillment of these three Buddhas. Complete fulfillment...

Therefore, there is no deficiency. Because their characteristics are identical, there is neither oneness nor difference. This intends to clarify that prior to the *Lotus Sūtra*, the three Buddhas were explained separately;

upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra*, one distinguishes the superior from the inferior, such that the three are precisely the one. [This occurs] below the section on the eight directions in the *Lotus Sūtra*.

The manifested response-buddha is none other than the perfect buddha. The Lotus Sūtra Buddha transforms the Sahā world, making it entirely pure so as to accommodate the various emanated buddhas from the ten directions.
Yet, even within a single direction, there was still not enough space;
therefore, he further transformed two hundred *koṭi-nayuta* worlds in each of the eight directions into purity to accommodate the emanated buddhas. Furthermore...
In each of the eight directions, two hundred trillion nayutas of lands were further transformed into purity so that the Buddhas might sit there in the future.
One should know that in each of the eight directions there are four hundred trillion nayutas of pure lands.
These emanation bodies of Śākyamuni are all Vairocana. This is cited as proof in the lower section of the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna-sūtra*. The sūtra clarifies the voice from within the void.

Regarding the practitioner: they practice the contemplative method of Samantabhadra’s Repentance. At that time, the practitioner asks a voice from the air, "Where am I currently practicing the dharma of repentance?
The voice from the air replies, "Śākyamuni Buddha is named Vairocana, who pervades all places.
The dwelling place of that Buddha is called the Constantly Quiescent Light (Nityapraśāntaprakāśa). All [the perfections]..."
In the place established by the Esoteric [Vehicle], one should contemplate the Buddhas of the ten directions in this manner. One knows that Śākyamuni is clearly Vairocana;
thus, one understands that the Responsive Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) is none other than the Dharma Buddha (dharmakāya), which clarifies the aspect of the perfected fruition of Buddhahood.
[Commentary on the *Wenju* (1.8): It says: "Concealing the previous three marks, it reveals only the inconceivable mark like empty space;

this is the Perfect Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others. (*Wenju* 1.8). [The *Miaole* (1.24) states: "If the previous three marks are concealed, it is spoken from the perspective of the most excellent [mark];
it does not mean that the great void itself is called the 'Perfect Buddha. (*Miaole* 1.24).
[Commentary] This reiterates the characteristics of the perfected fruit of the Perfect Buddha (*yuanfo*), yet it has not yet specified exactly what those characteristics are. The *Wenju* states:

"A body sixteen feet tall with the appearance of an old bhikṣu" refers to the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka [Teaching], who, having awakened himself and awakened others, manifests a *zunte* (lokanātha/viśvabhadra) body while still bearing the form of an old bhikṣu.
The Buddha of the Shared Teaching, having awakened himself and awakened others, manifests solely the *zunte* [body] upon a lotus pedestal.

Regarding the assumption of office: in the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka*), the Buddha’s self-awakening and awakening of others conceals the previous three marks and manifests only the inconceivable mark, which is like empty space;

this is precisely the self-awakening and awakening of others of the Perfect Buddha. In the *Miaole* commentary, the concealment of the previous three marks is explained from the perspective of what is predominant, not to suggest that the "Great Void" constitutes the Perfect Buddha. For if the Buddha of the Separate Teaching is already said to be discussed in isolation...

This conceals the former two characteristics; therefore, the Perfect Buddha is discussed here alone. This means that the former three characteristics are concealed, and only the characteristic of being like empty space—which manifests the superior by means of the inferior—is presented.
It does not mean that empty space itself is the Perfect Buddha, for emptiness is a phenomenon of form (*rūpa-dharma*) and is subject to arising and ceasing.

[Supplement] "Concealment" does not mean that the person of the Perfect [Vehicle] is obscured; rather, when observing the former three characteristics, they are seen as being solely phenomena (*dharma*).
The nature refers to what is called wondrous form and wondrous mind. The *Shenbao ji* states: "It is not the same as the preceding three;

therefore, it is said to 'conceal the former. It reveals only the inconceivable aspect that is like empty space. Nevertheless, it does not depart from the aspects constantly manifested, because the capacity of the perfect vehicle is singular.
Thus, one may speak of the mind being identical to empty space, its measure equaling the dharma-realm. This is what is meant by..."
It is the ultimate Dharmakāya; therefore, this present body is itself the Dharmakāya—contemplate this.

[Note] The *Guangming ji* (Record of Radiance), fascicle 1, part 8, states: "Because this teaching explains that the characteristics of the world are eternally constant, there is not a single dharma that is not the Middle Way.

Although they [the followers of the Separate Teaching] see the same *zhunti* (lofty and distinctive) form as we do, they cultivate it through a separate practice, whereas these [teachings of the Perfect Teaching] are all intrinsically complete by nature."

The Dragon Girl said: "The subtle and wondrous pure Dharma-body possesses the thirty-two marks. To manifest the complete nature, it is therefore designated by its preeminent name as the 'Dharma-body' (text)."
[Commentary] This citation explains that the Buddha-dharma body (*dharmakāya*) is taught from the perspective of its preeminence.

[Sub-commentary] Regarding the "Land of Constant Quiescent Light": the *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), fascicle 6, states: "The 'Constant' is the Dharma-body; the 'Quiescent' is Liberation; the 'Light' is Prajñā.
These three points are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither parallel nor distinct; they are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*). This is what all Buddhas and Tathāgatas..."
The place where one dwells and roams is the ultimate, true, and eternal, which is the most supreme Pure Land (*Sukhāvatī*).
[Commentary] The *Miaozongchao* states: "Names are established based on their essential nature. The first three lands pertain to phenomena;

therefore, their names are established according to the causes and effects of cultivation and severance belonging to those who dwell therein. This land pertains to principle; therefore, its name is established according to the three virtues of its fundamental essence. Question:

Regarding the partial realization of the *sukhāvatī* (Peaceful Light) realm, since the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*) have not yet been exhausted, how can one establish its name by relying solely on the principle? Answer:

While the aspect of the obstacles not yet being exhausted belongs to the *vipākaphala* (Retribution of Reality), here we establish the names "Superior," "Middle," and "Inferior" *nitya-sukhāvatī* (Eternally Peaceful Light) based on the stage where cause and effect are partially forgotten.

That is to say: from the first *bhūmi* (stage) upward is called "Inferior"; *Samyaksambodhi* (Equal Enlightenment) is called "Middle"; and *Suyojana* (Wondrous Enlightenment) is the "Superior. All [the Buddhas]...
The Buddha descends. This is shown by way of the abode. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* states:

"The Tathāgata dwells in the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, the sphere of action of all Buddhas, which surpasses the pure spheres traversed by all Bodhisattvas. Here, "immeasurable" is quiescence (*śānti*);
"profoundly deep" is radiance (*prabhā*); and "*dharmatā*" is permanence (*nitya*). The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-caryā-darśana-sūtra* states: "Śākyamuni is named Vairocana."
Vairocana. This dwelling place of the Buddha is named the Light of Eternal Quiescence (*nitya-prabhāsvara*).

It is a place established by the perfection of permanence (*nitya-pāramitā*), a place where the perfection of bliss (*sukha-pāramitā*) transcends the characteristics of the body, a place established by the perfection of self (*ātma-pāramitā*), and a place where the perfection of purity (*śubha-pāramitā*) extinguishes the characteristics of existence.
Therefore, this land is established from the ultimate state of these four virtues; it is by means of the four perfections (*pāramitā*).
This reveals the three virtues: permanence and self are the Dharmakāya; bliss is liberation; and purity is prajñā.
These three treatises mutually encompass one another, with each treatise containing all three. Thus, the Dharmakāya and the others each possess four virtues, which is termed the "Secret Treasury."
The major section on the Correct Exposition of the Stages and Ranks is concluded.
△ Second, skillfully clarifying the six levels of "immediacy" (liù jí) in four parts. First, a brief account of the reason:

However, regarding the stages and ranks of the Perfect Teaching (Yuánjiào), if they were not distinguished by the six levels of immediacy, there would be much confusion with those of superior sages; therefore, the six levels must be employed.
This is the determination of the stages.

[Commentary] Regarding the six stages: their meaning is contained within the Buddha’s sutras and is known by the wise. They are illustrated in various texts, such as the poor woman’s treasure store and the wrestler’s forehead jewel.
Some clarify the loftiness and profundity of the Dharma gates, while others elucidate the sequence of positions for the cultivation of contemplation.

Now, after the *Jinguangming jing wenzhu* (The Commentary on the Text of the Lotus Sutra) has fully elucidated the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanwei*), it further explains the "six identities" (*liuji*). This is intended to prevent the fault of overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and self-deprecation.

The *Fuxing zhuanhongjue* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), Volume One, Part One (33), states: "This doctrine of the six identities originated with our own school; it deeply accords with the intent of the Perfect Teaching and is forever free from all faults.
Those who practice meditation in the dark often harbor overweening pride, while those who rely on the written word attribute merit to others; both [errors] arise from a failure to..."
"Understanding the six [perfections] and yet realizing 'immediacy' (ji).

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* says: First, it reveals that the perfect teaching of all dharmas is such that phenomena and principle are non-dual, and the essence of all ordinary beings and sages, as well as living beings and Buddhas, is identical.

To prevent the arising of despondency or discouragement, the word "immediacy" (*ji*) is clarified; although the whole body [of reality] consists of the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment.
Their characteristics differ, so as to prevent the arising of overweening pride; thus, the six characters are clarified. Second, it rectifies the弊 (defects) of those who obscure Chan through texts.
Textual Dharma Masters seal themselves in words and stagnate in meanings, clinging solely to names and marks, attributing merit to others while resigning themselves to inferiority.
To remedy such faults, it is said that "the whole body is itself [Buddha]. Conversely, those who practice Chan in obscurity reject cultivation.
[The text] says: "Practice. It merely states that 'mind itself is Buddha' and does not distinguish between the shallow and deep stages [of practice].

This leads many to conflate themselves with the supreme sages and give rise to *adhimāna* (arrogance). To remedy this defect, the six stages are clarified. Furthermore, the *Wuji zi* (Master Wuji) records:

"Those of deluded meditation follow their impulses, conflating themselves with the supreme sages out of pride; those of wild wisdom follow their passions, demeaning themselves by remaining among the lowly commoners. Because of this...
This is the Tiantai teaching known as the "Six Identities with Buddhahood" (*liu ji fo*). It refutes two kinds of views:

it eliminates the error of overestimation by distinguishing the six stages where the phenomena of cause and effect differ, and it eliminates the error of underestimation by showing that the principle of the holy and the ordinary is equal. Regarding the "poor woman’s treasure" in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are six stages:

first, the existence of the treasure; second, the person’s finger [pointing it out]; third, the weeding and digging; fourth, coming close to it; fifth, the opening of the treasure; and sixth, the taking and using of it.
This is correlated with the six stages of realization (*liù jí*). The metaphor of the pearl on the forehead also appears in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (Dà jīng), and its meaning is the same.
[Commentary Note: The *Fǔ xíng* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua xuanyi*), Vol. 1, Part 1 (16), states: "As for 'immediate' (*jí*): the *Guǎng yá* says it means 'to join.

If one follows this interpretation, it would seem that two distinct things must join together to be called 'immediate,' which leaves the principle somewhat remote. Now, seeking it through its essential meaning: because the essence is non-dual, it is so named."

It is "identity" (ji). The *Myōshū* (Jingzhong), Volume Upper, section thirteen, states: "The six kinds of identity are all names for the meaning that phenomena and principle are non-dual in essence. (Text)
[Commentary: This demonstrates that the essence is non-dual; therefore, it is called "identical" (*ji*). The *Miaozong* states: "Phenomenal events (*shi*) may be either adverse or favorable.

The five [practices], beginning with 'name,' are favorable phenomenal events of cultivation. Only the single principle of nature (*li-xing*) is purely an adverse phenomenal event of cultivation. These are the adverse and favorable phenomenal events.
It is non-dual with the fundamental principle of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*). The commentary states: "To know this non-duality is for all phenomena to accord with principle;

this is called 'conformity' (*anuloma*). For those who do not know it, all phenomena contradict principle; this is called 'opposition' (*pratiloma*). Whether superficial or profound, the five categories beginning with names (*nāman*) and so forth [are thus categorized].

All are known and all are accordant. If, at the initial stage of "principle-as-such" (*li-ji*), one is solely deluded and solely contrary, yet the events of that delusion and contrariness have never for a moment deviated from the awakened principle;
therefore, it is called "identical with the Buddha. This is what is meant by the non-duality of "identity."
△ Second, the detailed enumeration of the stages [of the fivefold identity] has six parts. First, the explanation of the identity of principle (*li-ji*).
This refers to the fact that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; whether a Buddha appears or not, the nature and its characteristics are eternally abiding.
Furthermore, such statements as "a single form or a single fragrance is none other than the Middle Way" are all instances of the identity of principle.

[Commentary] The *Vajracchedikā-ṭīkā* states: "Regarding the term 'Buddha-nature': 'Buddha' refers to one who has attained the fruit. To say that all sentient beings possess the nature of one who has attained the fruit [is the meaning]. (Text)
[Commentary] This explanation clarifies that "principle" (*li*) is itself the person. The Buddha said:

"With my Buddha-eye, I observe that within the afflictions of greed, anger, and ignorance of all sentient beings, there exists the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s eye, and the Tathāgata’s body, sitting in the full lotus posture."
Steadfast and unmoving. [Supplement] The term "Buddha-nature" (foxing) is derived from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. It establishes the designation of the fruit by relying upon the nature of the cause;
it is intended to lead those who are deluded toward awakening.

[Commentary] The *Guanjing shu* (Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra), fascicle 2, states: "This principle is self-evident: the world is eternally abiding. Whether a Buddha appears cannot benefit it, nor can its absence harm it.
To attain it does not constitute loftiness; to lose it does not constitute lowness. Therefore, it is said that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas;
this is 'identity in principle' (*liri*). (*Wenzong*, upper volume, section 15) states: "The world is eternally abiding" refers to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*).
The ten worlds each abide in the dharma-position of *tathatā*. Because the dharma-position is eternal, the worlds are also eternal.
(Text) Here, "nature and characteristics" refers to the first two of the ten suchnesses (*daśa-tathatā*). Nature refers to the internal; it is self-contained and unchanging.
Characteristics refer to the external; they are grasped and can be distinguished.
[Commentary] The subsequent passage in the *Myōshū* states: "The permanence of the mundane world refers to the ten dharma-realms and the thirty mundane worlds;
each and every one of these abides in the station of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because the station of dharmas is eternal, the phenomenal characteristics of the world are also eternal.

Ten Similes: Gold wrapped in tattered cloth; an image within an earthen mold; jars and basins in a dark room; the seven treasures in a well—all these have existed inherently from the beginning and are not merely of the present.
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are suchness (*tathatā*). The *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* states: [All sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature].
The Buddha-realm and the sentient-being realm are one realm; there is no separate realm (text).
[Commentary] This cites various sutras to clarify the meaning of "identity" (*jiri*). The *Miaozongchao* states: First, it cites the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Sentient beings are themselves the Buddha. Why? Because apart from sentient beings, one cannot attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Such is the Tathāgata-nature."
The chapter states: "The term 'I' has the meaning of 'Buddha. All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; this is precisely the meaning of 'I.
This meaning of 'I' has, from the very beginning, been constantly shrouded by immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*);
therefore, sentient beings are unable to perceive it. It is like a poor woman who possesses a vast store of pure gold, yet no one knows of it. At that time, there was...
A strange man immediately excavated a hidden store of gold from his own house. It is also like a strongman who has a diamond jewel between his eyebrows;
when he wrestles with another man, he strikes the jewel with his head, and it sinks into his skin so that he does not know it is there.
A sore forms at that spot and requires treatment, until finally a physician takes up a mirror and the jewel appears clearly within it. Thus it is in the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*, chapter ten.
Regarding the analogies: that sutra contains one dharma and nine analogies. One is the object of analogy (*dṛṣṭāntika*), and nine are the illustrative analogies (*dārṣṭāntika*).
Because the object is derived from the illustrations, they are called the "ten analogies. As for the single dharma, the sutra says:

"With my Buddha-eye, I behold within the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion of sentient beings the Tathāgata’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s eye, and the Tathāgata’s body, sitting cross-legged in solemn majesty."

Yet it remains unmoving. Although all sentient beings dwell within the bodies of affliction across the various realms of existence, they possess the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is eternally undefiled and fully endowed with virtuous marks, no different from my own. He then cites nine matters as metaphors for this Dharma.
The nine metaphors are: first, the Buddha’s body within a withered flower; second, pure honey at the peak of a mountain; third, polished grain within the husk and chaff.
These are: (4) gold amidst filth; (5) a treasure-trove in a poor man’s house; (6) the kernel within a mango; (7) a golden image wrapped in rags;
(8) the noble fetus in a poor woman; and (9) a cast image from a scorched mold.

In the present text, only the "jewel in a dark well" is cited to prove *li-ji* (the identity of principle), thereby manifesting the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-li*). This is not like the *Zhiguan*, which uses these examples to manifest the Distinct Teaching (*bie-li*). Therefore...

It is said that this has existed inherently from the beginning and is not merely something of the present. Next, regarding the *Vimalakīrti*, it states that all things are suchness (*tathatā*); yet these words still involve a degree of conceptual penetration.
Now, one must possess perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). Next, the *Ratnakaraṇḍa* says: "One's own realm and the dharma-realm, and the realm of sentient beings, are equal.
One's own realm is the mind-dharma; the dharma-realm is the Buddha-dharma. Since the Buddha takes the dharma-realm as his essence, he is thus contrasted with the realm of sentient beings.

This constitutes three dharmas: the mind arises in the cause, while the Buddha-dharma resides in the fruit; yet these three are without distinction. Therefore, there is one realm and no separate realms.
[Note] Regarding "identity in principle" (*liri ji*): the *Miaozong* (Vol. 13) states: "It is truly because the sentient beings' nature is replete with defilement and evil that it cannot be altered."
They are distinct. Its nature is perfectly luminous; this is what is called the Buddha. When its nature manifests as defilement or evil, it arises as the totality [of that state].

Cultivated defilement and cultivated evil have no separate essence; the entirety of cultivation is the nature itself. Therefore, even when deluded regarding phenomena, there is nothing that is not the Buddha of Principle.

Yet, by using this very Principle to give rise to delusions and create karma, one transmigrates through birth and death, remaining entirely unaware that phenomena are in their entirety the Principle. Thus, for long kalpas, one...

The Principle (*li*). Though it remains unknown throughout long kalpas, it does not follow that because it is unknown, the Principle is not the Buddha. Because it is complete in its essence, it is called "the Principle as the Buddha" (*li-ji fo*).

Because it is [currently] unknown, it is not [identical to] any of the latter five stages of "as-is-ness" (*ji*). Nevertheless, "the Principle as the Buddha" represents the ultimate degree of depreciation;

for it utterly lacks the stages of understanding (*jie*), practice (*xing*), and realization (*zheng*), and consists merely in the fact that the nature of the Principle is inherently such "as-it-is-ness. Furthermore, "the Principle as the Buddha" does not pertain to phenomena (*shi*).
Externally, pointing to principle as Buddha means that the principle of the three obstacles is entirely Buddha.

Furthermore, one should know that it is not called "obstacles-as-Buddha," but rather "principle-as-Buddha," because this intends to manifest that the latter five [stages] possess cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), whereas this single stage consists solely of the nature of principle (*tathatā*).
Moreover, while the name "obstacles-as-Buddha" is still general, the latter five persons have all realized the three obstacles.
"Because this is precisely the Buddha" (text).
[Commentary] Jieyi states: Regarding the principle that the three obstacles are entirely the Buddha, the *Guangming shu* says: "Whenever explaining the methods of contemplation..."
At the beginning, one mostly proceeds from what is easy; when the contemplation is perfected at the level of ease, there is nothing difficult that will not be understood.
This is the discourse on the Master’s realization of the meaning: thus, the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—are all the three causes of Buddha-nature.

These are the dharmas of the three obstacles and saṃsāra. When the mind is real, the three obstacles remain firm and distinct; when the emotions are empty, the three virtues are perfectly integrated. Within the realm of the three virtues, nothing is diminished.

The three types of cultivated evil—namely, those of the hair-tip, the minute, and the subtle—are called the "three natures. These constitute the entirety of the wondrous realm, which is precisely delusion, karma, and suffering.
They penetrate thoroughly to the very limits and depths of the Dharma-realm. This concludes the explanation of the "Li-ji" (the stage of reality as it is).
△ Second, clarifying the identity of name.
Next, hearing or seeing these words from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or from a scriptural volume constitutes the identity of name.
[Commentary] *Zhiguan* 1 (21) states: "Although the principle is indeed identical, one is unaware of it in daily life because one has not yet heard of the three truths."
They have no understanding of the Buddha-dharma at all; their vision is like that of oxen or sheep, and they do not comprehend the cardinal directions.

Having heard what was described above regarding the single reality of bodhi—whether from a spiritual teacher or from a scriptural volume—they attain a thorough understanding and mastery of these names.
They know that all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma. This is "the identity with names" (literally: *mingzi ji*).

[Commentary] This explains that [birth-and-death] is identical to the Name. As the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "Not knowing that birth-and-death is identical to principle is called 'not knowing in daily life.
It is like a person who, in their daily life, does not know the grace of light; thus it is said they do not recognize the cardinal directions."

Among oxen and sheep, many do not understand the cardinal directions; therefore, the "directions" (fang) serve as a metaphor for the ultimate within the real, while the "corners" (yu) illustrate the provisional within the real.
Alternatively, from the perspective of names and words, this is the formal explanation of the meaning.

[Commentary] The *Myōshū* (The Wondrous Commentary), Volume Upper, section 16, states: "That 'name' is itself Buddha refers to the beginning of the cultivation of merit. Upon hearing that the preceding principle can express names, there is both inclusion and exclusion.
In terms of inclusion, those whose ears pass over the sounds of the Dharma—whether clearly or obscurely—and those who hear nothing at all, are both included within this stage.

In terms of exclusion, they have not yet attained perfect hearing equal to that of the distinct [teachings] or the internal stages of worthiness; thus, they still belong to the stage of 'principle-identity' (*ri-jaku*)."
Those at the seven stages of expedient means have not yet understood the profound meaning of the name; how could they know that it is itself the Buddha?

[Commentary] "To gather" means that upon merely hearing that the principle of the three obstacles is entirely the name of the Buddha, one’s perfect understanding is awakened, and this is precisely "the name is itself the person.
"To distinguish" means that even though those within the thirty stages of the ordinary beings—the stages of abiding, practice, and heading—of the Separate Teaching exert effort...

Practice by means of application. Because their perfect understanding has not yet opened, and because their stages remain sequential and unmerged, this stage belongs entirely to the level of principle (*li-ji*).
△ Third, the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing-ji*):
practicing according to the teachings constitutes the stage of contemplative practice (the five grades of rank).
[Commentary] *Zhiguan Yili* (23) states: "If one merely hears the names or speaks them verbally, it is like an insect eating wood that happens to form characters;

the insect does not know whether these are characters or not. One must have clear mental visualization and ensure that principle and wisdom correspond, such that what is practiced accords with what is spoken, and what is spoken accords with what is practiced. This is called 'contemplative practice' (*guanxing*). (Text)
[Commentary] This explains the identity of contemplative practice (*guanxing*). The first line serves as a metaphor for the meaning of the identity of names (*mingzi-jie*).

Regarding the phrase "like insects eating wood," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "It is like insects eating wood that happen to form characters. The insects do not know whether these are characters or not;
the wise person will never proclaim that the insects understand characters, nor will they be surprised or alarmed. This scripture provides the analogy.

The old physician did not distinguish between them and gave milk medicine for all illnesses; thus, "stopping" (*śamatha*) and "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) are metaphors that do not grasp the underlying intent.

Hearing the names is merely verbal recitation. One must proceed to the correct explanation: the meaning is that the object and the contemplation must clearly accord, and speech and practice must correspond.
This is called the stage of "name-only practice" (ming guanxing ji).

[Commentary] The *Miaozong* (Vol. 17) states: From the initial hearing of the perfect teaching and contemplating the wondrous realm of the Buddha, up until recognizing the stages of the path and diligently practicing the five repentances—if one has not yet attained the stage of "seed-germination" (fa pin)—all such practitioners belong to the category of "name-only. Thus, we know that "name-only" refers to this stage.

It is extremely long. Only when the object of contemplation and the contemplation itself mutually support one another, such that worldly thoughts have no interval between them, can one finally enter the stage of contemplative practice (the text).

[Commentary] This section cites the text to analyze its meaning, stating that from the initial sympathetic joy in hearing the perfect and wondrous principle, one gives rise to the perfect understanding.

Cultivating the Perfect Practice: From the first contemplation, the inconceivable realm, up to the eighth stage, the position of the consciousnesses, one should also diligently perform the five repentances.

Thus, the primary and auxiliary practices proceed in tandem. Even if one has not yet been able to give rise to the [true] stages, it should be understood that the contemplative practice is not yet perfected;

all such cases are subsumed within the stage of "names and words. The following section, "The Realm and Contemplation Support Each Other," demonstrates the correct principle of contemplative practice.

[Supplement] In the *Contemplation Sūtra*, one relies upon the Buddha to cultivate contemplation; therefore, it is called the "wondrous object of contemplating the Buddha. Question: What are the characteristics of the stage of "arousing the aspiration" (*fa-xin*)? Answer:

At the initial stage of the "name" (*ming-zi*), what is lost is easy to lose and what is gained is difficult to attain. In the "mind" (*xin*) within the name, gain and loss are roughly equal. In the subsequent mind, they are forged into a single whole;

there is only gain and no loss. This is precisely the stage of "arousing the aspiration. One must certainly reach the point where the object (*jing*) assists contemplation (*guan*), and through contemplation...

It becomes increasingly clear. As one contemplates the objective realm that serves as the support for contemplation (*ālambana*), the realm becomes ever more manifest, yet worldly thoughts (*rajas-citta*) remain uninterrupted; only then does one truly enter the stage of "Generating the Thought" (*cittotpāda*).

Because the objective realm and contemplation mutually support one another, those at the level of the five stages (*pañca-varga*) know the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, yet worldly thoughts remain uninterrupted.
Therefore, for those of the five grades, the five stages are fully subdued.

the arising of similar understanding constitutes the "Similar Identity" (the ten faiths).

[Commentary] *Zhiguan Yili* (1.23) states: "Because the more one contemplates, the clearer it becomes; the more one quiets [the mind], the more tranquil it becomes. It is like diligently shooting at a target;

[Commentary] This explains "semblance-identity" (*sādṛśya-abhisambodhi*). This person, through the diligent application of power derived from prior contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), achieves the correspondence between the object and the contemplation.
Having first shed the coarse defilements of the afflictive hindrances, the subtle principle of the Middle Way manifests in semblance;

therefore, it is called "semblance-identity with Buddhahood. Regarding the phrase "diligent archery," as stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "For example, in learning archery, one first establishes a large target, and subsequently..."

First, one practices with a small target; next, one shoots at a mark; next, one shoots at coins; and finally, one shoots at a single hair divided into a hundred parts—this is called having mastered the skill.
Then, even in the darkness of night, upon hearing a sound, whether from a human or a non-human, one shoots without exerting mental effort and invariably hits the mark.
The practitioner of samādhi is also like this. To borrow that analogy, one does not employ its actual method;
having already hit the mark of the neighbor, it is no longer the same as the previous training in aiming at the target.

[Commentary] The *Wangsheng jing shu* (Commentary on the Sutra of Contemplation), fascicle 2, states: "Regarding 'resemblance' (*xiangsi*): two things are similar to one another, like brass resembling gold, or a melon compared to a gourd;
it is like fire that is first warm, or the sea that is initially level. (*Miaozong chao*, fascicle upper [20], states: "Based on four metaphors, the practitioner of resemblance is clarified.
When the original enlightenment’s quiescent illumination and its union arise in a manner that resembles them, the stage of resemblance is established. There are three types.")
This awakening resembles the true; it is like brass resembling gold, or a gourd resembling a melon. These two objects serve as metaphors for the initial resemblance to the fundamental.
It is like first perceiving the warmth of heat when about to reach a fire, or observing the level surface when about to approach the sea.

These two matters serve as metaphors for a resemblance that is close to the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-tathatā*). The former two cases discuss resemblance in terms of phenomena (*dharma*), while the latter two discuss it in terms of stages (*avasthā*).
Treatise on the Apparent (Text).
[Supplementary Note] Regarding "quiescence and illumination" and "the two": The *Miaozong* states that within a single awakening, one speaks in terms of quiescence and illumination:
illuminating while constantly quiescent, quiescent while constantly illuminating; neither quiescent nor illuminating, yet both quiescent and illuminating—this is inconceivable. This is...

This is the awakening of stillness and the awakening of illumination; it is both a simultaneous negation and a simultaneous affirmation. The "illumination-awakening" arises in a manner that is similar [to the preceding].

The term *tūguā* (鍮瓜) is discussed from the perspective of its formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and thus the analogy pertains to the phenomena (*dharma*). The "fire-sea" is discussed from the perspective of its functional capacity (*kāritra*), and thus the analogy pertains to the stages (*avasthā*).
These three types—namely, stillness, illumination, and their union—are also the three perfect contemplations (*pariniṣpanna-tri-vipaśyanā*). The character for *hù* (瓠) is pronounced *hú*.

△ The partial realization of the identity of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) means to break through and see partially; this constitutes partial realization (from the first stage up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment).
[Note] *Zhiguan* 1.21 states: "By the power of the contemplation that accords with reality, one enters the stage of the copper wheel and for the first time breaks through ignorance."

To see the Buddha-nature, open the precious treasury, and manifest True Suchness (Tathatā) is called the Stage of Initial Resolve (Cittotpāda-vihāra), continuing up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi).

At this point, ignorance is attenuated and wisdom becomes increasingly manifest. If there are those who should be delivered by means of the Buddha-body, he manifests the eight phases of attaining enlightenment;
if there are those who should be delivered by means of the bodies of the nine realms of existence, he manifests them through the Universal Gate (Samantamukha-prakāśana). (Text)
[Commentary] This explanation clarifies the partial realization of identity. The commentary cites the first two lines of the *Zhi guan* to elucidate the merit of self-benefit;
the section beginning with "If a person... elucidates the merit of benefiting others. Both may be understood according to the text.

[Commentary on the Miaozong (20): It says: "Although the marks attained may appear similar, they still belong to conditioned cultivation (*yuánxiū*). Now, however, it is direct realization, which belongs to true cultivation (*zhēnxiū*).

By breaking through ignorance, the *Awakening of Faith* refers to this as 'partial awakening' (*suífēn jué*). Here, tranquil illumination is fused as one, and the true Buddha of original enlightenment (*běnjué*) is manifested bit by bit.
From the perspective of what is manifested, it is called 'partial truth' (*fēnzhēn*); from the perspective of that which manifests, it is called..."
Partial realization. All forty-one stages receive this name (text).

[Commentary] This section cites the text to provide an explanation. The first two phrases cite the preceding stage of semblance; although one perceives the principle with semblance, it is not yet true realization.
Because ignorance has not yet been shattered, it remains a conceptualization of the deluded mind; therefore, it is called "cultivation through conditions" (*pratyaya-bhāvanā*).

Now that ignorance has been shattered, the wondrous nature of *tathatā* (suchness) is revealed in its very essence. The three profound and wondrous contemplations manifest spontaneously; therefore, this is called "true cultivation.
That the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* refers to this as "partial awakening" (*anupūrva-bodhi*) is because one is free from the characteristics of coarse discursive thought. Now...
This clarifies that although the names differ, the meaning is the same; there is no difference in intent.
△ Sixth is the "Ultimate Identity" (niṣṭhā-niṣpanna).
Because wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions are perfected, it is called the Ultimate Identity (the stage of wondrous enlightenment).
[□ Note] As previously cited from the *Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra*, this explains the meaning of "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*).
[■ Record] This explains "ultimate identity" (*jiujing-ji*). When the wondrous principle is ultimately manifested, it is called the perfection of wisdom;
when ignorance is ultimately destroyed, it is called the perfection of severance. Therefore, this constitutes ultimate identity with the Buddha. The *Zhi-guan* states: "Ultimate identity..."

When wisdom-light is perfectly complete and can no longer be increased, it is called the fruit of Bodhi. When Great Nirvana has severed all that was to be severed and nothing further remains to be severed, it is called the fruit of fruits.
This state is not accessible even to those at the level of Equal Enlightenment; only a Buddha can fully realize it, and is thus called the Perfectly Complete Buddha.
△ Third, the correct explanation of the names and meanings:
In terms of the stages of practice, they proceed from shallow to deep; therefore, they are called "six. In terms of the essence of the principle revealed, each stage is non-dual;
therefore, they are called "identical" (*ji*).
【□Note】 Regarding the stages of practice and so forth: *The Great Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā* (Zhiguan Dayi) states: "Because they are identical, the beginning and the end are both one;
because there are six, the beginning and the end do not overlap. They are identical because the principle is the same; they are six because the phenomena differ" (text).
[Note] This explains the reason for establishing the names of the "six identities" (*liu ji*) by means of both stages (*wei*) and principle (*li*).

Because phenomena (*shi*) possess distinctions, six names are established from the shallow to the deep. Because principle is fundamentally without difference and is non-dual from beginning to end, the name "identity" (*ji*) is established.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation to profound understanding:

Therefore, one who deeply understands these six characters will not give rise to arrogance; one who thoroughly clarifies the meaning of "immediacy" (ji) will not give rise to self-deprecation. It is that to which one may return and upon which one may rely.
Contemplate it and choose it! This concludes the brief explanation of the stages of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

[Note] The six stages are names [for the same reality]. Since they all signify the non-duality of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*), each of the six stages possesses both the three thousand realms of phenomena and the three thousand realms of principle.

Therefore, because the principle is identical, it is "identity" (*ji*); this refers to the creation of principle. Because phenomena are differentiated, there are "six"; this refers to the creation of phenomena. As the *Yishu* says:

"Cultivating good and cultivating evil are the creation of the three thousand realms of phenomena (the six stages). Principle-identity is delusion and contrariety, which is the cultivation of evil. From the stage of 'name' (*mingzi*) onwards, one accords with..."

Nature. This is the cultivation of goodness. Whether nature is good or nature is evil, in principle it creates the three thousand [realms] (this is "immediate identity"). However, this immediate identity does not obstruct the six; the six sense bases are constantly identical.
Therefore, one attains the six stages and yet returns to the state of immediate identity (*ji*).

[Note] This demonstrates both the phenomenal and the principial aspects, correlating them respectively with the six stages of identity. As Siming (Sima Guang) stated: "The three thousand realms of *pratītyasamutpāda*..."

The cultivation of good and the cultivation of evil are both fundamentally endowed with the three thousand [dharmas]. These are categorized as the "intrinsic goodness" and "intrinsic evil" of nature. When correlated with the six stages of realization (*liujì*), this is identical to the present commentary.
Question: Why is it that the six stages are explained only in reference to the Perfect Teaching (*yuán*)? Answer: The dharmas of the three preceding teachings are not "stages of realization" (*jì*).

Although the Shared Teaching (*tōng*) speaks of realization, it pertains only to within the realm of *saṃsāra*. Therefore, the name "realization" (*jì*) belongs exclusively to the Perfect Teaching. Nevertheless, the three preceding teachings also...

One may establish six stages of "immediacy" (*jī*). In the Tripitaka Teaching, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the stage of Principle-immediacy (*lǐ-jí*). That which articulates the truth is Name-immediacy (*míngzì-jí*). The external ordinary person (*bāiwǎn*) is Practice-immediacy (*guānxíng-jí*).

The internal ordinary person (*nèiwǎn*) is Similar-immediacy (*xiāngsì-jí*). The Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is Partial-Truth-immediacy (*fēnzhēn-jí*). The Arhat is Ultimate-immediacy (*jiùjìng-jí*).

The Bodhisattva of the Tripitaka [Vehicle], up until sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, still abides in the stage of Similar-immediacy; it is only with the thirty-four moments of mind that they attain Partial-Truth-immediacy.

The ultimate [truth] is understood through both the general and specific teachings by analogy with what has been said. However, as these are all shallow and superficial, they do not teach "immediacy" (*jia*).
This concludes the brief explanation of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Explaining the Correct Practice of the Expedient Means of the Sublime Dharma. Part One: A General Account of How the Dharma Encompasses the Four Capacities.

However, when practicing according to the four aforementioned teachings, each has its own preparatory methods (*upāya*) and formal cultivation—namely, the twenty-five preparatory practices (*pañcaviṃśati-upāya*) and the ten vehicles of contemplative practice (*daśayāna-dhyāna-dharma*).
If these were explained individually for each teaching, the text would become somewhat cumbersome; yet, although their specific meanings differ, their numerical categories do not.
Therefore, they are explained collectively so that they may be understood through reflection.

[Note] However, while the preceding explanation of the four teachings as a method for interpreting the scriptures was primarily intended to open up understanding (*kai-ge*), if one is to establish practice based on that understanding, it is necessary to clarify the provisional means (*hōben*) and the correct cultivation (*shō-shu*) for each.
Therefore, the provisional means listed here apply across all four teachings; yet, the ten vehicles (*jū-jō*) are discussed here specifically from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*en*).
This is because the establishment of practice takes the Perfect Teaching as its standard.

[Commentary] This concludes the general exposition of understanding; from here on, one shall establish practice. It is said that to have understanding without practice is like having eyes but no feet;
to have practice without understanding is like having feet but no eyes. These two cannot both reach the Pond of Coolness.
Therefore, the preceding section clarified understanding by explaining the teachings; from this point forward, one shall establish practice based upon that understanding.
Practice. One desires that understanding and practice support one another, just as the eyes and feet jointly provide guidance.

Nevertheless, within the practices of the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), each has its own preliminary expedients (*upāya*) and formal cultivation (*bhāvanā*). The expedients listed here are common to all four teachings;

however, the ten vehicles (*daśa-yāna*) are discussed exclusively from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). This is because the practices established therein must necessarily take the Perfect Teaching as their standard.

[Note] This does not clarify the four kinds of samādhi (constant sitting, constant walking, half-walking-half-sitting, and neither-walking-nor-sitting), nor the ten realms (skandhas, afflictions, illness, karma, demons, meditation, views, pride, vehicles, and *sattvas*).
These merely record the essential outlines of the Great Text and do not constitute the actual intent of the *Zhiguan*; therefore, they are not treated in detail here.
[Commentary] This section explains why the four practices and ten objects are not clarified here. The first line points out the names of the four practices and ten objects;
the subsequent portion properly explains the reason for their lack of clarification.

That is to say, these are detailed in the second fascicle of the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (Mohe zhiguan), whereas here only the essential framework is briefly presented. Therefore, they are not explained in full detail.
Now, to speak briefly: first is *nityaparyaṅka* (constant sitting). This appears in the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where it is called the *ekavyūha-samādhi*.
It states that one should maintain constant sitting, avoiding walking, standing, or reclining. Whether among a community or living alone is better;

however, dwelling in a single quiet room upon a single rope-cot for a period of ninety days—or seven days, as the duration is not fixed—is recommended. Thus one should bind oneself [to this practice].
1. Seated in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), one focuses one-pointedly on a single Buddha (and so forth). 2.

Constantly practicing the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* (Banzhou Sanmei Jing), which means exclusively practicing circumambulation for a period of ninety days; it is also called the "Samādhi of the Standing Buddha.
When this samādhi is accomplished, one sees the Buddhas of the ten directions standing in the air. 3. Half-walking and half-sitting, as taught in the Vaipulya and *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtras*.
In the *Vaipulya Sūtras* it is said: "Circumambulate [the stupa] one hundred and twenty times, then sit back and engage in contemplation for an indefinite period of time.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Whether that person is walking or standing while reading and reciting this sūtra, or sitting while contemplating this sūtra, I shall at that time mount a six-tusked white elephant and appear before that person; for a period of twenty-one days..."
One period. Fourth, neither sitting nor walking: in reality, this practice is performed while seated. The methods appear in various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Avalokiteśvara-ādhyeṣaṇā-sūtra*.
Whether walking, sitting, or even performing manual labor, it may be cultivated even amidst the bustle of business and haste.
Nanyue referred to this as the Samādhi of Following One’s Own Intent. The ten realms do not transcend the three obstacles and four māras:
the realm of the five aggregates is the obstacle of retribution; the realms of illness and various views are the obstacle of afflictions;
the realms of arrogance, karma-characteristics, demonic activities, meditative concentration, the two vehicles, and bodhisattvas are the obstacle of karma.

The aggregates (*skandha*), karma, dhyāna, vehicles (*yāna*), and *sat* constitute the māra of the aggregates (*skandhamāra*). Afflictions (*kleśa*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), and pride (*māna*) constitute the māra of afflictions (*kleśamāra*). Illness constitutes the māra of death (*mṛtyumāra*).

*Māra* refers specifically to the celestial Māras. [Supplement] The *Yizhu* (Explanatory Notes) states: Regarding the "aggregates" (*skandha*), when a beginner practices contemplation, they must first focus on the internal mind;

therefore, from among the three categories [of dharmas], the spheres (*āyatana*) and bases (*dhātu*) are excluded. Furthermore, from among the five aggregates, the first four are set aside, and one specifically takes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as the object of contemplation.
This is like discarding the *zhang* to take the *chi*, or discarding the *chi* to take the *cun*; this constitutes the "general negation."

Illuminating the mind is like cutting down a tree by reaching its root, or cauterizing a disease by hitting the correct acupuncture point; thus, thousands of branches and myriad ailments will naturally wither away.

If one does not enter [the state of concentration], then one proceeds through the remaining "one-mind" stages, applying this principle to the other sense bases (*āyatana*) and even the nine objects (*viṣaya*), observing them only when they arise and not observing them when they do not.
As for "afflictions" (*kleśa*), these refer to the heavy delusions accumulated since beginningless time.

Now, by means of contemplation, one observes that these delusions have long persisted and cannot be controlled. For those who are ill, they contemplate the delusions regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), which agitate the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Having identified their fundamental cause, they treat them through contemplation, therapeutic techniques, or medical remedies. Thereafter, they further cultivate through the practice of contemplation.
As for the characteristics of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*): it refers to tainted karma (*sāsrava-karman*) whose retribution is due in the future. Now, by means of...

Contemplating the arousal [of the mind]. Although the characteristics of this arousal are numerous, they do not exceed the categories of obscuration and transcendence (*pāramitā*). Each possesses six characteristics; some arise due to *śamatha* (calm abiding), while others arise due to *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Regarding demonic activities (*mārakarma*): because one contemplates various objects, although delusions have not yet been destroyed, the celestial Māras fear that [the practitioner] will transcend their realm.
Thus, the lords of the world all come to disturb the practitioner, as do the terrestrial yakṣas such as Trāyastriṃśa, Pīḍaka, and others.
The realm of ghosts (preta) is governed by the celestial Māras, who obstruct practitioners and do not permit them to transcend their boundaries. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva who does not speak of Māra is called a bodhisattva-cāṇḍāla. Regarding dhyāna, this refers to the four fundamental dhyānas and so forth.

When one gains power through such cultivation, there will inevitably be manifestations of past habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). These signs are most difficult to discern, as explained extensively in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi* and the *Zuochan Sanmei Jing* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation).

Regarding "Views": these arise from contemplation, including the one hundred and forty views and so forth. Regarding "Pride": having already suppressed [wrong] views, one claims to have reached profound realization and improperly assumes the status of a supreme sage;
therefore, one must recognize this. Regarding "the Two Vehicles": they formerly set their aspirations on the Small [Vehicle], which arises through the cultivation of compassion.
Regarding "Bodhisattvas": there are three types of Bodhisattva minds—those of the Tripitaka, the Shared, and the Distinct—which arise through cultivation.
Manifestation. All the aforementioned objects must be subdued through the power of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). However, these ten objects constitute the general outline of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

[Note] The *Miaoxuan* clarifies the gateway to entering the essence: the four teachings and four gates, with ten vehicles within each gate. If one follows the ten [vehicles] of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*...

"Object. Regarding the ten vehicles of the objects of contemplation (*daśa-viṣaya-yāna*), this clarifies only the practice of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanxing*). The *Yili* states: "If there were no ten objects, the vehicles would have no substance;

if there were no ten dharmas, it would be called a 'ruined donkey-cart. (Text). This is because the ten [categories] beginning with the aggregates (*skandha*) serve as the objects of contemplation (*ālambana-viṣaya*), while the inconceivable object (*acintya-viṣaya*) and so forth serve as the contemplating subjects (*ālambaka-darśana*).

[Note] This citation from the *Myōgen* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) clarifies the extensive application of the ten vehicles (*daśayāna*). Regarding the phrase "the gate of entering the essence" (*tattva-dvāra*): "essence" (*tattva*) refers to principle (*li*).
That is to say, the Tripitaka Teaching takes arising-and-ceasing as its essence, and so on, up to the Perfect Teaching, which takes non-action as its essence, and so forth.
Regarding the "four gates of the four teachings": the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect Teachings each possess the four gates of emptiness, existence, both, and neither. [Practice...]

These four gates must all be driven by the ten vehicles to reach the ground of cool serenity. In the section on "Cessation and Contemplation" (Zhiguan), it clarifies that the establishment of practice must be complete;
in the section on "Principles and Examples" (Yili), it clarifies the reason why both the objective realm and the vehicle must necessarily consist of ten.

△ Second, a brief exposition of the two types of practice and establishment. Part one: clarifying the preparatory practices (*upāya*) that assist the path, which opens into twenty-five sections. First, the outline:
regarding the "twenty-five expedient means," they are condensed into five categories: 1. possessing the five conditions; 2. reviling the five desires; 3. ... [text continues] ...
