Abandoning the five hindrances; the four adjustments of the five matters;
the five practices and the five dharmas. [Commentary] The four skillful means (the first) of śamatha and vipaśyanā are called "skillfulness.
Through skillful cultivation, even with a minute root of goodness, one can cause immeasurable practices to achieve liberation and realization, entering the stage of a bodhisattva (text).
[Commentary] This explains the term "expedient means" (*upāya*). The *Zhiguan* states: "Expedient means refers to the convergence of various conditions.
Because it can harmonize [conditions] to form a cause, and also can harmonize them to attain the fruit. The *Fuxing* states: "Because it is skillfully able to harmonize [them]."

Therefore, it is called "expedient means" (*upāya*). Now, only through the harmonious integration and regulation of these twenty-five factors can one fulfill the cause for the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) and realize the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

Expedient means is termed "skillful" because, by means of minor practices, one is able to skillfully dedicate them so that these minor practices may be transformed into sublime causes; hence, it is called "skillful. That which is not skillful is merely provisional...

In reality, there is no duality. By understanding non-duality, one harmonizes ritual practices so that a single practice can encompass all practices, thereby perfecting the true understanding of the three modes of discipline.
With a single arousal of the aspiration, all aspirations are aroused; this is entry into the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*). As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Even small virtues can produce great fruits," such as seeking the fruit of Buddhahood by reciting a single verse of praise, invoking a single name, or offering a single burnt offering.
Offering a single incense stick and a single flower—through such minor practices, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.

Thus we know that what is called "skillful means" (*upāya*) consists in the power of guidance through wisdom by means of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Regarding the statement "practice is perfected and understanding arises":

this refers to the initial stage of the path, where understanding precedes practice. However, regarding the entry into the [bodhisattva] stages, if practice is not perfected, true understanding will not arise.

[Commentary on the Fourfold Cessation and Contemplation] The first [section] states: In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), the stages of the five ranks of provisional names (*jiaming*) and the stage of contemplative practice (*guanxing*) are still far removed from the Truth;

thus they are called "distant preparatory means" (*yuān fangbian*). The stage of the purification of the six faculties (*liu gen qingjing*), which resembles and borders upon the Truth, is called "near preparatory means" (*jin fangbian*) (referring to the stages of the outer and inner ordinary persons).
Now, within the stage of provisional names prior to the five ranks, we further distinguish between the distant and the near: the twenty-five dharmas constitute the "distant."
The preparatory practices (*upāya*). The ten kinds of objects serve as the proximate preparations; they encompass [the practice] both horizontally and vertically.

When the ten contemplations are complete, one attains the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), capable of producing the true and the semblance [realizations]. This is called the proximate preparation. (Text) Fully explained in the first volume of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).
[Commentary] This demonstrates the meaning of skillful means (*upāya*), which varies according to distance and proximity. Regarding the term "provisional name" (*prajñapti-nāman*):

although within the preceding stage of "names," one may have heard the principle of the true reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*) of the Three Truths from a teacher or from a scripture, and thereby attained a thorough understanding and realization of all phenomena, one has not yet practiced meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Thus, although it is called "names," it is in fact a "provisional name. (5)

Within the stage of "Refined Taste" (Gonp'in), although one practices the three contemplations perfectly and suppresses the five stages of dwelling (gojū) completely, one has not yet severed the delusions; one still remains separated from the ten levels of faith (juppishin).
Therefore, it is said that one is "distant from the Truth. The "six sense organs being adjacent to the Truth" refers precisely to the ten levels of faith.

This is because the first level of faith severs the delusions of views (ken), the second through the seventh sever the delusions of thought (shi), and the eighth severs the coarse defilements of the "dust-sands" (jinsha) both internal and external. First, [the coarse defilements are removed].

It falls [into the category of the semblance stage], yet it is called "pure" because it has perfectly subdued ignorance. According to the principle within the semblance stage of insight, when compared to the first dwelling (bhūmi), there is only the interval of a single mind;
therefore, it is said to be "adjacent to the truth. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "The twenty-five dharmas in the present text..."
Regarding the discussion of further expedient means prior to the distant and near expedients of the Perfect Teaching, these are established as the expedient means for the five grades of practice.
Within the six identities, this corresponds to the identity of name; therefore, it is called "provisional name. It should be understood that this is the intended meaning here.

Furthermore, prior to the ordinary practitioners (pṛthagjana) within and outside the four teachings, these collectively constitute the distant preparatory means (*dūram upāya*) for all four teachings.
As for the "ten kinds," they refer to the ten objects (*daśa-viṣaya*). If one contemplates them or brings them forth, entry into the [definitive] stage is not far off; thus they are called "near.

Because the twenty-five phenomena are distant from the Truth, they are termed "distant. Question: The aggregates (*skandha*) are the primary object of cultivation, while the remaining nine await their manifestation. Why is this so?
Why are these termed "expedient means" (*upāya*)? Answer: In this treatise, the reason all ten objects are called expedient means is that they are all that which is observed.
Only when there is an observer do they properly belong to correct cultivation. Therefore, the first eight pertain only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The latter two names constitute the skillful means (*upāya*) of the sages; thus, one knows that the ten realms are all the proximate skillful means for perfect practice (*yuanxing*).

If one follows the three previous teachings, the distinctions are not uniform: in the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), one contemplates only the realm of the bodhisattva; in the Common Teaching (*tongjiao*), one contemplates only one;
in the Tripitaka Teaching (*sanzang*), there is none at all, as one contemplates only nine realms; and in the Two Vehicles (*er sheng*), one contemplates eight realms.

Half. Regarding the two vehicles’ contemplation of the eight objects in their entirety: although this is the case in general discourse, the present intention lies in the Perfect [Teaching]. "Horizontal and vertical" and below explain the functional power of the contemplated objects.
As for "the ten objects encompassing horizontally and vertically," it is as explained at the beginning of the fifth fascicle of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation).
Ten pairs arise alternately; I shall now record them in full. *Zhiguan* states: "There are ten ways they arise alternately:
namely, sequential and non-sequential, mixed and unmixed, complete and incomplete, with mental attention and without mental attention, accomplished and unaccomplished, beneficial and non-beneficial."
"Long or not long; difficult or not difficult; further or not further. Regarding the "three obstructions, four maras, nine pairs, and seven singles," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:
"The first nine are paired, hence they are called 'nine pairs. The last one is not paired, hence it is called 'seven singles.

Furthermore, there is "horizontal possession and horizontal non-possession," as well as "vertical possession and vertical non-possession. This is, for example, like progressing from the four dhyānas up to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). This is [the meaning].

Vertical completeness (*ūrdhva-saṃpanna*): reaching up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Vertical incompleteness: the non-attainment of the supernormal powers, clear knowledges (*abhijñā*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and so forth.

Horizontal completeness: the attainment of the seven liberations. Horizontal incompleteness: ceasing at the attainment of the [first] seven liberations. Furthermore, the nine grades of the first dhyāna constitute vertical completeness; from the eighth grade downward constitutes vertical incompleteness.
Moreover, the fulfillment of the five factors (*pañca-aṅga*) within a single grade constitutes horizontal completeness; from four factors downward constitutes [horizontal incompleteness].
The horizontal [arrangement] is not complete; the rest may be understood by analogy with this. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states:

"Because they arise from the object, the arising of contemplation is further termed 'horizontal' and 'vertical. Furthermore, these ten dharmas have both general and specific aspects. The specific aspect is the inconceivable object (*acintya-viṣaya*)."
Reaching the ultimate depth of the true reality (*dharmatā*) is called "vertical" (*ūrdhva*). Encompassing the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*) is called "horizontal" (*tiryak*).

Arousing the aspiration for enlightenment to seek what is above is called "vertical"; transforming sentient beings below is called "horizontal. Furthermore, seeking what is above and transforming those below is called "vertical"; relying on the objective realm to make vows is called "horizontal.

Settling the mind so as to penetrate the principle is called "vertical"; the sixty-four stages [of practice] are called "horizontal. Destroying pervasive delusions to reach their limit is called "vertical. [These are] the various gates.
Mutually facing one another is called "horizontal" (transverse). Reaching through to the place of treasure is called "vertical. Examining and blocking [delusions] is called "horizontal.

The stages of the path (mārga-aṅga) reaching their culmination is called "vertical. Each stage facing the others is called "horizontal. The primary and auxiliary practices reaching their culmination is called "vertical.

Each dharma facing every other dharma is called "horizontal. Successive stages reaching the ultimate is called "vertical. Each stage universally encompassing all is called "horizontal. Patience and progress reaching what follows is... [the text continues].

"Vertical" (*yǔ*) refers to the mutual correspondence of the contrary and the compliant; this is called "horizontal" (*héng*). To enter and abide in non-attachment is "vertical," while being free from the three semblance-dharmas is "horizontal.
This explanation is provisionally based solely on the Perfect Vehicle (*yuánshèng*). If viewed in contrast to the partial vehicles (*piānshèng*), one may speak of horizontal and vertical.

To manifest that which is neither horizontal nor vertical is the inconceivable; it is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet it can produce both the horizontal and the vertical, and thus is called horizontal and vertical. Furthermore, in general...

Regarding the commentator’s view: within each individual stage, the ten [factors] are mutually related as "horizontal" (transverse). As each stage reaches its ultimate limit, the progressive deepening of the dharma constitutes the "vertical.
Alternatively, the first seven dharmas may be termed "horizontal," while the sequential progression through the stages of consciousness is termed "vertical."
[Note] Furthermore, the twenty-five dharmas constitute the universal expedient means because they apply universally to the four samādhis.

The *Vaipulya-mṛgendra* and the six-period fivefold repentance of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitute the specific expedient means because they are employed specifically for one particular type of samādhi among the four.

[Commentary] This clarifies the general and specific preparatory practices (*upāya*). The first two phrases clarify the general preparatory practice, because the four samādhis serve as the general preparation for the twenty-five dharmas.
The subsequent half-verse distinguishes the specific preparatory practice;
among the four samādhis, one specific type—half-walking and half-sitting—is used for the *Vaipulya*, the *Svapnarāja*, and the five repentances of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This is for the sake of providing an expedient means (*upāya*). Regarding what is called the "Dream King," the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The Vaipulya [sūtras] are most supreme; they must not be treated with levity.

If one wishes to practice them, the spiritual deities (*śrīmanta*) shall serve as witnesses. First, one seeks the Dream King; if one obtains a vision of him, this signifies that he permits practices such as repentance.
Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*, it specifically prescribes five repentances during six periods of the day and night; the explanation for these is found previously in section nine.

[Commentary] Regarding the grouping [of the conditions] into five categories: the *Zhiguan* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation), Part 4, states: "Now, the Way does not operate in isolation; it is propagated by persons.

Persons propagate the sublime Dharma, which relies upon conditions to advance one toward the Way. Therefore, one must possess the five conditions (*pañca-pratyayāḥ*). Once these causal powers are complete, one should sever all cravings and desires.
Having screened off external cravings and desires, one should internally purify the mind. If the mind is tranquil, one should then regulate and test the five [senses]."

Matters. Once the five matters have been harmonized, one practices the five dharmas and will certainly reach the destination. This extends even to the three categories. One version is from the *Mahā-śāstra* (Great Treatise);
one version is from the *Dhyāna-sūtra*. (It possesses five conditions. First, it was established by various meditation masters (*dhyāna-ācārya*) (the text harmonizes the five matters).

[Commentary] This citation from the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) clarifies the text concerning the sequential arising of the five categories. The first four lines explicitly explain this arising.
The initial two phrases clarify that the Way depends on the person to flourish—what is meant by "the person can expand the Way; it is not the Way that expands the person.
The subsequent two phrases clarify that although one relies on the person for its expansion, it must necessarily depend on auxiliary conditions. Therefore, the following points out the five...

The section headings from "Contact" down to "Lower" manifest that there is a source from which they derive. Regarding the statement "must reach the place of arrival," the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) takes the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) as that "place of arrival.

However, proceeding from the first stage is not the intended meaning of the present text; therefore, the subsequent passage states: "The merits of entering and abiding in the stages are not discussed here.
As for the three sections being extracted from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the treatise asks: "What is skillful means (*upāya*)?"
Attaining the Dhyāna-pāramitā means: setting aside five matters, eliminating five dharmas, and practicing five conducts. The text is extensive and not recorded here;
one version appears in the *Dhyāna Sūtra*, namely the passage on the next page beginning with "Although the four conditions are fully complete" (etc.).

One [version] was established by various dhyāna masters, though this remains uncertain. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Although this was established by humans, its practice is most essential; therefore, it is used here."

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan* says: It is like a potter who, wishing to produce a vessel, first selects a good location (providing the necessary conditions), ceases other worldly affairs (reproving desire), treats internal ailments of the body (abandoning the hindrances), adjusts the clay and the wheel (harmonizing the five matters), and works without ceasing (practicing the five dharmas). Thus he attains [his goal].

The meaning of this analogy is that the five [categories] are as clear as one’s own fingers and palms. If you wish to practice cultivation, you should seek out *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* (and so forth). [Commentary:
This citation from the *Śikṣāsamuccaya* separately lists the five sections to clarify the teaching through an analogy. The first seven lines directly cite the text and present the analogy.
The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Record) states: "Táo" refers to the city of Táoqiu south of the present-day Púzhōu, where Yao once resided.
Therefore, it is called "Yao’s City. For this reason, he is called Yao. He belonged to the lineage of Tàodáng; "Táo" (陶) refers to earthenware or brickwork.
Because he was named after this, he is called the "Master of Táo" (陶師). If the name were derived from what he produced, it should be written as "Táo" (陶), meaning earthenware vessels.
The following two lines clarify how one attains the analogy and thereby knows the Dharma. The *Lunyu* says: "Is it not like looking at one's palms? This refers to pointing at one's own palms.
"Pointing at the palm" means it is very clear. The final two lines refer to the full text; I shall now record it in its entirety. The *Śikṣāsamuccaya* (or *Zhiguan*) says:
"For example, a potter who wishes to produce a vessel first selects a good site—one free of sand and salt, with an abundance of grass and water—where he can establish his workshop.
Next, he must cease all distracting activities. If one's affairs are not settled, how can success be achieved? 'Jì' (際) means 'to connect'."
This refers to engaging with worldly affairs. Although one may cease external conditions, if there is illness within the body, how can one perform tasks?

Even if the body is healthy and strong, if the clay wheel is not properly adjusted, no vessel will be produced. Likewise, even if superior conditions are complete, if one is not dedicated to the task, the work will be abandoned and fail to continue;
there will never be any accomplishment. It is the same for the five conditions of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; they depend upon these factors.
This body must necessarily rely upon external supports. Just as one seeks out a favorable location, so too should one loathe and detest worldly desires and abandon the five hindrances.
Just as one treats an internal illness, so should one regulate the five factors. Just as one turns a clay wheel, so should one practice the five dharmas without ceasing.
In worldly affairs, even minor matters do not harmonize without the proper conditions; how much more so for the great matters of transcending the world?

If there were no preliminary guidance, how could one easily ascend? Therefore, one proceeds through twenty-five dharmas, taking phenomena as the basis for contemplation. By this, one adjusts the coarse and enters the subtle, examining and calming the distracted mind;
thus, these serve as the remote preparations (*dūrasāmagrī*).
△ Second, the citation and explanation of the five [conditions] has five parts. First, the complete enumeration of the five conditions has two parts.
First, the formal citation. First, explaining the five conditions:
[Note] The *Dhyāna-sūtra* says: "Although the four conditions may be fully present, guidance depends upon a good teacher; therefore, one employs the five dharmas as the entry."
The ladder of the Path: even a single missing rung obstructs progress.
[Commentary] When it says that the single method of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* originates from the *Dhyāna-sūtra*, it specifically refers to this passage.
【□Note】 The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), Fascicle 4, Part 1, states: "The two vehicles, Great and Small, take the precepts as their foundation; therefore, they are explained first.

Although internal prohibitions are strict, one must rely upon food and clothing. To advance in the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), one requires seclusion. Even if the dwelling is secluded, it depends upon the severance of external entanglements.
Although these four conditions are complete, guidance and instruction depend upon the teacher. (Text).
[Commentary] This section clarifies the sequence of the five conditions for the *Dhyāna-sūtra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"To maintain pure precepts, sever the fetters and proclivities, and attain the path of Arhatship; yet to maintain the precepts with a great mind and have compassion for sentient beings—this is the Bodhisattva."
Therefore, both the Great and Small Vehicles take the observance of the precepts as their foundation; this should first be clarified. The remainder is understandable.
[Note] The *Great Meaning of Śamatha and Vipaśyanā* (Zhi guan da yi), fascicle 4, states: First, the sufficiency of clothing and food, because it removes the conditions of longing and hope.

Second, the purity of the observance of the precepts, because it removes the causes for rebirth in the evil realms. Third, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place, because it removes the affairs of clamor and distraction. Fourth, the cessation of all...

Regarding the causal conditions: one must abandon trivial and miscellaneous activities. Fifth, one requires a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), for there is a ground for consulting and resolving doubts.

[Commentary] This clarifies that practicing the Path takes these five conditions as essential tasks; they are indispensable. The intent is that clothing and food are the provisions for assisting the Path;
they benefit the physical body, and therefore they must be fully provided. As it is said: "When the Wheel of Dharma has not yet..."

The wheel of food turns first; it is the primary sustenance. Pure precepts are the direct cause for hastening toward the ultimate fruit and the sublime practice for binding the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Therefore, one must first maintain them with purity in order to avoid the evil realms. A quiet place is the ground for applying effort and entering the Way;
as the saying goes, "one should seek pearls when the waves are calm," for it would be difficult to retrieve them from rushing waters. Thus, one should cease all external conditions.
This is the essential method for gathering the mind: that which is called "concentrating it in one place. There is nothing that cannot be accomplished thereby.
A spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the complete causal condition for attaining the Way; it is like an infant who must rely on its mother, or a fledgling whose wings must cling to a branch.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of the five [purities]. First, the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).

Regarding the purity of ethical discipline: as stated in the Sūtras, "By relying upon and depending on this ethical discipline, one attains the various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus, you should maintain pure ethical discipline. This applies to both householders and renunciants, and to all levels of the Great and Small Vehicles.

Same. [Note] The *Fajie Cidian* (Gradual Order of the Dharma Realm), Volume Upper (12), states: "The meaning of precepts (*śīla*) is prevention. (Text) The first part of the *Jieshu* (Commentary on Precepts), Volume Upper, states:
In the Sanskrit language, it is *śīla*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that in the language of Qin it means "innate goodness" (*xing shan*), and it is also called "coolness" (*qing liang*).

It is so named because it can arrest the feverish afflictions of violating the precepts; thus it is designated according to its function. It is also called *pratimokṣa*, translated as "preserving liberation" (*bao jie tuo*).
It is further termed "pure livelihood" (*jing ming*), and is also said to mean "accomplishing dignified deportment" (*chengjiu wei yi*). (Text)
[Commentary] To prevent wrongdoing and cease evil is called "prevention. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* was translated by Master Kumārajīva;

therefore, it is referred to as "the language of Qin. Regarding "inherently good": its nature is fundamentally good and free from defilement; such is the essence of the precepts (*śīla*). Regarding "cooling":

when a person who has broken the precepts is scorched by the flames of desire, the precepts are able to provide prevention and relief. Regarding "preserving liberation": this means they are able to maintain and protect [liberation].
The three karmas are free from all fetters. Pure livelihood means sustaining oneself with purity, forever remaining aloof from wrong livelihood.
Accomplishment in dignified deportment means possessing a majestic presence that inspires awe and a code of conduct that serves as a model.
[Note] Regarding "as stated in the sutra," this refers to the *Śāriputra-parivarta-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), fascicle 4, part 1, page 5, states:
"To cite evidence for the concentration of the Path, it further takes the Vinaya discipline as its foundation. (Text)
[Commentary] The *Śāsanānuśāsanī-sūtra* states: "O bhikṣus, after my parinirvāṇa, you should revere, treasure, and honor the *prātimokṣa*.
It is like encountering light in the darkness, or like a poor man finding a treasure. You should know that this is your Great Teacher;
it is no different from my remaining in the world. It continues: "The precepts are the direct path leading to liberation."

This is the foundation [of all virtues]. Relying upon and depending on this precept, one attains various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) as well as the wisdom that extinguishes suffering.

For this reason, a bhikṣu should maintain pure precepts and not allow them to be broken or deficient. (From the *Fuxing* [Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*], Part 2, explaining the meaning of "realization.")
[Note] Regarding the precepts for laypeople: there are the five precepts and the eight precepts. The eight precepts are so named because they add to the five precepts the following three:
not sitting on high or wide beds, not wearing flower garlands or perfumed clothing, and not going to watch or listen to singing and dancing.

[Commentary] Regarding the five precepts: they are [the prohibitions against] killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and intoxicants. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* clarifies four distinct categories:
first, those who merely receive the three refuges are called "partial" (*amśika*) upāsakas; second, those who receive one precept are called "small-part" (*parītta-aṃśika*);

third, those who receive two, three, or four are called "large-part" (*mahā-aṃśika*); and fourth, those who receive them all completely are called "full-part" (*pūrṇa-aṃśika*) upāsakas, as is the case with the five precepts.
If these were entirely lacking, the path of humanity would be cut off. These five precepts are the root of the *śīla* (ethical discipline) for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna;
thus, a sutra says: "The five precepts are the great prohibitions of the world. If one violates the five precepts, in heaven one opposes the five stars;

on earth one opposes the five sacred peaks (*wu yue*); in the quarters one opposes the five emperors (*wu di*); among humans one opposes the five constants (*wu chang*); and in one's person one opposes [the five organs]."
The five viscera [are thus protected]. Therefore, when the Buddha attained enlightenment and had not yet turned the Wheel of Dharma, he first bestowed the Five Precepts upon the Elder Trapusa;
this is called the "Human Vehicle," which stands at the head of the Five Vehicles. It is by means of these Five Precepts that one is transported out of the three miserable realms.

Furthermore, regarding the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), four are of a natural nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and one is a prohibitive offense (*prajñapti-sāvadya*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Among the prohibitive offenses, one abstains from alcohol alone in order to protect the remaining rules of discipline;
if one commits a transgression even when the rule has been established by convention, it constitutes an additional prohibitive offense on top of the natural one.

Regarding the eight precepts (*aṣṭāṅga-śīla*), they are received on the six days of fasting (*ṣaḍ-upavāsa-dina*). A treatise asks: "Why are the eight precepts received on the six days of fasting to cultivate merit? The answer is: "On these days..."
Evil spirits pursue people, seeking to snatch away their lives; they cause illness, misfortune, and decline, bringing ill omen to men.
For this reason, at the beginning of the kalpa, the sages taught people to observe the fast, cultivate goodness, and perform meritorious deeds in order to avoid such calamities.

It is said that the fasting methods practiced in former times did not involve receiving the eight precepts, but rather took simply one day of not eating as the fast. This continued until the appearance of the Buddha.
The World-Honored One said: "You should, for one day and one night, observe the eight precepts as the Buddhas do, abstaining from food after midday.

By this merit, you shall be able to reach Nirvana. As the Buddha taught in the *Cāturmahārājakāyika-sūtra*, on the six monthly fast days, the messengers, the crown princes, and the Four Great Kings descend in person to observe whether sentient beings are practicing giving and upholding the precepts.

Regarding the precepts: if those who are filial toward their parents and few in number report this to the Lord of Heaven (Indra) and the various devas, they all become displeased and lament, saying, "The hosts of devas are diminishing, while the asuras are flourishing.

If those who are many in number do so, their hearts are all filled with joy, and they praise it, saying, "The hosts of devas are increasing, and the asuras are being diminished. Furthermore, on these six days of fasting, wherever...
In villages and hamlets, those who observe the fast and receive the precepts cause malevolent spirits to depart far away, and their dwellings become peaceful and secure.
For this reason, observing the fast and receiving the precepts on these six days increases one's merit and virtue. Regarding the prohibition against sitting on high, wide, or large beds:
according to the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, Kāḷodāyin, knowing in advance that the Buddha was coming, immediately spread out a high and fine bed and seat along the road.
The Buddha, knowing that [the monk] harbored malice within, addressed the bhikṣus: "This foolish man acts only for his own sake; he has now censured others and established this precept.
If one makes a rope bed or a wooden bed, the legs should be as high as eight fingers of the Tathāgata; to exceed this constitutes an offense. The Āgama states:
"A leg length of one chi and six cun is not considered high; a width of four chi is not considered wide; and a length of eight chi [is the standard]."
It is not large. That which exceeds these dimensions is called a high, wide, and large bed, and thus violates the Buddha’s prohibition.
As for those who do not wear flower garlands or fine robes, it is appropriate that they wear garments of plain cloth.
【□ Note】 Regarding the precepts for those who have left the household life: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās (here translated as "women training in the precepts").
[Commentary: There are two hundred and fifty precepts for the characteristics of a bhikṣu. As for the bhikṣuṇī, the term "ni" is used as a general designation for women.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that a bhikṣuṇī attains immeasurable restraints (*saṃvara*), and thus she should follow after the bhikṣu. However, because the formal procedures (*vidhi*) would have been inconvenient, the Buddha [placed her after the śrāmaṇera].

Therefore, [the section on] Bhikṣuṇīs follows after that of the Śramaṇas. The *Nizhong pian* (Section on the Assembly of Nuns) states: "The Buddha initially did not permit women to leave the household life and become ordained, as this would cause the True Dharma to perish five hundred years earlier.

Later, he preached the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) and allowed them to ordain. Because they practiced according to these teachings, the duration of the Dharma was restored to one thousand years.

In the present age, these are not practiced; consequently, the Dharma perishes wherever it goes. The *Huizheng ji* (Record of the Correct Assembly) states: "Ten years after the Buddha attained enlightenment..."
Four years later, her maternal aunt requested to leave the household life. The Buddha did not permit her ordination. Ānanda made the request three times on her behalf.
The Buddha then instructed Ānanda to convey the Eight Rules of Respect (*aṣṭau gurudharmāḥ*) to her, saying: "If she can practice these, I will allow her to leave the household life.

She replied, "I shall receive and uphold them with the highest reverence. As for the Eight Rules of Respect, the verse says: She bows [to monks]; she is not to be reviled or slandered; she must not expose their faults; she receives the precepts from the Saṃgha; she practices [the rules].

Mānava, every half-month one should seek instruction within the Saṃgha; during the rainy season retreat (varṣā), one should approach the Saṃgha to request the invitation for the Prātimokṣa ceremony (pravāraṇā).
The precepts of the Bhikṣuṇīs consist briefly of five hundred articles. Śrāmaṇera: this is translated as "resting from affection" (xi cí), meaning to cease worldly defiled passions.
This means to rescue sentient beings through loving-kindness (*maitrī*). The underlying sense is that when one first enters the Buddha-dharma, worldly sentiments often persist;
therefore, it is necessary to cease evil and practice loving-kindness. In the Tang translation, this is *Bhikṣu-pāramitā-laukika*, which is translated here as "Diligent Encourager" (*Pravrajita*).

There is a distinction between male and female [novices]. From the age of seven until the thirteenth year, they are all called *Kūca-śrāmaṇera* (Crows-Driving Śrāmaṇeras). From fourteen to... [text ends]
Nine: One who is named an *anurupa-śrāmaṇera* (a śrāmaṇera in accordance with the Dharma). Only those aged twenty and above are designated by the title *nāmadheya-śrāmaṇera* (a śrāmaṇera by name).

Their precept characteristics are ten; the same applies to the community of nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*). A *śikṣamāṇā*—which is translated here as "a woman training in the Dharma"—is referred to in the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* as an eighteen-year-old girl who should train in the precepts for two years. It is also said that a young woman who has previously been married may be [admitted] at the age of ten.

Regarding this, she is granted the six dharmas. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The six dharmas are for training the mind; only when one is able to maintain these six dharmas may one receive full ordination.
Regarding the two years, this is for training the body, so that it may be known whether or not there has been pregnancy. The *Shishi Yaoyong Chao* states: "Śikṣamāṇā."

One must be fully trained in three sets of dharmas: First, training in the fundamental rules (*mūla*), which refers to the four *pārājika* offenses. Second, training in the six dharmas (*ṣaḍ-dharma*), namely those mentioned in the *Karmavācanā*:
intentional physical contact with a man, stealing four *kārsāpaṇa* or more, taking the life of an animal, speaking minor falsehoods, eating at improper times, and drinking alcohol.
Third, training in the rules of conduct (*ācāra-dharma*), which refers to all the disciplinary practices of a *bhikṣuṇī*; these must all be observed.
One studies these. If one commits an offense within the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), one is granted another two-year *karmavācanā*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"She sits below the *bhikṣuṇīs* and above the *śrāmaṇerīs*. The verse on the six rules (*ṣaḍ-dharma*) says:

"Touching with a defiled mind, stealing four *kārsāpaṇas*, taking the life of an animal, false speech, eating at improper times, and drinking alcohol—these are called the six rules for training in the *śikṣamāṇā*."
Dharma. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "In the case of the ten precepts for a śrāmaṇera, one immediately receives full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Why is it that in the Dharma for bhikṣuṇīs, there is the stage of śikṣamāṇā before one may receive full ordination? Answer:

"In the time of the Buddha, there was the wife of a householder who, unaware that she was pregnant, left the household life and received full ordination. Later, her body became visibly large with child. The other householders criticized and disparaged her."
The Bhikṣu Kātyāyana said to the Buddha: “For this reason, it was established that there is a two-year period of training in the precepts.
One must receive the six rules before receiving full ordination. Question: “If it is for the sake of avoiding public censure, how could the śikṣamāṇā herself not feel resentment?
Answer: “The śikṣamāṇā has not yet received full ordination; she is like a small child, or like a servant. Although she possesses faults and impurities, people do not [censure her].”
This is not permitted. There are two types [of cases]: first, eighteen-year-old girls who receive the six rules; second, daughters of noble families who may receive the six rules at the age of ten.
If they are to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*), it should be conducted within the assembly of both orders (*ubhayasaṃgha*). They must use the five robes and an alms bowl.

A bhikṣuṇī serves as the preceptor (*upādhyāyī*) and the instructor (*ācāryā*), while a bhikṣu serves as the preceptor for the precepts (*śīlācārya*). The remainder is as in the ritual for receiving ordination; this is a brief summary.

Five hundred precepts were taught; extensively, eighty thousand precepts were taught. Upon the completion of the third *karmavācanā*, one immediately attains immeasurable restraint (*saṃvara*) and becomes a member of the community of bhikṣus.
Alternatively, three hundred and forty-eight precepts are taught in brief, as is currently in circulation today.
[Commentary] The ten precepts for *śrāmaṇera* of the Hīnayāna and the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣu*. The verse says: "Four grave offenses, thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, two *aniyata*;
thirty-nine *niḥsargika-pāyattika*, one hundred *pāyattika*, fourteen *pratideśanīya*, one hundred *śaikṣa*, and seven rules for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
Altogether, these constitute the two hundred and fifty precepts (parājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, and śaikṣa)."

[Supplement] The Buddha ordained that those who have left the household life must devote themselves exclusively to the Vinaya for five summer retreats (*pañca-varṣa*) before they are permitted to study the teachings or engage in Chan meditation.
Therefore, when a *śrāmaṇera* shaves his head, he first receives the ten precepts;
subsequently, he ascends the altar to receive full ordination (*upasampadā*). These ten precepts were taught by the Buddha to Rāhula through Śāriputra.

[Note] Regarding the five categories (*pañca-varga*): *pārājika* (the four offenses of sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying), *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (the thirteen *saṃghāvaśeṣa*), *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (the thirty *niḥsargika* and ninety *pāyattika*, totaling one hundred and twenty), *pratideśanīya* (the four *pratideśanīya*), and *duṣkṛta* (the *duṣkṛta* and the one hundred rules of training). If discussing the six groups (*ṣaḍ-varga*), the *sthūlātyaya* is added.

[Commentary] The five categories [of offenses] are derived from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*. The six groups [of offenses] are derived from the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*. The Sanskrit term *pārājika* is translated here as "abandonment" (*qi*).

In the Hīnayāna, it is said that these cannot be expiated; in the Mahāyāna, they are called "points of defeat" (*tashengchu*). *Saṃghāvaśeṣa* is translated as "residual for the community" (*zhongcan*);

this is because, like a person whose head has been severed but whose vital breath remains in the throat, [the offense remains within the community]. *Pāyattika* (or *pāyittiya*) is translated as "falling" (*duo*). One commits this by falling away due to the accumulation of wealth.

Because they have fallen [into these offenses] but have not yet repented, there are the *pāyattika* (which is translated as "reproachable"), the *dukkaṭa* (translated as "wrongdoing" or alternatively as "evil speech").
Furthermore, these five categories of offenses may be correlated with the five punishments and the five elements: *pārājika* is correlated with death and earth;

*saṃghāvaśeṣa* with exile and water; *sthūlātyaya* with penal servitude and metal; *pāyattika* with the staff and fire; and *dukkaṭa* with... [the remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
*Pei-chai* (to flog) means to strike with wood. According to the *Mingyi* (Explanation of Terms): one *pārājika* corresponds in meaning to the utmost evil.
It is explained through three senses: first, "retrogression and submergence," because by violating this precept, one has no share in the fruits of the Path;

second, "not dwelling together," because not only is the Path lost, but one may also not participate in the *śīla-vyākhyāna* (recitation of the precepts) or the *karmavācanā* (formal ecclesiastical acts), as one cannot dwell together within the two types of Saṃghas.
Third is falling away. Having abandoned this body, one falls into the Avīci Hell.

If one commits this offense, one will fall into *niraya* for sixteen thousand years, which is the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods. Regarding the two *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses, the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states:
"The beginning of the *saṃgha* refers to the initial granting of the *parivāsa* (concealment) *karmavācanā*. 'Remnant' (*avaśeṣa*) refers to that which is granted at the end."
This refers to the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (expiation) *karma*. If one commits this offense, it is named after its objective because the Saṃgha performs a formal act (*dharma*) to remove it.
Furthermore, regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (requiring suspension from the community): it is like being struck by another, where the throat remains partially intact; thus, it must be remedied early.

The duration of this offense is equivalent to the lifespan of the Nirmāṇarati devas—eight thousand years—after which one falls into hell. The three *sthūlātyaya* offenses are here called "great obstacles" (*mahā-āvaraṇa*). [The term] *kuśala* means wholesome.
The *Jianyun* (Mirror of Views) states: "It greatly obstructs the wholesome paths and leads to falling into evil realms in the future. Its essence is base and defiled;

it derives its name from this unwholesome nature because it can bring about the offenses described in the preceding two chapters. The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* (or *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā*) translates this as "gross transgression" (*sthūlātyaya*).

There are two kinds of "gross": first, the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for a grave offense; second, that which can sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*). This offense is like that of [the deity] Dova.

The full lifespan of the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven is four thousand years; [if one commits this offense], one falls into hell for that duration. This constitutes four *pāyattika* (offenses involving falling).

The term is translated as "falling. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The retribution for this sin is equal to the lifespan of the Yāma heaven, which is two thousand years, after which one falls into hell.

*Naiḥsargika* is translated as "abandonment and falling. This offense arises from matters concerning wealth; when greed and arrogance are strong, one is enjoined to relinquish the object to the Saṃgha. Thus it is named *naiḥsargika*.
*Śaya*. The five *pāṭidesanīya* rules: the meaning is translated as "confessing toward another. They are named after their remedial object; these offenses should be disclosed.
The duration of this offense is one thousand years by the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, after which one falls into hell.
The six *duṣkṛta* rules: translated as "badly done" (*akṛtya*). The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: *śaikṣakāraka*; the meaning is translated as "should be practiced."
One should train in this. This offense is subtle and extremely difficult to maintain; therefore, it is named according to its practice and observance.
Other precepts are easy to maintain but carry heavy offenses, whereas this precept is difficult to maintain and easy to violate. One must constantly be mindful of training in it;
the retribution for violating it is to fall into hell for five hundred years, equal to the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings.

[Note] If one speaks of "the seven groups," the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) is opened out as *dauḥśīlya* (misconduct). [In this reckoning,] the offenses are equalized at five; the retributive kalpas are equalized at six; and the combined inclusion of cause and effect is equalized at seven.

The three grades of *laṇ* (fragrance) do not enter the formal sections; they are indeterminate. The seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamathā*) are not subsumed under the [five] categories of offenses (*varga*), yet they also belong to the *duṣkṛta* (minor offense). Regarding the phrase "the retribution kalpas are equal to six": this means that the number of kalpas for receiving retribution for the six categories of offenses is equal to the number of kalpas for the six upper hells, such as Sañjīva.

Regarding the phrase "cause and effect are mixed and subsumed as seven": because *duṣkṛta* and *durbhāṣita* (ill-spoken) are the causes of the *duṣkṛta* category, together with the effects of the preceding five categories, they constitute seven categories (as in the *Fanyi mingyi*).

[Commentary] Regarding the explanation of the names and meanings: it is said that while the *duṣkṛta* (minor offenses) constitute one category, they are divided into two groups because those of the body are termed "evil deeds" (*duṣkṛta*) and those of speech are termed "evil utterances" (*durbhāṣita*).
The *Xiaozhu* (Small Commentary) provides a judgment and interpretation of the three types of categories and groups. The first three lines correctly judge the limit [of the offenses].
The phrase "there are three grades of *sthūlātyaya*" explains the judgment of the five limits; that is to say, the *sthūlātyaya* consists of the three grades of superior, middling, and inferior.

This means that stealing four coins and thereby breaking the master who turns the Wheel of Dharma constitutes the highest offense; stealing three coins and thereby breaking a companion constitutes the middle offense;
and stealing one coin and thereby causing [the offender] to go naked, wear a stone bowl, or don outer robes constitutes the lowest offense.

However, these merely constitute the methods for completing the first two categories of offenses (pārājika and saṃghāvaśeṣa); therefore, they are not included in the formal articles themselves. Regarding the two indeterminate cases: the first three rules are indeterminate.

The next two rules are indeterminate. The Vinaya states: "If a bhikṣu sits alone with a woman in a secluded, concealed, or private place suitable for sexual intercourse, and speaks improper words, and a trustworthy upāsikā reports one of three matters—whether it is a pārājika, a saṃghāvaśeṣa, or a pāyattika offense."

If a monk who is sitting [in private] says of himself, "I have committed this offense," he should be dealt with according to each of the three rules, just as was stated by the laywoman of established faith;
he should be disciplined according to the Dharma. This is called the three indeterminate rules (*aniyata-dharmas*).
If a monk sits together with a woman in an exposed place, an improper place for sexual intercourse, and speaks coarse words...

Regarding harsh speech: if there is a laywoman (*upāsikā*) established in faith who, concerning two categories of offenses—one by one—declares it to be either a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* or a *pāyattika*, and that seated monk himself says, "I have committed this offense," he should be dealt with according to each of those two categories exactly as declared by the laywoman established in faith; he should be disciplined in that manner. This is [the rule].
Monks, these are called the two *aniyata* dharmas. Regarding the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), the Vinaya states:
"If a dispute arises among the monks, it should be immediately settled. One should apply the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*; one ought to apply the *pratyakṣa-vinaya*."

If the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted, it shall be granted as the *smṛtivinaya*. If the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one not insane) should be granted, it shall be granted as the *amūḍhavinaya*.

If the *pratijñākāraka* (settlement by confession) should be granted, it shall be granted as the *pratijñākāraka*. If the *yadbhūyaiṣīya* (settlement by majority vote) should be granted, it shall be granted as the *yadbhūyaiṣīya*.
If the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (settlement like covering with grass) should be granted, it shall be granted as the *tṛṇaprastāraka*.
"Grass-covering the ground" (tṛṇaprastāraka). These are the seven ways of settling disputes; thus it receives this name. Generally, disputes do not exceed four types:

first, disputes by speech (vādādhikaraṇa), wherein bhikṣus engage in verbal disputes with one another, citing eighteen grounds for dispute—ranging from "dharma" and "adharma" to "what has been spoken" and "what has not been spoken.
If they engage in such verbal disputes with these characteristics, then [the parties] mutually...

2. Disputes arising from accusations (*anuvāda-adhikaraṇa*). A bhikṣu accuses another bhikṣu of an offense based on three grounds for accusation: namely, violation of the precepts (*śīla*), violation of views (*dṛṣṭi*), and violation of conduct (*ācāra*).
He seeks out the offense through seeing, questioning, or suspicion, acting in such a manner. 3. Disputes arising from transgressions (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*).

This refers to the commission of seven kinds of offenses: first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *pāyattika* (pātayantika); fourth, *pratideśanīya* (pratikarman); fifth, *sthūlātyaya* (sthūlātyaya); sixth, [the sixth]; seventh, [the seventh].

A *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing). There are seven types of evil speech and four matters of dispute (*adhikaraṇa*). Among these, the first three concern the performance of an action; among them, the dispute regarding words (*vāda-adhikaraṇa*) is settled by two *vinayas*:

namely, by the presence of the assembly (*saṃmukha-vinaya*) and by the majority vote (*yadbhūya-saṃmata-vinaya*). Or it may be settled by only one *vinaya*: namely, by the presence of the assembly alone.

Disputes concerning accusations (*adhikaraṇa-śāthya*) are settled by four *vinayas*: namely, presence (*sammukha*), recollection (*smṛti*), non-delusion (*amūḍha*), and presence regarding the locus of the offense (*sthāna*).

Disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti-adhikaraṇa*) are settled by three *vinayas*: namely, presence, confession (*pratijñā*), and disciplinary action (*tāpanīya*); or presence and the "covering with grass" (*tṛṇaprastāraka*).
Disputes concerning matters (*kṛtya-adhikaraṇa*) are settled by all *vinayas*, according to the specific offense committed. These constitute the categories of the *skandhas*.

As for those not subsumed [under the formal categories], they are settled by *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense) or as indeterminate (*aniyata*); since they all lie outside the formal sections and clusters (*varga*), they are not included within the sections and clusters.
Nevertheless, they also belong to the category of *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), which is why it is said that the determination of the offense is uniform across these five.
The *Kṣudrakavastu* (Miscellaneous Explanations) limits [the transgressions] to six; the *Upāliparipṛcchā* (Questions of Upāli) limits them to seven, as seen above.
[Note: In the Mahāyāna, this refers to the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*. Any being possessing a mind may receive them.

Furthermore, there are the ten precepts of the *Mahā-śāstra*, the ten precepts of the *Mahā-sūtra*, and the five-limbed precepts (*pañcāṅga-śīla*), which are common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

These are fully detailed in the third fascicle of the end of the *Miaoxuan*, the fourth fascicle of the *Shiqian* (24), the fourth fascicle of the *Zhiguan* (3), and the first part of the fourth fascicle of the *Fuxing* (6).
[Commentary] The number of the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Brahmajāla Sūtra is as stated in that scripture.

One who commits a grave offense incurs a *pārājika* offense; one who commits a light offense incurs an offense of "light defilement. These are collectively termed the fifty-eight articles of the Great Precepts.
The phrase "anyone with a mind may receive them" means that when bestowing the precepts upon others, one must not engage in discrimination.
All kings, princes, ministers, and officials; the fourfold assembly, and even lustful men and women; Brahmā gods and desire-realm gods;
those without sexual organs, those with two sexual organs, and eunuchs; slaves and all ghosts and spirits—all may receive [the precepts].

Regarding the ten major precepts, the text says: "From the first moment of generating the aspiration for enlightenment, one should contemplate the noble precepts, which are precepts without deficiency," and so forth.
The precepts that follow meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the ten precepts in the Mahāyāna sūtras, they range from purity up to the complete accomplishment of the *pāramitā* precepts.
As for the five-limbed precepts, the text states: "The bodhisattva abandons desire, maintains the precepts of essential gravity, and puts an end to worldly reproach."

They are equal and without distinction. One does not allow the rākṣasas of craving and views to destroy the life-preserving float of the precepts. By upholding these, one fulfills the fundamental precepts;

the purity of action constitutes the primary precepts, while the preceding and succeeding factors constitute the secondary precepts. These remaining pure precepts are free from all unwholesome thoughts.
The precept of awakening to purity; guarding and maintaining right mindfulness; mindfulness of the pure precepts;

and the dedication toward the precepts for fulfilling the unsurpassed path—these are the five branches of the precepts. Furthermore, what is called the "root precept" refers to the ten wholesome natures as the fundamental precepts.
Because they are maintained by an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), they are termed "pure. The preceding and following "retinue" precepts refer to the *sthūlātyaya* and other offenses.

The former [three] branches are the primary retinue; *saṃghāvaśeṣa* and the others are the secondary retinue. These two sets of branches pertain to the precepts obtained through the formal ritual procedure (*vidhi*).
The latter three branches are not formal procedures; rather, these precepts arise at the moment one attains the dharma.

Regarding "not perceiving impure thoughts while perceiving the pure precepts," this refers to the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*). When the *śīla* (ethical discipline) is not pure...
Samādhi does not manifest because, through the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*), the obstacles of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*) are removed, and [the discipline] arises in the future;

because the obstacles of nature (*svabhāva-āvaraṇa*) are removed, it gives rise to the fundamental [state] that extinguishes unwholesome thought and observation (*vitarka-vicāra*). This is called the "discipline concomitant with concentration" (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).

Within the desire-realm discipline and concentration, the body, head, bed, and seat constitute the obstacles of phenomena, while the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm constitute the obstacles of nature. This continues up to the *vitarka* of the first dhyāna, which serves as the obstacle for the second dhyāna.

Regarding the hindrance of objects: the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna serves as the hindrance to the object of the third dhyāna. "Maintaining right mindfulness" refers to the right mindfulness that contemplates the principle through the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Although true [realization] has not yet arisen, by means of the similar right mindfulness of the four stages of application (*prayoga*), one is able to give rise to the untainted (*anāsrava*) true path of the first fruit (*phala*) and achieve the precepts concomitant with the Path;
this is called right mindfulness. Furthermore, there are the precepts concomitant with meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*).

That which arises from the mind of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) pertains to the meaning of virtue as tranquility (*śamatha*). That which arises from the mind of discernment (*pravicaya*), namely the precepts concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*), pertains to the meaning of virtue as cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

Both the mobile and the immobile are *vinaya*. Why? Because the treatises on precepts concern prevention; once one attains the precepts concomitant with concentration, the mind cannot give rise to evil.
Once one attains those concomitant with the Path, one gives rise to the truth and is forever free from transgression. Therefore, both constitute accomplishment. Dedication.

As for "being fully endowed": it refers to a bodhisattva who, within the various precepts, fulfills the four great vows and the six perfections, making a resolute aspiration and dedicating [the merit] toward Bodhi;
therefore, it is called the Mahāyāna precept. Regarding the six perfections: one feels weary of and afflicted by the constraints of the household life.
To joyfully delight in leaving the household life and renounce all that is beloved is *dāna*. To not transgress even by a hair’s breadth and resist the rākṣasas is *śīla*.
To restrain body and mind and remain patient under beating and abuse is patience toward beings (*satvākṣānti*).

To endure the eight winds, cold and heat, the favorable and the adverse, greed and anger, and so forth, is called patience toward phenomena (*dharmakṣānti*). That which cannot be harmed by attachment or views is *kṣānti*. To guard one's precepts and [not] transgress...
The non-arising of the mind is diligence (*vīrya*). To maintain the precepts with certainty, not being deceived by doubt, and to remain single-mindedly unmoving is called meditation (*dhyāna*).

To clearly discern cause and effect, knowing that the precepts are the fundamental basis for correctly following the path to liberation and giving rise to all the noble fruits of the three vehicles—rather than the sixty-two views or the "chicken-and-dog" precepts—is called wisdom (*prajñā*). This is a brief [explanation].
The explanation of the first condition is concluded.
△ Second, the sufficiency of clothing and food, in two parts: first, the combined heading;
second, the sufficiency of clothing and food.
[Commentary] The *Zhiguan si* (45) states: "Clothing serves to cover the body and conceal its ugliness; food serves to sustain life and fill the wounds of hunger.
When the body is at peace, the Way flourishes; when the Way flourishes, the foundation is established. Form, life, and the Way all depend upon these necessities of clothing and food.

Although these are minor conditions, they can accomplish great matters. If one is naked and hungry and lacks peace, where can the Dharma of the Way be found? Therefore, clothing and food must be fully provided."
[Commentary] Master Fuxing says: "To support the branches of the Path, one must first preserve the physical life. If the physical life is established, the foundation of the Path exists;
therefore, it is said 'and so forth' (*ji*). Furthermore, these provisions of food and clothing are fundamentally the conditions for the retribution of the physical body and its life."
Therefore, it is called a "small cause. Relying upon this, one is further able to practice and realize the Way; thus, it is called a "great matter. △ Second part:
the detailed explanation, which has two sections. First, the explanation of the robe.

There are three types of robes. First, like the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains, one is satisfied with whatever robe is obtained merely to cover the body and does not travel among people, because the power of endurance has been perfected.
Second, like Kāśyapa and others, one collects discarded rags (pāṃśukūla) or possesses only the three robes (tricīvara), without storing any extra clothing.
Third, in lands where it is very cold, the Tathāgata also permitted the storage of robes in addition to the three robes.
The one hundred and one requisites.
[Commentary: The Great Being of the Snowy Mountains dwells in remote mountain ravines, never venturing into the human world. He spreads a seat of woven grass and wears a garment of deerskin.

He has no need for the practices of receiving, maintaining, or declaring the purity of items; having perfected the power of endurance, he requires no warmth or comfort and does not frequent the human realm.
There is no need for assistance from others; such a person is superior. Regarding the twelve *dhūta* practices: one possesses only the three robes, neither more nor less.

Whether leaving the village or entering the mountains, one’s attire is always orderly and proper; thus, the three robes are established. This refers to the middling practitioner in lands where it is very cold.

Regarding the one hundred and one requisites for sustaining the body, one must certainly perform the ritual of "purifying" (śuddhi) them. They are intended merely to suffice for the performance of services; one should not seek much.

To seek much leads to hardship, and guarding them is likewise painful. It obstructs and distracts from one's own practice and further disturbs the donors. When one obtains even a little, one should immediately be content;
such is the person of inferior capacity (as per the text).

[Supplement] This commentary distinguishes three categories of robes. Regarding the statement that there are no matters such as formal acceptance (*parigraha*), recitation of the *śikṣāpada*, or disputes, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:
"The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: 'In a previous life, Śākyamuni dwelt on the Snow Mountains and consumed only various fruits.

Only in such circumstances can one forget matters such as the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-uddeśa*) and formal acceptance. This is the Buddha’s own narration of his past lives (*jātaka*). Because he was capable of enduring [such conditions]..."
At the time when [the precepts] were established by force, there was no Buddha-dharma in the world; therefore, there were no such matters as receiving, maintaining, or declaring purity (*śuddhi*).
Nevertheless, regarding the method for declaring purity, one first requests a donor with these words: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.

I, the bhikṣu [Name], now request the Venerable One to act as a successive purifier (*parivartaka-śuddhi-dāyaka*) for robes, medicine, and alms-bowls. May the Venerable One act for me as a purifier for robes and medicine..."

The bowl is passed on through successive acts of pure giving (*viśuddhi-dāna*) by the donor out of compassion. Having recited this three times, all clothing and requisites subsequently obtained are designated by mentioning this person’s name when declaring them pure to others.
Furthermore, the words for declaring purity are as follows: "Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind.
This long robe belonging to me, [named] so-and-so, has not yet been purified. Now, for the sake of purification, I give it to you, Venerable sir."
For the sake of mutual purification, the recipient says: "Venerable sir, attend to me with one-pointed mind. You have an extra robe that has not yet been purified;
for the sake of purifying it, I give it to you. Having accepted it, he says: "To whom do you give it?"
The donor shall say: "I give this to [Name]. The recipient who purifies the cloth shall say: "Venerable one, attend to me with a single mind. You have this long robe which has not yet been purified;
for the sake of purification, you give it to me. I have accepted it. You give it to [Name]; this robe already belongs to [Name].
For the sake of [Name], you must guard and maintain it well, wearing and using it according to the proper causes and conditions. The donor then says: "I give it."
"To so-and-so"—this refers to the name of the donor invited; whether within or outside the boundary, one may speak by naming them specifically.
Furthermore, the method of declaring purity through mental recollection (*cittavijñapti*) is permitted for a bhikṣu living alone.

This contains two methods: first, the explanation of the method of declaring purity; second, the explanation of the method of relinquishment and acceptance. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "One should bare the right shoulder..."
Kneel on the right knee with hands holding the robe. Mentally resolve and speak these words: "I, the bhikṣu [Name], offer this long robe as a pure gift to [Name].
Among the five groups of renunciants, it may be given away at will; let it be taken and used by them. This may continue until the eleventh day.
Then, again assuming the same posture as before, speak thus: "I, [Name], have received back this long robe from [Name]."
It may be kept for up to ten days. Furthermore, as previously stated: "I, [Name], offer this long robe as a pure gift to [Name];
may he take and use it as he sees fit. In this way, by relinquishing the old to take up the new, one changes them every ten days.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*), Fascicle 4, Part 1 (19), states: "The twelve *dhūta* practices, etc., are here translated as 'shaking off. First is the *araṇya* (wilderness)."
1. Always begging for food; 2. Wearing rag-robes; 3. Eating in a single sitting; 4. Moderating the amount of food consumed; 5. Not drinking liquids after midday; 6. Dwelling among burial mounds;
7. Sitting at the foot of a tree; 8. Sitting in the open air; 9. Always maintaining a seated posture; 10. Begging from house to house in regular order.
Twelfth, the three robes (*tricīvara*). In the present text, the "three robes of refuse-rags" from among the twelve *dhūta* practices are combined to constitute the practitioner of the middle grade.
Regarding the "three robes," this refers simply to the three robes themselves. When leaving the village, one wears the *saṃghāṭī* over the other two robes.
When entering a great assembly, one wears the *uttarāsaṅga* over the five-strip robe (*pañcaka*). When entering mountain forests, one wears only the *antarvāsaka*.
For the sake of modesty and because of the intense cold, it is permitted to wear them layered. In all cases, one’s deportment is orderly and solemn;
as this is a source of merit for those with long-standing roots of goodness, it is said that "the robes are worn in a neat and proper manner."

[Commentary] *Dhūta*. Translated into the new terminology as *duṭo* (抖多). This is translated as "shaking off" (*dousou*). It is also translated as "cultivating and purifying" (*xiuzhi*), or "winnowing and refining" (*taotai*).
The *Chuiyu ji* states: "Because it shakes off afflictions (*kleśa*). The *Sutra of the Devaputra Susthitamati* says:
"One who practices *dhūta* shakes off greed, anger, and delusion, as well as the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) internal and external to the three realms. If one does not grasp..."
Renunciation. Not practicing and not clinging—of such a person I say that he is called a *dhuta*. Nowadays, this is erroneously referred to as *touduo* (head-tooth).
However, the Vinaya and the Śāstras differ. In the Vinaya, there are the practices of sitting wherever one happens to be, not taking extra food, and eating only a single morsel;

the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* calls these "moderation in quantity," adding "not drinking after midday" and "begging in sequence. Furthermore, what the Vinaya calls "wearing rag-robes" (*pāṃsukūla*), the Śāstra calls...

Regarding "pāṃśukūla" (rag-robe from a dust heap): the Vinaya simply says "begging for food," while the Śāstra says "constantly begging for food. These two names differ, but their meaning is the same. The remaining ten [items] are all identical.
Although there are also points of difference in the various schools' Āgamas and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the general principle is not distinct.
Now, based on the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, I shall briefly set forth their characteristics. First, "araṇya" (ārañña), translated as "a place of tranquility. [This refers to] the laity...
Because there is much affliction, one abandons one’s kin and associates; yet even among teachers, disciples, and fellow students, there may still be attachments that lead to mutual disturbance.
Therefore, one dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage) so as to distance the body from them—at least three *li* away, though the further, the better.

Having distanced the body, one should likewise mentally detach from the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) and the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). Second, regarding those who constantly beg for food: they sustain themselves by begging for alms. Much...
This is what is accomplished. As will be explained in detail below in the section on *piṇḍapāta*, there are ten benefits to begging for food. Third, regarding rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*):

if one were to wander about in all directions seeking [food], one might fall into wrong livelihood; or, if accepting gifts from others, one would experience joy or sorrow depending on whether they are good or bad, or feel anxiety over the possibility of theft and so forth.
Since rag-robes are free from such concerns, this is the third [practice]. Fourth, sitting in one session (*ekāsanika*).

Regarding food: it means that a bhikṣu practicing the Path should reflect thus: "Even seeking a single meal still presents an obstacle; how much more so for eating breakfast, midday meals, and afternoon meals?
They waste half the day's effort and prevent one from practicing the Path with a single mind. As for the five measures of moderation in eating:
if one eats until full, the belly becomes distended and the breath is stifled, which obstructs the Path; therefore, one should practice moderation in eating, as Śāriputra did.
No. Having eaten five or six mouthfuls, one should supplement it with water. Regarding "not drinking liquids after midday": this refers to a bhikṣu practicing the Path;
if the day has passed the meridian, he must not drink any of the various kinds of liquids. If his mind develops attachment or craving for them, [he commits an offense].
Seeking various kinds of drinks, one cannot single-mindedly cultivate wholesome dharmas; it is like feeding a horse while wearing its bridle—the horse’s mind then becomes weary.
Seventh, regarding those who dwell among graves: they easily awaken to impermanence and easily attain the fruits of the Path.

This is because the contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness is the initial gateway to the Buddha-dharma, capable of inducing weariness with and detachment from the triple world. Eighth, the trees...
As for those of lower status, their task is accomplished through the attainment of the Way; they abandon [the monastery] and go beneath the trees.

This means that if a bhikṣu does not attain the Way while among the burial mounds, he should go beneath the trees. Just as when the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma and entered nirvana, both occurred beneath trees.
When corpses are putrid, rotting, and strewn about, being burned by fire or pecked at by birds, the contemplation of impermanence and impurity is easily accomplished.

Ninth, regarding sitting in the open air: some say this refers to sitting under a tree, which is like a half-roofed shelter; because one still experiences the pleasure of shade and protection, attachment arises.
Furthermore, there are two faults in sitting under a tree: first, the concern over cold and dampness from rain; second, the presence of bird droppings and poison.

Regarding "insects": he then reflects upon this and sits in the open air. He experiences ease and joy according to his will; the moonlight shines everywhere, making the mind clear and sharp, so that it is easy to enter the samādhi of emptiness.
Therefore, it is called "sitting in the open air. Regarding "the ten constant sitters": they put on their robes and take them off [at fixed times].
One may dwell in ease according to one's preference. Among the four modes of deportment, sitting is foremost; food is easily digested and the breath is harmonized.
For the great matter of seeking the Way, one must exert great effort. If one is indolent or succumbs to sleep, various thieves will constantly watch for an opportunity;
thus, one should not lie down in comfort. Whether walking or standing, it is difficult to restrain the mind; therefore, one should practice constant sitting. One should not [lie on one's side].

11. Regarding the sequence of begging for food while wearing a mat: one does not dwell on flavors, does not treat sentient beings with contempt, regards them with equal compassion, and makes no distinction between the poor and the wealthy.
12. Regarding the three robes: this refers to a bhikṣu who has few desires and is content;
he takes only as many robes as are necessary to cover his body, neither more nor less. Laypeople, because they seek much, therefore accumulate many. Externally...

The Path consists of ascetic practices. For this reason, one remains naked, neither more nor less [than necessary]. Therefore, one maintains three robes (*tricīvara*). In the *Nanshan lüchao* (Commentary on the Nanshan Vinaya), the categories are divided into four.

Regarding clothing, there are two types: first, the patched robe (*pāṃsukūla*); second, merely the three robes. Regarding food, there are four types: first, begging for food; second, not performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa* rite (the practice of consuming leftover food);
third, eating in a single sitting (*ekāsana*); fourth, eating in a single morsel (*piṇḍapāta*). "Morsel" (*piṇḍa*) means a mixture; it refers to a single kind [of food].
Regarding "mixed": that which is not stored in various vessels is called a single morsel of food (*piṇḍapāta*). There are five locations: first, an araṇya; second, a cemetery;

third, at the foot of a tree; fourth, sitting in the open air; and fifth, sitting wherever one happens to be. Regarding deportment, there is always the practice of constant sitting. This does not include begging for food in regular sequence;
however, the location category adds "sitting wherever one happens to be. The *Tongyuan ji* (Record of the Source) quotes Nanshan as saying: "In the Dharma of the Final Age..."
Those who seek honor through official rank are men of mere chance and fortune, who recklessly form factions and wings. May they reflect upon themselves by means of these words.
As for those who regard material gain as a hair-thin rope and view noble mansions as thatched huts, yet still long to trail their tails like a dog—this already invites derision;
how much more so when one treats a cough and a sneeze as an act of grace, regards a sidelong glance as an ornament, and secretly cultivates favors while forcibly [assuming authority]?
Matters move swiftly; even if one were to indulge in grandiosity for a time, one will ultimately be ridiculed by the multitude. Honor does not compensate for disgrace—how great is this error!
Thus we know that in the final age, those who do not lack in the practice of *dhūta* can cause the Buddha-dharma to abide permanently and never perish.
In the following passage, it is clarified that the present *śamatha-vipaśyanā* combined with the three robes of discarded rags constitutes the practice of the "middle-grade practitioner."
[Commentary on the Square Symbol] Regarding those of inferior faculties: this land is generally cold, and their spiritual capacities are thin.

Because the Great Sage granted one concession, three grades were opened up (therefore, in addition to the three robes, he permitted the keeping of the "one hundred and one" items and the keeping of extra robes). However, the three robes are considered superior, keeping the "one hundred and one" is middling, and keeping extra robes is inferior; thus it is said they were "opened up universally. This is according to the Vinaya explanation, which differs slightly from the present [tradition].
Here, the Snowy Mountains are taken as the superior grade.
[Commentary] This explanation takes the possession of the one hundred and one articles of equipment in addition to the three robes as the "lower" category.

The *Dazhu* (Great Commentary) clarifies that there are differences based on both the local conditions of the land and the spiritual capacities of sentient beings; therefore, it universally permits all three grades.

The *Xiaozhu* (Small Commentary) clarifies the reasons for the three grades as explained according to the Vinaya. The final two sentences clarify the three grades according to the Sūtras, as will be explained below.

[Commentary] If one keeps the "one hundred and one" items, one merely needs to keep them in mind. Some say there is an "addition of the formula" (the Sarvāstivādins state that one may keep one of each of the one hundred and one items;

anything beyond the one hundred and one is considered surplus property). Regarding "merely keeping in mind," this means that among the one hundred and one items, one simply remembers one kind within the mind, thinking, "This is my possession. Regarding "adding the formula," this refers to receiving and maintaining [the items] by adding the formal ritual, as illustrated in the diagram of the six requisites.

[Commentary] "Recording" (*ji*) means to identify or recognize. "Recalling" (*yi*) means to remember. It refers to stating, "This is a *niṣīdana* (sitting mat)," "This is a *vraṇapaṭṭa* (wound-covering cloth)," "This is a *varṣāśāṭī* (rain-bathing robe)," and so forth.
