Regarding the expression "one hundred and one items of memory," it is further stated that they are "added by means of a ritual" (*jiafa*). As the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) says:

this is because the two chapters concerning "adding by means of a ritual" and "purification through declaration" (*shoujing*) are discussed together, and thus they are termed "one hundred and one. Originally...
The first line of the commentary clarifies the possession of the "one hundred and one" items. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:

"If money or precious objects have been purified (*viśuddha*), they may be exchanged for all kinds of clothing and wealth to produce the three robes, the alms bowl, and other utensils; these then enter the category of the 'one hundred and one' items and do not require further purification. It further states:
"Among all one hundred items, the three robes, the [other] requisites, and the alms bowl must necessarily be formally accepted and maintained (*parigraha*). As for those outside of this..."
If one accepts them, it is permissible; if one does not accept them, there is no fault. A detailed illustration of the six items is provided below. [Commentary:

If one keeps extra robes, one must perform the *śuddhi-vyākarana* (declaration of purity) by adding the ritual formula for formal acceptance. (Regarding items beyond the "one hundred and one" [allowable possessions], if one keeps extra items, one must certainly perform the *śuddhi-vyākarana*. The wording is as follows: "Venerable One, please attend to me with a single mind.
This is an extra robe belonging to me, [so-and-so]. It has not yet been purified. For the sake of purification, I offer it to you, Venerable One.")
[Commentary] The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "Apart from the one hundred and one items, everything else must be declared as pure (*śuddha-vyavahāra*).

It further states: "In the general procedure for receiving robes, if they are in excess, they should be declared as pure; if they are not so declared, they enter into the category of 'excess' (*atireka*) within the property.
Regarding the rules on possessing precious objects, it says: "One should perform a *pāyattika* confession before the Saṃgha. This applies to money and items resembling precious gems.

Excluding the count of one hundred and one items, all others should also be relinquished; although they may be kept if visible, they must certainly undergo the ritual of *śuddhi-vyākaraṇa* (purification by declaration).
Next, regarding the words for the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-vyākaraṇa*), the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "The method of declaring purity accords with the Mahāyāna;
therefore, that which is possessed by a Bodhisattva according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* is offered as a pure gift to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. It then proceeds with...

Regarding the pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*) of the Śrāvakas, it is illustrated as follows: For example, suppose a bhikṣu were to relinquish his own robes and belongings to his preceptor (*upādhyāya*) or teacher (*ācārya*) to perform a pure gift.
If one realizes the single reality (*eka-tattva*), then this very pure gift becomes the Dharma of a Bodhisattva.
Some say: "Regarding all things that exist, if one perceives them as not being one's own property, what is the purpose of performing the ritual of 'purification' (*śuddhi*) for their beneficial use?
Now I ask: since these are not one's own wealth, why not entrust them to the four seas? If they are beneficial, why not simply hand them over to the two fields [of merit]?
Instead, you lock them away in deep chambers and seal them in chests and boxes. This is truly to harbor the perception of another's property; to use them will inevitably bring retribution."

[This would constitute] a transgression. Yet, one might suddenly claim it as one's own property and still perform the *śuddhika* (purification) ritual; having performed the purification, one then gives it away. What contradiction would there be in principle?
However, this accords with one's own biased attachment, and others will subsequently imitate it. Therefore, the dharma of *śuddhika* must not be absent.

In the fourth volume of the *Vibhāṣā*, within the inquiry regarding the causes and conditions for the initial formulation of the precept on long robes, it asks: "Is this *śuddhika*-gift a real gift or a provisional gift? The answer is: [it is a provisional gift].

Regarding all pure gifts (*śuddha-dāna*): among the ninety-six types of non-pure giving, the Buddha, out of great compassion and through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), taught how to purify such gifts. These are gifts of skillful means and not true [pure] gifts.

They enable his disciples to possess surplus wealth (*atireka-lābha*) without violating the precepts. Furthermore, it was asked: "Why does the Buddha not simply allow his disciples to possess surplus wealth directly?"
Yet he forcibly establishes precepts and devises these skillful means. Answer: The Buddha-dharma takes few desires as its foundation;
therefore, the precepts are established so that one does not accumulate surplus wealth. However, the faculties and natures of sentient beings differ.

There may be sentient beings who, after accumulating much, then practice the Way and attain the realization of the noble fruits. For this reason, the Tathāgata first establishes the precepts and then—
Skillful means (upāya) are unimpeded regarding the Buddha-dharma and bring benefit to sentient beings.
[Note] Regarding "rag-robes" (pāṃśukūla): Nanshan says that these are things discarded by worldly people that are no longer fit for use; their meaning is the same as "filth-swept."
Its substance is that of a lowly object; it is free from one's own attachment and cannot be coveted by kings or thieves, thereby constantly providing sustenance for the cultivation of the Path.
[Commentary] The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "Refuse rags" (*pāṃśukūla*) refers to clothing other than that of the deceased. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* clarifies its origins.
There are five distinctions: first, those from the road; second, those from the riverbank; third, those from an open space;
fourth, those from a refuse heap; and fifth, those that are tattered. Regarding the substance of these robes, there are seven types in total based on differences in material and origin:
first, woolen cloth (*ūrṇā-vastra*); second, *kṣauma* cloth; third, *śāṇaka* cloth; fourth, *kārpāsika* cloth; fifth, *dukūla* cloth... [and so forth].
1. *Loka-vastra* (garment from a village); 2. *Ghoṇa-bhoga-vastra* (garment from a high place); 3. *Āpān-daka-vastra* (garment from a cesspool).
Furthermore, there are five more: 1. chewed by cattle; 2. gnawed by rats; 3. pierced by ants; 4. burned by fire; 5. discarded by a wet-nurse.

One should know that those who wear such refuse rags (*pāṃśukūla*) internally abandon their own greed and externally quell the greed of others, constantly obtaining the sustenance to maintain this illusory body.
It nurtures the Noble Path. [Note] Regarding the three robes:
first is the *saṃghāṭī*, which is translated as "the robe of many fragments," because it consists of many strips.

In terms of its function, it is called "the robe for entering royal palaces and villages. Second is the *uttarāsaṅga*, known as the "robe of medium value. In terms of its function, it is called [the robe for... entering...
Regarding the various robes: first, the *antarvāsa* (inner robe), known as the "lower garment. It is so named because it is used for walking within the monastery grounds or for miscellaneous tasks.
If one refers to it as *kāṣāya*, this means "dyed with improper colors," and it is also called "discolored" (*prakṛti-varṇa-viparivartita*).

These correspond to the three types of dyeing prescribed in the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, all of which are in accordance with the Dharma: first, blue; second, black; and third, madder-brown (*mūlāna-varṇa*). As stated in the [Sixth]...
Illustration of Objects. [Commentary] *Saṃghāṭī*. This is translated as "joined" (*he*) or "layered" (*chóng*). It refers to that which is composed by cutting and sewing together pieces.
Yi Jing translates it as *saṃkāṭi*, rendered as "repeatedly layered robe. The *Linggan zhuan* states: "Whenever the Wheel of Dharma was turned, he donned the *saṃghāṭī*."

Nanshan says: Regarding the names of these three robes, none of the various schools provide a direct translation. This current commentator has instead provided translations based on their meaning for the sake of citation.
Specifically, the *saṃghāṭī* is called "the many-fragmented" because it consists of a great number of strips.
If named according to its function, it is called "the robe worn when entering royal palaces or villages," or "the robe worn when begging for food or preaching the Dharma. (Sarvāstivāda...)

The *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-śāstra* (or *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*) states that the great robe (*saṃghāṭī*) is divided into three grades: those with nine, eleven, and thirteen strips, each having two long and one short panel, are called the three lower grades;
those with fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen strips, each having three long and one short panel, are called the three middle grades;
and those with twenty-one, twenty-three, and twenty-five strips, each having four long and one short panel, are called the three upper grades.
Although these are divided into nine grades, they are not considered superior based on the number of strips;
rather, the number of strips is determined by the size of the cloth and the material. The *uttarāsaṅga*—translated here as the "upper robe"—is the seven-strip robe.
Master Nanshan refers to it as a robe of medium value because it occupies the middle position between the two other types of robes, both in terms of its price and its utility.

It is said that those who enter among the assembly wear the *antarvāsaka*. This is worn during all occasions of ritual repentance, reciting sutras, sitting in meditation, attending vegetarian feasts, and listening to lectures.
*Antarvāsaka* means "clothing for dwelling near [the body]," referring to its proximity to the person. Master Nanshan refers to it as the "lower garment" (*adhovāsa*).
Among the three robes (*tricīvara*), this one has the fewest strips and is thus the most inferior.
It is called the "miscellaneous work robe" (*jāyikā*) because it is used for such purposes; it may be worn at all times while performing labor or service within the monastery.
*Kāṣāya*—the full term being *kāḷāśāya*—is translated as "dyeing with improper colors" or "discolored. It is named after its color.
Huizheng says: *Kāṣāya* is the name of a plant; because its fibers can be used to dye robes, the term is now applied to the garment itself as a designation for it.
The *Zhendi zájì* (True Meaning’s Miscellaneous Records) states: *Kāṣāya* is the name for the three robes (*tricīvara*) in foreign lands.
The name contains multiple meanings. It may be called the "dust-free robe" because it severs the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).
It may be called the "emaciated robe" because it cuts through the afflictions (*kleśa*). It may be called the "lotus robe," for the wearer is free from defiled attachment.

It may be called the "intermediate-colored robe," as it is composed of three colors that are in accordance with the Dharma. According to the *Yèshū* (Commentary on Karma), the robes of a śramaṇa are made by cutting them with a blade.
Because one is not stripped by enemies or bandits. The *Zhangfu yi* (Ritual of Robes) states: "The appearance of the vertical and horizontal stripes is like the ridges of a field;
they hold water to nourish fine seedlings. This serves as a metaphor for how wearing this robe generates merit. The Buddha commanded that it be made like this; its significance is not in vain.
Regarding the three colors—blue, black, and madder: "Blue" refers to verdigris (copper-green); "black" refers to...
*Mṛd* (mud) refers to *muraṅga*, which is birch bark. The Vinaya states:
"When a bhikṣu obtains a new robe, he must apply one of three types of dyed discoloration (*kaṣāya*): blue, mud, or wood; he must prepare it according to one of these.
If he uses it without applying the three types of discoloration, he commits a *pāyattika* offense. It is only when the robe has been dyed and discolored that it may be worn.
These are called the "requisites according to the Dharma. As for the illustrations of the six articles: first, the *saṃghāṭī*; second, the *uttarāsaṅga*;
third, the *antarvāsaka*; fourth, the water filter; fifth, the *pātra*, translated as "proper vessel"; and sixth, the *niṣīdana*, translated as "sitting mat.
These are excerpted from the *Saṃyuktapiṭaka-dharmasaṃkhyā*.
[Commentary] According to the Vinaya texts, the *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) and the mere three robes (*tricīvara*) are considered superior; the one hundred and one items are middling;
and the remaining surplus items are inferior. In the present text, however, the Great Being of the Snowy Mountains wearing a deer-skin robe is taken as superior;
therefore, the *pāṃśukūla* and the mere three robes are considered middling; and possessing the one hundred and one items, as well as possessing the remaining surplus, are considered inferior.
[Commentary] This clarifies that the Vinaya text differs from the present text; however, neither is obstructive [to the meaning].

[Note] It was stated above that "one does not keep extra or surplus items," yet it should further state "one does not keep more than the one-hundred-and-one items. Below, it says "one keeps the one-hundred-and-one requisites for the community."
One should also further state: "keeping other surplus [robes].
[Commentary] The textual meaning for supplementing the two robes of medium and small size is clear.
△ Second, the explanation of food.

There are also three kinds of food: first, those of superior capacity, great beings who dwell in deep mountains far removed from the world, sustaining themselves with whatever roots, tubers, and fruits they happen to find;
second, those who constantly beg for alms; and third, those who receive food sent by donors—pure food provided within the Sangha.

[Commentary on the Fourfold Cessation and Contemplation (16): First, one dwells in deep mountains where no tracks remain, far removed from people, subsisting only on sweet fruits and fine water, or perhaps merely on a single vegetable or fruit.
Or one may consume pine and cypress to sustain the vital essence, such as the sweet and fragrant lotus roots of the Snowy Mountains.

One who eats in this manner is an "upper-grade practitioner" (*uttama-pudgala*). Second, one dwells in an *araṇya* (forest hermitage), practicing the *dhūta* (ascetic) purifications and begging for alms.
To support oneself: the seven Buddhas all clarified the method of begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*). The Vaipulya, Pratyutpanna, and Lotus Sūtras all speak of begging for food.

If the route is too far, the toil of wandering for alms becomes an obstacle; if it is too near, there is the clamor of people and things. Begging for food is most convenient when the location is neither too far nor too near; this is the practice of the "middle person.
Since the third type cannot abstain from grain to subsist on fruits, yet cannot practice the *dhūta* of begging for food, [they must rely on other means].

Regarding food: one may also accept food offerings sent by lay patrons (*dānapati*) as external support. Furthermore, one may also accept food that is pure and prepared according to the Dharma within the Sangha.
This refers to the person of inferior capacity (as stated in the text).
[Commentary] He eats fruit and pine nuts; having finished eating, he sits in meditation, with no other affairs. He is a superior man (*uttama-pudgala*).
An *āraṇya* is a place of stillness and tranquility, free from the sounds of cattle herding; it is a place for practicing the Way. Therefore, one must dwell there to practice the *dhūta* austerities.
Master Zhaolun said: "Conflict and rivalry arise in crowded assemblies; freedom from contention emerges in empty solitude. Thus, the Buddha praised it.
The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "Among the twelve dhūtas, there are five methods of eating; here we shall cite but one.

If one engages in plowing, sowing, pounding with mortars, husking with pestles, or grinding with mills—and by 'mill' is meant a stone grinder—one maintains the eight impure things and involves oneself in the four types of wrong livelihood.
This defiles the donors and is not the practice of an araṇya-dweller. Those established in recent times are far removed from the words of the Sage. [This applies to] both men and women."
Constantly traveling back and forth invites both ridicule and disgrace. If one were to follow the Buddhist teachings, the benefits would not be slight.
The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* states: "One should always practice begging for food and not accept invitations. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Enter the village to beg for food.

However, the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) should not be too far from or too near to the city. If it is too far, it will cause exhaustion and interference. The *Avadāna-śataka* (Piyu jing) relates: "In the past, at Vārāṇasī, five..."
Ten *li* away there was a mountain where five bhikṣus resided. At dawn they would enter the city to beg for food, and after midday they would return to the mountain at dusk;

thus, they eventually became utterly exhausted and were unable to settle into meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This continued for many years, such that they labored in vain without any attainment.
The Buddha transformed himself into a man of the path and went to comfort them. The bhikṣus said, "This body of the four great elements constantly suffers from hunger and deprivation."
"If you wish to beg for alms, the road to the city is far; what joy is there in it? You should simply resolve to remain here until the end of your lives.
The transformed śramaṇa said, "I pray that none of you venerable practitioners go tomorrow; I shall provide the provisions for one day's meal."
It is recorded that when the Buddha sent food, the five companions ate it and all attained arhatship; thus, one's place of residence also serves as a condition for the Path.
If it is too close, there will be the clamor of speech and noise, which likewise makes it difficult to enter meditative concentration. One must ensure that the distance is moderate.

To beg for food is simple; this is the practice of a person of middling capacity. If one accepts offerings sent by a donor (dānapati) and is permitted to receive food using tongs or a ladle, this is the practice of a person of inferior capacity. [Supplement] Regarding "pure food": "pure" means it should be consecrated (*pariṣkāra*).

Within the *karmavācanā*, it cites the Buddha’s words, permitting the consecration of a pure kitchen (*kalpi-kula*) in a quiet location within a monastery. [Preparation] Since clothing and food are the conditions for the Path, hunger and cold...

"How can you endure when your skin is being tormented? He replied, "If one practices the Way with a sincere heart, one will surely receive the protection and empowerment of the Triple Gem, the devas, and the dragons.
One need only feel shame and remorse, and apply oneself diligently to repenting for past karmic retributions. A practitioner of the Path relies on a single almsbowl throughout the ten directions."

When encountering circumstances that provide the conditions for practice, one should simply act without obstruction. For those who observe the Mahayana precepts, they should practice by means of skillful expedients so as to swiftly accomplish the fruit of the Way.
If one encounters situations resulting from past karma, one should realize that the mind possesses the true nature (*dharmatā*), maintain contemplation in the present, and wait for the end of life.
Alternatively, one may single-mindedly focus on the Pure Land; when the retribution of this life is exhausted, rebirth there is likewise acceptable.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 4, Part 1, states: "Pindapāta" means "begging for food. The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* says: "There are ten benefits to begging for food... [and so forth].
Food obtained through purity within the Sangha is still intended for those of inferior capacity; how could one simply remain seated in one's room?
[Private Note on "Fenwei" (文)]. [■ Record]:

"Fenwei" refers to begging for food (*piṇḍapāta*). The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "Begging for food and distributing it to the monks and nuns protects them, enabling them to cultivate their spiritual practice;
therefore, it is called 'fenwei'. The phrase "and so forth" (*yún yún*) indicates that this is not exhaustive. The term "yún" signifies a statement or an explanation.
This refers to the form of clouds and vapors revolving in the sky; when spoken from the mouth, it is like clouds nourishing all things. As for the ten benefits:
first, one sustains one's own life, belonging to oneself and not to others. Second, regarding those who give to me, one causes them to abide in the Three Jewels before partaking of the food.
Third, one constantly gives rise to a heart of compassion. Fourth, one accords with the Buddha’s teachings. Fifth, one is easily satisfied and easily contented.

1. To nourish [the body]. 2. To break the six types of arrogance. 3. To possess the roots of goodness of the "unseen summit" (anavalokitamūrdhatā). 4. When others see me begging for alms, they will all follow my example.
5. To avoid entanglements with men, women, the elderly, or the young. 6. To beg in sequential order, thereby generating a mind of equanimity. These are the ten benefits.
The final item refers to the meaning of taking food from the lowest-ranking person, used as an admonition against turning one's back on the multitude.
Eating. △ Third, dwelling in seclusion and stillness. Regarding "dwelling in seclusion and stillness":
not engaging in various affairs is called "seclusion" (*khan*); a place free from clamor and bustle is called "stillness" (*ching*). There are three types of such places.
For example, clothing and food can be understood accordingly.
[Commentary] *Zhiguan* 4 (17) states: "If one is in deep mountains or remote valleys where the paths are perilous and human tracks are forever cut off, who could disturb or distract one?

One may then practice dhyāna and contemplation at will; such a place is most excellent. Second, regarding the dhūta practice of 'shaking off' (doubts), it should be performed at a distance of no more than three li."
Social interaction is also sparse; one perceives and restrains the afflictions. This place is the intermediate [level]. Third is the araṇya-vihāra, a secluded monastery.
Dwelling alone in a single room, one does not attend to worldly affairs but correctly contemplates with true discernment. This place is the inferior [level] (text).

[Commentary] To settle the body and enter the Way, one must exercise careful selection; be cautious not to act impulsively. Once a suitable location has been found, there is no need to move frequently.
One should know that this *araṇya* (hermitage) is distinct from the *araṇya* mentioned previously among the twelve *dhūta* practices.
Previously, an araṇya was a central location, a place of open and remote terrain. This araṇya, however, is a lower location, a dwelling in open and remote terrain.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* explains that there are ten benefits to an araṇya: first, freedom to come and go; second, the absence of "mine-ness";
third, rejoicing without obstruction; fourth, the mind’s delight in the araṇya location; fifth, [having] little...
1. To desire few affairs; 2. To be unstinting with one's body and life; 3. To be fully endowed with merit and virtue; 4. To avoid clamorous speech; 5.
Although practicing meritorious deeds, not to seek gratitude or recompense; 6. To easily attain single-mindedness; 7. To easily give rise to the thought of non-obstruction.
Now, an *araṇya* monastery is distinguished from the lay communities of market towns; a secluded temple is distinguished from the narrow alleys and bustling markets;
dwelling alone in a single room is distinguished from the companionship of fellow students; not attending to worldly affairs is distinguished from wandering amidst secular dharmas;
and correct, profound contemplation is distinguished from perverse thoughts and delusive imaginings.
△ Fourth, ceasing all worldly affairs.
Ceasing all worldly affairs means ceasing livelihood, ceasing social obligations, and ceasing crafts, technical skills, and the like.

[Commentary] *Zhiguan Fuxing Chuanhong Jue*, fascicle 4 (18), states: "Worldly affairs obstruct dhyāna; this has been so from the beginning. A bhikṣu in an araṇya should distance himself from clamor."
One should remain close to stillness. Why engage in the affairs of construction and management? To do so destroys the practice of the *araṇya* (forest hermitage);

it is not what is appropriate. There are four kinds of such affairs: first, livelihood; second, social obligations; third, technical skills; and fourth, study. First, regarding the affairs of livelihood: managing the means of subsistence involves entanglements at every turn.
Gaining one thing while losing another leads to the loss of the Way and the disturbance of the mind. Second, regarding social obligations: these consist of attending to celebrations and funerals.
They look up and down, bowing low and rising high, coming here and going there; their coming and going never cease. As for the three skills:
they consist of medical arts, divination, and the crafting of clay, wood, and painted images, as well as chess, calligraphy, incantations, and the like. As for the fourth, learning:

it consists of reading and reciting sūtras and śāstras, engaging in debates of question and answer, and so forth—maintaining and memorizing which exhausts the mind and tires the will, while the exchange of discourse continues.
When the water is turbid and the pearl obscured, what leisure is there to further cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? If one abandons even this matter, how much more so the three prior duties?
(Text) Now, regarding the word "equal" (*deng*), it means equal to academic study.
[Commentary] Regarding the first three types of duties, it is logically appropriate that they be ceased; yet, one might ask, why should study and recitation also be ceased? The answer is:

The cultivation of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) is fundamentally based upon a single mind. Reading and reciting obstruct stillness; how then could the mind be unified? Therefore, these too should be ceased.
To investigate the root of a difficult point is a "perilous question"; to strike at the essential joints of an explanation is a "skillful answer. This is the meaning.

To prevail is deemed victory; to fall is deemed defeat. Even if one engages in debate on extensive learning, thorough inquiry, and clear discernment—though such qualities may mutually enhance one's insight—in truth, one cannot avoid the fault of victory and defeat.
Because of this victory and defeat, one incurs transgressions through the Dharma, creating enmity that spans generations and constantly inflicting harm upon one another.
Therefore, victory and defeat, right and wrong, must be entirely abandoned. This you should understand and uphold.
Regarding the term "and so forth": if one studies and learns, one must necessarily grasp the characters and memorize their meanings; thus, one cannot avoid mental exhaustion and weariness of will.
Furthermore, in the process of questioning and answering, one must inevitably formulate statements and establish arguments; how then can one avoid the turbidity of water and the clouding of a pearl?

One should know that the nature of the mind is like water, ultimate truth is like a pearl, external affairs are like churning, a distracted mind is like turbidity, and delusion regarding truth is like darkness.

Since the mind is disturbed by concerns and truth is obscured by darkness, what leisure is there for the refined cultivation of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*? For this reason, it is appropriate to also bring such activities to rest.
Furthermore, among these external studies and within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, one is permitted to practice and study for only one period out of every twelve periods of the day.
To subdue non-Buddhists, those of the Mahāyāna do not permit beginners to practice [the Lesser Vehicle] exclusively;
rather, they cause them to progress until they reach the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*), at which point learning will not be difficult.

Thus, even when studying and memorizing the authentic sūtras and śāstras—which are beneficial for the factors conducive to enlightenment—one still abandons them at that time, let alone the three [lower vehicles].
△ Fifth, associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
There are three types of associating with virtuous friends: first, the virtuous friend as external protector; second, the virtuous friend who practices together;
and third, the virtuous friend who provides instruction.

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan si* (Four Chapters on Stopping and Contemplation), section 49, states: "As for external protection, one does not discriminate between 'black' and 'white'; it simply consists of being able to provide whatever is required."
Like a mother nourishing her child, or like a tigress carrying her cub, one must harmonize [the practice] with due moderation; only those who have long practiced the Way are capable of this.

This is called external protection (*bāhya-rakṣā*). Second, as for fellow practitioners, they should mutually exhort and inspire one another, remaining without sleep or distraction, so that there is new progress every day.

They refine one another through chipping, carving, polishing, and grinding; they share the same heart and align their wills as if riding a single boat, respecting one another as they would the World-Honored One.

This is called "practicing together. Regarding the three types of instruction, they are able to decisively resolve all internal and external skillful means, as well as all points of obstruction, impediment, and hindrance.

He skillfully expounds the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening others, thereby transforming and breaking through the minds of men. Regarding various skillful means, he is able to understand them decisively on his own and may proceed alone;
yet, as he is not yet conversant with potential obstacles and difficulties, it is not appropriate for him to abandon [the company of others]. (Text)

[Commentary] This explains the three kinds of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). The first two and a half lines explain the "external protection" (*bāhya-rakṣā*). The *Fuxing* (Notes on Practice) states: "Regarding 'external protection':
one's own body and mind are considered 'internal,' while the body and mind of others are considered 'external. Because one is protected by what is external, it is called 'external protection.
Since both monastics and laypeople may serve this purpose, it is said that there is no distinction between 'black' and 'white' [i.e., ordained and unordained]. They are like a mother or a tigress."
As for this: though a mother is compassionate, she must discipline her child; though a tiger is fierce, it carries its cub with gentleness.

To protect traveling practitioners, one should neither disturb nor annoy them. Regarding those who have long practiced the Way: if they have not personally practiced, they will be ignorant of what is permissible and what is not;

if they remain entirely immersed in worldly ways, they will fail to understand the distinctions between what is allowed and what is prohibited. Furthermore, how could one simply entrust protection solely to lay outsiders? One must protect oneself as well.
One should also carefully protect [the donor]. As it says in the Āgama: When the Buddha was at Jetavana, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should revere the donors and patrons as you would your own parents. You must support them and attend to them; their giving enables the fulfillment of precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
It brings great benefit, for they are able to provide the four requisites. Therefore, O bhikṣus, with a heart of loving-kindness..."
Toward a donor, one should not forget even a small kindness, let alone a great one.

One should apply oneself diligently through the three karmas so that merit is not squandered—acting like a guide for the lost or providing provisions for the destitute; this is what is meant by "protecting and guarding" from the outside.

As for fellow practitioners, when wisdom is shared with wisdom, there is the merit of daily renewal; it is like rubbing two pieces of wood together to produce fire. It is like an elephant [being urged on].

Thus, jade is polished, gems are carved, and stones are ground; these are all methods for refining vessels. Now, it is said that by mutually "cutting and polishing" one another, one becomes a vessel of the Dharma.
As for those who are of like mind, this means they can share the same aspiration and respect one another; thus, the teachings of the Way will increase for both.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When Bodhisattvas dwell together and look upon one another, they should regard each other as the World-Honored One.
Why? Because he is my true companion; it is like traveling together on a boat, for what he learns, I learn. Regarding the teacher, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) says:
"One who acts as a guide must necessarily possess both eyes and feet. If understanding and practice are not balanced, how can one benefit others? This extends even to conduct and understanding.

It is fully endowed; such virtue resides therein. That which benefits me exists solely within understanding. Regarding internal and external skillful means: this refers to the skillful means prior to the Path.
Furthermore, there are internal and external [categories]: the ten objects serve as the internal skillful means, while the twenty-five dharmas [serve as the external].

These serve as external expedients (*bāhya-upāya*). Furthermore, among the twenty-five [factors], they are divided into internal and external: the complete conditions (*pratyaya*) are exclusively external;

the condemnation of desire (*kāma-nindā*) and the abandoning of hindrances (*āvaraṇa-prahāṇa*) have meanings that encompass both internal and external; the regulation of the five matters (*pañca-vastu-parīkṣā*) is both internal and external; and sleep and food are external.

The remaining three belong to the internal [realm]. One practices the five dharmas, which are exclusively internal. Regarding "penetration and obstruction" (*tō-soku*): when skillful means (*upāya*) reach their proper object, it is penetration;
when skillful means turn away from practice, it is obstruction. "Expounding the Dharma to transform the mind" refers to attaining understanding. It is further said:
"The ten objects mutually provoke one another, and the ten vehicles increase or decrease; within each and every dharma, there is both penetration and obstruction. If one can master this...

One who can master the points of penetration and obstruction, remove hindrances, and further skillfully expound the Dharma to guide and lead the human mind may then be called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who provides instruction.

Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening": pointing out the way is "showing" (*darśana*); instructing and admonishing is "teaching" (*anuśāsana*); causing others to obtain benefit is "benefiting" (*anugraha*);

and rejoicing because one sees others obtain benefit is "gladdening" (*saṃpraharṣaṇa*). As for "turning to break the minds of others": once the Wheel of Dharma has been turned, it is able to shatter [delusions].
That is the mind of beginningless false conceptualization. Once a practitioner has received these instructions on the perfection of understanding and practice, they should examine themselves.

If they are able to proceed through their own skillful means, they may travel alone; however, if obstacles and difficulties are not yet familiar to them, it is appropriate that they remain close to others and should not abandon them.
【□Note】 Regarding "the instructor" (*śāstṛ*): the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*), fascicle 4, part 2, page 6, states:

"To proclaim the words of the Sage is called 'teaching' (*jiao*); to instruct and admonish me is called 'bestowing' (*shou*). (Text). Regarding the general term "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*): the *Lotus Sūtra Commentary* (*Fahua shu*) states:
"To hear their name is 'knowing,' and to see their form is 'recognizing. Such a person benefits my path to Bodhi; therefore, they are called a 'good spiritual friend. (Text).
[Commentary] The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-śāstra* (Fu-fa-zang) states: "One practices and approaches the noble Dharma to attain nirvāṇa by means of a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Ānanda asked the Buddha, "Is a spiritual friend a partial cause and condition for attaining the Way? The Buddha replied, "No.
A spiritual friend is a complete cause and condition for attaining the Way. Ānanda, you should know that in this Jambudvīpa, with the exception of Mahākāśyapa..."
Śāriputra, as for other sentient beings, if they do not encounter me, there will be no time of liberation.
Therefore, I say that a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) can bring great benefit. The *Ekottarika-āgama* says: "Do not associate with evil friends or engage in affairs with fools;
you should associate with and commune with virtuous friends and the wise. If one enters into the fundamental absence of evil, one draws near [to them]."
If one associates with evil people, one will inevitably become an evil person, and an evil reputation will spread throughout the world. A virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is the opposite of this;
therefore, one must draw near to them. According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, there are two causes and conditions for attaining the unsurpassed path:
first, internal self-reflection; second, obtaining a virtuous friend. In the *Mahāvaipulya-mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, King Ajātaśatru came to where the Buddha was, and the Buddha told him:
O Great Assembly, as for the proximate cause of Bodhi, none surpasses the virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra). Had King Ajātaśatru not encountered Jīvaka, he would have fallen into hell;
therefore, one must draw near to a true spiritual friend. This concludes the brief explanation of the five requisite conditions.

△ Second, the reprimand of the five desires. Part one: the general summary. Part two:
the reprimand of the five desires.

[Commentary] *Zhiguan* 4.20 states: "The five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) are not themselves desire, yet within them there is flavor that can give rise to the mind of craving in the practitioner;

therefore, they are called the 'five desires' (*pañca-kāma*). They constantly draw people into the realms of various demons (*māra*). Even if one possesses the preceding conditions, it is difficult for the mind to be established in concentration.
For this reason, they must be reviled. Furthermore, these five faults are such that form (*rūpa*) is like a hot iron ball; if one grasps it..."
If one approaches it, it burns. Its sound is like a drum smeared with poison; hearing it brings certain death. Its fragrance is like the breath of a raging dragon;

smelling it causes illness. Its taste is like boiling honey; if it touches the tongue, it sears it. It is like a blade smeared with honey; licking it results in injury. To touch it is like lying near a sleeping lion;
drawing near leads to being bitten. A famous monk of a former age wrote in verse: "To distance oneself from it is easy for a man of virtue; to draw near to it is difficult."

The five passions—sensual desire, malice, ignorance, pride, and doubt—arise from the six sense objects. Form and color cause the body to perish; sound causes the mind to become agitated; fragrance and flavor cause lofty aspirations to decline; and touch causes the spirit to wither. (Text) Within these five [passions], there are both the primary and secondary retributions (*niṣyanda-vipāka*).
[Commentary] The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "Restraining the six passions is like tethering a dog, a deer, a fish, a snake, a monkey, and a bird. As for the dog:
Deer delight in mountain thickets; fish delight in ponds and marshes; snakes delight in dwelling in holes; monkeys delight in deep forests;
birds delight in relying upon the sky; and the six sense faculties delight in the six sense objects. These cannot be subdued by those of shallow wisdom or weak resolve;
only through wisdom, a firm mind, and right mindfulness can they be subdued. This serves as a general metaphor for the six sense faculties, to which the Great Master addressed himself.
That is to say: the eye covets forms; forms possess substantiality and image, like a dog coveting a village. The ear covets sounds;

sounds lack substantiality or obstruction, like a deer coveting deep mountains. The nose covets fragrances, like a fish coveting a pond. The tongue draws toward flavors, like a snake coveting an empty burrow.
The body clings to tangibles, like a monkey coveting a dense forest. The mind conditions dharmas, like a bird coveting its dwelling in the sky.
At present, we do not speak of the dharmas themselves, but clarify the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). Therefore, it is said that the five sense objects are not themselves desire;
rather, within them there is a distinct kind of lovely flavor capable of generating in the practitioner a mind of longing and craving, which is what is called the "five desires" (*pañca-kāma*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Alas for sentient beings! They are constantly troubled and disturbed by the five desires, yet they still seek them."
Thus it is. These five desires, once obtained, only intensify further, like roasting scabies with fire. The five desires are of no benefit, like a dog gnawing on a dry bone.
The five desires increase contention, like birds competing for meat. The five desires burn people, like holding a torch against the wind.
The five desires harm people, like treading upon a venomous snake. The five desires lack reality, like what is gained in a dream. The five desires...
It does not last long; it is but a borrowed moment. Worldly people are deluded and ignorant, greedily attached to the five desires, never relinquishing them until death.
Consequently, they undergo immeasurable suffering in future lives. It is like a foolish person who, greedy for fruit, climbs a tree to eat it and refuses to descend immediately;
when others cut down the tree, he falls and dies. Thus one can see that the five desires are the very place where one’s body is lost, yet people—
Why suffer by being near rather than far? *Pie* (pronounced *pi*) means resentment, anger, or malice.
△ Second, the detailed explanation has five parts. First, the condemnation of sensual desire.
1. Condemnation of form: This refers to the handsome and dignified physical appearance of men and women—long eyes, high eyebrows, crimson lips, and white teeth—as well as worldly...
Various treasures, such as black, yellow, red, purple, and all kinds of wonderful colors.
[Commentary] The commentary lacks a specific explanation for the term "reproaching form" (訶色). I shall now provide it. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If a person is attached to form, the fires of the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) will all blaze up intensely, burning and harming the human body, just as fire burns gold."
Silver and boiling hot honey may possess color and flavor, yet they burn the body and scorch the mouth; one must urgently abandon them.
Furthermore, when discarding these, one must not leave the gold while discarding the fire; one must discard both the gold and the fire together.
This is like King Bimbisāra, who for the sake of beauty entered an enemy kingdom and stayed alone in the chamber of the courtesan Ambapālī.
King Udayana, because he was stained by [the desire for] form (*rūpa*), cut off the hands and feet of five hundred *ṛṣis*. Such is the harm caused by it;

form is indeed to be censured. The *Zhiguan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) states: "Desire for form refers to the so-called red and white, long and short, bright eyes with a fine gaze, fair necks and emerald brows, white teeth and vermilion lips, and even to the secondary environment (*upabhoga-pariṣkāra*), such as the various colors of black, yellow, crimson, and purple."
Precious objects delude and agitate the human mind. As described in the Chan Gate (Chanmen), the harm caused by sensory forms (*rūpa*) is particularly profound;

they cause people to become crazed and intoxicated, for this is the very root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). This is clearly evidenced by the case of Nanda, who, though he attained Arhatship while observing the precepts out of desire for [a woman], still possessed many residual habits (*vāsanā*);
how much more so for ordinary sentient beings who remain bound by all fetters? Thus, kings may become addicted and dissolute beyond measure.
Disregarding the gravity of the ancestral temple and the altars of the state, for the sake of sensual pleasure, he personally entered the enemy's country.
In the high antiquity of this land, the ruin of states and the destruction of families have mostly arisen from desire. The majestic House of Zhou was extinguished by Bao Si;
this is precisely such an instance. As the Sūtra observes: "Driven by the passions of form, one becomes a slave to affection and love, losing all autonomy. If one knows...
Regarding the defects of form (*rūpa*): one will not be deceived by form. Having thus rebuked it, desire for form immediately ceases.
2. Rebuking the desire for sound (*śabda*).

The second part, the rebuke of sound, refers to the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, the tinkling of bracelets and pendants, as well as the sounds of men and women singing and chanting, and so forth.

[Commentary] Regarding "strings and bamboo": strings refer to lute strings; bamboo refers to flutes. These comprise the eight musical categories: metal, stone, string, bamboo, gourd, earth, leather, and wood.
Regarding "rings and pendants": those worn on the fingers are rings; "pendants" (pei) refers to sash ornaments. Both are used to adorn the female body.

Regarding "singing and chanting," the *Zhiguan* (Treatise on Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 4, part 1, states: "This refers to seductive and alluring lyrics, lewd sounds, and defiling speech. (Text).
The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), fascicle 4, part 2, cites the case of the seer Tīpayaṇa, who lost his supernormal powers upon hearing the voice of Śacī.
Furthermore, five hundred seers dwelling in the Snowy Mountains lost their various meditative concentrations upon hearing the singing voice of the maiden Kāñcanamālā, and so forth.
[Commentary] This explains the faults of sound. The harm it causes is no small matter; it must certainly be censured. Both sentient and insentient beings possess sounds that incite desire in people.
First, let us clarify that the sounds of stringed and wind instruments, as well as those of bracelets and pendants, are all sounds of insentient things.
Now, when "stringed and bamboo instruments" are mentioned, two of the eight musical sounds are cited; these refer to having attendants strike them against one another to initiate the music.

"Bangles and pendants" refers to such items as *linglang* jade pendants and the like, all of which serve as ornaments for a woman's body and cause those who hear them to fall into the error of generating sensual desire. Next, "singing and chanting" refers to the voices of sentient beings.
The first line cites the *Zhiguan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) for the correct interpretation. The next two lines cite the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) to prove the error.
Regarding the seer losing his supernatural powers upon hearing the words: before the Buddha appeared in the world, Śakra frequently visited the seer Vādi to listen to the Dharma.
The lady Śacī became suspicious and thought, "Śakra is abandoning me and desires other women," and she immediately concealed her form.
They ascended the chariot and arrived at the place where the seer was. Śakra first spoke to him, saying, "The seer does not wish to see this woman;
you should return to your palace. Śacī refused to go. Śakra then struck her with a lotus stalk. Śacī apologized to Śakra with gentle words.
Upon hearing her voice, the seer’s desire was aroused; his spiral-tufted hair fell to the ground and he lost his supernatural powers. Five hundred [others] heard it.
Regarding "losing meditative concentration through song," the treatise states: Five hundred rishis lived on Mount Himavat. There was a woman bathing and singing in the mountains;

when the rishis heard the sound of her singing, they immediately lost their meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). Their minds became intoxicated and wild, and they were unable to regain self-control.
Therefore, the treatise states that the characteristic of sound is impermanent; it perishes as soon as it is briefly heard.

Fools, failing to understand impermanence, falsely give rise to attachment toward sound, which subsequently gives birth to perverse thoughts and a defiled mind. This causes them to lose benefit in the present life and leads them to fall into the evil realms hereafter;
therefore, one must censure it.
△ Third, the prohibition of fragrances. Regarding the three prohibitions of fragrance: this refers to the bodily fragrance of men and women, as well as the fragrance of worldly food and drink, etc.

[□ Note] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 4, Part 2, Section 13, states: "People say that there is little fault in using fragrances; however, this is not the case here. It opens the way for the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to arise."
[This] gate blocks the true path. Though one may maintain the precepts for a hundred years, they can be destroyed in a single moment. [Commentary]:
This statement indicates that the great affliction of desire for fragrances is why they should be censured. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:

There was an Arhat who frequently entered the dragon palace to accept a meal invitation from the dragons. After eating, he had a śrāmaṇera wash his bowl. Inside the bowl were some leftover grains of rice.
A few grains [of rice]. The śrāmaṇera smelled them and found them very fragrant; he ate them and found them extremely delicious. He then devised a stratagem:
he went under his teacher’s rope bed and held up its legs with his hands. When the teacher entered the dragon palace, he always took the rope bed with him.

Because of this, the śrāmaṇera was also able to enter the palace. The dragon said, "This one has not yet attained the Way; why have you brought him along? The teacher said, "I was unaware. The dragon said: [text continues]
The śrāmaṇera obtained food and also saw that the dragon girl’s body was upright and graceful, with a wondrous fragrance beyond compare.
His mind became stained with attachment, and he secretly made a vow, saying: "I pray that through my merit, I may seize this dragon's place and dwell in her palace.
The dragon said: "Henceforth, do not bring this śrāmaṇera here. After the śrāmaṇera returned, he single-mindedly practiced the precepts and devotedly sought to become a dragon. Later...
At that time, as he walked around the monastery, water welled up from beneath his feet.

Realizing that his karmic destiny as a dragon was fulfilled and that he would certainly become one, he went straight to the edge of the pond, covered his head with his *kāṣāya*, and entered the water to die. He transformed into a great dragon;
because of the greatness of his merit, he immediately killed the previous dragon, turning the entire pond crimson. Before he died, the various masters rebuked him, O śrāmaṇera.

He said, "My mind is already settled; the characteristics of the mind have already emerged. Then the teacher and the monks went to the pond to observe him, and they sighed in admiration, saying, "It is because of his attachment to the fragrance that he has become thus.
Furthermore, there was a bhikṣu who was walking up and down by the edge of a lotus pond.
He smelled the fragrance of the lotuses, and his nose perceived it with mental attachment. The deity of the pond rebuked him, saying, "Why do you abandon meditative concentration?"
[The fragrance] was settled, yet someone stole my incense. Because of this incense, those fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*) that had long lain dormant have now all awakened and arisen.
At that time, there was a man who entered the pond to gather flowers; he dug up and pulled out the roots and stalks, departing in a state of disorder.
When the deity of the pond saw this, she remained silent and said nothing. The bhikṣu asked: "This man has destroyed the pond to take its flowers, yet you [did not speak]."
He remained silent. I was merely walking along the bank of the pond when I saw him rebuke me, saying, "Why do you steal my incense?
The deity said, "Worldly evil people constantly dwell amidst the filth of sin and impurity; therefore, I do not speak with them.
You are a good person practicing meditation, yet by wearing this incense, you ruin your virtuous practice; that is why I rebuked you."
This is called the condemnation of fragrance.
△ Fourth, the condemnation of desire for flavors.
Regarding the four condemnations of flavor: this refers to various foods, delicacies, and delicious tastes, and so forth.
[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 4, Part 2 (12), states: "Because of attachment to flavor, one constantly receives molten copper poured into one's mouth;
because of attachment to flavor, one falls into impurity. (Text)
[Commentary] This statement indicates that the harm caused by sensual desire is not slight. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
In the Copper Stake Hell, the hell-wardens ask the sinners, "Where do you dwell? They reply, "My mind is bewildered and distressed; I do not know where I have come from."
They suffer only from hunger and thirst. At that time, the hell-wardens immediately drive the offenders to sit upon hot iron spikes.

They force their mouths open with iron tongs and pour molten copper into them. They swallow iron balls; these scorch the mouth as they enter, rot the throat as they pass down, and burn within the belly until all five viscera are destroyed.
Passing straight through, they fall to the ground. This is due to the causal conditions of the person’s past conduct.

They plundered the wealth of others to provide for their own sustenance. As for those who have left the household life, some would feign illness at times to seek out large quantities of ghee, oil, and rock honey;
therefore, they receive molten copper poured into their mouths. Regarding those said to fall into impurity:
if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas touch food from a field of merit with impure hands, or eat it first, or place impure substances upon it—

Furthermore, there was one who violated the pure livelihood of begging for food; due to the causes and conditions of sustaining himself through wrong livelihood, he fell into the Boiling Excrement Hell.
Moreover, there was another śrāmaṇera whose mind was constantly attached to curd. Whenever donors sent curd to the saṃgha, the śrāmaṇera would always receive the leftover portions.
He became mentally attached to them, delighting in them without ever letting go. After his life ended, he was reborn in the Curd [Hell].
Inside a jar. His teacher had attained the path of an Arhat. When the monks were dividing the curd, he spoke slowly, saying, "Do not harm the novice who was so fond of the curd.
When the others asked for the reason, he replied, "This insect was originally my novice.
Because of his craving for the curd, he was born in this jar. For this reason, one must censure the desire for flavors."
△ Five condemnations of the desire for touch.
The five condemnations of touch refer to the softness and smoothness of the bodies of men and women; their bodies being warm in cold weather and cool in hot weather.
And various pleasant tactile sensations, etc.
[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Fascicle 4, Part 2 (13), states: "Tactile desire (*spraṣṭavya-kāma*) is the root of birth and death and the condition for bondage. Why is this?
While other desires each obtain their respective domains within the four sense organs, only this tactile desire pervades the entire body and arises in every place."
Because it is vast, it gives rise to much defiled attachment; this attachment is difficult to abandon. If one falls into hell, one again experiences myriad forms of suffering through bodily contact.
This contact is called the place of great darkness (text).
[Commentary] This is called the harm of sensual desire for touch; it is especially great. Regarding what is called the root of birth and death, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"If in all worlds, among all species—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation—all take their life and nature precisely because of lustful desire.
It further states: "Desire arises from craving; life exists because of desire. Sentient beings..."
Attachment to life still relies upon the root of desire; attachment to desire serves as the cause, while attachment to life serves as the effect.
Therefore, it is called the "root of birth and death. Regarding the conditions for bondage, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "You love my mind, and I cherish your form."
For these reasons, one remains constantly bound throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas; therefore, it is called the "condition of bondage.

Why is this? [The following] interrogates and explains the reason for this. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the seer Kapila, who, due to contact with desire, walked out of the palace and lost his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), becoming unable to fly. Likewise, the seer Mṛgaśṛṅga, through his defilement by desire...
To mount a lustful woman upon one's neck destroys long-accumulated merit and the fruits of many years of diligent cultivation.

The *Mokṣa-varga* (Chapter on Liberation) explains that the retribution for the fault of contact with desire is as follows: there are two divisions of hell, the first named Cold Ice (*śīta-hima*) and the second named Blazing Fire (*jvalana*).
Within these two hells, all suffer punishment through physical contact; the agonies are manifold, and this contact is termed "Great Black" (*mahākṛṣṇa*).
The dark place is a perilous path of danger. This concludes the brief explanation of the refutation of the five desires.
△ Third, the abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

The third vehicle employs the five hindrances, namely: sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), sloth and torpor (*styānamiddha*), restlessness and remorse (*auddhatyakaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan* (4.22) states: "They are collectively termed 'hindrances' (*āvaraṇa*) because they cover and entangle the mind, causing the spirit to become dark and obscured, such that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do not arise;

therefore, they are called hindrances. The previous condemnation of the five desires refers to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*) as they encounter the five present sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*)."

The five consciousnesses arise; now, one abandons the five hindrances, which are precisely these five consciousnesses. They transform and enter the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), where they retrospectively take past objects as conditions and anticipate future phenomena such as the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). These constitute a great obstacle within the mind.

[Commentary] This section generally clarifies the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). All are capable of obscuring the true nature (*dharmatā*), thereby destroying the Buddha-way and opening the path for Māra;

their harm is by no means slight. The first line explains the meaning of "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*). From "The preceding reprimand" (*qian he*) onwards, this distinguishes [the current section] from the previous topical division.

From "Tracing back the conditions" (*zhui yuan*) onwards, it correctly clarifies that if the five hindrances are not abandoned, they will flow and inflict harm throughout the three periods of time; hence it is said:
It constitutes a great internal obstacle to the mind.

[Commentary] This extends to the arising of the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), wherein one recalls past coarse and base fivefold desires, engages in discursive thoughts and calculations,
becomes intoxicated and deluded in mind, and loses right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).

[Commentary] The following section specifically clarifies the characteristics of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). The intent is that there is no separate entity for the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*);
its characteristic lies precisely in the moment a thought of greed arises. When that thought does not cease, one pursues past, coarse, and base objects of the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).

Following this, one further engages in mental deliberation and calculation, whereby the mind becomes intoxicated and deluded, losing right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Or, one employs skillful means, hoping to obtain them once again. Because of this...

This is the coarse awakening-covering (vitarka-āvaraṇa) of the immediate [uninterrupted] dhyāna; it is the essential characteristic of the covering of greed (*rāga-āvaraṇa*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used in the sense that greed is never satisfied;
this should be understood from subsequent examples. [Note:
As for the covering of ill-will (*vyāpāda-āvaraṇa*): it refers to recollecting how a person has harmed oneself, harmed one's kin, or praised one's enemies throughout the three periods of time.
The nine grounds for resentment (*navāghātasthānāni*): harboring enmity and hatred toward an adversary, the mind becoming feverish and coarse, and the persistence of anger and so forth.

[Commentary] This means that there is no other covering of aversion (*vyāpādāvaraṇa*) than this; its characteristic lies precisely in the retrospective recollection of how a person from the past vexed me.
"Either my parents and other relatives are harmed, or those whom I detest and resent are praised; this is anger in the present life.
Since there are three types of affliction in one lifetime, there are nine types across the three lifetimes. Thus do these objects of resentment correspond."
Consequently, the mind becomes feverish and the breath coarse, leading to a continuous succession of anger; this is the essential characteristic of the hindrance of hatred (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) asks: "The past has already passed and the future has not yet arrived; how can these be called 'affliction' (*pratigha*)? It answers:

"Although affliction belongs to the past or the future, its object is actually present. When it encounters that [present] time, afflictive agitation arises. This is because the past once afflicted me."
Furthermore, for one who is free from hatred, although there may be provocative circumstances, the provoking mind does not arise.

[Note] Regarding the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*): the state in which the mind and spirit are murky is "sloth" (*styāna*); the six consciousnesses being darkened and obstructed, while the four limbs are slumped and relaxed, is "torpor" (*middha*).
Torpor is called an increased mental factor (*caitta-dharma*). It is like a dark, heavy cloud that descends secretly to cover a person, making it difficult to protect or guard against.

[Commentary] The meaning is that the hindrance of torpor (*middha-nīvaraṇa*) has no other [nature]. It is simply the mind relying upon the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), whereby ignorance (*avidyā*) increases;

thus, the mental consciousness becomes dull and weary, and the five sensory faculties become dark and obscured, such that nothing is perceived or known—this constitutes sleep. The Saṃghabhadra school explains it as an increased mental factor (*caitta-dharma*).

It still belongs to what is abandoned by insight and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*), and is subsumed under the latent tendency of delusion (*moha-anuśaya*). The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "In this context..."

This is a general explanation of the nature of sleep. It causes the mental factors (*caitasika*) to increase without ceasing. Regarding this, the *Abhidharmakośa* states from the perspective of dharmic characteristics:
"Sleep is universally non-opposed; if it coexists with any [other state], it increases by one. This is because it pervades the three natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* censures it, saying: "Sleep is a great darkness in which nothing is seen; day after day it deceives, maddens, and robs [one of clarity]."

People are like those standing on the battlefield amidst their own blades, like those dwelling in the same room as a venomous snake, or like a person bound and led away to be executed—at such times, how could one sleep in peace? Sleep hinders dhyāna; its fault is most grave.
This is the characteristic of the hindrance of torpor and drowsiness.

[Note] Regarding restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*): if initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) arise in isolation, they are subsumed under the preceding hindrance [of restlessness]. Now, however, when initial and sustained applications arise together, they take all phenomena as their object;
momentarily taking desire as an object, then again thinking of ill-will, and furthermore of false views and delusion, they flicker without ceasing, surging up repeatedly.

Lack of stability; rising and subsiding abruptly, with all manner of agitation; the body wanders aimlessly and the mouth engages in useless chatter and laughter—this is called restlessness (*auddhatya*).
If one is restless yet feels no remorse, it does not constitute a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*). Because of this restlessness, the mind’s reflections lack caution and restraint.
How could one perform such useless deeds? This is truly shameful, and thus one feels sorrow and regret within the heart.
When the knot of remorse (*kaukṛtya*) entangles the mind, it constitutes the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtyanīvaraṇa*).

[Commentary] "Vitality" (*vitarka*) refers to coarse mental discrimination; "sustained thought" (*vicāra*) refers to subtle mental reflection. The *Fuxingyu* (Sub-commentary on the *Fahua Xuanyi*) states:

"The dharma of restlessness (*auddhatya*) destroys the mind of one who has left the household life. Even when collected, it is not yet settled, let alone being further agitated and scattered. 'Restlessness' means agitation. (From the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*)
The treatise says: "You have already shaved your head and donned the kashaya; why do you delight in clinging to the dharmas of frivolous debate?

Why are you negligent and self-indulgent, thereby losing the benefits of the Dharma? There are two kinds of regret: first, the regret that arises after becoming agitated; second, the regret like that of one who has committed a grave offense.

One constantly harbors fear, and the arrow of regret enters the heart, becoming so firmly rooted that it cannot be extracted. Thus, the *Fajie Cidi* (The Graded Arrangement of the Dharma Realm) states:
"The movement of thought with a deviant mind is called *auddhatya* (restlessness). To withdraw in thought and become distressed is called *kaukṛtya* (remorse).

If one erroneously grasps through ignorance, then frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) stirs and the mind of restlessness arises. Once one's actions have gone astray, one withdraws in thought and becomes afflicted by sorrow; thus, the mind of remorse is born.

This is also an increase in mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*). It belongs primarily to that which is abandoned by the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) and is subsumed under the latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*).

There is also a small portion abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). [Supplement] If one enters meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one should merely know the faults and not harbor attachments or thoughts.
One does not attain liberation merely through remorse; rather, one should cultivate the pure dharmas of meditative concentration. How could one possibly rely on remorse for such glory?
The mind obstructs great matters; therefore, it is said: "Once you have repented, do not worry about it later. You should not constantly dwell upon it with attachment.

If resentment and entanglement coil around the mind, they constitute the hindrance of regret (*kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*). This hindrance covers meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), preventing its development. All such states are characteristics of the hindrance of regret.

[Commentary] Regarding the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*): this is not the doubt that obstructs the realization of principles by seeing the truths; rather, it is the doubt that obstructs meditative concentration (*samādhi*). There are three types of doubt:
first, doubt regarding oneself, which means thinking, "My own person is lowly and inferior; I am certainly not a vessel for the Path," and thus doubting oneself.

Second, doubt regarding the teacher, which means thinking, "This person’s body and speech do not accord with my expectations; how could he possibly possess profound meditation and excellent wisdom? and thus doubting the teacher.
And one serves it; thus it will not mislead me. Third, regarding doubt concerning the Dharma: one wonders whether the Dharma received is necessarily consistent with principle.

This third type of doubt and hesitation remains constantly in one's breast; meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) does not arise, and even if it were to arise, it would be lost forever. These are the characteristics of the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).

[Commentary] This clarifies the fault of the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*). It is a great affliction that acts as an obstacle to the Path. The first two lines distinguish what it is not and identify what it is.
"Doubt is threefold," etc., correctly explains that the objects of doubt are not singular; namely, when one seeks the truth with a deluded mind, being hesitant and indecisive, this is called doubt.

If one practices the dharmas such as the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), due to the dullness and darkness of ignorance (*avidyā*), one cannot distinguish between the true and the false. Because of this—
To give rise to hesitation and for the mind to lack resolution—these are all forms of doubt. "Hesitation" (*yòuyù*) is the name of a beast; it serves as a metaphor for the state of indecision.

[Commentary] If the hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*) is heavy, one should employ the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to cast it aside. If the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*) is prevalent, one should contemplate loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*) to extinguish the fire of resentment.
If the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa*) is prevalent, one should apply diligent effort (*vīrya*), exerting both body and mind. If...

For one who is prone to agitation and distraction, one should employ the practice of counting the breaths. If three doubts persist in the mind, one should form this thought: "I am like a blind child born into great wealth;
though I possess the treasure-trove of the unsurpassed Dharma-body, it is obscured by afflictions and the eye of the Path has not yet opened.

I must cultivate and purify it, never abandoning the effort. Furthermore, considering the causal practices cultivated throughout immeasurable kalpas, what concentration could it possibly be? How could it be...
One suspects that one has lost the opportune time and forfeited the benefit. If one doubts the teacher, [one thinks]: "I am currently without wisdom;
while the supreme sages and great beings all seek the Dharma, they do not grasp at the person. If one doubts the Dharma, [one thinks]: "My Dharma-eye is not yet open;
I cannot distinguish right from wrong and rely on it only through faith. The Buddha-Dharma is like the ocean; only through faith can one enter it. (Text)

[Commentary] This passage clearly elucidates that the single word "abandon" (*prahāṇa*) is an excellent prescription for curing disease. The preceding text describes the illness; the present text provides the medicine.
It means that for those whose greed is heavy, because they take exquisite sensory desires as their sustenance, one must employ the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as the remedy.
As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Because [the practitioner] previously spoke of the five desires as pure, becoming entangled in attachment to them, now..."
Contemplate this body as a sack of pus and a bag of blood; from head to foot, there is not a single part to be rejoiced in.
A sense of revulsion arises: what wise person would take pleasure in this? Therefore, this contemplation is employed as the medicine to cure greed.
If this hindrance of sloth-and-torpor is removed, the mind immediately attains peace. The next two lines treat the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda*):
that is to say, this ill-will affects many people, as it takes the perception of enmity as its nutriment; one should employ a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) to extinguish the fire of hatred.

This is because the fire of hatred can burn away the merit of both worlds, making one unpleasant for others to behold; being poisonous, harmful, and cruel, one is no different from a beast, [trapped] in birth and death.

Enmity persists through successive kalpas without ceasing; a slight resentment in this life becomes a great hatred hereafter. Now, by cultivating a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one abandons this evil.
One should regard all people as one would one's own parents, perceiving them with thoughts of kinship, and cause them all to attain happiness.
How could one then give rise to enmity toward them? When one contemplates in this way, the mind of anger immediately subsides, and one enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in tranquility.
The next two phrases concern the abandonment of the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (*styāna-middha*). This hindrance affects many people because it is nourished by five factors:
namely, mental dullness, lack of joy, yawning, irregularity in eating, and weakness of mind.

Now, one should apply diligence to exert both body and mind, abandoning it through the observation of *vipaśyanā* (insight). That is to say, one should apply focused attention to guard against it and reflect upon it.
Contemplate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and distinguish between wholesome and unwholesome states, so that the hindrance of drowsiness (*middha-nīvaraṇa*) may not gain entrance.

Furthermore, you should discern between the wholesome and unwholesome mind, causing the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*) to arise. Once the mind is clear and pure, the hindrance of drowsiness will naturally be eliminated.
Do not, on account of sleep, lose the happiness of both worlds; to live or die in vain, with nothing at all gained, is to have failed. You must diligently restrain the mind.
This is skillful defense. The next two lines concern the abandonment of the hindrances of restlessness and remorse;

that is to say, many people find nourishment for this hindrance of restlessness in four things: namely, thoughts of relatives, thoughts of one's country, thoughts of immortality, and thoughts of recollecting past events.
One should employ counting the breaths (*ānāpānasmṛti*) to abandon it. This agitation is so sharp that one does not perceive its arrival until after a long time.

Now, by employing the counting of breaths, if the counting is not accomplished or if one occasionally forgets, one will immediately know that [the mind] has already departed; having become aware of this, one counts again.
When the practice of counting is perfected, the agitation will be subdued. If one does not treat it in this way, one will remain covered by it for the rest of one's life.
The next two lines provide a general demonstration of how to abandon the veil of doubt. This refers to a person who harbors these three doubts;

they are nourished by three characteristics and countered by dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). There are both general and specific ways to counter these three doubts. The general method is as follows:
one should reflect that this body is like a blind child of a wealthy man; although it possesses the wealth of the unsurpassed *dharmakāya*, [it remains deprived of its vision].
The Jewel is obscured by afflictions; the eye of the Path has not yet opened, so one cannot clearly perceive the treasury of True Suchness and its wealth of meritorious dharmas.
If one wishes to enjoy this, one must treat these cataracts of the eyes.

Therefore, day and night one contemplates the dependent origination of phenomena, never relinquishing this practice. This is the total abandonment of the three doubts. Furthermore, there is no inferiority below.
This is the specific method for abandoning self-doubt: one should consider that there is no fixed certainty regarding the causes accumulated by oneself since beginningless time.
Between the two kinds of roots of goodness—mundane and supramundane—one may have practiced either previously.

Just as when a person has debts, the heaviest is paid first, so too, having now obtained this human body, it is precisely the right time to practice in order to seek transcendence; how could one possibly doubt oneself?
Consequently, one loses both time and opportunity. As the ancients said: "If this life is not saved, what other life can be saved?

And again: "Everyone’s nostrils reach toward heaven; every person’s heels touch the ground. Since that person is a man of great capacity, so am I; one should not disparage oneself and succumb to despondency.
How can you harbor self-doubt, thinking your body is not a vessel for the Way? Second, regarding abandoning doubt concerning the teacher:
I am now foolish and lacking in wisdom; I must rely upon others to seek the Dharma.

Furthermore, when the supreme sages and great beings sought the Dharma, they did not cling to the person—just as the Snow Mountain [sage] requested the Dharma from a ghost, and the Lord of Devas prostrated to an animal as his teacher.
What kind of person am I that I would dare to doubt my teacher? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If a disciple perceives a fault in their teacher, whether it be real or..."
Indeed, their minds will naturally be ruined and they will lose the superior benefits of the Dharma; therefore, an empty voice proclaims: "Do not look for faults in the teacher.
