You should reflect upon your own meager merit for failing to encounter a Buddha and instead encountering an evil teacher. You must not look for faults, lest you obstruct your own prajñā."
If the teacher has faults, they do not pertain to me; I seek Prajñā from the teacher.
It is like a leather bag made of dog skin containing precious jewels—one does not discard the jewels because of the stench of the bag. As the Sūtra says, "Rely on the Dharma, not on the person.

What doubt could there be? Third, regarding the abandonment of doubt concerning the Dharma: this means that my Dharma-eye is not yet opened, and thus I am unable to distinguish [between right and wrong].
Whether it be right or wrong, how could one possibly fathom its depth? One should simply rely upon faith alone. A treatise states: "The Buddha-dharma is like a great ocean;
faith is that which enables entry, and wisdom is that which enables crossing. Therefore, one should believe in the Dharma and harbor no doubts.
Regarding the three types of doubt explained above that must be abandoned, among them, one should also skillfully discern between the teacher and the Dharma, so that... [the text continues].

If one is stained by an evil teacher or evil teachings, yet the teacher and the teachings are correct, then one should practice in accordance with that Dharma; at that time, the three doubts should all be abandoned.
Someone might object: "In the Gate of the Patriarchs (Zongmen), it is said that great doubt leads to great awakening and small doubt leads to small awakening; why then should they now be abandoned?"
Answer: It should be understood that regarding the principle of clarity, true doubt is indispensable; whereas regarding the matter of darkness, false doubt must not exist.

Therefore, one should abandon it. [Note] In the Chan school, doubt is taken as a gate of expedient means; this is different from the present case. The explanation of abandoning the five hindrances is complete.
△ Four ways of training in five matters.
The fourth is training in five matters, namely: training the mind so that it is neither sunken nor agitated; training the body so that it is neither lax nor strained; and training the breath.
Neither too astringent nor too slippery; this is the regulation of sleep. Neither too restrictive nor too indulgent; this is the regulation of food. Neither hungry nor satiated.

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan si* (Four Gates of Stopping and Contemplation), fascicle 4, states: "If earth and water are not in harmony, they cannot be used to make a vessel. If these five matters are not well-managed, one cannot enter dhyāna.

The two matters of sleep and food are regulated outside of formal concentration; the three matters [of posture, clothing, and environment] are regulated during the entry, exit, and maintenance of concentration."

Regarding the moderation of food: one should not consume food that increases illness, increases drowsiness, or increases afflictions (*kleśa*). That which sustains the body and heals disease is what should be eaten.
In brief, eating neither to the point of hunger nor to the point of satiety is the characteristic of moderate eating.

Regarding the moderation of sleep: sleep is the nourishment for the eyes; it should not be excessively restricted, as this increases mental factors (*caitta*) and causes a loss of effort. Furthermore, [it should not be excessive].
One may indulge [in sleep] at will. This is because, as stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it must be strictly abandoned as a hindrance to entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

Here, during the state of the distracted mind, one complies with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), each having its own purpose. To speak briefly: neither restraint nor indulgence constitutes the characteristic of balanced sleep.
When these three factors are harmonized, they depend upon one another and cannot be separated. This occurs at the very moment of first entering meditative absorption.

Regulate the body so that it is neither too relaxed nor too tense. Regulate the breath so that it is neither too constricted nor too slippery. Regulate the mind so that it is neither too sunken nor too flighty.

Transition from the coarse to the subtle and abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Should any part remain unregulated, one must become aware of it and examine it, regulating it until it is peaceful and secure.
If one emerges from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the process proceeds from the subtle to the coarse, as detailed in the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Sequential Gate of Dhyāna).
[Commentary] The *Chanmen* states: It is like a potter preparing clay; he makes it neither too hard nor too soft, after which he can apply it to the wheel and cord.
It is also like tuning a lute; first one must adjust the strings so that their tension is appropriate, only then can one proceed to play. Thus it is with emerging from meditation.
Just as with various exquisite melodies, it is the same now: when these five factors are harmonious and appropriate, samādhi arises easily.
In the *Boluozhi*, Huangfu Mi asks the "Master of the Blue Ox" about the methods for nourishing life, who says: "A person should desire constant labor and a constant small amount of food.
Labor should not exceed the limit, and eating should not reach the point of emptiness. Eliminate fatty and greasy foods and regulate sour and salty tastes; this is the method of worldly nourishment."
Those who give rise to [unwholesome] states constantly cause themselves toil. How could one who aspires to the Way overeat and be indolent?
It is not merely that they lose their benefit; it also increases illness and diminishes life. In the *Nirgrantha Sūtra*, the Nirgrantha replies to King Yañcī (Yan-chi) saying:

"King Prasenajit eats in excessive measure; his body is heavy and he is indolent. He loses benefit in both the present and the future. Therefore, it is said that one should not be hungry [to the point of weakness]."
"Satiation" is the characteristic of balanced eating. Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* states: While the Buddha was teaching the Dharma at the Jeta Grove, Aniruddha fell into deep sleep.
The Buddha rebuked him, saying: "Alas! Alas! Why do you sleep? You are like the species of snails, conches, and clams. He asked again:
"Have you gone forth [into homelessness] out of fear of royal law or fear of bandits? He replied: "No. I am weary of..."

"Because of birth, old age, sickness, and death, one seeks to leave the household life. Now that you have left the household life with such firm faith, why do you sleep with your eyes while the Buddha himself preaches the Dharma?

Aniruddha rose from his seat and said to the Buddha, "From this day forward, even if my form dissolves and my body decays, I shall never again sleep with my eyes before the Buddha. Because he did not sleep for seven days, he lost his sight in both eyes. The Buddha said:
Those who exert themselves with excessive diligence are associated with restlessness; those who are indolent and lazy are associated with the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
You should practice the Middle Way; you should rest and sleep. Why? Because all things exist by means of nutriment:
the eye has sleep as its nutriment, and so on, up to the mind which has mental objects (*dharma*) as its nutriment; even Nirvāṇa has non-negligence (*apramāda*) as its nutriment. I have none.

"By being heedless, one may attain Nirvana. He replied, "I dare not disobey. Later, having attained the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), he realized that sleeping is a fruit of retribution belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since he had not yet attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he could only maintain moderation;

he must not practice extreme austerity. If one sleeps at will and indolently, there are two faults: first, it increases the mental factors (*caitta*); second, it causes the loss of one's spiritual labor.
Furthermore, one must maintain equilibrium; it is also improper to be self-indulgent. This is the characteristic of balancing sleep.

Next, the upper section rebukes the lower practice by half [a verse], clarifying the distinction between the contextual meanings of the preceding and following passages. Regarding the harmonization of these three factors, *Zhiguan* states:

"It is like when first conceiving a fetus: first, warmth (*ūṣman*); second, vitality (*jīva*); and third, consciousness (*vijñāna*). Warmth is the physical form of the inherited body; vitality is the vital wind (*vāyu*)."
Continuity: Consciousness is the sovereign of the mind throughout a single lifetime. Upon entering the womb, these three factors are present;
as these three factors grow, they undergo a transformation every seven days. After thirty-eight such transformations have been completed, the emergence of these three factors is called infancy.

When the three factors remain stable, it is called middle age. When the three factors decline and weaken, it is called old age. When the three factors undergo transformation and cessation, it is called death.
Since from the very beginning these factors merely depend upon one another and are inseparable, the body, consciousness, and mind should be harmonized together and not discussed separately;
there are only differences in the methods for the beginning, middle, and end, as well as distinct characteristics for entering, abiding, and emerging.

Regarding the initial harmonization of the three matters when first entering meditative absorption: when a practitioner wishes to enter samādhi, it is appropriate to harmonize the body while still outside of the state of concentration.

Whether walking, standing, advancing, or halting, in movement or stillness, and in all activities, one must be thorough and discerning. If one's actions are coarse and violent, the breath will follow suit and become coarse;

because the breath is coarse, the mind becomes distracted and difficult to collect. Furthermore, while sitting, one will experience agitation and distress, and the mind will not find tranquility or joy.
Therefore, even when outside of meditative concentration, one must still apply the mind and employ skillful means to ensure that movement and stillness are both thorough and discerning.
To state the essential point: neither lax nor strained—this is the characteristic of a well-regulated body.

Second, there are four types of breath to be regulated: first, wind; second, panting; third, qi; and fourth, breath. To fixate on wind leads to distraction; to fixate on panting leads to congestion; to fixate on qi leads to exhaustion.
By guarding the breath, one attains concentration (*samādhi*). If the aforementioned three [factors] are not regulated, the mind will likewise be difficult to concentrate.

If one wishes to regulate them, one should rely on three methods: first, settle the mind; second, relax the body; third, imagine that the breath pervades all pores, entering and exiting through them freely and without obstruction.
If one refines the mind, the breath will become subtle and faint. When the breath is thus regulated, various afflictions will not arise.
The mind becomes easily concentrated. To state the essentials: being neither constricted nor slippery is the characteristic of balanced breath.

Third, there are two ways to regulate the mind: first, to subdue distracted thoughts so they do not wander; second, to ensure that sinking, floating, laxity, and tension are brought into their proper measure.
Regarding "sinking": when sitting, if the mind is dark and obscured, one has no capacity for recording [objects], and the head tends to droop.
"Sinking" (*līna*) refers to this state of dullness. At that time, one should fix the mindfulness on the tip of the nose, causing the mind to abide within its object.
"Floating" (*uddhata*) occurs when, while sitting, the mental faculty is restless and the body is likewise uneasy, and mindfulness dwells upon extraneous objects; this is the mark of floating.
At such a time, one should settle the mind by directing it downward and binding it to the object, thereby restraining all distracted thoughts; thus the mind will become stably concentrated. This...
The mind then becomes easily tranquil. To state the essentials: being neither sunken nor floating is the characteristic of a balanced mind.

When wishing to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one proceeds from the coarse to the subtle; the body is coarse, the breath is intermediate, and the mind is most subtle—this is the initial expedient for entering concentration.
Regarding the section on "Abiding in Dhyāna," it clarifies the balance of abiding in concentration, meaning that while abiding in dhyāna, these three factors are not...

Adjustment: If the mind does not enter the dharma, it is like tuning a lute for a performance; if the melody cannot be completed later, one realizes that the strings or pegs are out of tune and adjusts them accordingly.
This is the adjustment of the three matters while dwelling in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). When emerging from concentration and descending [to daily activities]:

This explains the preparatory adjustments for emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*). When one wishes to emerge from absorption, one should first release the mind toward external objects, open the mouth and exhale the breath, and imagine that the vital energy (*prāṇa*) disperses freely through the hundred vessels. Thereafter, one should very gently move the body.

This serves as the skillful means for adjusting the body, breath, and mind upon emerging from absorption, because it involves transitioning from the subtle back to the coarse. These three matters [body, breath, and mind] must be harmonized.
This is called skillfully entering, exiting, and abiding. As the verse says: "Advancing and halting follow a sequence; the coarse and the subtle do not conflict.
It is like a well-trained horse, which desires both to go out and to stay. This is it.

【□Note】 *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 4, Part 2 (23), states: "Therefore, in the Chan Gate, regarding the regulation of the body, it is said: 'Now, as for sitting, one must first establish a stable posture so that it remains comfortable for a long duration.
If sitting in half-lotus, place the left leg over the right, drawing it close to the body so that it is level with the left and right thighs.
If one wishes to sit in full lotus, further cross the right leg over the left. Loosen the waistband and adjust the body to be perfectly upright. Do not... [text continues].
While sitting, ensure that [the robes] do not slip off further. With the left hand, press down upon the right, stacking them so they are aligned.

Place them upon the right foot, keeping them close to the body and positioning them at the level of the heart. Then, extend and move the limbs about seven or eight times, according to the method of massage.
Neither bending nor raising [the head], keep the head upright and the neck straight, so that the nose is aligned with the navel. Do not lean to either side; do not nod or tilt.
Let the body be like an anchor stone, without any agitation or movement, and free from the faults of being too loose or too tight. This is the characteristic of bodily regulation.
Once the body is thus regulated, next open the mouth and exhale the air within the chest at will, allowing it to flow out until all the hundred channels throughout the body are completely [cleansed].
Exhale with the breath. Next, close the mouth and inhale pure air through the nose. Do this three times; if the breath has already been regulated, once will suffice.
Next, close the mouth and let the lips and teeth just barely touch. Turn the tongue upward toward the palate.

Close the eyes just enough to cut off external light. Next, examine the wind-like breath; if the breath is regulated, it is easy to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Next, to regulate the mind: first...
First, to regulate the agitation [of the body], so that it does not become excessive or unruly. Second, to regulate the mind, so that sinking and floating are brought to their proper state.
When the mind sinks, fix the mindfulness on the tip of the nose; when the mind floats, settle the mind by directing it downward (and so forth).
[Commentary] The *Jianzhousanmeijing* (Sūtra on the Three Samādhis) states: "The Buddhas sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), and the Bodhisattvas sit in the half-lotus posture.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "There are many methods of sitting; why is only the lotus posture shown? It answers: "Because it is the most stable; because it holds the hands and feet so that the mind does not waver;
and because it strikes terror into Māra. A verse says: "One who has attained the Way and possesses a sense of shame sits peacefully like a coiled dragon."
Seeing him depicted in the full-lotus posture (paryaṅka), even Māra was struck with awe and fear. This posture differs from the ordinary worldly sitting or the heterodox standing on one foot;
therefore, only the full-lotus posture is shown. The explanation of the five matters is concluded.
△ Two sections on the five practices and five dharmas. First, the general summary:
the fifth practice consists of five dharmas.
【□ Commentary】 *Zhiguan Sanwei* (3.11) states: "Although the aforementioned twenty dharmas are complete, if one lacks the aspiration and longing [for them], the body and mind..."
If one possesses bitter resolve, mindfulness, skillful means, and a single-minded determination, yet lacks the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, these will have no way to manifest before them.

If, however, one can joyfully cultivate [the path] without weariness, remaining untiring day and night, with thoughts succeeding one another in continuity, and thus skillfully attains its essential meaning, maintaining a single mind without distraction—such a person can advance upon the path.
Single-mindedness is like the rudder of a ship; skillful wisdom is like the helm; and the three types [of practice] are like the oars and the sweeps.
"If even one thing is lacking, then there will be no peace" (text).

[Commentary] This is a general explanation of practicing the five dharmas. Regarding the first two practices, they serve to clarify the underlying intent. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states:

"If the word 'if' were not present, it would apply throughout the following sections. That is to say, 'if there is no joyful aspiration and longing,' this corresponds to 'lacking joyful aspiration'; if there is no..."
If there is suffering in body and mind, it is appropriate that there be no vigor. If there is no mindfulness, it is appropriate that there be no thought.

If there are no skillful means, it is appropriate that there be no wisdom. If there is no single-mindedness, there is no way for cessation and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) to manifest; thus, correct practice cannot be accomplished.

Even if one possesses the aforementioned twenty factors, if five factors are lacking, it still will not be accomplished, let alone if there are omissions among those twenty, or if they are entirely absent.
"Are there not five dharmas? If one can practice even half of the lower [stages], this accords with the intended meaning. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) states:
"The two characters 'If one can' (*neng*) should also be understood as penetrating through the following five phrases; when applied sequentially and correspondingly, all five dharmas are present.

The single mind and the subsequent line clarify the dharma and its analogy together. The *Fuxing* further states: "The preceding metaphor refers to the guide; though all matters were prepared, he did not act."
If one acts without earnestness, does not maintain the proper method, acts without skillful means, acts without single-minded focus, then the task will not succeed.
Acting without beginning is like having no desire; acting without diligence is like having no vigor; not maintaining the proper method is like having no mindfulness;
acting without skillful means is like having no wisdom; acting without single-minded focus is like having no concentration. Thus, the task will not be accomplished.
[The practice] is accomplished. This is illustrated by the failure of right practice. The *Chanmen* (Dhyāna-gate) says:

"As for 'skillful wisdom,' when a practitioner first cultivates goodness, if they recognize the internal and external expedient means and apply them skillfully without losing what is appropriate, they will swiftly attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*);
therefore, it is called skillful wisdom."
△ Second, the specific exposition in five parts. First, the exposition of the aspiration for the Dharma.
1. Aspiration: The aspiration to leave behind all worldly delusions and inversions; the aspiration to attain all gates of meditative concentration and wisdom.

[Commentary] "Desire" (chanda) means desiring to abandon the delusions of ignorance and distraction, and desiring to attain the gateway of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Desire is the wish to proceed from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to the first dhyāna. The *Dhyānāmukha-śāstra* states:
"Desire is simply the mind of great resolve that accomplishes the aspiration for joy; one should not give rise to longing or recollective thoughts at the time of applying the mind."
Regarding perception (*saṃjñā*): if a mind of longing arises, the mind will not be clear and tranquil, and samādhi cannot possibly be brought forth.
△ Second, showing the method of diligence (*vīrya*).

Second, as for diligence: one firmly maintains the prohibitive precepts, abandons the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), and practices with diligent effort during the first, middle, and last watches of the night. Therefore, [it is called diligence].

[Commentary] Regarding diligence: the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is difficult to transcend. If one is not diligent, one cannot emerge from it; it is like a rebel returning to his own country, for the frontier of the realm is difficult to pass.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: Generosity, ethical discipline, and patience are the common laws of the world, like the etiquette between host and guest, which ought to be provided as a matter of course.
When one sees an evildoer, one must suppress and reform them so that they dare not commit further offenses, or [restrain them] by force.

When one is young, it is sufficient to practice patience; there is no need for intense diligence. Now, wishing to give birth to *prajñā*, one must rely on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and require great diligence.
It is because only when body and mind are applied with urgency can [the goal] be accomplished.
△ Third, the teaching on mindfulness.
There are three types of mindfulness: mindfulness that the world is deceptive, contemptible, and base; and mindfulness that meditative concentration and wisdom are venerable and noble.

[Commentary] "Mindfulness" means constantly dwelling on the first dhyāna and not attending to other matters. "Other matters" refers to everything outside of concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā);
these are all termed "other matters," namely the defiled passions of the five worldly desires.
△ Fourth, the teaching on skillful wisdom (*kauśalya*).

There are four types of skillful wisdom: weighing worldly pleasure against the pleasure of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), as well as [weighing] gain and loss, or light and heavy [consequences].
[Commentary: Regarding "skillful wisdom," it is the discernment that the First Dhyāna is honorable and precious, while the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) is deceptive and contemptible. The First...
Dhyāna refers to the aspiration for the superior, sublime, and transcendent. The desire realm refers to the aversion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstructions below.

When cause and effect are discussed together, there are twelve contemplations (*vipaśyanā*). These share the same names as the six practices of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), yet their meanings differ.

However, while the non-Buddhists practice these solely to seek meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), the disciples of the Buddha employ them to enter the correct path from the erroneous; by cultivating them with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), they instead bring about the fulfillment of the True Dharma. This is [the distinction].
This is skillful wisdom (*kauśalya*).
△ Fifth, showing the dharma of the single mind. 5. Single Mind:

When mindfulness and wisdom are distinct and clear, one clearly perceives the world as something to be afflicted with and loathed; one skillfully recognizes meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The merit of wisdom is venerable and noble.
[Commentary] Regarding "single-mindedness": when practicing this Dharma, one maintains a single mind and focused resolve, without engaging with other conditions.

This single-mindedness is the single-mindedness of definitive resolve, not the single-mindedness of entering meditative concentration. The demonstration of the practice of the five dharmas is complete.
△ Third, the summary of the intent:
These twenty-five dharmas must be fully possessed as the preliminary expedients for the four teachings.
If one lacks these expedients, even mundane meditative concentration cannot be attained; how much less so the wondrous principle that transcends the world? Thus, it is clarified:
Since the teachings differ as gradual and sudden, their expedient means (*upāya*) likewise differ. Depending upon which teaching one practices, one must carefully deliberate on each occasion.

[Commentary] The *Zhi guan si mo* (The End of Stopping and Contemplation) states: "These twenty-five dharmas serve generally as the expedient means for all meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because various contemplations differ, the expedient means also vary accordingly. It is like how, when the musical pieces performed are distinct, the tuning of the strings is also distinct. (Text)
[Commentary] This section concludes the explanation of the transition from the general to the particular. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) states:

"All" does not exceed the mundane and the four teachings. Through the meditative concentrations of the mundane world and the contemplative understanding of the four teachings, these guide the twenty-five dharmas.

Thus, what is practiced is entirely distinct; hence it is said that [the practice] also "turns. However, when the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) employs this as a skillful means (upāya), it is as stated in the *Zhi guan*:
"Now, these twenty-five methods are used as external skillful means for concentration (*samādhi*); they are also called 'distant' skillful means.
By means of these, one regulates the mind and suddenly perceives the principle (*li*). When perceiving the principle, who would discuss internal or external, distant or near? Great!

The chapter says: "This wisdom is not attained through internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*), nor through external contemplation (*bahirdhā-vipaśyanā*), nor through both internal and external contemplation.
It is not apart from internal contemplation, nor apart from external contemplation, nor apart from both internal and external contemplation; yet it is also not attained by means of non-contemplation.

Now, for the time being, we shall clarify the external expedient means based on this. However, one must not dogmatically cling to this and give rise to a state of "neither-nor" (*ubhayābhāva*). For now, let us rely upon...
Before one has seen the principle, it is necessary to establish twenty-five dharmas as internal and external expedients (*upāya*).

If one understands this intent, one will find the proper balance between sinking and floating, such that both the internal and external become perfected expedients. "Playing with the curve" refers to the playful application of the correct curve itself.

It is called "playing the melody. This serves as a metaphor for contemplating the Dharma. "Tuning the strings" refers to the sequence for rectifying the melody; it is called the "prelude," serving as a metaphor for skillful means (*upāya*).
This concludes the brief explanation of the auxiliary practices of skillful means, consisting of twenty-five sections.

△ Second, the correct cultivation through the contemplation of phenomena further opens into ten vehicles. This has two parts: first, a general indication that the Dharma is applied to four types of capacities;

second, an explanation of the ten-vehicle method of contemplation. Although the names of the ten vehicles are the same across the four teachings, their meanings differ. For now, I shall explain the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao); the other teachings may be understood by analogy with this.

[Note] Although the ten vehicles (daśayāna) of the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) apply generally to all four teachings, their names are identical while their meanings regarding the partial (*pian*) and perfect (*yuan*) differ.

Here, the partial is excluded to clarify the perfect; thus it says, "for now, we clarify the Perfect Teaching. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Vol. 5, Part 1 (26), states: "The dharmas of contemplation are not ten."
There are distinctions among the faculties; yet, despite these differences in faculty, it is but a single inconceivable contemplation.

One contemplates the inconceivable realm until one is free from craving, for one does not depart from that realm. Furthermore, although the lower three stages and positions are not themselves contemplative methods, they are all termed "contemplation" by association with the power of contemplation.
Thus, they are called the "Ten Contemplations. Moreover, because one is fully equipped with these ten, contemplation can be brought to fruition; therefore, they are called "Completion."

Contemplation is also called "accomplishing the vehicle. The first four dharmas function without priority or sequence; the three [dharmas] of penetration, obstruction, and so forth, accomplish the preceding four;
and the three [dharmas] of stages, positions, and so forth, serve to distinguish the preceding seven. (Text)

[Commentary] This clarifies the ten meanings of the method of contemplation (*guanfa*). The first two lines clarify that contemplation is not separate from its object; thus, they constitute ten [meanings].

Furthermore, the subsequent section below clarifies how the final three dharmas together complete the ten contemplations. Moreover, the section beginning with "fully equipped" (*bei*) clarifies the completion of contemplation and the completion of the vehicle (*yāna*).
One must prepare ten dharmas. The preceding section below clarifies that both the accomplished and the judging each have their respective objects and agents.

That is to say, the first four dharmas are the "accomplished" (the object), the middle three dharmas are the "accomplishing" (the agent), and the seven dharmas comprising the total of the preceding accomplishing and accomplished are the "judged" (the object), while the final three dharmas are the "judging" (the agent).
[Supplement] Regarding the absence of priority and sequence in their application: it is like contemplating the inconceivable.
When deliberating upon the realm, one realizes that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are of one essence; thus, one naturally accords with bodhicitta.
When observing the manifestation of the realm, one realizes that this mind is eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating; thus, one naturally accords with sublime śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One is then able to universally shatter all [obstructions]. Therefore, the four preceding dharmas function without sequence. As for the accomplishment of these four: if...
When contemplating the object, one cannot maintain continuous correspondence from moment to moment;

there may be interruptions by miscellaneous thoughts, or the arising of attachments regarding contemplative wisdom, or the factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) may not yet be well-balanced, or many obstacles may arise on the right path. It is for these reasons that one employs the three [criteria] of penetration, obstruction, and so forth;
thus it is said that the first four [stages] are accomplished.

[Commentary on the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), Vol. 7, Part 2, Section 27] states: "Therefore, one should know that the first seven [factors] correctly clarify the body of the vehicle (*yāna*) as well as its equipment and provisions.
The latter three are merely what the vehicle traverses. If there were nothing to traverse, the meaning of 'transportation' would not be established.
For this reason, these ten factors are collectively termed a 'vehicle' (*yāna*). (Text)

[Commentary] Master Zhili’s *Fuxing* (Supplementary Notes) states: "The 'great carriage' in the *Lotus Sūtra* is a metaphor for the ten dharmas. For now, I shall follow the sequential order of the sūtra text rather than the sequential order of the ten dharmas themselves.

That is to say, the 'high and broad' [carriage] refers to the inconceivable object [of the Mahāyāna]. The 'canopy' of compassion and the 'precious ropes' interlaced together refer to the arousal of the bodhicitta.
As for the 'scarlet pillow' placed within—it has both an internal and external aspect; if it is the pillow inside the carriage, it signifies rest..."
The cessation of all activities is the settling of the mind. Whether the carriage is on the move or at rest—this is the meaning of "penetration" (tong) and "obstruction" (se).

To break through obstruction and preserve penetration, or to be penetrated while remaining obstructed, is to be as swift as the wind; this is the breaking of ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the meaning of "breaking through" (*po bian*).
Furthermore, beginning with the white ox and ending with the level and upright path, these represent the meaning of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*). Moreover—
"Many attendants" refers to the primary and auxiliary practices. "Wandering in the four directions" refers to the successive stages.

"Patience" (kṣānti) simply means enduring the two conditions of adversity and favorability within the five grades, thereby enabling entry into the six sense faculties. "Detachment from craving" simply means detaching from the craving for phenomena that resemble [the truth] within the six sense faculties.
Thus, one should know that the first seven [sections] primarily clarify the body of the vehicle and its constituent perfections, while the final three...
This is what this vehicle traverses.
△ Second, the specific elucidation of the ten vehicles for those of perfect capacity. First, the elucidation of contemplating the inconceivable realm.

1. Contemplating the inconceivable realm: This means contemplating that within a single thought-moment, the three thousand nature-and-characteristics are fully present without deficiency. One hundred...
The thousand suchnesses of the realms are precisely this very object: it is simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way. There is no sequence of before or after;

it is vast, perfect, and sovereign both horizontally and vertically. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "That chariot is high and broad" (the person of superior capacity correctly contemplates this object).

[Commentary] This is the contemplation of the first vehicle (*śrāvaka-yāna*). Because it forgets both subject and object, it is named after its object. Furthermore, as the foundation for the nine vehicles, one practices the nine [contemplations] based on this foundation;

only then is one capable of entering the stage (the stage entered is the stage of contemplative practice). Regarding the phrase "contemplating a single thought-moment," etc.: this refers to the deluded mind of a single *kṣaṇa* within the present aggregates.

One contemplates it in accordance with its true nature (*dharmatā*), wherein it fully possesses the three thousand phenomena (*sanqian fǎ*). This is not merely selecting the objects of the three categories (*triskandha*) as the field of observation.

This clarifies the single thought-moment (*ekacitta*). It means that at this very point, one must distinguish the conceptualizing mind (*cintya-citta*) and grasp the inconceivable mind (*acintya-citta*).

Therefore, the *Myōraku-ki* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) states: "Distinguishing both the object and the mind. And the *Kōku-ki* (Record of the Radiant Verses) states: "One must eliminate the conceptualizing [mind] and grasp the inconceivable [mind]."
This is precisely what is called "discerning the mind. (Text) It means that one immediately penetrates the realm of the five aggregates (*skandha*), thereby accomplishing the inconceivable realm.

As for the statement that there are "the natures and characteristics of the three thousand" and further that there are "the ten realms, the thousand suchnesses," this is because the three thousand dharmas are discussed in relation to the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses, traversing the three worlds.
[Commentary] This clarifies that a single thought-moment is replete with the three thousand [realms].

Regarding the statement that one contemplates in accordance with the nature (dharmatā) so that the present momentary thought is replete with the three thousand, the *Detailed Explanation* (*Suyō*) states:

"As in the entire work of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, its essentials lie in understanding (*jie*) and practice (*xing*). Understanding means understanding that all phenomena are fundamentally true; practice means establishing the path of cultivation."

In the state of meditative concentration, one employs contemplation (*guan*). When correctly employing contemplation, one clearly contemplates that the deluded mind of the present moment possesses the three thousand dharmas;

the three thousand are identical to this single thought-moment, and this single thought-moment is identical to the three thousand. They are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither preceding nor succeeding.

If one contemplates this without ceasing, the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) transforms into the inconceivable. This constitutes contemplating in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*), wherein a single momentary mind (*kṣaṇika-citta*) is endowed with the three thousand phenomena (*trīṇi-sahasra-dharmāḥ*).
Regarding the statement that the three categories (*tri-skandha*) are used to select the object and clarify the single-moment mind, as stated in the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary):

"The aggregates, bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) can all serve as objects; however, because they are so vast and diffuse, they are difficult to demonstrate. Therefore, one proceeds directly to..."
The aggregates (*skandha*). This is like discarding the *zhang* (ten feet) to focus on the *chi* (one foot), or discarding the *chi* to focus on the *cun* (one inch).

Because they are subsumed within the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), which are broader in scope, the aggregates consist only of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*). Within the conditioned, the meaning encompasses both mind and matter; therefore, matter is set aside and the mind is retained.
Furthermore, "mind" includes both the primary mind and its mental factors (*caitta*); for now, however, we shall observe the primary mind alone, setting aside the mental factors. Thus...

The first contemplation concerns consciousness (*vijñāna*). Regarding the selection of the inconceivable mind (*acintya-citta*) over the conceivable mind (*cintya-citta*), the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:
"As for contemplating the inconceivable mind, this object is difficult to explain. First, clarify the conceivable realm so that the inconceivable realm may be easily revealed.
As for the conceivable, even the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) teaches that the mind gives rise to all phenomena; that is, the six realms of existence.

Cause and effect, the revolving cycle of the three realms: if one abandons the mundane and aspires for the sacred, one discards the lower and ascends to the upper, extinguishing the body and annihilating wisdom;
this is the Four Noble Truths of conditioned action (*saṃskṛta-satya*), for it is a dharma of conceptual thought.

The Mahāyāna also clarifies that the mind gives rise to all dharmas, namely the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). If one contemplates that the mind exists—possessing both good and evil, and if the evil is... the three [realms]... [text fragmentary].
This is the category of the causes and effects of the three miserable realms. Goodness consists of three grades; this is the category of the causes and effects of the asuras, humans, and devas.
Contemplating that these six paths are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing, one finds that the mind which contemplates them likewise does not abide for even a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, one realizes that both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are entirely produced by conditions, and that what is conditionally produced is empty. This is the dharma of the causes and effects of the Two Vehicles. If one contemplates this...
To fall into the two extremes of emptiness and existence, to sink in emptiness or stagnate in existence, and then to give rise to great compassion,

entering into the realm of conventional reality to transform sentient beings— truly having no body yet assuming a body, truly having no emptiness yet provisionally speaking of emptiness to guide and convert them—

this is precisely the dharma of the cause and fruit of a Bodhisattva. Contemplating this dharma, one sees that both the one who saves and the one being saved are entirely the dharma of the Middle Way and the True Mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Ultimate purity. Who is good? Who is evil? Who exists? Who does not exist? Who is delivered? Who is not delivered? All phenomena are thus;
this is the Dharma of the Buddha’s cause and effect. These ten dharmas proceed in gradual stages of depth and shallowness, all emerging from the mind.
Although they are subsumed within the immeasurable Four Truths of the Mahāyāna, they still belong to the realm of conceptual thought and are not—
This is now the object of contemplation in *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Regarding the "inconceivable realm" (*acintya-viṣaya*), as the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "The mind is like a master painter;
it creates the various five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Within all worlds, there is nothing that is not created by the mind. As for "various":

This refers to the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*). Regarding the dharma-realm, there are three meanings. First, the number "ten" is that which depends (*āśrita*), while the dharma-realm is that upon which it depends (*āśraya*);

when the dependent and the supported are spoken of together, they are termed the "ten dharma-realms. Second, these ten dharmas each have their own causes and each have their own fruits, being distinct and not confused with one another;
thus they are called the "ten dharma-realms. Third, each and every one of these ten dharmas, in its very essence, is itself the dharma-realm; thus they are called [the ten dharma-realms].

This refers to the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Now, a single mind contains the ten dharma-realms, and each of these ten dharma-realms mutually contains the others, thereby forming one hundred dharma-realms.

Each realm possesses the "ten suchnesses" (*daśa-tathatā*); thus, the hundred dharma-realms constitute one thousand suchnesses. Furthermore, each of these is individually endowed with the three kinds of worlds:
namely, the world of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha-loka*), the world of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-loka*), and the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*).

A thousand such [aspects] constitute the three thousandfold world. Therefore, it is said that there are "the natures and characteristics of the three thousand," which refers to the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses.

These three thousand exist within a single thought-moment (*citta*). If there were no mind, they would simply not exist; yet, with the slightest movement of the mind, the three thousand are immediately present.
Furthermore, it is not said that the single mind comes first and all phenomena come after, nor is it said that...
All phenomena precede; the single mind follows. For example, when the eight phases transform an object, the object precedes the phases;
yet the object is not transformed. The phases precede the object; yet the phases are not transformed. To say they precede is untenable; to say they follow is also untenable.
One merely discusses things by means of their mutual transformation; one merely discusses things by means of their mutual transformation. Now, the mind is also like this.
If all phenomena arise from a single mind, this is "vertical" (longitudinal). If the mind simultaneously contains all phenomena, this is "horizontal" (transverse).
Verticality is untenable; horizontality is also untenable. Thus, the mind itself is all phenomena, and all phenomena are...

The Dharma is the mind; therefore, it is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither one nor different. It is profound and wondrously transcendent, not that which can be known by consciousness, nor that which can be expressed by words.
This is why it is called the "inconceivable realm" (acintya-viṣaya). The intent lies herein: this serves to exclude the conceptualizing mind and to grasp the inconceivable mind.
Thus, at the beginning of the *Myōraku* [Commentary], it is established that the three categories [of dharmas] serve to distinguish the realm.

Regarding the "Explanation of the Mind" (*Mingxin*), the *Wenju Guanshin Shi* (Exegesis on the Contemplation of the Mind in the Textual Phrases) comments on the concluding passage, stating: "That is, the two contemplations of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]...

Master Miaole’s commentary notes that the phrase "and so forth" (*yunyun*) is an incomplete expression. Now, one should distinguish the characteristics of their similarities and differences at this point:

specifically, the provisional and correct cultivation, the differentiation of objects and mind, as well as the contrast with the preceding two [teachings] to distinguish between the provisional and the real, and so on. This is...

Up to the fourth contemplation, one must also engage in analytical investigation. Here, I shall briefly cite only a single phrase to demonstrate how the three categories [of dharmas] distinguish the objective realm and clarify the mind.
The passage from "The Record of the Light Phrase" (Guangju ji) below serves as proof that it distinguishes the conceivable from the inconceivable.

The phrase "that is, to penetrate the realms of the aggregates" and so forth explains the intent of the aforementioned "Record of the Light Phrase. The "Record" states below: "It elucidates the three thousand natures and characteristics..."
The realms are like a thousand suchnesses. [Note] Regarding "this very object," etc.: it means taking the object itself as the contemplation. It is emptiness, the provisional, and the middle;

object and contemplation are non-dual. The three and the one mutually interpenetrate; they are neither sequential nor simultaneous, neither vertical nor horizontal. They transcend thought and transcend discourse. This...
Because its objects are all-pervasive, it is vast; because no dharma is lacking, it is complete. It extends horizontally across the ten realms and penetrates vertically through the three truths.
Since the horizontal and vertical are mutually identical, it is called "sovereign. Is this not the very essence of the Lotus Wagon?

[Commentary] Taking the object itself as the contemplation, and the contemplation itself as the object, the object and the contemplation are non-dual. Nevertheless, while there are three types of contemplation, the object is but one.
Since the object and the contemplation are non-dual, this constitutes the mutual fusion of the three and the one: because the one fuses with the three, they are not sequential;
because the three fuse with the one, they are not simultaneous. Being not sequential means they are not vertical (not arranged like a stack); being not simultaneous means...

It is not horizontal; because thought and speech are severed, it is called the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*). This realm is all-pervasive, existing everywhere among the four types of noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings, as well as among sentient and insentient things;
therefore, it is called "vast. It encompasses all phenomena of the mundane and supramundane, the defiled and pure, both form and mind;
therefore, it is called "perfectly complete. Horizontally, it extends to the limits of the ten realms; vertically, it penetrates the three truths.
The horizontal is the vertical, and the vertical is the horizontal; these aspects accord with the mind, and thus they are called "sovereign.
Is this not the very essence of the Great White Ox Cart of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*? It lies herein.

[Note] Its carriage is high and broad. The *Wenju* (Commentary on the Text), fascicle 5, section 27, states: "The provisional designation of the carriage possesses the characteristics of height and breadth.

For example, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are profound and far-reaching; horizontally, they encompass the limits of the Dharma-realm, and vertically, they penetrate to the very source and bottom of the Three Truths. (Text)

[Commentary] The width of the chariot is like the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision extending horizontally; the height of the chariot is like the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision penetrating vertically.
The three truths of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are neither horizontal nor vertical. Because the dharma-realm is all-pervasive, it is convenient to speak of it as "horizontal";
because the three truths have distinct names, it is convenient to speak of them as "vertical. They are non-dual and mutually manifest—this can be seen through reflection.

[Commentary on the Square Symbol] Regarding "those of superior faculties" (*uttama-indriya*), the *Yili* (Exemplification of Meaning) states: "A person of superior faculties produces the fruit directly from the seeds within the objects of perception.

For those of middling and inferior faculties, the nine vehicles are further discussed. The general meaning says: "Furthermore, although these ten dharmas are all perfect and eternal, there are three grades of faculties among those who realize this perfection.
Those of superior faculties have only one dharma; those of middling faculties have two or seven; and it is only for those of inferior faculties that [the full range is required]."
[Endowed with] ten [aspects]. [Commentary]:
Regarding "the superior faculty" and so forth, this means that the superior [faculty] initiates contemplative observation precisely upon this inconceivable realm.
"Observing this realm for a long time gives rise to the fruit. The *Fuxing* (Supplementary Commentary) states: "Take, for example, the ten realms (*daśa-viṣaya*).
They are the ground upon which a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) practices. Second, the differing characteristics of the realms are the seeds of practice.

Each one gives rise to the ten vehicles of contemplative methods (*daśa-yāna-dhyāna-dharma*), which are the rain for practice. Each one is transformed into the inconceivable realm (*acintya-viṣaya*), which is the sprout of practice."
Each and every arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is the trunk of the practice; each and every settling of the mind (*śamatha*) is the foliage of the practice;

each and every breaking through the pervasive [delusions], up to the primary and auxiliary practices, are the flowers of the practice; each and every stage and position, up to the attachment to the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), are the fruit of the practice.
If these six matters were absent, the tree of the Path would not stand upright, even though the sequence is thus. This is explained from the perspective of human [attainment].
Those of superior faculties produce the fruit directly from the seeds within the object. As the text says: "Upon merely hearing these words, the illness was immediately cured.
For those of middling and inferior faculties, the nine vehicles are discussed. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "For those of middling and inferior faculties, further dharmas are required.
As the text says: "He went to the elder's place to compound various medicines. This is the general meaning of the lower section of the proof.
The distinction between the ten dharmas and the three roots.

[Commentary] However, this inconceivable realm is fully elucidated within *Zhiguan* (Calming and Contemplation) through three types of realms: first, the realm of inherent virtue (*xingde*), which contemplates that a single thought-moment is replete with the three thousand dharmas;
second, the realm of cultivated virtue (*xiude*), which traces back to the mind inherently possessed and departs from the four modes of attachment to self-nature (*sìxìng*). Third...

The realm of transforming others involves the understanding that is free from the four positions (*catuskoṭi*), which does not obstruct the fourfold teaching. This is because inherent qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*) constitute cultivated qualities (*bhāvanā-guṇa*).

As the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*) states: "In reality, it merely traces back to the mind of the intrinsically present principle. (Text) At the time of cultivating qualities, there is the understanding of transforming others;
this is not yet the act of preaching the Dharma. As the *Fǔxíng* states: "The beginner relies on the principle to give rise to understanding," which is distinct from initiating the teaching.
"The subsequent mind is not the same" (text). [Commentary]:

This refers to the fact that *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* fully clarify the three objects. The first half-verse provides the heading and indication; "one nature" and below demonstrate the inherent virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
To observe that a single thought-moment (*citta-kṣaṇa*) is replete with the three thousand dharmas is precisely what is called the inconceivable inherent virtue.

This is the section on the "Object" (*viṣaya*). Second, "Cultivating the Lower [Levels]," which demonstrates the cultivation of merit. Regarding the inquiry into correct contemplation: when the mind arises, it necessarily takes an object as its condition (*ālambana*).

Is this because the mind itself possesses the three thousand realms? Or is it because the object possesses them? Or do they possess them together? Or do they possess them separately? If the mind possessed them, then the arising of the mind would not require an object.
If the object possessed them, then the possession by the object would not concern the mind. If they possessed them together, then prior to their union, each would lack them; yet once united...
At that time, how could there be "possession"? If one is separated from possession, then since the mind is already separated from its objects, why would the mind suddenly possess them?

Even the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) cannot be established; how then could it possess the three thousand dharmas? Answer: Others say that all delusions and awakenings, as well as the true and the false, rely upon and are supported by the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena).
The *dharmatā* supports the true and the false, and the true and the false rely upon the *dharmatā*. This is according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
It is said: "The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither defiled by delusion nor purified by truth; therefore, the nature of phenomena is not the support (āśraya).
What is called the 'support' is the ālayavijñāna, which, being free from extinction, thoroughly sustains all seeds."

"Non-extinction" means that the eight consciousnesses have existed constantly since beginningless time; therefore, it is called non-extinction. If one follows the Master Di (Dilun), then the mind possesses all phenomena (*dharmas*).
If one follows the Master She (Shelun), then conditions possess all phenomena. These two views each rely on one side [of the truth].
If it is held that all phenomena arise from the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), then the *dharmatā* is neither mind nor condition. It is not mind...
Therefore, if all phenomena arise from the mind, then by the same principle, all phenomena should also arise conditioned by non-conditions.
How can you claim exclusively that the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is the support for both the true and the false?

If you say that the *dharmatā* is not the support and that the *ālayavijñāna* is the support—implying that there is a separate *ālayavijñāna* support existing apart from the *dharmatā*—then it would have no bearing upon the *dharmatā*.
If the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not separate from the ālayavijñāna, then that which is the support of the ālayavijñāna is itself the support of the nature of phenomena.

How can you claim exclusively that the ālayavijñāna alone is the support? Furthermore, this contradicts Nāgārjuna, who said: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another;
they do not arise from both, nor without a cause. He even went so far as to say: "One should know that the mind cannot be found when sought through the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi)."

It is so. Even the three thousand dharmas sought cannot be obtained. Since the three thousand dharmas arising from the four propositions are crosswise unobtainable, must the three thousand dharmas arise from the cessation of the non-contemplating mind?
When the mind has ceased, it should be unable to produce even a single dharma; how then could it produce three thousand dharmas? If they arise from a mind that is both ceasing and not ceasing—
As for the production of the three thousand phenomena, they are both extinguished and not extinguished; their natures are contradictory, like water and fire, such that neither can be established.

How, then, can they produce the three thousand phenomena? If the mind produces the three thousand phenomena while being neither extinguished nor non-extinguished, then being neither extinguished nor non-extinguished, it is neither the agent nor the object. How, then, can it produce the three thousand?
The Dharma is both vertical and horizontal, yet neither vertical nor horizontal. Even when seeking the three thousand dharmas, they cannot be found;

the path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases. Therefore, it is called the "Inconceivable Realm. Third, regarding "transforming others": this demonstrates the transformation of others. As the *Zhi guan* says:
"One should know that within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), not even a single dharma can be found, much less the three thousand."

Regarding the Dharma: within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), even a single mind possesses immeasurable dharmas; how much more so the three thousand worlds? As the *Shulun* (Treatise on Trees and Dragons) says:
"Not self-arisen," and so forth. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The arising of arising is ineffable," and so forth.

Because there are four conditions, it can nevertheless be explained—namely, by way of the four *siddhāntas*. Thus, from here below, the text specifically clarifies the realm of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*); the details are omitted in this passage.
Citing the *Sub-commentary* (*Fuxing*), the full record states: "Regarding the 'inconceivable realm of cultivated virtue' (*xiude bushiyi jing*), this refers to one's own practice (*zixing*).

It is necessary to clarify its phenomenal characteristics (*xingxiang*); therefore, the *Sub-commentary* employs questions and answers to investigate and establish it as the essence of practice (*xingti*).

Just as with the preceding 'nature of reality' (*lixing*), which originally lacks the fault of having a fixed nature, here, when speaking from the perspective of cultivation (*xiu-men*), it is necessary to clarify the departure from conceptual reckonings (*jiji*). Thus, by means of the four modes of being (*siding/sixing*)," [it is explained].

This constitutes a correct inquiry. However, within this question, we provisionally employ the principle that what arises is inherently complete within the fundamental reality (*li*) as the basis for investigation.
In truth, this analysis is intended solely to examine the mind that inherently possesses the fundamental principle, lest conceptual attachments arise; therefore, such an investigation is necessary.

Consequently, the subsequent answer merely dispels the fourfold attachments of "vertical" and "horizontal" and so forth, returning once again to the fundamental principle: the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment (*yīniàn sāqiān*).

One should cultivate the lower [stages]. This further clarifies the realm of transforming others: whether they be sages or ordinary beings, if one wishes to benefit others, one must employ the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) to horizontally and vertically shatter their attachments;
only then can one exercise the four propositions of compassion for the sake of others. However, this benefiting of others differs in meaning from the subsequent "arising of the teaching.
The latter refers exclusively to the manifestation of the eight phases of the true reward body (vipākaphala-kāya) to reach sentient beings, thereby initiating the provisional and the real.

Regarding "bestowing, opening, abolishing," and so forth: this refers solely to the initial mind that, relying on principle, gives rise to understanding and is free from the grasping at intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

It is taught as the four [truths] for others, and it also extends to the subsequent mind; it remains within the stage of the fruit of cultivation, the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), where the four graspings at reality are destroyed. This is the teaching of the four [truths] according to the capacities of beings.
[Note] Although three objects are distinguished, they reside solely within the one mind. To employ contemplation to investigate them is precisely the cultivation of virtue.

For practitioners of the final age, there is no place for cultivating contemplation outside of the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*). The present text states that [the Buddha-nature] is "complete and without deficiency," which refers to the virtues of the nature (*xingde*).

This is [the realization of] emptiness, the provisional, and the middle; it is cultivation based upon the nature itself. As stated in the *Yishu* (Second Meaning): "The mind is endowed with the three thousand [dharmas]."

This is the provisional (the three thousand realms). (The contemplation of the provisional) is not the dharma-nature. (Arising from self) refers to ignorance. (Arising from other) refers to its being produced through the combination of self and other, or by excluding them.

(The contemplation of emptiness) regarding this emptiness and the provisional, where cessation and illumination are not partial, is called the Middle Way. (Text) Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*) explains the cultivation of merit, stating:
"That which cannot be attained is attained; the Three Truths are perfectly distinct. (Text) "Cannot be attained" means that the contemplation of emptiness negates deluded attachments. And...

That which is attained is the provisional contemplation of the nature of illumination. When illumination and negation are not biased, the Middle Way is present therein. As for the current omission of the clarification regarding the sphere of transforming others:
when one cultivates virtue and distances oneself from the four natures, there arises an understanding that does not obstruct the fourfold teaching; this is precisely the transformation of others.
[Note] This section reconciles the three realms through the present text. The first two phrases reconcile the realm of inherent virtue (*xing-de*).
The next two phrases reconcile the realm of inherent cultivation (*xing-xiu*). As cited in the *Yi-shu* (Commentary on the Meaning), this demonstrates that cultivation is identical to nature.

Furthermore, the *Fu-xing-ji* (Record of the Aids to Practice) provides additional evidence for the identity of cultivation and nature. The subsequent half-phrase clarifies the textual meaning of the *Fu-xing-ji*, though the current version lacks this clarification.
This indicates the point for transforming others. Although there is no explicit textual indication, it exists implicitly according to the meaning.
The intent is that within these three objects, the instruction to employ contemplation and investigate specifically pertains to the stage of cultivating virtue (*śikṣā*).

This is the jade-like teacher’s sincere heart, pointing out the starting point for practicing contemplation. Later generations [should understand] the three thousand realms in a single thought-moment as inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
It may appear as if clearly understood, yet one is unable to penetrate deeply because the fault lies in not employing the fourfold analysis (*catuskoṭi*).

This fourfold analysis consists in observing this aggregate: does it arise from the *dharmatā*, or from ignorance (*avidyā*), or from both *dharmatā* and ignorance together, or does it arise apart from them?
None of these can be found. It is precisely this "unfindability" [that constitutes the realization].
The locus is itself the inconceivable realm; it is itself the inconceivable contemplation.
If such a realm does not manifest before one, then repeatedly raise the four propositions to investigate walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, never departing from them for even a moment.

Diligently apply the five repentances regardless of the passage of days or months, until the three truths are attained with crystal clarity and the single mind has no place of attachment. Then, concealment and illumination occur simultaneously within the Dharma-realm.

"Dònglǎng (Penetrating Clarity). This is the functional aspect of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Once the true mind has been attained, by taking the true object as its condition, then true conditions will naturally arise in succession.
True states flow one after another, and momentary thoughts follow one another without interval. How could there be anything that does not enter into the true principle?
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) asks: "In the previous section on 'objective realms' (*svabhāva-viṣaya*) and in the preceding analysis by Zhǎn’ān, it was stated in each case that [the mind] is one..."
The mind is spontaneously and fully endowed [with all phenomena]. How can it now be examined by confronting its objects? Answer:

Here, we are precisely examining the arising of a single thought-moment which already possesses the three thousand realms. Therefore, we examine this endowment to determine whether it is the mind or the conditions. If one examines its arising:
Arising cannot be apprehended; mindfulness and the three thousand [dharmas] are both unapprehendable. To attain through non-attainment, the Three Truths are perfectly manifest.
One must know that the fourfold negation—"if one investigates this arising, arising is unapprehendable"—is precisely the application of contemplation to seek out reality.

The two phrases, "not obtaining yet obtaining," precisely represent the simultaneous nature of cessation and illumination (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). This is the moment when the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is brilliantly clear.

From this point, one gives rise to the stages of faith, contemplation, practice, and realization—both the semblance and the partially true levels—without ever departing from this境 (realm/境). This constitutes the person of superior faculties.

If, after pushing [the mind] forward, it still does not enter and dullness and distraction increase further, then one should give rise to great vows to assist the contemplation and settle the mind through the skillful means of the general and the specific.

If it still cannot enter, this must be due to the obstruction of dharmas; therefore, use the gate of non-arising to universally break them down and examine them by distinguishing between what is penetrating and what is obstructed.
Furthermore, apply the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment in their proper sequence.
Adjusting and testing: there are eighty-four thousand matters that serve as remedies to assist in the opening [of the path].

If one can act in this way, there will be none who fail to attain realization—namely, those of medium capacity, whether two or seven [lifetimes]. As for those of inferior capacity who employ all ten [stages], these are also categorized according to a general classification.
Therefore, the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice) says: "For those of medium and inferior capacities, further methods are required; it is not necessarily [the case otherwise]."
Fix the mind firmly. Furthermore, during the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), an object will inevitably arise—such as afflictions, views, meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), and so forth.
If the mind is settled in the Truths (*satya*), there is no need to change it. However, if the object is powerful and the contemplation is weak, one should then employ the object that has arisen.
Within the practice of relying on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), one specifically takes it as contemplation so that the objective realm dissolves and returns to the inconceivable;
or, one may enter realization through the very realm that has been manifested. This is for the practitioner to examine for themselves; this is the essential point for initiating cultivation.
Do not weary of detail; please do not omit anything. This concludes the explanation of the Inconceivable Realm.
II. Truly and Correctly Arousing the Bodhicitta.
This refers to relying upon the wondrous realm to arouse the four great vows of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Out of compassion for oneself...

Out of compassion for others, one seeks the higher [enlightenment] and transforms those below. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, above it, one spreads out a canopy. [Fǔxíng Commentary, Vol. 5, Part 14] Question:
One should first give rise to the vow and subsequently contemplate the wondrous object. Why is it that the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) is mentioned only after the object?

Answer: It is not that the mind is not aroused prior to the object; this is fully in accordance with the meaning found in the *Wǔlüè* (Five Abridgments). What is stated here is the arousal of the mind in its most profound sense.
The contemplation is accomplished; therefore, one must rely on principle to benefit others (text). [Commentary] The *Fuxing* says:
"First, to give rise to a great resolve and to set out toward that which is expected is called 'initiation' (*fa*). Not relying on the path of the teachings is called 'true' (*zhen*).
Relying on the principle of the three truths is called 'correct' (*zheng*). Bodhi is precisely the fruit expected; it is the wondrous object."

This is precisely the path upon which one travels. The mind is that which can travel and can proceed toward it. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have followed after the defilements of sensory objects;
they do not know that the essence of non-conditioning pervades the entire Dharma-realm, but instead follow only the realm of deliberative cognition belonging to the deluded self.

Now, relying on the sacred teaching, one turns away from delusion; therefore, it is called "arousing" (*fa*). To regulate this contemplative knowledge so that one seeks the higher and transforms those below is also called "arousing.
Regarding the five summarized meanings: these refer to using the five summaries to encompass the ten detailed expositions—namely, first, the general meaning;
second, the explanation of names; third, the essential nature and characteristics; fourth, the inclusion of all phenomena; and fifth, the partial and the perfect. This is "arousing."
1. Great Resolve; 2. Six Expedient Means; 3. Right Cultivation, which is the cultivation of the great practice; 4. Fruition, which is the realization of the great fruit; 5.

Arising of Teaching, which is the tearing asunder of the great net; 6. Ultimate Destination, which is the returning to the great place. Therefore, it is not that one does not resolve before these objects.
Now, by resolving for the "lower," one correctly answers the reason for resolving for the future.

[Commentary] The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states in the fifth fascicle: "If one contemplates the object of practice (*ālambana*) and does not attain awakening, one must further cultivate the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Since this person has, from time immemorial, given rise to great vows, they now require a renewed vow because their contemplation of the object does not accord with the principle. Within stillness, they should contemplate 'self' and 'other.'"

To alleviate the pain of others' obstructions, throughout immeasurable kalpas I have wandered and revolved within birth and death; even when I gave rise to a small aspiration, I became deluded regarding the bodhicitta.
Although I now possess this knowledge, my practice remains incomplete; therefore, I again make this vow, and so forth. (Text)

[Commentary] This citation indicates the purpose of restating the vows after clarifying the objects of the realm. First, it clarifies that because his own practice of contemplation did not accord with the objective, he restated his vow.
Second, it clarifies that because his practices for benefiting both himself and others were not yet complete, he restated his vow.
Regarding the phrase "contemplating with aching pain," the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states: "Contemplation is the beginning of the great vow; aching pain is..."
The compassionate vow has been cultivated until it is perfected. "Choking" refers to a fishbone piercing the throat; "painful" refers to the extreme intensity of injury and suffering.
For this reason, he again makes a solemn vow.
[Commentary] Regarding "spreading out canopies and awnings," the *Wenju* (Volume 5, Section 27) states: "This is a metaphor for the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*). Among all virtues..."
Compassion is supreme; it universally covers all.
[Commentary] This explains the phrase "spreading the canopy": because compassion can protect and shelter all beings, it is like a canopy that provides shade and cover for everything.
△ Third, the skillful settling of the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding the skillful settling of the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: it means that realizing the wondrous principle mentioned previously as being eternally quiescent is called "concentration" (*samādhi*).
That which is quiescent yet constantly illuminating is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Therefore, a sutra says: "Place a vermilion pillow (the pillow used in a carriage) [upon your head]."
[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), fascicle 5, part 17, states: "One skillfully brings peace to the mind through the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);

therefore, it is called 'peace of mind' (*anxin*). (Text). The *Daiyi* (Great Meaning), fascicle 6, states: "Regarding 'peace of mind,' there is first the general [explanation], followed by the specific. As for the general:

taking the *dharmadhātu* as that which is to be pacified, and taking tranquil illumination (*jizhao*) as that which performs the pacifying. If one knows that the fundamental nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is intrinsically pure, this is called..."
Its quiescence is its intrinsic nature, which is like space; its illumination is what it is named for. These afflictions and the cycle of birth and death are further named the *dharmadhātu*.

This is the mutual manifestation of the essence and function of the *dharmadhātu*: the essence is the *dharmadhātu* that is established, while the function is the quiescence and illumination that establish it.
As for what is called "distinct," although they are thus established, they become increasingly obscure and increasingly dispersed; this is truly due to the habitual tendencies from time immemorial.
They are not the same. Therefore, we now follow their natures and settle them accordingly: namely, that they should listen, reflect, remain in stillness, and illuminate;

according to their inclinations, according to what requires treatment, and according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Why is this? Because there are those for whom roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) increase due to stillness and illumination, while for others they do not increase;

there are those for whom afflictions (*kleśa*) are destroyed by stillness and illumination, while for others they are not destroyed. It is the same regarding the vision of principle (*tattva*): for some...

It is through hearing and reflection that one turns [toward awakening]. Alternatively, hearing and reflection support one another; these cannot be fully realized at once, but must be sought out in detail before they are understood.
(Text) The present passage briefly clarifies the general method of settling the mind (*anxin*); therefore, it speaks of "permanence," "constancy," and so forth.
[Commentary] This explains the skillful method for settling the mind. First, regarding the initial practice, I have briefly cited the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) to provide a general explanation.
Below, I shall present in detail the general and specific methods for settling the mind. First, two lines indicate the headings; next, four lines explain the general settling of the mind.
The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "In the initial 'General Establishment,' it is simply that the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*) is first emphasized as the object of establishment.

What is this essence of the Dharma? It is the wondrous object (*myōkyō*). If one knows that the fundamental nature of afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is pure, this is called 'quiescence' (*jaku*);
this explains the quiescence that performs the establishing. This is what the text of the *Zhiguan* says: 'Ignorance and delusive confusion are, in their original nature, [pure]...'"
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā), through the delusion of ignorance, transforms into avidyā, giving rise to various inversions such as the wholesome and the unwholesome.
It is like the arrival of cold that causes water to solidify into ice; or like the onset of sleep that transforms it into dreaming.
Now, one should realize that all afflictions are themselves the nature of phenomena—neither identical nor different—even though they arise and cease through inversion. Just as...
It is like a whirling firebrand; one does not believe in the arising and ceasing of delusions, but believes only in this mind as being solely the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).
Its arising is the arising of the dharma-nature; its ceasing is the ceasing of the dharma-nature. In reality, it neither arises nor ceases;
