what is falsely called arising and ceasing is merely a designation for deluded thought, which is itself the dharma-nature. Thus, one binds the dharma-nature with the dharma-nature, and contemplates the dharma-nature with the dharma-nature.
This is eternally the dharma-nature; there is no time when it is not the dharma-nature. Once its essence is fully realized, one neither grasps at delusive thoughts nor grasps at the dharma-nature.
Returning to the source and reverting to the root, the entire dharma-realm is simultaneously quiescent. This is called *śamatha*. When one abides in such *śamatha*,...
All transmigration is brought to rest. That "the original nature is like space" refers to the illuminator; this explains the illumination that brings about tranquility.
The *Zhiguan* states: "Observation" means observing the mind of ignorance. Looking upward, one sees that the dharma-nature is fundamentally empty;
looking downward, one sees that all good and evil deluded thoughts are like empty space—non-dual and without distinction. This is...
It says: "When the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is profoundly clear and all things are universally illuminated, this is called 'contemplation' (vipaśyanā).

That these afflictions and birth-and-death are further termed the 'Dharma-realm' clarifies that the essence of cessation (śamatha) and contemplation is one. This explains that the Dharma-realm in which one rests has no separate essence;
it is precisely by taking what was previously realized as the object of contemplation that it is further termed the 'Dharma-realm. This is the function of that which is able to rest."
Regarding "quiescence and illumination" (寂照): although they are called quiescence and illumination, their essence is not distinct.

As for what is termed *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, *śamatha* is simply wisdom (*jñāna*), and wisdom is simply *śamatha*. Immovable *śamatha* is immovable wisdom; immovable wisdom is immovable *śamatha*. The *Fuxing* commentary explains:
"Though non-dual, they are treated as two; quiescence and illumination are without difference. This refers to the mutual interpenetration of the essence and function of this very *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the phrase "manifesting, etc.": this clarifies that both *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) equally illuminate the *dharmatā*.
Since the *dharmatā* inherently possesses the function of quiescence and illumination, it is able to manifest its functional utility from its essence.

Because quiescence and illumination are not separate from the essence of the *dharmatā*, one takes quiescence and illumination as the means of stabilization while correctly abiding in the *dharmatā*. This is as it is said: "Immovable Wisdom illuminates the *dharmatā*. That is to say—

The attainment of peace through contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā*) is also the peace of tranquility (*śamatha*). Being unmoving in accordance with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is the peace of tranquility;
it is also the peace of contemplation. These two are non-dual and without distinction. Next, the five practices explain the specific method of settling the mind (*anushthāna*).

First, half of the initial practice clarifies the basis for the specific settling of the mind, first stating its specific intent: although one settles the mind by means of the nature of phenomena, it remains increasingly obscure when contrasted with contemplation.
This is what is meant by "dispersing" and "stopping. It arises precisely because, since beginningless time, habitual tendencies have differed:
some have practiced hearing the Dharma, some have practiced seated meditation, and some have practiced *śamatha* (calm abiding) or *vipaśyanā* (insight); these various differences exist.

Therefore, we now employ the four *siddhāntas* (the four methods of teaching) to fulfill their respective aspirations and settle them accordingly. As it says in the *Zhi Guan*: "The spirit and mind are darkly [unified]..."

Obscure. "Suoli" (梭利) means to be dazed and bewildered. "Suo" (梭) means haste. Rising and ceasing in rapid succession, it is difficult to grasp; departing and arriving in an instant, it is not easy to restrain.
Even though one attempts to stop it, it rushes away with fiery speed; even though one attempts to observe it, it is darker than lacquer or ink.

Though effort is applied with extreme diligence, the dispersion of delusions only increases twofold. The enemy is strong while one's own strength is weak; like the warbler and the clam locking horns, once [the situation] has reached this point...
One must not advance, nor may one retreat. One should sacrifice one’s life to serve the Way, offering up one’s flesh and bones.
Vowing to skillfully settle the mind and employing expedient means to transform it, one brings it into accord, thereby achieving the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

This refers to the following section, which introduces the characteristics of the Fourfold *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (the four *siddhārtha* methods), as found in the "Transforming Others" chapter of the *Mohe Zhiguan*, where there are eight turns for the sake of faith and practice (*śraddhā-carita*).
For individuals, one preaches the calming and contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) that pacifies the mind according to the four *siddhāntas*.

There are eight variations for those who follow the Dharma by way of practice (*dharmānusārin*), wherein one preaches the calming and contemplation that pacify the mind according to the four *siddhāntas*. The *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:

"The characteristics of the calming and contemplation of the Dharma-faith are established as a method for instructing others for the sake of future generations. "Those who should listen and reflect" refers to those who follow the Dharma through faith (*śraddhānusārin*).

Their practices differ. The *Zhiguan* states: "If one has little personal insight into the Dharma but relies heavily on the power of hearing [the teachings], and later attains awakening through hearing the Dharma, this is called 'practice through faith' (*śraddhā-carita*).

If one has little reliance on the power of hearing but possesses much personal insight into the Dharma, and later attains awakening through contemplation, this is called 'practice through the Dharma' (*dharma-carita*).
To investigate their origins from afar: having listened and studied for many kalpas and practiced seated meditation for many kalpas, one comes to possess faith.
The seeds of the Dharma, through repeated cultivation from lifetime to lifetime, become the nature of the roots. Each attains awakening through hearing and reflection.
The teacher should ask: "Regarding concentration and wisdom, what do you aspire to?

If they say, "I have heard the Buddha teach that a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is like the light of the moon’s form, gradually becoming full; and like a ladder, gradually ascending higher," [the teacher should respond with skillful means].

To speak of transforming the human mind: attaining the Way depends entirely upon causes and conditions. When one’s aspiration is joyful and thirsty for understanding—like a calf following its mother—one should know that such a person is a "practitioner by faith" (*śraddhānusārī*).
If one says, "I have heard the Buddha's teaching," it is like a bright mirror: its substance is unmoving, yet forms and images appear clearly;
or like clear water without ripples, where fish and stones manifest of themselves. One joyfully abandons unwholesome thoughts as if discarding [filth].

The heavy burden—know that this refers to the practitioner of the Dharma (dharmānusārin). For the practitioner of the Dharma, one should reflect; for the practitioner through faith (śraddhānusārin), one should listen.

Regarding "being fit for tranquility and fit for illumination," this refers to what is called *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*; or, according to what is most suitable, one should settle the mind through tranquility.

Alternatively, it may follow what is convenient; this refers to settling the mind through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The above constitutes the *puruṣapudgala-siddhānta* (the standpoint according to the person).
Following inclinations and so forth constitutes the three *siddhāntas*. As stated in the *Zhi guan*: "Either following one's inclination, one settles the mind through calming (*śamatha*);

or following one's inclination, one settles the mind through contemplation; or following the application of remedies, one settles the mind through either calming or contemplation; or following the stages..."

This is the first meaning. To settle the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one knows that according to their respective root-natures (*gotra*), there are eight ways of settling the mind for a single person;
when combined with those of the faith-practitioner (*śraddhā-carita*) and the dharma-practitioner (*dharmānusārin*), there are sixteen ways of settling the mind.

"For what reason? and so forth is the general inquiry. The reasons for employing the four *siddhārtha* (fourfold means of integration) are as can be seen in the text. Next, the five phrases explain what is appropriate.
"Quiescent illumination. Within this text, one can discern [the stages of] the world, the generation of goodness, the destruction of evil, and the entry into principle.

The following two lines explain what is suitable for hearing and reflection (*śruta* and *cintā*). Regarding those who turn back from hearing and reflection, the text on the practice of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* states:
"The mental activities of sentient beings are not fixed; they may be dull for a moment and sharp for a moment, occurring spontaneously and naturally of their own accord. It is not...

Regarding the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*): it may not be achieved through repeated practice, or one’s contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) may lack penetration, leading instead to awakening through hearing from a teacher;

or, despite long-term listening, one may fail to understand until a momentary reflection brings resolution. For these reasons, the transformation of faculties and the settling of the mind (*citta-praśamana*) are discussed further.

If one of the Dharma-practitioner type (*dharmānusārin*) transforms into a faith-practitioner type (*śraddhānusārin*), the transformation follows their specific faculty, and they are granted the settling of the mind by employing the eightfold *siddhānta*. If it is a faith-practitioner who transforms...

The accomplishment of the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*) also proceeds according to the faculties (*indriya*). By employing the eight methods of settling the mind (*citta-sthāpana*), one attains this profound meaning and may explain it at length or in brief as one pleases.
Regarding whether these methods involve shifting or not shifting, there are in total thirty-two ways of settling the mind. Furthermore, it says within the section on the four shifts:

If the mind that practices according to the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*) transforms into the mind that practices through faith (*śraddhācaryā*), or if the mind that practices through faith transforms into the mind that practices according to the Dharma, one should skillfully investigate each according to what is appropriate for it.
There are thirty-two [aspects] for one's own practice and thirty-two for transforming others; these combined constitute the sixty-four points of settling the mind (*cittasthiti*).
Regarding the mutual support of hearing and reflection: if the Dharma is predominant and faith is scarce, this is called "faith supported by the Dharma" (*śraddhopastabdha-dharma*).

When faith is abundant and the Dharma is meager, this is called "the Dharma supporting faith. Since it is said that they support one another, it means that both the practice of faith and the practice of the Dharma are mutually beneficial.
As the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Faith and the Dharma do not exist in isolation; they must support one another through hearing and reflection.
This means that in the practice of the Dharma, hearing supports reflection, while in the practice of faith, reflection supports hearing. Within this mutual support, furthermore...

Regarding the discussion of turning and not turning, there are likewise thirty-two ways of settling the mind (*anxin*). Regarding the mutual support of transforming others, there are also thirty-two. Combined, these make sixty-four;
together with the preceding, they total one hundred and twenty-eight ways of settling the mind. The *Text on Stopping and Contemplation* (*Zhiguan wen*) states:
"If stopping (*shi*) is separated from the three truths, there is no place for settling the mind. If one is separated from stopping and contemplation (*zhiguan*), there is no settling of the mind."
Regarding the Dharma: if one settles the mind within the Truths (*satya*), a single phrase suffices. If one cannot so settle it, there are skillful means to bring the mind to rest.

Furthermore, by means of the three sequential contemplations (*anupūrva-vipaśyanā*) to clarify the three non-sequential contemplations (*ananupūrva-vipaśyanā*), with one hundred and twenty-eight [methods] for each, there are five hundred and twelve variations of discourse on the settling of the mind through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. [The final two...]
[End of] sentence. This concludes the brief exhortation to seek out the extensive text. The phrase "now, below the text" is a term used to conclude the reference.

[Commentary] Regarding "placing a vermilion pillow," the *Wenju* (Volume 5, Section 27) states: "If one uses a pillow within a carriage to rest the body and head, it is analogous to the *Ekavyūha Samādhi*, which brings rest to all wisdom and all practices."

[Supplement] This explains, by means of the *ekavyūha-samādhi*, the significance of placing a vermilion pillow. To speak of "one practice" (*ekavyūha*) means to directly take the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as one's object.

The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "Simply binding the object to a single thought-moment of the *dharmadhātu*; binding the object to the *dharmadhātu* is *śamatha*, and the single thought-moment is *vipaśyanā*.
For although there is binding and although there is mindfulness, they do not transcend the *dharmadhātu*; although there is *śamatha* and..."
Contemplation: tranquility and illumination are simultaneous; this is called the "single practice.
[Note] "Cinnabar" (dan) refers to red light, which serves as a metaphor for the dharma of non-discrimination. The *Miaole* (Wondrous Joy), fascicle 6, section 24, states:

"Wisdom is the head and practice is the body; samādhi is like a pillow. That which rests upon it attains the principle, for such is the nature of the Dharma-principle. As for 'red light' and so forth, there is no other dharma."

The space between is called "non-discrimination. Since light is used as a metaphor for wisdom, it is termed "wisdom-light" (*jñāna-prabhā*). Because red is positioned between black and purple, crimson is used here to represent light that is free from admixture.
The *Nanshan Zhujing Yin* (Pronunciation Guide to the Scriptures by Nanshan) states: "In the Western Regions, there are no wooden pillows; they are all made from red leather."
The interior is stuffed with cotton wool for the purpose of reclining and sleeping. It is red and glossy. (Text) *Fuxing* 7b (27) states:
"If one uses a pillow within the carriage to rest all activities, this is precisely 'settling the mind' (*anxin*)."

[Commentary] This explains the meaning of the "red pillow" (*dan-zhen*) from the sutra text. The first line cites the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) for the primary explanation; "Miaole" (Joyful Subtlety) below provides a further explanation;
and "Fuxing" (Aid to Practice) below provides a reconciliatory explanation. The intent is that resting upon an inner pillow is precisely the "settling of the mind" (*anxin*).
△ Fourth, the pervasiveness of destroying delusions.

Regarding the pervasiveness of destroying delusions: this means that by means of the three contemplations, one destroys the three delusions. These three contemplations are unified within a single mind; there is no delusion that is not destroyed.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Its swiftness is like the wind."

[Commentary] The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states in section seven: "Among the various gates of the manifold teachings, each 'great' category has four [aspects], extending even to eighty-four thousand different types.

There is not one that does not take non-arising (*anutpāda*) as its primary principle. Now, we shall follow this from the beginning: within the gate of non-arising, one universally destroys all delusions;

furthermore, by means of non-arising, one enters the remaining gates. Thus, both vertically and horizontally, all are destroyed, causing the essence of consciousness to be pervasive throughout. (Text)

[Commentary] The *Zhiguan* states: Regarding the "pervasive destruction of dharmas," the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is pure; it is neither conjoined nor dispersed, severed from the path of language, and extinguished as the sphere of mental activity.
It is neither destroyed nor not destroyed. Why, then, do we speak of "destruction"? It is simply because sentient beings are largely subject to inversions.
Because it is not inverted from the start, it destroys inversion and causes one to be non-inverted; therefore, it is said that "the destruction of phenomena is universal.
When the aforementioned skillful settling of the mind is achieved, concentration and wisdom are developed, and there is no need for further destruction.

If one has not yet attained such correspondence, one should employ the wisdom inherent in concentration to purify it completely; thus, it is said to "destroy. Furthermore, regarding the inconceivable realm, it is a single realm and a single...

The realm of all things. All minds, whether horizontal or vertical, and all phenomena, entirely converge within the mind. When the mind is shattered, everything is shattered; therefore, it is said to be "pervasive.

From the phrase "it is said that" below, the vertical is briefly explained as encompassing the horizontal. From "the three contemplations" below, the non-duality of the one mind—both horizontal and vertical—is pointed out and shown.
When there is no delusion left unshattered, then there is no phenomenon that is not revealed. This is the self-nature of cessation and illumination.
When delusions are destroyed, one can advance; one can destroy the "unpeak" (anuttara) fall, which is precisely the destruction of the ignorance of attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
Entering the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge), one gives rise to true and rapid progress; this is what is called "swift as the wind.

Regarding the statement that each of the various gates of the manifold teachings has four [aspects], the text on *śamatha-vipaśyanā* says: "Furthermore, in destroying dharmas, one must rely upon gates; the sūtras present different explanations."
Sometimes letters serve as the gateway, as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, where the forty-two characters are such a gateway.

Sometimes the practice of contemplation serves as the gateway, as in the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), which clarifies that Bodhisattvas cultivate the three samādhis by taking the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as their object.

Sometimes wisdom serves as the gateway, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, where it says, "its gateway of wisdom. These variations extend even to the eighty-four thousand different [teachings]. This...

This refers to the expansion of the various gates; that is to say, sentient beings have eighty-four thousand afflictions and defilements, and the Buddhas possess eighty-four thousand gates of *pāramitā*.
There are none among them that do not take non-arising (*anutpāda*) as their primary principle.

The *Zhiguan* states: "The Gate of Non-arising can lead one through both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, reaching from the causal stage to the fruition. Furthermore, it can manifest non-arising so that the gate may shine forth.

*Śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are practice; the Gate of Non-arising is the teaching. By practicing in reliance upon the teaching, one penetrates to the realization of the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby perfecting the causal stage.
For now, we shall follow the beginning by universally refuting all [views] within the Gate of Non-arising."

Regarding the "confused": the *Zhi guan* states: "First, the gate of non-arising (*anutpāda*). From beginning to end, exhausting its source and bottom—this is the 'vertical pervasiveness of breaking through dharmas' (*shu po fa bian*).
Regarding "entering all gates by means of non-arising," the *Zhi guan* states: "Second, traversing the various dharma-gates.
Within each gate, from beginning to end, exhausting its source and bottom—this is the 'horizontal pervasiveness of breaking through dharmas' (*heng po fa bian*). This is precisely...
By practicing this single mind and threefold contemplation through other gateways, one is likewise able to universally shatter [delusions]; hence it is called "transcending and entering.

Regarding "shattering both horizontally and vertically so that the essence of consciousness is pervasive," the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: "The three horizontal and vertical [dimensions] are non-dual from beginning to end."
To exhaust its source and bottom means that it is neither horizontal nor vertical, yet it pervades all phenomena. "Vertical" refers to height; "horizontal" refers to breadth.
When the vertical enters the horizontal, there is no horizontal that is not high. When the horizontal enters the vertical, there is no vertical that is not broad. This is what is meant.

[Commentary] The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary), Fascicle 7, Part 1 (6), states: "Now, one mind possesses the three [contemplations], thereby subverting the sequential three. Hence it is called 'one mind, three contemplations. As for subverting the vertical [sequence] of penetration and obstruction:

the three contemplations that can subvert the horizontal [distinctions] are those where the three contemplations are separated and assigned to three different persons, all of whom remain at the initial stage;
thus, the three do not coincide as one. Now, because the three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) are one, this subverts that [sequential view]."
They are divided into three; thus it is said that "the three contemplations are one mind.

One should know that "one mind and the three contemplations" and "the three contemplations and one mind" are identical in principle despite their reciprocal phrasing, being spoken as mutual counterparts to refute both horizontal and vertical [delusions] (text).

[Commentary] This cites the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) to elucidate, through mutual illustration, the horizontal and vertical aspects of penetration and obstruction. First, it addresses the vertical penetration and obstruction of the sequential [stages]. Regarding "the threefold contemplation within one mind":
the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) and birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) constitute obstruction;

the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*pratītyasamutpāda*) constitutes penetration. Ignorance and birth-and-death through skillful means (*upāya-jāti-maraṇa*) constitute obstruction; the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitutes penetration.
Penetration (*tong*). Ignorance, the causes and conditions of birth and death, and so forth constitute the obstruction (*se*); the Middle Way and correct contemplation constitute penetration.

When practitioners successively cultivate the breaking [of these obstructions], it is called "vertically penetrating the obstructions. Question: These three obstructive dharmas must naturally be broken;
however, why must the dharma of penetration also necessarily be broken? Answer: Although these three penetrative dharmas can break the three delusions when cultivated, they nonetheless...
This is the third penetration (*abhijñā*). If one examines it with respect to a single mind, the penetration remains obstructed; therefore, the vertical penetration enters gradually.
Although it belongs to a single person, there is a sequence of before and after, such that the three periods are each distinct. Because they are each distinct, it is not a single mind.
Therefore, now, by means of the three contemplations within a single mind, one breaks through the vertical obstructions and openings.

Next, for two and a half lines, by means of the single mind within the three contemplations, one breaks through the three horizontal obstructions and openings that are divided and scattered: suffering and accumulation are obstructions, while the path and cessation are openings.

Ignorance within the twelve links of dependent origination constitutes obstruction; the cessation of ignorance constitutes penetration. The six hindrances covering the mind constitute obstruction; the six perfections constitute penetration.
Even this penetration must be further broken through, for one uses the three contemplations to break the three delusions; although it is fundamentally penetration, it must still be overcome.
Having already departed from the three distinct persons, if one does not know that the three contemplations are the one mind, then the pervasive will again become obstructed.
Now, the one mind and the three contemplations are used to break this through. The phrase "one should know" below is an exhortation;

its meaning is that the two phrases "one mind and three contemplations" and "three contemplations and one mind" are mutually interwoven to manifest the breaking of horizontal and vertical [distinctions]. This is logically appropriate.
It is sufficient to understand this through the mind.
[□ Note] One practices within the Eightfold Noble Path and swiftly arrives at *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge); therefore, it is said that "its swiftness is like the wind.
[■ Record] This refers to the swift accomplishment of merit through the threefold contemplation within a single mind; from cause to fruit, one proceeds via the Eightfold Noble Path.
This is the Middle Way. △ Five.
Penetration and Obstruction of the Five Consciousnesses.

Regarding the penetration and obstruction of the five consciousnesses: suffering, accumulation, the twelve links of dependent origination, the six obscurations, the dust-sands [of afflictions], and ignorance constitute obstruction; the Path constitutes penetration.

Cessation. Wisdom regarding the causes and conditions of cessation. The six perfections. One mind and three contemplations. These constitute "penetration. If there is penetration, it must be protected; if there is obstruction, it must be broken.

When obstructions arise within penetration, one must be able to break them just as one breaks what is to be broken. Examining and verifying at every stage is called "recognizing penetration and obstruction. As the Sūtra says:
Place a red pillow (the pillow for the exterior of the carriage).

[Commentary] Regarding the "passing through and being obstructed" of the five consciousnesses: this means that suffering (*duḥkha*) is the fruit of the origin (*samudaya*), and the origin is the cause of suffering.
Cause and effect entangle one another; this is the cause of birth and death, and is termed an "obstruction. This obstruction must be broken.
The twelve links of dependent origination are like twelve concentric walls; when they are firmly established, one cannot advance. The six hindrances obscure the mind-nature of the practitioner.
The dust and sand obstruct the practitioner's eye of the Path. Ignorance clouds the wondrous principle of the Dharma-nature. These constitute obstructions; only when the Path is [clear]...
The cessation of the causes of the household is the fruit of the Daoist path. When cause and effect are interconnected, one can reach the place of treasure.

Through the wisdom that ceases causal conditions, one can clarify the mind and perceive its nature. The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) ferry one across this shore of birth and death to reach that other shore of nirvāṇa.
With single-mindedness and the three contemplations, one breaks through the views, afflictions, and the dust-like ignorance to attain penetration. If...
That which is open must be protected; that which is obstructed must be broken through. Within the cessation of the path, to give rise to attachment is called an obstruction.

This obstruction must be broken through. To break through what has become an obstruction to the open passage—breaking it just as one would break anything else—and to examine and verify this step by step, is called "discerning the open and the obstructed."

[Commentary] The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states in section seven: "Although one knows that birth-and-death and afflictions constitute obstructions (*saṃvara*) and that bodhi and nirvāṇa constitute the path (*mārga*), one must further recognize that the path can give rise to obstructions.
These obstructions must be destroyed; from within obstruction, the path is attained, and this path must be protected.

It is like the case where a general becomes a bandit—how could such a general remain [as a general]? Or if a bandit becomes a general—how could such a bandit be destroyed? One must examine and verify this at every stage. There is no [other way].

This causes attachment to arise. Because of attachment, there is obstruction; by breaking through obstruction, one preserves penetration. This is not a single fixed path. It is thus for all who possess a mind.
In every thought-moment, one must constantly examine and verify what is obstructed and what is penetrated. (Text)

[Commentary] This explains the penetration and obstruction of consciousness (*vijñāna*). The first line allows for the horizontal and vertical penetration and obstruction of that which is already known.
The subsequent three lines demonstrate that one must recognize how obstruction arises from penetration, as stated in the *Zhi guan*:

"If one is like the non-Buddhists who are attached to the wisdom of contemplating emptiness, one should universally shatter it with the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*); the means of shattering should be like that which is shattered, so that all obstructions may be removed."
Penetration. If one does not cling to the wisdom that contemplates emptiness, then one can destroy what is not as it should be destroyed.

One merely removes obstructions while preserving penetration, like removing the film to nurture a pearl, or destroying rebels to protect a general. If the general himself were to become a rebel, then that rebel must also be destroyed.
If the thief acts as the general, this general will likewise protect [the thief]. Thus, by turning back upon one another, all generals become thieves; they are broken down section by section.

Therefore, in the *Dà yì* (Great Meaning), only the universal breaking is mentioned. The *Fǔ xíng* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "The first is the general path of both penetration and obstruction."
Taking that which is to be refuted as "obstruction" (sai) and that which is able to refute it as "penetration" (tsū). These two are the specific characteristics of obstruction and penetration.

Taking the arising of attachment to that which is able to refute as obstruction, and non-attachment as penetration. Since the characteristics of dharmas have varying depths, there will inevitably be instances of penetration and obstruction;

therefore, one must examine and verify at every stage so as not to allow attachment to arise. Regarding what is called "examining and verifying at every stage," the *Zhiguan* states: "By means of the horizontal..."
Weave vertically and inspect for obstructions and openings. This is like entering from the provisional into the empty to destroy delusions.

Furthermore, use horizontal weaving and vertical inspection to enter from the empty into the provisional to observe obstructions and openings. Again, use horizontal weaving and vertical inspection for the correct observation of the Middle Way.
It is said that for each and every phenomenon (dharma), each and every capacity, and each and every object, if the three obstructions arise, one must break them to allow passage;

if the three passages are open, one must nurture them to bring them to fulfillment. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "First, horizontal passage and obstruction; second, vertical passage and obstruction."
The third is the distinction between the obstructions and the openings of the three horizontal [delusions]; the fourth is the obstruction and opening of the single mind.
In all cases, one must examine them through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). If obstructions arise within the four openings, one must break through those obstructions to preserve the openings.

Proceeding thus in succession, one takes the breaking [of obstructions] as the goal. Therefore, regarding each capacity, each object, and each thought, one must conduct this examination. Furthermore...
This must be analyzed through four propositions: first, obstruction within penetration; second, penetration within obstruction;
third, obstruction that is self-obstruction; fourth, penetration that is self-penetration. The first two propositions concern the mutual obstruction and penetration of the particular;

the latter two concern the universal penetration once obstruction has been broken. Therefore, it is said that there is not only one path. Since all who possess a mind have [this capacity], it is thus.
One must constantly examine and reflect upon this in every thought-moment.
[Commentary] Regarding the placement of the vermilion pillow, the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), fascicle five (27), states: "When a carriage is driven and transported, wherever it reaches,"
"One must brace the *zhī'áng*. This is like being in motion yet still, and being still yet in motion. (From the *Wénjué*, Fascicle 6, Section 24):

"The *Dānzhěn* says that 'bracing the *zhī'áng*' refers to the pillow outside the carriage. When the carriage stops, it must be braced; one braces it for fear that it might tip upward, hence it is called 'bracing the *zhī'áng*.
*Zhī* means to support; *'áng*' means to lift. As for the analogy of the mutual identity of motion and stillness: when the carriage moves, the pillow is at rest—this is motion [within stillness]."
Yet it is quiescent. When the carriage stops, its function as a pillow is employed; thus, while quiescent, it moves. At the time of its activity, it is always quiescent;

at the time of its stillness, it is always moving. The reality-essence and its function are likewise so. From cause to effect, the dharma-nature is unmoving; therefore, it is like the wind that does not shift.
It arrives in stillness; the myriad practices are without action, and the various wisdoms cannot observe it. This is because the three virtues are all non-dual.
It is precisely because the three are identical to the one that it is thus. (Text: *Fuxing* 7b [27] states: "If the pillow is outside the carriage...")
"Either moving or still; movement and stillness are simply the meanings of penetration and obstruction" (Text).
[Commentary] This explains the passage in the sutra concerning "placing a vermilion pillow. The first three and a half lines provide the direct explanation of the text.

From "Miaole" (Wondrous Joy) onwards, it provides a further interpretation. The first three and a half lines cite a metaphor to explain the meaning: the essential substance and its function are likewise so.

These two phrases correspond to the principle and the phenomenon. "Substantial entity" refers to the nature (*prakṛti*); it corresponds to the carriage. "Function" refers to cultivation; it corresponds to the pillow.

Since the carriage and the pillow are such that movement is itself stillness and stillness is itself movement—where movement and stillness are non-dual—so too are the substantial entity and its function.
It is precisely nature while practicing, and practice while being nature; nature and practice are non-dual. Therefore, it is said, "it is likewise so.

From the line beginning with "from its own cause" for two stanzas, the non-duality of the three virtues is clarified: the Dharma-body is the essence. Since it is said that one arrives at it through stillness, it is movement within stillness.
Prajñā and liberation are the function. Since it is said that the myriad practices are without effort, [they are activity within non-action].
When no wisdom can observe it, then movement is itself stillness. Since essence and function are mutually identical, it is said that the three virtues are all non-dual.

The final two lines conclude by clarifying the reason for this non-duality. In the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary), the reconciliation of movement and stillness corresponds to the meaning of "penetration" (*tong*) and "obstruction" (*se*).
△ Section on the Harmonization of the Six Realms.

Regarding the harmonization of the six realms: this refers to the individual adjustment and balancing of each factor of the path of non-action (anabhisaṃskāra-mārga), entering them according to what is appropriate. As the Sūtra says:
There is the great white ox, etc. (The above five refer to those of middling capacity).

[Commentary] The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states in section seven: "To refute [the self] by means of the universal gate while remaining ignorant of the underlying principle is insufficient; one must instead subject [the practitioner] to sequential training through the seven categories (*saptavastu*).
If this is not done, for whom was this path of practice (*dharmaskandha*) established? Although one contemplates the aggregates (*skandha*), one merely refutes the universal gate."

Regarding the objects (*viṣaya*): since the name "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*) has not yet been differentiated within the aggregates (*skandha*), how much more so when there are six categories that mutually balance one another?
Therefore, this gateway is employed to examine and discern [the phenomena] (text).
[Commentary] This explains the "Appropriateness" (*yathābhūta*) within the Chapter on the Path (*mārgavarga*). The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

Although the preceding sections have extensively analyzed phenomena, identified what is permeable and what is obstructed, if one does not harmonize and balance the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*), how can one swiftly correspond with the True Dharma? The True Dharma is termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*);

the factors of the path are "with-outflows" (*sāsrava*). While that which is with-outflows can serve as a skillful means (*upāya*) for the outflow-free, if these skillful means lose their proper application, the True [Dharma]...
The principle is difficult to comprehend. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the methods for practicing the Path.

The City of Nirvāṇa has three gates; these three gates are the proximate causes, while the factors of enlightenment are the remote causes. For this reason, one must employ the factors of enlightenment in balanced harmony.

If the following three phrases were not present, it would clarify the failure of applying the factors of enlightenment in vain; by refuting this [in the subsequent section], it clarifies [the correct application].
Now, regarding the intent of employing the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) for the sake of harmonious adjustment:

since the objects of observation—the aggregates (*skandha*)—discussed in the preceding "Pervasive Destruction of Phenomena" section have not yet been distinguished by the names of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), how could there be the activities of the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*) and so forth for the sake of harmonious adjustment?
Therefore, we employ them now as a means of inspection and evaluation to elucidate the underlying principles and to determine their practical application.

[Note] The true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) constitutes the body of the vehicle, while the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) serve as the vanguard; therefore, they are likened to white oxen. Regarding the phrase "white oxen and so forth," this corresponds to the descriptions in the sutras:
"the skin and color are pure and clean, the physical form is beautiful and excellent, possessing great strength and endurance, and walking with a level and upright gait.

The general meaning is that while those of middle capacity reach the seven vehicles, those who have now reached the sixth [vehicle] are divided into middle and lower capacities based on the distinction between the direct and auxiliary practices.
[Commentary] The *Wenju* says: The wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) destroys the darkness of the eight inversions; this is called "riding a white ox.

Within the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the two types of future good are fulfilled, like the fullness of the skin; the two types of future evil are exhausted, like the purity of the complexion. The four [bases of psychic power]...

The "satisfactions" (*iddhipāda*) accord with the practitioner’s mind, just as a beautiful form does. The "tendons" (*bala*) are analogous to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); their meaning is that they provide the basis for the ability to arise [in practice].

The "powers" (*bala*) are analogous to the five powers (*pañcabala*); their meaning is the function of crushing and subduing [the hindrances]. The evenness of one's gait is analogous to the balance between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).

Furthermore, it is like the seven factors of enlightenment being balanced and harmonious. Although these factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) share names with those preceding them, their meaning is actually restricted to the perfect [stage].
△ Seven: Aids to Counteraction for Opening.
Regarding the seven aids to counteraction for opening: if the right path is heavily obstructed and the perfect principle does not open, one must cultivate practical aids. That is to say:
The five *sthāpanā-citta* (stabilizing minds) and the six *pāramitās*, etc. The Sūtra says: "Furthermore, there are many attendants" (the following refers to those of inferior faculties).
[Note] The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning), fascicle 8, states: Regarding the seven types of antidotes for the path of assistance, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says:

"The afflictions of sentient beings are not of a single kind; the Buddha has taught immeasurable gates of antidotes. One should know that a person who does not believe in the existence of such antidotes is...

One has not yet understood correct practice. If one recognizes that one’s own correct practice is not yet perfected, it is truly because mundane evils assist in obscuring ultimate evils, which together veil ultimate goodness so that it does not manifest before one.
If mundane evils are eliminated, ultimate goodness can easily be clarified; therefore, one first cultivates the mundane perfections (*pāramitā*) to remedy mundane evils.
Once mundane evils have been overturned, ultimate goodness can arise (as stated in the text).
[Commentary] *Zhiguan* states: "If one’s faculties are sharp and there are no obstructions, it is easy to enter the Pool of Coolness; there is no need for remedial practices (*pratipakṣa*).

If one’s faculties are sharp but there are obstructions, one simply focuses exclusively on the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣamukha*); the obstructions cannot hinder [progress], and there is likewise no need for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

For those whose faculties are dull and whose obstructions are heavy: because their faculties are dull, they cannot open the three gates of liberation; because their obstructions are heavy, they pull down and destroy the contemplative mind."
For this reason, one must apply the path of remedies to break through and eliminate these obstructions; thus, one attains peace and enters the three gates of liberation.
When the *Mahāśāstra* refers to "all remedies," it means precisely this: that they are the dharmas which assist in opening the gates.
△ Eight: Knowing the Stages of Progress.
Regarding "Eight: Knowing the Stages of Progress": this means that for practitioners, it is in order to avoid the arrogance of overestimating one's own attainment (*adhimāna*).

[□ Commentary] The *Great Meaning* (Dàyì) states in the eighth section: "Those of inferior faculties have heavy obstructions; not only do they lack clarity regarding the primary and auxiliary practices, but they instead give rise to arrogance, claiming:"

One who equates themselves with a Buddha, claiming to have attained what has not been attained and realized what has not been realized, must understand the successive stages [of the path] so that the red and the purple are not confused.
If one claims to have realized what has not been realized, one not only loses their station but falls back into hell.

Thus, in the Hīnayāna sūtras, bhikṣus of the four dhyānas claimed to have attained the four fruits; and in the Mahāyāna sūtras, Māra grants bodhisattvas the prediction of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).

Commentary: If one gives rise to grasping and attachment, one will inevitably become a follower of Māra; one will lose even the realms of humans and devas, so how could this have anything to do with the Ultimate Path?
Therefore, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras clearly elucidate the sequence of stages (text).
[Commentary] Regarding "the followers of the Hīnayāna and others": this refers to sons of noble family who, during the Buddha's lifetime, left the household life within the Buddha-dharma;
yet, without cultivating the skillful means of extensive learning (*bahuśruta*), they dwelt in forest hermitages (*araṇya*) and, due to past causes, were able to transcend the mundane first dhyāna.
They claim for themselves the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to and including the fourth *dhyāna* which transcends the world, claiming it to be the fruit of *arhatship*.
Throughout their entire lives, they claim what they have not attained as attained, what they have not understood as understood, and what they have not realized as realized;

they no longer seek the path of further advancement. When their life later comes to an end, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth *dhyāna* manifests before them. At that time, they think to themselves:
"I have severed all conditions for rebirth; I should enter parinirvāṇa and should not be born again. Now, by what cause has this intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arisen within me?
Certainly there is no liberation. If there were liberation, I should have attained it. Thus he gives rise to the false view that denies nirvāṇa.
Because of this false view, his intermediate state of the fourth dhyāna is extinguished, and the intermediate state of hell appears before him.

Upon the end of his life, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell; this is it. Regarding the phrase "and so forth in the Mahāyāna," this clarifies that one gives rise to pride based on the causal records of the Mahāyāna.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Māra assumes the form of a bhikṣu and goes to where the bodhisattva is, saying these words:
'If a bodhisattva realizes the *prajñā*, they will attain the stage of *srotāpanna*, up to that of *pratyekabuddha*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "This is Māra’s speech."

“Bodhisattva, regarding the prediction of enlightenment bestowed upon you by the Buddhas—such as [the names] of your parents, brothers, and so forth—if you become attached to these, you will fall into overweening pride.
[Commentary: Within this stage of realization, one should further cultivate the fivefold repentance.

[Commentary: These five repentances are skillful means that assist in opening the right path. From the very beginning of the causal stage until its ultimate limit, one should practice them at all times.
Therefore, it is known that within the stages and positions, one practices the five repentances even more intensely; it is not that they are absent when there are no specific stages.
"Even more" (mi) signifies diligence.
△ Ninth, the ability to practice patience.

Ninth, the ability to practice patience. This means remaining serene and unmoved amidst both adverse and favorable conditions, thereby exerting oneself through the five stages and entering the six sense faculties.

【□Note】The *Dàyì* (Great Meaning) states in section nine: "When a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching first enters the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāiwǎn*), they attract fame and profit externally while stirring up latent obstructions internally.
Even if their past obstructions are thin, fame and profit arrive all the more; surrounded by a multitude, they neglect their own practice and thereby come to ruin. How could they advance on the Path?
To outsiders, they appear as if they were great sages—like a tree harboring a scorpion; the exterior resembles the interior."

"Empty. One should merely exert oneself and remain unmoved by [external conditions]. Upon attaining entry into the stage of the internal ordinary person (*ābhyantarapṛthagjana*), it is called the 'Stage of Similitude' (*sādṛśyāvasthā*) (text).

[Commentary] The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states: From the initial contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and elements (*dhātu*) up to the stage of consciousness (*vijñāna*), the hindrances are transformed and wisdom opens.

Whether one has not yet entered the [spiritual] categories or has entered the first category, one’s spiritual intelligence becomes sharp and keen. One may observe that the lecturer does not accord with principle, or observe the practice..."

The Way does not follow fixed tracks. When he spoke words of compassion, he was immediately surrounded by a crowd; he would then speak a sentence or two of Dharma, or demonstrate a section or two of Chan.

Initially, he addressed only one person at a time, but as these teachings were circulated, they gradually spread widely. At first, it was thought that there was benefit, yet the benefit to others was slight while his own practice was neglected.
Thus we know that for those on the outer stages of the Perfect Teaching, the benefit to others is truly meager, while the harm to oneself is indeed real.
At the end, he exhorts [the practitioner] to exert themselves so as to enter the stage of semblance (*sabhāga-bhūmi*), where the six sense faculties are purified.

This clarifies that the teachings spoken by the person upon whom one relies can likewise be accepted with faith; for his single voice pervades everywhere, and those who hear it rejoice. Therefore, one should strive to advance.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "inversely and favorably," etc.: "inverse" refers to afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, fixed views, pride, and so forth, which destroy [the tree] from within;

these should be treated with the three internal methods, namely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*upāya*), and the middle (*madhyama*). "Favorable" refers to fame as the *rāhu* net, gain and offerings as the hair-rope, and relatives as the gathering trees;
these obstruct and infest from within, while branches and leaves are exhausted from without—these are what destroy [the tree] from the outside.
One should eliminate it by means of the three external methods: first, neither receiving nor clinging; second, contracting virtue and exposing flaws;
third, lifting [the mind] ten thousand miles away. As stated in the *Zhi guan* (Contemplation and Observation), fascicle 7 (32).

[Commentary] This indicates the two conditions of adverse and favorable. That is to say, when the practitioner encounters adverse conditions internally that cause disruption, they employ the three internal arts to treat them;
this is not difficult. When favorable conditions externally cause encroachment, they employ the three external arts to treat them; this is not easy.
Therefore, it is said that there are three methods for ceasing and contemplating to rectify external conditions:

If one is ensnared by the net of fame and reputation, even to the point where the branches and leaves are completely exhausted externally, one should promptly cast them aside; do not accept them, and do not become attached to them.

If, despite casting them aside, they do not leave and instead cause one to be stuck and bound, one should contract one's virtues, expose one's flaws, proclaim one's madness, and conceal one's reality, secretly covering over one's "gold and jade" so as not to let [them be seen].

The thief sees [the treasure]. If one’s tracks cannot be hidden and one is not yet liberated, one should at once travel ten thousand *li* to a remote frontier or another land, where there are no signs and one is unobserved.
There, one may joyfully study and attain the Way. Even if fame, profit, or kinsmen come from without to destroy [this resolve], one should remember these three methods and endure with clenched teeth.
Though entreated by thousands or tens of thousands, remain firm and difficult to uproot. Be yielding, be hidden, and depart!
[Supplement] Hair-cord. In the Western Regions, this is used to bind the waist; it is made from dragon-whiskers (*nāga-veṇu*).

It will surely break one’s bones when entering water, serving as a metaphor for how attachment to gain and honor (*lābha-satkāra*) will surely sever the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). Fame and profit are like wood-worms (*gandaka*);

they cause internal contemplation (*adhyātma-vipaśyanā*) to scatter and perish—this is called "internal invasion. Retinues gather like a crowd, causing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to decay—this is called "external exhaustion. It is just like a great tree.
Externally it gathers various birds; internally it harbors insects and scorpions. The tree will surely wither and perish.
△ Tenth, detachment from attachment to dharmas:
Do not cling to the semblance-path of the ten faiths; you must enter the true principle of the stage of "Sharp Abiding."
The Sūtra says: "Riding this precious vehicle, one travels through the four directions (traversing the forty stages) until reaching the site of enlightenment (the stage of wondrous awakening).
[Commentary] Section Nine states: "If one dwells exclusively in the stage of semblance, it is called 'attachment to dharmas.

Having already attained the mutual functioning of the six sense organs in their semblance state and having already destroyed the two types of delusion, one will never again fall into suffering; yet to crave this stage of semblance is called 'falling from the summit' (*mūrdha-pāta*). If one practices..."
Free from craving, one enters the Copper Wheel, which is called the Ten Abodes (*daśabhūmi*). One’s body manifests throughout a hundred worlds, such that the one and the many are mutually identical.
As it is with the body and the land, so it is with self and others. With the ten bodies one benefits sentient beings, and with the four lands one gathers in all things. (Text)

[Commentary] Regarding the mutual functioning of the sense organs: as stated in the "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma-Master" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the text of the section on the nose-faculty says:
"One knows what is good and bad, distinguishes between the noble and the lowly, and perceives the adornments of celestial palaces. This indicates that the nose possesses the function of the eye.

Furthermore, when reading scriptures or preaching the Dharma, one is able to know [the content] by smelling the fragrance; this constitutes the function of the ear. One also smells the fragrances of the flowers and fruits of various trees, as well as the scent of clarified butter.

If one is able to know, then there is the function of the tongue. Entering and emerging from dhyāna involves the eight tactile sensations; the play of the five desires is likewise the object-field of touch.
If one can know by smelling fragrances, then there is the function of the body. One also knows the arousal of desire and anger, as well as the cultivation of goodness.

If one can know by smelling fragrances, then there is intentional application; the faculty of the nose is sovereign. If its superior function is such as this, the same applies to the other five faculties.
Regarding "falling from the summit," the *Zhiguan* says: "By practicing the nine matters above, one transcends internal and external obstacles."
One ought to enter into the truth. If one does not enter, it is because of dwelling in attachment through craving for the Dharma (*dharmatṛṣṇā*), and thus one does not advance.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The three samādhis constitute the stage of the semblance-path (*saddharmapratirūpaka-mārga*). When the true [path] has not yet been generated, there is a fondness for the craving for the Dharma;

this is called 'falling from the summit' (*mūrdha-pāta*). It is like a boat on the same current: one moment moving forward, the next moment stopping. This stopping is attachment; neither advancing nor retreating is what is meant.

"Peak-falling. This refers to when one breaks through attachment to the Dharma and enters the three gates of liberation. The commentary explains: Upon reaching the stage of the Ten Faiths, if one generates a mind of attachment, one will not enter the First Abode.
However, at the stage where the six sense organs are purified, one certainly does not fall into the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Because one dwells at the "peak," it is called "falling";
this does not mean falling back [into delusion], for there is no possibility of regression in the stage of the six purified organs. How much more so for those who further engage in [wholesome] deeds?
Is it not a grave transgression? Therefore, one falls from this "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). This differs from the previous [explanations] of the *Āgama* and *Abhidharma* schools.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that there are two distinct meanings for falling from the Summit: first, falling from the Summit is called "falling"; second, remaining at the Summit is called "falling.

Although the Lesser Vehicle possesses both meanings, because those who remain at the Summit mostly fall, in the present Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), where view-delusions and thought-delusions have already been cast off, there is only the single meaning of "falling" as remaining at the Summit.
The remainder may be understood. This concludes the brief clarification of the major sections on the skillful means and the correct cultivation of the Sublime Dharma (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra).
△ Third, the conclusion of the abridgment, the pointing toward the extensive, and the indication of differences—three parts. First, the conclusion of the abridged record.
I have respectfully consulted the expanded version of the Tiantai teachings and have transcribed the Five Periods and Eight Teachings; a brief understanding of them is thus provided.
[Note] This concludes the transcription of the Five Periods and Eight Teachings, which represent the ritual format for Tiantai’s doctrinal analysis and interpretation.
[Commentary] This explains the concluding passage. The meaning is that the Great Master established these names based on their underlying significance;

if one uses these to provide judgment and interpretation, none but those of saintly brilliance and exceptional penetration can unravel them. Nevertheless, within each phrase of the "Five Periods and Eight Teachings," there lies a profound and wondrous purport.
That is to say, in a single matter of the Buddha, both principle and phenomena are fully present.
△ Second, the detailed version of the "Pointing to the Goal.

For those who wish to understand this in full detail, please consult the ten fascicles of the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra), which provides a meticulous analysis of the ritual procedures for the preaching of the Dharma by all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, like a clear mirror;
as well as fascicles four through seven of the *Weiming xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra), which provide a complete analysis.

The "Teaching Aspect" (Jiaoxiang). [Note] This refers to the characteristics of the holy teachings as they were judged and the manner in which they were bestowed during a single period of transformation. *Miaole* (Vol. 17) states:

"The *Jingming qianxuan* (Profound Mystery of the Vimalakīrti) originally comprised ten fascicles in total. Because he composed the *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti) for the Prince of Jin, he separately prepared the *Lüexuan* (Brief Profound Mystery), which was then separated from the former."

The *Xuán* (Profound) was originally divided into three separate sections with individual titles: the *Sìjiào* (Four Teachings) in six fascicles, the *Sìxī* (Four Aids) in two fascicles, and the *Sānguàn* (Three Contemplations) in two fascicles.
Later generations merged these six into four; what is currently known as the four fascicles of the *Jìngmíng xuányì* (Profound Meaning of the Vimalakīrti Sūtra) refers to this.
[Commentary] This explanation refers to the extensive classification of the teachings (*jiaopan*). The first two phrases refer to the *Miaoxuan*. "Below the *Miaole*" refers to the *Jingxuan*.
The first two phrases refer to the fact that the previous *Xuan* was divided into ten fascicles. "Because of... below explains why the name "three" was established apart from the "ten.
"Prince of Jin" is the posthumous title of Emperor Yang of the Sui when he was still the Crown Prince. "Later people... below explains...
The combination of six into four—the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*’s profound meaning (*Ming-hsüan-i*)—is precisely what is found in the present *Chiao-i* (Meaning of the Four Teachings).

Should students wish to understand the characteristics of the teachings in detail, they should seek out the extensive versions such as the *Miao-hsüan* (Profound Meaning) and other works; it is appropriate that they study them with a meticulous mind.
△ Third, showing how this differs from other schools.
From here on below, I shall briefly clarify the methods of doctrinal classification (*panjiao*) employed by various schools.

[Note] Now, relying upon the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Daban* (Great Text), I have transcribed its essential outline. That text was composed after the present Master had completed his own system of doctrinal classification; it is comprehensive and detailed.
The accounts of various schools have been omitted here for brevity and are not explained.
[Supplement] It is said that the *Siji yaoyi* (Essentials of the Four Teachings) consists of two fascicles in total;

the present fascicle is the upper one, which exclusively clarifies the specific school’s system of doctrinal classification (*panjiao*) and its established tenets. The phrase "from this point downward" refers to the lower fascicle.
As for its lower fascicle, it demonstrates the differing tenets and divergent views of the various masters of the North and South.

Later, when it reached Gushan, he examined and collated it and remarked that the lower fascicle’s refutation of ancient [teachings] was still somewhat premature; therefore, only the upper fascicle has been circulated.
[Note] This thus clarifies the ritual for the classification and interpretation of the scriptures mentioned above, as practiced today at Tiantai.

However, that which is classified is the ritual for the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, while that which performs the classification is the ritual for the Great Master’s (Zhiyi) doctrinal classification.
These two aspects are inseparable yet distinct; one must understand this well.

[Appendix] Tiantai’s doctrinal classification and interpretation accord perfectly with the Buddha’s intent. Although one serves as the object of classification and the other as the means of classification, let students pay close attention to this point.
